author: Unknown
title: Two Kurdish women missing after being detained
content:
The Voice of Iranian Prisoners Organisation issued a statement concerning two Kurdish women detained in Rojhilatê Kurdistan (East Kurdistan).




The statement said that 17-year-old Perya Nasirî was detained by Iranian intelligence forces at her school in Nexede on 21 October. Six days after her disappearance, her fate and whereabouts remained unknown.




It also stated that Sedrî Bexşî, 43, from the village of Weştape in Bokan, had been held at the Urmiye Intelligence Directorate since her detention a month earlier and was facing serious security-related threats.




After being detained over posts shared on digital media platforms, Sedrî Bexşî had been allowed only one brief telephone conversation with her family, according to the statement. Iranian intelligence forces reportedly threatened the family with severe punishment if they publicised her detention in the media.




According to the report, Iranian Revolutionary Guard forces raided Sedrî Bexşî’s home in the village of Weştape a month ago, using eight armoured vehicles. Following a search of the house, they seized her phone.

author: groundxero
title: ‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power
content:
“I see the glimpse of hope that this is our future and that actually we can say to our kids, our grandkids, we changed the system, we were the change.”




Gavin Brent Sullivan

 and 

Tereza Capelos







 




Serbia’s student-led political movement has secured a historic election victory. Preliminary results suggest the so-called Student List has won 141 of the 250 seats in parliament, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party taking 104. The result brings the 12-year rule of Alexander Vučić to an end.




 




The Student List’s story is remarkable. It has no standalone leader and fielded candidates without political experience from across 

Serbian

 society. Stemming from student-led protests against the entrenched corruption and 

creeping authoritarianism

 of the ruling regime, it has now achieved an improbable dream.




 




In late 2025, one of us (Gavin Brent Sullivan) conducted focus groups with members of the student protest movement as part of the 

Pledge EU Horizon project

. The project explores the emotional dynamics of political grievances and their democratic implications.




 




The protesters’ grievances were centred on the 2024 collapse of a roof at the newly renovated 

Novi Sad train station

 in northern Serbia, which killed 16 people. Allegations of state involvement through corruption in the procurement process and lowered building standards have been denied by the government. But they nonetheless sparked large nationwide protests.




 




Focus group participants expressed anger and underlying fear about harassment during the protests by what they said were government-funded gangs. They also spoke of their concern at the threats and violence directed towards them, not only as they protested but also when walking in areas near government buildings in main cities. Several students reported feeling threatened even in their own homes.




 




At the same time, the students voiced dissatisfaction with teachers who were not supportive of their movement, and other students who opposed them. This dissatisfaction extended to older family members and relatives who repeated government-controlled media fabrications about the protests. These included claims that the students were being paid by foreign anti-Serbian groups.




 




Despite the fear of arrest or worse, and despondency that change could really occur, the students who took part in the focus groups were resilient. They were focused on their long-term goal of regime change, with many students talking with pride about creating a leaderless movement that was organising candidates to challenge Vučić in an election.




 




Several participants reported feeling spontaneous, intense experiences of national pride when taking part in the protests. Some spoke of taking back national symbols such as the Serbian flag to counter propaganda that they were not patriotic and wanted to destroy the country.




 




Feelings of solidarity 

were also experienced

 when minority Bosniak Muslim students from Novi Pazar University in south-western Serbia joined the protests. As one participant said:




 




They’re a minority which was at odds with Serbia, with Serbian nationals actually. So now we had that part of reunification with them and they’re a Muslim minority. They are really active in these protests and student protests and it’s been wonderful.




 




Another member of the focus group noted that they expected elections to be “brutal”. But they were optimistic about the prospect of unseating the Vučić government. They said: “I see the glimpse of hope that this is our future and that actually we can say to our kids, our grandkids, we changed the system, we were the change.”




 




At the same time, most of the students did not dare to dream that they would succeed in ousting a government that had held a 12-year grip on power. It is stunning now after Vučić’s concession speech in which he admitted “it is clear that we have lost these elections” to know that they were successful just one year later.




 




What’s next?




 




The remarkable victory of the Student List should give hope to any group opposing a corrupt, authoritarian regime that a core commitment to democracy is precisely what attracts voters to choose progressive change.




 




However, while there will be euphoria, pride and tears of joy in Serbia as the election result sinks in, there may also be groups who are fearful of change and that the new government 

may seek accountability

 for members of the ousted regime. Some theorists of political emotions talk about the 

possibility for revenge

 to be enacted by winners, especially when a fight for power has been bitter.




 




For those on the losing side, meanwhile, electoral defeat 

can bring grief

, anxiety and anger. But acknowledging these emotions and coming to terms with loss can bring openness to change. In his concession speech, 

Vučić said

: “I do not want unrest, I do not want killings, I do not want anything like that on the streets.”




 




The Student List’s commitment to democracy, pluralism and justice should also override any desire for redress. The movement has 

actively avoided developing

 a victim identity, taking responsibility for enacting change themselves.




 




As one focus group participant said:




Of course, they [the government] are the problem. I’m not trying to deny that. But I would blame us more … because, I mean, we chose them, we keep choosing them. Okay, they do steal when it comes to the elections, they do many things, they hide, they try to control the media and everything. But at the same time, we don’t have the opposition and we have that state of mind that is allowing them to do everything they’re doing.




 




There are various other challenges facing the Student List. These include adapting the movement’s leaderless organisational assemblage into a government capable of delivering the reforms required for EU membership.




 




But regardless of what happens next, it was certainly a privilege to talk to the students at a time when change did not seem possible and to provide encouragement and support when there was little outside recognition of their struggles and sacrifices.







 










Gavin Brent Sullivan

, Professor of Social Psychology, 

International Psychoanalytic University Berlin

 and 

Tereza Capelos

, Professor of Political Psychology, Department of Politics and International Relations, 

University of Southampton







 







This article is republished from 

The Conversation

 under a Creative Commons license. Read the 

original article

.

author: anred
title: Bolsonaro desconoce la derrota y Trump cuestiona las elecciones en Brasil
content:
Flávio Bolsonaro anunció que pedirá la anulación de los comicios tras perder frente a Lula da Silva por más de 4,4 millones de votos. Donald Trump también cuestionó el resultado sin presentar pruebas de fraude. La ofensiva vuelve a poner en escena una estrategia de desconocimiento electoral que ya tuvo como antecedente el asalto a las instituciones brasileñas en enero de 2023. La remontada de Lula descoloco la estrategia hegemonista del gobierno de Trump. Por ANRed.




El resultado de las elecciones presidenciales de Brasil abrió un nuevo conflicto político. El senador Flávio Bolsonaro, candidato del Partido Liberal (PL) e hijo del expresidente Jair Bolsonaro, se negó a reconocer la victoria de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva y anunció que recurrirá a la Justicia para solicitar la anulación de la segunda vuelta. La decisión se conoció el domingo 25 de octubre, luego de que Lula se impusiera por más de 6,65 millones de votos.




Brasil: Lula remontó 6,65 millones de votos, derrotó a Flávio Bolsonaro y puso a las big tech en el centro de la disputa







“Es imposible reconocer el resultado de las elecciones en el contexto en que ocurrieron estas cosas”, sostuvo Flávio Bolsonaro ante la prensa, al cuestionar una decisión judicial que extendió el horario de votación hasta las 19 horas en determinadas mesas electorales.




El argumento del candidato derrotado apunta contra el juez del Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) Cristiano Zanin, quien dispuso la extensión ante las dificultades denunciadas para trasladar votantes, especialmente en ciudades de Bahía y São Paulo. Sin embargo, la medida había sido solicitada por ambas candidaturas, incluida la del propio Partido Liberal. Además, la prórroga alcanzó a las mesas que continuaban abiertas, mientras que los votos de las que ya habían cerrado fueron contabilizados normalmente.







Los bolsonaristas bloquearon con autos el camino para impedir que pase el autobús con la gente que iba a votar. ¡Mirá cómo los sacan! Sea cual sea el resultado, lo que están haciendo los jóvenes brasileños para esta elección es heroico. https://t.co/MsQ8HS5Yqt




— PERIODISTA DE PERÓN (@PERIODlSTAPERON) 

October 25, 2026







Flávio Bolsonaro calificó la decisión de inaceptable y denunció una supuesta ruptura de la igualdad electoral, aunque no presentó elementos que demostraran que la medida hubiera alterado el resultado general de los comicios.




Trump se suma a los cuestionamientos




El presidente estadounidense Donald Trump también cuestionó el resultado electoral brasileño. Según declaraciones difundidas por la prensa internacional, afirmó que en Brasil se había aplicado el “manual de Joe Biden” y sostuvo que los comunistas no abandonan el poder una vez que lo consiguen. Sus acusaciones tampoco estuvieron acompañadas de pruebas que acreditaran irregularidades capaces de modificar el resultado.




La intervención de Trump se produce en un escenario de estrechos vínculos políticos entre el trumpismo y el bolsonarismo. Durante los últimos años, ambos espacios compartieron discursos contra sus adversarios políticos y cuestionamientos a las instituciones electorales. La reacción del mandatario estadounidense refuerza el enfrentamiento político en Brasil, aunque no equivale a una presentación formal ante las autoridades electorales ni demuestra la existencia de fraude.




El antecedente del asalto a Brasilia




La negativa a reconocer una derrota electoral tiene un antecedente reciente en Brasil. Tras perder las elecciones de 2022 frente a Lula, Jair Bolsonaro mantuvo una postura de cuestionamiento al sistema electoral, mientras sectores de sus seguidores bloquearon rutas y acamparon frente a instalaciones militares.




El 8 de enero de 2023, grupos de manifestantes bolsonaristas invadieron las sedes de la Presidencia, el Congreso y el Supremo Tribunal Federal en Brasilia, en un intento de desestabilizar el orden institucional. Jair Bolsonaro fue posteriormente condenado a 27 años de prisión por su participación en una trama golpista, según informaciones difundidas por Reuters.

author: Tam Saavedra
title: WEI and UN Women Co-Launches Guide for Disability-Inclusive
content:
Setting the Agenda: WEI Co-Launches Guide for Disability-Inclusive Peace in Asia and the Pacific




Across Asia and the Pacific,

 350 million women and girls with disabilities

 navigate conflict, crisis, and climate instability

. While they are frontline peacebuilders, community leaders, and human rights defenders, they remain systematically excluded from formal peace and security decision-making

.




To break down these barriers, 

Women Enabled International (WEI)

 and the 

UN Women Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific

 have officially launched a landmark publication today: the 

Guidance Note on Disability-Inclusive National Action Plans on Women, Peace and Security in Asia and the Pacific

. Released ahead of the annual UN Security Council high-level debate in New York, this first-of-its-kind guide provides a practical, policy-oriented blueprint for governments, policymakers, and civil society

.




Read the full 

Guidance Note on Disability-Inclusive NAPs on WPS in Asia and the Pacific

 




Shifting from “Vulnerability” to Setting the Agenda




Historically, women with disabilities in peace policies have been viewed narrowly as victims or passive recipients of protection. Co-drafted through consultations with 26 women and gender-diverse people with disabilities, in collaboration with Women Enabled International and the UN Women Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific, this guide directly challenges that narrative. It grounds its framework in a human rights model of disability and the core movement principle: 

“Nothing about us without us”.




As WEI Executive Director 

Maryangel García-Ramos Guadiana

 stated during the launch:







“The true value of this Guidance Note is that it exists, not as a siloed document, but as a means to ensure we, as feminist disabled change-makers, are not left out of the agenda, but we are the ones who get to set the agenda.”







UN Women Regional Director for Asia and the Pacific, 

Christine Arab

, added:







“National Action Plans on WPS that include everyone lead to peace that lasts.”







Grounded in Lived Experience




The publication was shaped by participatory research, drawing on focus groups and surveys with 26 grassroots leaders with diverse disabilities across the region

. It addresses critical ground-level hurdles—including digital exclusion, inaccessible evacuation infrastructure, and ableism in mainstream spaces

—ensuring that the voices of women, girls and gender-diverse people with disabilities form the foundation of the guidance

.




Core Pillars of the Guidance Note




The publication urges stakeholders to align National Action Plans (NAPs) with international standards—including the CRPD, CEDAW, and UN Security Council Resolution 2475—across all 

four WPS pillars

:










Participation:

 Reserve seats for organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs)—especially women-led OPDs—on NAP steering committees with full accessibility support

.










Prevention:

 Recognize women and gender-diverse people with disabilities as active peacebuilders and integrate intersectional early-warning indicators

.










Protection:

 Address unique forms of violence (such as caregiver abuse or institutionalization) and guarantee accessible shelters and evacuation procedures

.










Relief & Recovery:

 Ensure transitional justice mechanisms, reparations, and post-conflict upskilling actively include women with disabilities

.










The guide also features a practical 

Disability-Inclusive WPS NAP Checklist

 to help stakeholders evaluate progress at every stage of policy implementation

.




Acknowledgments




This Guidance Note was made possible with the generous support of the 

Government of the Republic of Korea

 (through the Ministry of Gender Equality and Family) as part of the project 

“Promoting Leadership of Future Generation Peacebuilders and Change-makers in Asia and the Pacific”

, and of the 

Australian Government

 under the 

Regional Framework Towards Peaceful, Inclusive Societies

 (2023–2027)

.




Access the Resource




 

Download:

 Read the full 

Guidance Note on Disability-Inclusive NAPs on WPS in Asia and the Pacific

 (available in designed PDF)

.




The post 

WEI and UN Women Co-Launches Guide for Disability-Inclusive

 appeared first on 

Women Enabled International

.

author: Daron Letts
title: Nunavut athletes honoured in Ottawa
content:
Two Nunavut athletes were honoured on Saturday night in Ottawa during the Aboriginal Sports Circle’s National Indigenous Sports Gala.




Rankin Inlet hockey player Lana Lindell and Sanikiluaq multisport athlete Andrew Kavik were named as Nunavut’s recipients of the Tom Longboat Award, established in 1951 in memory of the late Onondaga distance runner from the Six Nations Reserve, near Brantford, Ont.




“It was a great night filled with celebration,” said Aboriginal Sport Circle spokesperson Julie Hawrishok, in an email. “The main ballroom was transformed with lights and a digital background that displayed images of the recipients and images from their home province or territory.”




Lindell accepted her award onstage at the Ottawa Conference Centre 

from former Aboriginal Sport Circle board member Brendon Smithson. Jeff Seeteenak, f

ormer chef de mission for Team Nunavut, accepted Kavik’s award on his behalf because the athlete was unable to attend.




Kavik was recognized for excelling in badminton and for helping his team earn bronze in volleyball during the 2026 Arctic Winter Games.




At the same event, Lindell captained Team Nunavut’s U19 female hockey team to a bronze. 

She also captained Saskatchewan’s U18AA Notre Dame Hounds while attending Athol Murray College of Notre Dame.




Alongside hockey, she has participated in volleyball, basketball rugby, and ultimate frisbee during four years at the sports development high school.
















“Anything that they provided I played at least a year of,” she said in a phone interview.




She is active in student leadership and volunteer initiatives while studying engineering at the University of Saskatchewan.




Although the Professional Women’s Hockey League remains a dream, Lindell’s plan is to return home to help build infrastructure in Rankin Inlet, she said.

title: Testimonianze dalla piazza di Torino del 24 ottobre: violenze poliziesche
content:
Sono state raccolte una serie di testimonianze video e foto rispetto alla violenza poliziesca attuata nei confronti del corteo contro il riarmo e il carovita tenutosi a Torino sabato 24 ottobre. 




Alla fine del corteo in particolare le forze dell’ordine hanno impiegato una gestione sconsiderata della piazza, chiudendo a morsa i manifestanti sotto una pioggia di lacrimogeni. Al di là di questo, durante tutto il giorno e anche a corteo concluso, si sono registrate modalità selvagge di attaccare il corteo, tramite cariche, inseguimenti, fermi e provocazioni. Il corteo però è rimasto compatto ed entusiasta del fatto di essere partito e arrivato a portare a termine la manifestazione con una partecipazione incredibile nonostante gli svariati tentativi atti a impedire che essa avvenisse. 




Dall’alto diversi video riprendono la sequenza in cui le forze dell’ordine eseguono la chiusura totale del corteo. 













A Torino la polizia e carabinieri stanno letteralmente INSEGUENDO in tenuta antisommossa e camionette gli ultimi manifestanti. 







In Corso Emilia e Via regio Parco, prova di forza della polizia per far vedere i muscoli davanti a qualche manifestante.













Un influencer, 

Andrea Borello

, ricostruisce il contesto di Piazza Castello in questo video




NB: La manifestazione era legale ed era stata precedentemente comunicata alla questura di Torino. E dico comunicata, perché ricordiamoci che le manifestazioni in Italia per Legge non devono essere autorizzate, ma semplicemente bisogna darne comunicazione preventiva.







Non è l’unico video fatto uscire da persone che hanno partecipato alla manifestazione sul proprio profilo per denunciare quanto accaduto, questo è un altro esempio: 




sakunamusic




Rispetto alla dinamica della macchina bianca che ha tagliato in mezzo ai manifestanti a folle velocità, qui viene documentato quando la polizia, dopo aver fatto passare la macchina in via Pietro Micca, ha manganellato chi chiedeva spiegazioni

author: ROAPE
title: Mining in contemporary African underdevelopment
content:
One of the defining characteristics of capitalism is its remarkable ability to emerge from every crisis even stronger.[1] History has shown time and again that war and militarisation serve capitalism’s interests. And even in the case of the climate crisis – for which capitalism bears the greatest responsibility – we are presented with an alleged ‘win–win’ solution. While multinational companies at least partly withdraw from coal mining (see Tsuji et al. 2026, in this issue), the massive rise in 

demand for metals and minerals

 that are needed for ‘clean energy’, digitalisation, consumer electronics, aerospace and militarisation has led to a renewed mining boom, notably of so-called critical raw materials (UNCTAD 2026). In a business-as-usual scenario, demand for these materials between 2024 and 2040 is projected to increase by 353% in the case of lithium, 131% for graphite, 69% for nickel and 49% for cobalt (UNCTAD 2026, 3).




Many of the deposits of these raw materials are located in the global South, with the African continent accounting for about 30% of the world’s critical minerals and metals: for example, 85% of global deposits of manganese (in South Africa and Gabon) and 21% of graphite reserves (in Mozambique, Madagascar and Tanzania). Guinea alone holds one-quarter of global bauxite reserves. South Africa is one of the world’s leading producers of chromium and platinum, while the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is the second-largest producer of copper, with a 13% share of global supply in 2024 (after Chile with 24%). Around 70% of the global supply of cobalt is extracted in the DRC (Boafo et al. 2024; IEA 2025; Cobalt Institute 2026; US Geological Survey 2026).




Lithium has become the epitome of the metal needed for energy transition: it ‘embodies the fantasy of a “technological fix”, capable of turning the climate crisis into a political and economic opportunity for those in power’ (Voskoboynik and Andreucci 2022, 803). Critical research, political debate and activism has focused on the catastrophic impacts of the expansion of mining in the ‘Lithium Triangle’ (Chile, Argentina and Bolivia) that holds the largest part of global lithium reserves (Ahmad 2020; Ciftci and Lemaire 2023; Mejia-Muñoz and Babidge 2023). Yet, less attention has been paid to Zimbabwe, for instance, which holds the world’s fifth- or sixth-largest lithium deposits, accounting for almost 10% of current global production (Manduna 2026b, 4; OECD 2026, 6); or to Mali, which has 700,000 tons of lithium reserves (Chandler 2022, 2). Possibly one of the largest undeveloped hard-rock lithium deposits lies in southern DRC: an exploration licence for the Manono Lithium Project was granted in 2023 to Manono Lithium SAS, a joint venture of Chinese company Zijin Mining and Congolese state-owned Société commerciale et Minière du Congo, whereby Zijin holds a 54.9% majority (Zijin n.d.).




Remarkably, Europe’s largest lithium deposits are located in Ukraine. Ukraine is estimated to hold around 5% of the world’s strategic raw material reserves, including reserves of lithium, graphite, titanium and rare earths. Half of these reserves are in territories currently under Russian control (Baranowski, Jabkowski and Kammen 2025; Crescenzi 2026). Multinational companies are interested in the other half: for example, Irish company TechMet Ltd, in a joint venture with Ronald Lauder (heir to Estée Lauder Companies and a personal friend of Donald Trump), was awarded the concession to exploit the Dobra lithium reserve deposit in Kirovohrad by the Ukrainian government in January 2026 (Barba 2025; Méheut 2026). Here, too, geopolitical competition for the decarbonisation markets turns out to be a driving force of the war.




‘Critical’ minerals, however, are critical first and foremost for the global North, not for local and national demand and supply on the African continent itself. Very few African countries process and use minerals and metals for low-carbon technologies. This is hardly surprising, given that African states have fewer industries and consequently contribute far less to global greenhouse gas emissions. The G20 states are responsible for almost 83% of global greenhouse gas emissions, notably the EU, the USA, China and India (or, based on per capita emissions, Saudi Arabia, Canada and Australia) (EDGAR 2025).




Resource nationalism on the rise?




In many African countries, the commodity supercycle fuelled a further wave of large-scale mining, with unequivocal consequences (such as constraints to natural resource-based livelihoods and infrastructure, increasing wage disparities, rising living costs, and tensions within communities and between communities and mining companies: Bowman et al. 2021) that recall the boom-and-bust cycles so familiar to mining-dependent economies (Fraser and Larmer 2010). The recent global growth in natural resources extraction has reinforced old, colonially inherited patterns of extractivism across uneven development as a result of global capital accumulation (Greco 2020; Radley 2023a). Even so, or precisely because of this, in many African states the rise in demand for metals and minerals for decarbonisation, militarisation, digitalisation and other uses has been at the centre of political debates on whether mining can drive national development.




Although we know that ‘–win’ is a myth, decarbonisation may, according to some scholars, political elites and corporate actors, represent a ‘window of opportunity’ for some countries in the global South to benefit from ‘green’ value chains, drive forward industrialisation and increase economic sovereignty (see Alami, Taggart and Chodor 2025; Cerioli 2026). Whether this is the case in Africa, or applies primarily to middle-income countries, namely those in South-East Asia, remains to be seen. As Ben Radley (2026) has recently argued in a comparative study of cobalt nationalism and 

structural transformation in the DRC

 and Indonesia, in a reversal of former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere’s famous dictum that in Africa’s quest to industrialise, ‘we must run while others walk’, it is Asia that is running while Africa walks.




It also remains an open question whether delinking will be enabled if the economy is based on a sector whose demand and markets are controlled by the North. Delinking, a concept developed by 

Samir Amin

, refers to ‘submitting the external relations to the logic of an internal development that is independent from them’ (Amin 1987, 442). If national sovereign projects are to become a reality this will require not only national but also regional industrial development that, if it relies on the extraction of raw materials, must process and use those materials locally. In Africa, attempts to establish resource nationalism policies have emerged in some countries, for example in Zambia, Zimbabwe and the Confederation of the Sahel States (Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso) (Caramento, Saunders and Larmer 2023; Saunders, Mlambo and Ovadia 2023; Manduna 2026a; Tull 2026). However, these attempts are ‘nowhere near as ambitious as those once attempted by African socialist governments’ (Greco 2020, 511). While Nyerere advocated leaving resources in the ground until the nation was in a position to exploit them for its own benefit (Greco 2020, 511), the current mining reforms being implemented by African governments essentially maintain the practice of resource exploitation by multinational companies. In Tanzania, Ghana and Guinea, mining permits are being revoked under a ‘performance first’ model if companies are not actively using them and do not fulfil their processing commitments and obligations to contribute to national development. Mali and Burkina Faso have increased the state’s ownership stake in industrial mines from 20% to 35% and from 10% to 15%, respectively – which is a significant step but still means that 65% or 85% stakes are held by multinational corporations (Engels 2021, 155).




While 

resource nationalism

 pushes the idea that resource extraction can deliver on development promises in Africa, Amin (1978), when discussing whether Marx’s ground rent theory applies to mining, had already warned that the narrow calculation of costs and benefits of extraction in the short term rules future generations out of the equation – reproducing the bourgeoisie’s dystopic ‘après-moi le déluge’ approach to the appropriation of social wealth:




The first of these [special features of mining] is the nonrenewability of the resources to be exploited. This feature imposes a specific cost of production that does not enter into rent, namely, the cost of replacement. … Mastery of social development by society itself implies a considerably longer time prospect than that of capitalist calculation, the rationality of which appears, in this respect, to be relative and short-term. (Amin 1978, 96)




Amin also reminds us that even the supposedly unlimited ‘free gifts of nature’ (Marx’s concept of Gratisnaturkraft: see Moore 2016; Battistoni 2025, Ch. 3), such as soil, wind, sun and water, are far from being inexhaustible (Amin 1978, 97). Capitalist accumulation is based on the appropriation and exploitation of nature, thereby abstracting from its physical and material qualities and limitations. This alienation from nature and the alienation of labour are two sides of the same coin (Foster 2018). Based on his understanding of the labour process as ‘a process between man and Nature’ (Marx 1894, 574), Marx concluded that ‘capitalist production [is] simultaneously undermining the original sources of all wealth – the soil and the worker’ (Marx 1976 [1867], 638). The capital–nature contradiction is thus part and parcel of the capital–labour contradiction. With the industrialisation of agriculture and increasing land concentration in nineteenth-century Europe, the peasant population was diminishing and industrial population in the cities increasing, with depletion and overuse of soil as one consequence. As early as in the late nineteenth century, Marx, referring to chemist Justus von Liebig, highlighted what we today refer to as ecological crisis. He described the separation of rural agricultural and urban industrial settings as ‘an irreparable break[2] in the coherence of social interchange prescribed by the natural laws of life’ (Marx 1894, 531; see also Foster 1999; Saito 2020).




Capitalist accumulation and uneven development are based on colonial and imperial dispossessions, for whom the oppression, exploitation and destruction of female bodies are constitutive, as emphasised by decades of feminist social reproduction scholarship (Federici 2004; Mezzadri 2019; Ossome 2024). Building on this, and following Amin, Patrick Bond has argued that the supposed development effects of resource extraction – regardless of whether they are introduced by proponents of resource nationalism or by NGOs such as Publish What You Pay – rely on an ‘environmental and gender eraser’, as they account neither for the ecological costs, nor for the gendered unpaid labour of social reproduction that make the extraction of metals, minerals and fossil resources so profitable (Bond 2025, 103). Class is another key factor that is systematically erased. Neoliberal representations of environmental and climate crises pretend that humanity as a whole was responsible for and affected by the consequences of fossil economies – reproposing the idea that ‘we are all in this together’. In contrast, we emphasise the importance of a class analysis of the current crises and proposed ‘transitions’ to solve them (Greco 2022). Class relations structure all forms of domination – resource extraction, in Africa as globally, remains structurally rooted in the domination of the working poor. So far, questions of labour and class relations have been strikingly absent from debates on extractivism, resource nationalism and green industrialisation – though it is obvious that, as elsewhere, in rent economies based on resource extraction, value is actually produced by workers who extract metal and minerals from the ground.




Artisanal cobalt miners in the Democratic Republic of Congo (wikicommons)




Sacrificed twice




While the debate on resource nationalism in Africa is ongoing, countries that more heavily depend on the mining sector have so far struggled to use it as a source of income to fund national economic and social development plans. Meanwhile, those same countries have borne the ecological and social impact of extractive enclaves which have few or no links with local suppliers, generate no intersectoral linkages at the national level, and often become territorial enclaves ruled by transnational companies (Bebbington et al. 2008; Bush 2008; Radley 2020). Increasingly, extractive areas are becoming sacrifice zones whose residents are considered by governments to be expendable. The concept of ‘green sacrifice zones’ – ‘the logic of sacrificing … places and populations that will be affected by the sourcing, transportation, installation, and operation of solutions for powering low-carbon transitions’ (Zografos and Robbins 2020, 543) – has been established to highlight the unequal distribution of costs and benefits of decarbonisation economies, within and outside mining countries.




The rural populations of Africa and elsewhere in the global South are thus being ‘sacrificed’ twice: they bear the consequences of the climate crisis, which stems largely from the industrial development and wealth of the global North and the ‘imperial mode of living’ (Brand and Wissen 2021) of the wealthy classes; and they now bear the consequences of a pathway of decarbonisation that is based on technology and perfectly in line with capitalism, and which relies on the intensified extraction of raw materials from precisely these rural areas. If all humankind were to adopt the wasteful lifestyle of the wealthy classes of the global North, we would likely wipe ourselves out within a few generations by exceeding the planetary boundaries. Instead, the Global Justice Report (World Inequality Lab 2026) proposes striving for sufficiency: reducing high private consumption, getting rid of status symbols, and working half the current average number of hours. The key to this is a radical redistribution that begins by abolishing the billionaire class – the richest 0.001% – and instead ensuring a decent minimum income for all people globally. This is not a utopia, but rather quite feasible (World Inequality Lab 2026; see also Parsons and STWR 2026). However, redistribution alone does not create justice, neither globally nor within societies. It must go beyond what the Global Justice Report proposes and begin before and during the production process – ‘pre-distribution’, so to speak – with regard to ownership and control of the means of production, and the different valuation of productive and reproductive labour.




The UN Human Rights Council Special Rapporteur defines as sacrifice zones those localities where ‘communities are exposed to extreme levels of pollution and toxic contamination’ (UN HRC 2022, 1; see also UN HRC 2021). In these areas, extraction has been modifying local ecosystems and landscapes, leading to long-term environmental damage that creates toxic environments that are not fit to live in, violating the ‘human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment’ (UN HRC 2022, 1). Sacrifice zones are often militarised areas where people endure permanent social crisis. It is not by accident that these zones are located in historical sites of extraction in Africa. In the Zambian Copperbelt city of Kabwe, environmental lead exposure is so serious that 95% of children have elevated blood lead levels, which impairs their neurological development, leading to long-term cognitive deficits and, in the most severe cases, ‘blindness, paralysis and death’ (UN HRC 2022, 7). In the Niger Delta of Nigeria, oil pollution causes ‘abnormalities in blood, liver, kidney, respiratory and brain functions, as well as asthma attacks, headaches, diarrhoea, dizziness, abdominal pain and back pain’ (UN HRC 2022, 8), shortening the average life expectancy for local residents to 40 years, below the already low national average life expectancy of 55 years.




 

Green talk




While the impacts are essentially the same and well known (for example, dispossession and expulsion of local land users, health risks, soil contamination, water scarcity, increase in costs of living and poverty in mining areas), the current resource boom is characterised by the fact that, in addition to the well-established storyline that ‘mining creates economic growth, national development and jobs’, it is increasingly justified by a ‘green’ narrative: the prospect of green modernisation and mitigating climate change. Alternative strategies for tackling the climate crisis are thereby silenced and rendered invisible, while movements and activists mobilising against the disastrous effects of extractive industries are delegitimised as backward and standing in the way of decarbonisation, and are frequently suppressed and criminalised (World Social Forum 2023). In such ‘green extractivism’ (Voskoboynik and Andreucci 2022; Riofrancos 2025), the extraction of raw materials becomes a means to an end, which is presented as a ‘win–win’ solution: ‘extraction and valorisation of mineral resources is rendered not only compatible with “sustainable development”, but necessary to it and the possibility of a “lowcarbon” future’ (Voskoboynik and Andreucci 2022, 803; emphasis in original).




Today, as in previous decades and centuries, the global South serves as a reservoir of cheap nature and cheap labour for the global North. Hickel et al. (2022; see also Hickel, Hanbury Lemos and Barbour 2024) have attempted to quantify this unequal exchange. Based on environmental input–output data and footprint analysis, they calculate that the total amount of resources (raw materials, land, energy and labour) appropriated by the North from the South between 1990 and 2015 was US$242 trillion (Hickel, Hanbury Lemos and Barbour 2024). Labour thereby plays a key role: the North appropriates roughly twice as much labour as it has available itself; consequently, this labour is not available to contribute to production and social reproduction in the South. The North’s wealth is clearly based on the immense global wage gap: workers in the South contribute 90% to the global economy but receive only 21% of global income (Hickel et al. 2022). This applies equally to the 

extraction of resources in efforts to supposedly combat the climate crisis

. The continuation of colonial relations of exploitation of labour and nature, and of dispossession for ‘renewable goals’, is therefore referred to as ‘green colonialism’ (Hamouchene and Sandwell 2023) and ‘green imperialism’: the way in which companies and governments of the North control territories outside their national borders in order to profit from decarbonisation through the extraction of raw materials there (Radley 2023b, 324).




Green technological modernisation, the strategy of decarbonisation promoted by governments to fulfil their promises regarding their climate targets (a technocratic euphemism for their hypocritic response to the climate crisis), fits perfectly into the logic of neoliberal capitalism. It represents a technological fix for capitalism’s crises: technological and market-based ‘solutions’ to the climate crisis. Green modernisation is based on a substantial and rising need for metals, minerals and land, cheap labour for the extraction of resources, and the ‘free gifts of nature’, such as water, wind and sun, for renewable energies. ‘Green’ capitalism, too, needs an outside from which raw materials are appropriated and into which the ecological and social costs are externalised (see Luxemburg 2003 [1913]). With this type of crisis management, the historically anchored structures between the centres of industrial production and the resource-rich countries of the periphery are reproduced in the form of unequal development (Smith 1984) and asymmetrical power structures, albeit under new auspices and changing conditions. The crisis of neoliberalism was clearly articulated in the 2007–08 global economic and financial crisis, disastrous neoliberal austerity policies in response to this, and food price increases and uprisings worldwide as a consequence. Despite all this, current crisis management strategies remain firmly rooted in neoliberal logic and are increasingly dominated by military and ‘security’ interests – in the reactionary sense of the security of national borders, rather than the security of the health, nutrition and well-being of people worldwide.




The articles in this issue




The first two contributions to this issue deal explicitly with the impacts of global decarbonisation. Hiroyuki Tsuji, Kei Otsuki, Joshua Kirshner and Griet Steel examine the effects on labour relations. In Mozambique, multinational companies such as Rio Tinto withdrew from coal mining and Indian companies entered the scene. This had a major effect on labour conditions, especially as Indian companies operate under looser conditions than Rio Tinto and are more prone to employ subcontractors who do not comply with safety regulations. This led to a drastic decline in workplace safety measures, which had a heavy impact on workers given that mining is one of the most dangerous sectors. The shift from Rio Tinto to Indian companies also had implications in terms of class relations.




Kennedy Manduna provides a detailed empirical analysis of Chinese investment in Zimbabwe’s lithium sector. Examining in four local case studies who benefits and who loses from lithium megaprojects, he argues that Chinese investment in resource extraction in Africa represents new forms of unequal ecological exchange. According to Manduna, the construction of processing plants in the country is more window-dressing, intended to appease public discourse: the lion’s share of lithium ores is still being shipped unprocessed. Political attempts to indigenise the extractive sector in Zimbabwe have also been reversed, with multinational companies again allowed to fully own and control a mine. Investments in resource extraction, Manduna concludes, might help to make a state richer but not to be independent.




Siyabulela Christopher Fobosi examines the agency and practices of resistance of precarious workers in informal sectors. His ethnography of minibus taxi drivers in Johannesburg outlines imali yesokisi, ‘money in the sock’, as a main strategy used by workers to navigate exploitative labour relations by keeping a portion of their earnings hidden. Fobosi understands imali yesokisi as ‘everyday resistance’, a ‘weapon of the weak’, in James Scott’s (1985) terms, in a setting where collective organisation of workers is weak and hindered by violent extortion and minimal state regulation and protection. By hiding some of their earnings from the taxi owners, drivers respond to their material precarity and exercise agency in a structurally constrained work environment.




 




Mebratu Kelecha builds on dependency theory to analyse Ethiopia’s debt regimes, arguing that unequal power relations among states, international institutions and private investors shape the political processes behind debt restructuring in Ethiopia. Far from being a neutral technical exercise, debt restructuring is an arena of struggle within the global financial order. Kelecha stresses that domestic political choices matter and details the specificities of different debt regimes across Ethiopian history; at the same time, political choices are restricted by the constraints posed by a global financial system that is structured around unequal power relations. These constraints have resulted in a narrowing of policy options for successive Ethiopian governments, leading to reforms that prioritised debt repayment over long-term development plans and public provisioning for social needs.




Laura Paramoer, Hamish Evans and Anne Pollock analyse the prospects of medical manufacturing in Africa in the post-Covid-19 period by contrasting it with the immediate post-independence period. They observe that while in the post-independence period medical manufacturing was promoted within the broader imperative of import-substituting industrialisation and broader paradigms of national development, in the neoliberal era priorities have moved away from social transformation and towards health security. In the post-Covid-19 conjuncture, this had a profound impact on the meaning of solidarity and sovereignty, and while contemporary initiatives in African medical manufacturing are not as radical as those proposed in the 1960s and 1970s, they still bear some potential to catalyse tangible transformations and should not be underestimated.




In their briefing, Bülent Gökay and Zehra Vildan Serin also deal with Chinese investments in Africa. They analyse the Belt and Road Initiative, in which Africa has become a leading region, with energy and mining being key sectors. Energy investments in Africa ‘represent both the “dirtiest” and “greenest” composition in BRI history’ (406), investments in fossil fuels more than tripled from 2024 to 2025, while at the same time investments in renewable energies (wind, solar and waste-to-energy) also reached record highs. Apposite to the extractive themes of this issue, Bettina Engels reviews Kennedy Manduna’s Extractive industry indigenisation in Zimbabwe: neoextractivism, resource nationalism and uneven development.




 




In addition to these pieces, we are delighted to announce that this year’s Ruth First Prize was awarded to Antonater Tafadzwa Choto for her article, ‘Zimbabwe 1995–2000: rereading Gramsci’s organic intellectual in contemporary working-class struggles’ (Choto 2025). ROAPE presents the award annually for the best article by an African author published in the previous calendar year in the journal for the first time. Our editorial notice discusses Choto’s article and sets out the reasons for this decision, along with a profile of the author and her work.




 




Finally, Jon Abbink and Mohamed Salih remember the late Fantu Cheru, a contributor and friend of ROAPE and former member of its international advisory board. Fantu left us on 31 May 2026. His countless critical analyses of African political economy and development have shaped a generation of young radical scholars and are a precious resource to inspire future ones.

Συγκέντρωση ενάντια στην άφιξη του crown iris







ΑΝΕΠΙΘΥΜΗΤΟΙ ΠΑΝΤΟΥ ΟΙ ΣΙΩΝΙΣΤΕΣ ΚΑΙ ΟΙ ΝΤΟΠΙΟΙ ΔΩΣΙΛΟΓΟΙ ΣΥΝΕΡΓΑΤΕΣ ΤΟΥΣ, ΓΙΑΤΙ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΓΕΝΟΚΤΟΝΟΙ ΚΑΙ ΣΥΝΕΝΟΧΟΙ ΣΕ ΓΕΝΟΚΤΟΝΙΑ




Υπάρχουν ακόμη άνθρωποι που αντιδρούν και αναρωτιούνται γιατί είμαστε με την Παλαιστίνη;




Ως ελάχιστη συμβολή στον αγώνα κατά του Ολοκαυτώματος των Παλαιστίνιων, είναι χρέος μας και κατεβαίνουμε για πολλοστή φορά στο δρόμο ενάντια στο πλοίο το οποίο μεταφέρει στρατιώτες του IDF οι οποίοι κάνουν ένα διάλειμμα από τις δολοφονικές τους ενέργειες, που κουβαλάει μέσα του στην πραγματικότητα προσωποποιημένο όλο το μίσος και την απανθρωπιά αυτού του κόσμου.


Δεν είναι ευπρόσδεκτοι στα λιμάνια, στις πόλεις, στα χωριά μας και πουθενά, γιατί είναι μισάνθρωποι, μισαλλόδοξοι και πάνω απ’ όλα ΓΕΝΟΚΤΟΝΟΙ.


Συγκεντρωνόμαστε γιατί πιστεύουμε στην αξία της ανθρώπινης ζωής και της αξιοπρέπειας ανθρώπων, όπως του παλαιστινιακού λαού, που εδώ και δεκαετίες υφίσταται τις γενοκτόνες πολιτικές του Ισραηλινού κράτους.


Συγκεντρωνόμαστε ενάντια στο ζόφο του πολέμου που επιβάλλουν οι ντόπιοι και ξένοι εξουσιαστές, ενάντια στις πολιτικές θανάτου που επιφυλάσσουν για εμάς τους “κοινούς θνητούς”, τους μετανάστες και κατατρεγμένους αυτού του κόσμου, τα βρώμικα και διεστραμμένα μυαλά τους.

Η παρουσία όλων των ελεύθερα σκεπτόμενων ανθρώπων κρίνεται απαραίτητη και θα μας τιμήσει ιδιαίτερα.













Συγκέντρωση στα γραφεία της Motor Oil







ΤΟ ΑΙΜΑ ΤΩΝ ΕΡΓΑΤΩΝ/ΤΡΙΩΝ – ΤΑ ΠΛΟΥΤΗ ΤΩΝ ΑΦΕΝΤΙΚΩΝ




Το πρωί της Παρασκευής 9 Οκτωβρίου ύστερα από έκρηξη στις εγκαταστάσεις της MOTOR OIL στους Αγίους Θεοδώρους τραυματίστηκαν σοβαρά 5 εργάτες εκ των οποίων ο ένας λίγες ώρες αργότερα κατέληξε, ενώ στις 11 Οκτωβρίου ένας ακόμα από τους πολυτραυματίες χάνει τη ζωή του. Την Πέμπτη 15 Οκτωβρίου μια νέα ισχυρή έκρηξη σημειώθηκε στις εγκαταστάσεις της Motor Oil, αφήνοντας πίσω της 4 τραυματισμένους εργάτες, 2 εκ των οποίων με πολλαπλά κατάγματα και εγκαύματα. Και αυτά τα προδιαγεγραμμένα φρικτά εργοδοτικά εγκλήματα έρχονται να προστεθούν στις ήδη περισσότερες από 140 δολοφονίες εργατών/τριών του 2026 (και πάνω από 220 τραυματίες) και στις αναρίθμητες των προηγούμενων ετών, στις οποίες αντανακλάται με κυνισμό η όξυνση της εργασιακής εκμετάλλευσης και η οικτρή πραγματικότητα των εργασιακών συνθηκών στις οποίες καλούμαστε να δουλέψουμε όλες και όλοι.




Η προώθηση των διαδικασιών της κρατικής και καπιταλιστικής αναδιάρθρωσης εντείνει με γοργούς ρυθμούς την επίθεση στον κόσμο της εργασίας με την ολοένα και μεγαλύτερη όξυνση των συνθηκών εκμετάλλευσης. Η επίθεση αυτή συντελεί στην εγκαθίδρυση ενός μεσαίωνα στην εργασιακή πραγματικότητα. Η εργοδοτική αυθαιρεσία σε συνδυασμό με την απελευθέρωση των απολύσεων επιτείνουν την επισφαλή και «μαύρη» εργασία, εντείνουν σε ακραίο βαθμό την εκμετάλλευση χιλιάδων εργαζομένων και θέτουν στο προσκήνιο τον διαρκή εκβιασμό της ανεργίας, την ίδια στιγμή που τα εξαντλητικά ωράρια οδηγούν στην συνεπακόλουθη μείωση ως και εκμηδένιση του ελεύθερου χρόνου όσων εργάζονται. Η κατάργηση των συλλογικών συμβάσεων και εργατικών κεκτημένων κατακερματίζει τις ταξικές αντιστάσεις και αποδυναμώνει τις συλλογικές διεκδικήσεις στους χώρους εκμετάλλευσης, γεγονός που σε συνδυασμό με την πλήρη αποθράσυνση των αφεντικών συντελεί στη ραγδαία αύξηση των εργατικών ατυχημάτων και δολοφονιών στα κάτεργα της μισθωτής σκλαβιάς στο βωμό της καπιταλιστικής και κρατικής κερδοφορίας και ανάπτυξης. Οι δεκάδες δολοφονίες εργατών στα κάτεργα της σύγχρονης δουλείας μαρτυρούν οτι οι εκμεταλλευόμενοι και οι καταπιεσμένοι συνεχίζουν να πληρώνουν με το αίμα τους τη διατήρηση και αναπαραγωγή του βάρβαρου εκμεταλλευτικού και καταπιεστικού συστήματος, που καταδυναστεύει, δολοφονεί, εξαθλιώνει. Αυτό ακριβώς καταδεικνύει η εργοδοτική δολοφονία 5 εργατριών στο εργοστάσιο της Βιολάντα στα Τρίκαλα, μετά από έκρηξη που διέλυσε τις εγκαταστάσεις στις οποίες εργάζονταν, και από την οποία τραυματίστηκαν άλλοι 7 εργάτες. Σήμερα, και αφού επιχειρήθηκε θεσμικά από την πρώτη στιγμή να συγκαλυφθούν οι ευθύνες της εργοδοσίας, το αφεντικό του εργοστασίου Τζιωρτζιώτης βρίσκεται ελεύθερος μετά από την απόφαση του συμβουλίου πλημμελειοδικών Τρικάλων με την οποία έληξε η προφυλάκισή του. Αυτό ακριβώς καταδεικνύει και η εργοδοτική δολοφονία 2 εργατών σε εργοστάσιο στον Ασπρόπυργο τον Ιούλιο του 2026 μετά από έκρηξη λόγω διαρροής εύφλεκτου αερίου, ο τραυματισμός άλλων 11, εκ των οποίων ο ένας νοσηλεύεται ακόμα με πολλά εγκαύματα. Η έκρηξη στα διυλιστήρια της motor oil, στη Βιολάντα και στον Ασπρόπυργο δεν είναι ούτε τυχαία γεγονότα, ούτε ατυχήματα, αλλά αντίθετα αποτελούν την κορυφή του παγόβουνου της άγριας ταξικής εκμετάλλευσης που επιβάλλεται στους χώρους δουλειάς, αποτελούν προδιαγεγραμμένα κρατικά και καπιταλιστικά εγκλήματα.




Οι εκατοντάδες δολοφονημένοι εργάτες/τριες στα κάτεργα της μισθωτής σκλαβιάς, οι χιλιάδες πρόσφυγες και μετανάστες/τριες, που όταν δεν βυθίζονται στη θάλασσα από το ελληνικό λιμενικό, βασανίζονται και φυλακίζονται σε στρατόπεδα συγκέντρωσης, οι 57 νέοι/ες που δολοφονήθηκαν στο κρατικό έγκλημα στα Τέμπη, οι απόκληροι που πέφτουν νεκροί στα αστυνομικά μπλόκα και οι χιλιάδες αγωνιστές/στριες που στους δρόμους και τις διαδηλώσεις χτυπιούνται με μανία από τους ένστολους δολοφόνους της δημοκρατίας αποτελούν μόνο ένα μικρό μέρος της πραγματικότητας της συνολικής βαρβαρότητας, που επιβάλουν στη μεγάλη κοινωνική πλειοψηφία κράτος και αφεντικά.




Το βάθεμα του σύγχρονου ολοκληρωτισμού εκδηλώνεται αφενός με τις συνεχείς και δυσμενέστερες αναδιαρθρώσεις σε κάθε πεδίο του κοινωνικού και ταξικού ανταγωνισμού αλλά και την προετοιμασία της κοινωνικής βάσης για μια εμπόλεμη κοινωνία, την εμπέδωση μιας συνθήκης σιωπής και ταυτόχρονα υποταγής στα σχέδια των κυρίαρχων και αφετέρου με το τσάκισμα του εσωτερικού εχθρού, κάθε αντίστασης που εκδηλώνεται από τα κάτω και στόχο έχει να θέσει ανάχωμα στις αντικοινωνικές και εγκληματικές πολιτικές κράτους και κεφαλαίου.




Απέναντι στην οργανωμένη επίθεση του κράτους και του κεφαλαίου που τοπικά και διεθνώς δεν έχουν να υποσχεθoύν τίποτα περισσότερο από την αγριότητα των πολεμικών σφαγείων και του φασισμού, η μόνη ελπίδα για τις κοινωνίες βρίσκεται στα οδοφράγματα των εκμεταλλευόμενων και καταπιεσμένων και την πολιτική, κοινωνική και ταξική οργάνωση του αγώνα στην κατεύθυνση της κοινωνικής επανάστασης για μια κοινωνία γενικευμένης χειραφέτησης και αυτοδιεύθυνσης.




– ΣΥΓΚΕΝΤΡΩΣΗ –

title: Art Basel, la foire du Pillage
content:
« L'époque contemporaine est finie (…). Autant en finir aussi avec les dîners de gala » La foire internationale du Grand Palais « Art Basel », supposée rassembler les nouvelles « scènes artistiques émergentes », a, pour la première fois de son histoire, été l'objet d'un véritable happening, d'une véritable émergence, le 24 octobre dernier : un appel à « reprendre le Palais », signé « Pillage de classe ». Il ne s'en est pas fallu davantage pour que les organisateurs spéculent sur l'irruption d'un peu de réel. La galerie fut suffisamment épatée pour fermer pendant trois jours. Spéculera bien qui spéculera le dernier !




Comme tous les ans à Paris, Art Basel – la foire internationale d'art contemporain – devait se dérouler la semaine dernière au Grand Palais dans un bêlement sédatif. Une foire préparée bien en avance pour laquelle il valait mieux ne pas se tromper, vu les prix de location astronomiques des stands à plusieurs dizaines de milliers de dollars. Depuis quelques jours, professionnels et pique-assiettes étaient dans les starting-blocks pour enchaîner jusqu'au dimanche soir les soirées en plastique dans des clubs en toc, pour courir les événements du off (en concurrence les uns contre les autres), et pour subir les programmes de discussion assommants habituels (« les nouvelles scènes émergentes »). Tout aurait pu continuer tranquillement jusqu'à dimanche. C'était sans compter l'intrusion d'un phénomène très concret au cœur de la machinerie d'Art Basel : celui du mouvement en cours.




Mardi soir, premier coup de semonce. Alors que des ultra-riches s'agglutinaient à la preview, le compte Instagram Documentations.art publiait un appel à « reprendre le Palais le 24 octobre » signé d'un collectif : Pillage de classe. Le 24 octobre, soit le jour de l'acte II du mouvement social et insurrectionnel en cours. Le post, liké par milliers et relayé par la presse bourgeoise fut interprété comme une invitation à piller la foire. Menace symbolique ou réelle, toujours est-il que des appels à se rassembler aux abords du Palais pour déborder l'appareil sécuritaire mis en place pour le protéger commencèrent à se répandre.







 

 










Pour enfoncer un peu plus le clou, et prouver aux organisateurs que l'énorme dispositif de sécurité mis en place était incapable d'empêcher les intrusions – et, donc, que la foire ne serait pas protégée le 24 octobre en cas de débordement –, des actions sont organisées le jeudi 22 lors du vernissage publique : distribution de vrais-faux programmes détournant le graphisme d'Art Basel, collage d'affiches dans les toilettes dénonçant « la foire du pillage », déploiement d'une banderole dénonçant la collusion du marché de l'art et de l'armement…




Jeudi, la rumeur est confirmée : Art Basel fermera définitivement ses portes dès le vendredi soir. Plus de temps à perdre. Les transporteurs et les régisseurs sont rappelés en 4

e

 vitesse pour décrocher. Il faut changer les billets de train et d'avion… Malgré le vernissage en cours, l'humeur en berne et le visage morose de certain

·

es galeristes trahissent la fuite de Varennes qui s'organise au même moment en toute discrétion.




Sans surprise, une partie du monde de l'art tente de décrédibiliser cette victoire éclatante d'une mobilisation collective, révélant une fois de plus la posture contre-insurrectionnelle qui échoit à ce secteur. Il était de bon ton chez les professionnels de minimiser l'action, affirmant que les plus grosses transactions ayant eu lieu dès mardi soir, la fermeture anticipée du week-end n'aurait aucun impact sur le marché de l'art. Et qu'a contrario, en contraignant la foire à fermer ce week-end, nous pénalisions le « grand » public qui avait payé ses billets (47 euros !) et les « petites » galeries courageuses qui faisaient « un travail formidable de prospection pour soutenir de nouvelles pratiques ». Nous n'avons que faire des leçons des anti-communistes de l'art, qu'elles soient morales ou stratégiques !




La fermeture du week-end est une victoire qui résulte de la force tactique conférée par la puissance des mobilisations débordantes qui ont souvent lieu le week-end depuis les Gilets Jaunes. Certains semblent avoir des leçons à nous donner. Les mêmes qui nous demandent pourquoi ne pas avoir organisé un rassemblement le mardi soir, sont ceux qui nous accusent aussi d'approximations. Les journalistes du Monde, du Figaro, les professionnel

·

les de l'art, vous vous plaigniez d'un manque de précisions. Et nous vous demandons : Qu'avez-vous à cacher derrière vos œuvres d'art ? Vos cours si bien révisés de défiscalisation ? Votre compromission avec les business les plus sales ? Ou bien nous avions mal compris et vous étiez prêts à piller le Palais dès le mardi ? Appelez-nous la prochaine fois. 







 

 










Quoi qu'il en soit, l'impact financier de cette mobilisation sur l'ensemble de la foire a été considérable. Il touche en premier lieu les petites et moyennes galeries – plus fragiles, moins résilientes –, et ce n'est pas notre affaire. D'un point de vue systémique, ce sont ces petites galeries qui apportent le vernis progressiste dont l'art a besoin de se parer. Elles ont une fonction structurelle intégrative : ce sont elles qui repèrent les nouveaux artistes, les nouvelles formes, les nouvelles pratiques pour les transformer en marchandises et les intégrer à l'ensemble du système capitaliste. les intégrer a l'ensemble du système capitaliste. Pour autant, les mégas galeries auraient-elles couru le risque de voir leurs booths pillés ? Ce n'est pas nous qui regretterons que les petites galeries n'ait pas pu vendre ce weekend. Nous ne faisons pas de distinction morale entre bonnes et mauvaises galeries, gros ou petits commerçants au sein d'Art Basel. Chacune d'elle participe d'un système que nous souhaitons abolir, et non réformer ! 







 

 







Programme distribué devant la foire :




Nous nous sommes glissé-es dans la brèche laissées par la mise en concurrence des nombreuses entreprises de sous-traitants à qui reviennent les missions de sécurité, d'accueil, de médiation et nous avons pris une mission de distribution d'un tract au public de la foire. « Art Basel, vous voulez le programme d'Art Basel ? »




Nous serions en droit de questionner l'intérêt stratégique d'attaquer une foire telle qu'Art Basel. Pourquoi perdre son temps en d'aussi vaines occupations alors qu'il suffirait juste de de s'en détourner ? Nos modes de sociabilisation et d'action n'ont pas besoin de ceux du monde de l'art pour s'épanouir. Nous savons en revanche pourquoi il existe, ce rendez-vous mondial qui rassemble inlassablement, année après année, artistes, galeristes, curateurs, public, collectionneurs, agents, commissaires-priseurs, etc.. Et nous connaissons le rôle qu'il a pris au sein du système capitaliste impérialiste. En 2025, la pièce la plus chère s'y est vendue à 23 millions d'euros. Les quelques acheteurs (les fameux 1 %) y font leurs emplettes dans les conditions les plus opaques possibles, et le tout financé grâce à l'enchâssement obscur de puissants fonds d'investissement et holdings états-uniennes (Art Basel by MCH by Lupa Systems).




Pendant ce temps, dans des quartiers et des lycées qui auraient besoin d'argent public, la jeunesse a lancé un puissant mouvement social. Le 17 octobre, ils ont été rejoints par toutes celles et ceux qui dénoncent l'augmentation indécente du coût de la vie et la captation des richesses par quelques-uns. Certain

·

es brisent courageusement les vitrines de Chanel au risque de leur vie et de la répression judiciaire. L'opulence, le style de vie, le luxe, ils prennent tout ce qu'ART BASEL et son monde présentent comme désirable. Et la presse bourgeoise appelle cela du pillage.




Comment s'appelle ce que fait ART BASEL ?




Un véritable pillage organisé ! Les ultra-riches s'y retrouvent pour acheter, vendre et spéculer sur des œuvres devenues des actifs financiers. À ce marché s'ajoutent les dispositifs de mécénat et les fondations privées, qui permettent aux grandes fortunes et aux entreprises de bénéficier d'avantages fiscaux considérables, tout en exerçant une influence sur la production et la consécration artistiques. Autant de recettes auxquelles les États renoncent, voyant de potentielles richesses publiques s'évanouir dans des manœuvres d'optimisation fiscale, grâce à l'entremise de fondations ou autres sociétés-écrans, alors qu'on entend sans cesse répéter que cet argent manque cruellement pour nos besoins élémentaires. La liste des cadeaux faits aux plus privilégiés s'allonge chaque fois qu'on se penche sur elle (retrait de l'ISF, refus de la taxe Zucman, augmentation du seuil de la taxation sur l'héritage...).




Les œuvres couvrent la violence de classe. Elles sont des « valeurs refuges » pour les bourgeois dans des moments où la spéculation est moins efficace ailleurs. Pour ne rien voir, tout doit briller ! D'ailleurs personne ne veut savoir que James Murdoch, via sa holding Lupa Systems, premier actionnaire de l'organisateur d'ART BASEL (MCH), a également un fonds « défense », étroitement lié au complexe militaire américain et dont le directeur a proposé une réforme ouvrant davantage le ministère de la défense des États-Unis aux géants de la tech.




ART BASEL incarne les deux faces d'une même bourgeoisie transnationale qui assure son hégémonie culturelle grâce aux conditions militaires et politiques de son enrichissement – au prix, s'il le faut, d'un génocide en Palestine.




Les foires d'art contemporain veulent se donner bonne conscience, et on aime citer Debord, Butler, Federici, Fanon et le "décolonial". Mais quand les artistes et les étudiant

·

es demandent une sécurité sociale de la culture et un salaire étudiant, le marché de l'art et son monde les traite de casseurs.




L'époque contemporaine est finie : son système capitaliste aussi. Commençons par en finir avec les dîners de gala.




Le Grand Palais et les fantômes coloniaux qui le hantent doivent disparaître en même temps que les projets qu'il accueille. À l'instar des enseignes du grand luxe de la rue Saint-Honorée, saccagées lors de l'insurrection du 17 octobre, nous avons contraint la vitrine somptuaire de l'art contemporain et du capitalisme à baisser précipitamment le rideau ! Et nous recommencerons, autant de fois qu'il le faut.

title: Families in Washokani Camp stage protest: We want to return to our homes before winter
content:
Families who were forcibly displaced from Serêkaniyê and Til Temir and are living in Washokani Camp staged a protest today. Blocking the Til Temir–Hesekê road, the families demanded to return to their homes as soon as possible.




The protesters stated that they were facing numerous difficulties in the camp and that no organization was providing them with assistance anymore.




Camp resident Mûsa Mihemed from the village of El Menacîr, said that no organization was helping them anymore and that their living conditions were poor. He explained that winter was approaching and that when it rained, water poured through their torn tents, leaving them exposed to the rain. He demanded that they be enabled to return to their homes as soon as possible.




Another resident of the camp, Cabir Ebdulrehman, said: “I am from the village of El Kêf in Til Temir. We are organizing protests because we want to return to our homes as soon as possible. Our situation is difficult, theft has increased, there is chaos, and we have no means of making a living. We want the return convoys to include all displaced people.”




Mihemed Ebdulrehman, from the village of El Kinêhir in Til Temir, stated: “The return convoys only include people from certain areas. We want to return to our village before winter arrives.”

title: 25 organizations in Europe seek to strengthen joint struggle and solidarity
content:
25 political and civil society organizations from Turkey and Kurdistan have agreed to establish a joint alliance for struggle and solidarity in Europe. The initiative aims to bring together different political currents and strengthen resistance against the rise of right-wing and fascist forces, imperialist war policies, and state repression. At the same time, the participating organizations intend to support the peace and democratic society process in Turkey and advocate for a democratic solution to the Kurdish question.




The agreement stems from a meeting held on October 17 at the Cologne headquarters of the Federation of Alevi Communities in Europe (AABK). Representatives from various political traditions and social movements gathered at the invitation of eight organizations. In a joint final declaration issued today, the participants reaffirm their determination to preserve their organizational independence while establishing a lasting foundation for joint political action.




Against militarism, fascism and imperialist war policies




In their declaration, the organizations describe a world marked by growing international tensions. They warn that wars and conflicts driven by imperialist centers of power are increasing the risk of a broader military confrontation, potentially escalating into a new global war over the redistribution of power and resources. While ever-greater resources are being devoted to armament and warfare, they say, poverty and social inequality are deepening. The consequences, they argue, are borne primarily by working and oppressed sections of society, women, and the natural environment.




The signatories view the growing strength of right-wing and fascist movements as part of this development. They argue that militarism, racism, sexism, hostility toward refugees and migrants, and the destruction of the natural foundations of life are interconnected. At the same time, social forces opposing these developments are increasingly being criminalized.




The organizations therefore call for stronger international coordination among movements of struggle. They remark that resistance movements from India to France and the United States, as well as Yemen and Rojava, must not remain isolated from one another. “Their experiences must be brought together and transformed into a shared framework of internationalist solidarity. Peace, democracy, and social justice cannot be expected from the very power structures responsible for war, exploitation, and oppression. Instead, the key lies in strengthening ties between working and oppressed populations across national borders.”













Joint resistance against AKP-MHP policies




Another key focus of the declaration is the political situation in Turkey. According to the organizations, the AKP-MHP government is exploiting the international shift to the right to consolidate its authoritarian system of rule on a permanent basis. They point out that repression against the political opposition, arrests, bans, and restrictions on democratic rights are aimed at suppressing social resistance and weakening organized opposition forces.




According to the organizations, those particularly affected include workers, trade unions, democratic organizations, intellectuals, artists, and opposition political groups. At the same time, the collective rights of the Kurdish and Alevi populations continue to be disregarded. Women face patriarchal violence and discrimination, while the protection of children and the right to life of animals, as well as the preservation of nature, are systematically neglected.




The organizations do not regard these policies as an isolated development in Turkey. Rather, they see them as part of a broader authoritarian offensive through which capitalist centers of power and reactionary governments are responding to social crises. This, they argue, makes it necessary to connect democratic and social struggles in Turkey with those in Europe and other regions of the world.




Democratic solution to the Kurdish question as a shared responsibility




The participating organizations explicitly address the peace and democratic society process, stating: “Although Abdullah Öcalan and the PKK have paved the way for political and democratic dialogue through their decisions to end the armed struggle, the AKP-MHP government and the Turkish state continue to refuse to take the necessary steps toward genuine progress.”




The final declaration stresses that the process initiated by Öcalan must enable the release of political prisoners, the democratic and political participation of former guerrilla fighters, and the return of exiled politicians. “It must also pave the way for full equality for the Kurdish population. This includes, in particular, collective rights to the mother tongue, identity, culture, and freedom of organization.”




According to the declaration, a democratic solution to the Kurdish question would serve not only the interests of the Kurdish population but also those of all peoples and oppressed social groups in Turkey. At the same time, the organizations oppose subordinating peace efforts to the political calculations of the government and the state or exploiting them for their own interests. Peace, democracy, and equal citizenship rights, they argue, are not concessions granted by those in power but must be achieved through collective social struggle.




Lasting cooperation instead of temporary alliances




In addition to the political situation, the Cologne meeting addressed the organizational requirements for building a joint movement. Previous experiences with alliances such as ABDEM, HDK-Europe, and ADGB were evaluated. The participants agreed that joint statements and occasional actions alone were insufficient. Instead, they aim to establish continuous cooperation that brings together different social movements and political organizations.




The aim is not to create a single organization in which the participating groups would have to abandon their political identities, structures, or programs. Rather, the alliance is intended to be based on shared objectives, mutual recognition, and equal participation. Political decisions are to be made through joint discussions, while solidarity is to be strengthened through concrete struggles. The alliance’s precise political orientation, organizational structure, and working methods will be developed through further consultations. To ensure that the alliance can take action even during its founding phase, the participants agreed to establish a joint communication group.




20 organizations declare their readiness to join as founding members




According to the final declaration, 20 organizations have expressed their willingness to participate in the new alliance as founding members. These include:







Federation of Alevi Communities in Europe (AABK)




Kurdistan Democratic Communities Congress in Europe (KCDK-E)




Socialist Refoundation Party (SYKP-Europe)




Confederation of Oppressed Migrants in Europe (AVEG-KON)




Confederation of Democratic Rights in Europe (ADHK)




Purple-Red Collective




Association of Migrant Workers in Europe (AGEB)




Confederation of Workers from Turkey in Europe (ATIK)




European Revolutionary Democratic Communes Initiative (ADDKI)




International Struggle Collective (EMK)




Green Left Party Europe




Socialist Women’s Union (SKB Europe)




Council of Revolutionary Communes in Europe (ADKM)




Federation of Democratic Dersim Associations in Europe (ADEF)




Kurdish Women’s Movement in Europe (TJK-E)




European Forum for Freedom and Peace (EFFP)




European Council in Exile (ASM)




Federation of Democratic Alevis (FEDA)




Democratic Alevi Women’s Union (YJAD)




New Woman and the TÜDAY Human Rights Association







The Platform for Workers’ Unity and the Brotherhood of Peoples (BIR-KAR), the European Front for Labour and Freedom, the Anti-Imperialist League (AIL), and the Red Alliance will initially participate as observers and actively contribute to the alliance’s further development. In the coming weeks, talks are planned with additional progressive, revolutionary, and democratic organizations from Turkey and Kurdistan that are active in Europe.




Call to build an internationalist solidarity front




In closing, the participating organizations issued a joint appeal to democratic and revolutionary forces in Europe, stating the following:




“We want the first step we have taken in Cologne to converge with the democratic struggles in Europe and Turkey, as well as with resistance forces in different parts of the world. We are convinced that this common platform of struggle must become part of an internationalist network of solidarity in which peoples and social forces from different regions strengthen one another.




In the face of rising fascism and international war policies, such cooperation is more urgent than ever. We must stand together for peace, democracy, fundamental rights and freedoms, and intensify our joint struggle against rising fascism, racism, sexism, hostility toward migrants, imperialist aggression, and anti-democratic repression.




Differences in political programs and organizational structures do not stand in the way of cooperation. We share a broad common foundation in our commitment to an equal, free, and just society.




To jointly institutionalize, firmly establish, and expand this common foundation, we call on all progressive, revolutionary, and democratic organizations and individuals from Turkey, Kurdistan, and migrant communities in Europe to join our founding process.”

title: Panel discussion on Jineolojî and self-defense in Marseille
content:
A panel discussion and commemoration event focusing on Jineolojî and the formation of women’s armed forces was held in Marseille, France, organized by the Association of Martyrs’ Families (KOMAW), the Marseille Arîn Mîrkan Women’s Council, and members of Jineolojî Provence. The event, held at the Marseille Kurdish Democratic Community Center, was attended by numerous Kurdish women from the region, as well as representatives of French internationalist women’s movements.




The event began with a minute of silence in memory of the martyrs of the Kurdistan freedom struggle, represented by Bêrîtan (Gülnaz Karataş), described as an immortal commander of the Kurdish women’s struggle, as well as international women revolutionaries who lost their lives defending life.




This was followed by a video presentation highlighting Bêrîtan’s commitment to the principles of women’s freedom and the resistance of Kurdish women in their struggle for liberation. During the screening, chants of “Şehîd namirin” (“Martyrs are immortal) frequently echoed through the hall.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/c389a11c_20261025174114_2026-10-25-marsilya-jineoloji-paneli-1.mp4













‘The formation of women’s armed forces and Jineolojî in the pursuit of women’s freedom’




Speaking at a seminar titled “The Formation of Armed Forces within the Kurdistan Women’s Movement and Jineolojî,” Sîdar Feraşîn, a member of the Kurdish Women’s Movement in Europe (TJK-E), discussed the historical development of the Kurdish women’s movement, awareness of self-defense, and the importance of organizing women’s armed forces.




Feraşîn emphasized that Jineolojî should play a greater role in women’s gatherings and areas of struggle, not merely as an institutional identity but also as a guiding perspective. She also highlighted the importance of the principles of women’s freedom.




Feraşîn stated that Kurdish women continue their organizing efforts in various fields, particularly politics, diplomacy, culture, and the arts, while work on Jineolojî is also ongoing. She noted that educational activities conducted across Europe through camps, seminars, workshops, and conferences have encouraged women to develop new ways of questioning and critical thinking. She emphasized the need to adapt organizational structures to the existing potential.




Discussions focused on the role of Jineolojî, as the science of women, in social transformation. Participants emphasized that strengthening the principles of women’s freedom is essential to building an alternative way of life. They also highlighted the resistance of Bêrîtan, who lost her life in the struggle, as one of the symbols of the Kurdish people’s and Kurdish women’s struggle for a free life.




Message of solidarity from internationalist women




In a statement issued by members of Jineolojî Provence and representatives of international women’s movements, violence against women and femicide were described as being linked to the persistence of the patriarchal system and fascism. The statement emphasized women’s determination to strengthen their struggle for freedom in different parts of the world.




The statement also stressed that keeping the memory of women revolutionaries alive provides strength and courage to continue the struggle, concluding with the message “Berxwedan Jiyan e” (“Resistance is life”).




Elefteria Hambi and Nagihan Akarsel commemorated




The event also commemorated Elefteria Hambi, an internationalist revolutionary who lost her life in Rojava, and Nagihan Akarsel, a member of the Jineolojî Academy who was killed in Sulaymaniyah in an assassination carried out by the Turkish state.




A speech honoring Elefteria Hambi (Eva Maria Steiger) recalled that she traveled to Rojava in 2018 and fought against ISIS in the ranks of the YPJ before joining the guerrilla struggle in the Garê and Qandil regions. A tribute written in memory of the German revolutionary was read aloud.




The portraits prepared jointly by Jineolojî Provence and the Third District Neighborhood Committee were described as symbols of remembrance and internationalist solidarity.




In the final part of the program, a poem written in memory of Nagihan Akarsel, the Kurdish journalist and academic who was killed, was recited.




The event concluded with a performance by a choir formed under the Arîn Mîrkan Women’s Council.
