title: Quelques mots sur Trappes, la nécropolitique et le traitement des « pillages »
content:
L'attentat raciste du 23 octobre, qui a tué Pengo Bossio Wangi et blessé cinq autres personnes dont une enfant de 12 ans, on aurait pu le prévoir, et on aurait dû l'empêcher. Malgré la violence et le harcèlement auxquels leurs luttes les exposent, c'est contre une telle actualisation de la violence raciste que se mobilisent chaque jour les militant.es antiracistes. Par son abjection monstrueuse, l'assassinat déchire la réalité mais il n'est pas moins le produit de cette réalité, et de tout ce qui en elle relève, jusque dans l'apparente normalité des discours quotidiens, de la mécanique organisée du racisme.




Que le racisme soit en cours d'intensification en France, et qu'il tue, on le savait. Que tous les discours, politiques, intellectuels, médiatiques, qui relativisent ou nient l'existence du racisme - allant même jusqu'à remettre en question le terme d'

islamophobie

 - partagent la responsabilité dans cet assassinat, on le sait. On savait aussi que le racisme ne s'arrête pas aux portes de l'extrême droite, qu'il structure le 

contrat racial

, non seulement comme un crime originel, mais comme une domination perpétuée et amplifiée par des discours qui sursaturent l'espace public et social, des négligences organisées, des lois, telles que la proposition de destitution de la nationalité (inextirpable d'un ancrage fasciste), ou par les différentes juridictions qui étendent la laïcité pour en faire un régime de disciplinarisation raciale. Que ce soit à Trappes, précisément dans la ville qui n'a cessé d'être visée par l'extrême droite, que l'assassinat raciste ait été perpétré, expose on ne plus clairement que le racisme fonctionne comme une chaîne de concaténation entre les discours qui désignent une population, l'assignent à une sauvagerie extérieure à la politique, au monde commun, à l'humanité même, et le passage à l'acte. Et il faut lire ce qui est clamé dans les rassemblements commémoratifs et écrit sur les les pancartes, il faut lire ce que les gens savaient déjà : « les mots tuent », « vos discours de haine tuent

 [

1

]

 », « le monde politique et les médias ont armé le terroriste

 [

2

]

 », « vous ciblez, ils tuent

 [

3

]

. »




On savait aussi que les vies non blanches sont constamment exposées à la violence d'État, et que cette violence est vouée à s'étendre. Rappelons un fait symptomatique : la Cour d'appel de Versailles a récemment décidé de retirer « l'intention d'homicide » du jugement du policier qui a assassiné en 2023, à bout portant, Nahel Merzouk, un adolescent non blanc de 17 ans, pour la remplacer par un jugement pour « coups mortels

 [

4

]

 ». Ce n'est pas seulement que la police et que l'État tuent, c'est que le racisme d'État organise d'un même geste le meurtre, sa non-reconnaissabilité comme homicide au sein du dispositif juridico-politique où celui-ci est commis, et sa possible répétition par d'autres meurtres, d'autres vies violentées, tuées, retirées du monde. L'extension de la brutalité policière et étatique prend également une autre forme. Depuis au moins les répressions contre les Gilets jaunes, les « forces de l'ordre » étendent leur capacité à violenter les corps pour exposer un peu plus clairement à chaque mouvement social la violence meurtrière qui les fonde, et que le gouvernement a encore confirmée et explicitée par la proposition, cette année, d'une loi sur « la présomption de légitime défense pour les forces de l'ordre », c'est-à-dire d'un 

droit de tuer

 (adopté par l'Assemblée nationale, et en cours d'examen au Sénat).




Ainsi, la violence aujourd'hui en France, c'est les vies tuées, les mains arrachées, les yeux explosés, les gaz contre la foule rassemblée, les nasses, les gardes à vue

 [

5

]

, les confiscations arbitraires de matériel des manifestants, les atteintes au droit fondamental de manifester, l'extension d'une logique autoritaire, la normalisation de l'état d'urgence, l'impossibilité pour les jeunes enfants de participer et de brandir des pancartes colorées pour affirmer leur appartenance au présent et au futur de la communauté sans risquer d'être gazé.es. La violence, ce sont toutes les raisons éminemment politiques qui ont mené les gens dans les rues : lycéen.nes, étudiant.es, gilets jaunes, parents, minorités, précaires, retraité.es, militant.es. Parce que la violence, c'est que dans ce régime capitaliste, hier mais spécifiquement aujourd'hui, la vie bonne n'est pas possible.




La violence, aujourd'hui, c'est que Pengo Bossio Wangi n'est plus en vie, qu'il n'y a plus que ses proches pour se souvenir des mille et mille petits tous qui composaient son existence. Et nous toustes qui le connaissions pas, qui n'avions jamais entendu ni son nom ni sa voix, jamais aperçu son visage, sommes tenus de prendre soin du trou béant qu'il a laissé dans le monde, de le pleurer, de faire résonner son nom et de lutter contre la possibilité que d'autres vies soient exposées à la domination raciale. La violence c'est qu'une petite fille de douze ans puisse non seulement craindre le racisme, mais se 

souvenir

 du moment où une arme a été pointée contre son corps pour la tuer.




Le meurtre de Pengo Bossio Wangi est le produit de la domination raciale et de toutes les complicités qui la légitiment et la reproduisent. Kevin T., le tireur présumé, l'a révélé explicitement : il voulait s'en prendre « aux Noirs et aux Arabes » afin de « venger » les commerçants victimes de « pillages » en marge des manifestations du 17 octobre

 [

6

]

. L'invocation de la vengeance pour les « pillages » expose que quelque chose d'autre est en cause dans ce meurtre. Non pas autre chose que le racisme, ou autre chose que le fascisme (un exemplaire de 

Mein Kampf

 a été découvert au domicile du tueur présumé), mais une actualisation spécifique de la domination qui désigne dans la configuration présente une responsabilité collective gravissime.




Dans un célèbre article publié en 2006, le chercheur Achille Mbembe analyse les « formes contemporaines de soumission de la vie au pouvoir de la mort » par « lesquelles de nombreuses populations sont soumises à des conditions d'existence leur conférant le statut de 

morts-vivants

 [

7

]

 

 », c'est-à-dire, pourrait-on commenter, d'individus et de populations surexposés à la possibilité de la mort tout au long de la vie. Le politologue relève plusieurs matrices et actualisations historiques de la constitution moderne d'un droit de tuer, d'un pouvoir qui s'exerce en faisant mourir ou en laissant expressément mourir certaines populations. Dans l'analyse qu'il consacre au colonialisme, il résume ainsi la brutalité de la rationalité coloniale, c'est-à-dire la manière qu'a celle-ci de percevoir et de traiter les colonisé.es : « Les colonies ne sont pas organisées sous une forme étatique ; et elles n'ont pas généré un monde humain. Leurs armées ne forment pas une entité distincte et leurs guerres ne sont pas des guerres entre armées régulières. Elles n'impliquent pas la mobilisation de sujets souverains (citoyens) se respectant mutuellement en tant qu'ennemis. Elles n'établissent pas de distinction entre combattants et non combattants ou encore entre « ennemi » et « criminel ». Il est donc impossible de conclure la paix avec eux

 [

8

]

. » Parce que la juridiction politique européenne fait dépendre le droit (et la politique) de la propriété d'un État, les espaces colonisés étaient catégorisés comme des territoires du non-politique, de non-droit, justifiant ce paradoxe essentiellement mortifère consistant à produire un 

droit de tuer

. En d'autres mots, les vies colonisées sont assignées à un statut d'exception extérieur à toute politique, et c'est notamment cela qui les rendait 

tuables

 pour le pouvoir colonial : « le droit souverain de tuer n'est soumis à aucune règle dans les colonies. Le souverain peut y tuer à tout moment, de toutes les façons

 [

9

]

. »




Dans la lignée des travaux de Foucault et d'Agamben, les analyses d'Achille Mbembe donnent à voir que l'assignation d'un groupe de personnes à l'extériorité du politique, et à une extériorité présentée comme menaçante, sauvage, essentiellement anti-politique, est non seulement constitutive de la rationalité coloniale, mais fonctionne comme l'une des manière de rendre des populations vulnérables à la violence, à l'homicide, de les désigner comme tuables, et donc de produire la chaîne de concaténation des passages à l'acte

. 

Or la 

dépolitisation

 de ce qui s'est passé le 17 octobre, l'obsession des médias et politiciens, non seulement d'extrême droite, mais du prétendu arc républicain lui-même, du désordre et du nécessaire retour à l'ordre, la racialisation des « pillages » qui n'a cessé de déferler à travers videos, modifications IA, discours, mais aussi la séparation entre les bons manifestants et les prétendus sauvages ainsi dépolitisés, tout cela n'est pas indifférent à ce qui s'est passé à Trappes le vendredi 23 octobre. Cela s'inscrit dans un dispositif nécropolitique qui désigne tout un groupe de personnes comme étranger à la communauté, voire comme ennemi, en le dépolitisant et en lui refusant l'accès au monde.




Critiquer cela ne signifie pas pour autant que nous devrions présumer toute action comme politique 

a priori

, mais plutôt qu'inlassablement, nous sommes ramené.es à l'exigence de 

penser

 la politique, de la dissocier de l'État, et d'en radicaliser l'extension afin que justice soit rendue aux vies assignées à l'invisible et donc à l'infra-politique — sans oublier de rester fidèles à la charge imprévisible et disruptive de l'action politique, jamais réductible à une simple gestion des existences. Double impératif donc, et toujours conflictuel, consistant à « faire entendre [que] ce qui ne semblait pas relever du « champ » politique se trouve en fait en son cœur

 [

10

]

 », et que c'est donc à nous, là, tout de suite, de résister à la séparation qui nous est faite, entre bons et mauvais manifestants, celleux qui pensent et celleux qui ne pensent pas, bonnes revendications et sauvageries pré-politiques, et à nous de donner sens et pratique aux gestes communs tendus vers un monde que nous voulons faire devenir commun.




Un monde où Pengo Bossio Wangi serait encore en vie.




Yuna Visentin










[

1

] 

Deux pancartes au rassemblent à Trappes.







[

]

Mediapart,

 24 octobre 2026.







[

] 

Paroles de la députée écologiste Léa Balage El Mariky, citée dans

Mediapart,

 24 octobre 2026.

]

Mediapart

, le 5 mars 2026. Voir aussi : Sylvain George, « Nahel Merzouk, acte II : La « deuxième mort » ou la souveraineté judiciaire », paru dans lundimatin#511, le 11 mars 2026.

author: groundxero
title: All Quiet on the Central Front
content:
The central front of Delhi’s agitation against Gyanesh Kumar isn’t made up of the 50 square kilometres of administrative real estate at its heart, but so too of her borders, her universities, her stadiums, her construction sites—every inch of her geographic territory. In truth, a ‘protest map’ of the national capital has little to do with ‘notified’ and ‘denotified’ protest sites, and everything to do with the people who constitute it. When battle is between citizen and state, every man’s a front.




 




by 

Mouli Sharma




 




25 October 2026, New Delhi:

 After three weeks of near constant on-street agitation and mass protests, the final week of October has brought to Delhi an apparent change of pace.




 




Hours after hundreds marched from the Bangla Sahib Gurdwara towards the Election Commission of India (taking a longer route from the main road after being blockaded by the Delhi Police (whose headquarters are incidentally close enough to be visible in their full glory en route), and were detained and/or dispersed on 23 October 2026, the nearby streets of Central Delhi carried within them an uncharacteristic calm in what has been a month of upheaval and unpredictability.




A protester attempts to climb a parked police van on the 12 October opposition rally against SIR and CEC Gyanesh Kumar along Barakhamba Road/12 october 2026/Mouli Sharma




“Usually people loiter around in CP after the protest. But today it seems everyone went home after the police dispersed people,” said Rajendra*, an auto driver in Rajiv Chowk. 




 




Rajendra was disappointed by the day’s efforts. According to him, a ‘decent number of people’ did eventually manage to gather outside gate number 3 of Gurudwara Bangla Sahib (opposite to the gate closest to the ECI office) on the Baba Kharak Singh Marg, but were quickly detained outside the Sacred Heart Cathedral barely a few hundred metres away.




 




This ‘decent number of people’ was somewhere between 200-300, with the crowd peaking close to 2PM and having been completely dispersed by the end of the hour, as estimated by independent reporters Saumya Singh (@saumyaa.singh on Instagram) and Harsh (@kahaniistaan on Instagram) who were on field at the time.




 




“Before they started the detentions, they attempted to separate the identifiable press personnel from the remaining crowd and specifically began pushing us back. Literally, they were shoving us back as the detention buses came in, creating a stampede like situation,” Saumya said. “I’m quite small, so I was completely smothered in the crowd.”




 




“AISA, AISF, RWPI, Disha, and KYS were among the organisations present in the march. People demanded an end to the fascist regime, an immediate resignation of Gyanesh Kumar.”




 




Naureen, from RWPI, confirmed that over 20 people had been detained, a handful of which were from RWPI. By sundown, she and others were still attempting to track down where the detainees had been taken, with no information of their whereabouts. 




 




“At least 23 people were detained yesterday,” says a representative of the Disha Student’s Organisation, 7 of whose members were among those taken. “They were taken to Dwarka Sector 23,” he says. “All were released at about 10:30 PM at night.”




 




By 5PM, the crowds, police, and press had all left. Some made their way to other protests ongoing parallelly within the city, such as the Race Course Club (where 100 year old race course property was 

recently acquired

 by the central government in May earlier this year, and a Mosque now stands under 

threat of demolition

, with 

water and power supplies 

having been cut) or Jamia Millia Islamia, where students who once represented the forefront of the country’s political dissent are now fighting for their right to partake in politics itself, demanding to bring their banned student’s union back from the dead. Others scattered to trace detained individuals, whose whereabouts remained unknown for hours thereafter and who wouldn’t be released until well into the night. Contrary to Rajendra’s belief, few had ‘gone home’.




 




Outside the Cathedral itself, which became the primary site of detention, a small protest of about 50 or so people continued between Gurudwara and Church, performing a quiet, gentler form of resistance, of the kind Rajendra describes in the post detention loitering that usually takes place in the three concentric circles of Connaught Place. 




 




Conversation, art, and crowd taking up the places ordinarily reserved for automobiles and silent-antipathy between strangers; chalk and spray paint spreading over the sidewalk and roads like transient, horizontal graffiti; a silent reclamation of the streets.




Chalk graffiti on the road outside Delhi’s Sacred Heart cathedral saying, “Modi has felled more temples than Aurangzeb”/23 October 2026/Mouli Sharma




In Erich Maria Remarque’s 1929 classic German war novel, 

Im Westen nichts Neues

, the line between enemy and ally is abstraction made concrete, and being an outsider or an insider isn’t metaphor for xenophobia, but territorial reality that makes the difference between who shoots and who gets shot. The English (and best known) title of the book is 

All Quiet on the Western Front,

 which has been adapted into film, parodied, and described as the “greatest war novel of all time”.




 




For over a century now, narratives like Remarque’s have dominated the cultural idea and mythos of battle, where silence, literal silence, at the warfront is potent and dangerous; when all is quiet on the Western front, one must run, for it means the attack is shifting eastward, for the enemy surrounds us, and is at all times on the outside trying to find a way in. 




 




Of course, not all battlefields have borders. 




A policeman holds former CJP spokesperson Vijeta Dahiya by the collar on the way to a detention vehicle during a massive road jam on the Safdarjung flyover/10 October 2026/Mouli Sharma




As writer after writer, publication after publication verbalises the 

siege of Central New Delhi

, 

attempts

 to ‘

map out

’ the living geography of protest in India’s capital, and attempts to rationalise and codify the collective excitement of a people into words and phrases and theories that might hopefully lend order to the chaos that has overtaken Delhi’s streets between 

emergency security measures

, an indefinite curfew, recurring internet and transport shutdowns and every day detentions, the 4km radius under the yet 

unspecified

 ‘prohibitionary magisterial order’ under Section 163 illegalising placards, sloganeering, demonstrations and public gathering of more than five persons in the region has become the primary ‘front’ of the war between state and citizen that are the ‘Gen Z’ protests demanding the resignation and criminal investigation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar and an immediate rollback of the controversial SIR. 




 




Remarque’s title, however, is referring to a different kind of silence—the kind found on Baba Kharak Singh Marg on 23 October, where over 200 people took to the streets knowing they could be prosecuted by law for it. When 23 people were detained, allegedly with excessive force, and remained effectively missing for hours till their alleged release well into the night, far past the Supreme Court’s requirements of releasing detainees, particularly women, before sundown. When young people travelled from overstate without home or shelter in the city, hitchhiking instead from dharamshala to dharamshala, Gurudwara to Gurudwara, just to be able to curse the government and have it echo back in other people’s voices. When people 

did 

loiter, leaving behind the evidence of their resistance on the ground beneath them itself. 




 




End Manual Scavenging. Repeal Delhi Police Act. Jal Jangal Jameen. Ban RSS. Save Manipur. Free Palestine, free Gaza. Rapist Brij Bhushan Out!




‘FREE PALESTINE FREE GAZA’ spray painted on the Baba Kharak Singh Marg near Sacred Heart Cathedral, New Delhi/23 October 2026/Mouli Sharma




All is quiet on the Central Front of India’s uprising against its own electoral bureaucracy during the last leg of October 2026 the same way all was quiet on the Western Front of Germany a hundred and ten years ago during the first World War.




 




Nichts Neues 

does not translate to ‘nothing is happening’. It translates to ‘nothing is new’.




 




No front, many fronts 




 




Weeks earlier, farmers’ groups, student organisations, and other civil society members had declared Friday, the 23rd of October as a day for nationwide protests against CEC Gyanesh Kumar and the incumbent Modi government’s ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls.




 




Among these organisations was the Samyukta Kisan Morcha, whose National Council/General Body convened at Jat Bhawan, Karnal, Haryana on 12 October 2026, deciding to intensify the farmers’ struggle and organise massive demonstrations on 26 November at New Delhi and across India after ‘large countrywide protests’ against the ‘illegal SIR’ on 23 October.




 




“The state bodies of SKM will decide the spots,” SKM representatives said. “Lakhs of farmers will participate in this protest action. 26 November marks the 6th anniversary of the historic farmers’ struggle at the Delhi borders.”




 




Further, the meeting explicitly added Punjab’s organised farmers—one of India’s most militant and powerful labour pressure groups, whose year long agitation in 2020 forced the Union government to retract three controversial parliamentary legislations on their industry—to those who have over the course of the past year joined the ever expanding national outrage against alleged corruption, discrepancies, and a massive conspiracy to add false votes and delete legitimate marginalised voters from India’s electoral rolls, posing a direct perceived threat to the country’s democratic republican constitution and its foundational principle of Universal Adult Franchise.




 




The meeting decided to rally farmers in support of the student and youth protesters on the SIR issue and called for mass demonstrations at all district/tehsil centres across India on 23 October 2026. This is what happened in Punjab, on Friday, says Abdul from SKM.




 




“We led protests across all DM offices. The following month, we plan to move to Delhi as well. We are in solidarity with the youth protesting the illegal SIR and demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.”




 




SKM also warned against the alleged brutal repression against, and torture of the protesters including young women students by the Delhi Police and the “criminal elements from RSS-BJP at New Delhi”.




 




“If the Modi regime continues to attack the protesters, farmers will come forward across India to protect them, especially women, students and youth,” they said. “The right to protest is a fundamental right and attacking peaceful protesters is against the Constitution and the rule of law.”




 




The SKM meeting criticised the Judiciary including the Supreme Court for not taking suo motu cognisance of the widespread crimes in the Capital and not taking immediate action, according to them,  resulting in the “collapse of law and order”.




 




“We call upon farmers and people across India to unite in the struggle to protect democracy. We demand the immediate end of SIR, the removal and prosecution of Gyanesh Kumar, the Chief Election Commissioner, restoration of voting rights for all 13.41 crore citizens eliminated from the electoral rolls without transparency, and amendment to the 2023 Act and the inclusion of the Chief Justice of India instead of the Cabinet Minister on the selection panel,” SKM said in a public statement on 13 October.




National Council/General Body convened at Jat Bhawan, Karnal, Haryana/12 October 2026/Special Arrangement




But SIR is not the only thing SKM’s farmers plan to fight.




 




“A long haul of struggles” to achieve seven principle demands, namely: “Enact law to guarantee MSP@C2+50%, No FTAs, Loan Waiver and Rs 25 lakh compensation to suicide victim families, Pension and Insurance, No Electricity Privatisation and Seed Bill 2025, Protect Land Rights of Peasants and Tribals, Repeal 4 Labour Codes, and Restore MGNREGA” means that a union of rising discontent against electoral and agricultural policy is underway.




 




This interconnection between political crises, said Habiba from the Disha Student’s Organisation in Jamia Millia Islamia all the way back in 

June 2026

 when Abhijeet Dipke’s internet brainchild had just started to take tangible form on the now blockaded Jantar Mantar Road.




 




“If this anger against Dharmendra Pradhaan has to organically evolve into a legitimate and sustained mass movement, then students have to extend their solidarity to the workers oppressed by the new labour codes, religious minorities, and all the oppressed peoples of the country,” she said. According to her, the essential ingredient often absent from civil agitations, like the 2025 India Gate protests against air pollution, the 2024 RG Kar protests against the murder of a senior resident in Kolkata, is this unification of demands. The ongoing protests against Gyanesh Kumar seemed to have rectified this shortcoming with interest.




 




With the spontaneous journalists’ protests spurred by one reporter’s complaint of sexual assault against a 

Delhi Police ACP

 on 3 October, a series of 

women’s protests

 triggered by the gangrape of a minor outside one of DU’s premier women’s college growing into a march against the ‘anti women SIR’ outside India Gate on 4 October, and a 

lawyer’s agitation

 that resulted in urgent and immediate intervention by the CJI himself on 10 October, India’s variant of Nepal and Bangladesh’s ‘Gen Z’ protests have taken a form as multi frontal as it is multi causal.




 




On 12 October, the same day SKM convened its GBM, an indefinite hunger strike began in Jamia Millia Islamia, demanding the reinstatement of the JMI Student Union—two decades after it was banned by the then incumbent UPA government.




Banner reading ‘LADO JAMIA ZINDABAD PADHO JAMIA ZINDABAD #JMISU’ on the outer lawns at the University’s Gate no. 7, where five students remain on an indefinite hunger strike since 12 October 2026/Intervening night of 24 and 25 October 2026/Mouli Sharma




The strike, which entered its 13th day on the 25th October, brought with it threats of girls’ hostel closures, suspension of offline classes, and the violent detention of over 20 students from outside the University’s gates, which have mirrored the ‘securitised’ and militarised radius of central Delhi since police entered the campus and opened fire back in December 2019, triggering the historic Shaheen Bagh protests against the controversial CAA-NRC-NPR legislations—whose backdoor implementation many experts allege is the true intent behind SIR. 




 




On 14 October, in his first remarks addressing the ongoing protests against Gyanesh Kumar, Amit Shah confirmed as much. 




 




“I want to tell Rahul Gandhi ji that the nation is well aware of your plan to save ghuspaithiyas (infiltrators) and now the people of Bharat are not going to fall for your ploy,” Shah said in an interview.




 




Jamia’s protests follow mere days after a major victory for the students of another central university making the same demands (reinstatement of the students’ union), albeit after a much shorter stint at institutional depoliticisation—JNU itself. 




 




On 20 October 2026, the suspended office bearers of the briefly deregistered JNUSU ended their 17 day indefinite hunger strike with 

success

, with the University agreeing on 19 October 2026 to revoke the suspension of union members in place since February earlier this year after a protest against 

casteist remarks

 made by VC Santishree Pandit on a private podcast and demanding the implementation of the ‘Rohith Act’. 




Day 13 of the JNUSU’s indefinite hunger strike, student encampment at Sabarmati T-Point, JNU/15 October 2026/Mouli Sharma




At Kashmere Gate, just a few hundred metres away from the office of Delhi’s Chief Election Officer, Alok Kumar’s office, where on 7 October opposition parties 

staged a road blockade 

and mass rally resulting in the extension of alleged Section 163’s prohibitions to yet another region and submitting a memorandum demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, an immediate deletion of the massive voter deletions and revisions in the state, and a switch to physical paper ballots from EVMs, 

another

 government university has been up in arms against an alleged institutional attack on democratic academia. 




 




Elected representatives of the university’s student body (specifically the Student Council from the Karampura Campus, AUDSC KP, and the Joint Action Committee of AUD PhD scholars, according to 

sources from PTI

) led by AISA, had been on indefinite strike since September 28 2026 against growing restrictions on independent student activity in the campus. In an “

advisory

” issued on 31 July to ‘students holding events’, which became one of the primary triggers of the protest, the University referred to student demonstrations, rallies, marches, and even public meetings as “unauthorised gatherings”, and issued a proforma for students to physically fill out and submit to the University seeking permission for every such event aforementioned, bureaucratising independent student activity and subjecting it to authoritative discretion. The guidelines also included a process of explicit profiling of speakers (

section 4, subsection iv

), as well as the requirement to submit applications at least four days prior to the proposed events, making spontaneous organisation ‘unauthorised’ by definition. 




 




On 14 October, eleven students were suspended after a 17 day sit-in protest in the university’s Kashmere Gate campus, which was allegedly met with a 

complete institutional lockdown

, though the university denied the claim. One of the 17 suspended students, Vivek, also 

told

 

Tarushi Aswani writing for

 The Wire 

that the University had “violated its own ordinances” by issuing suspension orders without a proctorial meeting or the issuance of show-cause notices to the aggrieved. AISA representatives told 

GroundXero 

that the protest is currently on hold, following the suspensions.




 




The very 

next day

, the construction workers from across the city alleging corruption and intentional obscurement of social security policies by the Delhi Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board (DBoCWWB) led a protest march to the Board’s office at Vikas Bhawan, demanding immediate registration of construction workers such that they should be able to seek the minimum wages for the 90 days of the work ban announced by the Rekha Gupta led BJP government in Delhi as a GRAP IV measure and payment of backwages from the same last year, which remain largely pending still. These builders, who work independently as daily wage labourers seeking work at local labour chowks across the city, or affiliated with workers’ unions, NGOs, or large scale third party contractors, hailed from the farthest corners of the city—Burari, Karwal Nagar, Okhla, Jahangirpuri, etc. 




Upinder, a mason part of the ongoing construction workers’ struggle climbs down from the second storey of an under construction building he is working on, Burari Main Market, Delhi/21 October 2026/Mouli Sharma




The aesthetics of reportage and the performance of ‘neutrality’ aside, it is a categorical falsehood to suggest that ‘nothing is happening’ in Delhi since Neha Bora’s arrest scare on the CJP led ‘Lehra Do Tiranga March’ on the evening of 16 October 2026, a day after which a magisterial notice was issued to the student activist, demanding her to sign a ‘peace bond’ committing to one year of political inactivity alongside producing a surety of Rs. 10,000 for the same (Bora has 

unconditionally refused

 to sign the bond, and the next hearing is set to take place on 29 October). 




 




The central front of Delhi’s agitation against Gyanesh Kumar isn’t made up of the 50 square kilometres of administrative real estate at its heart, but so too of her borders, her universities, her 

stadiums

, her construction sites—every inch of her geographic territory. In truth, a ‘protest map’ of the national capital has little to do with ‘notified’ and ‘denotified’ protest sites, and everything to do with the people who constitute it. When battle is between citizen and state, every man’s a front. If anything, resistance has become the capital’s new normal, and as the old journalist’s adage goes, news is not when dog bites man, but when man bites dog. 




 




All is quiet, because nothing is new.




 







 

Mouli Sharma

 is a journalist from New Delhi, currently reporting for the Kolkata based independent news platform, GroundXero. Her work has appeared in publications like The Mooknayak, Frontline, Maktoob Media, The Observer Post, The Leaflet, Nivarana, The Polis Project, Article 14, Feminism in India, SabrangIndia, NewsClick and others. Photographs taken by her.

author: dev
title: Génération niketout
content:
Pour évoquer la journée du 17 octobre, nous parlions la semaine dernière d'une vengeance des enfants face à l'écrasement répressif et policier et à l'étouffement du quotidien. La catégorie d'"enfance" doit néanmoins être manipulée avec précaution, le retour à l'ordre adulte se tient toujours en embuscade. Il nous faut par ailleurs acter le caractère générationnel de la révolte en cours qui prend appui sur la fin des espérances contemporaines et une fin du monde annoncée. Ce texte que nous avons reçu, propose de circonscrire le plan d'action de la GenZ qui pourrait aussi se nommer la « génération niketout ».




Qu'est-ce qu'on se marre bien dans vos rues ternes devant vos faces consternées par nos feux de joie. Ne vous méprenez pas chers spectateurs, il y a beaucoup de peur dans nos gestes, plus que de désespoir ou de haine. Chaque poussée émeutière est un coup de dès jeté à la face de votre république. On sait que ça va être dur et on assume le conflit ouvert.




On ne sait pas de quoi le futur sera fait et on se doute que les jours sombres ne feront que grandir. On ne sait même pas contre quoi ou qui s'énerver et vos flics on en a rien à foutre. Le pouvoir est impersonnel, alors on détruira tout, même si on a compris que les bâtiments que les flics protègent et les zones urbaines sécurisées sont les points 

où il faut aller

. On ne s'arrêtera pas tant que vos schmits ou vos treillis ne nous mettront pas des balles... et on se doute bien que ça va bientôt déraper, 

ça dérape déjà.




On sait juste qu'il y a quelque chose qui cloche dans votre système de merde et qu'il part en couille. On a juste pas envie de crever avec lui et nous allons tout donner. Tu sais ce truc qui fait une boule au ventre et qui donne envie de crier de toutes ses forces tellement ça oppresse. Ton béton ? tes caméras ? tes flics ? tes injonctions ? tes pubs ? ton futur de merde ? ça doit être ça, on a besoin d'air.




Nous, les moins que rien, les petites guêpes, les pue-la-pisse, les crèves la dalle, les shlags, les « autonomes », les « ultra-gauchistes », les casseurs, les racailles, ça nous fait sortir les jours de manifs toute cette frustration.




Les jours où ça sent la lacrymo, ça nous libère du dogme, ça nous fait vivre quand on sent que tout vacilles. Les faces blêmes de tes pantins à la télé qui répètent les mots du pouvoir nous en disent beaucoup sur le niveau de décomposition de ta république de fantoches. Maintenant on sait que tes forteresses sont pénétrables ! Et plus les images se répètent, plus on comprend qu'on est proche de tout péter.




On ne s'aime pas particulièrement dans la rue. On est pas des « camarades » ou des « frères » ou d'autres conneries de gauchistes de ce genre, mais ce système pourrie nous a fait nous retrouver au même endroit, dans les mêmes pratiques et avec une certaine connivence de pirate de ton monde et on partage tous un certain goût de la piraterie une envie de changer d'air.




C'est vrai que l'on ne crache pas sur quelques butins qui sont comme une petite récompense face aux risques que l'on prend. Mais c'est pas avec trois polos Lacoste et une paire de TN que l'on va s'assagir. ça nous rend juste moins nerveux et on a l'impression d'avoir un peu travaillé dans ta ville qui nous fait miroiter toute l'année des marchandises qu'on pourra pas souvent se payer.




C'est Noël ! Et comme les jours de fête, le lendemain la gueule de bois est sévère parce que rien n'a vraiment changé. L'adrénaline passée, on se dit que l'on aurait pu faire mieux et que la prochaine émeute sera la bonne. On se demande même quand on ne fuira plus face à tes agents Smith.




En direct de la fin du monde, ou plutôt d

'un monde

, on va continuer gentiment à foutre le zbeul et à frapper là où vous ne nous attendrez pas.




Tu crains encore pour ta place dans ce système moisi ? Tu y crois encore un peu hein ? Avoue ? Tu t'imagines pénard dans 10, 20, 30 ans à cotiser pour ta retraite, pour une place au soleil, échappant au cancer ou à la guerre ? Si tu crois encore à toutes ces conneries, c'est qu'ils t'ont bien eu et que tu es cuit. T'es qu'un petit pion dans l'armée de réserve de l'ordre existant, t'es bon pour la chambre à gaz des banquiers type Soleil Vert, le four à crématoire du capital, le camp de consommation du Leclerc !




Et on veut pas finir comme toi !




Avec la force de nos petit essaims, sans stratagèmes et complètement désorganisés, on a compris depuis 2018 avec les Gilets Jaunes qu'on pouvait avoir le dessus et te déstabiliser. Des milliers d'essaims frappant de partout. Nous avions besoins de nous revoir et de comprendre notre détermination ce 17 octobre. Et maintenant que tout flambe, les occasions ne vont pas manquer d'éprouver les résistance de tes murailles.




La pratique de l'émeute, les gestes de l'émeute, les habits de l'émeute sont maintenant universellement partagés. La mode sera au jogging noir pour tous ! Continuons et faisons confiance à cette 

intelligence des foules, 

elles ont montré qu'elles comprenaient sans réfléchir, comme le vol des étourneaux.




Un culture du zbeul est maintenant bien ancré qui, au-delà des accoutrements et des messages muraux, est en fait 

la négation en acte 

qui refait surface. Elle ne peut pas être récupérée car c'est un parricide des générations d'avant, type Bernard Tapie, golden boy, clope au bec et insouciance des grands magasins. On prend notre revanche contre cet héritage qui va nous filer les leucémies et le 50°C l'été. Toutes vos merdes laissées valent bien quelques barricades enflammées, non ?




Mais du coup cela promet d'autres beaux 'soubresauts' historiques voire même des moments intéressants révolutionnairement parlant. Il n'y a pas besoin de manuel, de plan ou de leaders maximo pour guider les foules sans visages. Car magasins détruit ou pas, le 

Mal de la démocratie

 touche la plus grande part de la jeunesse qui n'y croit plus et qui a vécu plus intensément en trois semaines de blocages que toute une année dans ton bagne climatisé qu'est le bahut, la fac ou le boulot de merde. Alors enfiler une cagoule et péter des trucs, sans rien attendre, est comme un entraînement face à ce qui nous attend. La barricade est le prolongement du blocus qui est le prolongement d'année a fulminer tout seul sur son banc..... sauf que maintenant nous sommes nombreux dans la rue à ne plus avoir de revendications et à ne défiler sous aucune bannière. Notre seul mot d'ordre : le feu.




Notre génération sait qu'elle ne récoltera pas la moindre miette des retombées de ton système nauséabond. Plus besoin de lire 

Das Kapital

 pour comprendre qu'à long-terme les contradictions de l'économie vont tous nous tuer et que nous somme arrivé à terme cher téléspectateur ! Le Métro Terre arrive au terminus ! Maintenant que les fruits pourris de ton marché empoisonnent directement nos corps et nos esprits, nos vies et nos quotidiens spectraux, plus besoin d'explications alambiquées et de mots en allemand. Nous le vivons et ça nous épuise, et ça nous fatigue et ça nous énerve et ça nous rend malade, ça nous tue et tue nos proches... nous avons compris la leçon, mais nous avons aussi compris qu'il existait des failles. Nous allons donc les exploiter pour le temps qu'il nous reste à vivre dans ce merdier-monde.




La génération Niketout n'est qu'un acte de survie d'une population qui n'a plus de faux rêves auxquels se raccrocher : 'démocratie', 'pouvoir d'achat', 'espérance de vie', 'retraite', 'avenir' sont devenus des 

running gag

 sortant de la bouche des politiciens et des syndicats.




La génération Niketout sait que le gâteau a été mangé et qu'il était empoisonné, alors elle n'a plus rien à perdre, elle n'a plus faim, elle veut seulement vivre.




La génération Niketout n'aura aucune aide de Papa-État ou de Maman-économie alors elle ne compte que sur elle.




La génération Niketout est une erreur. Mais une erreur qui va vous péter à la gueule !




Beaux cauchemars pour les prochaines années. Peut importe qui nous sommes, ce qui compte c'est ce que nous allons faire.

title: Camcı: Urban Commune must be established to combat poverty
content:
Deep poverty in Diyarbakır (Amed) is reflected in unemployment, precarious working conditions, food insecurity and difficulties accessing basic necessities. According to 2024 data from the Ministry of Family and Social Services, 196,530 households in the city received social assistance, with the total amount reaching 4.47 billion Turkish lira. These figures reveal that poverty is not merely a matter of individual income loss but a structural problem affecting different aspects of social life.




Field research conducted in the Bağlar and Sur districts of Diyarbakır also reveals the tangible effects of deep poverty on neighbourhoods. Approximately 93 per cent of the women who participated in the research reported reducing their food purchases, while 95 per cent said they had cut spending on clothing. Many families are forced to take on debt to meet their basic needs.




Children living in damp homes affected by water leaks and inadequate heating are reportedly experiencing health problems. The fact that 196,530 households in Diyarbakır received social assistance in 2024 further illustrates the scale of poverty across the city.




Mehmet Şerif Camcı, former chair of the Sarmaşık Association, which was shut down by a Decree-Law (KHK), said that poverty was rooted in the economic policies pursued by the state in Kurdistan over the past century. He stressed that the solution could not be reduced to distributing aid. Camcı called for the establishment of an “Urban Commune” in the city to carry forward the principles and vision of the Sarmaşık Association.




‘State policies are deepening poverty’




Şerif Camcı discussed the reasons why poverty has become increasingly visible in the city, stressing that the problem cannot be understood solely in terms of unemployment and inadequate social support. While acknowledging the global dimensions of poverty, Camcı said that state economic policies were the decisive factor in Kurdistan and Diyarbakır.




Camcı said, “The primary factor deepening poverty in Kurdistan is policies created by human intervention, or more precisely, by the state. Poverty is, of course, a global problem. Another major cause lies in the choices made by capitalist modernity regarding production and distribution. However, what gives poverty its particular character and depth in Kurdistan, and especially in Diyarbakır, is the economic policies that the state has pursued in Kurdistan for the past century.”




‘After Sarmaşık, people were left at the mercy of the state's charity culture’




Camcı said that the closure of the Sarmaşık Association by decree-law had left a significant gap in the city's solidarity networks. He stressed that the association had not merely provided support to people in need but had also developed a model that strengthened social solidarity. Camcı also addressed the social consequences of capitalist relations of production and distribution: “Capitalist relations of production and distribution do not merely produce negative economic consequences. They also erode society's moral foundations, weaken its political reflexes and render people passive and powerless. The most important aspect of the Sarmaşık experience was that it enabled citizens to support one another through solidarity. At the same time, through the model and methods it developed, it helped turn solidarity and a sense of collective responsibility into a shared public consciousness capable of resisting the forces that undermine society.”




Camcı said that the closure of the association had weakened the ability of the city's poor to organise on the basis of solidarity. Criticising existing social assistance mechanisms, he continued: “After Sarmaşık, the urban poor were deprived of their capacity for self-defence. They were pushed back into the traditional relationship between the state and its citizens and left at the mercy of the state's culture of charity. Through its charity-based practices and the handouts it presents as support, the state is effectively telling people: ‘You depend on me. You can only survive through the assistance I provide.’”




‘An Urban Commune should be established based on Sarmaşık's principles’




Camcı also discussed the responsibilities of local authorities, civil society organisations, professional associations and the business community in combating poverty. He stressed that these actors should not confine their efforts to mechanisms that simply distribute aid.




Camcı stressed the need for a fundamental change in existing approaches to poverty: “Local authorities in particular, along with other actors in the city, must abandon assistance programmes that merely reproduce a poor imitation of the state's practices. Above all, these local actors must return to the principles of Sarmaşık. They should update the Sarmaşık model in keeping with the needs of the present and implement solidarity policies through an Urban Commune.”




‘Citizens must become active participants in solidarity’




Camcı added that combating poverty should not be limited to meeting basic needs such as food, housing, education and healthcare. He stressed that people should not be placed in a position of permanent dependence on assistance. Instead, the solution lay in developing a solidarity model in which citizens participate directly in decision-making and governance.




Mehmet Şerif Camcı emphasised that independent citizens' organisations should form the foundation of his proposed Urban Solidarity Commune. Camcı said, “Independent citizens' organisations must be the driving force behind the Urban Solidarity Commune. Institutions and other actors in the city should be involved from the outset and take the lead in establishing it. However, responsibility for managing the commune must be transferred to citizens themselves, particularly those experiencing poverty, as soon as possible. In other words, it must become a model of solidarity built by citizens for one another.”

title: ‘Terror-free Turkey’ rhetoric and security directive mark new university term
content:
The new academic year has begun under the shadow of security-oriented policies, alongside chronic problems such as inadequate student grants, safety concerns in dormitories run by the Credit and Dormitories Institution (KYK), dysfunctional democratic mechanisms and sexism on campuses. The Ministry of Interior's 17-point circular on “Security Measures at Universities”, issued on 9 September 2026, effectively treats campuses as “crime scenes”. Together with the Council of Higher Education's (YÖK) instruction to address the theme of “Terror-free Turkey” in the first lecture, it reflects the government's efforts to tighten its control over universities.




ANF spoke to Sude Şener from Labour Youth, Yasin Incekara from the Revolutionary Youth Union (DGB) and Özcan Berber from Student Activity about the new academic year, the government's security policies at universities and how students plan to organise in the coming period.




‘The Council of Higher Education promotes nationalism under the guise of peace’







 







Sude Şener from Labour Youth said the government and the Council of Higher Education were seeking to reduce the question of peace to a matter of “terrorism” through these measures. Şener said, “We must establish our own perspective in response to the presidential regime's attempts to restrict struggles for rights. Although the government fuels nationalist sentiments, what matters to us is the Kurdish people's struggle for freedom and peace.”




Özcan Berber from Student Activity said the government's recent policies, including its “Terror-free Turkey” initiative, were fundamentally aimed at neutralising social opposition. Berber said the demands of workers, students and the wider public, including growing calls for peace and democracy, were being suppressed through the rhetoric of “counterterrorism”. He said the government's rhetoric served a political agenda extending beyond security concerns, adding that even the most basic gatherings, information stands and awareness-raising activities on campuses were being treated as potential criminal offences.







 







Berber described the policy as follows: “As a continuation of neoliberal policies, they want to divide students, make them focus solely on their individual careers and prevent them from questioning social issues. They want a system in which we cannot trust one another or act collectively. They know that when we come together, we will begin to question this system. By isolating us, they aim to make us remain silent as even our most fundamental rights are taken away.”




Yasin Incekara, a member of the Revolutionary Student Union, said they had witnessed a series of attacks by the capitalist state against social opposition in general and universities in particular. Incekara said, “Organising events at universities under the banner of ‘Terror-free Turkey’ is seen as a means for the capitalist government, the reactionary AKP administration, to continue spreading its ideological and cultural propaganda on campuses. The events announced by the Council of Higher Education today are being presented as part of ‘Terror-free Turkey’. Yet we live in a country where even the most fundamental democratic rights and freedoms of all sections of social opposition are being trampled upon. The Council of Higher Education, which has promoted chauvinism, nationalism and other misguided ideas and attitudes in previous years, now appears to be taking certain steps under the banner of ‘Terror-free Turkey’ with an insincere approach.”




Incekara said the presidential regime viewed the peace process as an opportunity to bring a national liberation movement under its control and, in a sense, confine it within the boundaries of the existing system. He added that the growing repression at universities and attacks against students, which amounted to a veiled threat, clearly demonstrated how insincerely the government was approaching the process and how it was proceeding through deception.




‘They want to create an atmosphere of fear’




Sude Şener described the ministry's 17-point circular as a reflection of security-oriented policies on university campuses, saying that the deployment of police officers and detention vehicles outside universities was intended to marginalise the student movement. Şener said, “They are trying to turn universities into places where people are afraid, as though only a handful of students were raising their demands or taking action. We have never experienced a period with so many plainclothes police officers on campus and university entrances filled with riot police, police cars and detention vehicles.”




Şener said the atmosphere of fear being created on campuses was intended to isolate students, adding that police measures had nothing to do with student safety. She recalled the killing of Hilal Özdemir, a 15-year-old child worker who was shot dead on 30 August 2025 while working at a wedding at Boğaziçi University's Kennedy Lodge Social Facilities, pointing to where the real security failures lay.




Özcan Berber said the security circular issued by the Ministry of Interior was a continuation of similar directives introduced periodically over the past five years. He argued that these regulations effectively served as “authorisation documents”, legitimising the harsh treatment of students by university security personnel and police officers.







 







Berber said restrictive measures had been introduced at universities as the student youth movement gained strength around 19 March 2025. He recalled that students who set up information stands, distributed leaflets or voiced their demands in university cafeterias had been placed on police watchlists, detained in raids on their homes or seized in the streets as though they were being abducted, and subsequently criminalised. Berber said the latest circular indicated that repression would intensify in the new academic year, but insisted that no amount of pressure could prevent students from demanding their rights and seeking accountability from those responsible for abuses.




Yasin Incekara said they had been confronted with a directive from the Istanbul Governor's Office immediately after 19 March 2025 that effectively declared a state of emergency inside universities. He said the Ministry of Interior's 17-point circular was not the first of its kind, recalling previous attempts to discredit the revolutionary youth movement by labelling it as “terrorist”. He also referred to Ulaş Yıldırım, a member of the Revolutionary Youth Union, who was detained after being subjected to torture on campus and subsequently imprisoned.




Incekara said: “We were forced to confront a similar circular four years ago. Our most fundamental democratic rights have already been trampled upon, yet they are now trying to discredit all progressive and revolutionary activities at universities through the demagogy of terrorism.




On 19 March, we witnessed a youth uprising. We saw masses of young people confronting barricades in Saraçhane Square and students breaking through barricades at Istanbul University. The capitalist government is undoubtedly aware of the potential of the youth movement. That is why it now seeks to discredit our struggle at universities and the activities of students fighting for their rights, freedoms and future by branding them as terrorism.




Our comrade Ulaş Yıldırım from Ege University was arrested for intensifying the call to struggle against the fascist circulars sent to universities by the Council of Higher Education. Our fellow students at Ege University also set up a stand against this fascist circular under the slogan, ‘The circulars are yours, the universities are ours.’ They raised the call for resistance against the fascist repression and tyranny of the presidential regime from their campuses.




Ulaş was among those detained and subjected to torture. Our comrade was subsequently imprisoned unlawfully. We know that his imprisonment was not directed merely against one individual or an information stand, but against the entire youth movement.”




The impact of the economic crisis on universities




Sude Şener said students were facing deepening poverty as a result of the Medium-Term Programme (OVP) and cuts to public budgets, alongside growing repression on campuses. She drew attention to rising prices for basic necessities, saying students at Boğaziçi University had staged mass protests against an increase in the price of a cafeteria meal to 85 Turkish lira. Similar increases had also been introduced at Middle East Technical University, Istanbul University, Namık Kemal University and several universities in Kayseri.




Şener said growing poverty was forcing students to work under harsh and precarious conditions. “Working while studying should not be a necessity. The most fundamental need of young people is to intensify the struggle for the right to free, quality education,” she said.




Özcan Berber said poverty and the economic crisis affected not only students but society as a whole, pointing to the direct connection between declining educational standards on campuses and the policies of the state and capital. He said students were effectively struggling to survive amid rising transport costs, inadequate nutrition and exorbitant dormitory fees.




Berber criticised the allocation of university budgets, saying funding for social sciences, literature, philosophy and other socially oriented disciplines was being reduced, while public resources and university funds were being channelled into security mechanisms and the arms industry.




He said even university cafeterias funded through public budgets were being operated for profit. Berber also recalled that academics at foundation universities were being dismissed en masse and replaced by government-appointed staff. He added that engineering students were being drawn into projects run by companies developing military technologies because of their economic hardship, placing them in an ethical dilemma.




Yasin Incekara said the Revolutionary Youth Union had identified the main concerns and priorities of young people, emphasising the importance of a united struggle. He outlined these priorities as follows: “We believe young people have four fundamental concerns. The first and greatest is the economic crisis. Closely connected to this is the lack of prospects for the future, alongside increasing fascist repression and tyranny. Another major concern is the imperialist wars and aggression taking place in our region and internationally. As university students and young people, we face many problems. We have called for an organised struggle against these problems from the very beginning. Therefore, as we develop our course of struggle, we must organise around these fundamental issues and build a united struggle based on our most concrete demands.”




‘United struggle against hopelessness’




Sude Şener said they would organise faculty by faculty in the new academic year under the slogan “Democratic, autonomous universities; an independent, democratic country”. She cited international student movements as examples of resistance to the wave of hopelessness created by the government and said: “From France to Germany, from young people taking to the streets for Palestine in New York to those resisting economic policies in Argentina, a powerful wave of protest is rising across the world. We know that the same anger is simmering in Turkey. We can only overcome the atmosphere of fear designed to isolate us by drawing strength from our unity.”




Şener added that femicides, violence against women, sexual harassment and many other issues facing young women today, including the killing of Hilal Özdemir, were among the most urgent concerns of the student movement. She said the struggle of young women on campuses, like many other areas of resistance, needed greater unity and strength. Şener announced that Labour Youth would enter the new academic year determined to mobilise all its resources towards this goal.




Özcan Berber said students and different sections of society, despite their diverse backgrounds, were suffering as a result of the same underlying crisis. He described the central task facing the student movement as follows: “The problems faced by a student who grew up in Istanbul and protests against rising cafeteria prices, a Kurdish student who comes from their hometown and faces discrimination because of their mother tongue or identity, a woman resisting sexual harassment on campus, or a miner killed in a workplace accident all stem from the same crisis. Campuses are our living spaces, and decisions concerning them must be made by the university community.”




Berber concluded by saying that resistance to war, poverty, declining academic standards and political repression could only succeed through a united social struggle that exposed the common source of all these crises.




Yasin Incekara said, “The Mecca Alliance is being signed, and messages are being sent that imperialist wars in our region will intensify.” He continued: “The AKP government aims to suppress all young people who speak out against this system and, beyond simply expressing their opposition, actively struggle against it. In response, we once again declare that our organised struggle will continue and that we will raise the banner of resistance. As the Revolutionary Youth Union, we call on young people to organise a struggle around our most concrete, legitimate and just demands during this period and to build a united revolutionary youth movement on common platforms.”

author: Unknown
title: Karamus: Joint national strategy essential for Kurdish UN representation
content:
The international conference organised by the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) to secure representation and observer status for the Kurdish people at the United Nations (UN) was held in Brussels, the capital of Belgium, on 3 October 2026. Political representatives, academics and experts from all four parts of Kurdistan and the diaspora attended the conference, which discussed the diplomatic path towards Kurdish representation at the UN and the next stages of the process.




KNK Co-Chair Ahmet Karamus spoke to ANF about the work to be carried out following the conference. He highlighted the importance of political contacts in South Kurdistan (Başûr), establishing a commission involving all four parts of Kurdistan and the diaspora, and preparing a joint roadmap.




Karamus said efforts to secure observer status at the UN should be developed with the participation of different political and social groups and coordinated through joint diplomatic work.




Karamus explained that the idea for the conference had emerged at a KNK congress and was followed by approximately a year of preparations. He said discussions had been held with different groups, proposals had been evaluated and efforts had been made to ensure broad participation in the conference.




Karamus described the conference's objectives and preparations: “This project was not the result of a single day's work. It was first proposed at a KNK interim congress meeting. We then spent approximately a year preparing, meeting with different groups and evaluating proposals. “Our aim was to launch a serious initiative to secure recognition of the Kurdish people's status and their representation at the UN. That is why we wanted all political parties, organisations, social institutions and experts to participate in the conference. Bringing together representatives from all four parts of Kurdistan and the diaspora was important to us.”




Karamus said the conference had attracted broad participation and received a significant response from the Kurdish public. He added that support for the initiative from different political groups was particularly important. He said the conference should not remain merely a meeting and that its decisions needed to be followed by organised and coordinated efforts.




Karamus clarified that the initiative was not seeking full UN membership. Instead, its objective was to secure international recognition of the Kurdish people and their representation through observer status. He pointed out that observer status differed from the full membership held by UN member states and underlined the importance of international recognition of the Kurdish people's existence.




‘This is no longer KNK's project, but the Kurdish people's project’




Karamus said the scope and responsibility of the initiative had changed following the conference and that it should no longer be regarded as a project belonging solely to KNK. He said the participation of different political and social groups in the conference and their support for the initiative were important in this respect.




Karamus said: “With the conference, this initiative ceased to be a KNK project and became a project of the Kurdish people. Therefore, responsibility for it no longer rests solely with KNK. The work to secure recognition of the Kurdish people's status and their representation concerns every section of society. All political parties, institutions, social groups and the Kurdish people as a whole must participate in this process.”




Karamus said advancing the initiative would require not only political support but also an institutional structure and a shared approach to working together. He added that the collective determination demonstrated at the conference needed to be translated into concrete action.




Political contacts in South Kurdistan




Karamus said they had held meetings with political actors in South Kurdistan during preparations for the conference, including representatives of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) and the Kurdistan Region Presidency. He said these meetings were important for assessing the positions of different political groups towards the initiative and broadening the scope of the work.




Karamus said the political contacts established in South Kurdistan should also continue in other parts of Kurdistan. He added that meetings would be held with political parties, institutions and social groups in North Kurdistan (Bakur), Rojava and East Kurdistan (Rojhilat). He also pointed to the importance of involving Kurdish institutions and representatives in the diaspora.




Karamus acknowledged that political conditions and approaches differed across the regions and said the views of all groups needed to be considered to develop a joint approach. He said the initiative for national representation should not remain confined to any particular political group but should be developed through the participation of different sections of Kurdish society.




A commission representing all four parts of Kurdistan and the diaspora




Karamus said one of the most important priorities following the conference was establishing a commission to coordinate the work. He said the commission should represent all four parts of Kurdistan and the diaspora, take responsibility for efforts to secure Kurdish representation at the UN and maintain relations with different groups.




Karamus said preparations for establishing the commission were continuing. He said: “Certain mechanisms need to be established for this project to move forward. Institutions, committees and commissions must be formed, and the scope of the work must be expanded. We want to establish a commission that will take responsibility for coordinating all these efforts. This commission should coordinate the work aimed at securing recognition of the Kurdish people's status and their representation at the UN.




We are continuing our discussions with all political parties, organisations and social institutions on this matter. The structure of the commission is also extremely important. Kurds from all four parts of Kurdistan and those living in the diaspora must be represented on it. Representation must be ensured democratically. Different groups must be able to express their views and participate in the work. This is not something that can be carried out by a single institution. If we are talking about representing the Kurdish people, the different sections of Kurdish society must also have a place on the commission.”




Karamus said the commission should not be limited to conducting political contacts and highlighted the importance of carrying out its work regularly and in a coordinated manner. He added that the commission's responsibilities needed to be clearly defined, proposals from different groups evaluated and these proposals developed into a joint working plan.




‘Academics, politicians and diplomats must contribute’




Ahmet Karamus said the commission would need contributions not only from political representatives but also from academics, intellectuals, historians, diplomats and people with experience in bureaucracy. Karamus said discussions were continuing with people who had knowledge and experience in different fields, adding that their expertise should be used in developing the initiative for Kurdish representation.




Karamus said: “We are holding discussions with academics, intellectuals, historians, diplomats and people working in diplomacy. We are also meeting with people who have experience in bureaucracy. We want to benefit from their knowledge and experience. However, our approach is not to carry out all the work ourselves and then hand it over to others. For this project to move forward, different groups must take responsibility and contribute to the work.”




Karamus said society should also be part of the process and announced plans to establish a digital platform through which people could submit their proposals directly. He said allowing Kurds living in different regions and countries to communicate their views to the commission, have their proposals considered and contribute to its work would further strengthen the process.




Karamus also said: “We are preparing a website where everyone will be able to send their views and proposals to the commission electronically. People must be able to make their voices heard and put forward their suggestions. These proposals should be taken seriously and considered in the work to be carried out. We want to create a space where everyone can express their ideas and make a contribution.”




Karamus said it was important for different sections of society to take ownership of the national representation initiative. He added that everyone working in political, academic, diplomatic and social fields could contribute according to their knowledge and experience.




Karamus also pointed to the need for the work to be conducted in an organised and disciplined manner, with clearly defined duties and responsibilities for the commission. He said that while the process should remain open to everyone's contributions, its coordination and institutional structure must also be secured.




‘We must properly analyse the threats to the Kurdish people's existence’




Karamus said the national representation initiative could not be considered separately from regional and international developments. He pointed out that developments in the Middle East, the policies of international powers and events across all four parts of Kurdistan were decisive for the future of the Kurdish people.




Karamus continued: “When we look at the global situation, developments in the Middle East and conditions in all four parts of Kurdistan, we see that we are facing serious dangers and threats. Of course, the Kurdish people have also made gains. However, the Kurdish movement has suffered serious setbacks over the past year or two. Developments in Rojava and other areas, the direction of international politics in the region and the conditions that have emerged are not working in favour of the Kurdish people. That is why we must analyse the current situation correctly. We must recognise the dangers we face and shape our assessments of the future accordingly.




We must achieve unity among the Kurdish people, strengthen our collective will and develop a national strategy. We must draw the necessary lessons from what has happened and develop a common approach that will secure our future. 




We need to struggle for recognition of the Kurdish people's existence. This recognition will not come about on its own. Work must be carried out in politics, lobbying, diplomacy and international relations. For this to happen, all political parties, organisations, social groups and individual members of the Kurdish people must assume serious national responsibility.”




‘We must build national unity while preserving our differences’




Karamus said the call for national unity did not mean eliminating the different political views and circumstances across the four parts of Kurdistan. He said it was necessary to identify common ground and act together while respecting those differences.




He said: “We may have differences and disagreements. Not everyone has to think alike. However, we must be able to identify what we have in common and develop mutual understanding while respecting our differences. We need a common national strategy for the future of the Kurdish people. In developing this strategy, we must take into account the conditions in each part of Kurdistan. We can no longer act according to the circumstances of the past. We are now in a period when the Kurdish people can protect their achievements through their unity, national will and collective strength. That is why political parties, organisations and social groups must act together on issues of common concern. We can develop a common strategy while preserving our differences and continue our work on that basis.”




Karamus added that national unity should not be limited to political statements but strengthened through joint efforts. He highlighted the importance of political parties and institutions developing relations on shared issues, strengthening ties between the different parts of Kurdistan and working towards common objectives.




Joint diplomacy, Newroz and national commemorations




Ahmet Karamus said the need for joint action should extend beyond diplomatic initiatives to social and cultural activities.




Karamus said: “In the coming period, we must work together in diplomacy, both in the diaspora and in our homeland. We must pursue joint diplomacy and collectively uphold our national symbols. We must also act together during Newroz celebrations, national days and commemorations of the tragedies experienced by the Kurdish people. We must conduct our political activities through democratic methods and organise joint activities in Europe, the diaspora and Kurdistan. Different groups need to act together and stand side by side on issues of common concern. This is a responsibility we all share.”




Karamus said the threats facing the Kurdish people made joint action even more necessary, adding that everyone could contribute to the process according to their resources and areas of activity. He said, “Every political party, every organisation, every institution and every section of Kurdish society must support this process. Everyone should contribute while maintaining their own distinct identity and perspectives. This is not merely an initiative. It is a responsibility concerning the existence, future and international recognition of the Kurdish people. We must all take on this responsibility.”

title: Announcement on Integration in Shengal to be made today
content:
Preparations are continuing on Mount Shengal ahead of the announcement. It has been learned that commanders from YBŞ and YJŞ, along with Iraqi army officials, will attend the ceremony.




The announcement is expected to outline the details of the official integration of the Shengal Resistance Units (YBŞ) and the Shengal Women’s Units (YJŞ) into the Iraqi army.




All preparations for the formal announcement of the integration have been completed, and the parties are expected to make a joint statement in the coming hours.




In addition to YBŞ and YJŞ commanders, 60 fighters, Êzîdî mothers, and Êzîdî religious scholars are also expected to be present at the announcement.




Representing Iraq, military commanders, the Governor of Mosul, Iraq’s Deputy Prime Minister, and numerous other Iraqi officials are also reported to be attending the ceremony.

title: Iraqi Government: We reaffirm our full responsibility to protect Yazidi rights
content:
Sabah Numan, spokesperson for the Iraqi Prime Minister’s Office, shared details of the Iraqi government’s statement regarding the integration of YBŞ and YJŞ into Iraq’s security institutions.




The statement read as follows: “Under the leadership of Mr Ali Zeydi, Commander-in-Chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, an official ceremony will be held today, 26 Monday October 2026, to formalise the military status of the Shengal Resistance Units (YBŞ) and integrate them into Iraq’s security forces. The ceremony will also mark the process of transferring responsibility for the security of Mount Shengal to federal forces.




This process is taking place within the framework of the policy of regulating weapons under state control, as decided by the Iraqi government and incorporated into its official programmes and ministerial directives. It is also regarded as an achievement that will establish the foundation for assuming responsibility for the security situation in Shengal.




In this context, the Iraqi government greatly values the significant and unique sacrifices made by the Yazidi community in the face of terrorism and extremist agendas targeting all of Iraq, and particularly the Shengal region.




This step once again demonstrates the commitment of members of the Yazidi community to national principles. On this basis, the Iraqi Constitution prohibits any activities outside the legal framework. This message also makes clear that bearing arms is not an end in itself, but a means of defending the country in accordance with the Constitution and the law.




Adhering to the decisions of the federal government will help strengthen state authority, support national decision-making processes, and enhance state institutions’ capacity to uphold their constitutional obligations and protect the rule of law.




The Iraqi government once again reaffirms its full responsibility to protect the rights of the Yazidi people, who resisted terrorism and suffered grave injustices in the process, including loss of life, injuries, the abduction of family members, and displacement. It also reiterates its commitment to providing compensation to those who lost loved ones as a result of terrorist attacks and to rebuilding Shengal.”
