title: Mihemed: We will continue our struggle for constitutional recognition of Kurdish in Syria
content:
Reactions continue in Rojava Kurdistan to the Damascus transitional government's decision concerning the Kurdish language. On 17 October 2026, the Initiative for the Constitutional Recognition of Kurdish and Its Adoption as an Official Language in Syria was announced in Qamishlo. Hesen Mihemed, a member of the initiative, spoke about its activities, aims and objectives.




Hesen Mihemed said there was an urgent need for such an initiative today. He said, “We worked to establish this initiative because our aim was to secure official status for our language. For the past 15 years, students in Rojava have generally been reading, writing and receiving their education in Kurdish, their mother tongue. Unfortunately, under the latest decision, the Syrian Minister of Education has allocated only a few hours, three hours in total, to Kurdish. Even if some other subjects, such as philosophy, mathematics and history, can also be taught in Kurdish, this is unfortunately not enough.




The Kurdish people are an indigenous people, as stated in Article 13 of the Syrian presidential decree. Kurds have rights as Syrian citizens. They must be able to speak, read and receive education in their own language. Unfortunately, however, there has recently been a retreat from these rights. That is why our initiative seeks recognition of Kurdish as an indigenous language alongside Arabic and aims to secure its official status. Just as Arabs can study and receive education in their own language, Kurds must also be able to receive education in theirs. This is why we considered it important to establish such an initiative.”




‘Efforts to secure official status for Kurdish will continue’




Hesen Mihemed stressed that efforts to secure official recognition of Kurdish would continue. Mihemed said: “Kurdish must be permanently recognised as an official language in Syria's future constitution. We will carry out our work towards this goal. They acknowledge that Kurdish is an indigenous language and that Kurds are Syrian citizens. But if the rights verbally acknowledged for Kurds are not reflected in practice and enshrined in the constitution, it cannot truly be said that those rights have been recognised. In such circumstances, there can be no genuine justice regarding Kurdish rights. That is why we are making these efforts. There are human rights organisations, civil society organisations and institutions such as the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). There are organisations that defend the right of every people to speak and receive education in their own language, particularly when it comes to children's education.




We believe that if we continue our efforts, maintain our activities and pursue our work with determination, we can secure our rights. We will establish relations with legal organisations, international institutions and all organisations working on children's rights and issues concerning children. We will also maintain contact with national institutions working in education and language teaching, as well as civil society organisations, intellectuals and individuals concerned with the rights of peoples. Our aim is to establish relations with every organisation working on language rights. We have already established contacts with international and civil society organisations both inside and outside Syria. We contacted and visited them before formally establishing and launching the initiative. We met with representatives of Assyrians, Armenians, Chaldeans and other communities. We developed relations with individuals and institutions representing different peoples.




We explained that we are a civil initiative, that we are not affiliated with any political party and that our work is peaceful. Our objective is to ensure that Kurdish is permanently recognised as an official language in Syria's future constitution. We do not want division. Demanding official status for one language does not mean diminishing or eliminating another language, nor does it mean dividing the country. On the contrary, it represents richness and diversity. In many countries around the world, education is provided in two, three, four or even five languages. We want this to be possible in our own country as well. We are asking for support in this regard. The people we met told us that they supported us, that they could join the initiative and that Kurds were entitled to this right. They also expressed their willingness to become part of the initiative.”




‘Multilingual education does not divide a country; it enriches it’




Hesen Mihemed stressed that multilingualism did not mean dividing a country but, on the contrary, represented a source of richness and diversity. Mihemed continued: “There will be no division in Syria over language or education. What we are demanding is constitutional protection for Kurdish. This would enrich both education and the country's culture. We want to carry out activities towards this goal and raise awareness among all the peoples around us. Allowing people to receive education in their mother tongue and recognising their languages as official languages in the constitution does not mean dividing the country. Nor does it mean weakening another language or diminishing the position of the language spoken by the majority in Syria. Take Arabic, for example. Granting Kurdish official status would not represent a loss for Arabic. On the contrary, it would enrich the country.




This would improve education, mutual understanding and linguistic diversity. One of our objectives is to make our voices heard by all relevant institutions and individuals. We are trying to reach organisations concerned with children's rights and education in the mother tongue. So far, we have managed to reach some individuals and organisations, particularly those outside Syria. Unfortunately, we have not yet been able to reach everyone or every organisation because our initiative was established only recently. Nevertheless, we are continuing our efforts to make our voices heard as widely as possible. The countries and organisations concerned have signed conventions recognising that children should be able to speak, learn and receive education in their mother tongue. Every child should be able to speak, learn and receive education in their own language. Speaking and receiving education in one's mother tongue is a right belonging to all citizens and peoples.




Syria signed a convention in 1993 concerning children's right to speak their mother tongue and the right of all peoples to receive education in their own languages. That is why we will work to reach the relevant institutions. They should also support us. We hope our efforts will succeed. I want to ask a question: Education is provided in five languages in Switzerland, two in Canada and four or five in South Africa. Have these countries been divided? Has multilingual education posed a threat to them? On the contrary, it has helped foster solidarity and equality in these countries. It has encouraged meaningful dialogue and mutual understanding between different communities and peoples. This is a form of richness. It helps develop cultural understanding between people.




Our demands are being misinterpreted. Our call for Kurdish to be constitutionally protected and recognised as an official language certainly does not mean that we want separation or to break away part of the country. Nor do we want to diminish the importance of Arabic as an official language of the state. Quite the opposite. We want Kurdish people to be able to speak, read and receive education in their own language, just as Arab people can speak, read and receive education in theirs. This creates richness and strengthens solidarity between peoples. As an initiative, we want to make one thing clear: Nobody should be afraid. We do not want separation or division, and we do not want to diminish the importance of any other language. We are simply demanding the right of a people to receive education in their own language.”




‘The Kurdish people must protect their language’




Mihemed said the establishment of the initiative had attracted considerable attention. He also said: “Everyone believes that the time has come for the Kurdish people to receive education in their mother tongue. Martyrs, students and teachers have made tremendous efforts towards this goal. Significant work has been carried out through activities organised in support of Kurdish, initiatives both inside and outside the country, and the many relationships established over the years. All these efforts have received support, and people have openly expressed their solidarity. We now want to carry out this work on an institutional basis and strive to secure official status for Kurdish. As an initiative, we have also visited Kurdish political parties. We met with all parties without discrimination because we are a neutral, civil, independent and peaceful initiative. Everyone should join this initiative, support it and contribute to our work. That is why we visited different political parties in Syria individually and invited them to participate. Kurdish is not the language of any particular group. It is the common language of the entire Kurdish people.




That is why we want to set politics aside and carry out this work as independent individuals. Our aim is for the initiative to achieve meaningful results and for Kurdish to be recognised as the language of the entire Kurdish people. We have therefore tried to bring everyone together. We hope that Kurdish parties will unite around the language issue through this initiative and that they will also be able to act together on other matters. We have worked to involve everyone in the initiative and secure their support. The vast majority of parties have expressed their support. They told us that our work and struggle were valuable and that they would join us. As an initiative, we call on the Kurdish people to take responsibility for their own future. Before turning to other institutions, we want the Kurdish people themselves, together with all sections of society, including political groups, intellectuals and academics, to fulfil their responsibilities. We expect everyone, including students, teachers and families, to take responsibility in this regard. Our hope is that the Kurdish people will protect their language. Today is a day of struggle to secure constitutional guarantees for Kurdish and ensure that it becomes a permanent official language in Syria's future constitution. This requires effort, hard work, resistance and struggle.




We hope that all families will send their children to school to receive education in their mother tongue. We also call on existing relevant institutions and those responsible for children and education to support us Together, we can make Kurdish an official language in the Syria of the future. We want a diverse, multilingual Syria founded on equality. Our hope is that, by working together, we can ensure that the Kurdish people also secure their rights.”

title: Sevda Karaca: War policies undermine unity and labour struggles - Part One
content:
Sevda Karaca, Deputy Chair of the Labour Party (EMEP) and MP for Antep, answered ANF's questions about labour struggles and the struggle for peace.




Karaca said, “War permeates every aspect of social life. Workers' demands for higher wages, the right to strike, women's struggle for equality and people's democratic demands can suddenly be pushed into the background by debates over 'national security', 'the survival of the state' or the 'domestic front'. The racism, nationalism and chauvinism being fuelled also prevent people, women and young people from coming together around shared demands.”




Karaca stressed that Turkish workers also had a responsibility to oppose the policies of their own ruling classes and support the Kurdish people's demands for peace, equality and democracy. She added, “This is necessary not only as an act of solidarity but also to defend the independent interests of their own class. Because in an environment where peoples are turned against one another, it becomes harder to develop a common struggle against capital.”




How do you assess the current state of the labour struggle in Turkey? Is it sufficient, and where does it fall short?




One of the greatest contradictions in Turkey's labour struggle is this: workers' anger is growing, working and living conditions are deteriorating, and individual pockets of resistance are continuing and spreading. Yet this accumulation of struggle has not developed into an effective nationwide class movement or an independent political force representing the working class.




Workers in textiles, metalworking, logistics, mining and the service sector are engaged in fierce struggles over wages, working conditions and trade union rights across industrial regions with very different characteristics throughout the country. They continue to resist despite the threat of dismissal, pressure from employers, obstacles to trade union organising and the corruption of the trade union bureaucracy.




These struggles show us that the working class has not surrendered. However, the experience gained in one factory or one struggle is not being carried over sufficiently to other workplaces, sectors and cities. Resistance often remains confined to individual workplaces and struggles to develop into a collective class consciousness and political force.




What do you attribute these difficulties to?




We cannot attribute these shortcomings to a lack of willingness among workers to struggle. The limitations imposed by trade union bureaucracy, the lack of organisation, fear of unemployment, increasingly precarious employment and political repression are significant obstacles. But socialists and labour organisations must also confront their own responsibilities. Exposing workers' problems and voicing their legitimate demands is not enough. We must establish connections between these problems, bring struggles together, help workers develop confidence in their own strength and link economic demands to a political programme.




The connection between economic and political struggle does not emerge automatically. What we need today is to unite the fragmented experiences of the working class around a common struggle. We must ensure that workers have a say not only in confronting the employers in their own factories, but also in challenging the economic and political system that determines their working and living conditions. The working class needs to organise itself as a force capable of shaping society as a whole. We need to develop a strategy of struggle that transforms workers' scattered anger into collective strength, builds political action out of everyday experiences and enables the working class to shape society according to its own demands and objectives.




Are socialists sufficiently self-critical? Is enough thought being given to why poorer sections of society turn to ruling parties?




The government does not merely control economic resources and the institutions of the state. It also intervenes in people's everyday lives, their sense of belonging, their expectations and their relationships of trust. It creates the everyday, consistent and long-term mechanisms needed to sustain this influence. We cannot explain the political choices of a worker or a poor family solely in terms of economic interests.




People also make political choices based on belonging, trust, identity, solidarity and expectations for the future. Through the networks of everyday relationships it has established among working people, the government controls not only material resources but also the power to shape what society regards as a problem and whom people trust. Confronted with this hegemonic relationship, correctly identifying the problem is not enough. We must also question how we reach workers and working people in their everyday lives and which of their experiences we are able to transform into a common struggle.




‘

We must return to the old principles of organising’




Which of the everyday, consistent and long-term mechanisms of engagement established by the government do we possess? Socialists do not have these material resources at their disposal. For socialist organisations that lack the power, money and resources available to the government, there is ultimately no substitute for consistent work rooted directly in workers' living and working environments, work that does not lose its direction regardless of circumstances, together with perseverance and determination. This is how we can build lasting foundations within everyday life that respond to people's sense of belonging and their expectations. Perhaps I can give an example from Antep. This is essentially what we are trying to do there. We insist on working in working-class neighbourhoods, at the grassroots, where such efforts often remain unseen and unrecognised. This work has taken concrete shape in the workers' resistance struggles in Başpınar. Our efforts are fundamentally aimed at giving working people's struggles an organised foundation. This is not work that attracts attention on social media or is loudly advertised. It requires accepting the demanding task of long-term organising rather than seeking short-term results.




This is the only way to become an organised force rooted in the everyday lives of working people in industrial areas that are regarded as government strongholds, where every mechanism of its hegemony is deployed.




We must become part of people's everyday lives, learn alongside them, develop shared solutions rather than arrive with ready-made answers to their problems, and build political consciousness out of these experiences. For the Labour Party, one of our central challenges is to go beyond being a party that says the right things. We must become a political force that workers trust through struggle, where they make decisions collectively and recognise their own strength.




But something else is even more important to us. Socialists know that the fundamental task is to strengthen the organised power of the working class. The growth of socialist organisations and the growth of the working class's political power are not the same thing. That is why I sometimes disagree with assessments on social media that measure socialist parties by their membership numbers and similar indicators. An organisation's membership may increase. Its visibility on social media may grow. It may win more votes in elections. But none of these, on their own, can measure whether the working class is becoming a historical political subject.




In periods of severe repression, discussions about turning workers and working people into an organised force tend to focus largely on finding new methods and approaches. I disagree with this. In periods such as these, when fear and political and economic repression become increasingly ruthless, we need to return to the old, time-tested methods of organising. Rather than searching for some magical 'new' form of organisation, we need to return to much older principles of organising.




Working-class organising is not glamorous. Spending years building an organisation in a workplace or a working-class neighbourhood is no easy task in a country where the aggression of the one-man regime constantly forces us to respond immediately to one attack after another. Winning a worker's trust or spending years building a lasting organisation in a neighbourhood is not highly visible work. In this climate of repression, it cannot be. Unfortunately, in an atmosphere of left-wing populism where visibility is sometimes valued more highly than becoming deeply rooted in workers' lives, discussions can proceed on entirely the wrong basis. It seems almost characteristic of our times to shy away from the long and demanding nature of organising working people, and to regard forceful rhetoric as more important than devoting time and effort to a street, a factory or three politically conscious workers in that factory. What I mean by time-tested knowledge is precisely this: revolutionary politics is built not so much on these visible displays, but on the often unseen labour of organising.




No matter how high poverty and hunger rates rise, how much anger repression generates, or how clearly the nature of the government becomes apparent to broad sections of society, social struggles will not develop automatically unless we become deeply involved in them as an organising force. Nor will it be possible to transform spontaneous eruptions of anger into purposeful political struggles. Those spontaneous outbursts will eventually subside. The conditions that gave rise to them will either be addressed by the system to some extent or, more often, become normalised in the minds of millions as circumstances that simply have to be accepted. The existing order will find a way to preserve itself.




We have seen numerous examples of this at different moments, from the Gezi resistance to the events surrounding 19 March. Transforming social energy from immediate reactions into lasting organisation requires time, effort and patience. Rather than constantly trying to respond to every new issue the government places on the agenda, our priority must be to build the foundations for sustained struggle. If we are to respond to attacks, our response must emerge from those organised foundations. We must concentrate our efforts in the vital centres of working-class life. Working-class neighbourhoods and industrial areas must be our priority. Only in this way can 'working people' cease to be an abstract expression and become a concrete political subject, conscious of their class position and shared interests. This requires persistence.




‘We must strengthen people's capacity to act collectively’




At the stage we have reached, repression and oppression may be presented as the only reality, and each new wave of attacks may leave people feeling overwhelmed, wondering how they can possibly respond to everything. Yet the issues at stake, and the foundations for resisting them, have actually become clearer. Whatever the government does, it cannot completely exclude people from politics in Turkey.




We can see how essential organisation is if people are to play a decisive role in political life. In recent years, we have repeatedly been told that everything depends on a leader, a saviour, the ballot box or electoral campaigns. Politics has increasingly been discussed as though it were simply a matter of the performance of professional politicians, party leaders and MPs. Yet these approaches have repeatedly proved ineffective. We must strengthen what really matters: people's capacity to act collectively through organisation. Political organisation is one of our most fundamental challenges. It is not simply about expanding political parties. It also means building women's associations deeply rooted in neighbourhoods, initiatives established by residents against local drug gangs, parents' groups fighting for free school meals, villagers coming together to protect their living environments, and students organising dormitory committees, corridor by corridor, because there is no hot water in their accommodation. We need to devote time and effort to strengthening these forms of organisation.




One of the most decisive factors in this period is ideological clarity and understanding. For nearly 50 years, not only in our country but across the world, we have repeatedly heard claims that ideologies are dead, that they destroy freedoms, and that politics is essentially a matter of pragmatism. The Justice and Development Party's (AKP) attempts to co-opt opposition politicians in order to divide and weaken the opposition, the lack of a political programme that may appear left-wing but is essentially rooted in liberalism, and the tendency to regard positions that remain within the existing system and fundamentally serve capital as preferable under conditions of repression all demonstrate how important ideological clarity and consistency become when political struggles intensify.




Professor Cangül Örnek made an observation recently that I agree with: for the first time in many years, the political situation in Turkey has become remarkably clear. There is no longer any political force that people can rely on other than their own capacity to organise and act. Perhaps for the first time since the military coup of 12 September 1980, we are living through a historical period that offers considerable opportunities to strengthen opposition to capital. Today, people are experiencing enormous anger towards capital, but that anger has not yet become fully politicised. We must give it a political direction and prevent it from being absorbed back into the existing system. This is also what we are seeing internationally, from France to Albania.




We are confronted with a brutal labour regime that condemns the working class to ruthless working conditions and extremely low wages, attempts to discipline workers through the fear of unemployment, and traps people in lives stripped of dignity. The scale, consequences and cruelty of poverty are frequently discussed, but there is very little discussion of the means of struggle. There is only diagnosis! It is not enough to define injustice, lawlessness and inequality solely through the government's most prominent attacks. General statements about justice and the rule of law are ineffective unless they are grounded in clear, fundamental demands that working people can embrace.




The subjects of opposition politics are not merely those who are politically active in some way and face repression because of it. The real subjects of opposition politics are the exploited and the oppressed. Politics that neglects this reality has no prospect of expanding its influence or bringing about change.

author: Unknown
title: Hawari: Syria could lose a century without guaranteed rights
content:
The transitional administration established in Syria following the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad's government faces fundamental challenges, including political legitimacy, economic recovery and the protection of the rights of the country's diverse communities. Journalist and writer Nidal Hawari spoke to ANF about a range of issues, from tensions in Hasakah (Hesekê) and the situation of Alawites and Druze to regional power struggles and strategic straits. He warned that the administration's failure to develop lasting solutions to these problems was increasing uncertainty and deepening social tensions.




Hawari stressed that developments in Syria could not be considered in isolation from one another.




‘The legitimacy of the transitional administration is disputed’




Hawari pointed to the structure of Syria's transitional administration, saying that the current political order had not been established by a government directly elected by the people. He said the way the administration had been formed, from the presidency to the transitional institutions, had raised questions about its legitimacy. He added that the structure established under the leadership of Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) was not based on a consensus encompassing all communities in the country.




Hawari said that the forces which had gained influence in Syria following the overthrow of the Assad government were attempting to reorganise their political and regional interests, but had failed to establish a common political position even among themselves. He pointed out that the administration had been unable to stabilise the country politically, economically or legally, placing the process of rebuilding state institutions at risk. Hawari stressed that a transition to a democratic system required the establishment of accountable institutions based on the will of the people and subject to public oversight.




‘The economic crisis is deepening and artificial crises are being created’




Hawari warned that Syria was facing a severe economic crisis, pointing to difficulties in paying public employees' salaries and the administration's dependence on external resources, which restricted its ability to act independently. He said uncertainty surrounding future support from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and other countries was increasing the pressure on the administration. Any reduction or suspension of foreign assistance would make it even more difficult for the authorities to maintain public services.




Hawari stressed that the economic crisis could not be separated from the political crisis. He said the administration's failure to resolve economic problems was intensifying social tensions and creating conditions conducive to new political crises and security problems.




He also expressed the view that artificial crises and hostilities were being created between different sections of society to conceal economic problems. Hawari said this was placing additional pressure on communities outside the central administration or those demanding recognition of their identities and rights.




‘Tensions in Hasakah and the provocation of tribes are not independent of external factors’




Hawari addressed attacks against Kurds in Hasakah and the positions adopted by Arab tribes. He said these developments could not be reduced solely to relations between the transitional administration and the Kurds, stressing the need to examine the political positions of the tribes and the regional influences shaping them. He pointed out that Arab tribes held differing positions among themselves. Some had previously issued statements supporting the agreement between the Kurds and the transitional government within the framework of integration, but had subsequently retreated from those positions.




Hawari stressed that this shift was significant in the context of regional power struggles. He suggested that the conflict of interests between Turkey and Israel could also influence the positions of local actors, pointing to the incitement of certain Arab tribes against the Kurds. He linked the continuation of attacks and tensions, despite the flexibility shown and concessions made by the Kurds on certain issues during the integration process, to the absence of a lasting legal framework in Syria and interference by certain states. Hawari stressed that lasting peace in Syria could not be achieved solely through temporary agreements between local actors.




Hawari also discussed the historical and social characteristics of the tribes, describing certain tribal structures around Raqqa and Deir ez-Zor as communities that had historically positioned themselves according to regional balances of power. Referring to the work of historian and orientalist René Dussaud, he recalled that these structures had been shaped by migration movements and had played important roles in military service and animal husbandry during the Byzantine and Sasanian periods. Hawari said power relations continued to determine their positions today. He pointed out that Turkey exercised influence over certain tribes and that local structures could act under its direction.




The future of the Druze and Israel's policy towards Syria




Hawari discussed the situation of the Druze community in southern Syria, saying that developments concerning its future could not be considered separately from regional power struggles. He pointed to Israel's influence in the region, saying that Druze areas were moving towards more independent military and administrative structures, with local forces preparing to establish autonomous administrative and military institutions with Israeli support. Hawari also addressed Israeli military activity around Damascus, noting that the regional objectives of Turkey and Israel did not always coincide and that tensions between the two countries could influence the positions of local forces.




He pointed to the potential impact of elections in Israel and the US midterm elections on regional policies, while stressing that states would continue to pursue their long-term strategic objectives. Hawari said the implications of any new political arrangement emerging in Druze areas for Syria's territorial integrity would depend on how the central administration responded to the demands of different communities. He added that efforts to secure local autonomy could gain momentum in an environment where rights were not guaranteed.




‘The problems facing Alawites are worsening’




Hawari warned that the problems facing Alawites in Syria were becoming increasingly severe. He said security concerns persisted, particularly in coastal areas, while allegations of attacks against Alawites and hate speech were intensifying social tensions. He said Alawites were being targeted during periods of crisis for the transitional administration, with employees and workers facing attacks. Hawari added that Alawites were also encountering difficulties in accessing public-sector employment. Hawari pointed out that past massacres were being brought back into public debate through allegations involving individuals associated with the former government, while responsibility for certain attacks was being attributed to Alawites.




He discussed accusations surrounding the Baniyas and Reyhanlı incidents, which have recently been debated in the media, in this context. Hawari stressed that claims concerning responsibility for these incidents needed to be verified through independent investigations. He also reported that an Alawite religious figure who had reportedly crossed into Syria through Hatay had disappeared, stressing that the person's fate needed to be established.




Hawari said protecting cultural rights would become increasingly difficult when even the right to work was not guaranteed. He stressed that independent investigations and legal accountability should take precedence over sectarian accusations.




The integration process of the Kurds




Hawari returned to the issue of integrating the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into central state institutions, saying that the Kurds had demonstrated flexibility and adopted a constructive approach throughout the process, but that their rights had not been permanently guaranteed. He stressed that Syria lacked a functioning state governed by the rule of law and pointed to the absence of the institutional framework needed to ensure the implementation of integration agreements.




Hawari warned that leaving recognised rights dependent on decisions made by the transitional administration posed serious risks. Hawari asked, “Can we really regard these rights as rights?” and stressing that they must be founded on social consensus, constitutional guarantees and independent judicial mechanisms. Hawari said the Kurdish people continued to face attacks against their flag and symbols expressing their identity. He stressed that integration must be accompanied by arrangements that protect education, security, political representation and cultural freedoms.




‘New balances of power are emerging along the Lebanon front’




Hawari discussed the relationship between Iran and Hezbollah and developments in Syria, noting that Syria had long occupied an important position in Iran's regional connections and the logistical routes extending to Hezbollah.




He said Iran had been forced to adapt to new circumstances following the overthrow of the Assad government. Hawari explained that Tehran was seeking to maintain contact with different political actors, viewing its longstanding relations with Muslim Brotherhood circles and the possibility of establishing contact with HTS within this framework.




Hawari said there were concerns that a possible military operation by HTS against Lebanon could alter the balance of power, adding that the Lebanese authorities were taking this scenario into account. He also addressed the conflict of interests between Turkey and Israel, saying that Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem's statements concerning relations with Turkey could not be considered separately from regional strategic calculations. Hawari pointed out that forces reaching agreements in Syria could find themselves confronting one another elsewhere.




Developments in Yemen




Hawari said developments in Yemen needed to be assessed alongside the changing balance of power in Syria and Lebanon. He drew attention to allegations concerning Turkey's military cooperation with Saudi Arabia and possible measures against the Houthis in Yemen. He also referred to reports that Egypt had sent military shipments towards Yemen, suggesting that these developments could indicate the emergence of a regional military alliance.




Hawari stressed the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, saying that Iran's power was not limited to its nuclear programme. He pointed out that control over energy transportation and maritime trade routes provided a major strategic advantage. He warned that any disruption in the Strait of Hormuz would affect the global economy. Hawari also highlighted the critical importance of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait because of its position between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Hawari said the establishment of a broader military front against the Houthis in Yemen, combined with Iran's involvement in the conflict, could draw the region into a much wider war.




‘Peoples could lose a century if they fail to protect their rights’




Hawari warned that Syria's transitional process would also shape the lives of future generations and said: “The region is preparing for the next hundred years. If peoples lose their rights today, fail to protect them and cannot secure their future, they may have to live with the consequences for perhaps a century.”




Nidal Hawari stressed that rights must be protected through concrete and lasting guarantees rather than temporary decisions. He said uncertainty about the future could not be overcome without establishing a system that safeguarded the rights of Kurds, Alawites, Druze and other communities, ensured political participation and resolved disputes through the rule of law.

title: YJA Star guerrillas: Martyr Beritan is the embodiment of a free life
content:
Throughout the history of the Kurdish people, there have been many heroic epics that live on in the people’s memory and are never forgotten. Martyr Beritan (Gülnaz Karataş), who shouted in the face of traitors and became a symbol of resistance and the free woman’s stance, represented the essence of the Kurdish woman.




Hesret Dilgeş Amed, one of the YJA Star commanders, spoke about martyr Beritan’s actions and resistance. Beginning her remarks by commemorating martyr Beritan and the martyrs of October.







 







Hesret Dilgeş Amed said: “Comrade Beritan joined the ranks of the freedom movement in the 1990s, at a time when the Kurdish people were rising up throughout Kurdistan. Comrade Beritan came to know Leader Apo by reading his books and studying his analyses. She organized her life through the knowledge she gained from Abdullah Öcalan and through her own efforts.




At that time, there were also liquidationists within our movement who wanted to dismantle it. Through her stance in life, her organizational commitment, and her free will, Comrade Beritan stood against these liquidationists. In this way, she upheld Öcalan’s line. Martyr Beritan put Öcalan’s ideas into practice in her own life. For this reason, no force could intimidate her or break her resolve.




Comrade Beritan is a pioneer of Kurdish women and a great fighter. During the 1992 war, martyr Bêrîtan’s stance against liquidationism, betrayal, and surrender became the embodiment of the heroic Kurdish woman’s resistance. Comrade Beritan played a major and important role in that war. At the most difficult moments of the conflict, so as not to fall into the hands of the enemy and the traitors, she broke her weapon and threw herself from the cliffs.




Through this act, comrade Beritan became a heroic symbol of the Kurdish woman who never surrenders. The banner that martyr Beritan carried forward affirmed the existence of the Kurdish people. From now on, too, we will struggle under this banner for the physical freedom of Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan]. We are the successors of Comrade Beritan.”




Martyr Beritan never bowed her head 




Emphasizing that martyr Beritan’s stance carried great significance not only in the military sphere but also in the ideological sphere, Hesret Dilgeş Amed continued: “In the military sphere, comrade Beritan was a commander for us women fighters. She showed everyone that a woman can accomplish anything if she sets her mind to it. For this reason, as the comrades of martyr Beritan, we will always take the stance she demonstrated as an example. Comrade Beritan was a fighter who never bowed before the liquidationists.”







 







YJA Star guerrilla Agir Zîlan also spoke about martyr Beritan’s connection with Abdullah Öcalan, saying: “What makes us happiest is the following statement that comrade Beritan made about Leader Apo in her report: ‘I want to write the novel of the Leadership.’




These words encourage us to develop ourselves and, at the same time, strengthen our bond with Leader Apo. The stance demonstrated by comrade Beritan was an answer to every kind of difficulty. She remained steadfast in the line of Leader Apo and the PKK. This line will always be the foundation of our struggle. We will have no choice but to recognize our own strength and will. Every one of us knows this. Martyr Beritan is not merely an individual to us; she represents a line, a path. She is a source of pride. We bow our heads in respect before comrade Beritan’s stance and struggle.”

title: Slovenian philosopher Slavoj Žižek writes letter to Öcalan
content:
Slavoj Žižek, a Slovenian philosopher and one of the leading figures in Marxist thought, wrote a letter to Abdullah Öcalan. The letter, which Žižek sent to the Imralı delegation, reads as follows:




“Dear Abdullah Öcalan,




Today, there are leaders whom we feel compelled to support only because they represent the least bad option among two or three bad choices. However, choosing between bad options never brings a solution; it merely produces a compromise that carries within itself the seeds of its own failure.




You are one of the very few leaders who can and should be supported unconditionally. This is because you combine a principled stance and a profound, theory-based approach with sound pragmatism and a willingness to make difficult decisions.




You are fully aware that the struggle you are waging for the Kurds is not a struggle against the Turks. If you succeed, it will not be only the Kurds who benefit; both sides will win. All citizens of Turkey will enjoy greater freedom, peace, and prosperity.”

author: groundxero
title: The Twilight of Trumpism
content:
Contemporary Trumpism is not the conservative attempt to return US society back to the 1950s. It is the attempt to return US society back to the 1850s – an attempt which will fail completely, disastrously and totally.




 




By 

Dionysius




 




Between 2016 and 2026, the political system of the United States has been dominated by Trumpism, a.k.a. the US variant of billionaire fascism or plutofascism. Its domination was so complete that even when non-Trumpist politicians won elections, they did not question Trumpism’s single most compelling argument. This argument, in a nutshell, was that the United States could solve the 21st century problems of a 

collapsing middle class

 and 

an economy being looted by billionaire monopolists

 by a magical return to 19th century tariff walls, territorial imperialism and settler colonialism.




 




The year 2026 marks the moment when a majority of US citizens have stopped believing in 19th century magic. One of the most telling signs of this shift occurred on October 9, 2026, when Pete Hegseth, the Trumpist official in charge of the US military, announced that the US would broadcast the execution of a former US soldier on live television.




 




Hegseth had fully expected the announcement would create a wave of hurrah-patriotism. After all, the soldier in question, a former US Army major, had shot and killed 13 fellow soldiers and wounded 30 others at a military base in Fort Hood, Texas in 2009. The soldier also happened to be Muslim and the US-born son of Palestinian American immigrants, two groups which have been constantly scapegoated and persecuted by Trumpism.




 




Instead, the announcement triggered a firestorm of condemnation. Numerous former soldiers and Pentagon officials criticized the announcement as tantamount to a lynching, while human rights advocates pointed out that the only two countries which hold public executions are Taliban-ruled Afghanistan and theocrat-ruled Iran. Ten days later, overwhelming political pressure forced the Trump administration to back down and 

call off the broadcast

.




 




To understand why Hegseth misread the situation so badly and why this moment is so significant, it is worth pausing for a moment to reflect on the group which forms the electoral core of Trumpism. This group consists of white males who are nostalgic for the settler colonial white masculinity which dominated US politics for almost two hundred years, i.e. between the creation of the US in 1783 and the civil rights and feminist struggles of the 1960s and early 1970s.




 




To understand why this group wants to return to the past, we must first understand that this white masculinity was responsible for 105 years of settler colonial land theft and genocide against the First Nations of North America. This period began with the 1785-1795 Northwest Indian War, and ended in the Wounded Knee Massacre in South Dakota committed by US soldiers against the Lakota people on December 29, 1890. Most of the surviving First Nations were confined to reservations thereafter, and none enjoyed full US citizenship rights until the Snyder Act of 1924.




 




This white masculinity was also crucial to perpetrating the horrors of 82 years of US chattel slavery (1783-1865) on African Americans and citizens kidnapped from Africa by slave traders. After the abolition of slavery in 1865, this white masculinity engineered systems of legal apartheid (commonly called “Jim Crow” laws) which privileged whites at the expense of African Americans. In addition to these laws, many US states had groups of white terrorists who regularly assaulted and murdered African Americans. The most notorious of these terrorists were the Klu Klux Klan, an organization so powerful that as late as August 12, 1925, an estimated 30,000 of their members marched openly through the US capital of Washington, DC without any legal repercussions whatsoever.




 




Official Jim Crow and unofficial racial terror ruled large parts of the US for 87 years (i.e. 1878-1965). They did not disappear until the 1965 Voting Rights Act granted African Americans the right to vote in all US states, and until Federal law enforcement agencies cracked down on white terrorist groups during the 1960s and 1970s.




 




Settler colonial white masculinity was equally predatory towards women, albeit with the proviso that property-owning white females were occasionally more privileged than African American males (conversely, African American females faced the double burden of racial as well as gender oppression). For almost two hundred years, US women were treated officially and unofficially as second-class citizens. Females had only limited rights to employment, education and property as compared to males, while wives were treated as dependents of their husbands.




 




US women did not achieve the right to vote on a national level until 1920, although it is true many US towns, cities and states had adopted female suffrage during the second half of the 19th century. It was not until the 1964 Civil Rights Act that discrimination based on gender was prohibited. It was not until the 1974 Equal Credit Opportunity Act that US banks were prohibited from requiring women who opened a checking or savings account to have a male co-signer. It was not until the 1980s that females entered the US workforce on a more or less equal basis with males.




 




To summarize a long and complex history, for nearly two hundred years large numbers of US white males could mercilessly exploit African American slaves who they owned as property African American sharecroppers who were their debt peons, and domestic partners who were essentially permanent indentured laborers. US white males also enjoyed a massive structural advantage in the job market vis-a-vis African Americans and females, who were subject to a variety of official and unofficial forms of exclusion.




 




Contemporary Trumpism is thus not the conservative attempt to return US society back to the 1950s. It is the attempt to return US society back to the 1850s – an attempt which will fail completely, disastrously and totally.




 




Hegseth is the perfect embodiment of this failure. Prior to becoming the head of the US military, he was a Fox News talk show host. He had no real training in military affairs and never displayed the slightest administrative capacity to run a vast organization which oversees 2.11 million soldiers. His sole qualification for the job was that he was a white male television entertainer who created heavily scripted performances designed to sell the ideology of settler colonial white masculinity to an audience of other white males.




 




Once installed in the Pentagon, Hegseth fired anyone with a degree of military competence and promoted incompetent sycophants. These latter view the military as a mere stepping stone on the path to becoming a highly-paid private consultant for the world’s most monopolized and wasteful military-industrial complex. In fact, Hegseth went so far as to impose 

mandatory testosterone testing

 of male US soldiers, on the wholly unscientific and frankly bonkers notion that high testosterone equals battlefield effectiveness (spoiler alert: it does not). In the words of a recent

 

CBS news report

: “The Trump administration has pushed out top female and Black officers, and Black and female officers have been disproportionately removed from promotion lists, a source familiar with the lists told CBS News. There are currently no active four-star women generals or admirals in the military. Many of those who failed to secure promotions have left the military.”




 




After gutting the US officer corps, Hegseth’s next achievement was to lose a war to Iran, a country without a modern navy or air force. The US spent a colossal $45 billion, lost 

most of its most advanced anti-missile interceptors

, and had 

81 of its aircraft

 shot down – for zero political results. Instead of collapsing, Iran’s theocratic regime was bolstered by an upsurge of patriotism, as ordinary citizens rallied against an unprovoked war against their country. Meanwhile, the wartime disruption of the strait of Hormuz increased the world price of oil from $65 on February 25, 2026 to $101 on October 20, 2026, triggering ruinous inflation in the world economy.




 




Thanks to these multiple catastrophes, Trumpism has become massively unpopular. 

Two out of three US citizens reject the war on Iran

, while 

two out of three US citizens reject the Trump presidency as a whole

. Interestingly, this rejection mirrors that of public opinion outside of the US, where two out of three people polled in thirty-six countries 

view the Trump presidency negatively

.




 




What will follow next is the political bankruptcy of settler white colonial masculinity, in the form of the crushing defeat of Trumpism in the 2026 midterm elections and the first possibility of progressive political reform in the US since the brief window of 2020-2022. Needless to say, any successful reform coalition must attack the exclusionary vision of this white masculinity through an inclusionary vision of the US as a truly representative democracy, one capable of bringing concrete improvements to the lives of every single one of its thousands of communities and all 350 million of its citizens.




 







The author is a social activist in U.S.

author: Rob Wipond
title: A Biological Psychiatrist Wins the Nobel
content:
O

ne could be forgiven for feeling wary rather than celebratory this October when 

Stanford University neuroscientist and psychiatrist Karl Deisseroth

, along with two German scientists, 

received the Nobel Prize

 for inventing a new, invasive brain technology dubbed “optogenetics.”




After all, the last time a psychiatric treatment garnered a Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine was in 1949—for the lobotomy technique of severing the arteries into the brain’s frontal lobes. The award further boosted excitement among psychiatrists worldwide, who ultimately administered lobotomies to tens of thousands of people (often by, infamously, hammering an icepick through both eye sockets) as a “calming treatment” for hundreds of different mental and emotional conditions. Mainstream psychiatry later moved on from lobotomies with the emergence of new drugs. But 

protest campaigns

 led by family members of lobotomized patients continued for decades as they tried (in vain) to get the Nobel Foundation to rescind its award for a practice that had killed an estimated 5 percent of patients and left countless others permanently stripped of major emotional, mental, and functional capacities.




So, in 2026, is optogenetics biological psychiatry’s long-sought breakthrough for understanding and rectifying dysfunction in the mechanisms of the brain? Or is it another damaging, dangerous tool? Reading some of the leading researchers in the field reveals that it could be a bit of both.




Karl Deisseroth: From Poetic Emoting to Policing Emotion




To understand the roots and likely future of this “revolutionary” new brain technology, it helps to first understand a little about its founder and leading developer.




In his book, 

Projections: A Story of Human Emotions

, and in a wide-ranging, three-hour 

interview

 with computer scientist Lex Fridman, Karl Deisseroth shows his appreciation for both scientific and artistic ways of viewing the human condition.




Alongside his neuroscientific research, Deisseroth works in both hospital inpatient and private outpatient psychiatric practice, and writes literary nonfiction. He believes in the value of talk therapy, is interested in extreme states of consciousness, frequently fuels his thinking with poets and novelists such as Jorge Luis Borges, Toni Morrison, and James Joyce and, when describing his conversations with his patients, uses words like “empathy” and “communion.”




Karl Deisseroth. Photo by Cmichel67, CC BY-SA 4.0




Yet Deisseroth also writes that he was “trained to see brains as biological objects, as they indeed are.” He describes many of those same patients as having “diseases” or “disorders” of the brain, and not infrequently authorizes that they be involuntarily committed and forcibly drugged against their protests. And he appears to have no serious sociological or scientific critique of common psychiatric research and practices. For example, he regularly discusses the lack of reliable lab tests in psychiatry to verify any diagnoses or positive emotional impacts from treatments, yet he also describes electroconvulsive shock therapy (ECT) as “very effective” for depression—with no acknowledgement of the 

dearth

 of quality scientific evidence supporting such a view. He describes lithium as “highly effective for bipolar”—despite 

broad scientific questions about such claims

. And he says studies in twins have proven that depression, bipolar, and other mental disorders have major genetic drivers—with no acknowledgement of the 

scientific gaps and biases

 common in twin and other behavioral genetics studies.




One of many stories from Deisseroth’s book that vividly illustrate these seemingly contradictory tendencies is that of a 67-year-old retired insurance executive he calls Alexander. After witnessing the 9/11 attacks on the World Trade Center, the man becomes swept up in a whirlwind of new interests and activities, hoping to find ways to help his country. Alexander’s family is worried about these dramatic changes and get into conflicts with him, but Alexander himself regards what’s happening as exciting, positive, a revitalizing surge of youthful energy, and a new, more meaningful lease on life. Deisseroth reflects on how a similar experience came over him after a rush to escape an armed robbery left him hyper-energized for weeks. Deisseroth also relates Alexander’s impassioned convictions and behaviors to those of literary figures, historical leaders, and mythical heroes of extraordinary achievements, and to an evolutionary need to respond intensely to threats and challenges that’s part of “a common heritage of humanity across cultures and continents” and “an elevated expression of what a human being can be.” He suggests Alexander is going through a deep, personal “metamorphosis.”




Unfortunately, Deisseroth then tells us, Alexander was “born in the wrong time and place” to harbor such intense energy. Deisseroth diagnoses Alexander as having “mania” and locks him up and drugs him against his will with tranquilizing antipsychotics. Alexander’s wife is relieved. But Deisseroth admits that this “normalizing” of Alexander was “not a clear-cut win”—even a year later, he writes, Alexander was no longer “manic,” but seemed “glum” in his inconsequential retired life and “still did not understand why we had acted as we did.”




In virtually every other story, Deisseroth’s empathy for his patients comes with a similar hard limit—his interest in them seems less a “communion” of equals than the fascination of a zookeeper for his caged animals. Could this be a cautionary metaphor for where the field of psychiatric optogenetics is headed?




What optogenetics is and how it works




For a breakthrough technique in brain research, the basics of optogenetics are nevertheless surprisingly 

easy to understand

.




In a single-celled alga, German researchers isolated a protein, called channelrhodopsin, that made the alga move towards light. Deisseroth developed a technique whereby the gene that produces channelrhodopsin is carried by a virus (a “viral vector”) and functionally embedded into selected brain cells, after which the firing of those brain cells can be turned on or off by exposure to a light source implanted in the brain.




Developed in the early 2000s, optogenetics was a massive leap in precision beyond brain scans and electrical brain stimulation devices for studying and changing the activities of specific brain cells and cell networks and circuits. Optogenetics has 

exploded

 in popularity, by 2022 engaging thousands of research institutions in over 51 countries, while genes, methods, and techniques have multiplied.




So far, most of the brain research has taken place in living mice—but theoretically, there’s nothing stopping it from being implemented in human brains. And though linking mice behaviors to imagined human-like thoughts, feelings, and experiences is an inexact science at best, still, the discoveries have been striking.




Using optogenetics, researchers have been able to 

isolate and control

 mouse brain circuits that switch on and off fear and anxiety reactions, addiction behaviors, and social avoidance, implant 

false memories

, block or enhance memory formation, and even break down into component brain circuits 

more complex behaviors

 such as how mice care for their young.




In his book, Deisseroth uses the word “eerie” to describe witnessing how mouse brain states and behaviors “could be added to or subtracted from” in these ways—such as making a mouse freeze with apparent fear over nothing, and then promptly become active again.




© The Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine. Ill. Mattias Karlén




Researchers 

believe

 this ability to turn cells on and off may have many applications—such as for stopping tremors, controlling epilepsy, healing deafness, curbing neuropathic pain, restoring bladder or bowel dysfunction after spinal cord injury, and treating amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Already in one 

case

, a blind person, through optogenetics on his eye and the aid of specially engineered goggles, partially recovered vision.




All of those applications offer cell targets in more safely accessible parts of the human body—but it’s the possible brain applications that animate Deisseroth the most. In a 

paper

 specifically about using optogenetics in psychiatry, Deisseroth and other researchers state that the main goal of experiments on animals is to identify “neurobiological mechanisms” of mental disorders and then target these in humans with new “pills that non-invasively cure or ease the symptoms of mental illness with minimal undesirable side effects.”




They add, though, that the “heavy burden” of mental illnesses “demands” that entirely new treatment options also be developed besides drugs—including, possibly, “optical tuning” of the brain through direct application of optogenetics on humans. They suggest, for starters, using optogenetics to tackle aspects of drug addiction, depression, anxiety and PTSD.




In his book, Deisseroth writes with enthusiasm about using “cellular precision” in manipulating “brain circuits” to rectify “human frailty,” ease human suffering, and cure the “causation” of psychiatric disorders.




However, pressed by Fridman in his interview, Deisseroth becomes more circumspect. He explains that optogenetics scientists may be able to “turn up or down” specific behaviors linked to specific brain circuitry—such as a particular compulsive activity—but acknowledges that it remains mystifying how or why most behaviors truly arise. Even in mice, he says, the “choice” to take any particular action appears to mysteriously “start” in innumerable places “all across the brain… all at about the same time.” Consequently, optogenetics interventions won’t truly be addressing the root causes of people’s suffering any time soon but, like psychiatric drugs currently do, Deisseroth says they could be used to “treat symptoms.”




This admission raises a spectre: An optogenetics intervention might well be experienced—by humans and mice—as an irrational, altered reality, where a behavior feels uncontrolled and completely disconnected from what’s perceived through the senses and desired through the thoughts. What would this kind of disassociation between desire and action, between self and reality, repeating over and over again, do to a vulnerable mind?




And what of the potential biological risks and harms?




The risks of optogenetics




 

Optogenetic brain interventions involve both viral delivery, through injection, of a genetic alteration to selected brain cells, and an implant to deliver light directly inside the brain. This has never been tested on humans.




Viral gene therapy alone is hazardous—experiments on humans have sometimes triggered 

life-threatening

 responses, especially from immune system reactions, including 

deaths

.




Certainly, some leaders in the field are openly grappling with the hazards, uncertainties, and ethics of optogenetics.




In one 

paper

, a team of British researchers summarize concerns about possible adverse effects of optogenetics, and identify a host of “currently unanswered questions.”




The initial injection will have to carry a substantial load of the virus and gene, because repeated deep-brain injections are simply “not feasible,” the researchers state—and that makes potentially dangerous immune responses even more likely. Cellular toxification or damage and instigation of brain tumors are also all possible.




Patients will have to accept hosting a “non-human” gene and protein inside their brains, they write, and this, along with any associated impacts, will be permanent and irreversible.




The light-producing devices must be implanted deep enough in the brain to reach the target area. Even very slight amounts of heat generated by the light could be extremely harmful to surrounding cells. The implant can damage the underlying brain tissue during placement or subsequent movement, while also potentially making it more difficult to detect these damages due to common implant materials disrupting MRI scanning. And the long-term effects of light itself on the cells of an enclosed brain are utterly unknown.




In a 2025 

Nature Science

 

paper

, Swiss and American researchers, including Deisseroth, note that additional unknown, long-term risks exist due to the comparatively short lifespans of the mice that have been so far tested, and the comparatively much lower threshold for the activation of immune responses in humans.




The human experimentation question




The Swiss and American researchers write that testing these potentially harmful techniques in more-similar non-human primates such as monkeys comes with “considerable regulatory and ethical burdens.”




The British researchers point out that new drugs are always clinically tested for safety in healthy human volunteers, but optogenetics is so hazardous that “it is ethically out of the question to deliver both a permanent gene therapy and to implant a novel device” into any healthy human.




Furthermore, because the brains of mice are hardly perfect analogues for much larger and more complex human brains, it’s questionable how much—if any—of the existing research learnings will translate to humans. Therefore, the British researchers note, “there can be no guarantee” that the first human groups submitting to optogenetics studies would get any clinical benefit at all.




In spite of this, neither team of researchers calls for banning experiments on humans. On the contrary: Noting that new medical devices (which aren’t as tightly regulated as drugs) are often used in trials on ill people with relatively little prior safety testing, the researchers lobby for jumping directly to experimenting on people who have severe physical or mental illnesses.




Enter the rationalizations




Both research teams acknowledge serious ethical concerns with such human experiments—albeit they do so in ways that can seem more worrying than reassuring.




The Swiss and American researchers write: “Direct optogenetics in the brain can alter cognitive processes such as mood, motivation and memory, as well as fundamental survival drives common to all mammals—including anxiety, fear, hunger, thirst, reward-seeking, aggression, mating, nurturing and parenting. Together, these capabilities underscore the profound ethical implications of optogenetics for altering human behavior, desires and decisions. The stakes are high…”




They propose “complete transparency” with patients, tight regulatory oversight, long-term monitoring of impacts, and “fostering a collaborative ethical discourse—encompassing scientists, ethicists, legal experts, patients, families and other public stakeholders.” They further pledge to “champion the principles of voluntariness” and safeguard “freedom of thought.”




Along the way, though, they invoke the somewhat Orwellian-seeming notion that even prospective patients with purportedly diseased, disordered, dysfunctional minds must nevertheless by all means be granted the “cognitive liberty” to submit to psychiatrists’ potentially deadly experiments in thought control.




The British researchers follow a similarly contorted line of reasoning to push for experiments on humans.




They note that, for example, a “schizophrenia patient suffering severe side effects to their medication” might likely welcome an optogenetic intervention as an alternative. However, because optogenetics is so nascent, they write, “there cannot be any suggestion of benefit put forward” to these patients—even though, of course, they themselves have already enticingly suggested optogenetics could produce fewer side effects than medications.




Establishing with a patient a correct “understanding” of the “risk/benefit balance,” they write, allows for the vital “informed consent” that will move ethical human trials forward—even though, again, they themselves acknowledge that the true risk/benefit balance is impossible to know and the “vulnerable” patients most willing to try optogenetics “may have an impaired ability to give informed consent.”




No mentions of coercion or power




And the most frightening part of these ethics discussions is what’s going unsaid. These researchers’ apparent collective naivete about the actual economic and socio-political context of their profession—whether from ivory-tower ignorance, willful delusion, or deliberate obfuscation—is profoundly disturbing.




For example, yes, many medical devices often are introduced into markets and used on ill humans 

without

 important kinds of safety and effectiveness testing first—however, as a recent Government Accountability Office report 

summarized

, this practice has contributed to millions of injuries and tens of thousands of deaths 

in the U.S. alone

 in just ten years. Indeed, electroconvulsive shock therapy (ECT) devices are arguably one of these—they’ve 

never been tested by regulators

 for safety or effectiveness despite 

widespread reports

 of permanent memory loss, heart attacks, and other serious adverse impacts.




Countless psychiatric patients were promised long-term support for submitting to treatments with experimental Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) devices but, 

across two decades

, such patients have been 

repeatedly left

 with dangerously malfunctioning and degenerating implants in their heads and no support from government regulators, health insurers, research institutions, or doctors. And the excitement and fervor among optogenetics researchers that’s tangible in their writings—now amplified by the Nobel Prize—suggest optogenetics has the potential to have impacts at exponentially larger scales than DBS.




Meanwhile, none of these papers discuss the heightened risks for patients created by the 

profit-driven motives

 that are widespread in psychiatric research, even as hundreds of 

commercial optogenetics patents

 have already been filed.




They don’t discuss the misleading coerciveness about the alleged effectiveness of psychiatric treatments that’s endemic in public communications from 

industry advertisers and physicians

, 

health websites

, and even 

health regulators

.




They don’t discuss the 

high and rising rates

 of uses of force against psychiatric patients, nor the fact that it’s 

not uncommon

 for extremely vulnerable psychiatric patients to be coerced into risky studies.




Either all of these researchers are unaware of these problems in their own profession, or, even in the context of specifically discussing psychiatric ethics, they simply don’t consider the ongoing, systemic, mass-scale harms of modern psychiatric power and coercion—nor the victims of them—to be worthy of mention.




In the end, it’s unclear which is worse—but it proves our society has nothing close to a safe environment for optogenetics trials on humans.

author: Unknown
title: Эррико Малатеста - Насилие и революция
content:
Автор

: Эррико Малатеста

Название

: 

Насилие и революция

Дата

: 25 августа 1921

Источник

: Umanità Nova, год 2-й, № 115







О МОЁМ ПРОЦЕСССЕ










––––––––––––










II.










Насилие и революция







 Недавно автор, подписывавшийся в 

Avanti!

 псевдонимом 

Скамполиста

, писал: «

Анархисты, согласно также последним заявлениям Эррико Малатесты, не являются сторонниками насилия и не ставят своей целью организацию революционной силы для насильственного преобразования капиталистического общества…

». 




 Из какого отчёта о миланском процессе можно вообще вывести, будто я не стремлюсь к организации революционной силы для насильственного преобразования капиталистического общества? 




 Анархисты против насилия. Это общеизвестно. Центральная идея анархизма – устранение насилия из общественной жизни; организация общественных отношений, основанная на свободной воле индивидов, без вмешательства жандарма. Поэтому мы враги капитализма, который принуждает, опираясь на защиту жандармов, рабочих позволять эксплуатировать себя владельцам средств производства или даже оставаться праздными и терпеть голод, когда хозяева не имеют выгоды их эксплуатировать. Поэтому мы враги государства, которое есть принудительная организация, организация насилия, насилия над обществом. 




 Но если порядочный человек говорит, что считает глупым и варварским делом доказывать что-либо палкой и что несправедливо и злобно принуждать одного исполнять волю другого под угрозой револьвера, разве разумно выводить из этого, что этот порядочный человек намерен дать себя избить палками и подчиниться чужой воле, не прибегая даже к самым крайним средствам защиты? 




 Я сказал в Милане то, что я сам и все анархисты повторяли тысячу раз: «Насилие оправдано только тогда, когда оно необходимо для защиты себя и других против насилия. Где прекращается необходимость, начинается преступление». И если бы государственный обвинитель дал мне возможность изложить в конце процесса, каковы наши цели и наши средства, я доказал бы, что раб всегда находится в состоянии правомерной обороны и что поэтому его насилие против хозяина, против угнетателя всегда морально оправдано и должно ограничиваться только критерием полезности и экономии – то есть минимизации – человеческих усилий и страданий. Это тоже вещь, тысячу раз повторённая всеми анархистами. 




 Нынешний режим несправедливости и угнетения держится на насилии, на грубой силе штыков и пулемётов, и поскольку индивидуальный бунт, хотя и хорош и полезен, когда применяется разумно, вообще бессилен против колоссальной силы государства, необходима организация революционной силы, достаточной для достижения цели. 




 Но как же так: социалисты, которые столько раз наперебой с королевским прокурором изображали нас сторонниками слепого насилия и почти не видели в анархизме ничего, кроме систематического насилия, – сегодня вздумали изображать нас пацифистами, которые ждут, что капиталистический режим тихо и мирно сойдет на нет сам собой? 




 Истина в том, что 

Скамполиста

 опьянён идеей «диктатуры пролетариата» и не мыслит революции без означенной диктатуры. А поскольку мы против этой диктатуры, которая есть одновременно угнетение пролетариата и издевательство над ним со стороны вождей (я сказал бы 

мелкобуржуазных

, если бы любил язык этой школы), со стороны, говорю я, вождей партии, которым удаётся господствовать и 

душить

 революцию, – 

Скамполиста

 выводит из этого, что «

анархисты

 

не ставят своей целью организацию революционной силы для насильственного преобразования капиталистического общества

». 




 А ведь 

Скамполиста

 должен был бы знать, что желание или нежелание делать революцию – революцию вооружённую, насильственную – всегда было главной причиной наших разногласий с социалистами, которых мы обвиняли в том, что они охотно говорят о революционной подготовке, но на деле противятся всякому возможному движению, усыпляя массы реформизмом, соглашательством и парламентаризмом вообще. 




 Помилуйте, пусть 

Скамполиста

 борется – спокойно или нет – с нашими идеями; но пусть не заставляет нас говорить противоположное тому, что мы думаем и говорим. 







Эррико Малатеста







––––––––––––




Карло Скарфольо, которого я назвал бесстыдным лжецом до смешного, отвечает: «Я цитировал письмо Малатесты. Ложь, если она есть, – на совести того, кто написал письмо».




Но кто написал письмо? Вернее, существует ли действительно это письмо, из которого следовало бы, будто я обещал английскому правительству оставаться тихим, если оно оставит в покое анархистов?




Я отрицал это самым решительным образом (тогда как Скарфольо лживо утверждает, будто я не отрицал факта) и потребовал опубликовать письмо, которое, по словам Скарфольо, будто бы появилось в английской газете

 The Daily Mail. 




Пусть Скарфольо опубликует его, если может; и тогда мы поищем, кто фальсификатор.




Пока же подтверждаю

: Бесстыдный лжец до смешного. 




Тот же Скарфольо, призывая осадное положение, говорит, что гражданская юрисдикция абсолютно некомпетентна в политических делах, и доказывает это примером миланских присяжных, которые нашли, что директор

 Umanità Nova 

не совершил подстрекательства к преступлению, тогда как управляющий его газетой совершил.




Нет, сударь: Малатеста был оправдан присяжными, тогда как управляющий, товарищ Пальяи, был осуждён профессиональными судьями. Разница существенная: присяжные не имеют карьерных интересов, которые надо охранять, не зависят от правительства и, даже будучи буржуа, живут среди людей и испытывают – к добру и к худу – влияние народной среды. Судьи же испытывают влияние тех, кто стоит у власти

. 




...

title: Farmers reiterate demand for genuine agrarian reform
content:
MANILA — Farmers, fisherfolk along with Indigenous peoples and advocates culminated this year’s Peasant Month on October 21 by marching from España to Mendiola after a week-long camp out, bringing longstanding calls for genuine agrarian reform.

The Super El Niño, land-use conversion and human rights abuses are among the key issues aggravating the plight of rural folk.

Farmers from Southern Tagalog and Central Luzon expressed deep frustration by the state’s suggestion to use buckets to collect water. They decried the lack of government aid like subsidies for the dry spells, leaving many without food to sustain themselves and their families.

Other issues they highlighted are the Pax Silica initiative and various renewable energy projects which will convert their farmland into infrastructure which they said “will serve corporate interests and the US military complex.”

They condemned the continuing U.S. intervention in many aspects of the nation’s affairs. They vowed to hold protest actions on the upcoming visit of U.S. President Donald Trump,or this year’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) forum. (RVO)
