author: By John Malamatinas, Contributor
title: TikTok Revolt in France: A New Generation Takes To The Streets
content:
On October 17, France witnessed some of the most intense urban unrest in its recent history. Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across the country, while clashes with police, widespread looting, and burning barricades transformed the streets of numerous cities. Activists described the events to Unicorn Riot as among “the fiercest riots France has experienced since World War II.”




The protests were not confined to Paris. From Marseille and Lyon to Bordeaux, Limoges, and numerous smaller cities, demonstrators confronted police, occupied streets, and attacked commercial and government buildings.
















The mobilization had begun weeks earlier. On September 7, a young TikToker called for a revival of the Yellow Vests movement, which had shaken France in 2018 and 2019. The immediate trigger of the original movement was the rising price of fuel, which had climbed above two euros per liter.




Meanwhile, an independent wave of high school protests was spreading across France. Students were protesting deteriorating school infrastructure, chronic underfunding of public education, and worsening conditions in classrooms. Hundreds of schools were reportedly occupied or blockaded during the preceding weeks.




These two mobilizations began to reinforce each other, turning October 17 into a focal point for broader social discontent. On TikTok, a veritable media storm unfolded. AI-generated videos, influencers, humorous memes, and countless short clips promoted the demonstrations and in the prospect of a Yellow Vests comeback. Old footage from the movement was recreated, remixed, and circulated to a new generation. High school students were particularly active. In videos shared across social media, groups of students danced to the viral song “Hey Mr. Policeman” in front of police lines during their demonstrations. By Saturday, the mobilization had reached an extraordinary scale.




According to organizers, approximately 800,000 people demonstrated across France. The Interior Ministry estimated 550,000 participants, including 110,000 in Paris. For comparison, during the massive mobilization against the Loi Travail labor reforms on June 14, 2016, organizers estimated that 1.3 million people had taken to the streets nationwide.







The protests developed into widespread urban unrest with 

more than 2,000 businesses

 attacked or looted, vehicles set on fire, and government buildings targeted. In Limoges, masked individuals entered the historic 19th-century city hall and set it ablaze. The fire destroyed large parts of the building, including its roof. In Marseille, protesters forced their way into city hall.







“Stop shooting out the eyes of high school students and ordinary people. These are people who are studying. And you’re blinding people, you’re blinding people who are studying. These are people, they’re victims, and you’re hurting them.”










Paris: The Streets Breakaway From the Official March




The morning in Paris began with relatively unsuccessful attempts to mobilize around several railway stations. Groups of protesters were repeatedly surrounded or dispersed by police, preventing them from gathering in larger numbers.




By approximately 2 p.m., however, the center of the mobilization had shifted to Place de la République, where tens of thousands of people assembled. 




As the first confrontations with police began, protesters gathered around the monumental statue of Marianne, the symbolic representation of the French Republic. Activists had dressed the statue in an enormous yellow vest. One side carried a message referring to October 17, 1961, when Paris police massacred Algerian demonstrators protesting a discriminatory curfew. The other side denounced the treatment of students by police in 2026.




The symbolism was unmistakable: the current revolt was being connected to France’s history of colonial violence and contemporary police repression.




What followed was difficult to describe: rather than following the conventional and thus predetermined demonstration route, large groups of protesters began moving in multiple directions.




Traditionally, major demonstrations in Paris follow routes negotiated between unions and authorities, often connecting large squares such as République, Bastille, or Nation. These routes allow police to concentrate their forces and contain demonstrations within relatively predictable boundaries. On October 17, that model collapsed.




Instead of remaining within a single march, protesters dispersed throughout the surrounding streets. Near Place de la République, supermarkets, tobacco shops, and other businesses were broken into and goods were taken and at times dispersed to those who are unhoused.




As the afternoon progressed, crowds formed in different parts of the city. Entire intersections and stretches of road were taken over, while police struggled to respond to simultaneous confrontations. In some neighborhoods, officers appeared to lose control of the streets for hours. 







The unrest spread across several Parisian arrondissements, or administrative districts. Barricades were erected, vehicles were set on fire, and police deployed large quantities of tear gas in attempts to disperse the crowds.




Groups moved through side streets, regrouped at intersections, and reappeared elsewhere as police attempted to contain them. Some areas were under total occupation of those groups.




The decentralized nature of the unrest made it exceptionally difficult for authorities to regain control. Only the following morning did the full extent of the destruction become visible. Shattered storefronts, burned vehicles, and debris covered streets across the capital. Similar scenes had unfolded in cities throughout France, extending far beyond the country’s major metropolitan centers.













Scenes from Paris, France on October 17, as nationwide protests brought together masses of people protesting rising fuel prices, in solidarity with the student mobilizations, and opposition to nearly a decade of Macronism. 




[image or embed]




— Unicorn Riot (

@unicornriot.bsky.social

) 

October 17, 2026 at 6:03 PM
















Hundreds of thousands marched across France today. Vandalism of state and corporate institutions were reported as tensions escalate ahead of next year’s presidential election. This video shows protesters attacking a surveillance camera in Paris as the crowd cheers when the camera gets knocked down.




[image or embed]




— Unicorn Riot (

@unicornriot.bsky.social

) 

October 17, 2026 at 6:07 PM
















“The economy is collapsing. There’s more demand than supply in France, with the recession and everything what’s going on. The problems in schools. So we’re here to demand our rights.”










The Youth at the Center of the Revolt




But who were the people taking to the streets? As Unicorn Riot’s 

video report

 shows, anyone who took the time to speak with protesters at Place de la République quickly discovered that many were young people fighting for a better future. Their grievances went far beyond fuel prices. 




Some were demonstrating for better schools and adequate funding for public education. Others spoke about the rising cost of living, declining purchasing power, and the lack of opportunities for employment or internships.







For many of these young people, Emmanuel Macron has dominated the political landscape for almost their entire adolescence. Since taking office in 2017, Macron has pursued economic reforms, reductions in certain taxes on wealth and capital, and controversial changes to France’s social welfare and pension systems. His policies have repeatedly triggered large protest movements.




The generation now entering the streets has grown up amid these conflicts, with little expectation that established political institutions will address their concerns.










Screen grab from frontline video report from Paris, France filmed on Oct. 17, 2026.










Screen grab from frontline video report contributed by John Malamatinas.










The original ambition behind October 17 was to bring together two different social forces: the young people who had been protesting outside their schools and the older Yellow Vests movement. So far, this convergence appears only partially successful.




Individual Yellow Vests could be seen among the demonstrators, but the broader social base that characterized the original movement was not present on the same scale. The Yellow Vests had mobilized significant sections of the working class and lower-middle class, including many people from rural areas and smaller towns who had previously felt excluded from traditional political movements.




The current revolt, by contrast, is driven predominantly by urban youth. Among them are high school students from different social backgrounds, but also large numbers of young people from the banlieues, the migrant working-class suburbs surrounding France’s major cities.




These neighborhoods have experienced decades of social marginalization, underinvestment, discrimination, and aggressive policing. The memory of 

Nahel Merzouk

 remains particularly significant. On June 27, 2023, the 17-year-old was shot and killed by a police officer during a traffic stop in Nanterre, outside Paris. His death triggered nationwide protests and several nights of intense unrest.




For many young people in the banlieues, police violence and racism are not abstract political questions but part of their everyday experiences.




The current mobilization therefore brings together grievances that cannot be reduced to the price of fuel or the condition of school buildings. It is also a revolt against social exclusion, racial discrimination, and a political system that many young people believe offers them little future.




Whether these different social forces can unite into a broader movement remains an open question. More people associated with the Yellow Vests are beginning to express solidarity with the protests. A larger convergence could still emerge in the coming weeks and months as the French elections approach.










“There’s a lack of resources. Petrol prices are rising too. There are too many problems in France. It’s all hard. There are no work-study placements. There are no jobs, there is nothing. We’re fed up.”










Macron’s Response, a Second Day of Unrest and Repression




In the aftermath of October 17, public debate quickly shifted toward the widespread looting and destruction. Political leaders and much of the media focused on the attacks against businesses and public buildings, often separating the political demands of demonstrators from the actions of those involved in the riots.




President Emmanuel Macron 

in a speech to the nation

 condemned the violence and argued that people protesting over legitimate social concerns should not be confused with those seeking to create chaos. The distinction between supposedly legitimate protesters and violent troublemakers became central to the government’s response. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation, but Macron refused to accept it.







On Sunday, October 18, demonstrators returned to Place de la République and the surrounding streets. Once again, predominantly young crowds confronted police, erected barricades, and set them ablaze. The confrontations continued for hours, with police using tear gas to disperse groups that repeatedly regrouped in nearby streets. While the government was calling for order, parts of the capital were experiencing another day of unrest.




Nuñez reported that more than 1,800 people had been arrested across France following the previous day’s demonstrations and riots.




In Paris alone, 

police reported 855 arrests

 connected to Saturday’s events. The figures continued to rise in the following days. By October 20, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin reported 2,513 placements in police custody since the beginning of the unrest.




Hundreds of detainees were being referred to the courts, with many facing accelerated criminal proceedings known as “immediate comparisons.” Under this procedure, defendants can be brought before a judge shortly after police custody, leaving limited time to prepare their defense. The government has demanded a particularly severe judicial response to attacks on police officers, public buildings, and businesses. Prosecutors have been instructed to seek pretrial detention in serious cases.




One case attracting particular attention concerns the destruction of Limoges’ historic city hall. Investigators reportedly 

detained a 34-year-old activist suspected of involvement in the fire

. French media described him as having connections to radical left-wing environmental activism and reported that he was classified as fiché

 S

.




This designation refers to a French security-intelligence file used to flag individuals considered potentially relevant to state security. It does not establish criminal guilt or prove membership in a terrorist organization.




The authorities are also preparing for further demonstrations. Reports of local curfews, discussions about restrictions on social media, and plans to deploy military personnel to protect strategic buildings have intensified concerns about the government’s security response.




Police themselves have faced criticism for failing to contain the unrest on October 17. In several cities, the simultaneous and highly mobile nature of the confrontations overwhelmed their capacity to respond.




Meanwhile, striking images of security operations have circulated online. One video shows a helicopter hovering over Paris at night, sweeping the streets with a powerful searchlight. The scene looks less like an ordinary evening in the French capital than something from Gotham City.







“

It’s simply about the economy. We no longer have any means to survive, we no longer have any means to live. Petrol at €2 a litre, wages going down, our money flying off to Ukraine

“










More Protests Planned




The next major day of protest is expected on Saturday, October 24.




Once again, calls to mobilize are circulating on TikTok and other social media platforms.




Further demonstrations are being promoted for October 31, coinciding with Halloween. It remains unclear whether the next mobilizations will reach the scale of October 17 or whether the government’s intensified security response will change the dynamics on the streets.




Protests in France are not likely to break down, especially because of the looming presidential elections in April. The far-right around Marine Le Pen from the National Rally, 

who is favorite in the elections

, together with many establishment figures blame the far-left party Unbowed France (LFI) for instrumentalizing the riots or even creating them as a plot themselves.




The chief of LFI is, according to the current polls, also a favorite to enter in the second round of the presidential election.




Protests and clashes last weekend also took place in Italy, including Milan and other cities. Elsewhere in Europe, social media users have begun circulating calls for similar youth-led demonstrations.




In Germany, TikTok videos are promoting protests on October 31 under slogans suggesting that Generation Z should take matters into its own hands. Student protests have also taken place in Greece, while calls are circulating for a broader European day of youth and student action on November 20.




Across Europe, young people are confronting rising living costs, deteriorating public services, uncertain employment prospects, and a growing sense that established political institutions are unable or unwilling to respond to their demands. France may be offering an early glimpse of how these frustrations can erupt into a much broader confrontation.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Cold Lake First Nations chief acknowledges conflict as he heads to First Nations meeting in Ottawa
content:
With no Assembly of First Nations regional chief in Alberta, individual chiefs and proxies from that province will be attending Monday’s First Nations-First Ministers meeting in Ottawa.




One of those attending is Cold Lake First Nations Chief Kelsey Jacko.




“A lot of conflict has happened,” he says of discussions over who would attend. “I know AFN is going to have a lot of seats in the house. Those seats should be filled with rights holders, you know, but this is a step in the right direction,” Jacko said in an interview with 

APTN News

.




“That’s the reason why I’m going there because nobody is going to be speaking for me, for our rights or for our people.”




Jacko said he understands why Onion Lake Cree Nation and two other First Nations, Tsuut’ina and Saddle Lake Cree Nation have issued a cease and desist notice to the AFN because they speak on their own behalf.




“And a lot of people are left out of the room, and I imagine a lot of other Nations feel the same way,” he said.




AFN election in Edmonton 




Jacko said the AFN election for national chief will be next year in Edmonton and Alberta chiefs are frustrated even with how that is set up.




“Because here in Alberta, we only got 48 votes, and B.C. and Ontario (First Nations) each have over 200 votes. And when you talk about treaty rights, some of these nations in B.C. didn’t sign the treaty. So, it’s very conflicting,” Jacko said.




Jacko also questions how beneficial the Ottawa meeting will be for First Nations in Alberta because Premier Danielle Smith has not confirmed her attendance either in person or virtually.




“And, we’re still in court with her,” Jacko said.




Cold Lake First Nations filed a Federal Court judicial review challenging Canada’s designation of the Pacific Link pipeline under the 

Building Canada Act

. The community was left out of consultation prior to the designation. It is also seeking clear impact assessments, and a substantial equity stake in the pipeline.




Cease and desist




Onion Lake Cree Nation

 issued a cease and desist letter demanding the “AFN refrain from speaking, negotiating or consenting on our behalf at the October 26 First Nations-First Ministers’ Meeting.”




“For us, we are participating (instead)in this National Day of Action alongside other nations in defense of our inherent, treaty and constitutional rights,” Okimaw Pete Chief says in an interview with APTN.




Onion Lake maintains that “the AFN does not represent, speak for, or hold any authority or agency on behalf of OLCN.”




“You are therefore directed to cease and desist immediately from making such representation and acting, or purporting to act, on behalf of OLCN,” the letter to the AFN says.




“The cease and desist notice is the formal assertion of our Nation’s independence and authority,” Chief says.




The Cree Nation, which straddles the Alberta-Saskatchewn border in Treaty 6 territory north of Lloydminster is an independent Nation.




“Our people voted to withdraw from AFN, and that decision must be respected. No meeting outcome, declaration or agreement may be presented as binding OLCN or carrying our consent,” Chief says.




“We will defend our rights, lands and waters for our people and future generations, including pursuing legal remedies where necessary,” Chief continues.




Onion Lake, alongside chiefs of Saddle Lake Cree Nation and Tsuut’ina Nation had earlier released an open letter addressed to fellow chiefs, leaders, Elders and other citizens in a call to action, similar to the 

Idle No More movement.




“Join us in peaceful gatherings, community meetings, teach-ins and public action in Ottawa on October 26 and in y(our) territories,” the letter urges.




“Let us be clear. We have not authorized the Assembly of First Nations, Regional Chiefs, selected representatives or any other organization to negotiate, make commitments or give consent on behalf of our Nations,” their letter emphasizes.




“Whatever the outcome, no declaration, agreement, document or decision adopted or signed at this meeting shall not apply to or bind the undersigned Nations, or alter, diminish or prejudice our inherent rights…”




The AFN National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak touted the gathering during the July 2026 Annual General Assembly (AGA) in Ottawa, saying the long-awaited forum would mark the first formal high-level forum between First Nations leadership, provincial/territorial Premiers, and the Prime Minister in several decades.




The forum is on Monday on unceded Algonquin Territory in Ottawa, however it will be preceded by a day for ceremony for First Nations.




Chief says Danielle Smith’s potential absence definitely sends a message to Canada.




“But again we want to send that message to the federal government, the AFN, and all Canadians that the independence, the authority and the treaty rights of individual First Nations must be respected. And this would be the same message to all levels of government including hers,” Chief says.







Read more:




AFN draft for upcoming meeting with prime minister, premiers, calls for a First Nations-controlled wealth fund




Few details released as First Nations–First Ministers meeting approaches







Chief says the AFN responded to their letter and the organization again shared that the purpose of the meeting was to establish a political dialogue between Canada and First Nations on a wide variety of shared interests.




Onion Lake has so far not initiated any court action against the AFN.

title: The Ahmedabad Reading Controversy and the Freedom to Read
content:
Who gets to decide what we should read? The question arose sharply in Ahmedabad this August, when two books were removed from a school reading list, and a silent reading session was later disrupted.

In August, an Ahmedabad school removed Malala Yousafzai’s I Am Malala and Anne Frank’s The Diary of a Young Girl from its reading list after objections from some parents and protests involving right-wing organisations. Later that month, a silent reading session organised in Vastrapur was reportedly disrupted by a group claiming affiliation with the Vishwa Hindu Parishad and Bajrang Dal. The gathering included students, lawyers, media professionals and others. The reading itself became the object of confrontation.

I Am Malala is the memoir of a girl who survived an assassination attempt after publicly advocating girls’ right to education. The Diary of a Young Girl records the experiences of a Jewish teenager hiding from Nazi persecution before Anne Frank died during the Holocaust. Whatever one thinks of Malala’s political views, or of the ways her story is interpreted, reading her memoir does not require accepting every view she holds. Anne Frank’s diary similarly allows readers to encounter the testimony of a young person caught inside one of history’s greatest crimes.

A book is not a political membership card.

Reading allows a person to encounter an argument without accepting it. A reader can examine its evidence, question its assumptions and reject its conclusions. The point is that judgement becomes possible through encounter.

Education is often described as the transmission of knowledge. But knowledge without the capacity to question it can become another form of conformity.

This question of who may read and what they may encounter carries a specific weight in the Indian context. For much of India’s history, access to formal education was deeply shaped by caste hierarchy. Ambedkar wrote that under the Chaturvarna system, the right to education was assigned to the Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas, while Shudras were denied it. He also discussed the denial of education to women. The control of education was therefore connected to the wider system of graded inequality that Ambedkar analysed.

This was one of the structures challenged by Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule. Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848, and Phule later set up schools for the Mahars and Mangs. In his 1882 testimony before the Education Commission, Phule criticised the concentration of education among the higher classes and called for a wider spread of primary and female education. His educational work treated access to knowledge as a social question rather than a privilege confined to a small section of society.

Dr B.R. Ambedkar’s conception of democracy makes this problem especially important. In Annihilation of Caste, he imagined an ideal society with “varied and free points of contact with other modes of association” and described democracy as “a mode of associated living.” For Ambedkar, fraternity was not sameness. It required people to participate in a common social world despite their differences. His writings on the Depressed Classes emerged from a context in which these communities faced restrictions on access to public wells and schools, and were subjected to social segregation and prescribed occupations. The “associated living” he imagined presupposes that those who were once excluded from classrooms are now full participants in the world of ideas.

A democratic society cannot expect citizens to form independent judgements while continually narrowing the range of ideas they are permitted to encounter. The democratic reader needs the freedom to examine an argument before deciding whether it deserves acceptance, rejection or further examination.

John Dewey understood education as inseparable from democratic life. For Dewey, democracy depended on communication, inquiry and shared experience. He saw education as a way of preparing people to participate intelligently in common life.

Not every book belongs in every classroom. Parents can question reading lists, teachers can challenge texts, and schools can make decisions about age, pedagogy and context. Citizens can protest. A democratic society must leave room for disagreement over education. The important distinction is between arguing that a book should not be taught and intimidating people who choose to read it. The first concerns the content and place of a text in education. The second makes the act of reading itself a political offence.

Contemporary concerns about caste discrimination in higher education, including its relationship to student distress and suicides, remain serious enough to have been examined by the Supreme Court-appointed National Task Force on student mental health and suicides.

The harder democratic principle is to defend the reader’s freedom even when we dislike the book being read. Otherwise, “intellectual freedom” simply becomes another name for allowing ideas with which we already agree.

This is why the Ahmedabad episode matters beyond the two books involved. The deeper question is who gets to decide what a citizen may encounter before that citizen has had the opportunity to form a judgement.

Once reading itself becomes evidence of political allegiance, we begin judging the person who has chosen to read a book rather than only the ideas within it. “What does this book say?” becomes “What does reading this book say about you?” The reader is then placed on trial alongside the ideas in the book.

A society that makes the second question more important than the first risks producing citizens who know which ideas belong to their side but have little opportunity to examine ideas outside that boundary.

The people who gathered for the silent reading session in Vastrapur had come to read. They were exercising their judgement through the simple act of sitting with books.

A democratic citizen should be free to encounter an idea, question it, and decide what to make of it. In India, defending that freedom is inseparable from defending the right of readers from the Depressed Classes and other communities historically excluded from education to full and equal access to the world of texts.

Rajat Kanti Satpati is an author of several books. His writing has appeared in SteinbeckNow, People’s Daily, and other publications.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: ‘Something big is coming’: climate advocates say Bill C-39 is a new version of an old issue
content:
First Nations activists say a federal bill approaching its third reading will fast-track environmental impacts that Indigenous communities have already been feeling for decades — with the same lack of consent.




Michel Koostachin, founder of Indigenous-led advocacy group 

Friends of the Attawapiskat River

, said that prophecies are a part of many First Nations cultures and he viewed the bill as that.




“There was an Elder that spoke about what was coming to us as First Nations. If you look at this legislation… he said that there’s something big coming, something that has no ears, no brain, no eyes, no mouth, no legs, no feet, no hands. And that’s that legislation,” Kootstachin said.




“You know, bulldozing the environment without primary informed consent, which is our Indigenous right, and contaminating the environment.”




Bill C-39, the 

Building Canada Strong Act

,

 is currently being studied by a special committee in the House of Commons, and pre-studied by the Senate.




If passed, the law would aim to expand on the government’s “one-project, one-review, within one-year approach” to major projects, such as mines and ports, that are predicted to have a positive effect on Canada’s economy.




Bill C-5, the 

Building Canada Act

,

 passed in 2025, introduced “projects of national interest,” which gives ministers the authority to fast-track major projects if they meet certain criteria.




According to the Major Projects Office set up to deal with proposed infrastructure, a project must “strengthen Canada’s autonomy, resilience, and security”; “provide economic or other benefits”; “advance the interests of Indigenous Peoples”; and “contribute to clean growth and to meeting Canada’s climate change objectives.”




If a project presents a case that aligns with those guidelines, it may be exempt from permits pertaining to different laws, such as the 

Species at Risk

 and 

Heritage

 Acts.




However, several First Nation governments, advocates and environmentalists have raised the concern that these projects of national interest do not align with their own criteria — specifically, advancing the interests of Indigenous Peoples and contributing to clean growth — due to the bill’s implications for the environment, as well as inherent and Treaty rights.




On Wednesday, 56 scientist fellows from the Royal Society of Canada 

published an open letter

 “concerning environmental stewardship and the proposed 

Building Canada Strong Act.

”




Among other points, the letter recommended that “additional time may be required to evaluate less harmful alternatives and impacts not yet studied by the proponents,” and to remove the “concentration of power” from a single minister “to dismiss conditions for permits and Impact Assessments.




“This is an extraordinary power,” the scientists wrote, “with potentially far-reaching consequences for the environment.”




They said that they “fully agree” with the goal of creating economic growth while protecting the environment, referencing Canada’s Force of Nature announcement, which included adding protective environmental measures when it came to the development of large-scale projects.




“As written, however, Bill C-39 countermands the environmental protections currently in place in Canadian law, laws written to avoid irreparable harms to species, ecosystems, natural resources, and human wellbeing and health,” the letter continued. “We call upon the House and Senate to uphold these laws and to consider our recommendations for the benefit of nature, Canadians, and the rest of the world.”




Webequie First Nation, approximately 60 km from the Ring of Fire mineral deposit in the James Bay lowlands of northern Ontario, is seen from the air in 2025. Photo: Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press.







Koostachin said that the bill is part of a larger issue of projects being approved without consent from First Nations.




This was in response to Ottawa’s announcement to invest $1 billion in the construction of the 

Webequie Supply Road

, an all-season gravel road into the Ring of Fire, a mineral-rich section of the James Bay Lowlands.




Currently, the Ring of Fire is only accessible by ice road or plane, and James Bay, more than 68,000 square kilometres and holding approximately 30 billion tonnes of carbon — is largely untouched.




The investment was only one line in a larger announcement about a “new action plan to protect workers from tariffs and strengthen Ontario industries,” done in collaboration with the provincial government.




While this project was not labelled a project of national interest, the beginning of construction was fast-tracked and began 10 years early because of a partnership with Webequie and Marten Falls First Nations.




Attawapiskat First Nation had not given consent for the project to be developed on their lands, Koostachin said, adding that he learnt about the new funding at the same time as everyone else.




He said his community still deals with a lack of safe drinking water due to an influx of mercury sent downstream by the 

Victor Diamond Mine

, which closed in 2019.




In order to mine in the Ring of Fire, the government will need to dewater areas of swamp in the James Bay peatlands, which essentially acts as a filter for any water sent downstream, Koostachin explained.




He added that fast-tracking the road also fast-tracks poisoning water that, according to the 

United Nations Water Strategy 2030

, should be safely maintained by a deadline coming up in only four years.




“So that billion dollars that were issued to fast-track, how come we don’t fast-track our water treatment?” he said.




When it comes to Bill C-39, his worries around consultation are the same.




“People don’t know what’s going on,” he said, “or they don’t know until the day after. That’s why it’s important to keep track of what’s being introduced, you know? The legislation itself, there’s no hearings for the public to make comments. And even though they have to pass those bills with the third reading, when are we given the opportunity to have a say?”




The Town of Churchill, Man. Photo: Charlotte Moritt-Jacobs/APTN.







Ramon Kataquapit, a member of Attawapiskat First Nation and co-founder of the 

Okinawak Youth Movement

, said that, “When we have a nation like Canada, pushing for mineral extraction, they often end up on the other side from where we are.”




“The Ring of Fire is going to be one of the biggest projects of North America,” he said, and instead of consulting with communities, the government is “cutting the red tape as fast as possible.




“There’s a bad precedent being set here, and our First Nations can really attest to that.”




Kataquapit was part of the 

Arctic Crossroads Tour

, a series of speaking events led by climate activist Clayton Thomas-Müller and a panel of youth activists, which began in Churchill, Man., and wrapped up in Winnipeg on Oct. 23.




“This is a very, very shady process,” Thomas-Müller said, referring to Bill C-39 and Bill C-5.




The event’s key message was, through sharing knowledge from advocates based in Ontario and British Columbia, that the large-scale infrastructure projects that handle liquefied natural gas are connected, including the 

Port of Churchill

, the 

Pacific Link Pipeline

, and the 

Robert Banks Terminal 2

 port expansion.




“We came here because we know what it’s like to fight the oil and gas industry,” said Denzel Sutherland-Wilson, a member of Gitxsan Nation, who has been advocating against the proposed 

Prince Rupert Gas Transmission project

 in southern B.C.




“We all have the same issues,” he said, reflecting on Manitoba, adding that “consent” and “consulting” in terms of legislation is a “relatively new thing.




“We just see the same narratives, the same dismissal of Indigenous systems and jurisdictions,” he said.




James Bay is located on the south end of the Hudson Bay, which connects the peatlands to northern Manitoba.




Hudson Bay is an anomaly, Thomas-Müller said, as the deepest part is only 30 metres, which makes it a perfect place for beluga whales to give birth.




The member of Mathias Colomb First Nation said that, because of the Port of Churchill expansion, wildlife, including the belugas and polar bears, which the Town of Churchill is known for, is “at risk.”







Read more:




First Nations oppose proposed ‘one-year, one-project’ bill following its first vote




Proposed federal law attacks environment, ‘stomps on’ leadership, says youth




Friends of the Attawapiskat River file for judicial review over road to the Ring of Fire







“When we think of environmental racism in Canada, it’s a very red and white issue … by far and large, Indigenous peoples pay the heftiest price, especially in moments like this,” Thomas-Müller said. “None of these are new ideas; it’s the same old climate criminals repackaging old ideas, for profit at the expense of these communities.




“At every part of the distribution of the oil gas sector,” he continued, “there are incredible impacts to communities, to water, to the climate, to the environment itself,” and those impacts “fall on the shoulders of Indigenous Peoples.”




Thomas-Müller said that he wanted “to make sure that our people knew what they’re being asked to consent to, that our people understand the many layers of geopoliticalness.”




A National Day of Action

 is planned for Monday, which coincides with the 

First Nations-First Ministers Meeting (FNFM)

 in Ottawa.




While the event will be a rally, Koostachin said he hoped that the public understands that “we’re not protesters, we’re protectors.”




APTN News reached out to the office of the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources for comment and will update the story if a response is received.




The post 

‘Something big is coming’: climate advocates say Bill C-39 is a new version of an old issue

 appeared first on 

APTN News

.

title: DEM Parti'den “Ekmek, barış ve adalet için bütçe” çağrısı
content:
İstanbul - DEM Parti, 2027 yılı Merkezi Yönetim Bütçe Kanunu Teklifi görüşmelerine ilişkin bir video paylaştı. Videoda, “Fedakarlık değil, adil bölüşüm; yoksulluk değil, insanca yaşam istiyoruz. Ekmek, barış ve adalet için bütçe istiyoruz” ifadelerine yer verildi.

Yapay zekâyla hazırlanan videoda ücretler, emekli maaşları, vergi politikaları, eğitim ve sağlık harcamalarına ilişkin eleştiriler dile getirilerek adil bölüşüm çağrısı yapıldı.

Videonun seslendirmesinde şu ifadelere yer verildi:

“Gece gündüz çalışıyoruz ama insanca yaşayacak bir ücret alamıyoruz. Asgari ücret yetmiyor. Emekli maaşları, temel ihtiyaçları bile karşılamıyor. Kiramızı ödeyemiyor, kredi kartı faizlerini dahi karşılayamıyoruz. Çocuklarımıza ücretsiz okul yemeği verilmezken eğitim ve sağlık giderek pahalanıyor. Çünkü iktidarın önceliği emekçiler değil, sermayenin çıkarları.

Çiftçi ve esnaf borç içinde boğuluyor. Biz daha ücretimizi almadan vergi kesilirken sermayeye milyarlarca muafiyet ve teşvik veriliyor. Vurguncuların ceremesi yeni vergilerle halka yükleniyor. Borçlanmadan yaşayacak gelir ve adil vergilendirme istiyoruz.

“Kaynakların savaşa değil yaşama ayrılmasını istiyoruz”

Eşit yurttaşlık, demokratik haklar, kadın özgürlüğü, ana dilinde eğitim ve sağlık hakkı için kaynakların savaşa değil yaşama ayrılmasını istiyoruz. Fedakarlık değil, adil bölüşüm; yoksulluk değil, insanca yaşam istiyoruz. Ekmek, barış ve adalet için bütçe istiyoruz.”

DEM Parti, sosyal medya hesabından 2027 yılı bütçesine ilişkin taleplerin dile getirildiği bir video yayımladı. Paylaşımda, “Ekmek, barış ve adalet için bütçe. Hepimiz için yarın başlıyoruz.” ifadeleri kullanıldı https://t.co/PaLletydkr https://t.co/txdAvoUnLr

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Car Crash Plot on Comedian Shows Increasing Violence of China’s Transnational Repression
content:
FIVE MEN WERE indicted earlier this week over a plot to run down stand-up comic Huang Yi-hao, in retribution for a comedy show in which Huang mocked Chinese president Xi Jinping.

The five men slammed into Huang with a car, injuring his pelvis, after being ordered to hurt Huang enough to hospitalize him. Subsequently, they acted as though the incident was an accident and assisted Huang with an insurance claim. They then forwarded the picture of the insurance documentation to their handler, a Chinese man referred to in media reporting as K., who refused to pay them the full 450,000 NT promised because Huang was not injured sufficiently.

News of the plot to attack Huang follows suit from the indictment of two men over a May attack on a comedy club where Huang was performing, during which the comedy club had a mixture of feces and paint thrown at its entrance. A 35-year-old man surnamed Kuo was reportedly paid 50,000 NT by a 33-year-old man surnamed Liu to carry out the attack. It is unclear whether the two were acting at China’s behest. The incident was not widely known before the indictment.

Since news of the plot broke, there have been calls to strengthen national security laws to deal with Chinese threats. In particular, the attack on the comedy club and the plot to run down Huang highlight China’s growing transnational repression within Taiwan itself.

It can be seen that there are several recurring tactics used by China when it comes to transnational repression. For example, attacks with feces and paint have occurred on several occasions. In 2020, Hong Kong pro-democracy singer Denise Ho and bookstore owner and publisher Lam Wing-kee, one of the Causeway Bay booksellers, were splashed with red paint by attackers. Some of these attackers were linked to Taiwanese pro-China organized crime groups such as the Bamboo Union gang.

Likewise, the same year, Aegis, a restaurant that assisted Hongkongers seeking refuge in Taiwan, was splashed with chicken feces by men who were paid by a Chinese national to carry out the act.

Earlier this year, a gym owned by a pro-democracy Hongkonger who had previously stood as an electoral candidate was splashed with red paint by two individuals who arrived from Hong Kong. The two individuals departed back to Hong Kong before they could be caught.

Nor would this be the only case in which China has apparently flown individuals to Taiwan to carry out actions that they try to quickly flee from in short order. This was also the case when political commentator Akio Yaita was attacked in a Taichung hotel where Yaita was giving a speech, with the individual in question having been flown in for the attack from Hong Kong, and subsequently attempting to flee abroad. The use of Taiwanese and Hongkongers, or Chinese nationals with Hong Kong passports, for such attacks, however, allows for plausible deniability that avoids being directly traced back to the Chinese government.

In other cases, China simply hires Taiwanese individuals to carry out such attacks, as occurred with Huang. But the attack on Akio Yaita, as well as the attempted ramming of Huang Yi-hao, shows that the level of violence of China’s transnational repression directed at critics may be increasing. Indeed, one notes that in 2025, news broke of a plot by the Chinese military attaché in Prague to ram a vehicle into the motorcade of Hsiao Bi-khim during a visit to the city, during a period when Hsiao was the vice president-elect. The plot could have been construed as either an act of intimidation or even an assassination attempt.

Presumably, the aim with such acts as the car crash plot against Huang would be to depict the Chinese government’s reach as inescapable and penetrating deep into Taiwan, meting out retribution for even simply making fun of the Chinese leader. Still, it is possible that such actions ultimately end up pushing Taiwanese further away from China, in showing the dangers of unification, rather than cowing Taiwanese into submission.

author: rti_admin
title: The Questions of Milinda: Publisher’s Note on Navayana Edition
content:
A river remains alive only so long as fresh water continues to flow through it. The same principle applies to language. Language is never static; it evolves with time. Its vocabulary, sentence structure, and modes of expression continually change. Whether one considers Hindi, English, or any other language, it becomes evident that literature written in the nineteenth century is often difficult for contemporary readers to approach without assistance.

For this reason, responsible publishers of classical literature frequently present ancient works in a renewed form, adapting their language, style, and presentation to the needs of modern readers. Such efforts enable timeless ideas to remain accessible to new generations.

When we turn to Buddhist literature, however, we find that relatively little attention has been given to this task. Many texts continue to be published in styles that remain largely unchanged from earlier translations. Regrettably, this has contributed to an increasing distance between younger readers and the rich intellectual heritage of Buddhism.

One remarkable work that has suffered from this situation is the Milinda Pañha (Questions of King Milinda). This extraordinary text preserves a series of profound dialogues between King Milinda and Venerable Nāgasena, offering readers an accessible gateway into the heart of Buddhist philosophy through reasoned inquiry and debate.

Today, this book can be found in many Buddhist households across India. Yet experience suggests that, although it occupies a place of honour on many bookshelves, it is seldom read in its entirety. Many readers begin it with enthusiasm but fail to complete it. This is not mere excuse-making; it is a practical reality. The difficulty arises largely from an archaic style of translation and a language that often feels distant from contemporary readers.

As publishers, we felt it insufficient merely to lament this situation. Instead, we resolved to seek a constructive solution. Our volume, The Questions of Milinda: Milindapañha in Navayana Perspective, represents the second step in that endeavour. The first was Navayāna Darśana: A Modern Interpretation of the Buddha’s Teachings, which presented Buddhist philosophy in a simple, rational, and contemporary style. The enthusiastic response it received, leading it nearly to go out of print, encouraged us to continue this work.

The present book is not a direct translation of the original Pāli text. Rather, it is a careful reworking based upon a comparative study of English, Hindi, and, to some extent, Marathi translations. Many existing versions contain accounts of previous births and other traditional elements that appear difficult to reconcile with modern scientific understanding and with claims concerning the rational and humanistic character of Buddhist philosophy.

In this edition, Author Ratnesh Katulkar has sought to remove such accretions and reinterpret the text through a Navayāna perspective, presenting it in a clear, modern, and accessible form for contemporary readers. Yet this undertaking presented a significant challenge. The original questions of Milinda and the replies of Nāgasena could neither be arbitrarily expanded nor fundamentally altered. How, then, could they be made more approachable?

The solution adopted was both simple and effective. The original dialogues have been preserved with only minimal modifications, mainly involving language and presentation. However, following nearly every question-and-answer exchange, explanatory sections have been added in which the discussion is interpreted afresh in the light of modern knowledge and contemporary concerns. In this way, the text has been connected to present realities while preserving the spirit of the original dialogue.

We are confident that this approach will appeal both to readers already interested in Buddhist philosophy and to newcomers seeking an accessible introduction to the Dhamma.

It is only natural, however, that some readers deeply attached to traditional interpretations and inherited assumptions may not feel entirely comfortable with this presentation. Any attempt to revisit established traditions is often met with resistance. Yet the Buddha’s path itself is one of inquiry, reflection, and continuous investigation. Following the spirit of the Kālāma Sutta, it encourages individuals to examine truth for themselves rather than accept doctrines solely based on authority or tradition.

Our purpose is not to provoke those committed to conventional views, but to ensure that younger generations become active participants in the Buddhist intellectual heritage. For that reason, it is perhaps best to pay little attention to reactionary criticism. Navayāna, after all, resembles an elephant that continues steadily on its path without being distracted by passing noises. This book is simply another step in that journey.

History repeatedly demonstrates that every significant intellectual and social transformation faced opposition in its own time. Yet it is often these very transformations that later shape the course of human civilisation. Generations afterwards, historians frequently look back with surprise at the resistance such movements encountered.

Navayāna is part of that continuing tradition of renewal. The flame first kindled by the Buddha illuminated vast regions of the world in the age of Emperor Aśoka. Though dimmed during periods of decline and reaction, it was rekindled in modern times by figures such as P. Lakshmi Narasu, Dharmanand Kosambi, and Dr B. R. Ambedkar, inspiring countless thinkers and reformers across the world. Each of these individuals encountered hostility from conservative circles; therefore, criticism of our own efforts should come as no surprise. Indeed, our author often remarks that a positive mind can transform even hostility and irritation into a source of strength and motivation.

This book was not written in isolation. The entire manuscript was taught and discussed online with students over an extended period. Every dialogue, criticism, observation, and suggestion emerging from those discussions was carefully considered and incorporated where appropriate. The final text was subsequently reviewed and approved by the wider Navayāna study group. Consequently, this volume should not be viewed merely as the private opinion of its author. It is, rather, a collective expression shaped through dialogue, study, reflection, and collaboration among the students of Navayāna. We sincerely hope that readers will find it worthy of their expectations.

We humbly request all readers to share their reflections, suggestions, and critical assessments after reading this book. Your thoughtful responses will guide and inspire our future work.

Book Title: The Questions of Milinda: Milindapañha in Navayana Perspective

Publisher: Navayana Prakashan, Nasik

author: Cooper Quintin
title: The Vulnerability Apocalypse and Why We Should Fund Open Source
content:
If you use the internet at all, you may have noticed that a large percentage of sites suddenly went down earlier this week

—

and all your nerdiest friends were talking about "The Vulnerability Apocalypse” and this thing called PHP that 

powers nearly 70% of the websites on the internet

. You may find yourself wondering: what is PHP, what just happened, what is the vulnerability apocalypse, and what do I need to do? 

 




To find out what you can personally do read the 

first blog post

 in this series! 

 




What Is PHP? 

 




PHP is a programming language used mainly to create interactive websites. Facebook, Wordpress, Wikipedia, Etsy, and other major sites all use or were originally built on PHP. It is a long-established mainstay of web development. But because it is open-source, maintenance of these critical systems depends on a small number of volunteers working on this in their free time. The disaster scenario that happened this past week is the perfect example of why we need more money and people supporting open-source projects. Corporations should be contributing both.

 




What Is the Vulnerability Apocalypse? 

 




Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) are the way that security professionals file reports about vulnerabilities in software. The 

National Vulnerability Database

 (NVD), run by NIST, is the official national database of CVEs. In other words, CVE reports managed by NIST are the closest thing we have to a canonical database of security vulnerabilities in software. The NVD currently has around 400,000 CVEs that have been filed and accepted since 1988. In just the month of October, 13,000 new CVEs have been submitted. This means that 3% of critical software security bugs that have ever been officially logged were found in the last month alone. And it's likely that by the end of the year over a quarter of the software vulnerabilities that have ever been found will be from 2026. 

 




 

Computer vulnerabilities reported are rising exponentially. Source: CVE Tracker




This research is being driven almost entirely by the cybersecurity capabilities of major AI models from companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. Historically it has been popularly assumed by cybersecurity experts that finding unknown (zero-day) exploits in any specific project and turning them into exploits was expensive. The knowledge to discover them was not widespread, and it was a hard task even for those initiated into the arcane ways of vulnerability hunting. Google even dedicated 

an entire team to it

. 

 




But now thanks to major AI models, vulnerabilities are cheap, and anyone of moderate technical skill with a few dollars and access to a frontier AI model can find vulnerabilities in a few minutes. For example, recent vulnerabilities in PHP were found with a prompt to an AI model that literally said "

find bad vulnerabilities in PHP

." 

 




What Happened This Week?

 




In 2024, a potentially severe vulnerability in PHP was 

discovered during an external security audit

. PHP’s maintainers couldn’t agree on a solution, but more importantly, they couldn’t find a way to exploit the vulnerability. Because it didn’t seem like an active threat, they ended up deprioritizing a fix in favor of working on more urgent security issues. Then, in August 2026, security researchers working with the latest models from OpenAI and Anthropic independently discovered the vulnerability again, and another one

—

and now, with a way to exploit them. 

 




We now know that the vulnerabilities 

were so severe that they would have allowed even moderately inventive hackers to take over any website that uses PHP and then steal customer data, launch further malware attacks, spy on users, take websites offline, or launch a massive denial of service attack.

[

1

]

 




Because of the severity of these vulnerabilities, several of the involved researchers got together with the makers of PHP to patch the vulnerabilities and disclose them in a coordinated manner. The idea was that hopefully everyone would get a chance to quietly release and then apply fixes for the vulnerabilities before the whole world found out about it.

 




But news already started to leak on October 20th. There was a 

post on a widely read forum

 “Hacker News” and other posts elsewhere. One of the researchers accidentally published a video early. Companies reported seeing active exploitation of the vulnerabilities going back as far as October 17th. On October 21st, six hours before the planned press embargo, one company, 

Chainguard, jumped the gun and released a patch early,

 essentially giving anyone instructions about exactly where to find the vulnerabilities and how to weaponize them. This sent system administrators everywhere scrambling to patch their systems before they were taken over by hackers. And it’s going to take a long time to patch all these systems. At the time of this writing over 33 million websites are 

still running on vulnerable versions of PHP

. 

 




The internet is run largely on open-source software, mostly maintained by a small handful of skilled volunteers occasionally getting a small stipend, not by major corporations and highly paid engineers. These are projects you have perhaps never heard of, like PHP, OpenSSL, and SQLite, but these programs run on nearly every computer in the world and are maintained by teams as small as one person. When a vulnerability is found in these projects, it can be devastating. 

 




PHP isn’t the only critical open-source software with a high severity vulnerability this week either. Other widespread open-source projects like Node.js and GitLab also had severe security bugs reported. 

 




The small number of already overworked open-source maintainers are now facing a deluge of vulnerability reports, some of which are false, but many of which are very real. 

Burnout in open source has never been higher

. 

 




We Need Stronger Support for Open Source Projects




Much of the foundation for the modern multibillion-dollar internet industry is built on open-source products that were created and still maintained

—

for free

—

by dedicated volunteers in their spare time. It’s an imperfect system, and it can lead to errors. 

 




One of those critical, under resourced open-source products is PHP. And while vulnerabilities in PHP were privately found years ago, they were left unfixed because they didn’t seem as impactful as other bugs at the time. These same vulnerabilities were recently rediscovered and proved to be trivially exploitable by security researchers using advanced AI models. While in the middle of the widespread, global effort to correct this mistake and deploy fixes, the problem was leaked by some of the security researchers who had gotten early access to the fixes. Unfortunately, this left millions of websites, ranging from personal blogs to government sites, vulnerable to hacking that could result in data theft, malware distribution, and worse. 

 




Open-source projects like PHP and others are the backbone of the entire internet. If they don’t get the resources they need, they and the internet they power, are at risk of falling apart. Corporations (whose products would not exist without these products) should be actively contributing to their maintenance.

 




1. A technical analysis of the vulnerabilities is out of scope for this post and has already been 

written by the original researchers

.

author: India McKinney
title: Computer Security Is About to Get a Lot Worse, Here’s What You Can Do
content:
It is a commonly held truth among computer geeks that there is no such thing as bug free software, or a secure computer. Any piece of software that anyone actually uses 

will have a security vulnerability somewhere in the code

. The more complex that software is, the more likely there will be a vulnerability. Fortunately for everyone, finding severe vulnerabilities was generally considered an expensive and difficult task requiring years of training and deep knowledge of how computers and software worked. Until recently there was a steady background hum of vulnerabilities being found and patched, with major vulnerabilities that could cripple the entire internet only happening every few years. Now that is no longer the case. 

 




You may have noticed your nerdiest friends freaking out about the “Vulnerability Apocalypse” this week and waving their arms in panic about something called PHP. You may have also noticed that some of your favorite websites were down for a bit. In the last two weeks of October alone, there have been multiple, potentially internet-breaking vulnerabilities reported and patched. Many of those vulnerabilities were in the open-source software that is the foundation of the vast majority of the internet. 




For more detailed information on what happened, and why supporting open-source projects matters, 

check out our other blog

.




This is all because frontier AI models, such as those created by OpenAI, Anthropic, and others, have made it incredibly cheap and easy to find previously unknown vulnerabilities (zero-days) in open- and closed-source code. 

Three percent of all software vulnerabilities ever found in history were found just in the month of October. This year alone researchers have found nearly a quarter of all software security issues which have ever been discovered.

 




If exploiting critical software is now cheaper and easier than ever, what does that mean for us as individuals and what does that mean for society as a whole? 

TL; DR

: It’s going to get worse before it gets better. But you can protect yourself with basic digital security hygiene that is now more important than ever. 

 




What Do I Need to Do?

 




There absolutely needs to be a bigger conversation about how we got here and how to fix the systemic issues involved, including how corporations that depend on open-source code should contribute to their upkeep, and how big tech should be regulated. 

 




But for now, this news is a compelling reason to tighten up your digital hygiene. 

A lot of computers are going to get hacked a lot more often, and unfortunately, it isn’t going to get better any time soon. 

Thankfully, EFF has compiled a comprehensive set of security advice in 

our Surveillance Self-Defense guides

.

 

To start

, 

we recommend making sure your browser and all applications are 

always up to date

 with the latest patches.  

 




You should also consider installing a tracker blocking tool, like EFF’s 

Privacy Badger (now on Safari),

 and remain vigilant for 

phishing attempts

. Additionally, 

install a password manager

 and 

use unique passwords

 for each website, so that if one site is compromised, the rest of your passwords are safe. You should also be aware that 

data breaches

 may now be more likely, and the websites you visit may experience more attacks than usual, which means that some services may be disrupted. 

 




If you host a blog or other website, make sure that either you or your hosting provider has 

patched

 this particular issue. 

 




For additional tips on protecting yourself and others, head over to our 

Surveillance Self-Defense site

. Additionally, if you’d like to support any of EFF’s open-source projects like 

Privacy Badger

, 

Rayhunter

, and 

Certbot

, visit our 

donate page

.

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: ‘Release tortured Mangyan organizer’
content:
“He needs immediate medical attention for injuries and trauma allegedly sustained during his detention.”

Indigenous Mangyan farmer and organizer Miguel Magbata was reportedly beaten and tortured while in military custody after his arrest in Bulalacao, Oriental Mindoro, on October 14, prompting human rights groups to call for his immediate release and to hold accountable those responsible.

According to Karapatan Southern Tagalog, Magbata was arrested after a reported armed encounter between the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and alleged New People’s Army (NPA) members in Sitio Badyang, Barangay San Roque in Bulalacao. He was reportedly subjected to physical abuse and interrogation by the 1st Infantry Battalion (IB) under the command of the 203rd Infantry Brigade (IBde).

After days of uncertainty over his whereabouts, reports emerged that Magbata was transferred to Roxas Municipal Police Station. Defend Mindoro said that he needs immediate medical attention for injuries and trauma allegedly sustained during his detention.

The group also raised concerns over a Facebook post from 203rd Infantry Brigade of Philippine Army about Magbata’s children and family, published without their consent, which it said could compromise their safety.

Despite his reported transfer to police custody, the military reportedly sought to retain custody of Magbata. Defend Mindoro demanded his immediate release and called for accountability from the 203rd IBde led by Brig. Gen. Melencio Ragudo, and the 1st IB, under Lt. Col. Edwin Mirador.

Defend Mindoro said that Magbata’s case shows a pattern of harassment and abuses against Indigenous Peoples, farmers, and community organizers in Mindoro where those asserting their rights are often accused of links to the communist armed movement.

The group cited the killings of Indigenous and peasant individuals Jay-el Maligday, Hulyo Agtay, and Juan Sumilhig which it attributed to military abuses. It also stressed the case of Dolores Solangon, an elderly Mangyan-Iraya woman who reportedly endured illegal arrest and nine hours of torture at the hands of elements from the 76th IB.

Maligday, a young Hanunuo-Mangyan, was allegedly killed by soldiers of the 4th IB while sleeping in his home. The same unit was accused of beating another Hanunuo-Mangyan, Minggo, in Mansalay early this year.

For Defend Mindoro, these abuses are inseparable from the land disputes and economic hardships confronting Indigenous communities and farmers.

In Bulalacao, the group said that large-scale mining and renewable energy projects threaten ancestral lands and local livelihoods. These include developments associated with CleanTech Global Renewables and Singapore-based The Blue Circle which is reportedly planning an offshore wind project involving 100 turbines across a proposed 40,050-hectare area.

Meanwhile, drought has exacerbated the farmers’ hardship. In 2024, an estimated 864 hectares of farmland in Bulalacao were damaged, resulting in P87 million (US$1.37 million) in agricultural losses and affecting around 1,000 registered farmers, according to Defend Mindoro. With another severe El Niño episode looming, communities face renewed threats of crop failure and water shortage.

The group criticized the government for prioritizing counterinsurgency operations over addressing rural poverty, landlessness, and the climate crisis. It said that militarization further endangers communities already struggling to protect their livelihoods and ancestral territories.

Defend Mindoro demanded an independent investigation into the allegations of torture and illegal detention. Torture is prohibited under international law and civilians must be protected from violence and cruel treatment in situations of armed conflict.

The group held the 203rd IBde and the Marcos Jr. administration accountable for the alleged violations, calling for an end to military harassment of Indigenous Peoples and farmers.

For Defend Mindoro, Magbata’s case underscores the dangers faced by community organizers defending the rights of rural communities. “No allegation of insurgency can justify torture or the denial of due process,” the group wrote in a statement. (DAA)

title: İsviçre’de aşırı sağa karşı ortak mücadele ve dayanışma çağrısı
content:
Geçtiğimiz hafta sonu İsviçre’nin Basel kentinde BastA! (Basels starke Alternative – Basel’in Güçlü Alternatifi) Tarafından düzenlenen Siyaset Evi etkinliğinde bir araya gelen toplumsal ve politik muhalefet güçleri Avrupa'da yükselen aşırı sağla mücadelede ortak politika imkânlarını harekete geçirmek konusunda görüş birliğine vardılar. 




“Faşizm, Karşı Güç ve Gelecek” başlığıyla gerçekleştirilen etkinlikte, Avrupa’da aşırı sağın yükselişi, otoriter politikaların yaygınlaşması ve bunlara karşı geliştirilebilecek ortak mücadele stratejileri ele alındı.




Konuşmaların, atölyelerin ve grup tartışmalarının gerçekleştirildiği etkinlikte, sol hareketlerin yalnızca mevcut politikalara karşı çıkmakla yetinmemesi, toplumsal sorunlara somut çözümler üreten ve gündelik yaşamda karşılık bulan dayanışma ağları oluşturması gerektiği üzerinde duruldu.




Bolliger: Sol, somut dayanışma yapıları inşa etmeli




Etkinliğin açılış konuşmasını yapan BastA! Başkanı Oliver Bolliger, artan kiralar, yükselen yaşam maliyetleri, ağır çalışma koşulları ve geleceğe ilişkin belirsizliklerin toplumun geniş kesimlerini doğrudan etkilediğine dikkat çekerek, sol hareketlerin bu sorunlar karşısında yalnızca eleştiri üretmesinin yeterli olmadığını söyledi.




Bolliger temel yönelimini çöyle özetledi:







“Kiralardaki artış, yükselen yaşam maliyetleri, stresli çalışma koşulları ve geleceğe yönelik belirsizlik, insanların günlük yaşamlarını doğrudan etkiliyor. Sol, eleştiriyle sınırlı kalmamalı. İnsanların bu sorunlarla başa çıkmalarına yardımcı olacak somut dayanışma yapıları inşa etmelidir.” 







Atölyelerde ortak mücadele yöntemleri tartışıldı




Etkinlik kapsamında düzenlenen beş atölyede feminist mücadele, iklim adaleti, demokratik konfederalizm, antifaşist sosyal politikalar, mahalle örgütlenmesi ve örgüt içi dayanışma konuları ele alındı.




Katılımcılar, farklı toplumsal mücadelelerin birbirleriyle nasıl ilişkilendirilebileceğini, ortak örgütlenme olanaklarını ve dayanışma ağlarının nasıl güçlendirilebileceğini tartıştı.




İsviçre merkezli ilerici kampanya ve dayanışma örgütü Campax’ın Genel Yöneticisi Itziar Marañón, aşırı sağa karşı mücadelenin yalnızca mevcut hak ve kazanımların korunmasıyla sınırlı kalmaması gerektiğini belirtti.




Marañón, alternatiflerin ortaya konulmasını istedi:







“Mücadelemizi mevcut kazanımları savunmakla sınırlamamalı, şiddet içermeyen ve adil bir yaşam için olumlu alternatifleri görünür kılmalıyız."







Faşizme karşı feminist stratejilerin tartışıldığı atölyede, kadın düşmanı erkeklik anlayışlarının gençler üzerindeki etkileri ve sosyal medyada cinsiyetçilikle mücadele yöntemleri değerlendirildi.




Aşırı sağa karşı mücadelede kullanılan dilin de belirleyici olduğunu vurgulayan Marañón, siyasi söylemin toplumun geniş kesimlerinin anlayabileceği ve kendi yaşam deneyimleriyle ilişkilendirebileceği bir biçimde kurulması gerektiğini söyledi.




İklim adaleti mücadelesi ve ekofaşizme karşı direniş




İklim adaleti üzerine gerçekleştirilen atölyenin sonuçlarını paylaşan Kolektif İklim Adaleti temsilcileri Zoë ve Mirjam, iklim krizi ile aşırı sağın yükselişi arasındaki ilişkiye dikkat çekti.




İklim adaleti mücadelesinin ırkçılığa, ayrımcılığa ve otoriter politikalara karşı mücadeleden ayrı düşünülemeyeceğini belirten Zoë ve Mirjam, ekofaşizme karşı örgütlü ve aktif bir direnişin gerekli olduğunu vurguladı.




Atölyede, büyük teknoloji şirketlerinin çevresel ve toplumsal etkileri de tartışıldı. Bu şirketlerin yüksek enerji tüketiminin yanı sıra gözetim ve denetim mekanizmaları aracılığıyla otoriter eğilimleri güçlendirdiği ifade edildi.




Katılımcılar, ekolojik krize karşı mücadelenin yalnızca çevrenin korunmasıyla sınırlı tutulamayacağını, toplumsal eşitsizlikler ve otoriterleşmeyle birlikte ele alınması gerektiğini belirtti.




Demokratik konfederalizm ve mahallelerde öz örgütlenme




Ronahî Kadın Konseyi adına değerlendirme oturumuna katılan Özen Aytaç, yerel örgütlenmenin, toplumsal katılımın ve mahallelerde kurulan dayanışma ilişkilerinin önemine dikkat çekti.




Suriye ve Rojava’daki demokratik konfederalizm deneyimlerinden örnekler veren Aytaç, özellikle kriz dönemlerinde insanların yaşadıkları mahallelerde örgütlenmesinin ve ortak karar alma mekanizmaları oluşturmasının önemini vurguladı.




Mahalle örgütlenmesinin yalnızca benzer siyasi görüşlere sahip kişileri bir araya getirmekle sınırlı kalmaması gerektiğini belirten Aytaç, gündelik yaşamda kurulan ilişkilerin uzun vadeli ve sürdürülebilir dayanışma ağlarına dönüşebileceğini ifade etti.




Aytaç yerel örgütlenmelerin çoğulcu kararterine dikkat çekti:  







“Mahallelerde örgütlenmek sadece benzer görüşlere sahip insanları bir araya getirmekle ilgili değil. Anketler yapmak, ortak buluşma yerleri oluşturmak, birlikte kahve içmek veya birlikte yemek pişirmek gibi basit adımlar, kalıcı ilişkilerin başlangıcı olabilir”.







Demokratik konfederalizm deneyiminin yerel örgütlenmenin toplumsal dayanışma ve katılım açısından önemli bir zemin oluşturduğunu gösterdiğini belirten Aytaç, bu faaliyetlerin yalnızca sosyal etkinlikler olarak kalmaması gerektiğini vurguladı.




Antifaşist mücadelenin temelinde sosyal dayanışma var




BastA! Başkanı Oliver Bolliger’in yürüttüğü “Antifaşist Bir Mücadele Alanı Olarak Sosyal Politika” başlıklı atölyede, dayanışmanın gündelik yaşamda nasıl somutlaştırılabileceği ve uluslararası ölçekte nasıl güçlendirilebileceği tartışıldı.




Aşırı sağın, ekonomik eşitsizliklerden ve toplumsal güvencesizlikten kaynaklanan sorunlara basitleştirilmiş ve dışlayıcı çözümler sunduğu belirtildi.




Sağ partilerin kendi seçmenlerine refah vaat ederken bu refahtan yararlanabilecek toplumsal kesimleri daraltmaya çalıştığına dikkat çekildi.




Atölyede, gençlik kampları, yaz kampları, işgal evleri, mahalle kafeleri ve komşuluk ilişkileri gibi alanlarda geliştirilen dayanışma deneyimleri ele alındı.




Bolliger kapıda bekleyen tehlikeye dikkat çekti:







“Gelecekte dayanışmayı daha geniş kitlelere nasıl yaymak istiyoruz? Bunu başaramazsak, insanların aşırı sağa yönelme riski çok yüksek."







İklim krizinin dayanışmayı daha da acil bir ihtiyaç haline getirdiğini belirten Bolliger, parlamentoya sunulan siyasi önerilerin önemli olmakla birlikte sonuç alınmasının uzun zaman gerektirdiğini ifade etti.




Bu nedenle sol hareketlerin mahallelerde doğrudan harekete geçmesi gerektiğini vurgulayan Bolliger, sıcak hava dalgaları sırasında iklim krizine uyum önlemlerinin hayata geçirilmesine destek verilmesini örnek gösterdi.




Sol içindeki bölünmelerin aşılması, ortak stratejik hedefler geliştirilmesi ve mevcut kaynakların nasıl kullanılacağının yeniden değerlendirilmesi gerektiği de tartışıldı.




Örgüt içi dayanışma ve sürdürülebilir aktivizm




Örgüt içi dayanışma ve sürdürülebilir aktivizm üzerine düzenlenen atölyeyi yürüten topluluk çalışmaları uzmanı Mona-Lisa Kole, sol ve toplumsal hareketlerin kendi iç işleyişlerini de sorgulaması gerektiğini belirtti.




Siyasi örgütlerde sorumlulukların dağılımı, aktivistlerin üzerindeki iş yükü ve giderek artan tükenmişlik sorununun ele alındığı atölyede, uzun vadeli mücadelenin yalnızca dışa dönük faaliyetlerle sürdürülemeyeceği vurgulandı.




Kole, dayanışmanın örgütlerin kendi iç ilişkilerine ve çalışma yöntemlerine de yansıması gerektiğini ifade etti.




Her toplumsal gelişmeye anında tepki verme ve sürekli aktif olma baskısının aktivistler üzerinde yıpratıcı etkiler yarattığına dikkat çeken Kole, siyasi mücadelenin sürdürülebilir olması için sorumlulukların ve kaynakların daha adil dağıtılması gerektiğini söyledi.




Kole toplumsal mücadelelerin tamamına hakim olma güdüsüyle başa çıkmayı önerdi:







“Her şeyi yapmak zorunda olduğumuz ve sürekli acele etmemiz gerektiği düşüncesinden kurtulmalıyız. Yorulduğumuzda ve tükendiğimizde kaynaklarımızı yeniden dağıtmayı, yavaşlamayı ve mükemmeliyetçi beklentilerden vazgeçmeyi öğrenmeliyiz.” 







Ortak siyasi değerlerin savunulmasının yalnızca aynı görüşü paylaşan kişilerle dayanışmak anlamına gelmediğini belirten Kole, kişisel yakınlık duyulmayan veya siyasi olarak aynı fikirde olunmayan insanların da temel haklarının ve ifade özgürlüklerinin savunulması gerektiğini vurguladı.




Stier: "Faşizme karşı mücadele parlamentoyla sınırlı kalamaz"




Etkinliğin kapanış konuşmasını yapan BastA! Genel Sekreteri Franziska Stier, gün boyunca gerçekleştirilen tartışmaları değerlendirerek aşırı sağın yükselişine karşı birleşik ve örgütlü bir toplumsal mücadelenin gerekliliğine dikkat çekti.




Faşizme karşı mücadelenin yalnızca parlamenter siyaset üzerinden yürütülemeyeceğini belirten Stier, toplumsal hareketlerin kendi örgütlenme kapasitelerini güçlendirmesi, farklı mücadele alanları arasında dayanışma ilişkileri kurması ve gündelik yaşamın somut sorunlarına yönelik ortak talepler geliştirmesi gerektiğini söyledi.




Stier, 2027 yılında gerçekleştirilecek Feminist Grev kapsamında gündeme gelen çalışma saatlerinin azaltılması talebinin de bu açıdan önemli olduğunu dile getirdi.




Çalışma saatlerinin kısaltılmasının yalnızca işçi hakları veya bakım emeğinin daha adil paylaşılması açısından değil, insanların toplumsal ve siyasi yaşama katılabilmesi bakımından da değerlendirilmesi gerektiğini belirtti.




Stier konuşmasını şu sözlerle sonlandırdı:







“Faşizme karşı mücadelede parlamentodan çözüm beklemek yeterli değildir. Asıl soru, aşağıdan yukarıya doğru nasıl örgütlenmek istediğimizdir. Gelecek yılki Feminist Grev kapsamında çalışma saatlerinin azaltılması talebi, insanların hem dayanışma hem de siyasi örgütlenme için zaman bulabilmeleri açısından çok önemli bir mücadele alanıdır.” 










BastA! hakkında




İsviçre’nin Basel-Stadt kantonunda faaliyet yürüten BastA! (Basels starke Alternative – Basel’in Güçlü Alternatifi), sosyal, ekolojik ve feminist hareketlerle yakın ilişkiler içinde olan radikal sol bir parti. Konut hakkı, güçlü kamu hizmetleri, göçmen ve mülteci hakları, iklim adaleti ve ayrımcılıkla mücadeleyi temel siyasi öncelikleri arasında görüyor.




Uzun yıllar Yeşiller ve Genç Yeşiller ile seçim işbirliği yapan BastA!, 2024 kanton parlamentosu seçimlerinde yüzde 6,7 oy alarak 100 sandalyeden 6’sını kazandı. Partinin kanton hükümeti adayı Oliver Bolliger ise 14 bin 566 oy almasına rağmen seçilemedi. BastA!’nın federal düzeydeki tanınmış isimlerinden Türkiyeli siyasetçi Sibel Arslan, 2015’ten itibaren Basel’i Ulusal Konsey’de temsil etti. Arslan, Ocak 2026’da partiden ayrılarak Yeşiller’e geçti.







(MMY/AEK)

title: Eski SPK Daire Başkanı Erman Çete hakkında gözaltı kararı
content:
Eski Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu (SPK) Daire Başkanı Erman Çete hakkında İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığınca yürütülen fon soruşturması kapsamında gözaltı kararı çıkarıldı. Ayrıca Çete'nin mal varlığına tedbir kararı da istendi. Çete'nin henüz gözaltına alınmadığı bildirildi.

Soruşturma kapsamında eski SPK Başkanı İbrahim Ömer Gönül hakkında da işlem yapılmıştı. İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı, Gönül hakkında "görevi kötüye kullanma" suçlaması kapsamında soruşturma yürütülebilmesi için Hazine ve Maliye Bakanlığına başvurmuştu. Hazine ve Maliye Bakanı Mehmet Şimşek, yapılan ön incelemenin ardından 14 Ekim'de Gönül hakkında soruşturma izni vermişti. Gönül, 30 Eylül'de de soruşturma kapsamında şüpheli sıfatıyla savcılığa ifade vermişti.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.
