author: Caitlyn Clark
title: Interview: How We Beat Back Nonunion Subcontracting at Kroger
content:
After more than six months fighting against Kroger’s use of non-union subcontractors, members of Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 700 in Indiana won a 

victory

 in August, when Kroger announced it would be ending the Retail Odyssey direct store delivery (DSD) program entirely.




This means more hours for union members—thanks to those who organized to enforce the contract, file grievances, and educate their co-workers. In this interview conducted by Caitlyn Clark of the reform group Essential Workers for Democracy, shop stewards Andrea Reynolds and Kristen Jackson explain how they did it.




Essential Workers for Democracy: What is Retail Odyssey and why is it a problem? 




Andrea Reynolds:

 Retail Odyssey is a nonunion third-party contractor that solely services Kroger stores. Normally RO does things like rearranging a store layout or auditing whether products are displayed the way the brand wants.




A few months ago, the Kroger Central Division here in Indiana developed a new program utilizing RO employees to stock direct store delivery vendor items on weekends. [

DSD items are delivered straight to the store by the supplier, rather than coming through a Kroger warehouse.

]




Why is this a problem? Kroger has employees who need hours. This isn't “extra help.” Kroger wants to phase nonunion third parties into the stores to cut hours of its union employees. If we don't speak up, it will only get worse. We’ve seen this happen already with cut fruit vendors, outdoor floral products, floor cleaning, and gift cards, just to name a few. 




How did you and your co-workers start taking on Retail Odyssey?

 




Reynolds:

 We immediately started gathering as much accurate information as we could and passing it along to our co-workers. We shared information in our Facebook group and we shared flyers with our co-workers.




We wanted them to know why this was a problem and what they could do about it. The company wants us to think that third parties are there to make our jobs easier. But time and time again, we see our hours cut and wonder why. 




We also passed along the feedback of our vendors. Their products were being damaged, mixed with other vendors, and stocked incorrectly. 




Kristen Jackson:

 Although in the pharmacy, I am not as impacted, my union brothers and sisters are. As a steward, I try my best to let others know what is wrong with RO taking our work.




I walked around and talked to my co-workers about what the RO workers were allowed to stock. I told them if they saw them, to please take pictures, talk to the RO workers, and be nice.













By having a standardized report form, members could make sure grievances were airtight.










How did you collect information to file grievances? How did you make sure grievances got filed and processed?




Reynolds:

 Retail Odyssey was scheduled to work Friday through Sunday, noon to 6 p.m. I had a lot of conversations with members I knew were normally there during those hours.




I instructed them to take photos, make note of the day, time, duration of stocking, what non-vendor products were stocked, and anyone who witnessed it. We had them send this info to our stewards or trusted employees who could contact our union rep.




Every week after the grievance was filed, we messaged our reps asking for status of the grievance. We didn't want it to fall through the cracks.




Jackson:

 I just went up to the RO workers, introduced myself as a steward, and let them know I would be taking pictures of them and why. I explained, “I'm not against you having a job. I'm here to document Kroger violating our contract.”




The RO workers were understanding, and would tell me that the manager told them to stock our product and let me file the grievances. The RO worker at my store location would tell me exactly what he stocked, so I could file the grievances effectively. We filed three grievances at my location. 




What advice would you give to anyone dealing with non-union subcontracting?




Reynolds:

 Document, document, document! You need to prove there was a contract violation.




Talk with your co-workers about how to document. Contact your rep. Don't hesitate to ask for help from a steward or a trusted member.




You have power in your numbers. The more members speaking up, the better! We filed so many grievances in six months that the third-party DSD program has officially ended. When we fight, we win. 			




Andrea Reynolds and Kristen Jackson are UFCW Local 700 shop stewards in Kokomo and Zionsville, Indiana. Caitlyn Clark is the director of Essential Workers for Democracy.

author: Chris Walker
title: Prosecutors Filed Over 900 Cases of “Pregnancy-Related Crimes” Since Dobbs
content:
Most of the charges being brought stem from laws that were never meant to apply to pregnancy.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A new report has found that, in the years following the Supreme Court’s overturning of abortion rights established in Roe v. Wade, hundreds of people have been charged with crimes related to their pregnancies.

Reproductive rights nonprofit Pregnancy Justice documented at least 902 cases of such charges in the three years after the court’s Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health decision. The data suggests that more cases likely exist, since the research only covers the period from the summer of 2022 through 2025, and doesn’t include instances where people were charged over the past year.

Most of the charges being brought against pregnant people relate to their actions while pregnant, pregnancy loss, or births, Pregnancy Justice noted in its report. The cases are primarily based on long-existing criminal statutes, not new abortion ban laws, with 876 of the 955 charges documented relating to allegations of child neglect, endangerment, or abuse.

While the report notes that 23 states charged people with pregnancy-related crimes during that three-year period, a majority of the cases were in just three states — South Carolina (381 cases), Oklahoma (222), and Alabama (204).

These charges included claims from prosecutors that individuals were abusing drugs or other substances during their pregnancies; failed to provide an adequate amount of prenatal care for their fetus or infant; and attempted to obtain, obtained, or even merely researched abortion services.

What’s more, prosecutors overwhelmingly charged pregnant people under statutes that allow them to obtain convictions without proving that there was any actual harm to a fetus or infant. According to the report, close to 95 percent of the cases involved such charges.

“These numbers show that the criminalization of pregnancy in this country is not some distant or hypothetical consequence of abortion bans,” said Lourdes A. Rivera, president of Pregnancy Justice. “It is already happening.”

Law enforcement is using laws that were never intended to apply to pregnancy to investigate, arrest, and punish women, and it’s only getting worse since the overturning of Roe. Pregnant people deserve health care, support, and dignity — not handcuffs.

Beyond criminal charges that pregnant people have faced, abortion bans and other restrictions on reproductive health care have also led to deadly outcomes in the years since the Dobbs decision.

A ProPublica report from last month, for example, found around 200 documented instances of people dying from ectopic pregnancies from 2020-2025 — a rate that is about double what it had been in the preceding six-year period.

The report noted that doctors, perhaps concerned that their action could be viewed as illegal by their state governments, may be hesitating to offer treatment when an ectopic pregnancy occurs. Such pregnancies, in which a fertilized egg implants outside the uterus, often in a fallopian tube, are in no way viable and can often lead to life-threatening complications.

In an op-ed for Truthout in the spring of 2025, Lauren Rankin, reproductive rights author and journalist, wrote: “Under abortion bans, the life of the pregnant person is a secondary concern.”

“Doctors are afraid of being prosecuted for treating a potentially life-threatening health issue; someone facing a miscarriage is afraid of being prosecuted for flushing the toilet; and a teenager and her mother were imprisoned because she didn’t know where else to turn for an abortion in her state,” Rankin said, discussing real-life examples of how abortion restrictions have detrimentally affected people’s lives.

“This isn’t an accident, but an intentional byproduct of overturning Roe and ending the constitutional right to an abortion,” Rankin added. “Ending Roe was meant to ripple far beyond abortion — it was meant to erode the personhood of pregnant people, to eradicate their full-fledged autonomy and ability to determine the course of their own lives. When you reduce someone to less than a person in the eyes of the state, criminalization is never far behind.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Jen Fifield
title: Ballot Rejections Soared in Rural Counties After USPS Cost-Cutting Measures
content:
The rates of primary ballots rejected for arriving late this year doubled or tripled in some areas compared to 2022.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

In early August, election workers north of Spokane, Washington, went across the street to the post office to check for late mail-in ballots. It was three days after the primary and they were expecting no more than a few dozen.

Instead, their mailbox was brimming with envelopes — more than 500 of them, each a vote that wouldn’t count. The sight was “jarring,” said Auditor Lori Larsen, a Republican who oversees voting in Stevens County.

Across the region, other election officials were getting similar jolts. In the 11 predominately rural counties in eastern Washington, nearly 2,000 ballots came in late, compared to about 600 in 2022, the previous midterm primary.

In recent weeks, concerns about mail-in voting disruptions have focused almost entirely on President Donald Trump’s now-shelved plan to sharply restrict who can vote by mail.

But a ProPublica data analysis shows that delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, not only in Washington, but across the country.

Over the past three years, as mail volume continued to plummet and annual deficits ballooned, the Postal Service started consolidating the processing of first-class mail at larger regional plants instead of at smaller hubs closer to local post offices. Then, in a little-noted switch that mostly took effect after the 2024 election, the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at many post offices 50 miles or more from these processing plants, from twice daily to once.

The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and, most importantly for ballots, pushed back postmarking, which doesn’t happen until mail reaches the regional centers.

In this year’s primary, the effects of the cuts were clearest in five states that make detailed data on mail-in ballots available: Washington, California, Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon. All have or recently had grace periods allowing ballots to count if they come in after Election Day as long as they’re postmarked by the deadline.

In these states, the number of ballots rejected for arriving late soared in counties affected by the service changes compared to 2022, ProPublica’s analysis showed.

Rejection rates in counties where services were cut doubled or tripled from what they were four years ago, dwarfing any increases in counties where postal pickups remained as they were, our analysis showed. In urban Spokane, for example, the number of ballots rejected for being late actually dropped this year.

Across the five states, the delays have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, ProPublica’s analysis shows. In Washington, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said he sees the service changes directed by Republican appointees leading the Postal Service as a way to undermine mail-in voting.

“I don’t think they realized how much it was going to affect their voter base,” he said, adding that Washington has “a lot of rural Republican voters.”

Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts into place for these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout. They have circulated a memo to the nation’s more than 30,000 post offices saying that for the 10 days before the election, managers should separate completed ballots from other first-class mail and deliver those intended for local election offices the day they come in.

At an Oct. 15 news conference, Postal Service leaders emphasized the agency’s longstanding recommendation that voters mail ballots back at least a week before their states’ deadlines, while defending the agency’s ability to fast-track ballots through the system.

“We work to identify and address issues quickly,” said Amber McReynolds, chair of the Postal Service board of governors, “so ballots can continue to move swiftly from election offices to voters and from voters back to election offices.”

Election consultants, researchers and former Postal Service officials told ProPublica that the guidance for the upcoming vote gave more detailed directions on how to expedite ballots. They said they hoped the agency’s special measures would limit delays, but some said mistakes were likely.

“I don’t think we can say with any kind of conviction that there will be no ballots rejected,” said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer of the National Association of Election Officials. “It isn’t a question of ‘if,’ but a question of ‘how many.’”

A pilot program instituting the delivery changes in 18 regions before the 2024 election ran into problems. An audit by the Postal Service’s inspector general found that agency staff in these areas sometimes didn’t handle ballots correctly, mainly because instructions weren’t clearly communicated. (A Postal Service spokesperson said “learnings from the pilot” have been applied as the program has expanded.)

After this year’s primary, reports by media outlets noted that mail-in ballot rejection rates were higher than in the past, but ProPublica’s analysis shows these increases were directly connected to Postal Service changes. Research published in September by the Brookings Institution also found this connection, projecting that if the pattern held in the general election, tens of thousands of mail-in ballots could be rejected.

At least seven closely contested congressional districts — including Washington’s 3rd, California’s 22nd and North Carolina’s 11th — are in areas that were affected by service changes in the primary, ProPublica found.

Elena Patel, who conducted the Brookings analysis, said service changes may still imperil mail-in votes in the general election.

“I think there remain risks to ballots,” she said, adding that the Postal Service’s plan for the general election “depends on flawless execution.”

Mail-in voting has become more popular over the last decade, with many states broadening access to it during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Nearly 1 in 3 Americans voted this way in 2022 and 2024. Trump himself frequently votes by mail, and in recent weeks has started to encourage his supporters to do so as well, though he has claimed without evidence that the process is rife with fraud.

The Postal Service has mostly ensured the timely delivery of hundreds of millions of ballots, even as mail volume overall has dropped 50% from its high in 2006.

When Louis DeJoy was appointed postmaster general in spring 2020, he inherited an $81 billion operating deficit and rapidly took steps such as eliminating overtime to reduce costs, under pressure from Trump and others in his administration. (DeJoy did not respond to questions from ProPublica.)

The NAACP sued that August, alleging the measures could affect mail-in votes in that year’s general election. Courts ordered DeJoy to reverse some of the cuts and the Postal Service agreed to implement special procedures to ensure ballots weren’t delayed. The Postal Service has continued following those procedures since.

Still, DeJoy went forward with a 10-year restructuring plan designed to save the agency billions. It ended evening pickups from some post offices, often in rural areas. Trucks serving these places travel long distances and at times were mostly empty. This part of the plan — called regional transportation optimization, or RTO — was projected to eventually save the Postal Service $4 billion a year.

The agency announced the national rollout of the RTO plan in 2024, but DeJoy agreed to pause it leading up to that year’s November election, leaving only about 4,000 ZIP codes in the pilot project affected by the service changes.

In January 2025, the Postal Regulatory Commission, which oversees the Postal Service, warned that moving forward with the plan would be disruptive to rural communities and might not save as much money as expected. The Postal Service rolled out the reductions anyway, extending the changes to almost 20,000 ZIP codes to date. Officials said they expect the system to be fully implemented within two years.

This January, the agency put out a statement saying the transportation cuts would mean it took longer for mail, including ballots, to be postmarked and delivered. But the Postal Service didn’t specify which voters would be affected by the slowdowns and which wouldn’t.

Though the delay from RTO is often only a day, mail can be delayed longer if it’s deposited in a mailbox after the daily pickup time, or just before Sunday or a holiday.

A Postal Service spokesperson said the agency told election officials that RTO would change schedules and reemphasized the need for voters to get their ballots in the mail at least a week ahead of time. Election officials in Washington said the Postal Service wasn’t direct enough about the fact that the changes would lead to delays in delivering and postmarking ballots.

“What they said was, ‘We are going to change the way we do postmarks,’” said Hobbs, Washington’s secretary of state. “That was it.”

Patel, the Brookings analyst and a former Postal Regulatory Commission employee, said that more direct communication to voters could have helped change their behavior. “That’s the part that I think has not been super transparent about the whole process,” she said.

Many of the areas that saw a spike in late ballots were in Western states, which were the earliest and most enthusiastic adopters of expanded mail-in voting.

In 2004, Washington became the second state to start conducting all-mail elections, in which every eligible voter automatically receives a mail-in ballot. Most residents vote by putting their ballots in drop boxes. Still, in 2024, about 33% put them in the mail.

In the 30 mostly rural Washington counties most affected by RTO, the percentage of ballots postmarked late more than tripled compared to the 2022 primary, ProPublica found.

In Garfield County, in southeastern Washington, 19 ballots — nearly 1 in 10 cast — had late postmarks this year. In 2022, only a single ballot was postmarked late. In Pend Oreille County, in northeast Washington along the Idaho panhandle, 6% of ballots were rejected for arriving late, compared to 1% in the 2022 primary.

“It was pretty awful telling people we couldn’t count their votes,” said Marianne Nichols, Pend Oreille’s longtime auditor. “They were quite upset because they felt like, ‘Why? This was in the mailbox on election day, the post office picked it up and had it.’ They felt like it should have counted.”

In Stevens County, the percentage of ballots rejected for having a late postmark jumped to 8%, from 1% in 2022.

Steve Hutkins, a retired professor who analyzes the effect of Postal Service changes on Savethepostoffice.com, also found that places in Washington with RTO had more ballot rejections during local elections earlier this year for school board and other measures. The patterns “set off the alarm bells,” he said.

Stuart Holmes, the state’s director of elections, said he reached out to Postal Service officials to find out what had happened, but got few answers and no specifics on delays related to RTO, which were a “total surprise,” he said.

Election officials in California and Oregon also reported thousands more ballots rejected for arriving late during their primaries. Counties affected by RTO, including Kern County, California, had substantially higher rates of ballots rejected for mail-related reasons, ProPublica found.

Kern County’s assistant registrar of voters, Laura Cantu, said election officials are urging rural voters to use drop boxes to cast their ballots in the general election.

The expansion of RTO had a similar effect in North Carolina and Ohio, where the rates of late ballots were about twice as high in counties affected by the restructuring as rates in counties that weren’t. Since 2022, these states have also eliminated grace periods in which ballots postmarked by Election Day could count even if they arrived later. Voters unused to the tighter deadlines also could have contributed to an increase in late ballots.

ProPublica didn’t find any association between RTO and higher rates of late ballots in Wisconsin, even though clerks reported delays involving mail-in ballots cast in its state election, held this spring. (Other Postal Service changes may have contributed to the delays.)

Wisconsin’s data does not distinguish ballots sent by mail from those cast in drop boxes or in person, making it impossible to definitively measure rejection rates just for ballots returned by mail. Election researchers said Wisconsin’s deadline for mail ballots, which must come into election offices by 8 p.m. on Election Day, also probably had an effect.

“If you know that you don’t have a grace period, it probably affects voter behavior,” said Patel, the Brookings researcher.

Recent Postal Service audits have found that RTO-related changes had saved the agency about $2.8 billion by the end of fiscal year 2025 — less money than expected — and are slowing down all first-class mail, not just ballots. Residents of rural areas are waiting longer for everything from prescriptions to bills, a report published in September by the Postal Service’s inspector general said.

A Postal Service spokesperson still defended the plan, both for financial reasons and to adjust to the changing marketplace. “These savings are both significant and necessary,” he said.

In the lead-up to Nov. 3, the agency’s plan is to route ballots meant for local election offices to a nearby postal facility or directly to their destination. They shouldn’t go to regional plants, which the Postal Service says should minimize delays.

Larsen, the Stevens County auditor, is encouraging Washington voters to deposit their ballots in drop boxes rather than relying on the mail. Since the primary, she’s increased the number of red, white and blue drop boxes that sit outside government buildings from seven to 12. Near each box, there’s a large sign encouraging people to take selfies when they vote and send the photos to Larsen.

In prior years, Larsen said, she avoided telling voters how or when to vote, concerned they might regret choices they made if critical information later emerged about the candidates. That’s no longer uppermost in her mind.

“Now we are more concerned that we get your ballot,” she said.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Sara Luterman
title: Nursing Home Residents Have a Right to Vote — Despite What Trump CMS Agency Says
content:
The Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 requires facilities to support their residents in exercising their rights.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Cindy Napolitan and her daughter Melissa have multiple sclerosis, a degenerative condition in which the immune system attacks the brain, spinal cord and nerves. They have lived together at a nursing home in Mesquite, Texas, for nine years. In previous elections, Cindy and Melissa Napolitan voted by mail, but this year they took an unusual step: They voted in person. They worried their mail-in ballots — and even their in-person votes — may not be counted.

“I’ve never worried like this before. I’ve never worried that I don’t have the proper ID. I’ve never worried that somebody is going to intimidate me. Will I encounter somebody that’s going to threaten me or make me feel less than? So yeah, I’m very worried, and I shouldn’t be,” Cindy Napolitan said. “I shouldn’t have to be worried about stuff like that. This is the 19th Amendment. I’m allowed to vote.”

Nursing home residents are guaranteed the right to vote. Around two-thirds of all nursing home residents in the United States are women, making aging and long-term care gendered issues.

There is no data on how many nursing home residents exercise that right. Cindy, 70, and Melissa Napolitan, 48, at least, feel like they’ve had good experiences with voting at their facility. Cindy Napolitan, in particular, has worked with the activities coordinator to organize rides to the polls for her, her daughter and other interested residents.

“We are scheduled to go on the first day of early voting. So in case there are any issues that we come across, we still have time to rectify the situation and be allowed to vote,” Cindy Napolitan said.

Cindy and Melissa Napolitan are more concerned this year than in previous years about government interference and voter suppression. Their fears are not unfounded: Experts and advocates for the rights of nursing home residents, older adults and people with disabilities are worried too.

In July, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services rescinded previous guidance affirming that nursing home residents have the right to vote.

“The memo does not alter the underlying law. Nursing homes are governed by the Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 and its implementing regulations,” said Nina Kohn, a professor at Syracuse University and expert on elder law. “That law still requires facilities to support their residents in exercising their rights as Americans.”

The memo also emphasized voter fraud in nursing homes, specifically around mail-in ballots. For years, President Trump has disparaged mail-in ballots, insisting without evidence that fraudulent votes by mail had a role in his loss during the 2020 presidential election. His comments have led to some states restricting who can use a mail-in ballot and in what contexts.

According to experts, including Kohn, there is no evidence that voter fraud is a serious or widespread problem in nursing homes. Instead, Kohn is concerned about the chilling effect that it may have on residents’ rights.

“The language in the memo itself is intimidating, and it may understandably make staff think that they could face criminal prosecution or be in some other form of legal trouble if they help residents vote,” Kohn said.

Cindy and Melissa Napolitan do everything together — and on Monday, they voted together. They are also roommates at the facility; most people living in nursing homes are assigned roommates who are strangers.

“Unlike other people that have roommates that don’t get along, I’m very lucky and fortunate that I have somebody that loves me and I love her,” Cindy Napolitan said.

This is the second time Cindy and Melissa Napolitan have voted in person since entering a nursing home. The first time was during the 2024 presidential election.

“I’ve been checking my status weekly to make sure that I haven’t been dropped off the voter rolls, making sure my daughter and I don’t have some sort of issue that says that we can’t vote,” Cindy Napolitan said.

People living in nursing homes and other long-term care facilities face specific barriers. Some residents may need assistance filling out their ballots because they lack the movement or dexterity to hold a pen or press buttons on a computer screen. People with dexterity or coordination issues may also be unable to produce the same signature twice.

“With some forms of voting, some states will use your ID to verify your signature. If your signature looks different than the one on your ID, your ballot might get thrown out. Or there is a ballot hearing process, so you could be notified of that and able to fix it, but it is a bunch of extra steps that impact disabled voters at higher rates,” said Alexia Kemerling, director of Accessible Democracy for the nonpartisan American Association of People with Disabilities.

An increasing number of states now require voters to show some form of photo identification. This can also be a problem for many nursing home residents because they may no longer have a driver’s license. They also may no longer have passports because they aren’t traveling internationally. States have other forms of identification, but getting them can involve complex paperwork and multiple trips.

Some states will accommodate voters in nursing homes and other facilities so they can acquire state identification that isn’t a driver’s license.

“My license expired, and so I had to apply for an identification card. I had to coordinate with them to come here instead of going to the DMV because I wasn’t about to do that. I didn’t know how long I would have to sit there. I didn’t have a ride,” Melissa Napolitan said. “They came and took our pictures, and filled out all the forms for us.”

Kemerling objects to the idea that this somehow renders nursing home residents and other people with disabilities incapable of making an independent choice.

“In the disability community, we don’t necessarily mean that independence means doing something alone. Independence is having control over how something is done,” Kemerling said. “Just because you need someone to assist you as part of the voting process does not mean that you are giving up your choice.”

There are steps nursing home residents and their families can take to advocate for their rights. Lori Smetanka is the executive director of the National Consumer Voice for Quality Long Term Care, which advocates on behalf of people living in nursing homes and assisted living facilities. Her organization produces a fact sheet for nursing home residents enumerating their rights and how they can advocate for themselves.

“For the generation of people that are living in long-term care facilities, it’s largely an older population of people,” Smetanka said. “It’s very important to them to exercise their right to vote. When we talk with residents, it is very important to them. Some of them have really advocated very heavily for themselves in order to be able to do that.”

Smetanka emphasized that it is not only up to residents and their families to advocate for their rights.

“If the resident has the ability to raise the questions about it, they certainly should be doing that, Smetanka said. “Families should be asking, but staff should be asking too — ‘What can we do to help you vote this year? Who is interested in voting? How can we get the requirements in place so you can cast your ballots?’” At some facilities, voting may not be on staff’s radar, despite the legal requirements.

Cindy Napolitan has been active in advocating for her right to vote, as well as the rights of her fellow residents, and she encourages others who are able to do the same.

“I’m very vocal and very into advocating for our residents here and making sure that they’re all able to vote,” Cindy Napolitan said. “I’m the one that will start telling our activity director that there’s a deadline for filing to become a registered voter. There’s a deadline to file for a mail-in ballot, and I’m usually the one that makes sure that those things get done.”

When asked what she wants people to understand most about voting in nursing homes, Melissa Napolitan pushed back against the insinuation that nursing homes are hotbeds of voter fraud and that she and her peers don’t have their own opinions.

“I think that people maybe don’t take the time to realize that people in nursing homes aren’t just here waiting to die,” Melissa Napolitan said.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

title: «No Data Center»: maxi scritta di Extinction Rebellion sull’edificio in cui dovrebbe sorgere il più grande data center d’Italia
content:
Riceviamo e pubblichiamo il comunicato stampa di Extinction Rebellion Torino.







22 ottobre 2026, Moncalieri (Torino) – 

Extinction Rebellion ha realizzato delle enormi scritte “No Data Center” sullo stabilimento dismesso dell’ex Ilte e appeso uno striscione con la frase “Fermare l’ecocidio”. Una protesta per denunciare l’impatto ambientale, sanitario e sociale dei data center e di quello che potrebbe diventare il più grande impianto del Paese. «In un mondo che sta collassando, non c’è spazio per altre strutture ecocide»




“No Data Center”. È l’enorme scritta realizzata da Extinction Rebellion sulla facciata dello stabilimento ex-Ilte di Moncalieri, alle porte di Torino, edificio al centro dell’iter per la realizzazione di quello che potrebbe diventare il 

più grande data center

 d’Italia. Accanto alla scritta principale, visibile anche dall’autostrada e da Moncalieri, una seconda scritta “Stop Tech Fascism” (Stop tecno-fascismo) è stata realizzata sulla facciata laterale e uno striscione srotolato su una terza facciata con scritto “Fermare l’ecocidio”.




«Lasciamo qui questo messaggio affinché sia visibile ovunque e serva da monito a tutte le amministrazioni»,

 spiega Extinction Rebellion. 

«Un data center di queste dimensioni ha impatti ambientali, sanitari e sociali pericolosissimi ed è incompatibile con qualsiasi obiettivo climatico. In un mondo che sta collassando e in cui il costo della vita sta soffocando la maggioranza della popolazione, non c’è spazio per investimenti miliardari per strutture ecocide».

 Al centro della protesta ci sono gli enormi consumi energetici e idrici dei data center, oltre ai possibili effetti sociali e sanitari. Un impianto come quello ipotizzato a Moncalieri, da 527 megawatt e 4,5 miliardi di euro, consumerebbe tanta energia 

quanto tutte le famiglie

 piemontesi. A ciò si aggiunge l’acqua necessaria a raffreddare i server, in una regione alle prese con una siccità cronica, che ad agosto ha 

avviato le procedure

 per chiedere lo stato di calamità naturale per l’emergenza idrica. Anche i refrigeranti identificati come soluzione al consumo d’acqua possono in realtà comportare rischi: 

molti contengono

 PFAS, le cosiddette «sostanze chimiche eterne», che si disperdono nell’ambiente e si accumulano nel corpo umano. Un problema che il Piemonte conosce bene: a Spinetta Marengo, nell’Alessandrino, la produzione di PFAS dello stabilimento Solvay 

ha già esposto

 gli abitanti alla contaminazione, e queste stesse sostanze 

sono state rilevate

 anche nell’acqua potabile di oltre 70 comuni del torinese. In ultimo, i data center sono diventati veri e propri 

bersagli militari strategici

 negli ultimi anni, trasformando le infrastrutture digitali e l’Intelligenza Artificiale in nuovi teatri di guerra.




«Moltiplicare queste enormi infrastrutture è folle: significa aumentare la pressione sulle risorse naturali e la dipendenza dai combustibili fossili, proprio quando la crisi climatica impone di azzerare le emissioni e contenere i consumi»,

 aggiunge Extinction Rebellion. Nel 

rapporto «Energy and AI»

 del 2025 dell’Agenzia Internazionale dell’Energia (IEA), la domanda dei maxi data center è infatti indicata come uno dei motori della crescita della produzione elettrica da gas e carbone fino alla fine del decennio. Lo stesso assessore regionale all’Ambiente, Matteo Marnati, ha ammesso che le rinnovabili non basteranno e ha annunciato che 

chiederà al governo

 di escludere i consumi dei data center dal calcolo degli obiettivi di decarbonizzazione. Durante un convegno all’Ordine degli Avvocati di Torino 

ha poi dichiarato

 che per alimentarli «è imprescindibile pensare all’energia nucleare». 

«Le scelte del governo e della Regione sono surreali: prima creano il problema, poi impongono una soluzione che ne genera un altro, ancora più grave, spacciandola per inevitabile»,

 replica Extinction Rebellion.




Il progetto del più grande data center di Italia ha già incontrato i primi ostacoli: a ottobre il sindaco di Moncalieri lo 

ha definito

 «non accoglibile», anche se il Comune ha tempo fino a fine mese per la decisione. Per questo la protesta è andata in scena proprio sullo stabilimento: mentre l’iter prosegue, la scritta resterà lì, visibile a tutti. Intanto i cittadini del posto 

hanno lanciato

 una raccolta firme per fermare il progetto. La richiesta di Extinction Rebellion è netta: fermare il maxi data center, bonificare l’area e restituirla alla comunità. 

«Al posto di altro cemento e di una nuova struttura energivora, si avvii un percorso partecipato per rinaturalizzare l’area o destinarla all’emergenza abitativa»,

 conclude il movimento.

author: Santana Dreaver
title: ‘Gratifying and humbling’: First Nation leads ghost net cleanup from Interior ‘B.C.’ rivers
content:
Volunteers Lyza Adoplh, John Redan, Nick Froese and Roxx Ledoux work to haul abandoned fishing gear out of the Fraser and Thompson rivers. Photo by Santana Dreaver




This article has been co-published 

with the Narwhal

 as part of their 

2026 Indigenous journalism fellowship

.







After starting the day with a prayer and a safety demonstration, a group of volunteers gears up in water-resistant clothing and lifejackets, ready to hit the water.




The crew is preparing to scour a stretch of the Fraser and Thompson rivers, removing any fishing gear or waste left behind. Fishing nets left underneath the water are commonly known as ghost nets, which trap and kill fish. 




As the saying goes on a volunteer call out poster, “ghost nets create ghost fish.”




TLKemchEEN (Lytton First Nation) has led the river clean-up program in the area for the past 20 years, all in an effort to preserve salmon populations and aquatic life following harvest season.




Over two days in September, a group of 40 volunteers spent a total of 20 combined hours on the water.




From Lillooet to Lytton during the first day, and from Lytton to Yale during the second day, volunteers passed through white-water rapids and rugged terrain such as the famously turbulent passage of Hell’s Gate.




When the raft leader yells “hold on,” that’s exactly what participants do, reaching down for a rope attached to the raft, laughing and hollering, ripping through the Fraser Canyon rapids. 




The cold river water splashes everyone — waking up the crew as countless bald and golden eagles watch from above.




“I didn’t realize how impactful everything is along the shores. I guess I didn’t realize that some leave their garbage and nets out there,” volunteer Rebecca Riley, who is from the Stʼatʼimc Nation, said.




“Once I saw that with my own eyes, I wanted to jump in and be a part of it.”




A newspaper ad about the river clean-up project inspired Rebecca Riley to get involved. She has helped remove ghost nets since 2018. Photo: Supplied by Rebecca Riley




‘That fishery is a communal right’




It’s a sentiment shared by many volunteers on the boat, who eagerly approach the shoreline when a ghost net comes into sight. 




Whether the net will take one person to remove, or up to five to pull out of the water, is unknown until people get their hands wet. 




During the non-rapid portion of the cleanup, countless stories were told, Indigenous people exchanged words in their languages to compare similarities and differences and folks even had hot chocolate along the shore, courtesy of Kumsheen Rafting, which was contracted to support the program this year. 




During the first year of the program, 126 ghost nets were collected.




“This year we picked up six nets and some garbage, some years prior we’ve picked up zero. We have to remind our fishermen not to be lazy and take their gear home,” Kevin Duncan told the Narwhal.




Duncan is an elected councillor for TLKemchEEN in “B.C.’s” Southern Interior, part of the Nlaka’pamux Nation Tribal Council. He has been involved with the program since its inception. He attended both cleanup days this year with his son, Aaron.




Kevin Duncan, an elected councillor for TLKemchEEN, has been involved in Lytton’s ghost net clean-up initiative since it started 20 years ago. He always leads a prayer before they begin. Photo: Supplied by Rebecca Riley




For TLKemchEEN, stewarding their waters as they always have is crucial — especially as salmon numbers decline. Life along the Fraser and Thompson rivers is deeply connected to salmon. And TLKemchEEn is home to where the two rivers meet, in the country’s largest salmon-bearing watershed.




“For future generations, sometime down the road, I’m afraid all they’re going to be looking at is pictures of salmon in a book,” said Duncan. 




The nets recovered by the program are given to those in need, including single mothers, low-income families and Elders from the nation. 




“As a Nlaka’pamux or Stʼatʼimc member … that fishery is a communal right, it’s not an individual right. It’s looked after by your nation,” Duncan said.




“Most times, you just get to see portions of the river from the highway, but once you’re down on the water, floating for eight hours from Lillooet to Lytton, it gives you a better perspective on where people fish.” 




Now 20 years into the program, volunteer spots fill up months in advance. Photo by Santana Dreaver




Removing fishing gear from the cold and fast-moving river can be dangerous, which is why Duncan starts each day of the program with a yémit, or prayer in Nlaka’pamxcín. 




“Salmon are the lifeblood of our people, and when these fish pass through coastal communities, they pray for them in the lower Fraser. We’re doing the same thing as they pass through our territories in the mid Fraser. … These fish hear that prayer.”




Nations collaborate to steward salmon




Volunteer Riley is Lillooet Tribal Council’s fisheries manager. She has participated in the river cleanup program three times, beginning in 2018 when she saw an advertisement in the newspaper. 




Although she’s been on the Fraser and Thompson rivers many times throughout her fisheries career, she said that the ghost net removal program was “eye opening,” regarding the number of fishers out on the water.




She said that Lillooet Tribal Council is happy to help as the neighbouring nation to Nlaka’pamux territory, given the large area to cover and the shared value of protecting salmon.




“When we’re having the long days and we’re getting splashed and it’s cold, if we save a salmon or two that are still alive and let them free, or we clear out a net so we know that other animals can’t go in, it’s very gratifying and humbling,” she said. 




“At the end of the day, when you’re riding the bus home and you’re cold and hungry, you know in the back of your mind it was so worth it.”




While the focus of the program is cleaning up the river, volunteers take the opportunity to support other initiatives while on the water, such as mapping traditional fishing sites to prove occupancy. 




According to 

Conservation Biology

, “Proof of occupancy is the foundational legal and moral requirement needed to establish Aboriginal Title, regain territorial sovereignty and protect ancestral lands from unauthorized exploitation.”




Lillooet Tribal Council’s extreme heat resiliency planner, Lyza Adolph, did a lot of heavy lifting over the two days removing ghost nets, but also had a mission of her own. 




A member of the Stʼatʼimc Nation, this was her first time participating in the ghost net removal program.




“It was very cold, but with the group that we had, it was very enjoyable and uplifting,” she said.




Despite the cold water, Lyza Adoplh, Roxx Ledoux, Doug Mitchell, Nick Froese and John Redan shared laughs and stories as they hauled abandoned fishing gear out of the Fraser and Thompson rivers. Photo by Santana Dreaver




With a focus on planning for extreme heat in her position at the tribal council, Adolph monitored fishing sites during the program to see if there were any shade trees nearby, scoping out areas to potentially plant some. 




“The program tied in with my traditional shade tree planting. I know more about the upper river, but from Lillooet to Lytton and beyond, I didn’t know too much about it. It was definitely nice to see the various fish camps and see if there were shade trees,” she told The Narwhal.




Shade trees are beneficial for both humans and aquatic life.




As spawning salmon break down, their nutrients feed the trees. In turn, trees offer shade to cool the water, which is critical for survival on a warming planet, and tree roots and branches give salmonids space to hide from predators while also preventing erosion.




In the Fraser Canyon, which includes the communities of Yale, Lytton and Lillooet, fishing sites can be hard to access. Adolph’s shade tree monitoring data, collected by boat, will be used in future tree planting projects. 




“I would definitely do it again,” Adolph said. “Although it was very cold, it was very refreshing and rewarding by the end of the day.”




The post 

‘Gratifying and humbling’: First Nation leads ghost net cleanup from Interior ‘B.C.’ rivers

 appeared first on 

Indiginews

.

author: Mehk Chakraborty
title: Inside the resistance to Spain’s crackdown on migrants in Ceuta
content:
This article 

Inside the resistance to Spain’s crackdown on migrants in Ceuta

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







On July 30, images streamed across TVs, social media feeds and newspapers of thousands of people approaching a fence along the beach, in boats and by foot. Migrants, including children and families, were attempting to cross into Ceuta, a Spanish enclave bordered by Morocco. Facing violent border guards and the threat of drowning, over 70,000 people made it to Ceuta, with hopes of eventually reaching the Spanish mainland. Officials in Ceuta 

said

 that 100 people died in the crossing — either by drowning or being crushed — and sources on the ground believe the number was higher. 




“I lost my phone, my money, my ID card, everything I had,” one Moroccan teenager recalled. “At one point I got pulled to the bottom, so far down that my feet touched the sand. When I looked around me, I saw women and babies who had drowned.”




“There was no proper humanitarian response from the local authorities — whether it is basic hygiene, food or shelter,” said Ric Fernández, coordinator and spokesperson for humanitarian and migrant advocacy group No Name Kitchen, or NNK, about the first days after the mass crossing. “Instead, there was an institutional response of pressuring people to ‘voluntarily’ return to Morocco. … There was repression, violence against people on the move in every form — legal, administrative and physical, and the forced expulsion of people.”   




Facing intense pressure and violence from both the Spanish police and military, within 96 hours most people returned to Morocco. Estimates about how many migrants remain are in flux, but the Spanish government 

said

 in late September that up to 10,000 people are still in Ceuta.




While the global mainstream media quickly moved on from this story, the situation in Ceuta has 

remained tense

 over the last three months, with increased violent harassment by the police, evictions and collective expulsions. In recent weeks, 

“voluntary returns” and evictions

 from makeshift camps on the beach have ramped up.




Embed from Getty Images




Irene Estébanez Gutiérrez, a family and community doctor in Madrid, spent two weeks in Ceuta as a volunteer. “An information campaign has been waged that portrays people on the move as invaders, violent and dangerous,” she said. The 

media coverage

, she believes, has failed to adequately address “the resulting humanitarian crisis, the systematic violation of rights, the lack of protection for minors, and the systematic violence and discrimination to which people are being subjected to, particularly by the military.”




Those who remain include Moroccan men and women, alongside Sudanese, Syrians, Palestinians, Malians and Nigerians. According to NNK, a significant number are minors. They are still stranded; the majority of them have slept in the street or in makeshift tents since they crossed into Ceuta over two months ago. 




Kora, who uses a pseudonym as an activist to protect her identity, arrived in Ceuta to volunteer in early August and found the violence and the lack of access to basic necessities particularly angering. The authorities were “not letting them access the supermarkets to get food or water,” she said. “They turned off the publicly and freely accessible water [to shower or drink] on the beaches and beat them or scare them in the middle of the night … to purposefully making their lives more miserable.” 




Organizing solidarity, facing criminalization




This 

violence

, however, did not prevent activists and migrants from developing forms of organizing and resistance. Hundreds of migrants 

staged a protest

 on a popular beach in Ceuta in August to demand asylum. On Sept. 21, Migreurop, a Euro-African network of organizations, activists and researchers that monitors European migration policies, noted in a 

joint statement

 with over 100 organizations: “We have witnessed forms of resistance in everyday survival practices.” They mentioned the sharing of information, food and medicine, as well as safety and protection practices. 










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










Besides migrants’ self-led efforts, civil society has stepped up to help, with the Spanish Red Cross 

distributing food

 at Trampolín Beach, the site of one makeshift camp. Other local charities like Luna Blanca, have been 

providing

 between 2,700 and 3,500 meals a day in five locations with initial funding from the Spanish government. NNK, a group started by Serbian activists in 2017 that supports migrants along the Balkan and Mediterranean routes to the EU, has been working in Ceuta since 2021. It has grown from a fixed team of four to more than 21 volunteers, after a call for help in early August through social media and Signal groups with other grassroots organizations providing aid to migrants in EU borders. Operations have shifted in the three months since the migrants arrived, and NNK is now cooking and serving over 1,200 meals a day in a new industrial-size kitchen. 




Fernández shared how the group has adapted its work on the ground to keep up with a crisis situation. “For more than a month [after July 30], we were not able to do proper legal accompaniment, because the system was broken and we were just trying to register people,” he said. “We tried to divide our work into four different teams: legal, health, cooking, awareness.” To keep things coordinated, aid groups in Ceuta hold a weekly meeting to share information and needs. The most pressing needs are for immediate humanitarian assistance, including clothes distribution, housing for vulnerable groups and phone charging. 




Volunteers arrive from Spain and mostly other European countries, contributing what they can based on their experience. “I provided direct basic health care because of the barriers to accessing medical care and the huge health needs due to violence and living conditions,” said Irene, the doctor who volunteered with NNK. She said she assessed dozens of cases involving wounds or injuries resulting from assaults, mostly perpetrated by the Spanish military. 




The 

hostility of authorities toward migrants

 has also extended to volunteers, who carry out their daily work under intense police monitoring. Police constantly ask for identification documents and conduct searches, including of food containers meant for distribution. Reprisals against volunteers and grassroots groups have taken multiple forms, from administrative fines to criminal charges of “trafficking.” A volunteer who had previously spent time in Ukraine and Syria reported that the seven-square mile enclave of Ceuta felt considerably more militarized than either of those countries.




Lessons learned and the way ahead 




Spain’s response to the people who crossed into Ceuta has been shocking to many observers, especially for a country that has been considered among the more progressive in the European Union on migration. This comes at a time when states are slowly beginning to implement the 

EU Pact on Migration and Asylum

, a new and comprehensive reform to migration management which includes a focus on 

external borders

. Legal advocates argue that 

this pact

, coupled with the use of 

emergency laws

, could suspend migration and human rights law in the EU during mass border crossings like the one in Ceuta. 
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













Solidarity groups 

have also come under attack

 and are looking for ways to move forward in this new atmosphere. Greece is among the first countries to implement the pact and one that has led the way in criminalizing humanitarian efforts to support migrants. This increasing criminalization is happening “through the misuse of the criminal justice system to target and persecute activists and people in solidarity for their work, as well as through administrative law, such as harsher requirements for the registration of civil society organizations,” said Eleni Sirri from the Border Violence Monitoring Network, a network of NGOs, associations and collectives that monitors human rights violations at and within European borders. 




Anna Gruber is the advocacy manager from Collective Aid, an NGO working with migrants in the borderlands of Serbia, Bosnia and Greece. She shared how Collective Aid also had to reorganize and strategize about the way ahead, given the increase in crackdowns on humanitarian work, as well as the anticipated changes because of the EU pact. “We are now focusing more on capturing conditions in detention, [and] mapping deaths and disappearances on the borders,” she said. “While these are hard to trace, bringing all the scattered evidence we can find together helps showcase the EU’s focus on detention camps and the containment of migration that is at heart of the new pact.” 




Like other groups navigating the criminalization of migration and anticipated changes under the new pact, NNK feels it is important for grassroots groups across the EU and beyond to come together around migrant rights. Fernández believes putting energy into growing networks and collectives of grassroots groups is the way forward. “The far-right in Europe and instrumentalization of migration will continue to grow,” he said. “We need to prepare for that and learn from each other to be stronger.” 




Kirsten Dimovitz, the advocacy coordinator for the Border Violence Monitoring Network and a volunteer in Ceuta, contributed additional reporting to the story

.




This article 

Inside the resistance to Spain’s crackdown on migrants in Ceuta

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.

author: C4SS
title: C4SS Panelists on the Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie
content:
The 

Markets and Society conference

 this weekend (October 23-26) will feature many interesting panels on topics from public policy to self-governance to digital privacy to immigration and beyond. There will also be longtime C4SSers presenting.




On 

Saturday from 9:00-10:30am

, Nathan Goodman is chairing the panel “The Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie” featuring:




Cory Massimino – National Economic Planning: What is Right?




Don Lavoie argued in “National Economic Planning: What is Left?” that economic planning was inherently reactionary and thwarted genuinely left-wing aims like peace and liberation. Despite the prevailing conservative-libertarian fusionism of Lavoie’s day, his study of economics and history helped him see the transience of such an alliance: libertarianism was left-wing until the left became obsessed with economic planning and the right was always about militarism and hierarchy no matter how much libertarian rhetoric it adopted. Lavoie’s new (yet old) framing went under appreciated during his time and deserves careful reconsidering for anticipating the contemporary right’s increasing authoritarianism. This essay will build on Lavoie’s framing of economic planning as essentially right-wing, apply that framing to the contemporary American political situation, and argue such a framing is essential for any coherent conception of the political landscape going forward.




Jason Lee Byas – A Role For Lavoian Democracy




Don Lavoie argues for detaching our concept of democracy from the particular institution of voting, and instead seeing it as “openness,” or accessible means to shaping the world around you and its rules. An advantage of this approach is its complementarity with markets and property rights, which might otherwise be seen as in tension with democracy — thus partially reuniting liberalism’s “libertarian” and “democratic” commitments. Yet there is still a tension here. Philosophically, many libertarians may think that any social rules involving force should simply be set by natural rights, and so leaving these open to adjustment by anyone at all (let alone with open access to everyone) will be a problem. Practically, open access to reshaping the rules may spell uncertainty in problematic ways. I resolve these remaining tensions by suggesting a specific role for Lavoian Democracy. In short, many things are left radically indeterminate by any socially-practiced system of rights, and so too are many things left radically indeterminate by a commitment to natural rights. Questions of interpretation and resolution loom large, and the process of interpretation and resolution can either be hierarchical and authoritarian, or a product of ground-up contestation. There are principled liberal grounds — both moral and epistemic — for favoring the latter, and this is the role for Lavoian Democracy. I then offer a handful of institutions and practices that Lavoian Democracy might favor, including unions (of a certain form), adverse possession, and the common law.




Akiva Malamet – Beyond Recognition: Identity, Cultural Discovery, and the Limits of Social Planning




Scholars in liberal theory and political economy have long emphasized what Don Lavoie called the “knowledge problem”: social information is dispersed, local, emergent, and personal, and thus inaccessible to centralized or “high modernist” institutions. Lavoie and others showed that state economic planning fails because planners cannot access or generate this kind of knowledge and often undermine its creation. Liberal institutions, by contrast, enable people to align diverse plans and generate forms of knowledge no top-down authority could anticipate. I extend these insights to issues of identity, cultural development, and interpersonal life. Identity and cultural formation are bottom-up, organic processes reflecting the nuances of how people self-conceive, relate, and find meaning. State planning and institutional treatments of identity often obstruct pluralistic self-concepts and cultural discovery, flattening human diversity and complex individual lives into simple, legible categories. Ironically, formal recognition can perpetuate the injustices it was intended to remedy and reinforce intergroup conflict. State recognition of identity undermines the processes through which identity becomes meaningful, and conflicts with core liberal values of pluralism, self-authorship, and cooperation. Immigration restrictions present an analogous case: they constrain the unpredictable ways natives and migrants associate, pushing societies toward narrower cultural configurations and limiting the scope of both native and migrant identities and life plans. Just as national economic planning distorts economies, national social planning limits the discovery processes through which identity, meaning, and belonging emerge. Lavoie’s work illuminates the epistemic complexity of cultural formation and inner life — offering crucial resources for rethinking identity in open societies.




Roderick Long will also be there, as part of a separate panel on Sunday at 9:00am, offering comments on Aeon Skoble’s “Deleting the State.”




We hope to see many of you there!

author: David Venn
title: QEC announces planned power outages in Kimmirut, Resolute Bay
content:
Qulliq Energy Corp. is planning outages in Kimmirut and Resolute Bay this weekend, with the possibility of an outage in Iqaluit as well.




The corporation announced the outages in a series of public service announcements Thursday as it gears up for a weekend of work.




In Resolute Bay, QEC is carrying out maintenance on the power lines to get them ready for winter. A planned outage is set to take place Saturday and Sunday from 7 a.m. to 11 a.m. to allow for this work.




In Kimmirut, QEC is installing a new generator in the hamlet’s power plant. An outage is scheduled for Sunday, from 6 a.m. to 9 a.m.




In Iqaluit, QEC says it expects to be able to connect a new generator to its power plant without interrupting power to the community.




“However, a temporary outage remains possible in the event of an unexpected equipment malfunction,” the announcement said.




The scheduled work in Iqaluit is scheduled for Saturday and Sunday, from 6 a.m. to 8 a.m.

title: Συγκεντρώσεις αλληλεγγύης σε διωκόμενους, Παρασκευή 23/10
content:
>Για την πλήρη αθώωση του Δ. Χαρτζουλάκη και της Χ. Χοτζόγλου, 9:00 ΠΔΕ Αττικής,


-συγκέντρωση και στις 14:00 στο ΥΜΑΘ, Θεσσαλονίκη


>Για τον Α. εκ των συλληφθέντων της υπόθεσης της 1/7 στη Θεσσαλονίκη, 9:30 δικαστήρια


>Για τους προφυλακισμένους της υπόθεσης της Marfin, 10:00 δικαστήρια Ευελπίδων










ΝΑ ΑΘΩΩΘΟΥΝ ΠΛΗΡΩΣ Ο ΔΗΜΗΤΡΗΣ ΧΑΡΤΖΟΥΛΑΚΗΣ ΚΑΙ Η ΧΡΥΣΑ ΧΟΤΖΟΓΛΟΥ!




ΠΑΡΑΣΚΕΥΗ 23/10

 

στις 09:00

 ΞΑΝΑ ΟΛΟΙ ΣΥΓΚΕΝΤΡΩΣΗ στην ΠΔΕ Αττικής




(Ξενίας 24, κοντά στο μετρό Μέγαρο Μουσικής)




ΝΑ ΑΘΩΩΘΟΥΝ ΠΛΗΡΩΣ Ο ΔΗΜΗΤΡΗΣ ΧΑΡΤΖΟΥΛΑΚΗΣ ΚΑΙ Η ΧΡΥΣΑ ΧΟΤΖΟΓΛΟΥ!




ΝΑ ΜΗΝ ΤΟΥΣ ΕΠΙΒΛΗΘΕΙ ΚΑΜΙΑ ΠΟΙΝΗ!




ΚΑΤΩ ΤΑ ΧΕΡΙΑ ΑΠΟ ΤΑ ΣΩΜΑΤΕΙΑ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΓΩΝΕΣ!




ΟΙ ΕΛΜΕ-ΣΕΠΕ ΚΑΙ ΟΙ ΟΛΜΕ-ΔΟΕ-ΑΔΕΔΥ ΝΑ ΠΑΡΟΥΝ ΑΠΟΦΑΣΕΙΣ ΑΠΕΡΓΙΑΣ (3+3 ή 24ωρη)




Ορίστηκε για τις 23/10 (Παρασκευή) το «τελικό» πειθαρχικό για τους αγωνιστές εκπαιδευτικούς Δημήτρη Χ. και Χρύσα Χ., που παραπέμφθηκαν με απόφαση του ΔΔΕ Πειραιά (και νυν ΠΔΕ Αττικής), με βαρύ κατηγορητήριο, που επισύρει μέχρι και την ποινή της απόλυσης

, για τη συμμετοχή τους σε κινητοποίηση ενάντια στην αξιολόγηση σε σχολείο του Πειραιά, μαζί με μαθητές και άλλους εκπαιδευτικούς!




Πρόκειται για την υπόθεση που κλιμάκωσε την βιομηχανία των διώξεων, αφού επιχειρήθηκε να ανοίξει ο δρόμος για τις απολύσεις στο δημόσιο σχολείο για συνδικαλιστικούς λόγους. Αφού επιβλήθηκε, με πολιτική απόφαση, για 18 μήνες το καθεστώς της δυνητικής αργίας στην Χρύσα και επιχειρήθηκε να γίνει το ίδιο και με τον Δημήτρη.




Τώρα λίγο διάστημα μετά που ανακοινώθηκε στη Χρύσα η επιστροφή στο σχολείο της, αποτέλεσμα όλου αυτού του επίμονου αγώνα που εξελισσόταν 2 χρόνια τώρα, οι 2 αγωνιστές εκπαιδευτικοί σέρνονται ξανά στο Πειθαρχικό για να κριθεί αν είναι ένοχοι ή όχι! Αν είναι ενοχή δηλαδή (που να επισύρει μάλιστα την ποινή της οριστικής παύσης) η συμμετοχή στην συλλογική πάλη, η υπεράσπιση του δωρεάν δημόσιου σχολείου, η υπεράσπιση των εργασιακών δικαιωμάτων των εκπαιδευτικών!




Γιατί αυτό επιχειρείται με όλη την βιομηχανία διώξεων! Η επιβολή οριστικής σιωπής απέναντι στον οδοστρωτήρα των δικαιωμάτων μας, απέναντι στην φτωχοποίηση στις πολιτικές που μας σέρνουν στην πολεμική εμπλοκή!




Δεν θα τους περάσει! Όπως καταφέραμε με τους αγώνες μας και είχαμε τις επιτυχίες στα πειθαρχικά και τις διώξεις το προηγούμενο διάστημα, έτσι θα συνεχίσουμε! Και όλα αυτά τα πετύχαμε με 

ΟΠΛΟ

 την 

ΑΠΕΡΓΙΑ

. Με τη 

μαζική κινητοποίηση του κόσμου στον δρόμο

 τόσο εκείνη την ημέρα όσο και όλο το προηγούμενο διάστημα. Που προσπέρασε τις αγκυλώσεις και τις υπονομεύσεις του αγώνα και του επέβαλλε μαζικά και πανελλαδικά χαρακτηριστικά! 

Έτσι ΠΡΕΠΕΙ ΝΑ ΓΙΝΕΙ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΡΑ.




ΕΛΜΕ-ΣΕΠΕ και ΟΛΜΕ-ΔΟΕ-ΑΔΕΔΥ να παρουν αποφάσεις έτσι ώστε εκείνη την μέρα να αποτελέσει μέρα πανελλαδικής απεργιακής κινητοποίησης ενάντια στις διώξεις (με 3+3 στάσεις εργασίας ή 24ωρη). Δε θα ανεχτούμε άλλο εκφυλισμό όπως αυτόν που είδαμε στα Πειθαρχικά στις 30/9 όπου ο κόσμος έφευγε, ενώ οι διωκόμενοι απολογούνταν στο Πειθαρχικό επειδή η πλειοψηφία στην ΟΛΜΕ (ΑΣΕ-ΔΑΚΕ-ΣΥΝΕΚ-ΠΕΚ) δεν έβγαλε καθόλου στάση εργασίας, με αστεία «επιχειρήματα»!




Καλούμε όλους τους συναδέλφους να κινητοποιηθούν μαζικά στα σωματεία τους ώστε να παρθούν οι απαραίτητες αποφάσεις για να υπάρξει για ακόμα μια φορά μια μεγάλη απεργιακή συγκέντρωση στις 23/10 έξω από την ΠΔΕ Αττικής αλλά και σε όλη τη χώρα.




ΠΑΡΑΣΚΕΥΗ 23/10

 στις 

09:00

 ΞΑΝΑ ΟΛΟΙ στην ΠΔΕ Αττικής (Ξενίας 24, κοντά στο μετρό Μέγαρο Μουσικής). ΝΑ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΜΕΡΑ ΑΠΕΡΓΙΑΣ ΕΝΑΝΤΙΑ ΣΤΙΣ ΔΙΩΞΕΙΣ




ΝΑ ΑΘΩΩΘΟΥΝ ΠΛΗΡΩΣ Ο ΔΗΜΗΤΡΗΣ ΧΑΡΤΖΟΥΛΑΚΗΣ ΚΑΙ Η ΧΡΥΣΑ ΧΟΤΖΟΓΛΟΥ




ΝΑ ΠΑΡΘΟΥΝ ΠΙΣΩ ΟΛΕΣ ΟΙ ΔΙΩΞΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΠΕΙΘΑΡΧΙΚΑ
















Στην εκδίκαση του οριστικού πειθαρχικού της Χρύσας και του Δημήτρη θα είμαστε και πάλι εκεί!




Το δικαίωμα στη συνδικαλιστική δράση και την απεργία είναι κατακτημένο με αγώνες! Θα το υπερασπιστούμε συλλογικά μέχρι τη νίκη!




ΟΛΕΣ/ ΟΛΟΙ ΤΗΝ ΠΑΡΑΣΚΕΥΗ 23/10/2026 ΣΤΙΣ 09:00 π.μ. ΕΞΩ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΠΕΡΙΦΕΡΕΙΑΚΗ ΔΙΕΥΘΥΝΣΗ ΑΤΤΙΚΗΣ (Ξενίας 24, κοντά στο Μέγαρο Μουσικής)







Την Παρασκευή 30 Οκτωβρίου 2026, οι συνάδελφοί μας Χρύσα Χοτζόγλου (μέλος της ΕΛΜΕ Πειραιά) και Δημήτρης Χαρτζουλάκης (μέλος της ΕΛΜΕ Δυτικής Αττικής) έρχονται αντιμέτωποι για ακόμα μια φορά με το πειθαρχικό συμβούλιο εκπαίδευσης διωκόμενοι πειθαρχικά, επειδή τόλμησαν να εκφράσουν τη διαφωνία τους ενάντια στην ατομική αξιολόγηση μαζί με άλλους συναδέλφους, αλλά και με μαθητές τους το Μάρτιο του 2024 στο σχολείο που υπηρετούσαν, ασκώντας το συνδικαλιστικό τους δικαίωμα και εφαρμόζοντας τις αποφάσεις του σωματείου τους.




Συγκεκριμένα κατηγορούνται για 

χαρακτηριστικώς αναξιοπρεπή συμπεριφορά

 που συνίσταται σύμφωνα με το κατηγορητήριο, σε φωνασκίες και άσκηση ψυχολογικής βίας (προπηλακισμό) ενάντια στον αξιολογητή- σύμβουλο, ο οποίος και κίνησε την πειθαρχική και ποινική διαδικασία. Η συγκεκριμένη κατηγορία μπορεί να επισύρει μέχρι και την ποινή της οριστικής παύσης, δηλαδή την απόλυσή τους!




Για πολλοστή φορά τα τελευταία χρόνια διώκεται και ποινικοποιείται το δικαίωμα έκφρασης άποψης και συνδικαλιστικής δράσης των συναδέλφων/ισων μας, δηλαδή το δικαίωμα των εργαζόμενων εκπαιδευτικών να αγωνίζονται ενάντια στο μηχανισμό πειθάρχησης που επιβάλλει η αξιολόγηση στα δημόσια σχολεία. 

Έτσι γίνεται ξεκάθαρο ότι οι παραπάνω διώξεις είναι πολιτικές και αποσκοπούν στην επιβολή ενός κλίματος φόβου και τρομοκρατίας για όλους και όλες μας ως εργαζόμενων, αλλά και ως εκπαιδευτικών μέσω της απόπειρας τιμώρησης των συνδικαλιστών συναδέλφων μας. Το μήνυμα του συστήματος είναι σαφές: «Μην αντιδράτε σε τίποτα γιατί θα μπλέξετε!»




Και το ερώτημα που τίθεται σε όλους και όλες μας είναι επίσης σαφές:

 θα τους αφήσουμε να ισοπεδώσουν κάθε δικαίωμα μας και κάθε έννοια της αξιοπρέπειας μας στο χώρο εργασίας μας; Θα τους αφήσουμε να προχωρήσουν σε περαιτέρω διώξεις και πολιτική στοχοποίηση των απόψεων και της δράσης μας;




Και η απάντηση συνάδελφοι είναι και πρέπει να είναι μια και μόνο μια: ΟΧΙ! Και το όχι μας αυτό πρέπει να γίνει πράξη μέσα από τη συμπαράσταση μας στους διωκόμενους συναδέλφους μας και από την ταυτόχρονη διαμαρτυρία μας για τις κατηγορίες που τους αποδίδονται με στόχο να καταπνίξουν και να ενοχοποιήσουν για ακόμα μια φορά τη συνδικαλιστική και πολιτική δράση!




Και το όχι αυτό πρέπει να το πούμε δίνοντας τη μάχη με την παρουσία μας κατά τη συνεδρίαση του πειθαρχικού συμβουλίου στις 23/10 έξω από το κτίριο της ΠΔΕ Αττικής στην οδό Ξενίας 24! Όπως κάναμε και στις δύο άλλες μεγάλες συγκεντρώσεις που προηγήθηκαν (23/10/24 και 29/4/26). Η συμπαράσταση στους συναδέλφους μας είναι ο δικός μας αγώνας για τα δικαιώματα όλων μας σε αξιοπρεπή εργασία, στη δυνατότητα προάσπισης της ελευθερίας έκφρασης και δράσης μας στο δημόσιο σχολείο, αλλά και της δημοκρατικής λειτουργίας της εκπαίδευσης!







Διεκδικούμε την αθώωση των συναδέλφων μας και την παύση κάθε πολιτικής δίωξης!




Κάτω τα χέρια από τους απεργούς συναδέλφους/συναδέλφισές μας!




Να μην περάσει το κλίμα φόβου και τρομοκρατίας στα σχολεία!




Κανένας και καμία μόνη απέναντι στις διώξεις – Η συνδικαλιστική δράση δεν ποινικοποιείται!




Η μάχη ενάντια στην αξιολόγηση συνεχίζεται

!










Ζ’ ΣΕΠΕ ΘΕΣΣΑΛΟΙΝΙΚΗΣ – ΨΗΦΙΣΜΑ ΣΥΜΠΑΡΑΣΤΑΣΗΣ




στους σ. Χρ. Χοτζόγλου και Δημ. Χαρζουλάκη – Στις 23/10 το οριστικό Πειθαρχικό – Να


μην επιβληθεί καμιά ποινή – Κάτω τα χέρια από τη συνδικαλιστική δράση




ΣΥΓΚΕΝΤΡΩΣΗ ΔΙΑΜΑΡΤΥΡΙΑΣ την ΠΑΡΑΣΚΕΥΗ 23/10, 2μμ, στο Υ.ΜΑ.Θ.




Για την Παρασκευή 23/10 ορίστηκε η εκδίκαση του Πειθαρχικού για τους Δημήτρη Χαρτζουλάκη


(νεοδιόριστος και μέλος της Α’ ΕΛΜΕ Δυτικής Αττικής) και Χρύσα Χοτζόγλου (μέλος της ΕΛΜΕ


Πειραιά) για την συνδικαλιστική τους δράση! Μάλιστα το κατηγορητήριο που τους έχει, απαράδεκτα,


απαγγελθεί μπορεί να επισύρει μέχρι και την ποινή της οριστικής παύσης (απόλυση)!


Υπενθυμίζουμε ότι ο Δημήτρης Χαρτζουλάκης και η Χρύσα Χοτζόγλου είχαν παραπεμφθεί στο


Πειθαρχικό με μόνο «έγκλημά» τους την έκφραση διαφωνίας και διαμαρτυρίας από κοινού με


μαθητές και εκπαιδευτικούς για την πραγματοποίηση αξιολόγησης σε σχολείο του Πειραιά, δηλαδή


εξέφρασαν την αντίθεση του κλάδου στην αξιολόγηση όπως αποτυπώνεται στις συλλογικές


αποφάσεις ΟΛΜΕ και ΕΛΜΕ. Και οι δύο έχουν διατελέσει μέλη του ΔΣ της ΕΛΜΕ Πειραιά.


Υπενθυμίζουμε επίσης ότι στις 29/4 παραπέμφθηκαν με το ερώτημα της δυνητικής αργίας, κάτι που


το Πειθαρχικό ομόφωνα απέρριψε κάτω από πίεση των κινητοποιήσεων, και αυτό είχε και σαν


αποτέλεσμα να πιεστεί η Υπουργός και να πάρει την απόφαση (25/8) της επιστροφής της Χρύσας


στο σχολείο μετά από 18 μήνες από την απαράδεκτη απόφαση του πρώην ΥΠΑΙΘ.


Αποτέλεσε κλιμάκωση της βιομηχανίας των 2500 διώξεων και της τρομοκρατίας ενάντια στους


εκπαιδευτικούς που αγωνίζονται για δημόσιο και δωρεάν σχολείο και συντάσσονται με τις


συλλογικές αποφάσεις των σωματείων τους. Το άνοιγμα του παράθυρου για απολύσεις και στο


δημόσιο σχολείο για συνδικαλιστικούς λόγους είναι το απόγειο αυτής της προσπάθειας!


Ξέρουμε πολύ καλά ότι η πολιτική των διώξεων πάει χέρι χέρι με την πολιτική της φτώχειας, του


πολέμου της διάλυσης των δικαιωμάτων μας! Για αυτό απαιτούν να σωπάσουμε! Αλλά δεν κάνουμε


πίσω!


Οι αγώνες και οι συνεχείς μαζικές κινητοποιήσεις όλου αυτού του διαστήματος έχουν παραγάγει


αποτελέσματα: όχι μόνο την επιστροφή της Χρύσας στο σχολείο και την αποτροπή αργίας για τον


Δημήτρη, αλλά και τις πρώτες μαζικές δικαιώσεις εκπαιδευτικών για την απεργία αποχή από την


ατομική αξιολόγηση αλλά και άλλες συνδικαλιστικές διώξεις!


Συνεχίζουμε κι απαιτούμε να μην επιβληθεί καμιά απολύτως ποινή στους 2 συναδέλφους!


Να σταματήσουν τώρα όλες οι διώξεις και τα πειθαρχικά!


Κάτω τα χέρια από τα σωματεία-τους αγώνες-τους αγωνιστές- την απεργία!
















Συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης στα προφυλακισμενα συντρόφια







Στις 10/7, 2 συντρόφια και ένα ακόμα άτομο συλλαμβάνονται από την «αντι»τρομοκρατική, ενώ η τελευταία συνδέει τις συλλήψεις με πρόσφατο εμπρησμό. Παράλληλα πραγματοποιούνται, μετά από 16 χρόνια, συλλήψεις για την υπόθεση της Marfin. Επιπλέον την Πέμπτη 16/07 συλλαμβάνεται ένας ακόμα σύντροφος με τα κανάλια να τον συνδέουν με την υπόθεση της 01/07 της Θεσσαλονίκης και την αντιτρομοκρατική να εισβάλλει σπίτι του, πραγματοποιόντας έρευνα. Τα τρία συντρόφια προφυλακίζονται με τα μίντια να επιτίθενται στον αναρχικό χώρο και τη δικογραφία να παραμένει ανοικτή.




Δύναμη ως την λευτεριά στα συντρόφια μας, που είναι στα χέρια του κράτους.




Αγώνας, αυτοοργάνωση, αλληλεγγύη




Ανοιχτή συνέλευση αλληλεγγύης στα 3 προφυλακισμένα συντροφια για την υπόθεση της 01/07 στη Θεσσαλονίκη













Τα ξημερώματα της 1ης Ιούλη πραγματοποιείται τριπλή εμπρηστική επίθεση σε σπίτια πολιτευτών της ΝΔ στη Θεσσαλονίκη. Η μία απο αυτές οδήγησε στον, υπό αδιευκρίνιστες μέχρι στιγμής συνθήκες, θάνατο της Βάγιας Νέστορα, μητέρας της πολιτεύτριας με τη ΝΔ, Αφροδίτης Νέστορα. Η κυβέρνηση και τα μίντια, ως είθισται, άδραξαν την ευκαιρία εργαλειοποίησης του εν λόγω θανάτου πραγματώνοντας το προεκλογικό τους σόου. Ως συνήθως, στο στόχαστρο των ερευνών, βρέθηκε για άλλη μία φορά ο α/α χώρος, με τα μίντια να συντηρούν το αφήγημα της κυβέρνησης, παρουσιάζοντας τον αντιεξουσιαστικό χώρο ως τη μήτρα παραγωγής υπόπτων, προδικάζοντας την υπόθεση πρωτού αυτή φτάσει στα χέρια της αστικής δικαιοσύνης.


Εννιά ημέρες μετά, η αντιτρομοκρατική προχωράει στη σύλληψη του συντρόφου Χάρη Σ., της συντρόφισσας Γεωργίας Β. κι ενός ακόμα ατόμου, ενώ στις 16/7 συλλαμβάνεται και οδηγείται στη ΓΑΔΘ ο σύντροφος Αίμονας Τ., με μοναδικό στοιχείο ενοχής την ψευδομαρτυρία του τρίτου συλληφθέντα. Ελλείψει στοιχείων, παρά την άρνηση όλων των κατηγοριών και ενώ δεν δόθηκε το περιθώριο εξέτασης μαρτύρων υπεράσπισης από την ανακρίτρια, αποφασίζεται η προφυλάκιση των δύο συντρόφων και της συντρόφισσας, οι οποίοι οδηγούνται στις φυλακές Λάρισας, Δράμας και Κορυδαλλού. προκειμένου να ολοκληρωθεί το αναγκαίο αφήγημα κράτους-μίντια, περί της ύπαρξης τουλάχιστον τριών δραστών και να αποκατασταθεί η “κοινωνική ειρήνη”. Παράλληλα, τα ειδησιογραφικά ασκώντας άριστα την ποταπή δουλειά τους διαρρέουν φωτογραφίες της συντρόφισσας και του συντρόφου από τυχαίες κάμερες της πόλης, ποινικοποιώντας για ακόμα μία φορά τις συντροφικές και φιλικές σχέσεις εντός του χώρου. Φυσικά, ο πολιτικός χρόνος στον οποίο συμβαίνουν τα παραπάνω δεν είναι τυχαίος. Είναι εμφανές πως το ελληνικό κράτος έχει εισέλθει σε καθεστώς πολεμικής προετοιμασίας και επομένως σε καθεστώς θωράκισης απέναντι σε εσωτερικούς εχθρούς. Εχθροί οι οποίοι κατασκευάζονται και παρουσιάζονται με μαεστρία από τον κρατικό μηχανισμό, με στόχο τον αποπροσανατολισμό του δημόσιου διαλόγου από τους υπαίτιους της εκμετάλλευσης και εξαθλίωσης των ζωών μας.




Δεν μας εκπλήσσει η χυδαία στάση μπάτσων, δημοσιογράφων και δικαστών απέναντί μας, αλλά ούτε και η αναξιοπρεπής μεταχείρηση και ο ευτελισμός του θανάτου ενός ατόμου της “δικής τους πλευράς”, με τα στελέχη της ΝΔ να παίζουν ένα ντροπιαστικό και συνάμα θλιβερό θέατρο στα κανάλια, προκειμένου να ασκήσουν συναισθηματικές πιέσεις στο κοινωνικό σύνολο. Οι τακτικές αυτές στοχεύουν διαχρονικά στην αποδυνάμωση και διάσπαση του α/α χώρου μέσα από ψεύδη και βρώμικα πολιτικά παιχνίδια.


Απέναντι σε όλη τη λασπολογία, τη χυδαιότητα και τη στοχοποίηση του αντιεξουαστικού κινήματος απαντάμε πως όχι μόνο τρόμο δεν αισθανόμαστε, αλλά τώρα, πολύ περισσότερο από ποτέ, μπροστά στην ολομέτωπη επίθεση που συλλογικά δεχόμαστε, δεν σκύβουμε το κεφάλι. Όσο προσπαθείτε να καταστήσετε κανονικότητα την υποτίμηση της ανθρώπινης ζωής, τόσο οι αγώνες μας θα μπαίνουν ανάχωμα στα σχέδιά σας. Στεκόμαστε πλάι στα συντρόφια μας με υπερηφάνεια, υψώνοντας τις φωνές μας ωστέ να μην σας αφήσουμε να ξεχάσετε πως οι δολοφόνοι είστε εσείς.
