author: Lillian Kollross
title: Texas Mother Sues Anti-Abortion Extremists Under Law Targeting Abortion Pills
content:
Last week, a Texas mother sued Kristan Hawkins, the president and founder of Students for Life of America, an anti-abortion organization, and three other staff members for breaking a law the group helped to establish.

In March 2026, Hawkins posted an Instagram photo with two other staff members in front of the Space Center Houston with the caption: “Guess what we are doing? Ordering abortion pills undercover? Yep. Stay tuned.”

The lawsuit was filed on Oct. 6 by Maria Puerto, who is using a pseudonym to protect her family. Ms. Puerto believes that the group violated House Bill 7, known as the Woman and Child Protection Act, and also mocked those Texans who were deeply affected by the bill.

In December 2025, the Texas legislature passed the Woman and Child Protection Act, which allows almost anyone to sue a person who imports, delivers, or prescribes abortion pills. Plaintiffs can win at least $100,000 per violation.

Despite being on birth control, in 2022, Puerto became pregnant. This unplanned pregnancy came right after Texas banned abortions. With no money or way to travel out of state, along with caring for her disabled mother, Puerto was unable to get an abortion and was forced to carry to term.

The pregnancy took a toll on every aspect of her life. Severe morning sickness caused her to miss class and lose her scholarship. She then lost her job at a convenience store and had to drop out of college. In 2024, Puerto had another unplanned pregnancy.

“I had everything in my hands,” Puerto said in a Spanish interview with The New York Times. “But the laws came like a hurricane and took everything away.”

Now, at age 26, she shares a room with her young children at her mother’s house and is unable to find a job that could cover the cost of raising two children. After seeing the Hawkin’s photo on social media, Puerto filed the suit.

“I’ve filed a lawsuit against those who helped build these horrible laws,” Puerto wrote in a statement, “And then had the privilege to break them in an attempt to trap women like me who still need help.”

From the four defendants, Puerto is seeking $459,782 – the average cost of raising two children until adulthood in Texas. Since Puerto is not connected to the defendants, if she wins the lawsuit, she will be awarded $10,000 while the rest of the money must be held in a trust for a charity chosen by the plaintiff.

According to Abortion in America, the organization supporting Puerto’s legal case, she has chosen to donate the money to Jane’s Due Process, a non-profit that helps young Texans access abortions and birth control.

Puerto’s lawsuit puts the law’s enforcement mechanism under scrutiny. HB 7 allows individuals to bring lawsuits over alleged violations, even when they were not personally affected by the conduct. Puerto is now using that mechanism to challenge anti-abortion activists who supported the law.

Her case highlights the consequences of abortion restrictions for people who cannot afford to travel for care. It also raises questions about how broadly Texas’s abortion pill law can be applied and whether those who helped establish it can face legal challenges under its provisions.

author: Sofia Little
title: Election Day is Not the Only Day to Vote
content:
October 24th is Vote Early Day, meant to encourage all eligible United States citizens to vote early and inform voters of their states’ early voting laws.

Early voting offers many voters the convenience and flexibility that match the demands of modern life. It can be especially helpful for people with demanding work schedules, long commutes, caregiving responsibilities or travel plans. For many, the option to vote early can make the difference between casting a ballot and missing the opportunity.

According to the Center for Election and Research (CEIR) nearly 97% of voting-age citizens live in states that offer at least one way to vote before Election Day.

However, access to the ballot remains a concern ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. The Trump administration has deployed a wide variety of intensified voter suppression tactics in an attempt to interfere with the 2026 midterm elections. These tactics range from plans to place federal officials at polling stations and an executive order targeting mail voting. Courts have blocked aspects of the administration’s mail voting order from taking effect.

The impact of these voter suppression maneuvers often harm communities of color. Strict voter ID laws and fewer polling locations in certain areas disproportionately affect voters of color, leading to longer wait times on Election Day and discriminatory intimidation tactics at these locations.

Joyce Vance, a Brennan Center senior fellow and former federal prosecutor, emphasized the importance of protecting voting rights in an interview. “Who you vote for, that’s a political decision. But the right to vote should be something fundamental that everybody in government works to guarantee for all Americans.”

Despite these threats, early voting methods remain secure and convenient ways to participate in the democratic principles our country was founded on. Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward, discussed these challenges in remarks about the role of the courts in protecting voting rights.

Perryman concludes with a request: “The lawyers will file these cases, but people have to be vigilant about their voter registration and about their plan to vote. That is what we need the American people to do.”

So, here are a few reasons why you should vote early:

You avoid the long lines of Election Day.

It can be more logistically convenient than Election Day voting.

It reduces the strain on polling locations on Election Day.

You don’t have to worry about any unforeseen circumstances on Election Day (the weather, flat tire, illness, etc).

It leads to greater election security as it creates more opportunity for polling officials to counteract any issues that might arise, such as a machine breakdown, any threats of voter suppression, human error, and more.

It narrows the opportunity for claims of a ‘rigged’ election.’

For the 2026 general election, 47 states and Washington DC will offer all voters the opportunity to vote early in person, with 37 of those states also offering voters the option to vote by mail without the need to cite a reason. Encourage your friends and family to use this opportunity to practice your constitutional right in upholding democracy.

Check your state’s rules and deadlines before making a plan. For voter registration information, election dates and voting resources, visit Vote411.org/feminist. Election Day is the last day to vote, but it is not the only day to vote.

author: Kiara Green
title: Beyond Indigenous Peoples Day: The Fight to Protect Indigenous Communities
content:
The second Monday in October is federally recognized as Christopher Columbus Day, commemorating the arrival of colonizer Christopher Columbus to the Americas. It’s undeniable that Indigenous communities lived in America long before Columbus docked his ship. Why, then, is he celebrated as the man who “discovered” America?

For years, public debate has challenged this Eurocentric narrative. In response, several states have recognised the second Monday in October as Indigenous Peoples Day. The day celebrates the resilience and the vibrant cultures of Indigenous communities in America.

Despite the lack of federal recognition, Indigenous Peoples Day continues to be celebrated while bringing attention to issues that Indigenous communities face. The day has been used to advocate for the removal of Columbus memorials, the returning of Indigenous lands, and awareness about Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women (MMIW).

The Trump administration has rejected this broader recognition. In 2025, Trump declared he was “bringing Columbus Day back from the ashes,” reinforcing the federal emphasis on celebrating Columbus rather than recognizing Indigenous peoples.

Meanwhile, proposed federal funding cuts of $2.3 billion from the administration continue to impact Tribal programs especially violence related programs and services that support survivors. These reductions could undermine essential services, including programs that address violence and support survivors.

The consequences are especially serious given the rates of violence facing Indigenous communities. On September 15, the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Federal Government Surveillance held a hearing titled “Missing and Murdered Indigenous People: Strengthening Public Safety in Tribal Communities.” Lawmakers and witnesses discussed how the federal government can help ensure the safety of Indigenous communities as they face some of the highest homicide and missing persons rates in the country.

According to the CDC, homicide was the fourth leading cause of death for American Indian and Alaska Natives men and sixth-leading cause for women ages one to 44 in 2023. Tribal communities rely on violence prevention programs and other services to address these disparities. Funding cuts threaten their ability to sustain this work.

During the September hearing, witnesses urged members to increase the funding for tribal communities to sustain these instrumental programs. Trent Shores, former U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Oklahoma, stressed that “Resources need to reach the people and stay there.” Myron Lizer, Former Vice President of Navajo Nation, similarly warned that “we have built programs but not continuous systems,” highlighting the gap between establishing initiatives and providing the sustained resources communities need.

Legislation like Savanna’s Act and the Not Invisible Act have started to address missing and murdered Native Americans by strengthening relations between federal and tribal law enforcement. However, significant gaps remain in preventing violence, investigating cases and supporting survivors.

As Indigenous communities continue to face high levels of homicide and missing person rates, Congress must continue to act and pass the Trace Act for a concise database. Honoring Indigenous resilience goes beyond annual recognition but a continued effort to guarantee sustained resources and legislative action that protect these communities from ongoing violence and funding cuts.

author: Bianca Blell
title: Women and Girls Severely Affected in Colombia’s 7.4 Earthquake
content:
On August 10th, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia, with its epicenter near San José del Palmar in the department of Chocó. It was the strongest earthquake recorded in the country in a decade. The disaster damaged homes and essential infrastructure across multiple departments, displacing residents and disrupting access to health care and other critical services.

Chocó, which has a large Afro-Colombian population, was among the hardest-hit areas. During this catastrophic tragedy, where 335 people died, 4,611 people were injured, and which left 111 people missing, it remains the country’s deadliest earthquake since the 1990s.

Though spread out through other nations and departments, most deaths occurred in Valle del Cauca and Risaralda, as the earthquake caused severe humanitarian and protection challenges for vulnerable populations, especially girls and women. More than 31,460 homes were destroyed. 4,996 community centers and 348 health facilities were affected due to conditions from the event. This large scale loss of housing, displacement, and disruption from essential networks have heightened risk of Gender-Based Violence (GBV), especially in rural communities.

In these communities, girls and women face heightened risks of exploitation, harassment, and sexual abuse due to the increase of displacement and chaos as a result of the earthquake. These risks can be categorized into three key impacts girls and women face in Colombia and in many other parts of the world. Protection risks are one key impact, as thousands of families rely on temporary shelters where inadequate privacy, lighting, and sanitation continuously increase exposure to GBV.

Chocó, among the most affected departments, is an area already suffering from pre-existing social and economic inequalities and vulnerabilities, now exacerbated by the 7.4 earthquake. This highlights the second key impact on women and girls, sexual and reproductive health gaps. Pregnant women, specifically those living in rural and remote areas where access was already limited, have suffered greatly from these further deepened barriers. Women and adolescent girls increasingly lack access to menstrual products, hygiene kits, and safe spaces.

These issues are interconnected and compounded by the last key impact, increased displacement and the loss of support networks. The loss of homes and community support systems have reduced girls and women’s access to education, healthcare, and protection services.

Large international actors, including the UNFPA have done tremendous work to aid Colombia’s response to this catastrophic natural disaster. This is a program the US cut all funding to under the current administration.

The earthquake highlights how decisions made by governments and international institutions can affect communities beyond their borders. In the United States, Congress plays an important role in appropriating federal funds, overseeing foreign assistance, and shaping trade policy. The administration also influences how foreign policy priorities are carried out.

The November 3 midterm elections will determine the makeup of Congress, whose members will help shape debates over federal spending, international assistance, and oversight. Voters who want to understand the United States’ role in international humanitarian response can review candidates’ public positions, examine federal funding decisions, and follow how elected officials approach foreign aid and trade.

author: Unknown
title: "Yunanistanlı Ortodoks keşiş Nikolaos Tsigkozis nerede?"
content:
Yunanistan’ın Yanniça şehrinden İstanbul’a gelen 58 yaşındaki Rum Ortodoks keşiş Nikolaos Tsigkozis’in (Keşiş Yosif), kaybolmasının ardından ailesi ve yerel topluluklar hayatından endişe ediyor.




DEM Parti Diyarbakır Milletvekili Serhat Eren, keşişin akıbetinin araştırılması ve bulunması için İçişleri Bakanı Mustafa Çiftçi’nin yanıtlaması istemiyle Meclis’e soru önergesi verdi.




Serhat Eren’in İçişleri Bakanı Mustafa Çiftçi’ye yönelttiği soru önergesinde yer alan bilgilere göre Tsigkozis, 23 Temmuz’da otobüsle İstanbul’a geldi. Ailesinin ve diplomatik misyonların aktardığı bilgilere göre keşiş, en son 25 Temmuz öğle saatlerinde İstanbul’daki Yunanistan Başkonsolosluğu’na gitti.




Başkonsoloslukta Trabzon, Sümela Manastırı ve Karadeniz bölgesinin yanı sıra Kapadokya’daki tarihi Rum manastırları, kilise kalıntıları ve ulaşım olanakları hakkında bilgi alan Tsigkozis’in, şehirlerarası otobüs terminaline yönlendirildiği belirtildi.




Münzevi bir yaşam sürmek amacıyla kırsal bölgelere gitmek istediği aktarılan Tsigkozis’in nerede olduğu ise bilinmiyor.




Ailesi ve yerel topluluklar endişeli







Soru önergesinde, Tsigkozis’in yaklaşık 1,64 metre boyunda, normal kilolu, kır saçlı, kır bıyıklı, kısa sakallı ve yeşil gözlü olduğu bilgisi yer aldı. Türkçe bilmediği ve son görüldüğünde sivil kıyafetler giydiği belirtilen keşişin bulunması için yürütülen çalışmaların durumu gündeme getirildi.




Eren, İçişleri Bakanı Mustafa Çiftçi’ye keşişin Türkiye’ye giriş yaptığı 23 Temmuz’dan itibaren fiziki ya da dijital izine rastlanıp rastlanmadığını, İstanbul’dan Trabzon’a, Karadeniz’e veya Kapadokya’ya gitmiş olabileceğine ilişkin otobüs terminali ve bilet kayıtlarının incelenip incelenmediğini sordu.




Önergede ayrıca, keşişin bulunması ve can güvenliğinin sağlanması için emniyet birimlerinin aktif bir arama veya soruşturma yürütüp yürütmediği soruldu.




Trabzon ve Kapadokya’da arama yapıldı mı?




Eren, keşişin gitmek istediği belirtilen Trabzon ve Kapadokya’daki kolluk kuvvetlerine kayıp ihbarı iletilip iletilmediğini de sordu. Önergede, bölgedeki tarihi kiliseler, manastır kalıntıları ve kırsal inziva alanlarında arama yapılıp yapılmadığına ilişkin bilgi talep edildi.




Eren, İstanbul’daki Yunanistan Başkonsolosluğu ve kayıp kişinin ailesiyle koordineli bir arama süreci yürütülüp yürütülmediğinin açıklanmasını istedi.




Önergede son olarak, konunun insani boyutu ve inanç özgürlüğü de dikkate alınarak yürütülen arama çalışmalarının hangi aşamada olduğu ve kaygılı aileyle kamuoyunun nasıl bilgilendirileceği soruldu.




Eren’den İçişleri Bakanı’na 5 soru




1. Yunanistan vatandaşı Rum Ortodoks Keşiş Nikolaos Tsigkozis’in (Keşiş Yosif) Türkiye’ye giriş yaptığı 23 Temmuz’dan itibaren fiziki veya dijital olarak izine rastlanmış mıdır? İstanbul’dan Trabzon, Karadeniz veya Kapadokya bölgelerine seyahat edip etmediğine ilişkin terminal, otogar veya bilet kayıtlarında inceleme yapılmış mıdır?




2. Kayıp keşişin bulunması, akıbetinin aydınlatılması ve can güvenliğinin sağlanması amacıyla İçişleri Bakanlığı ve emniyet birimleri tarafından başlatılmış aktif bir arama-kurtarma veya soruşturma çalışması bulunmakta mıdır?




3. Keşişin gitmek istediği belirtilen Trabzon ve Kapadokya bölgelerindeki kolluk kuvvetleri ile yerel güvenlik birimlerine kayıp ihbarı ve bilgilendirme iletilmiş midir? Bu bölgelerdeki tarihi kiliseler, manastır kalıntıları ve kırsal inziva alanlarında arama yapılmış mıdır?




4. İstanbul’daki Yunanistan Başkonsolosluğu ve kayıp kişinin ailesiyle koordineli bir bilgi akışı ve arama süreci yürütülmekte midir?




5. Konunun insani boyutu ve inanç özgürlüğü de dikkate alınarak, kamuoyuna ve kaygılı aileye yürütülen arama faaliyetlerinin hangi aşamada olduğuna ilişkin yakın zamanda bilgilendirme yapılması planlanmakta mıdır?

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: John Amagoalik scholarship recipient calls win motivating
content:
Nunavut Sivuniksavut student Jamie Comeau is the winner of this year’s $10,000 John Amagoalik scholarship.




Qikiqtani Inuit Association announced winner Oct. 16 in a news release.




“With this scholarship, it gives me more motivation to keep going into universities after second year, so much more motivation to come to school and do better,” Comeau said in an interview.




The John Amagoalik scholarship scholarship is presented to an Inuk student who is pursuing journalism or studies that promote Inuit language and culture. This year QIA doubled its value from $5,000 to $10,000.




After graduating from Inuksuk High School in Iqaluit, Comeau enrolled in Nunavut Sivuniksavut, an Ottawa-based college program for Inuit.




She graduated her first year of Inuit Studies with honours and an award for her dedication to learning Inuktitut. Now in her second year, Comeau is studying Advanced Inuit Studies.




“I feel a little more at ease when it comes to financial stability. Last year I was struggling,” she said, adding that the scholarship allows her to enjoy the south and focus on her education rather than stress about affording food and housing.
















After graduating from Nunavut Sivuniksavut, Comeau plans to attend Carleton University in Ottawa, though she’s unsure of which program. She says she wants to finish her education at Dalhousie University in Halifax.

author: Blanca Missé
title: As More Unions Oppose ICE and Israel, the Right Is Cracking Down
content:
The right is trying to gain access to labor unions’ minutes, membership lists, and Zoom chats.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

On September 22, The Free Press attacked the California Faculty Association (CFA), which represents about 29,000 faculty, librarians, counselors, and coaches across the California State University (CSU) system. Drawing on private discussions about a proposed Jewish caucus, including communications from a union Zoom meeting, the article accused CFA of antisemitism. How those communications reached the publication remains unclear. Two days later, the Jewish Journal amplified those allegations, urging Gov. Gavin Newsom to consider them as he weighed California Assembly Bill (AB) 2551, CFA-sponsored legislation challenging campus protest restrictions imposed after the 2024 Palestine solidarity encampments. Less than a week after The Free Press story was published, Newsom vetoed the bill.

Pro-Israel and Jewish advocacy organizations had already campaigned against AB 2551 before the union’s internal deliberations were targeted, arguing that greater scrutiny would weaken rules needed to protect Jewish students from harassment and intimidation. Newsom’s veto does not prove coordination, but the campaign portraying CFA as hostile to Jewish students had become entangled with the union’s fight against campus protest restrictions.

The CSU’s systemwide policy prohibits encampments, overnight demonstrations, and unauthorized structures. The CSU Academic Senate immediately condemned the restrictions as undermining academic freedom when it was instituted in 2024, while CFA warned that vague definitions of disruption threatened constitutionally protected speech, assembly, protest, and future strike activity. A major 2026 ACLU-Amnesty study, investigating 80 campuses over two years, documented sweeping repression of Palestine solidarity protests. As the report found, universities “have imposed sweeping restrictions on student speech, initiated disciplinary actions against students, and imposed severe punishments, including expulsions and suspensions.” The ACLU has insisted that even legitimate time, place, and manner restrictions “must leave ample room for students to express themselves.”

The controversy reaches beyond CFA and CSU. Unions and rank-and-file organizations committed to Palestine solidarity have been forced to relitigate, again and again, whether anti-Zionism and solidarity with Palestinians constitute antisemitism — and whether such organizing should be systematically policed, investigated, or surveilled. At stake is a more fundamental right of the exploited: Can workers democratically connect economic struggles with Palestine solidarity, resistance to anti-immigrant and anti-Black racism, and the defense of civil liberties without exposing their organizing and deliberations to external pressure or repression?

We already have a word for the use of legal process as a political weapon: lawfare. You do not necessarily have to win. Investigation, expense, compelled disclosure, and possible sanctions can exact their own price.

Call its media counterpart pressfare: leaked material, selective or doctored quotations, and public identification can turn people into political targets and invite pressure on employers, universities, or government agencies.

The leaked CFA meeting should not be adjudicated through fragments selected for publication, especially when CFA’s statewide record contradicts the portrayal of a union indifferent to antisemitism. During the 2024 encampments, CFA opposed antisemitism and Islamophobia “in all forms” while supporting the encampments. Amid a 2025 federal antisemitism investigation, it stated that “as CFA members, we are united against antisemitism; it has no place in our communities,” while defending members’ academic freedom. CFA’s Palestine, Arab, and Muslim Caucus likewise defines its mission as confronting racism “in all its manifestations,” explicitly including antisemitism. The Free Press story — a clear example of pressfare — sought to overwrite this legacy with weaponized accusations, undermining the trust that workers place in the sanctity of their union spaces and processes.

Antisemitism demands to be taken seriously — which is why accusations of anti-Jewish discrimination should not be instrumentalized. Kenneth Stern, director of the Bard Center for the Study of Hate, has warned that using the International Holocaust Remembrance Association (IHRA) definition of antisemitism as a regulatory code threatens academic freedom by equating criticism of Israel with antisemitism, while the Jerusalem Declaration warns that the definition’s ambiguities have generated confusion and controversy, “hence weakening the fight against antisemitism.” And as Jewish Voice for Peace and Jerusalem Declaration scholars have argued, combating antisemitism is not helped by conflating hostility toward Jews with anti-Zionism, criticism of Israel, or Palestine solidarity. Requiring Palestinian and anti-Zionist unionists to prove otherwise reverses the burden of proof, allowing accusations to substitute for evidence and cultivating fear and suspicion that inhibit collective action while fueling an ever-expanding search for evidence.

That ever-expanding search has taken the form of several federal antisemitism inquiries targeting universities and their workers.

Federal antisemitism investigations have extended scrutiny to faculty speech and Palestine solidarity organizing, with consequences for unions. At Cal State LA, CSU disclosed employees’ personal information to federal investigators, prompting CFA to sue over violations of workers’ privacy.

What drove these federal inquiries on antisemitism? A 2025 study from the American Association of University Professors and the Middle East Studies Association examined 102 complaints that prompted federal civil rights investigations; pro-Israel and right-wing organizations were involved in 78 percent. All but one of the complaints concerned speech critical of Israel, and in 80 percent, complainants characterized criticism of Israel or Zionism that made no reference to Jews or Judaism as antisemitic. In at least half, the complaint rested solely on constitutionally protected political speech.

The study separately examined 28 Title VI antisemitism lawsuits brought against universities by pro-Israel groups. As of its cutoff, not one had produced a final judicial finding of discrimination in favor of the plaintiffs, although some resulted in settlements imposing new restrictions on campus speech and protest.

CFA’s political commitments long predate the renewed Palestine solidarity movement. In 2023, the union challenged CSU administrators on First Amendment grounds for restricting classroom discussion of strikes. In 2020, after years of organizing, CFA helped secure passage of AB 1460, the landmark law making Ethnic Studies a graduation requirement across the CSU system — a major victory for racial justice and educational equity in one of the nation’s most racially and ethnically diverse states. Since then, it has continued fighting CSU over its implementation, defending faculty control over curriculum and the integrity of Ethnic Studies programs.

Now, at the bargaining table, CFA is seeking protections against retaliation for faculty speech, assembly, and protest through an academic freedom article that would make those protections enforceable through the union contract.

Why are state agencies and outside political organizations seeking access to the networks through which workers organize political solidarity?

The Free Press article published names and private union messages, exposing faculty, particularly faculty of color vulnerable around employment and tenure, to potential retaliation. Among those identified was Omar Zahzah, whose scholarship includes the book Terms of Servitude, on U.S. technology companies and Israeli settler colonialism. He had also recently written about the “Michigan 8,” warning of “a broader targeting of the pro-Palestine movement.” Whatever the intent, the chilling message is clear: Continue this scholarship, political writing, or union organizing, and you, too, risk public exposure and targeting.

The consequences of this attack reach into union democracy itself: Fear of exposure changes what members dare to say, whom they trust, and how they are willing to organize together. In 2025, CFA sued CSU after Cal State LA disclosed faculty and staff members’ personal contact information to federal investigators conducting an antisemitism inquiry. The union secured a January 2026 settlement requiring CSU to notify employees before complying with any specified federal demands for personal information, unless legally prohibited.

The exposure of CFA’s internal deliberations raises a question beyond leaked communications: Why are state agencies and outside political organizations seeking access to the networks through which workers organize political solidarity? In Minnesota and Michigan, that scrutiny has taken a more coercive form: undercover surveillance and federal subpoenas.

In Minnesota, federal agents infiltrated political meetings and activist chats under “Operation Puppet Master,” a surveillance operation exposed during the prosecution of the “Minnesota 15,” activists charged with conspiracy to impede federal officers. A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) slide titled “The Conspiracy” mapped 18 organizations, including unions, while Homeland Security Investigations used administrative subpoenas — requiring no judicial approval — to obtain years of financial records connected to Service Employees International Union (SEIU) and Communications Workers of America (CWA). Defense attorney Kevin Riach challenged the surveillance as lacking any “articulable criminal predicate” and violating constitutional protections; federal prosecutors maintained that the charges concerned criminal conduct alone.

At a February workers’ assembly at Minneapolis’s United Labor Centre, roughly 400 workers debated labor’s response to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). One undercover agent reported “no real threats”; another sought to “get phone numbers.” Defense attorneys are seeking federal surveillance reports, undercover device downloads, and communications between local prosecutors and Washington to establish the extent of infiltration and whether anti-ICE activists were selectively prosecuted.

Defense attorneys are seeking federal surveillance reports, undercover device downloads, and communications between local prosecutors and Washington to establish the extent of infiltration.

In Michigan, following the indictment of the Michigan 8 — eight Palestine solidarity activists accused of conspiracy — a federal grand jury subpoena demanded Graduate Employees’ Organization (GEO) records dating to January 1, 2023: current and former membership information, officers, meeting minutes, personnel, and finances.

GEO President Hiab Teshome faced felony embezzlement and false-pretenses charges over alleged misuse of student organization funds. University police also sought to bar her from campus, potentially excluding a member of the union’s bargaining team from her workplace. Both charges were dismissed on August 6 — the day the federal subpoena was signed. GEO denounced the prosecution as politically motivated and moved to quash the subpoena. The dismissal does not establish a political motive behind the federal investigation, but the juxtaposition is striking: The charges against one union leader collapsed, yet federal scrutiny extended to the entire union — who belonged to GEO, who led it, what its members discussed, and how they spent their money.

Those records could reveal how solidarity was organized. Meanwhile, GEO says university management struck proposed contract language barring disclosure of workers’ union membership to the federal government. The constitutional stakes are hardly new: In the 1958 case of NAACP v. Alabama, the Supreme Court recognized that compelled disclosure of membership lists can expose people to retaliation and deter lawful political association.

Membership lists, meeting minutes, financial records, and private communications reveal who organizes with whom. Historian Ellen Schrecker identifies a disturbing historical precedent in McCarthyism’s system of “guilt by association”: Private groups compiled dossiers, government investigated political affiliations, and employers and universities imposed punishment. She sees today’s assault on higher education as even more dire: “Today, what’s happening is worse, so much worse that we have to really find a new phrase for it,” she told Democracy Now!.

Labor has its own answer to “guilt by association”: solidarity by association — where association is not a risk to be feared, but a means of repairing what injustice or oppression has torn apart. In the words of the Minnesota 15 solidarity campaign, “Community Is Not Conspiracy.” Rather than accept the social hierarchies that divide and oppress workers, union organizers build relationships that can dismantle and transform them. In organizing with those under attack, workers discover capacities for collective action that none could exercise alone. An injury to an immigrant family facing deportation, a Black community confronting police violence, or Palestinians facing repression thus becomes a concern for workers beyond those immediately targeted.

“An injury to one is an injury to all” means little if solidarity becomes competitive or selective — if defending Jewish workers requires silence about Palestinians, if defending citizens means abandoning undocumented workers, or if wages are labor’s concern while police violence, deportations, and attacks on civil liberties belong to somebody else.

Workers need room to reflect, make mistakes and acknowledge them, disagree, organize, persuade one another, and make collective decisions without employers, the state, or outside political organizations dictating the limits of debate.

Union meetings, caucuses, and other forms of association create spaces where workers connect economic and political struggles, building solidarity across sectors rather than dividing struggles against racism, gender oppression, political repression, and exploitation into separate constituencies. Through these relationships, workers build collective power, expanding their capacity to think, feel, and act together beyond the narrow and isolated roles assigned to them in the workplace and, more broadly, under capitalism.

Yet none of this is possible without preserving unions’ internal democracy and political independence. Workers need room to reflect, make mistakes and acknowledge them, disagree, organize, persuade one another, and make collective decisions without employers, the state, or outside political organizations dictating the limits of debate. Pressfare undermines that democracy when unproven allegations and internal deliberations become material for public targeting; lawfare erodes the independence of unions when accusations and investigations impose political costs before wrongdoing is established. Undercover agents mapping worker assemblies and prosecutors demanding years of union records bring far greater coercive power to bear on those same democratic spaces.

These methods differ in form and intensity, but they reproduce the same political effects: fear, suspicion, sadness, and isolation. These are effects that weaken the relationships through which workers might act together and change their circumstances. Solidarity, by contrast, nurtures compassion, courage, and the joy of gathering in assemblies, discovering what we can accomplish together. It strengthens our capacity not only to resist oppression and exploitation but to transform the social relations that sustain them. Perhaps that is what those who fear organized labor solidarity find most threatening.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

title: Xê, hesabê Halk TVyê yê ku 3 milyon şopînerên wê hene sansûr kir
content:
Xê ji 21’ê Cotmehê pê ve hesabê Halk TVyê yê ku 3 milyon şopînerên wê hene ji bikarhênerên li Tirkiyeyê re girt. Projeya EngelliWebê ya Komeleya Azadiya Derbirînê (İFÖD) ku sansûra li ser înternetê dişopîne, heman rojê ev geşedan ragihand.




Platformê biryara astengkirinê ya 14ê Cotmehê ku li gorî xala 8/A ya Qanûna bi hejmar 5651ê hatibû girtin, piştî heftiyekê xist meriyetê. Her weha hesab li cihê navê @halktvcomtr dest bi bikaranîna navê @halktveu kiribû.




Hîn jî nayê zanîn ka sedema vê sansûrê çi ye û ji ber kîjan naverokê biryara astengkirinê hatiye dayîn. 




Qeyûm hat tayînkirin




Polîsan di sibeha 14’ê Cotmehê de bi ser navenda Halk TVyê ya li Stenbolê de girt û qeyûm hat tayînkirin. Heyeta qeyûm daxwaza rêveberiya kanalê ya berdewamkirina weşana zindî qebûl nekir.




Serdozgeriya Komarê ya Stenbolê ev midaxele bi lêpirsîna li dijî xwediyê kanalê Cafer Mahiroglu re girê da ku bi îdiayên "bertîl" û "gendeltî"yê tê tohmetbarkirin. Mahiroglu jî got ku hemû îdia bêbingeh in.




Di heman rojê de hesabên Halk TVyê yên YouTube, X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok û Telegramê jî hatin astengkirin.







bianetê jî di nav de biryara astengkirina hesabên saziyên wekî T24, Kısa Dalga, Evrensel, soL Haber, Ajansa Mezopotamyayê, Komeleya Xebatên Medya û Hiqûqê (MLSA), İFOD, EngelliWeb, Şaxa Tirkiyeyê ya Rêxistina Efûya Navneteweyî, Partiya Karkerên Tirkiyeyê (TİP), Akademîsyenên Aşitiyê, Weqfa Ali İsmail Korkmaz, UMUT-SEN, Federasyona Komeleyên Jinan a Tirkiyeyê, Kaos GL, SPoD, Pembe Hayat, UniKuir, 17 Mayıs, Lambdaistanbul, Komeleya Têkoşîna li Dijî Tundiya Zayendî û Velveleyê hate dayîn. 




Her weha biryara astengkirina hesabên rojnameger Hikmet Adal, Tugçe Yılmaz, İrfan Değirmenci, Şirin Payzın, Burak Acerakis,Erdal Sağlam, Dinçer Gokçe, Sarya Toprak, Esra Tokat, Onur Dalar, Furkan Karabay, Bahadır Özgür û Yaman Akdeniz jî hat girtin.

title: Günaydın AKP'nin transfer bilançosunu açıkladı
content:
YENİ Parti Grup Başkanvekili Gökhan Günaydın, 31 Mart 2024 yerel seçimlerinden bu yana muhalefet partilerinden seçilen 106 belediye başkanının AKP'ye geçtiğini söyledi.




Günaydın, 32 belediye başkanının tutuklu olduğunu belirterek, operasyonların ve belediye başkanı transferlerinin muhalefet belediyelerini hedef aldığını söyledi.




Günaydın, TBMM'de yaptığı basın açıklamasında gündemdeki konuları değerlendirdi. 31 Mart 2024 yerel seçimlerinden bu yana muhalefet belediyelerine yönelik operasyonlara ve belediye başkanlarının AKP'ye geçmesine dikkat çekti.




Günaydın, seçimlerin üzerinden iki buçuk yıl geçtiğini belirterek, “O gün diğer siyasal partilerden seçilmiş olan 106 belediye başkanı, havuç ve sopa ilişkisiyle AKP'ye geçirilmiş” dedi.




Günaydın'ın paylaştığı bilançoya göre, CHP'den 36, Yeniden Refah Partisi'nden 41, İYİ Parti'den 11, diğer siyasi partilerden ise 18 belediye başkanı AKP'ye geçti.




Belediye başkanlarının tutuklanması yoluyla belediyelerin yönetiminin de el değiştirdiğini söyleyen Günaydın, İstanbul'da Gaziosmanpaşa, Bayrampaşa, Beykoz, Şile, Üsküdar, Adalar ve Ataşehir'in yanı sıra Bursa Büyükşehir Belediyesi, Hakkari Derecik ve İzmir Menderes'i örnek gösterdi.




Günaydın, “İki buçuk yıl evvel halk, açıkça AKP dışında çoğu o dönemin CHP, bu dönemin YENİ Partili belediye başkanlarına oy vermiş. Ama sen bunları, başkanlarını tutuklamak suretiyle belediye başkan vekili yoluyla AKP'ye transfer etmişsin” dedi.




32 belediye başkanı tutuklu




Günaydın, halen tutuklu bulunan belediye başkanlarının isimlerini sıraladı. Bu isimler arasında İstanbul Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanı ve Cumhurbaşkanı adayı Ekrem İmamoğlu, Şişli Belediye Başkanı Resul Emrah Şahan, Beylikdüzü Belediye Başkanı Mehmet Murat Çalık, Beşiktaş Belediye Başkanı Rıza Akpolat, Antalya Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanı Muhittin Böcek, Bursa Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanı Mustafa Bozbey ve Bayrampaşa Belediye Başkanı Hasan Mutlu da yer aldı.




Günaydın, toplam 32 belediye başkanının tutuklu olduğunu, bu isimlerden yalnızca Akçakoca Belediye Başkanı Fikret Albayrak'ın yakın zamanda tahliye edildiğini söyledi.




Tutuksuz yargılanan belediye başkanları arasında Esenyurt Belediye Başkanı Ahmet Özer, Adana Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanı Zeydan Karalar, Adıyaman Belediye Başkanı Abdurrahman Tutdere, Beyoğlu Belediye Başkanı İnan Güney ve Avcılar Belediye Başkanı Utku Caner Çaykara'yı saydı.




Eski belediye başkanlarından İzmir Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanı Tunç Soyer, Manavgat Belediye Başkanı Şükrü Sözen ve Nilüfer Belediye Başkanı Turgay Erdem'in tutuklu olduğunu da belirten Günaydın, 13 belediyede kayyım uygulamasının sürdüğünü söyledi.




Bu belediyelerden üçünün Esenyurt, Şişli ve Ovacık olduğunu, diğer belediyelerin ise DEM Partili olduğunu belirten Günaydın, muhalefet belediyelerinin hedef alındığını ifade etti.




Günaydın, “Türkiye'de bin 400 belediye varken gördüğünüz gibi gözaltı, tutukluluk, belediye başkanı transferi hep muhalif belediyeler üzerinden yapılıyor. Şimdi bunun demokratik olmadığı çok açık. Millet iradesi üzerinde bir etki yaratıyor mu, yaratmıyor mu? AKP'nin bu vahşilik, bu demokrasi dışılık, bu demokrasi tanımazlık işine yarıyor mu?” diye konuştu.




(EMK)

author: Robert Narai
title: Hungary 1956: a workers’ revolution against Stalinism
content:
Seventy years ago, Hungarian workers and students rose up against a brutal dictatorship that justified itself in the language of Marxism. In its place, they built workers’ councils: organs of working-class democracy, giving future generations a chance to discover the essence of revolutionary Marxism.

My grandfather, Vendel Koroknai, often played Beethoven’s Egmont Overture on his record player and spoke fondly of its role in the 1956 revolution. The overture tells the story of Lamoral, count of Egmont, who defied Spanish tyranny under the duke of Alba. His execution sparked a broader rebellion that led to Dutch independence. For the Hungarians who heard it, the parallels were striking: the Russians as the oppressive occupiers, themselves as the Dutch seeking self-determination.

They heard it because on the evening of 23 October 1956, workers and students defeated the hated AVH, the secret police of the dictatorship that had ruled Hungary for the previous eight years, in fierce street fighting and gun battles, and took control of Magyar Radio in central Budapest. They turned it into a hub for broadcasting news, appeals, morale-boosting content and, importantly, political arguments about the way forward for their revolution. Between announcements, they played the overture over and over to lift people’s spirits and give them the resolve to fight a much better-armed enemy in the form of Russian tanks. It became the unofficial anthem of the revolution. My grandfather, who at the time was a farm labourer on the outskirts of Debrecen (Hungary’s second-largest city) and a delegate and militia leader in one of the workers’ councils, recalled: “It wasn’t just filler. It was a prophecy, articulating the hopes, dreams and aspirations of a people fighting for their liberation.”

Whether they knew it or not, Hungarian workers and students were also creating a radical alternative to both Stalinist and Western barbarism. At the height of the Cold War, they broke the so-called communist regime’s repressive arms—the secret police were dispersed, the police defected or stood aside, the army disintegrated—even as parts of its executive and bureaucratic machinery kept functioning. Into the space that opened up, they built workers’ councils, elected and recallable, running factories, farms, whole cities and towns. My grandfather was one of those workers, and it was his first taste of any political freedoms.

Stalinists who defend the bureaucratic monstrosities of the Soviet Union have always called this a counter-revolution, the work of fascists and Western agents, and used that claim to justify sending in the tanks. (The term “tankie” is derived from this argument.) The Hungarian far right, Viktor Orbán chief among them, calls it something else: a rehearsal for 1989 and the fall of the “communist” system, proto-capitalists fighting to restore private property and the free market. Neither is true. Hungarian workers were not fighting for capitalism, Stalinist or Western. The councils they built were organs of workers’ power and the basis for a democratic society run by the working class: genuine socialism and communism. This was a workers’ revolution, and the people who made it included men like my grandfather, who had lost his family’s farm to the regime that now called him a fascist.

As the American Trotskyist Hal Draper wrote at the time: “Hungary opens a new era with the first revolution against the Stalinist system.” Hungarian workers and students proved the working class could still make revolutions. They proved the so-called communist regimes were counterrevolutionary. And they cracked, for the first time on this scale, the grip Stalinism held over communist parties across the world.













PART ONE: THE OCTOBER UPRISING

Background

The Red Army occupied Hungary at the end of World War Two. With the tacit approval of the West, a Russian-backed dictatorship was installed under Mátyás Rákosi, who called himself “Stalin’s best Hungarian disciple”. Like the other Eastern European regimes established at this time, Hungary called itself a “workers’ state”. It was anything but. Workers like my grandfather had to perform backbreaking labour to meet production targets set by bureaucrats. They had no say in what was produced or how, or in any broader political decision. They were paid pitiful wages that could hardly buy bread and milk.

Peasants were driven into collective farms at gunpoint, and the hatred this produced never went away. (My grandfather’s family farm was seized in the late 1940s and he was forced to work in the coal mines of Bátonyterenye, in the north of Hungary.) Much of the Hungarian countryside became a grain colony for the Russian Empire, producing hunger, starvation and famine. Workers lived in fear of torture, imprisonment or death at the hands of the secret police, the AVH, and the system of prisons and concentration camps they ran. All opposition within the Communist Party was eliminated through regular purges. My grandfather used to say there were only three kinds of people in Hungary in those years: those in prison, those who’d just got out, and those waiting to go in.

This was Stalinism: a bureaucratic dictatorship ruling over the working class, dressed up in the language of the movement it had strangled. It was never a continuation of October 1917, when Russian workers, peasants and soldiers seized state power through soviets (the Russian word for “council”), but a complete break from it. Civil war and isolation had ruined the Russian economy and decimated the working class that made the revolution. The soviets were reduced to empty shells, and a bureaucracy stepped into the vacuum and began to develop a will of its own as the revolutionary movement ebbed. By the time it had consolidated its grip, the language of 1917 survived only as camouflage for its opposite. After 1945, this system, not the one workers had built in October 1917, was exported into Eastern Europe: bureaucratic state capitalism.

Clockwise from top left: The Stalin monument in Budapest, 1953 (Photo: Gyula Nagy); Compulsory grain deliveries in a rural village, 1951 (Photo: Fortepan); Woodworking factory hall, 1951 (Fortepan); Workers’ lodgings in the 1950s (Fortepan); Ganz Ship Repair Yard workers build a Soviet merchant vessel as part of reparations, 1940s (Fortepan).

Stalin’s death in 1953 created a crisis at the top of these regimes, since most of their authority derived from him as a figure. His replacement, Nikita Khrushchev, cynically acknowledged Stalin’s crimes in a bid to expand his own power base and present a more “liberal” face. But “de-Stalinisation” did nothing to challenge the fundamental structures of the system. Workers remained exploited and oppressed. It did, however, open space for opposition and dissent and raised expectations among certain sections of society. In Hungary, Rákosi was briefly replaced by the reformer Imre Nagy in 1953. Rákosi returned in 1955, but Moscow removed him in July 1956, replacing him with his ally Ernő Gerő, another hardliner. Nagy’s brief rule inspired hope among Hungarian workers, students and intellectuals, and his ousting was remembered with outrage. And Hungary wasn’t alone. Working-class rebellions had already broken out in East Germany in 1953 and in Poland, at Poznań, in June 1956.

Opposition circles started meeting inside the Hungarian Communist Party: the Petőfi Circle in Budapest, the Kossuth Circle in Debrecen, and the Writers’ Union. They were made up of intellectuals and students who supported Nagy and wanted reform. They were hardly radical, but they attracted new members who believed change was possible.

Pictured here is Emil Horn, later a historian of the Revolution; At the meeting of the Petšfi Cercle on 27 June 1956, social democrat Arpad Szakasits talks with philosopher George Lukacs; A meeting of the Writers’ Association on 28 December 1956. Tibor Dery has the floor. In the foreground is Gyula Hay, chin in his hand. Several weeks after this meeting, both men were sentenced to prison terms.

Workers weren’t involved in these groups. But some of their ideas, such as giving workers a greater say in how production was run, influenced some workers and intersected with the dissent already rumbling in the factories and on the farms. My grandfather recalled the climate at the time, which was reflective of the attitudes of many workers:

“We had no interest in joining any of these [official opposition groups] ... but all the talk of change and infighting at the top did start to make many of us think that this so-called monolithic party was not so monolithic after all.”

That is how the cracks began to appear. At a Budapest factory that autumn, a shop committee meeting turned into something closer to a trial. The minutes record the chairman, Horváth, defending the wage computation system against workers who no longer accepted being told to sit down and listen:

“Never before has anyone so harshly attacked the wage computation system”, roared Horváth.

“But are we right? Answer this question”, a voice interrupted.

“I am speaking now”, shouted Horváth. “When I finish, comrade, you may ask for the floor.”

“We cannot be forbidden to ask questions ... we have the right”, declared foreman Lengyel.

Small scenes like this multiplied across Budapest; in the countryside, they appeared in muted forms. In the oil fields of southern Zala, the tightening of production norms throughout 1955 met with little open protest, but plenty of “low-level sabotage, undisciplined behaviour and simple neglect”, as one party official put it. It wasn’t yet directed at the government. But it was the same thing happening in factory after factory and on farm after farm: a worker-peasant workforce that had never accepted the regime’s right to rule, and men like my grandfather, who had lost their land and spent years resenting it.

Months before the revolution, steelworkers began striking at the Stalinvarosz steel plant, the Hungarian state industry’s flagship and pride. Photo: Erich Lessing

How the revolution began

My grandfather recalled:

“It was the first demonstration I had ever attended, given such things had not taken place in Hungary for my entire life. I will never forget how jubilant everyone was—something also very rare in Hungary. Everyone was distributing their political literature with their demands, talking, discussing, arguing. I did not like the Communists [reformers], but I did like what they were saying. And I also did think Nagy was one of the better guys who meant well. But here we were, out on the streets, demanding such things that seemed unthinkable just a few days earlier. How to guarantee these demands would be met?”

This was Piac, Debrecen’s main street, on 23 October 1956. It was a good question, and the reformers had no answer. It took thirteen days, and a great deal of blood, for Hungary’s workers to find one. Student meetings across the country had called the demonstrations in solidarity with the workers’ movement in Poland. At first, the regime permitted them and broadcast the details on official radio stations. “This was something completely unheard of in Hungary,” my grandfather continued:

“We did not think highly of the people organising the demonstrations. It was the chance to show some sort of opposition to the government that attracted us. But we also had some sense that in Poland workers had been demanding change and that was also something worth coming out for. Myself and some of my co-workers agreed that we would attend the demonstrations in the city after we finished work.”

Then came the radio announcement that permission had been withdrawn. “If anything”, my grandfather said, “it only steeled our resolve because we were now telling the government to go fuck themselves”. By the following morning, the regime could do nothing to stop the crowds from gathering. One intellectual close to the Petőfi Circle, Tamás Aczél, later described the shock of realising this wasn’t going to stay a debate among writers: “[I]t was then that we realised, that everybody realised, that this wasn’t just an affair of a few Communist intellectuals but that everyone felt as strongly, the same way, against the regime”. Another prominent intellectual admitted afterwards that “the idea of an uprising never entered our minds”.

At this stage, the demonstrators did not want a revolution. No one carried guns, not even stones. Members of the Communist Party led the demonstrations, carrying portraits of Lenin and Imre Nagy, and the most common demand was for Nagy to take over the government. In Budapest, the crowds gathered before the statue of Józef Bem, a Polish hero of the Hungarian revolution of 1848, where the Writers’ Union read out its demands: a more independent policy for Hungary within the Soviet bloc, factories co-run by workers and specialists, peasants free to decide whether they joined a cooperative, and Nagy reinstated as prime minister. The demonstrators sang Sándor Petőfi’s “National Song”, the revolutionary song of the 1848 uprising against the Austrian Empire (a poem my grandfather can recite by heart).













The crowds then began moving toward Parliament Square, in Debrecen as in Budapest. Nagy tried to address the crowd in Budapest, but his calls for calm and order did not match their mood. The demonstrations were drawing in people who wanted more than a few reforms. “Many of us began to shout, ‘Out with the Russians! Death to Rákosi! Free and fair elections!’”, my grandfather said. “Others shouted ‘Nagy to power!’”

Then news broke that Gerő had denounced the demonstrators as wanting to “poison Hungary and create disorder”. A section of the protest in Budapest broke off towards Magyar Radio to insist on the right to broadcast a reply. Another marched to the huge statue of Stalin in the city park and tore it down with hammers and ropes, leaving only the boots. In Debrecen, demonstrators like my grandfather were tearing the symbols of the regime from buildings and public spaces.













At Magyar Radio, massive lines of AVH blocked the building. The crowd sent a small delegation inside. Time passed with no sign of the delegates, and the crowd surged towards the police lines. First came tear gas, but the crowd was undeterred. Then came a burst of machine-gun fire.

With that single action, the revolution had begun. A few demonstrators fell. For thousands of others, the purpose of the demonstration changed: if they did not destroy their enemy, it would destroy them. They fought with stones and petrol bombs, and demonstrators serving in the armed forces called on their units to distribute arms to the crowd. Workers, who had stood on the sidelines, were drawn into the fray. Street fighting raged through the night. Barricades went up, party offices and AVH stations were burned, and hated AVH men were lynched on the streets. Russian tanks were sent in but were met block by block by small battalions of youths with petrol bombs. By the end of the night, the radio was in the hands of the insurgents, and Beethoven’s 

Egmont Overture

 was blaring out of its speakers.

The answer to my grandfather’s question was being given in Debrecen as well:

“Soldiers had refused to fire upon us when we reached the parliament building. But the AVH had opened fire and killed maybe 30 or 40 people. Those of us who weren’t already armed were given arms by the soldiers or went home to fetch their hunting rifles. We went back to our farms, factories and neighbourhoods and told our co-workers and neighbours what was happening, formed ourselves into armed units and delegations and prepared to take on the AVH. By morning, news had broken of the fighting in Budapest and the fall of the Gerő government. Delegates from all the big factories and farms, officers from the barracks, representatives of those who had led the demonstrations—we all met at the Lajos Kossuth University to discuss and decide upon a course of action. A general strike was called and within days the government had been overthrown.”

The violent suppression of peaceful demonstrators unleashed a well of bitterness fed by almost a decade of dictatorship, poverty and AVH brutality. In days, the state’s repressive apparatus, seemingly all-powerful the week before, collapsed, even as parts of its administrative machinery kept ticking over underneath. Police and soldiers handed their weapons to the insurgents. Army tanks carried Hungarian flags with the Russian insignia cut out.

A new government was declared on 24 October, led by Nagy. One decree demanded Russian troops “restore law and order” and another proclaimed martial law. This did nothing to stop the fighting. A general strike spread across the country demanding the removal of all Russian forces and that those responsible for the massacres be held to account.

The rise of the workers’ councils

The struggle against the dictatorship was not confined to armed confrontation with Russian tanks and the remnants of the AVH. By the third day of the revolution, 26 October, people everywhere were establishing institutions to express their new power. Revolutionary councils formed in the towns, the villages and the quarters of the cities, in newspaper offices and government ministries, in colleges, on collective farms and above all in the factories. The running of factories, the distribution of food and the publication of newspapers all passed from the disintegrating apparatus of the old state to the new organs of popular power. My grandfather described how this system of workers’ democracy was set up and how it functioned on his own collective farm and across the wider city of Debrecen:

“In every factory, farm, government building, army barracks, university, and school we had established these councils to respond to the massacres and determine how we would smash the AVH and the Communist regime. On our farm, instead of some stupid bureaucrat telling us what to do, we got rid of the ones we didn’t like and elected the ones who were actually helpful, alongside other workers like myself—the ones who were the most opinionated or showed the most initiative. I had authority because I’d been one of the first to take up arms, and for many, because I wasn’t a member of the Communist Party.

“We had armed detachments as well: a militia. We’d elect and re-elect roles whenever we thought it was needed, so you’d often change what you were doing depending on what needed to be done. I was a delegate to many of the initial meetings in Debrecen, then changed my role when I went to Budapest to bring food and medical supplies to the fighters. Every morning, or any time we thought it necessary, we called meetings and argued about what to do. If your colleagues didn’t like what you were saying or doing, they could call a meeting, raise their concerns, call a vote, and if you lost, have you recalled. It was the total opposite of a dictatorship. This was working-class democracy.”

In Győr, the Revolutionary Council assumed control over the whole area. Győr’s National Council was one of the most powerful bodies to emerge outside Budapest, and it had a clear leader, Attila Szigeti, who, unlike many younger delegates elsewhere, had been a political functionary under the old Communist government before the revolution. The councils drew their leadership from wherever it actually existed, including from inside the apparatus they were now overthrowing. In Miskolc, the Workers’ Council and the Student Parliament held power. In Debrecen, the Debrecen Socialist Revolutionary Committee assumed authority over the entire city.

Peter Fryer was a member of the British Communist Party and correspondent for its newspaper, 

Daily Worker

. Sent to Hungary to report on what he was told was a fascist counter-revolution, he found “a genuine workers’ revolution”. At the Győr town hall, he wrote that the committees, in their striking resemblance to the councils of Russia in 1905 and February 1917, were remarkably uniform:

“They were at once organs of insurrection—the coming together of delegates elected by factories and universities, mines and army units—and organs of popular self-government which the armed people trusted. Of course, as in every real revolution ‘from below’ there was ‘too much’ talking, arguing, bickering, coming and going, froth, excitement, agitation, ferment. That is one side of the picture. The other is the emergence to leading positions of ordinary men, women and youths, whom the AVH domination had submerged. The revolution thrust them forward, aroused their civic pride and latent genius for organisation, and set them to work to build democracy out of the ruins of bureaucracy.”













As the councils grew, the government announced more concessions to re-establish its authority, including recognising the councils themselves, in a bid to let the party machine seize control. In many instances, the plan backfired. At a telephone factory in Budapest, a worker who had spent 25 October fighting in the streets went back the next day to find 800 of his 3,000 colleagues gathered in the factory hall, listening to management try to get ahead of what was coming. The SZOT, the National Trade Union Council, had appealed for workers’ councils to be constituted so workers would have a say in the factory.

The workers interpreted the appeal differently from how the SZOT and party headquarters expected—they took it seriously. They proceeded to elect workers, their own representatives, to the council and not the men suggested by the leadership. Nineteen or twenty of the 25 council members were workers rather than staff, roughly half in their twenties, radicalised by the previous two days’ fighting. The director asked to stay on, but only as an ordinary toolmaker, the job he’d had before his promotion, and the workers let him.

Recognition was meant to bring the councils under the party’s control. Instead, it gave the youngest and most militant workers official sanction for what they were already doing, and they came to dominate the councils rather than the party officials.

The better-organised councils sent delegations to see the ministers and press their demands. My grandfather joined one of these delegations to bring food and medical supplies to Budapest and to press the central government for its demands. Across the councils, he related, the tone of their statements was always the same: “We will give our full support to the new government ... when the new government accepts our programme, particularly the withdrawal of Russian troops”.

The central government had two choices: crush the revolution mercilessly, using enormous numbers of Russian troops and tanks, or make huge concessions to the insurgents. The government and party leaders chose the second. Nagy appeared on a broadcast, saying most insurgents were not counter-revolutionaries, and promised to withdraw Russian troops from Budapest immediately. By the night of 31 October, no Russian units were seen in any major city. Nagy also announced a new government that abolished the one-party system and said the workers’ councils and local councils would be officially recognised. The revolution, it seemed, had been successful.
