title: Freedom guerrillas: We will uphold women martyrs’ legacy of resistance
content:
Freedom guerrillas commemorated pioneering women martyrs, highlighting the significance of October in the history of their struggle. People's Defence Forces (HPG) guerrilla Cumali Ararat emphasised the legacy of struggle left by Azime, Canda, Ronahî (Andrea Wolf) and Berîtan (Gülnaz Karataş), saying that the women's liberation movement has gained support around the world.




Cumali Ararat said that October holds particular significance in the history of women's military organisation and the tradition of resistance.







 







He reflected on the month's place in the history of their struggle and said: “Every month has its own significance in our life of struggle. October is also a meaningful month in the history of our struggle and women's military organisation. It is a month of resistance. Looking back at history, we see that our women comrades played a pioneering role and fulfilled a leading mission in the tradition of struggle during this significant month. For example, there were comrades Azime, Canda and Ronahî the German. Comrade Ronahî was an internationalist. Abdullah Öcalan's ideas and philosophy had a profound influence on her. Comrade Ronahî refused to surrender to the enemy and was martyred when the enemy riddled her body with bullets.




October is also associated with our comrade Berîtan, a pioneering commander in women's military organisation and a symbol of this month. Comrade Berîtan, who was martyred in the Xakurke region after refusing to surrender to the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) forces, became a guiding principle and a legacy for us. Today, we follow the path of comrade Berîtan.




There are many similar examples throughout the history of Kurdistan. Kurdish women demonstrated a pioneering stance in the resistance struggles of Dersim, Koçgirî, Ağrı and Kela Dimdimê. Within the history of our organisation, comrade Berîtan became a pioneer of this tradition.




Throughout Kurdistan's history, those in power have disregarded the values of the Kurdish people and subjected them to a life they did not deserve. Comrade Berîtan confronted this mentality and, by refusing every call to surrender, delivered a powerful response to the path of betrayal. Comrade Berîtan, who chose life over surrender, lives on in our hearts today.”




HPG guerrilla Cumali Ararat said that the women's liberation movement, embodied by Abdullah Öcalan and comrade Berîtan, has inspired widespread support across the world. He continued: “Today, it is not only women but also men who march behind the slogan ‘Jin, Jiyan, Azadî’ (Woman, Life, Freedom). This slogan represents a manifesto unlike anything seen anywhere else in the world. This cry for freedom and the passion for liberation centred on change have all been made possible through the determined struggle of Abdullah Öcalan, the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) and the many comrades who were martyred for this cause.




If we fail to understand comrade Berîtan properly and analyse her struggle correctly, we cannot achieve freedom by following her path. We cannot fulfil the dreams of our martyred comrades or achieve the goals for which they sacrificed their lives.




The greatest dream of our martyred comrades was to live alongside Abdullah Öcalan and ensure that the Kurdish people could live peacefully in their own land, with a free identity and freedom of thought. On this basis, we will strive to be worthy of our pioneering women martyrs, particularly those who were martyred in October, and the path of free women's identity established by comrade Berîtan. We will continue our struggle to realise their dreams.




We also bow with respect before the memory of all our revolutionary martyrs, represented by martyrs Delal Amed, Berwar Dersim and Berîtan Nurhak, and pledge to uphold their comradeship.”







 







HPG guerrilla Ferman Penaber also spoke to ANF about the significance of October for himself and the freedom guerrillas. He said: “I commemorate all the martyrs of Kurdistan's freedom struggle, particularly comrade Berîtan, and bow before their memory. This month, we remember comrades who were martyred through heroic struggle and self-sacrifice. Throughout our party's history, we have had pioneers such as comrades Besê, Azime, Berîtan, Zîlan, Sema, Sara, Delal Amed and Leyla Sorxwîn. Some of these comrades may not have been martyred in October, but they remain our pioneers. Their memory lives on in our hearts.




Comrade Berîtan chose resistance against colonialist forces and betrayal in the Xakurke region in October 1992. She had deepened her commitment to Abdullah Öcalan's path and the tradition of women's resistance. The mentality of male domination sought to break the will of free women to live. But comrade Berîtan refused to bow down. She resisted that mentality and rejected surrender. She always chose the path of resistance and Abdullah Öcalan's ideas. She became an enduring symbol for us, and we will always follow her path.




At that time, colonialist forces seeking to exploit Kurdistan wanted to attack the free will of Kurdistan and its guerrillas. They were met with tremendous resistance. This tradition of resistance has continued to the present day. That is why the path of women's freedom has always served as an example for us. The path of women's liberation is the path of Abdullah Öcalan. The spirit of self-sacrifice reached its highest levels. We also witnessed this in 1996 through our legendary commander, comrade Zîlan. Comrade Zîlan carried out a self-sacrificial action against the colonialist enemy in the heart of the enemy's territory. She did not hesitate for even a second.




We, too, have never accepted surrender. We will continue to resist and struggle along the path of resistance, down to the last fibre of our being. We will struggle without hesitation to secure Abdullah Öcalan's physical freedom. We must intensify our struggle to the highest level so that we can see him and live alongside him. That is why we will never stop. We will place even greater emphasis on the struggle and deepen our commitment to Abdullah Öcalan's path.




Once again, through comrade Berîtan, we respectfully commemorate the martyrs of October and all the heroic martyrs of Kurdistan, and renew the promise we made to them. We will struggle until victory. We say, ‘Bijî Serok Apo’ (Long live President Apo (A.Öcalan)) and ‘Şehîtler Ölümsüzdür’ (Martyrs are immortal).”

author: Unknown
title: Democratisation is not about imposing conditions
content:
Mehmet Uçum (Chief Adviser to the President and Deputy Chair of the Presidential Legal Policies Board) wrote an article about the process on 17 October. Judging by his remarks, Uçum appears to be acting as the spokesperson for a group seeking to undermine the process. He claims to advocate dialogue, yet he is trying to dictate terms to the Kurdish Freedom Movement. He seems to think he is intelligent and everyone else is a fool. The article Uçum wrote is precisely the kind of article that opponents of the process, those seeking to sabotage it, would write. If it reflects the views of Tayyip Erdoğan, whom he advises, the situation is even more serious and troubling. If that is the case, the government is attempting to lay the ideological groundwork for undermining the process. Tayyip Erdoğan has repeatedly said that the process is progressing well. If Mehmet Uçum wrote his article based on information received from the presidential palace, it means the process is not going well.




Even before the law approved on 18 August was enacted, government officials had said that the status of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan would change, that he would meet with various groups and that even those who would work alongside him would be able to visit Imrali. These commitments were made before the law was passed. Following its enactment, the deputy chair of the Justice and Development Party (AKP) parliamentary group publicly stated, in front of television cameras, that journalists and many others would be able to visit Imrali. However, more than two months have passed since the law was enacted, and there has been no change in the Kurdish People's Leader's status.




Mehmet Uçum believes that the Kurdish People's Leader can play a role in achieving negative peace, but not genuine peace, or what is known as positive peace. He also argues that freedom for Abdullah Öcalan cannot be demanded. Who could possibly believe that genuine peace can be achieved while the central figure in the peace process remains imprisoned? Did Devlet Bahçeli not say from the very beginning that, if Öcalan called on the organisation, he could address the DEM Party parliamentary group and fully exercise his right to hope? The right to hope envisages the possibility of release from prison. Does declaring that freedom for the Kurdish People's Leader cannot be demanded, contemplated or achieved not amount to announcing the end of this process?




The Kurdish People's Leader is the principal interlocutor in this process. However, the Kurdish Freedom Movement is also a key actor in putting the process into practice. This movement has consistently insisted that Öcalan must be able to work freely. It maintains that enabling him to work freely is the first step towards securing his freedom and that nothing can be achieved without it. Yet Mehmet Uçum tells those making this demand that what they are asking for will not happen. In doing so, he blocks every possibility of practical progress. One thing is clear: the way a people's or movement's leadership is treated reflects the way that people and their organisation are treated. The Kurdish People's Leader understands this very well. In this respect, Uçum's approach represents a new version of the policy pursued towards the Kurdish people for the past century.




Democratic participation is not possible under the existing laws and legal framework. The current laws allow people to be imprisoned for even the slightest expression of opposition. Those demanding the fundamental democratic rights of the Kurdish people are immediately imprisoned. This is also how the current government operates. Opportunities for democratic participation can only emerge through new legislation. After all, it was the existing laws that created this problem in the first place. What kind of reasoning suggests that people should enter the democratic political sphere without changing these laws? Such reasoning fails to understand the essence of the process. Or perhaps it views the process as a means of achieving an entirely different objective.




Mehmet Uçum has also used the concept of “ethnic politics”, a term Turkish state officials have employed for decades, indeed for a century, to deny Kurdish existence and fundamental rights. Demanding the fundamental rights that arise from the Kurdish people's very existence is not engaging in ethnic politics. It is the state and those who share Uçum's mentality who have been practising ethnic politics for the past century. The cliché “do not engage in ethnic politics” is one of the expressions most frequently used by fascists and those who deny Kurdish existence. The Turkish state, its politicians and people like Uçum constantly speak about the rights of Turks in Cyprus and elsewhere. Demands they consider perfectly legitimate for themselves suddenly become “ethnic politics” when Kurds make them! And this is treated as the most serious offence.




Mehmet Uçum is not merely trying to dictate terms to the Kurdish Freedom Movement; he is also threatening those engaged in democratic politics. He says that measures will be taken. Presumably, by “measures”, he means resorting to state repression and oppression, and mobilising the military and police. This is the same mentality that has prevailed for a century. People with such a mentality used to be mocked for being as thick-headed as they were stubborn. Uçum could also be described as someone who merely echoes the woodcutter's grunts, blindly supporting those wielding power.




Mehmet Uçum may interpret integration in his own way. However, neither the Kurdish People's Leader nor the Kurdish Freedom Movement nor the Kurdish people understand integration as Uçum does. If the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government shares his interpretation, then it, too, has misunderstood the concept. Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan speaks of democratic integration. This requires, first and foremost, freedom of thought and organisation, the legal recognition of the right to engage in democratic politics without obstruction, and guarantees for the Kurdish people's linguistic, cultural and identity rights. All obstacles to organising around these rights must be removed. Democratic integration can be achieved on this basis through the recognition of local democracy and the right of local administrations to exercise initiative in social, economic and cultural affairs. This is how reconciliation and integration between the Kurdish people, the state and Turkish society can be achieved. Old approaches and impositions, however, will only perpetuate division. This will benefit no one. The Kurds will resist such policies, just as they have done for the past century. No force can now stand in the way of this resistance.




Mehmet Uçum's understanding of democracy is also based on the notion that rights are granted as favours. His article makes it even clearer that he lacks a democratic mentality. In other words, democratic steps might be taken only if everyone submits completely to those in power! He openly denies that the Kurdish question stems from misguided policies and an undemocratic system. Consequently, he does not see democratisation as the solution to the problem. Demanding democracy can never be regarded as imposing a condition. Those who are genuinely democratic take steps towards democratisation without waiting for others to demand them. Democratisation is not only for the Kurds but for all the peoples of Turkey. Those who fail to recognise this cannot carry any process forward; they can only sabotage it.




The Kurdish Freedom Movement consistently raises the issue of its leadership's status to ensure that the process proceeds in a healthy manner. This is not because it has a hidden agenda, as Uçum suggests, but because it recognises how important this issue is for the progress of the process. The movement will certainly not abandon this concern. Those who disregard this demand are the ones with other agendas.




Resolving the Kurdish question is fundamentally a matter of democratisation. Those who do not share this understanding cannot resolve any of Turkey's problems. Mehmet Uçum continues to voice the views of those who want Turkey to be governed on an authoritarian basis. His remarks therefore reveal what that camp is thinking.




Source: Yeni Yaşam newspaper

title: Zübeyir Aydar: Kurds have the right to speak at the UN
content:
The Kurds' struggle for international recognition and representation is entering a new phase. Zübeyir Aydar, a member of the Executive Council of the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK), said that despite their population of approximately 60 million, Kurds are not represented internationally through their own political will. Aydar said, “We also want to be represented. Our demand is equality.”




Aydar spoke to ANF and emphasised that the initiative to secure representation at the United Nations (UN) is not merely a diplomatic demand but an important part of the Kurds' struggle for recognition as an equal people.




We spoke to Zübeyir Aydar, a member of the Executive Council of the KNK, about the demands raised and decisions taken at the conference organised by the KNK in Brussels on 3 October, as well as the importance of Kurdish national unity.




What challenges do Kurds face today in terms of international recognition and representation?




As a people and a nation, we are not officially recognised. Our struggle is for the Kurds to be recognised by everyone, just like other nations around the world. Yes, the existence of the Kurds is acknowledged, and Kurds are recognised, but this recognition has not yet acquired the legal, political and diplomatic status we seek.




There has been official recognition in Iraq since 2004. Kurds have federal status within Iraq. In Syria, there is partial recognition. However, Kurds are not recognised as a nation in either Turkey or Iran. No international institution, including the United Nations, recognises an institution or representative body that represents the Kurds as a nation and a people.




In this sense, one dimension of our struggle for freedom is to achieve recognition within the countries where we live, while another is to secure recognition internationally. Like other nations around the world, we need to be represented both domestically and internationally. Kurdistan must be recognised as a geographical entity and the Kurds as a nation. A representative body authorised to speak on behalf of the Kurds must also be recognised.




As in other areas, we face a major lack of representation internationally. We have launched an initiative to address this. The Kurdish population is approximately 60 million. Despite this, Kurds remain a nation living without a state, without representation and without recognition. This situation cannot continue.




The majority of Kurds live in Turkey, Iran, Iraq and Syria. Each part of Kurdistan is under the sovereignty of one of these states. Although the situation varies from one country to another, the fundamental problem remains the same.




We are not represented in the government of Turkey, nor are we partners in the state. The situation is the same in Iran. Although Kurds have a different status in Iraq, there are still shortcomings in their international representation. A similar situation exists in Syria.




Yet Kurds are one of the indigenous and ancient peoples of this region. Just like Turks, Arabs, Persians, Azerbaijanis, Greeks, Armenians and other peoples of the region, Kurds must also be represented internationally.




The United Nations General Assembly discusses issues affecting the entire world. Representatives of the world's peoples and nations take the floor there. Kurds are also discussed from time to time, but their own representatives are not present. Kurds, too, have the right to speak from that podium and to be represented.




Demanding this right does not mean opposing Turkey, Iran, Syria or Iraq. We favour cooperation and shared solutions. However, we are not Turks, Persians or Arabs. We are a distinct nation. We have our own culture, our own language, our own people and our own country. This reality must be recognised.




This is the international dimension of the struggle for freedom. The struggle for freedom is not limited to securing certain rights within a particular country. We must also have a voice and a say in decisions at the international level. We are launching this process. This is also a right of the Kurdish people.




We are demanding the restoration of a right that has been usurped. We do not oppose the representation of other peoples. We want to be represented too. Our demand is equality. We want to live in this world as a nation and people with equal rights. We must have equal rights and representation not only in the countries where we live but also among the peoples of the world.




How did the initiative to secure international representation for the Kurds take shape?




We conducted extensive diplomatic discussions as part of this initiative. We met with experts, exchanged views and held consultations. We brought the issue onto the agenda of the KNK General Assembly held on 6–7 June. The General Assembly decided to launch such a process following the discussions.




For the first time, a Kurdish organisation has officially initiated such a process on behalf of the Kurdish people. As part of this initiative, a letter was also personally delivered to United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres on behalf of the KNK.




We organised a conference in Brussels on 3 October to bring the initiative to the attention of both domestic and international audiences, particularly the Kurdish public. The aim of the conference was to place this issue on the agenda of all Kurds and their friends, bring everyone together around a common position and raise awareness.




Everyone was invited to the conference. Participation was largely successful, although there were some gaps. We will work to address these. The decision was shared with all Kurds. A KNK delegation travelled to South Kurdistan and held high-level meetings with all the major political figures and parties there.




We want everyone to participate in this process. So far, no one has expressed opposition to the initiative. However, discussions are continuing about how different parties will participate and how the process will be conducted.




What decisions were taken at the conference, and what plans do you have for implementing them?




The conference decided to establish a broad national committee involving all parties, organisations, institutions and relevant figures. This committee will be responsible for coordinating the initiative and advancing the process.




It was also decided that, once the committee has been established, a signature campaign will be launched for submission to the UN and international institutions. The aim is to organise a petition campaign involving millions of people.




However, the campaign has not yet begun. The committee must first be established. Once it is formed, it will begin its work and develop further plans. 




The committee will then take steps to submit the signatures collected during the campaign to the UN. We plan to visit the UN headquarters in New York to present the signatures and hold meetings.




What stage has the establishment of the international representation committee reached? Which groups will participate in its work?




We held discussions with all the parties before the conference and consulted everyone. We now have a decision and a document outlining the basis of this process. The committee has not yet been established. We will begin a new round of discussions to form it.




We will ask the parties, organisations and institutions we have consulted to nominate their representatives to the committee if they agree to participate. We want to know who will represent them on this committee. We are currently at the initial stage of the process.




Delegations will probably travel to South Kurdistan and Rojava in the near future. Discussions will be held with all groups, including those in these regions. The views and participation of different parties, groups and political representatives are important. The KNK will coordinate these efforts and hold discussions with everyone involved.




The committee will not consist solely of political representatives. Lawyers, diplomats and experts must also participate in this work. Different subcommittees involving specialists could be established. These structures, organised around law, diplomacy and other areas of expertise, could carry out their work through a broad network.




What diplomatic steps are needed to secure observer status for the Kurds at the UN? How can the experiences of other peoples provide guidance?




Since we do not have a state, observer status is the option available for our representation at the UN. To achieve this, a state or group of states must bring the issue before the UN General Assembly, where it must secure majority support.




This is not an easy process. A country must place the issue on the General Assembly's agenda. We cannot set the agenda ourselves because we do not have that right. There are approximately 192 member states at the UN. At least one of these states, or a group of them, must bring the issue forward. This requires us to conduct international lobbying efforts.




There are also examples of other peoples securing observer status at the UN. We can look at how the Palestinians achieved representation with observer status. The Arab League first recognised the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) as the legitimate representative of the Palestinian people. It then brought this decision before the UN General Assembly. In the subsequent vote, a majority accepted the PLO's representation of the Palestinian people with observer status.




A similar process took place in South Africa. While Nelson Mandela was in prison, the African Union recognised the African National Congress (ANC) as the legitimate representative of the Black population of South Africa. An application was then submitted to the UN, and this representation was accepted. Today, the ANC is South Africa's ruling party. Since South Africa is already a member state of the United Nations, there is no longer any need for its former observer status.




A similar process took place in Namibia with the South West Africa People's Organisation (SWAPO). The African Union recognised SWAPO as the legitimate representative of Namibia. The issue was subsequently brought before the UN, which accepted this representation and granted observer status.




These examples demonstrate that there is also a path towards international recognition of legitimate Kurdish representation. However, we face a long, difficult and challenging road ahead. We have taken a step, but we are still at the beginning of the process.




We have embarked on this journey, and we will continue. This initiative represents another dimension of the broader struggle for freedom being pursued in different fields.




One of the fundamental conditions for establishing strong international representation is for Kurdish political forces to develop a common position. What do you see as the main obstacles to Kurdish national unity today?




The question of unity has long been an open wound for the Kurds. Kurdistan was first divided between the Safavids and the Ottomans. This division emerged in practice in the 1500s. The Treaty of Qasr-e Shirin, signed in 1639, formalised the division, leaving one part of Kurdistan within Iran and the other within Ottoman territory. The separation continued after this formal division. Later, the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 divided Kurdistan into four parts. This remains a deep wound for the Kurdish people.




The fundamental causes are occupation and division. Alongside these historical circumstances, there are also obstacles preventing Kurdish organisations from coming together. The process of national awakening and nation-building among the Kurds began relatively late, and sufficient national unity has not been achieved.




We are trying to bring everyone together through a different approach. The KNK has been working towards this goal since 1999. National unity is one of the KNK's most important priorities. We have not yet achieved all our objectives, but this remains on our agenda.




The call for a national conference at the 3 October conference was also important in this respect. The lack of national unity is felt everywhere. We maintain relations with parties and groups from Kurdistan and with all sections of society. Our fundamental objective is to come together around a common strategy and establish an institution capable of representing all of us.




For example, we can find common ground on representation at the UN. Even if we have not yet established a sufficiently developed institutional structure, we can make a joint decision on international representation for the Kurds, establish a joint committee and work together.




We can celebrate Newroz together in the diaspora, organise joint events and conferences, and hold emergency meetings whenever an important issue arises in Kurdistan. We are putting these proposals to everyone we meet. We are not committed to a single formula; we are open to everyone's suggestions.




There is now more dialogue among Kurds than in the past. The region also faces considerable dangers. If we cannot come together, we risk losing the gains we have achieved. If we unite, we can both protect our existing gains and build on them. All these developments are compelling us to come together. The people want this too.




Everyone must therefore put party interests aside and prioritise national interests. Parties can continue to exist, but we must also come together under a common national umbrella and within the framework of a shared strategy. This is a matter of vital importance.




How does the “Peace and Democratic Society Process” in North Kurdistan affect efforts towards Kurdish unity and international representation?




Kurds now have greater opportunities to come together. The Peace and Democratic Society Process also contributes to unity among Kurds. The success of this process is of vital importance to all Kurds.




If the obstacles to resolving the Kurdish question in the North begin to be overcome and the issue moves towards a solution, this will have positive effects on the other three parts of Kurdistan. It will also have a positive impact on the region and contribute to bringing Kurds together.




The current period and circumstances are favourable in this respect. We need to take steps towards both national unity and international representation. We have taken the first step, and we will continue to develop this process.

title: Commemoration in Kobanê for 68 martyrs
content:
A tent has been erected at Martyr Dicle Cemetery in Kobanê to commemorate 68 YJA Star/HPG guerrillas who fell as martyrs in different years while serving in the ranks of the Kurdistan Freedom Movement.




On Tuesday, a convoy of people from the cities and towns of Til Temir, Hesekê, Zirgan, Dirbêsiyê, Qamişlo, Dêrik, Girkê Legê, Til Koçer, Amûdê, Tirbespiyê and Çilaxa gathered at the Kandil Junction in Til Temir before setting off for Kobanê to attend the ceremony.




In observance of the commemoration, all shops and markets in the city of Kobanê were closed.




According to information provided by the Council of Martyrs’ Families, speeches will be delivered at the ceremony on behalf of the Council of Martyrs’ Families, the Kongra Star Coordination, political parties, the Democratic Islam Congress and numerous other organizations.




In addition, a video message from Murat Karayılan, central commander of the People's Defense Headquarter, will be shown. A video presentation documenting the lives, struggle and sacrifices of the fallen fighters will also be screened.

title: Submission to the Council of Europe: ECtHR ruling on Öcalan remains unimplemented after 12 years
content:
According to Mezopotamya Agency (MA), Asrın Law Office, which represents Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan, submitted a communication to the Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers over Turkey’s failure to implement the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) ruling issued in 2014.




The submission recalled the Committee of Ministers’ interim resolution of September 17, 2025, concerning the Gurban group of cases, which includes the “Öcalan No. 2” judgment.




It noted that the Committee had requested information from Turkey by the end of June 2026 on progress made in implementing the judgments, but that Turkey had failed to submit the required information or an action plan within that period.




The law office stated that Turkey had not established any legal mechanism allowing aggravated life sentences to be reviewed after a specified period.




Öcalan excluded from the scope of the legislation




The submission also addressed the bill on 

Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Cohesion

. Prepared as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, the bill was submitted to the Parliamentary Speaker’s Office on 5 August and subsequently passed by Parliament’s Justice Commission. It was also debated in the General Assembly and adopted with 468 votes.




The law office stated that the legislation did not remove the categorical exclusions from eligibility for conditional release or introduce a general, periodic, and individualized review mechanism for aggravated life sentences.




It noted that Article 6 of Law No. 7595, which provides an exception for life and aggravated life sentences imposed for crimes committed before June 1, 2005, effectively excludes Öcalan from the scope of the law.




Asrın Law Office stated that this provision demonstrates the persistence of the structural problems identified by the ECtHR in its “Öcalan No. 2” judgment.




Constitutional Court application remains unresolved




The submission recalled that an individual application was filed with the Constitutional Court (AYM) on December 3, 2021, seeking to remedy the violation identified in the ECtHR judgment, but that no decision has yet been issued.




The law office also pointed out that Turkey’s action plan, submitted on October 5, 2026, did not specify any legislative measures aimed at implementing the “Öcalan No. 2” judgment.




It noted that Turkey submitted the action plan only after the deadline set by the Committee for providing information on the implementation of the judgments and following the inclusion of the Gurban group of cases on the agenda of the Committee’s December 1–3, 2026 meeting. The law office called for this timing to be taken into account as part of the process of supervising the implementation of the judgments.




Five demands to the Council of Europe




Asrın Law Office called on the Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers to take the following steps:




- Place the Gurban group of cases, which includes the “Öcalan No. 2” judgment, on the agenda of every human rights meeting under the enhanced supervision procedure.




- Reaffirm that the violation is ongoing.




- Request legislative measures in line with the findings and principles set out in the ECtHR judgment and require progress reports on their implementation.




- Move the supervision process out of its current state of stagnation by introducing new and effective mechanisms.




- Given that more than 12 years have passed since the judgment, ensure that the process is monitored jointly with the Secretary General of the Council of Europe and the President of the Parliamentary Assembly.




The law office emphasized the need for an effective, regular, and consistent supervision mechanism to ensure the implementation of the ECtHR judgment.

author: Ayurdhi Dhar, PhD
title: Being Mindful of Agony: How to Incorporate the Sublime in Our Daily Life—An Interview with Will Adams
content:
H

ow does a wounded world wound us in return? Can we be mindful and offer intimate attention to pain and trauma? We answer these and other questions with Will Adams who is an Associate Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychology at Duquesne University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. He holds a PhD in Clinical Psychology from Duquesne and completed his clinical psychology internship at McLean Hospital, affiliated with Harvard Medical School.




Dr. Adams is the author of 

A Wild and Sacred Call: Nature-Psyche-Spirit

, published by SUNY Press, a book that explores the deep connections between human psychology, the natural world, and spirituality. His work brings together phenomenology, relational psychoanalysis, Gestalt therapy, transpersonal psychology, and contemplative traditions, particularly Zen Buddhism and Christian mysticism.




His scholarship invites us to reconsider the relationship between self and world, mind and nature, and psychological healing and spiritual life. In this very personal interview, we’ll be speaking with him about how a lifetime of contemplative practice came to his rescue during the most traumatic time in his life, the possibilities of a relational understanding of human and more-than-human experience, and what psychology might learn from contemplative traditions and our relationship with the natural world.




The transcript below has been edited for length and clarity. Listen to the audio of the interview here.







Ayurdhi Dhar: Dr. Adams, you’ve learned from multiple traditions—Christian mysticism, Buddhism, and phenomenology, which is the study of lived experience. How did all of these come together?




Will Adams:

 First, I want to say that I appreciate this opportunity to have this conversation. I want to thank you and thank Mad in America for touching folks in a deep way, especially many folks that have been marginalized and wounded.




This was during my undergraduate years at University of North Carolina which got me interested in humanistic and existential psychology. I had powerful experiences with a roommate in college and then later volunteering at a state psychiatric hospital. I started reading people like Martin Buber and R. D. Laing, and I found my way to a wonderful master’s program at University of West Georgia. You and I both are alums from that program. That program changed my life.




I went to London to study with R. D. Laing. Then I came to Duquesne as a PhD student and immersed myself in not just phenomenology, but the larger human science psychology tradition. I became interested in meditation. I practiced Vipassana meditation for 11 years, and then a wonderful Zen teacher fell into my life, Bruce Harris; I’ve been practicing with him for 26 years now.




I’m practicing psychotherapy and bringing these sensibilities into the therapy. Later I realized that with all the ecological destruction and desecration, with our human plundering of the natural world, the more-than-human natural world, that psychology has something to say about this, because it’s not only a biological problem—habitat destruction, mass extinction, climate change. It’s a malady of consciousness and culture, and psychology has something to say about consciousness and culture. All of this sparked me to do work in eco-psychology.




Dhar: You spoke about suffering; a lot of our readers are privy to what suffering is. They’re often people with lived experience of terrible psychological distress and also of horrid institutional responses that we have to that distress. You mentioned working at the state psychiatric hospital, and how that was an important experience for you. Could you share your experience at the Halloween carnival at the institution?




Adams:

 That experience, and also the one with my college roommate were life-changing. We were roommates and dear friends. He was realizing that he was gay, and this was at a time when it was much more dangerous to express than today. We had long, intimate conversations about his excitement, his suffering, his confusion, and his inspiration. This is before I studied psychology, but through those conversations, his trust and generosity, and his opening to me, I realized that really being with another person, and listening intimately and openly is transformative.




That was right at the time I volunteered at the state psychiatric hospital. It was a bleak place, not quite as extreme as the depiction in 

One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest

, but similar. I was working on a unit that was locked, a unit with schizophrenic men, and there was a Halloween carnival coming up. Most of the men had lost contact with their family and friends. This was a time when folks were hospitalized for decades. They didn’t have any Halloween costumes and they asked me if I would bring face paints so that they could have some kind of costume decoration.




We painted each other’s faces and went to this carnival. I went up to this booth that had basketball, and the person behind the booth, the nursing staff, said, “This is a basketball, do you see? You take this and throw it through that hoop, and you win a prize, you see?” It seemed a little strange, but I just took a couple shots and went to the next booth.




There was another booth and the person that was handling the booth talked to me in the very same way—really slowly “this is a game, and you get those rings on those bottles, and you win a prize, and do you see how this works?” It was just really weird, but it struck me that this is how the nursing staff thinks they’re supposed to talk to psychiatric patients. This is their view of what it means to be suffering psychologically, that it’s like being a little kid or having brain damage. Even today, 40 years later, I feel this sort of uneasy chill running through my body because it was horrible to be treated that way.




That experience coupled with these conversations with my roommate, made me realize that we don’t really need that much from each other; we just need someone who listens, is open and cares, doesn’t judge us or quickly put us in a box.




Dhar: About 15 years ago, I did my clinical internship at a state psychiatric hospital in India, about 9,000 miles away from where you were, and it was the same. There was both an infantilization of the patients, so treating them like they were kids, but also something punitive about it, punishing them like they were kids.




I remember psychiatrists during our morning rounds talking about patients like they were not there in the room. It’s interesting that across culture and time, that kind of punitive infantilization of some of the most vulnerable people, remains.




I have found that with many people going through extreme states, people with lived experience, some form of spirituality was important in recovery. What do you think about how spirituality can help some people heal through some really adverse experiences, from trauma and self-harm to psychosis or depression. Have you met such people?




Adams:

 Yes, and one of those people was me, because four years ago I had a horrible trauma where my neck was broken, and I could have easily died, been brain damaged, or paralyzed. My contemplative practice and some spiritual realizations that came as a blessing were profoundly life-saving. It saved my life and saved my sanity.




There have been so many people that I’ve known for whom spirituality has been crucially important in healing, growth, transformation, and in navigating the ongoing pain that life sends us. Sometimes it’s formal, organized religion, other times not. The common ground is a deep experiential realization that we’re not separate from each other, from the community, from the rest of nature, and we’re not separate from this great unfathomable, infinite, all-encompassing, all-pervasive mystery that goes by different names in different spiritual traditions.




That realization about the lack of separation that we’re not in it alone, but we’re in it with each other and even for each other—in service of each other—is crucial. One of the most profoundly healing experiences is offering ourselves in the service of others. Spiritual traditions differ in many ways, but the heart of these traditions seems to be a surpassing of a supposedly separate, self-centered, narcissistic stance. Once one realizes this, then the natural response is kindness and compassion, not because the Ten Commandments or the Buddhist precepts or the APA ethical principles tell you. It’s just completely obvious and natural.




Dhar: When I’ve talked to people with lived experience, apart from spirituality, the other important thing has been being of service to others. Peer support is built on that, but I know people who take care of animals, often at great personal cost, but it allows them to heal and not get lost into throes of psychosis or pits of depression.




You said that this idea that we are separate is a delusion. A lot of psychological theories would come in and dispute that, saying achieving a sense of separation is the foundation for a healthy ego. Many of these become pop psychological theories. On Instagram or Facebook, we have overwhelming narratives around strong boundaries or that you must only care about your own truth or anybody who doesn’t agree with you is toxic and should be cut off. I’m sure cutting people off is absolutely needed sometimes. There are some truly awful people out there, but the push towards disconnection and separation is real. Why do you think psychology equates health with a strong sense of separateness?




Adams:

 Contemporary psychology often does advocate for separation as the pinnacle of health, autonomy, that version of a strong ego. That’s happening in 2026 and this was a concern that Shakyamuni Buddha raised 2,500 years ago in a very different culture.




The fantasy of being a supposed separate self, or I would add a supposedly separate species—humans elevated above the rest of nature—that’s a delusion. It’s a delusion that’s based upon confusion and paranoia and greed, and it amplifies each. When I say that it’s a delusion, I’m not critiquing the affirmation of difference. You and I are different people, but we’re having a wonderful conversation. I’m different from the plant, and from the water, but I’m feeling its coolness, and I know I can get a drink. I’m not separate.




But separation, the felt sense that I’m actually independent, that my well-being can be separate from and independent from the well-being of my brothers and sisters, both human and more-than-human, this is a dangerous delusion. It arises because life is really painful and scary at times. We’re all going to die. The people we love are going to die.




There’s something alluring about the fantasy of reinforcing my supposedly separate, independent, autonomous self. 

David Loy

 says it’s not just that humans are aware that we and all of our loved ones will die, but deep inside we are aware that our taken-for-granted notion of our “self” isn’t real from the start. Historically, modernity gave us a lot of gifts. But modernity joining with the technological power of science and technology also led to an overreaction, where a core ethos of modern Western European culture was that we would be separate from and elevated above the rest of nature and dominate and control and exploit the rest of nature. Masters and possessors of nature—this is total madness!




Dhar: We are part of it. We are it.




Adams:

 We are it, nature. That’s the thing. You can’t be separate from what you most deeply are, but you can have the fantasy that you’re separate. There are developmental processes in an individual’s life that lead to a sense of supposedly separate self, partly to help us navigate this strange, wild, confusing, and sometimes dangerous world that we’re growing up in.




It’s helpful to distinguish between so-called ego strengths, like the capacity to reflect, to think, to not act on impulses, to be able to hold painful or pleasurable experiences without immediately acting, the capacity to remember and to plan. All of these ego strengths are valuable. They are different than the representational aspect of the ego, where we give ourselves a self-representation—“I’m smart, I’m kind, I’m a psychology professor.” The self-representation that’s the most bedeviling is “I’m a separate self.”




Dhar: In your book you discuss what I’m calling are cultural determinants of mental health—these larger narratives in the culture. You write that our suffering is partly because of these larger cultural stories that we are told. For example, a homeless person is depressed because there’s a whole world telling them that you should pull yourself up by your bootstraps and they’re not able to. We professionals say, “The problem is in you. It’s your personality, it’s your neurotransmitters.” As a professional, how do we respond to cultural pain and how do we not harm people more than we already have by individualizing their issues?




Adams:

 It seems to me, the basic structure of suffering goes like this. Life is painful and scary so I separate myself or I separate my tribe. Me and my tribe are separate. Because we’re frightened, we elevate ourselves above others as a defense mechanism, a security move. Out of elevation, we devalue others. This happens individually, but it also happens collectively. Out of that devaluation, we feel entitled to exploit, control others. Fear, separation, elevation, devaluation, domination, right?




This happens interpersonally and collectively. The collective systemic structural pathologies that Mad in America addresses operate according to that dynamic. There needs to be an interdisciplinary multifocal psycho-cultural therapy with different people and groups working in different ways that complement each other. This has to be according to one’s personal inclinations and gifts. We need psychotherapy and we need friendship. We need interpersonal exchange. But we also need people working on the legal system, the political system, the educational system, larger collective systems.




It’s crucial that we find a way for ourselves and in support of each other to take the most painful as well as the most joyful experiences, experiences that feel like they’re ineffable, unsharable, unspeakable, no one will understand. We need to find at least one other trusted person who can listen openly, non-judgmentally, non-punitively, and dare to say what can’t be said, because it can be said, in the right relationship. This happens individually, but it also happens collectively, to speak up and challenge the pathological madness of our contemporary culture.




Dhar: Let’s shift gears a little. People can have very profound spiritual or peak experiences that leave them shaken and in awe. How can we turn the altered states of consciousness into altered traits of consciousness? How can we incorporate the sublime into our daily life and pay “intimate attention” to the world around us?




Adams:

 This is the heart of psychological and spiritual practice to me. I learned this phrase from Huston Smith. He says that the point of spiritual practice is not to just have altered states of consciousness, but to cultivate altered traits of character. The point of spiritual practice, and even of psychotherapy, is not to have special experiences on a meditation cushion or in conversation with a psychotherapist, as valuable and profoundly important as those can be. The point is living differently day to day with each other and for each other.




These powerful experiences are often fleeting and ephemeral. The opportunity, and indeed the responsibility is to find a way to integrate them without reifying them, to integrate them into our more consistent reliable ways of being with each other. How to do this is a beautiful question. First is to not make those experiences so special. To really open to the deep intuition that the depths of life and of myself are ceaselessly being revealed and are playing out all the time. It’s not like we have to get anywhere else. The deepest realization is that there’s no distinction between spirituality and the rest of life. This is it.




My Zen teacher says mindfulness practices are helpful but the deepest practice is one of re-mindfulness—how do we remind ourselves many times a day to open, to release, and respond with the best understanding, compassion, love, and justice we can bring forth in actual nitty-gritty everyday encounters. We make a devoted commitment while knowing that we’re going to forget, that we get lost. We’re fallible, we get confused, frightened, and shut down. This is just the territory of being human with each other. Make a commitment to many times a day, pause and recognize the depths that are ceaselessly flowing forth, the overtures of life that are being sent to us and to say yes to those overtures.




I think a daily meditation practice is immensely helpful, that you consecrate a certain time and space to do a meditation practice. But then the deepest meditation, the deepest spiritual practice is everyday life, everyday relationship. In Zen, we say the world is our Zendo. For example, there is a stone in my pocket. Whenever my hand touches this stone accidentally—I reach for my keys or I’m just sitting with my hands in my lap—it’s a re-mindfulness stone. It’s a spiritual touchstone, literally. I touch the stone and I pause, and silently to myself I open and savor that this is my life. How do I want to live? How do I want to respond? That helps me integrate things.




Dhar: That is lovely but it makes me think—let’s say a person who’s listening to the interview is going through devastating grief or brutal withdrawal from psychiatric medications. They might say, “Well, if I were to sit down mindfully and consider that this is my life and feel the pain of withdrawal or of grief, it would not help!” So, I want to go back to what you shared with us in the beginning.




What was it like to have to deal with a broken neck, near-death trauma, and have that stone in your pocket where the moment by moment was incredibly painful and deeply terrifying? What was it like to be mindful of agony?




Adams:

 First, I would say there are times to get away from pain. If things are too overwhelming, we need to find ways, maybe it’s distracting ourselves, taking a medication, just moving away from pain. We need to learn the difference between pain as a danger signal that we need to take seriously and protect ourselves from and pain that isn’t actively threatening us and that we could open to and understand and learn from and even grow from. How can we be scared but not scared away? Pain says pay attention, something important is happening. I don’t want to romanticize the pain.




But we also know, and Freud and the other depth psychologists, but also the spiritual teachers show us that a habitual response of avoidance towards pain doesn’t work over time. What we try to push away is going to come back to haunt us. It’s important to cultivate our capacities to allow pain to come into our awareness so that we can discern how we want to respond. Meditation practice really helps with this.




In particular, you ask about my trauma. I went to hang out with my son and we went mountain bike riding. We were riding through the woods at a park in Pittsburgh. He skillfully rode over this small wooden bridge that didn’t have any rails, that was over a creek. My bike hit a bump at the beginning of the bridge. I lost control of the bike, fell over the handlebars into the creek, and really hit my neck—it snapped. I could feel it instantly. I knew, “Oh, this is really bad.”




To make a long story short, my years of meditation practice came in because I knew I needed to lay as still as possible because if I moved, I could die or get paralyzed. My spinal cord would be severed. I was hurting in the worst way I’ve ever hurt. My 14-year-old son saved my life and got paramedics there and got me to a hospital. I had multiple vertebrae fracture, especially cervical vertebrae, lumbar vertebrae, broken ribs, broken skull, but I was alive, thanks to my son, and I would say also thanks to my Zen practice.




They needed to do neurosurgery to fuse my spine; it was scheduled for two days later. The first night, after everything quieted down, everyone left, I was in the worst pain I had ever felt. Even though they were giving me morphine, it was barely touching it. But the physical pain was only part of it because I was aware that I could die. I could die that night; I could die on the operating table. My meditation practice came into play there. Whenever my eyes were open, the pain was excruciating. Whenever I closed my eyes, I was thrown into this kind of hell realm where these insidious presences, beings, I couldn’t really see them exactly, but they were like evil destructive presences that were trying to kill me. It was like I was in a game that was a deadly serious game. They knew the rules, but I didn’t.




They would attack me and I would try to avoid them and survive, and then they would attack again, surge after surge of these attacks. I knew that if I didn’t win this game, I would actually die. As a psychologist and a long-time contemplative, part of me knew that this was my psyche working out my death dread that helped a teeny tiny little bit, but it was mostly really, really horrible. Again, to make it short, I found a way to make peace with the fact that I might die. I’ve made plenty of mistakes in my life and hurt people that I love, but I’ve also lived a good life, a loving life. I said, okay, if it was just me dying, I could make peace with that. But I wanted to live to be a dad and a husband.




I made a commitment to myself, which was also a promise to my family, I’d do what I could to stay alive. The next day doctors started coming, I got to see my kids, I got to see my wife again. Then the night came, people left, I told my wife to go home and be with my kids. It got quiet, the pain was there all the time, my fear of dying was there, I didn’t want to die and leave my family bereft, and the hell realm started coming back. I felt like I was helpless, I couldn’t do anything, I couldn’t do anything to stop the pain, I couldn’t do anything to get out of the hell realm. But then I remembered, well, what I can do is breathe. I can breathe consciously, and I can open to the painful stuff without letting it totally tyrannize me, control me, captivate me. I could make a contemplative meditative space for the stuff to arise and hit me but not dominate me. That I could find a capaciousness of awareness that allowed this.




Eventually as I was breathing, meditating, this was like minutes by minutes by hours by hours, breathing out, opening, breathing out, releasing. Suddenly, unexplainably, everything released. The pain released, my death dread released, I released, I was gone, and all that was there was love. Boundless love, boundless spaciousness, suffused with love, imbued with love. I was gone. I died, but I died into love. I don’t know how long I was gone. I was outside of clock time. It was eternal, not everlasting.


Eventually I returned to something kind of approximating ordinary consciousness, although still resounding with this boundless love, absolute openness, peace. My neck pain and my fear of dying came back, but they weren’t grabbing me like before. In that experience, as I was coming back, I realized this is the way it always is. This is our nature. This is what life is, this dynamic presencing of what felt like love. That was pretty darn important, but Ayurdhi, what was even more important were two things that happened after that.




As my pain and dread of dying and leaving my family came back, it was totally clear to me that that the pain and death dread were an expression of that boundless love. Even though I didn’t want them, even though I didn’t like it, even though I was ready to move past them, that’s just the way it was; and seeing them, feeling them, knowing them as strangely perfect expressions of love was liberating.




I realized that my surgery was the next day, but I was already healed in the deepest way possible. That I could die that night or on the surgeon’s table, and I would still be well. That somehow, I had fallen into or been carried into a wellness that’s deeper than any wound. Coming through that experience, I knew that my spiritual practice was to live up to the gift of that boundless love day to day in my everyday relationships, to embody and convey that love in the nitty-gritty encounters of day-to-day life. Ever since then, these experiences are more vividly present for me day by day.




Dhar: I want to thank you for sharing that story; it was extremely powerful and quite beautiful, and equally horrifying—all of those things at the same time.




Adams:

 All of those things. This experience that I lived through, and I’m still trying to live up to is what inspired me to be writing this next book that’s almost done. That’s the one on trauma, love, and meditation, and where I tell my story.




***

author: cnt.es
title: CNT, por el derecho a una pensión pública y a un salario digno por nuestro trabajo
content:
La anarconsindical apoya la manifestación en defensa del Sistema Público de Pensiones del 24 de octubre

.







Tenemos un ojo puesto en la indisimulada intención de desmantelamiento y saqueo de las pensiones públicas por parte de la oposición política, pero tampoco perdamos de vista las medidas regresivas para las futuras pensionistas, introducidas por el gobierno en las últimas legislaturas. La última entró de lleno en la negociación colectiva con la Ley 12/2022. Ahí se regulaba el impulso de los planes de pensiones de empleo, modificando la Ley de 2002. Con ella, un fondo que es de promoción pública puede ser gestionado por el sector privado, sin que el propio Ministerio garantice el valor de las aportaciones efectuadas, ni la rentabilidad de estas.




Un fondo de promoción pública, gestionado por el sector privado nos lleva a un sistema de pensiones mixto, donde nuestra pensión pública resulte más miserable. Y esto se puede hacer en un convenio colectivo en tu nombre, con rúbrica sindical.




Viene de atrás




En julio de 2006, algunas centrales sindicales pactaron con el Gobierno del PSOE y la patronal el Acuerdo sobre Medidas en Materia de Seguridad Social. Desde una perspectiva anarcosindicalista, aquel acuerdo representó una nueva renuncia del sindicalismo institucional: en lugar de impulsar la acción directa y la defensa intransigente de las pensiones, subordinó los intereses de la clase trabajadora a la lógica del Estado y del capital. Así se abrió un proceso que, desde entonces, no ha dejado de generar polémica, incertidumbre y alarma social.




Ya entonces denunciamos las consecuencias del acuerdo en un celebrado dossier donde advertíamos que el pacto no protegía el futuro de las pensiones, sino que profundizaba la dependencia de las y los trabajadores respecto de unas instituciones concebidas para preservar el orden capitalista. Nuestra idea era sencilla: Frente a la concertación social y la delegación en burocracias sindicales, defender la organización desde la base, la solidaridad de clase y la movilización sostenida. Y el tiempo nos da la razón.




Los derechos y las condiciones de vida de la clase trabajadora —en activo o jubilada— no pueden quedar en manos del Estado, de la patronal, ni de sus mecanismos de concertación. Para CNT, las pensiones son salario diferido y una conquista colectiva; su defensa exige autonomía obrera, apoyo mutuo, acción directa y control de los propios trabajadores y trabajadoras. Y eso solo puede impulsarse desde organizaciones independientes del poder político y económico capaces de impedir que estos derechos se conviertan en moneda de cambio.




Está claro que si no nos resignamos y empleamos las herramientas reales que tenemos a nuestro alcance, abrimos una oportunidad de avance como ya estamos experimentando en el tema de la vivienda.




La amenaza al Sistema Público de Pensiones




Tras la firma de aquel acuerdo de 2006, los sucesivos gobiernos adoptaron medidas que debilitaron el sistema público de pensiones.




CNT puede hablar claro porque no tiene ninguna atadura que le impida identificar la pasividad y el colaboracionismo de algunas centrales sindicales, que obligó al surgimiento de un movimiento importante movimiento de ámbito estatal en defensa del Sistema Público de Pensiones (SPP).




El movimiento social en defensa del SPP nació para frenar los retrocesos impulsados por los gobiernos, la patronal y las burocracias sindicales mediante la organización desde la base y la movilización sostenida en las calles, junto con la presión hacia los grupos parlamentarios más sensibles a la defensa de las pensiones públicas. Esta combinación de presión social e intervención institucional marcó su estrategia.




Con una constancia infinita, se han logrado pequeños avances, pero la confianza depositada en la vía institucional ha dificultado una respuesta autónoma, sostenida y capaz de imponer cambios y blindaje mediante la presión social y la acción directa.




Desde CNT no se ha dejado de advertir la intoxicación mediática, política y sindical destinada a saquear el sistema y debilitarlo, para luego presentarlo como inviable y justificar así su privatización. Esta estrategia se apoya en el denominado modelo multipilar, promovido por el Banco Mundial en 1994 y actualizado en 2005, que amplía progresivamente el espacio reservado a los sistemas privados de ahorro y previsión. Y la UE no anda lejos, pues fue la que obligó a la reforma de 2022.




Presentadas como ajustes técnicos o medidas de sostenibilidad, estas reformas avanzan gradualmente hacia una aspiración liberal: convertir las pensiones de la clase trabajadora en una mercancía gestionada por fondos financieros. Nos toman por tontas, si no son viables, ¿por qué quiere entrar el capital financiero? La realidad es que nuestro sistema era tan bueno que nuestra hucha que llegó a tener 67.000 millones en 2011, gracias a Rajoy cayó en 2018 hasta su nivel más bajo, con 5.000 millones. Sin devolver el dinero a la caja, ahora ya tenemos 18.000 millones otra vez. Es un caramelo más que sostenible.




La experiencia demuestra que la privatización va más lenta de lo que quisieran, en parte, por la correlación de fuerzas en el Congreso. Esto puedo cambiar enseguida porque los buitres financieros no renuncian a apropiarse de nuestros recursos de clase destinados a garantizar una vejez digna o la suficiencia ante la incapacidad laboral, orfandad o viudedad, y seguirán presionando a los partidos políticos para conseguir reformas favorables a sus intereses. Muchos de los fondos de inversión depredadores son principales accionistas de bancos que, a su vez, presionan a los gobiernos y  también lo son de los principales medios de comunicación, con BlackRock a la cabeza.




La pensión pública digna, reivindicación esencial de CNT y el internacionalismo obrero




Aunque CNT tiene sus matices respecto a la estrategia institucional del movimiento social pensionista, siempre ha respaldado en el ámbito local las movilizaciones semanales en distintos puntos del Estado. Asimismo, cada año llama a su afiliación a participar en la concentración estatal de octubre.




No obstante, confiamos más en la acción directa de la clase trabajadora y defendemos que la lucha por las pensiones públicas debe situarse en los centros de trabajo y muy especialmente, en la negociación colectiva, pues este es el último agujero que se abrió en el edificio del S.P. Pensiones. Es ahí donde es más necesaria la sensibilización y organización conjunta de trabajadoras en activo y pensionistas, fortaleciendo la solidaridad de clase y convirtiendo la defensa de la pensión pública suficiente en una reivindicación esencial del conjunto del movimiento obrero -al mismo nivel que el salario o la vivienda- después de toda una vida sometida a la explotación y de contribuir a la obscena riqueza de unos pocos. Porque ellos sí que son los parásitos.




Necesidad de una respuesta global




Considerando que el ataque a los Sistemas Públicos de Pensiones es transnacional, en 2023 la Confederación Internacional del Trabajo (CIT), a propuesta de CNT, remarcó que la lucha debe ser internacional, porque los atacantes también actúan a escala mundial. En las escasas zonas del planeta donde el movimiento obrero había arrancado este derecho, esas sabandijas quieren convertirlo en una nueva fuente de negocio. Es un hecho que hoy están en peligro las pensiones en Francia, Alemania, Italia, Suiza, …, algo impensable hace pocos años. Aunque nuestro sistema resiste mejor, no lo permitiremos.




Lucha por las pensiones públicas: Pocos puntos, pero muy claros




Para CNT, el derecho a una pensión digna se defiende y se consigue, si luchamos decididamente por estos tres puntos:




– Pensión pública = SMI o 60% del salario medio de la comunidad autónoma, siempre y cuando sea superior al estatal.




– No a la obligatoriedad de planes de pensiones privados. No a los planes de pensiones de empleo.




– No al aumento de la edad de jubilación. No al aumento de periodo de cómputo.




Y lo vamos a conseguir.




La entrada 

CNT, por el derecho a una pensión pública y a un salario digno por nuestro trabajo

 se publicó primero en 

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

author: dev
title: Pour Ritchy Thibault, premier prisonnier politique du mouvement lycéen
content:
Ritchy Thibault est Gilet jaune depuis ses 14 ans, voyageur depuis toujours, écrivain quand il le faut. Étudiant brillant sur son temps libre, assistant parlementaire interdit d'accès à l'assemblée, journaliste quand ça lui chante, il est aussi le premier prisonnier politique du mouvement lycéen en cours pour avoir appelé au soulèvement. Placé à l'isolement à la prison de Fleury-Mérogis, les contacts vers l'extérieur lui sont théoriquement interdits, nous avons proposé à ses amis de lui écrire en vidéo et à ses avocats de raconter comment en France, en 2026, on peut finir en prison pour des mots.







Ami et un collaborateur de lundimatin, il tient désormais dans une page une chronique hebdomadaire depuis sa détention.




Pour lire les deux premières :




Le 17 octobre depuis le quartier d'isolement de Fleury-Mérogis




Pourquoi les lycées brûlent-ils ?
