author: Brenda Medina
title: Departamento de imigração dos EUA diz que Ramagem é imigrante ilegal e violou leis
content:
A detenção-relâmpago de Alexandre Ramagem nos EUA no começo deste ano parece ter criado uma guerra de narrativas dentro do próprio governo americano. 




Enquanto o Departamento de Estado afirma que a Polícia Federal “manipulou” o sistema legal americano, 

o Departamento de Segurança Interna (DHS, na sigla em inglês) diz que Ramagem é um “imigrante ilegal” e está sujeito a detenção e deportação.

 Segundo o DHS, o fato de Ramagem ter feito um pedido de asilo político não lhe dá proteção. 




Ex-diretor da Abin e ex-deputado federal pelo PL, Ramagem foi condenado a 16 anos de prisão pela tentativa de golpe de Estado durante o governo do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro. Ele está nos EUA desde que foi condenado pelo Supremo Tribunal Federal, em setembro do ano passado, quando fugiu do Brasil através da Guiana

 

com auxílio de um criminoso

 condenado por garimpo ilegal na terra Yanomami.  




Em abril, o ICE, a polícia imigratória dos EUA que responde ao Departamento de Segurança Interna, prendeu Ramagem em Orlando por permanecer além do prazo do seu visto de turista, mas ele foi libertado dois dias depois.

 Ele não pagou fiança, segundo Paulo Figueiredo, que afirmou diversas vezes que sua 

empresa

 de consultoria de imigração, a Immigrex, está auxiliando Ramagem. Procurado pelo ICIJ, Figueiredo afirmou que não sabia como localizar Ramagem e não podia falar em nome da Immigrex.




“Obrigado, Presidente Trump e todos na administração”, escreveu Figueiredo no X. 

Eduardo Bolsonaro agradeceu a Trump e ao Secretário de Estado Marco Rubio. Sóstenes Cavalcante, líder do PL, disse que Rubio ajudou a acelerar a libertação

, ou ela teria levado pelo menos duas semanas.




Diferentemente de outros casos, nenhum juiz precisou ordenar sua libertação. Imigrantes detidos geralmente precisam comparecer diante de um juiz de imigração para solicitar libertação sob fiança. No caso de Ramagem, a reportagem não encontrou nenhuma petição judicial. 




O próprio Ramagem já havia sugerido antes que tinha costas quentes. 

Em um 

vídeo

 publicado em novembro de 2025, após o Supremo Tribunal Federal do Brasil ordenar sua prisão, ele disse que estava nos Estados Unidos com o conhecimento do governo americano. “Nas palavras até do governo americano para mim: ‘que bom que temos um amigo que está em segurança a salvo aqui nos Estados Unidos’.

 Então a gente tem esse apoio dos norte-americanos”. 




Em 20 de abril, cinco dias após a libertação de Ramagem da custódia de imigração, 

o Departamento de Estado dos EUA suspendeu o credenciamento do policial federal Marcelo Ivo de Carvalho, que era o oficial de ligação da PF lotado em Miami para trabalhar com o ICE e que ajudou na localização e detenção de Ramagem. 




“Nenhum estrangeiro pode manipular nosso sistema de imigração para contornar pedidos formais de extradição e estender perseguições políticas ao território dos Estados Unidos”, escreveu o assessor do Bureau de Assuntos do Hemisfério Ocidental do departamento no X. “Hoje, pedimos que o funcionário brasileiro envolvido deixe o nosso país por tentar fazer isso”. A embaixada dos EUA no Brasil 

compartilhou

 o texto. Em resposta, Paulo Figueiredo tuitou: “tchau, querido”.


































No entanto, o Brasil havia protocolado um pedido formal de extradição no Departamento de Estado em 30 de dezembro de 2025, mais de três meses antes da prisão, segundo o Ministério da Justiça.




Em resposta, o governo Lula suspendeu a permissão de um agente de imigração americano lotado em Brasília, que deixou o país em 22 de abril. 

Em um comunicado, o Ministério das Relações Exteriores disse que os EUA falharam em consultar o Brasil primeiro, como exige o acordo entre os dois países sobre adidos policiais

, e ignoraram a “boa prática diplomática de diálogo entre nações amigas, como Brasil e Estados Unidos, ao longo de mais de 200 anos de relações”.




Agora, o porta-voz do Departamenrto de Segurança Interna confirma que Ramagem está ilegal no país. Em resposta para a ICIJ (Consórcio Internacional de Jornalistas Investigativos), parceiros da 

Agência Pública

 nesta investigação, o porta-voz afirmou: “Em 13 de abril, o ICE prendeu Alexandre Ramagem Rodrigues, um estrangeiro ilegal do Brasil. Ele entrou legalmente no país em 11 de setembro de 2025, em caráter temporário, com permissão para permanecer no país por seis meses, mas optou por permanecer ilegalmente além do prazo autorizado, em violação às leis da nossa nação. Ele foi liberado da custódia do ICE em 15 de abril, enquanto aguarda o resultado do seu processo de deportação”. 




Segundo o DHS, “um caso de pedido pendente NÃO confere nenhum tipo de status legal nos Estados Unidos. Se uma pessoa entra ilegalmente no nosso país, ela está sujeita a detenção ou deportação”. O porta-voz reforçou o recado destacando o “NÃO” em caixa alta na resposta. 




O DHS garante que Ramagem receberá o devido processo legal. E conclui: “Sob o Presidente Trump e o Secretário Mullin, nossa mensagem é clara: estrangeiros ilegais não são bem-vindos em nosso país”.




Procurada, a Casa Branca não respondeu ao pedido de comentário.   
















Foto de Alexandre Ramagem após a detenção em Orange County (EUA)




Um caso que foge à regra 




O caso de Ramagem se destaca em relação aos de centenas de milhares de imigrantes que buscam asilo nos Estados Unidos.




Desde que Trump voltou ao poder em 2025, juízes de imigração ordenaram a remoção de mais de 440.000 solicitantes de asilo, mais do que nos oito anos anteriores, segundo uma análise recente do Washington Post. A libertação da detenção tornou-se a exceção. 




No final de 2025, o ICE estava deportando mais de 14 pessoas diretamente da detenção para cada uma que liberava para aguardar uma audiência, segundo o American Immigration Council, um grupo de defesa que analisou dados do ICE. Em dezembro, a administração pausou o processamento de todos os pedidos de asilo pendentes. 




Um daqueles que ainda esperam é Luis Galeano, um jornalista nicaraguense que fugiu da repressão do governo Ortega à mídia independente e teve sua cidadania nicaraguense cassada em 2023. Em setembro, o ICE o deteve em Orlando enquanto ele dirigia para o Uber. 




Como Ramagem, ele havia entrado legalmente nos Estados Unidos com uma estadia temporária, segundo o Departamento de Segurança Interna, e permaneceu após o prazo enquanto buscava asilo, que ele havia solicitado em 2019. 




Diferentemente do ex-diretor da Abin, ele passou quase duas semanas detido e só foi libertado depois que um juiz de imigração fixou uma fiança de 10 mil dólares. 




O Departamento de Estado, que disse em fevereiro que o governo da Nicarágua havia silenciado e banido a mídia independente, não se pronunciou publicamente sobre o caso de Galeano.

author: radical.guide
title: Emotional support is material
content:
The speaker describes caring militancy as a concept that deliberately collectivizes care. Support becomes a core part of political life, and emotional support and material support are not separate layers. Emotional support is material because it affects who can survive, who can organize and recover, who can refuse work, who can leave harmful situations and who can stay involved in the struggle.




From the Plan C segment of the "The Revolt of Care: Anarchist Mutual Aid in the 21st Century" workshop at the 2026 International Workshops.




A Radical Guide is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that builds movement infrastructure, including a global directory of radical spaces, mutual aid programs, and educational resources for people doing liberation work around the world.




The full day: 

https://www.radical-guide.com/anarchist-international-workshops-2026/

author: radical.guide
title: You are not alone: the most silent form of revolt
content:
Tasos Sagris says real change begins with a gaze turned tenderly to one another and a voice that tells you someone is there, someone is thinking of you, you are not alone. In a world that treats indifference toward others as a sign of maturity and success, every moment of care and spontaneous selfless concern is the most silent form of revolt, an uprising of care.




From the workshop "The Revolt of Care: Anarchist Mutual Aid in the 21st Century" at the 2026 International Workshops.

author: dev
title: « Assommons les groupuscules d'extrême gauche ! »
content:
Détournement du célèbre « Assommons les pauvres ! » de Charles Baudelaire (Les idées s'améliorent. Le sens des mots y participe. Le plagiat est nécessaire. Le progrès l'implique.).




Pendant quinze jours je m'étais confiné dans ma chambre, et je m'étais entouré des journaux et des chaînes d'information à la mode dans ce temps-là ; je veux parler de ces émissions où il est traité de l'art de rendre les peuples libres, tranquilles et obéissants, en vingt-quatre heures. J'avais donc digéré, — avalé, veux-je dire, — toutes les élucubrations de tous ces entrepreneurs de sécurité publique, — de ceux qui conseillent aux Français de sacrifier leurs libertés individuelles sur l'autel de la sécurité collective, et de ceux qui leur persuadent qu'ils vivent dans un pays livré aux professionnels du chaos. — On ne trouvera pas surprenant que je fusse alors dans un état d'esprit avoisinant le vertige ou la stupidité.




Il m'avait semblé seulement que je sentais, confiné au fond de mon intellect, le germe obscur d'une idée supérieure à toutes les formules de maintien de l'ordre dont j'avais récemment parcouru le dictionnaire. Mais ce n'était que l'idée d'une idée, quelque chose d'infiniment vague.




Et je sortis avec une grande soif. Car le goût passionné des mauvaises informations engendre un besoin proportionnel du grand air et des rafraîchissants.




Comme j'allais entrer dans un café, je rencontrai une manifestation. Des étudiants défilaient en brandissant des pancartes sur lesquelles étaient inscrites quelques revendications que je n'eus pas le loisir de déchiffrer. L'un d'eux, un jeune homme d'apparence chétive, portait un sac à dos et tenait à la main une pancarte sur laquelle on pouvait lire : « Moins de flics, plus de frites ! » Il avait un de ces regards inoubliables qui renverseraient les gouvernements, si les regards renversaient les gouvernements, et si les slogans faisaient tomber les ministres.




En même temps, j'entendis une voix qui chuchotait à mon oreille, une voix que je reconnus bien ; c'était celle d'un bon Ange, ou d'un bon Démon, qui m'accompagne partout. Puisque Socrate avait son bon Démon, pourquoi n'aurais-je pas mon bon Ange, et pourquoi n'aurais-je pas l'honneur, comme Socrate, d'obtenir mon brevet de civisme, signé du subtil Retailleau et du bien-avisé Bardella ?




Il existe cette différence entre le Démon de Socrate et le mien, que celui de Socrate ne se manifestait à lui que pour défendre, avertir, empêcher, et que le mien daigne prévenir, neutraliser, réprimer. Ce pauvre Socrate n'avait qu'un Démon prohibiteur ; le mien est un grand sécurisateur, le mien est un Démon d'ordre, ou Démon de pacification.




Or, sa voix me chuchotait ceci : « Celui-là seul est libre, qui vit en sécurité, et celui-là seul mérite la sécurité, qui ne trouble jamais l'ordre public. »




Immédiatement, je sautai sur mon étudiant. D'un seul coup de poing, je lui bouchai un œil, qui devint, en une seconde, gros comme une balle. Je cassai un de mes ongles à lui briser deux dents, et comme je ne me sentais pas assez fort, étant né délicat et m'étant peu exercé aux opérations de maintien de l'ordre, pour neutraliser rapidement ce jeune homme, je le saisis d'une main par le collet de son blouson, de l'autre, je l'empoignai à la gorge, et je me mis à lui secouer vigoureusement la tête contre un mur. Je dois avouer que j'avais préalablement inspecté les environs d'un coup d'œil, et que j'avais vérifié que, dans cette rue momentanément déserte, je me trouvais, pour un assez long temps, protégé par les agents de police, qui, à quelques pas de là, observaient avec une bienveillance toute républicaine les progrès de mon intervention.




Ayant ensuite, par un coup de pied lancé dans le dos, assez énergique pour briser les omoplates, terrassé ce dangereux représentant de l'ultragauche, je me saisis de sa pancarte tombée à terre, et je le battis avec l'énergie obstinée des gouvernements qui veulent rétablir l'ordre public.




Tout à coup, — ô miracle ! ô jouissance du citoyen qui vérifie l'excellence de sa théorie ! — je vis ce jeune corps se retourner, se redresser avec une énergie que je n'aurais jamais soupçonnée dans un individu si manifestement hostile aux valeurs de la République, et, avec un regard de haine qui me parut de bon augure, le petit professionnel du chaos se jeta sur moi, me pocha les deux yeux, me cassa quatre dents, et avec la même pancarte me battit dru comme plâtre. — Par mon énergique intervention, je venais donc de démontrer l'extrême violence de ces groupuscules !




Alors, je lui fis force signes pour lui faire comprendre que je considérais l'opération comme terminée, et me relevant avec la satisfaction d'un ministre de l'Intérieur qui vérifie l'excellence de sa doctrine, je lui dis : « Monsieur, vous êtes un danger pour la République ! Veuillez me faire l'honneur de reconnaître que votre réaction confirme exactement ce que nos meilleurs experts avaient annoncé ; et souvenez-vous, si vous êtes réellement attaché aux libertés publiques, qu'il faut désormais vous abstenir de participer à ces manifestations où l'ordre public se trouve si gravement menacé.




Il m'a bien juré qu'il avait compris ma théorie, et qu'il renoncerait désormais à manifester.




Qu'en dis-tu, citoyen Retailleau ?

author: Jim McIlroy
title: The giant ‘swiftie’ begs for an end to coal
content:
More than 50 people joined the protest which was organised by Lock the Gate Alliance (LGA).

The swift parrot, which won the Bird of the Year prize in 2023, has been described as the world’s fastest parrot.

Nick Clyde from LGA told the rally that the swift parrot was being endangered by NSW Labor's approvals of new coal and gas projects. “There are currently 17 coal mine expansion projects in the pipeline in NSW.”

Raymond “Bubbly” Weatherall, an Gomeroi man, said: “State and federal governments have approved every coal and gas project that they can. Enough is enough! The end game is to get coal and gas out of our country.”

Doro Babeck, NSW campaigner for the Bob Brown Foundation, said the campaign to save the swift parrot and other species focused on protecting the native forests in Tasmania and elsewhere. “The swift parrot flies from Tasmania across Bass Strait to the mainland in three hours. That trip takes up to 12 hours by boat.”

Sally Hunter, an anti-coal mine campaigner and a Maules Creek farmer, asked people to send a message to the government to let the Maules Creek mine lease lapse.

“We need a plan for the transition of mining jobs out of coal and gas and into renewable industries. The Maules Creek mine has already bought out around 80 farms in the area, and this has to stop.”

The model swift parrot, which was constructed in Muloobinba/Newcastle, will now be transported to Maules Creek for a gathering with the local community.

[For more information on the Swift Parrot campaign visit Lock the Gate Alliance.]

title: Communiqué de presse de la Coordination nationale lycéenne, réunie à Paris le 18 octobre 2026.
content:
Lors de cette seconde réunion de la Coordination Nationale Lycéenne, nous étions plus de 100 lycéen.nes venu.es de 27 villes, mandatés par nos Assemblées générales interlycéennes respectives.




En plus des délégations d'Île-de-France étaient présentes des délégations de : Nantes, Toulouse, Rennes, Brest, Bordeaux, Tours, Angers, Montpellier, Aix, Marseille, Grenoble, Lyon, Besançon, Montbéliard, Nancy, Strasbourg, Lille, Dunkerque, Rouen, Caen.




Notre mouvement, né dans les lycées de banlieues et d'Outremers, s'est propagé durant ces dernières semaines dans toute la France et gagne en ampleur chaque jour. Des centaines de milliers de lycéen.nes se mobilisent contre le manque de moyens dans l'éducation et le mépris indifférent du gouvernement.




Nos revendications sont claires : plus de moyens et de personnel pour de meilleures conditions d'étude et de stage, suppression de Parcoursup et des classes limitées à 25 élèves, la fin des inégalités entre les beaux quartiers et les quartiers populaires, et entre les lycées privés et publics.




Face à nos demandes, le gouvernement n'a su répondre que par une violence extrême et disproportionnée. Nous exigeons donc aussi la libération de tous·tes nos camarades et l'arrêt de toute poursuite judiciaire. Au lieu de nous écouter, l'État ferme les lycées et met en place des pseudo «

 

espaces démocratiques

 

» qui étouffent nos revendications et ne nous représentent pas. Ces réponses prouvent que le gouvernement craint ce mouvement, à nous de lui donner raison en poursuivant la mobilisation




La journée de mobilisation de samedi a encore une fois prouvé la puissance du mouvement : les étudiant.es et travailleur.euses nous ont rejoint par centaines de milliers dans la rue, partout en France. Nous appelons donc à poursuivre le mouvement en se liant avec tous.tes celleux qui veulent continuer ou rejoindre le mouvement : les lycéen.nes, les alternant.es, les apprenti.es, les étudiant.es et les travailleur.euses. Par conséquent, nous appelons les lycéen.nes à sortir dans la rue le jeudi 22 octobre et le samedi 24 octobre à leurs côtés et appuyons toutes les suites de la mobilisation – blocages, manifestations, occupations etc.




Les vacances ne nous arrêteront pas, bien au contraire : profitons-en pour intensifier la mobilisation et revenir encore plus forts à la rentrée pour une semaine noire. Nous appelons déjà à une grande journée de mobilisation nationale le mardi 3 novembre et nous nous joignons aux travailleur.euses dans leur journée de grève du 5 novembre contre le budget d'austérité. Et s'il y a un deuxième «

 

17 octobre

 

» dès le samedi de la rentrée, on en sera

 

!




Seule l'unification et l'organisation des lycéen.es à l'échelle nationale permettra la poursuite du mouvement. Nous appuyons toutes les tentatives d'organisations à la base : comités de lycéen.nes mobilisé.es, assemblées générales de lycées ou inter-lycées, coordinations à l'échelle des villes, départements ou régions. Nous appelons donc tous.tes les lycéen.nes mobilisé.es à nous contacter et à s'organiser pour envoyer des délégations élues à la prochaine 

CNL

 qui se tiendra le jeudi 29 octobre.




Le Comité de Liaison de la Coordination Nationale Lycéenne.

author: Unknown
title: Suite à la répression et à la mort d'un manifestant ivryen
content:
Communiqué de la Coalition antiraciste 2027, du Collectif Romain Rolland Ivry, de la Convergence Citoyenne Ivryenne, et de l'Assemblée des Quartiers




Le 19 octobre 2026




Depuis le début de l'année scolaire, les lycéen-nes mobilisé-es font entendre leurs revendications légitimes sur la dégradation du système scolaire : manque de moyens humains et matériels, d'enseignants et de personnels éducatifs, inégalités de traitement, d'orientation via ParcourSup, opacité, affectations aléatoires et impasses de ce système de sélection, discriminations négatives et territoriales des établissements avec un 

IPS

 (indice de position sociale) faible situés dans les quartiers prioritaires de la politique de la ville, emplois du temps surchargés du fait de la réforme Blanquer, bâtiments vétustes et conditions d'enseignement indignes qui participent à la reproduction des inégalités scolaires et sociales...




Toutes ces revendications sont connues de longue date des autorités, et sont portées depuis des années par les élèves, leurs familles et les personnels de l'éducation nationale sans que les pouvoirs publics apportent de réponses à la hauteur des besoins.




Des collectifs militants dénoncent également ces injustices et soutiennent les mobilisations de la jeunesse.




Les lycéen-nes et étudiant-es tiennent depuis des semaines, malgré la répression policière et institutionnelle inédite qui s'est abattue sur les blocus. Violences policières, interpellations massives, tentatives d'interdire les rassemblements ou de fermer les lycées... les jeunes résistent face à cette violence visant à entraver leur liberté d'expression, de réunion et de manifestation.




Le 17 octobre, les mobilisations de la jeunesse ont convergé avec celle contre la vie chère et ont réuni des centaines de milliers de personnes. Cette mobilisation du 17 a été émaillée de graves violences policières, dans la continuité du mois précédent - les forces de l'ordre rouant de coups des manifestant-es de tous âges, faisant un usage massif de gaz lacrymogènes jusqu'à noyer des zones entières, y compris des espaces fermés, et à mettre en péril la santé, lasécurité et la vie des protestataires ou des passants.




De nombreuses et nombreux manifestant-es ont été blessé-es dans des circonstances qu'il reste à élucider et nous n'avons toujours pas de nouvelles d'uncertain nombre d'entre elles et d'entre eux.




Le 18 octobre, l'exécutif reconnaissait un mort, par arrêt cardiorespiratoire, près de la Place de la République, où la répression était particulièrement violente et l'air massivement saturé de lacrymogène.




La victime est ivryenne. Nous manquons d'informations sur sa place dans la manifestation, sur les circonstances de son décès et des soins qu'il a pu recevoir.




Les autorités doivent communiquer sans délai la réalité du bilande ces deux derniers jours de mobilisation et d'action, le nombre exact de mort-es et de blessé-es et les conditions dans lesquelles des manifestant-es sont tombé-es et ont été pris-es en charge.




La sécurité et l'intégrité physique des manifestant-es ont été mises en danger par les pratiques de «

 

maintien de l'ordre

 

». Savoir ce qui s'est passé pour ces manifestant-es, et en particulier pour cet ivryen décédé, devrait être la priorité absolue de ces prochaines heures.




Nos collectifs demandent aux élu-es et organisations politiques, notamment locales, de presser l'exécutif par tous les moyens de déliver les informations que nous attendons toutes et tous. Des proches des victimes, leurs soutiens, leur entourage, veulent plus de transparence sur le bilan du week-end et sur les responsabilités en jeu.




Nous demandons donc en premier lieur à Monsieur le Maire d'Ivry, Philippe Bouyssou, à Madame la députée d'Ivry, Mathilde Panot et à Monsieur le Sénateur, Pascal Savoldelli, de tout faire pour obtenir les informations exactes sur les conditions de décès du manifestant ivryen.




Nos collectifs se tiennent à la disposition de la famille et des proches du manifestant décédé samedi pour les épauler dans la recherche de la vérité et les accompagner dans leur deuil.




Soutien au mouvement, solidarité avec les victimes

 

!




Coalition antiraciste 2027, Collectif Romain Rolland Ivry, Convergence Citoyenne Ivryenne, Assemblée des Quartiers

author: Unknown
title: Après le 17, approfondir la rupture
content:
La société de l'abondance trouve sa réponse naturelle dans le pillage, mais elle n'était aucunement abondance naturelle et humaine, elle était abondance de marchandises - Guy Debord







Une inversion systématique de la réalité




 




"Chaos insoutenable", "horreur", "guerre civile", "République assassinée", politiciens et éditorialistes s'apitoient en chœur sur les dégâts matériels du 17 octobre.




A droite comme à gauche, tout l'échiquier politique condamne et stigmatise. Danger pour l'ordre institutionnel pour les uns, défaut de respectabilité sociale pour les autres. Et dans ce marasme d'indignations morales, pas un mot pour les mutilé⸱es, ni pour l'incroyable courage de celles et ceux qui sont descendu⸱es dans la rue.




Faut-il rappeler à ces donneurs de leçon que les principaux acquis sociaux ont été le résultat de moments insurrectionnels

 

? 

Que l'ébranlement d'un pouvoir verrouillé dans sa tour d'ivoire n'est pas un dîner de gala

 

?

 Qu'il n'y a pas de Révolution française sans incendie des hôtels aristocratiques, sans attaques des barrières d'octrois chargées de percevoir les taxes, sans mise à sac du couvent Saint-Lazare et sans pillage des arsenaux

 

?




En définissant la violence par la seule destruction de biens matériels , 

le pouvoir revendique le monopole du langage et l'inversion systématique de la réalité.

 Les mains arrachées deviennent alors de simples accidents et le pillage d'un magasin de luxe - pourtant couvert par des assurances privées - se transforme en un crime odieux. En réalité, dès la matinée, Laurent Nunez n'a cessé d'agiter les épouvantails de l'ultragauche et de 

LFI

 pour justifier une répression sanglante.




À nous de remettre les mots à l'endroit. 

La première violence, c'est la violence sociale qui prive une majorité de la population de toute perspective d'avenir et les maintient dans la misère

. C'est celle qui nous contraint de trimer tous les jours et de perdre notre vie à la gagner. C'est celle qui multiplie les lois racistes, accordent des permis de tuer aux flics, expulsent les pauvres de leurs logements, et laissent crever les gens aux urgences dans les hôpitaux publics.




La vraie violence, c'est aussi la violence policière. Ce sont les

 8 000 arrestations de lycéennes en deux semaines

, c'est un mort place de la République dans des circonstances troubles, ce sont les mains arrachées à Lens la semaine dernière, et celle d'un adolescent de 17 ans à Saint-Étienne samedi. La vraie violence, c'est un homme de 27 ans qui a perdu un œil un Strasbourg, c'est une adolescente qui a été éborgnée à Mulhouse, c'est des tirs de 

LBD

 dans la tête à Clermont et Saint-Nazaire, c'est encore les 2 300 arrestations pour la seule journée du 17 octobre dont on sait qu'une grosse partie risque de finir en prison.




La vraie violence, c'est auss

i le mépris de ce gouvernement face à l'ampleur de la révolte

, c'est la droite de Retailleau qui appelle à l'état d'urgence, ou celle d'Édouard Philippe qui appelle à un retour des «

 

peines planchers

 

».










"On récupère ce qu'on paye toute l'année"





 




Quand ça fait plus de 30 ans que l'État fait la sourde oreille aux revendications sociales, il ne faut pas s'étonner que ça pète.

 Il ne faut s'étonner que les gens se saisissent d'une situation où l'autorité est provisoirement contestée pour s'affranchir des règles qui disciplinent notre quotidien (travail, boulot, dodo). Il ne faut pas s'étonner que les gens se libèrent pour un temps des règles de la marchandise qui nous obligent à avoir des taff de merde pour payer notre bouffe et notre logement, sans jamais avoir assez pour s'offrir les fringues étalées dans les vitrines de luxe. Alors oui, samedi, pendant quelques heures, Hugo Boss, Louis Vuitton, 

HM

, MacDo ou Apple ont fait les frais de leur obscénité.




Dans les médias, tous les politiciennes et éditorialistes de plateaux rejouent l'opposition classique entre les bons et les mauvais⸱es manifestant⸱es, les bons et les mauvais pauvres, les lycéen⸱es respectables et les voyous sans scrupules, la "belle jeunesse" pacifiste et les "jeunes de banlieue" descendus en bandes. Cette opposition, minée par un racisme latent, montre également une ignorance crasse de ce qui se joue en ce moment.




Dans tous les cas, ce n'est pas à nous de dire ce qu'il "faut faire" ou "ne pas faire"

. Ce qu'on a vu samedi, c'est 

un large mouvement de révolte avec plusieurs composantes

. Une composante qui expose des revendications légitimes sur ses conditions de travail et d'étude et qui pointe les manquements de l'Etat

 

; une composante qui

 met à nu la logique du capital

 dans sa plus simple évidence : la propriété privée, la marchandise et les forces armées qui la protègent.




La journée de révolte du 17, mélange de déambulations festives, d'affrontements avec la police et de pillages, est tout simplement

 la forme actuelle de la lutte des classes.

 Ces différentes modalités de contestation, parfois contradictoires, sont à l'image des différentes fractions de classe engagées dans cette mobilisation contre la vie chère 

 : des étudiant⸱es qui voient leur condition d'étude dégradées mais espèrent encore décrocher un boulot correct, des travailleur⸱euses déclassé⸱es qui attendent une meilleure répartition des richesses de la part de l'État, mais aussi des

 lycéen⸱nes qui n'ont aucun espoir dans avenir

, des jeunes racisés qui ne savent que trop bien que l'État ne lâchera pas une miette, et que le mythe de l'intégration est une vaste mystification pour domestiquer une main d'œuvre surnuméraire.




Il n'y a pas de bons ou de mauvais manifestants, il y a seulement des contestataires aux situations différentes, avec des places différentes dans les rapports de production et de reproduction du capital. 




Certain·es partagent encore l

'illusion citoyenniste que l'État va un jour céder à leurs revendications

 

; d'autres, soudé·es par un ensemble d'expériences quotidiennes, scandées par le harcèlement policier, l'exclusion économique, le racisme institutionnel, sont tout à fait conscient· es que

 l'État actuel n'a plus rien à leur offrir

. Certain· es espèrent encore tirer leur épingle du jeu de la précarité, en jouant le jeu de la respectabilité, là où d'autres ne voient aucune perspective d'ascension professionnelle à l'horizon et refusent de jouer avec des dés pipés d'avance.




Car émeutes et pillages sont largement le résultat d'une

 incapacité totale de la part de l'Etat à assurer une quelconque perspective d'avenir

. Ils sont le revers de la médaille néolibérale, et la somme des humiliations et des défaites passées.




Si des mairies, des commissariats et le siège de CNews ont été pris pour cible, ce n'est pas pour rien. Ce sont les symboles d'un État qui garantit la reproduction des rapports capitalistes, et qui répond aux conséquences de ses choix néolibéraux par la répression la plus brutale.




Si une fraction des insurgé· es ne se contente pas de défiler avec une belle pancarte, ce n'est pas parce qu'ils et elles ne savent pas parler, mais parce qu'ils et elles savent pertinemment qu'

il est impossible d'obtenir satisfaction auprès de l'État 

 en utilisant les répertoires d'action traditionnels du mouvement ouvrier dont l'affirmation comme unité de classe n'existe plus.




Les décennies de défilés pacifiés et de cortèges encadrés, de 

NAO

 et de journées nationales sans lendemain, de grèves perlées et de revendications corporatistes ont prouvé leur inoffensivité. Place désormais aux écarts et aux brèches, et qu'importe si cela passe par quelques éclats de vitre et des mairies en feu.




Dans un contexte d'inflation massive, on ne va pas pleurer sur ces actions de réappropriation directe qui ne sont que

 l'aboutissement du règne de la marchandise et de la publicité

 auprès de celles et ceux à qui on impose la consommation de masse, mais dont l'accès aux "meilleurs" produits est réservé à une petite minorité.




Approfondir la révolte





Malgré l'offensivité inédite de ce samedi, rien ne garantit que ça continue comme ça. 

 Il nous faut un horizon, ou à défaut, la chute du régime macroniste.

 Avec l'instauration d'un couvre-feu, une justice aux aboies et des appels à l'état d'urgence, 

les réactionnaires de tous bords sont prêts à monter au créneau pour rétablir l'ordre. 

 Comment approdondir la rupture entamée samedi sans tomber dans le piège de la répression

 

? Comment amplifier sans canaliser les forces en présence dans des formes trop éprouvées

 

? Il ne faut pas se leurrer : ce n'est pas la gauche, ni extrême, ni ultra, qui va orienter le cours des choses. 

Notre rôle n'est pas de fisseler un mouvement éparse pour l'unifier dans un cadre clair. 

 Mais d'accompagner les modes d'organisation et d'action émergeants, de les défendre face aux disqualifications systématiques, et de répondre présent· es chaque fois que nécessaire. 

Approfondir la révolte, c'est aussi prendre conscience de ses limites objectives et subjectives en vue de son dépassement. 

 Maintenir des liaisons avec les franges les plus radicales de la contestation, dans la rue, devant les lycées, dans nos quartiers.




D'ici là, espérons que la mairie cramée de Limoges, ne soit pas le nouvel incendie du Reichstag...

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Residents rally against Inner West Council’s pro-developer plan
content:
About 300 people rallied outside the Inner West Council meeting at Ashfield Town Hall on October 20 to demand real consultation time and more information about its so-called Fairer Future Plan 2 (FFP2).

The Fairer Future Part 1’s rezoned large sections of the inner west for luxury high-rise apartments.

The rally was organised by No High Rise Lilyfield and supported by a range of community groups, including the Better Future Coalition, Leichhardt Matters, Save Marrickville, Save Dulwich Hill and Action for Public Housing.

Lucy Wynter from No High Rise Lilyfield said the Fairer Future plan is “ill-conceived, underdone, under-prepared, not explained to the public and the time we’ve had to digest it has been paltry”.

Wynter said that when FFP2 was announced, she started a WhatsApp group chat with neighbours and friends in Lilyfield. A few weeks later, there are 700 members of the group chat, “about 10% of the population of Lilyfield. That shows how much this matters to people.”

Lilyfield residents did not receive a notice about FFP2 until two weeks into the six-week consultation period and many have still not received any information at all.

“That means we can’t provide informed consent; we cannot provide feedback to a plan we don’t understand or have not seen,” Wynter said.

“We are ordinary mums and dads, and we think it's unfair to implement the biggest change in the history of the Inner West, on such a broad scale, without actually asking us.”

John Stamolis, a former independent councillor on Inner West Council, and a member of the Better Future Coalition, which includes resident action groups opposed to Fairer Future, told the protest that the Inner West is already one of the most-densely populated local government areas in the state.

He said it is wrong that there had been so little information, consultation or debate about the plan.

Kobi Shetty, Greens MP for Balmain, also spoke. “We are a closely connected community; we care about each other. They are proposing to remove heritage restrictions, to massively rezone our entire neighbourhood, including public housing estates that are only 15-years old.

“We know that it is not fair; it is not going to fix the housing crisis.

“We’ve seen what happens when developers get their hands on the most affordable places in our communities … they demolish those and create luxury housing.”

The crowd then entered the chambers to address and observe the meeting.

Under pressure, Labor Mayor Darcy Byrne had attempted to neutralise residents’ anger about the proposal by offering an extra week of consultation — but only for the suburb of Lilyfield. He promised a number of concessions to reduce the increased density in the area.

Speakers at the council forum questioned why only Lilyfield had been granted an extension, arguing that the consultation period should be extended to all of the Inner West.

A motion to extend consultation to February to allow residents to better understand the plans and make submissions was put by Greens Councillor Liz Atkins and seconded by independent Councillor Victor Macri. It was voted down by the Labor majority, 8–7.

Byrne was noticeably absent from the meeting while residents outlined their concerns. He later suggested that only “activists and socialists” opposed the plan, disregarding the concerns of many community groups.

[The deadline for submissions is October 28. Isaac Nellist is the Socialist Alliance candidate for Balmain in the NSW elections.]

author: Tom Bramble
title: US imperialism in the 21st century
content:
At the start of this century, US imperialism was at its peak. It had been a decade since its chief adversary, the Soviet Union, had crumbled; the country was now the unchallenged global superpower. Washington was bringing countries into the North Atlantic Treaty Organization that had been the USSR’s satellites in Europe, and it could rely on its allies to extend US influence into every corner of the world.

The US dominated the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund and was the most powerful nation in the United Nations. Its economy was booming, and the federal government ran surpluses. US multinationals found new markets and investment outlets worldwide. It was the heyday of “globalisation”. The US ruling class boasted that the country was a beacon to the world. As Democratic candidate Al Gore put it in one of the presidential debates in 2000:

“It is a great tribute to our founders that 224 years later this nation is now looked to by the peoples on every other continent and the peoples from every part of this Earth as a kind of model for what their future could be … The power of example is America’s greatest power in the world.”

Twenty-five years later, US rulers are not so assured. The country has suffered a series of crises, and the global balance of power has shifted. The US remains the world’s leading power, but it is wracked by dysfunction on a series of fronts. Its allies are increasingly estranged. Wars in the Middle East have exposed its diminished military power. Its tech sector and banks still lead, but its industrial base is now much weaker. Its political system is seen not as a model for what to do, but what to avoid. 

The decay of US power can be understood as the result of four interrelated phenomena: an imperial crisis in the Middle East, an economic crisis that crashed the world, the challenge from China and a political crisis that reflects and exacerbates these three trends.

The imperial crisis

The 9/11 attack on the World Trade Center in 2001 was a devastating blow to America’s sense of invulnerability. But US strategists also recognised the attack as an opportunity to advance US power—justification for a new round of wars that would intimidate the country’s rivals and allies alike and overcome the Vietnam-era legacy of widespread domestic opposition to far-flung and lengthy land wars. 

The idea of an aggressive revival of US military interventionism had been germinating in the ranks of the Republican Party for some years in its “neoconservative” wing. The leading think tank was the Project for a New American Century, founded by William Kristol and Robert Kagan. Its supporters and associates included Dick Cheney, Donald Rumsfeld, Paul Wolfowitz and John Bolton, all of whom held senior positions in the George W. Bush administration, which had won the 2000 election. 

The October 2001 invasion of Afghanistan was the first step in this wider project. Bush’s cabinet believed that the US would topple the ruling Taliban in Kabul and then lead a triumphal march through the capitals of its defeated enemies. Iraq, Iran and Syria were the main targets and, further afield, North Korea. Regime change was the objective.

In the short term, the invasion of Afghanistan was a stunning success. The Taliban were overthrown within two months. Domestic support for the war was overwhelming. It seemed US imperialism was back. Next was Iraq. The Bush administration justified its invasion by associating the country’s president, Saddam Hussein, with the 9/11 attacks and claiming that he had built an arsenal of weapons of mass destruction to threaten the West. On 19 March 2003, the US and its allies invaded Iraq. Within three weeks, US forces had taken Baghdad, and on 1 May Bush appeared on the deck of the 

USS Abraham Lincoln

 to declare “mission accomplished”. 

Yet things turned bad for the US in both countries. In Iraq, local resistance to the occupation soon emerged. By the following year, it was raging. The US responded by flattening whole neighbourhoods, deploying white phosphorus and uranium-tipped weapons. Regular sweeps of suspected resistance activists terrified neighbourhoods and filled the jails. The US destroyed civilian infrastructure providing clean water, power and health care. And it sacked more than 100,000 government employees, creating mass unemployment and impoverishing millions. The death toll rose steadily. A study by the 

Lancet

 journal in 2006 estimated 655,000 excess deaths in Iraq in the first three years of the war. Anger towards the US ran white-hot. 

The US now turned to classic colonial divide-and-rule tactics, stoking sectarian conflict on religious lines. Tens of thousands of Iraqis died in a civil war the US occupation had provoked. Actual terrorist groups now began to grow in Iraq, including the group that became the Islamic State. The Bush administration dispatched 20,000 more US troops supposedly to quell internal conflict while promoting collaborators. 

It was all to no avail. Hatred of the occupation meant the US never “pacified” Iraq. In 2009, Britain pulled its troops out, and the US followed in 2011. In 2014, the Obama administration sent troops back into Iraq to fight the Islamic State, but this was a rearguard operation. The US was eventually forced to shut its last base down on 30 September this year. American hubris had given way to humiliation.

In Afghanistan, the US occupation also ran into the sand. The US propped up a corrupt government in Kabul that depended on warlords. Resistance soon appeared. In 2009, Democratic President Barack Obama ordered a 100,000-troop surge. The Taliban gradually regained territory based on popular hatred towards the predatory US-backed government. With war weariness widespread at home, the Trump administration in 2020 negotiated a withdrawal with the Taliban to take effect in 2021. Once the US withdrew air support and contractors left, the Afghan army collapsed in a matter of days, and the Taliban took power once again.

Bush’s dream of a victory parade through the region, a springboard for US global revival, had ground to a halt. At home, the cost of two decades of war and occupation—7,000 military personnel dead, US$3 trillion spent by the Pentagon and on care for veterans and interest payments on war borrowing—killed off any patriotic surge or any notion that the Vietnam Syndrome could be finally buried. For many American victims of domestic repression, the attacks on civil liberties and anti-Muslim racism spawned by the “War on Terror” could be added to the total cost.

Such was popular revulsion at home that the next Republican to win the presidency after Bush, Donald Trump, won support in 2016 by pretending to be against war.

The US’s war on Iran this year has only added to US military failures in the Middle East. Iran was one undisputed beneficiary of US defeats in Iraq and Afghanistan, extending its influence on a range of fronts. The Trump administration, egged on by Israel, believed that years of sanctions, serious reversals among its allies and massive internal opposition had sufficiently weakened the government that a combined attack would quickly break the Islamist regime. 

But the US has failed in Iran so far. Trump’s regular proclamations of imminent victory are now treated as a joke. Despite not having landed a single Marine in Iran, the US armed forces are running out of munitions. The generals tell Trump the war is unwinnable. Arab allies see that US promises of protection have amounted to nothing. The operation is also stoking inflation in the US. The US is spending hundreds of billions of dollars on a war with no path to victory. The US military has demonstrated that it can pulverise humans and essential infrastructure but cannot extract strategic gains from its bloody wars.

Economic crisis

For all the boasting about America’s economic power at the turn of the century, the US soon suffered two heavy blows. The first was the dot-com bust. The explosion of US tech corporations in Silicon Valley in the 1990s was held up by boosters of American capitalism as vindication of the country’s strength. The Nasdaq stock market index tracking the industry rose fivefold from 1996 to its March 2000 peak. 

But by October 2002, the Nasdaq had lost more than three-quarters of its value, dragged down by rising interest rates, doubts that the dot-com businesses would ever show a profit and an end to the supply of easy venture capital. Major businesses collapsed under heavy debt. Enron, an energy trading business and among the country’s largest companies, went bust. The media, which had praised these companies for years, were now forced to expose their corrupt dealings. Tens of thousands of workers lost their jobs, while most executives cashed out and walked away scot-free. 

The global financial crisis of 2008–09 was even more severe. It started in the US housing industry, then spread to the US stock and credit markets, triggering the biggest economic bust since the Great Depression of the 1930s. In eighteen months, trillions of dollars of wealth were destroyed. Household-name banks went under. The crisis dragged down the entire global economy. Whole regions of world capitalism teetered on the brink of collapse. 

Of course, the suffering was not shared equally. The working class was shafted with job losses, wage cuts, evictions and savage austerity. Unemployment did not fall back to its pre-crisis level until 2016. Many corporations, however, received enormous government subsidies and cheap loans. The recovery was slow by historical standards, GDP rising by just 2 percent annually over the decade that followed. The US economy has never recovered the production lost during this period.

The US is currently faring relatively well compared to other advanced economies: a huge investment boom is under way, centred on tech companies, unemployment has fallen and corporate and household debt are down. But weaknesses lie beneath the surface, and the scars of the ten-year crisis are still visible. 

Federal debt has grown over the years as the government responded to the dot-com bust, the financial crisis and the pandemic by throwing trillions of dollars in subsidies to the capitalists. Successive tax cuts to corporations and the wealthy have added to the debt, as has spending on wars and war preparations. The federal government is now running budget deficits of 6 percent of GDP, unprecedented outside deep crises.

The successive crises encouraged the US central bank to keep interest rates low. This contributed to a long bull market in equities that benefited wealthy investors and exacerbated already high inequality. Since 2022, however, the Federal Reserve has raised interest rates sharply. This has not yet burst the stock market bubble, but it has increased interest payments on government debt and on companies now feverishly borrowing to invest in AI infrastructure. Annual federal interest payments now stand at nearly $1 trillion, the second-largest item on the government’s books after Social Security. Rising bond yields in turn drive up interest rates on home loans and consumer debt, hitting working-class living standards. The US economy may not be in crisis yet, but the fault lines are obvious.

The China shock

The China shock added to US troubles. At the time of Bush’s inauguration, the US regarded China as a potential rival but not a serious threat. China’s GDP was just one-eighth the size of America’s, and it had little ability to project power beyond its shores. Far from a threat, US imperialism saw China’s rise as an opportunity. Washington calculated that US capitalists could use China as a low-wage manufacturing platform and market and, on that basis, sponsored China’s entry into the World Trade Organisation in 2001.

US plans in China soon came unstuck. China grew rapidly; by 2011, its economy was half the size of the US’s. China adopted US methods and techniques to develop its own capitalist enterprises, which soon challenged the US in its domestic and export markets. China began to exert a magnetic pull on its trading partners, which increasingly looked to it for new economic opportunities.

In response, the Obama administration announced a “pivot to Asia” in 2012. Sixty percent of US naval power was to be directed to East Asia and the Pacific, and the Middle East was downgraded as the main theatre for US imperialism. In 2017, the incoming Trump administration ratcheted up the US offensive against China. Trade policies are always a weapon. Previous presidents had promoted “free trade” to advance US interests. Trump argued that this had only enriched China at the US’s expense; a high tariff wall was the only way to “Make America Great Again”. 

In the alternating Trump-Biden-Trump presidencies, different economic and diplomatic strategies have been pursued, but the common theme has been the desire to hold China at bay. These attempts have failed. China’s GDP is now two-thirds of US GDP. It produces 30 percent of global manufacturing, nearly double the US share. China now dominates global production across a range of high-tech and advanced manufacturing; its universities lead the world in science and tech research; and Chinese labs are catching up to the US’s expensive AI frontier models despite the US’s strenuous efforts to block them. 

Crucially for US imperialism, Chinese industrial capacity is powering a growing military presence that reaches hundreds of kilometres from its shores. China now has more ships than the US Navy, and its shipyards can build them much faster. US attempts to “reshore” manufacturing for military purposes have had extremely limited success. 

The Chinese ruling class now believes that it can go toe to toe with the US. The latter’s relative decline and its failed wars in the Middle East have also encouraged Russia to test US resolve in Ukraine. The turn-of-the-century unipolar moment has given way to a multipolar world. All talk of a “new American century” has receded.

Political paralysis

Imperialist failure abroad, the failures of American capitalism at home, and the China shock have shaken American politics. At the turn of the century, more than 40 percent of respondents to Gallup polling said that they had “a great deal” or “quite a lot” of confidence in US institutions. Today, the figure is just above a quarter. On the left, young people in particular were drawn to anti-capitalist politics, fuelling the Bernie Sanders surge in 2015. But most of the radicalisation has been expressed on the right. The ruling class proved incapable of stopping Donald Trump’s rise; he transformed the Republicans into a party of radical disruption and chaos. 

It speaks volumes about the state of official politics that the federal government of the world’s most important imperial power is run by con artists, grifters and anti-science nutters. Trump is attacking America’s traditional allies, one of the country’s major sources of strength, antagonising the military and foreign policy establishment, and blatantly using executive power to go after his critics and reward fealty. His budget policies are unashamedly pro-billionaire, but many of his economic policies appear little more than thought bubbles. 

Trump’s tariffs and the broader program of economic nationalism do, however, have one important goal for US imperialism: to unwind the offshoring of US manufacturing and rebuild production at home, preparing for war with China. That has been a consistent theme of both Trump’s and Biden’s terms in office. Trade and economic policy are now squarely aimed at winning the competition between the superpowers. The problem for US imperialism is that Trump’s administration is so chaotic and unpredictable, and the manufacturing base so degraded, that it may be very difficult for it to be rebuilt, short of actual war breaking out when the Pentagon will simply take over the industrial base, as it did in World War Two.

In the immediate aftermath of 9/11, Bush’s rhetoric focused on the need for the country to stand as one against a common enemy. For the Trump administration, the enemy is at home—critics of the administration and progressives more generally. Any idea of “national consensus” has gone, except perhaps in one area: Trump has the lowest favourability rating of any president since polling began.

The US may still be the world’s number-one imperial power, but compared to the turn of the century, it has declined and appears less confident and more divided. The ruling class has no strategy to stop China’s ongoing economic rise, or to lift the living standards of its own working class. It seems incapable of providing a credible narrative justifying its own economic excesses or its ongoing and obscene levels of military spending. 

But that doesn’t mean the story is over. This is a wounded beast, and wounded beasts can lash out in many directions.

author: Rachel Sherrington and Hazel Healy
title: How Big Pharma Tried to Weaken the Rules of the UN’s Nature Fund
content:
As the COP17 nature summit gets underway in Armenia, evidence has emerged of lobbying by a leading international pharmaceuticals group to weaken the terms of a flagship fund for nature.




Documents analysed by DeSmog show that the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations (IFPMA) 

called

 for a “radical rethink” of the rationale for the 

landmark

 Cali Fund – the first mechanism built to take voluntary payments from large companies that profit from genetic sequence data.




The IFPMA states that the “modalities of the decision” to establish the Fund – which was ratified by 196 countries in 2024 at the COP16 summit of the UN Convention on Biological Diversity in Colombia – should be “significantly reviewed, revised and clarified”.




In the consultation submission, the trade group – which 

represents

 the pharmaceutical sector at the UN – also challenged the indicative rates at which companies were invited to contribute to the Fund, agreed at COP16 as 0.1 percent of revenue or 1 percent of profit.

The IFPMA labelled these indicative rates as “premature”, set “without any rational analysis”, and “commercially unrealistic”, suggesting instead that companies be allowed to contribute to the voluntary fund at a level of their choosing. 




Other demands from the IFPMA included a guarantee that any contribution would explicitly substitute payments for digital sequence information required under national or international laws.

Despite contributions to the Cali Fund already being voluntary, following a fierce 

lobbying push

 at the last summit, the IFPMA also seeks a guarantee they will remain so, stating that “there are elements in the decision that do not go far enough in creating a truly voluntary mechanism”.




Responses from other sectors, such as biotechnology and cosmetics – which are listed alongside pharma and artificial intelligence firms in the treaty text as industries that should contribute – echo some of the IFPMA’s objections, and appear to be reluctant to support the Fund as it is currently conceived. 




The UK Bioindustry Association (UK BIA), which 

has

 600 biotech and life sciences companies among its members, 

says

 the CBD’s expectations for what the Fund can raise are currently set “unrealistically high”, in its consultation response dated March 2025. 




UK BIA states that “for the Fund to succeed in the long term”, questions over its design and operationalisation must be addressed, and “clear incentives” created. 




The revelations come as negotiators gather for the UN biodiversity summit in Armenia this week, with just $10,000 

pledged

 by companies to the Cali Fund. 




It falls far short of the $1 billion to $10 billion that the UN had 

hoped

 the Fund could draw in every year, half of which is mandated to flow directly to the Indigenous and local communities that steward biodiversity.




“The tiny amounts contributed to the Cali Fund so far, combined with continued delays from industry, send a clear signal: voluntary contributions are simply not delivering,” An Lambrechts, a biodiversity politics expert at Greenpeace International, told DeSmog. 




The latest UN report shows that the world is 

off track on

 all but one of 23 targets aimed at reversing catastrophic nature loss, with the total funds raised to date from both private and public bodies falling far short of what is needed to close a $200 billion “biodiversity finance gap”.

“Big multinational corporations are turning massive profits by exploiting nature,” Lambrechts says, “while leaving people all over the world to face the impacts of the biodiversity crisis.”







Subscribe to Desmog




Get the weekly intelligence you need to hold polluters accountable
















Email Address







Sign Up










Send me intelligence from:







All




US/Global team




UK/Europe team

























A spokesperson for the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) Secretariat admits that the sums in the Fund “sit well below the scenarios that were discussed in Cali”, but puts this down to the evolving “operational infrastructure” and its low profile.

“Substantive decisions expected at COP17 are expected to give in-scope companies more solid ground to commit,” they said.




“I do believe companies have legitimate concerns, but there’s also a sense in which they don’t want to pay,” said a source close to the negotiations, who preferred to remain anonymous. “If these industries were really supportive then someone would have put the money in by now, even just as a token, a show of good faith.”




Guilherme Cintra, Director, Innovation Policy at IFPMA wrote in an email that the group had “long supported the goals of the Convention on Biological Diversity and continues to deliver against the targets set out in the Global Biodiversity Framework”.

He added: “The level of participation in the Cali Fund reflects ongoing questions about the design and implementation of the mechanism, rather than a lack of commitment to biodiversity. Governments should use COP17 to rethink the Cali Fund to attract broader participation and ensure it supports biodiversity and preserves scientific openness.” 




UK BIA declined to comment on the record. 




“It’s concerning that, nearly two years after the agreements reached at COP16 in Cali, funding for biodiversity protection remains an unfulfilled promise,” Juan Bay, leader of the indigenous Waorani nation of Ecuador told DeSmog.




“This reflects a situation we have been denouncing for years: Indigenous peoples protect some of the most biodiverse territories on the planet, yet we continue to face enormous difficulties in directly accessing the funding needed to protect them.”




History of Pushback

 




When the Cali Fund was launched in February last year, the UN 

hailed

 it as the beginning of “a new era for biodiversity finance”.




The new financial instrument aimed to address a new reality: that genetic data, known as digital sequence information, or DSI, is now available online. This allows companies, or researchers, to access material from plants, animals, bacteria and fungi without ever setting foot in the country of origin – and bypass 

rules

 that require payment. 




As a result, the genetic code that underpins a range of lucrative products – everything from sweeteners to the 

vast majority

 of cancer drugs – is available with few rules to limit access. 




The Cali Fund, Carbon Brief 

writes

, was aimed at “closing this loophole”. It was agreed that 50 percent of funds would go to Indigenous communities and local communities that steward fragile ecosystems, with the rest going to Global South countries and scientific research.




At the COP16 summit where the Fund was agreed, the business lobby 

reached a record high

, including from sectors that the mechanism was built around: pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, cosmetics, and information services associated with DSI, including artificial intelligence.




An Indigenous delegate taking part in UN talks in Colombia two years ago, when the Cali Fund was first agreed. Half of any funds raised are  ear-marked for Indigenous and local communities that care for fragile ecosystems. Credit: Photographer: Fernando Vergara / Associated Press /Alamy




A Global South government 

push

 at the UN talks for the Fund to be a mandatory mechanism was defeated in the wake of a strong lobbying effort by the 

pharma

, 

agritech

 and 

biotech

 industry, which dubbed the proposed levy a ‘global tax’.

In the lead up to the summit, UK-based pharma giant AstraZeneca, which 

posted

 $12.4 billion in profits last year, had 

warned

 the British government it “might cut jobs” if a levy were introduced, according to The Guardian. An AstraZeneca spokesperson denied the comments. 




Another pharma giant, GSK, also pushed back against the Fund, which it called “disproportionate”, telling the UK government it could “hinder the development of new medicines and vaccines”, in emails 

obtained

 by Carbon Brief.




A spokesperson from GSK told DeSmog it had set ambitious targets and was investing in nature protection. “We support the intent behind the Cali Fund and will make a decision regarding voluntary contributions when there is more information about how the Cali Fund will work alongside other national and multilateral Access and Benefit Sharing mechanisms,” they said. 




“

As a company, we are committed to advancing our research and development in response to the needs of patients,” an AstraZeneca spokesperson said in an email. “An assessment of the full impact on our operations will be conducted once there is more clarity from governments on the implementation of the DSI MLM [Cali Fund].”




Since 2024, the pharmaceutical industry’s global lobby group the IFPMA appears to have continued to focus its energy on weakening the rules that were agreed in Colombia.

The COP16 agreement established key elements of the Fund: contribution rates, a list of sectors that should contribute, and set thresholds to ensure large companies were expected to give to the fund, defining qualifying entities as those that exceeded two of three financial thresholds: $20 million in assets, $50 million in sales, or $5 million in profit.

However, rates and thresholds were marked as ‘indicative’ and set to be finalised at the current talks in Armenia. 




Cali Fund Push Back

 




To build on what had been agreed in Cali, Colombia, the CBD sought to engage industry over how to make the Fund operational – inviting responses on what sectors should contribute and how.




DeSmog analysed 22 responses, which were submitted by 14 groups in response to stakeholder consultations issued by the Convention of Biological Diversity secretariat, along with available public statements from industry groups that have engaged publicly with the Fund.

In their submissions, industry groups pushed back on a range of fronts. The IFPMA, which claims to represent over 90 percent of the world’s leading research-based pharmaceutical companies, emerges as the Fund’s most outspoken critic.

It 

called

 for a “radical rethink” of the Fund’s rationale, and states that the MLM (multilateral mechanism that gives rise to the Cali Fund) does not “effectively advance biodiversity goals”. 

The group criticised everything from contribution levels, a lack of clarity “on how funds will be allocated or guarantees that funds will directly support conservation efforts”, and proposed that the treaty decision text be “significantly reviewed, revised and clarified”.




’A Tax on Innovation’




The IFPMA states that the MLM “essentially imposes a financial burden on the free exchange of scientific data, which is critical for medical, environmental and other societal research”. It adds that: “by taxing DSI use, the MLM risks creating disincentives for global scientific cooperation, slowing the pace of innovation”.

The IFPMA also stated that it is “critical” that indicative contribution rates (0.1 percent of revenue or 1 percent of profit) be “reconsidered”.

“Establishing indicative contribution rates in Decision 16/2 was premature and the rates themselves are commercially unrealistic, are not based on the underlying value that DSI brings, lack scientific justification, do not take into account sector-specific differences, and serve as a disincentive to participation,” it wrote. 




The IFPMA’s view that setting indicative rates was “premature” is 

echoed

 in the submission from the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC). 




The ICC was approached for comment. In its consultation submission, it states that the ICC is seeking “clarity, certainty and enabling conditions that are essential to incentivise businesses to actively engage”.




“Not Voluntary Enough”




The IFPMA goes on to suggest that the size of any contribution should be left to companies’ discretion, writing that “the expectation of contribution as well as the level of contribution must both be voluntary”.

While IFPMA recognises that payments into the Fund are already “voluntary in principle”, it argues that the wording of the treaty decision does “not go far enough in creating a truly voluntary mechanism” – taking issue with a clause that invites signatories to the CBD treaty to enact laws that incentivise company contributions.




The IFPMA goes on to add: “Given that the indicative rates were chosen without any rational analysis – as acknowledged by the decision itself, which calls for a study to propose replacement realistic rates – it is critical that these placeholder rates are truly indicative.”

In 2026, the UN’s CBD secretariat produced a 

study

, in which it modelled the impact of contribution rates on the competitiveness of eligible companies, and found “the direct cost burden […] to be modest, relative to sector margins”. The IFPMA 

disputed

 these findings too, stating that “even modest reductions in expected returns can be enough to delay, scale back or halt a project”.




“Obligation Stacking”




The CBD negotiating text (

Decision

 16/2), which established the Fund, stated that the treaty would not override national “benefit-sharing” laws that already 

exist

 in at least 20 countries – which require companies to pay, or otherwise compensate, communities for their use of digital genetic data.

The IFPMA and BIA trade groups both expressed their concern at what they call “obligation stacking”, in consultation documents analysed by DeSmog. The IFPMA said that any payment into the Cali Fund should rule out paying governments for DSI again under any national laws, and both ask for “legal certainty”.

In response to a request for comment, Guilherme Cintra, IFPMA’s director of innovation policy, said: “The current mechanism overlaps with existing law, relies on inaccurate assumptions about how data is used in the discovery of medicines, and asks companies to hand over a share of their total revenue whether ‘digital sequence information’ was used to develop a medicine or not.”




‘Artful Arguments’




Dr Siva Thambisetty, associate professor of law at the London School of Economics (LSE), describes industry’s core arguments as “artful”.

She explains that the Fund decision to base contributions on revenue or profit, was an attempt aimed at securing “oversight and transparency” in the absence of comparable publicly available data from companies on how they use DSI.

“I think it’s interesting that the very companies that wanted a voluntary mechanism are now claiming that there is no legal certainty,” says Thambisetty. “We have to be careful that national ABS [access and benefit-sharing] laws are not damaged for a system that not many users appear to have any intention of paying into”.

She suggests that industry objections raised touch the fund’s viability and the terms already agreed, rather than how it should be rolled out. “It’s the operational clarity that the negotiations in Armenia should ideally focus on, rather than reopening the basis for the normative clarity, and multilateral will – which is clearly set out in CBD decisions,” she said.  

A paper released on the eve of the summit by the Common Initiative think tank acknowledges that the fund is empty due to structural problems, not just to low company ambition. 




It highlights a lack of consensus on how to define DSI, no clear mechanism for counting contributions, and a lack of harmonization between national governments’ implementation.




But these structural problems are not “bad luck,” they write. Rather, “it is what happens when a mechanism designed to extract money from some of the most profitable industries on earth is built on the assumption that those industries will simply volunteer to pay it.”




Indigenous Agency




Finalising the Cali Fund will be top of the agenda at the upcoming Cop17 talks in the Armenian capital Yerevan, which will run from 19-30 October. 

Parties are expected to pin down the details on disbursement of the fund between Global South countries, thresholds for company participation and fund governance, as well as measuring countries’ progress against 

targets

 to protect 30 percent of land and seas and restore the earth’s degraded ecosystems.

For June Rubis, an Indigenous representative who sits on the Cali Fund Steering Committee, the question of where money ends up has great importance. “I would like to see Indigenous communities be given meaningful agency over priorities, access and delivery,” she tells DeSmog.




The final Cali Fund text agreed at COP16 stated that half of any funds 

raised

 would go to Indigenous and local community stewards 

for self-defined projects that support biodiversity protection like

 forest restoration, or the transfer of ecological knowledge between generations.

Indigenous communities 

manage

, or have rights over, 

around 37 percent of the earth’s natural areas, despite making up just 6 percent of the global population.

“What I want to avoid is a situation in which money is nominally allocated for Indigenous Peoples and local communities, but the project priorities are determined elsewhere or communities have to pass through an institution they did not identify,” says Rubis.




Rubis believes it’s important to take the time to build a financial mechanism that works for company contributors, countries, and Indigenous peoples and local communities alike. “Of course,” she adds, “for all this to apply, we also need to have the money coming in.”




More Action From States




Although businesses are expected to pay into the Cali Fund, national governments have the power to negotiate, agree and enforce decisions reached through the CBD process – and bear the responsibility to ensure funds are raised. 




To date, governments have played a mixed role. Some Global North countries, including the EU bloc and UK, appear to have lobbied alongside industry 

to push

 for the Cali Fund to be non-binding and voluntary.

However since then, through the Friends of the Cali Fund – which is chaired by the UK and Chile and 

includes

 Norway and Armenia – both the UK and the EU are now working to incentivise contributions.




Other countries such as Switzerland, where pharmaceutical companies 

make up

 7 percent of GDP, as well as Japan and Korea, have continued to push back on key elements of the fund architecture.   




“I have been surprised to see industry arguments amplified by some Global North governments,” says Nithin Ramakrishnan from the nonprofit Third World Network,




“Including on areas – such as the relationship with national laws – that appear to go against the text that was agreed in Cali.”

For her part, Thambisetty tells DeSmog she would like to see “more coordinated action” on the part of countries where most of these large firms are situated. 




Thambisetty suggests a global push is needed to frame contributions as a moral responsibility for companies and investors: “a good public narrative about why these payments are necessary”. 




Learning By Doing




So far, the Cali Fund has raised no money from large firms. The only companies to contribute are Prozomix, a small UK-based biotech company that paid in July this year, and UK technology start-up TierraViva AI which 

contributed

 in November 2025.




The smaller outfits are encouraging others to follow suit. The first, TierraViva AI, which deposited $1,000, 

called

 on companies to embrace “learning by doing”, in an open letter penned last November. 




A second company, the biotech firm Prozomix, which handed over $5,000 in July, 

states

 on its website: “We feel companies of our size, and at any and all stages of development, should pay for the privilege of exploiting public DSI”.

Business for Nature, an alliance of more than 100 progressive businesses, has encouraged contributions from its members, pointing out they depend on healthy ecosystems to maintain their business model. It 

writes

 in an August briefing that “companies do not need to wait for the final rules to engage”.

It’s a sentiment echoed by the CBD executive secretary Schomaker, who called on companies to commit, ahead of this week’s summit. 




“Maybe if you think it’s too new for you, make a gesture and start paying, and increase over time,” she 

told

 environmental news site Mongabay.




“It’s frankly not good enough for a company to say, ‘We have many questions,’ and just sit there and wait.”

With editing by Emma Howard

How Big Pharma Tried to Weaken the Rules of the UN’s Nature Fund
