author: Ben Hillier
title: ‘Post-truth’ politics is business as usual
content:
Since Donald Trump’s arrival on the scene more than a decade ago, lying in politics has become ever more shameless. It’s the “post-truth politics” era, apparently. Oxford Dictionaries, which crowned “post-truth” the word of the year when Trump first took up residence at the White House, noted that “it describes not just particular assertions, but a general characteristic of our age”. The 

Economist

 wrote at the time:

“His brazenness is not punished, but taken as evidence of his willingness to stand up to elite power … [Post-truth politics] picks out the heart of what is new: that truth is not falsified, or contested, but of secondary importance. Feelings, not facts, are what matter in this sort of campaigning.”

Yet if “post-truth” is characterised by emotional appeals and relegating facts to the sidelines, it’s not clear that politics has fundamentally changed at all.

On a 2008 autumn night in Grant Park, Chicago, Democratic president-elect Barack Obama, promoted as an articulate Harvard Law graduate with a firm grasp on reality, addressed an enormous crowd. The backdrop was an emerging economic depression: millions of workers were being sacked, more than 3 million homes had been foreclosed in the previous 24 months, the financial system had collapsed, and tent cities of the newly homeless were springing up on the edges of cities across America.

“The true strength of our nation comes … from the enduring power of our ideals: democracy, liberty, opportunity”, Obama promised. “This is our time … to reclaim the American dream and reaffirm that fundamental truth, that, out of many, we are one.” His optimistic gesture was one of the finest moments for the politics of feeling, the culmination of a campaign run on vague notions of hope, change and the slogan “Yes, we can”—appropriated from the mass struggle of undocumented migrants, millions of whom he would go on to deport as president.

Yet Obama’s oration wasn’t considered “post-truth”, because the sentiments, similarly articulated by most political leaders in the democratic West for the last century, were underpinned by unchallenged liberal certainties: that under capitalism, anyone can “make it”, that improvement is the child of hard work, that all individual interests can be accommodated within the national interest. 

“Dream, believe, achieve.” Vacuous aphorisms of this variety are the bedrock of capitalist politics. They aren’t facts or truths, but expressions of an idealised liberal-democratic world whose promises have never been realised. Yet they endure. So why only now are we said to live in a world of post-truth politics? Probably because the empty pledges of progress and prosperity have given way to messages and tones that reflect an era of social decline and political decay at odds with the vision of the world that liberals remain desperate to believe. 

Marketing the truth

Many have pointed out that the last four decades of rapacious free trade and economic and political crises sowed the seeds of this post-truth age. Soaring inequality, greater economic precariousness, more and more people expected to fend for themselves against the forces of globalised capitalism. So British commentator George Monbiot wrote in the 

Guardian

 that “Donald Trump’s election started in England in 1975”, when Margaret Thatcher took over the leadership of the Conservative Party and got everyone reading, and later implementing, the work of Frederick Hayek.

This focus on a purportedly neoliberal economy in producing the “Trumpian moment” (and the broader rise of the far right) misses the universal aspect of this so-called post-truth era. Capitalism is based on theft, and all pro-capitalist politics—far right, conservative, libertarian, liberal, even social democratic—exists to cover up or justify it. Pro-capitalist politics is fundamentally about deceiving people into thinking the system is either fair or natural, when it is neither. 

Nearly 200 years ago, Karl Marx and Frederick Engels first wrote of the stripping away of humanity that came with capitalism’s emergence from the old medieval order:

“The capitalist class, wherever it has got the upper hand, has put an end to all feudal, patriarchal, idyllic relations. It has … left remaining no other nexus between man and man than naked self-interest, than callous ‘cash payment’ … It has resolved personal worth into exchange value, and in place of the numberless indefeasible chartered freedoms, has set up that single, unconscionable freedom—free trade.”

Pre-capitalist feudal markets, with guilds and heavy regulation, often operated as limited sites of “justice”: prices and incomes were reasonably assured, all things being equal, and fixed to create economic stability for the people doing the work. Capitalism removed these certainties, shattering the regulated social and economic order. As it did, the market became a site of “truth”: prices increasingly reflected the true costs of production, which were falling. Falling costs facilitated trade and wealth accumulation among a small section of the population at a disturbing pace and on an unlimited scale. But at the same time, they ravaged the labouring classes, whose relationship with the world was now mediated through the capitalist market.

Much later, Michel Foucault, in a series of lectures at Collège de France, noted that this capitalist turn had profound political implications—the market itself became the adjudicator of governments: “The market determines that a good government is no longer quite simply one that is just. The market now means that to be a good government, government has to function according to truth”. But the market’s truth is nothing more than one of capitalism’s adages: every man has his price, there’s no such thing as a free lunch, and so on. There is now no humanity, no solidarity, no intimacy in truth.

We can recognise the continuity from those early years of capitalism. Governments and representative institutions today are characterised less by political discussion than by managerial procedures focused on economic efficiency. Policies themselves are “tested” not by their social value but by the Treasury, which usually produces a “business case” for whatever it is.

Yet if the truth of government lies in the judgment of capitalist markets, then the latter’s crises expose the deceptions of official politics. In “normal” times, people don’t buy all of the system’s “truths”—for example, not many people would look at Gina Rinehart and think she must have worked really hard for all that money. In extraordinary times, when events like the 2008 financial crisis occur, reality is laid bare, and politics is forced to respond. 

Obama made some gestures toward the idea that greed and a lack of regulation caused the economic catastrophe. But by and large he regurgitated the old pro-capitalist economic nostrums. That was hardly surprising—pro-capitalist politics mostly hinges on exploited people’s hopes for a better life. Tens of millions wanted to believe what the president-elect was saying—even the ones who didn’t vote for him. Yet as the economic “truth production” process struggled to revive in the following years, trust and certainty evaporated for large sections of the population.

According to the Pew Research Center, by the third year of Obama’s presidency, just 15 percent of Americans trusted the federal government to “do what is right” at least most of the time. The question, given the circumstances, was always going to be how the breach of trust, the lack of certainty and honesty and the breakdown of “truth” would play out politically.

Truth in identity?

The above tells only part of the story, however, and a peculiarly economic one at that. Yet capitalist political “truth” is not only about market rule. And public trust in government collapsed faster during George W. Bush’s presidency than under Obama’s, not for economic reasons. Indeed, the longer-term trend shows a general decline over the last 60 years.

A range of factors—including the atomisation of society, the failure of the radicalisation of the late 1960s and early 1970s to overcome capitalism, and a collapsing labour movement from the 1980s—created the conditions for hyper-personalised political expression in which “truth” became relative long before Trump. 

Political theorist Wendy Brown was one of the first to note this in a seminal 1993 essay, “Wounded attachments”. Brown was trying to come to grips with the increasingly toxic nature of 

progressive politics

, searching for the reasons why “politicised identity” becomes self-absorbed, rancorous and self-destructive. In the liberal progressive political universe, oppressions deemed irreducible to a single logic or cause such as capitalism, and to be unintelligible to anyone but the bearer of the particular “wounded attachment”, become owned truths—the property of individuals. 

Indeed, progressive political minds were behind the original theorisations of what is now labelled post-truth, valorising diversity for its own sake and shunning calls for class unity as authoritarian and blind to the many variants of “truth” contained in individual experience. As Andrew Calcutt explained at the 

Conversation

 some years ago:

“More than 30 years ago, academics started to discredit ‘truth’ as one of the ‘grand narratives’ which clever people could no longer bring themselves to believe in. Instead of ‘the truth’, which was to be rejected as naïve and/or repressive, a new intellectual orthodoxy permitted only ‘truths’—always plural, frequently personalised, inevitably relativised.”

This framework remains widely accepted and promoted on the liberal left. Hence the oft-used comment that someone is speaking “their truth”—something private, unshared. It’s truth as a commodity—individual, marketable, something to trade off, like owning a rare collectable or a customised car. This viewpoint, which is little more than the political expression of foundational capitalist ideology—that private property is the foundation of society and that individuals are the basic unit of the economy—is somehow considered radical and progressive.

How ironic then, that this “progressive” framework is today the guiding principle of far-right politics, in which the burdens of class, both working and middle, are articulated forcefully as white racial identity (and anxiety) and in the yearning to witness humiliation as a means of avoiding it—the impulse to be uplifted by putting, or even beating, others down (something identity-obsessed progressives know a thing or two about).

“The truth has become so devalued that what was once the gold standard of political debate is a worthless currency”, wrote Matthew Norman in the 

Independent

 on the day Trump was first elected. “How internet-reared and internet-addled generations can be taught to venerate provable fact over the lies which reinforce whichever truth they have chosen, I have no idea.”

The US president is a liar and a fraud. Yet liberal commentators like Norman and the editors of the 

Economist

 don’t grasp the nature of capitalism’s marketable truth and its uneasy relationships with politics and identity. If they did, they would see that Trump, in a disturbing way, is arguably more real precisely because his mendacity is so transparent.

This is a revised version of an article first published in 2016.

author: Tim Arnot
title: Repressive one day, strike-breaking the next: Queensland workers under attack
content:
As if the right to strike hasn’t been curtailed enough. On 14 October, the Queensland Liberal National Party government accepted a raft of recommendations from a review into the state’s industrial relations laws. Restricting the right to strike is central to the changes the LNP plan to implement, including giving the industrial relations minister sweeping new powers to stop workers from taking protected industrial action. 

Under the proposed amendments, protected industrial action can be terminated by the minister “if it would ... cause significant damage to the state’s economy”. The same goes for action that would “significantly disrupt the delivery of a public service”—a direct attack on the ability of schoolteachers, paramedics, hospital workers and others to take protected action. According to industrial law firm Maurice Blackburn, the laws will also restrict the window in which protected industrial action can be taken and give employers the right to dock workers’ pay even in cases where they are still performing some duties while on strike.

The proposed amendments also target any action taken in the lead up to, or during, events such as the Brisbane Olympic games, where the minister simply needs to be satisfied that such action has “a significant effect that is contrary to the public interest” to have the power to terminate protected action. 

Disruption is the point of strike action. The only power workers have to reliably improve their living standards is the collective withdrawal of their labour, and the chaos this causes is precisely what compels bosses concede to their demands and give workers a greater share of the value their work produces. A willingness to take such action is the reason why workers have sick leave, the eight-hour day, weekends, paid leave and more. It has been the actions of generations of workers that have gone before who have taken strike action, caused disruption and won the things that we value today. None of it was conceded willingly by bosses or governments.  

The LNP make no secret of who their planned changes are intended to benefit. Their press release touting these reforms is all about protecting business interests, and as such they have inserted the buzz-word “productivity”—i.e. workers producing more for the same pay—into the industrial relations legislation multiple times. Among backers of the LNP’s changes are the CEOs of Business Chamber Queensland, Queensland Hotels Association and Master Builders Queensland.

Attorney General Jarrod Bleijie has cited the ongoing Queensland Rail dispute as an example of where, had these amendments been in effect, protected action by rail workers could have been terminated. The eight-month long dispute was initiated because workers refused to accept the government’s low-ball offer of an 8 percent wage rise over three years. In those eight months, the government has been forced to grant some minor concessions—something they do not want to repeat. 

Premier David Crisafulli and his government have attempted to downplay the severity of the legislation, stating they are simply bringing Queensland’s industrial relations laws into line with the federal Fair Work laws brought in by the Rudd Labor government in 2009. That the LNP can point to Labor’s harsh anti-strike legislation at a federal level to justify their attacks is an indictment of the Labor Party, and its record in helping make Australia’s industrial relations laws some of the most draconian in the developed world. But the LNP’s amendments will go beyond the Fair Work provisions, particularly by giving the minister the power to stop strikes, not simply the industrial courts which at least have the pretence of being impartial.

In defending the new legislation, Bleijie told the ABC that “We’ve kept arbitration. We’ve kept conciliation.” No surprises there! Workers get nothing of substance from arbitration and conciliation—certainly not without winning it in the streets and in the workplaces first. The dispute between public school teachers and the Crisafulli government was referred to arbitration at the end of 2025, but it won’t be settled until next April at the earliest. Meanwhile, teachers’ pay and conditions continue to languish.

Another way in which the amendments break new ground in eroding workers’ rights is by undemocratically exerting control over who can and cannot be a union official or employee of a union. The amendments impose a significant number of restrictions, including a “fit and proper” test that can be applied by the Industrial Commission in relation to anyone employed by a union. If only the likes of Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk or Gina Rinehart were subject to a “fit and proper” person test. 

Any union official who has, or who incurs, a conviction for an offence against industrial law can be removed from their role. Given the extremely draconian nature of Australia’s industrial laws, and the necessity of breaking them in the course of even routine union organising, this represents significant government interference in union activity. It is taking the precedent of the administration of the construction and general division of the CFMEU and applying it across unions in the state. 

There is a raft of other attacks in the proposed amendments. One is to allow direct employer ballots to settle disputes, to circumvent the government having to come to agreement with unions first. This opens the door to employers negotiating with other organisations such as the LNP-aligned Nurses Professional Association of Queensland and the equivalent body for teachers. These were set up and are run by ex-LNP staffers such as Graeme Haycroft and Jack McGuire to undercut the existing unions. These associations had been restricted by the Palaszczuk Labor government in 2022.

These two changes complement each other. Direct ballots already happen but take place only after union members vote to accept an offer. The proposed changes would mean that employers can proceed with a direct ballot when “the employer has reached agreement with at least one employee organisation but cannot reach agreement with any of the other negotiating parties; and wishes to proceed with the proposed agreement despite not reaching agreement with all of the negotiating parties”. So, the legislation seeks to remove the requirement that employers come to an agreement with unions, opening the door to negotiation with LNP-aligned associations and then presenting direct employee ballots on inferior agreements. 

Workers’ compensation is also in the firing line. Law firm Slater and Gordon state the changes will make it more difficult for workers to access compensation for psychological injuries. 

There’s little standing in the Liberals’ way to getting this through parliament. Queensland’s unicameral system means that having a majority in the legislative assembly is enough to get bills adopted. 

Union cannot go silent in the face of such attacks. Union leaders held a joint press conference with Opposition Leader Steven Miles to express their opposition to the proposed changes. Zac Beers, Australian Workers’ Union organiser, told the media, “The minister is coming to systematically dismantle your right to fight and organise in this state”. However, we can’t simply look to Labor to fend off these attacks. Looking to Labor is how we got Rudd’s Fair Work laws in the first place, after all. 

What is needed, but is sorely missing from the overall union response, is a 

fight

 against these laws. The unions ought to be organising mass protests at the very least. This would draw attention to these attacks, force the media to engage with workers’ objections and send a message to workers everywhere that we don’t have to accept the constant erosion of our rights—we can fight back. This is exactly what the laws are trying to restrict—the power workers have when we act collectively. Protesting can also help make Crisafulli a pariah akin to Campbell Newman, the last LNP premier who was kicked out in a historic landslide. To do this, there needs to be visible resistance to the government, including industrial action against attacks like these. The reality is, such action would risk falling foul of the 

current

 anti-strike legislation, and is therefore something that our current union leaders have no stomach for. By this logic, we will continue to watch our hard-won rights and conditions be legislated away. At some point we need to fight, and there’s no time like the present.

Tim is a public school teacher in Brisbane.

author: Unknown
title: Пётр Кропоткин - В память о чикагских мучениках
content:
Автор

: Пётр Кропоткин

Название

: В память о чикагских мучениках

Дата

: декабрь 1892

Источник

: Freeom, №72







 В ПАМЯТЬ о ЧИКАГСКИХ МУЧЕНИКАХ 










В Лондоне







Эта речь была опубликована в газете Freedom (№72, декабрь 1892). В ней Кропоткин в общих чертах обрисовывает как обоснованность анархистских теорий, так и необходимость их применения в рабочем движении. В оригинальной статье был также текст, не принадлежащий Кропоткину, здесь он не включен.













 П. Кропоткин: Мы не можем лучше почтить память наших братьев из Чикаго, чем бросив взгляд на прогресс идей, ради которых они жили и погибли, после того как их так жестоко пытали в течение 18 долгих месяцев американские грабители земли и денег. 




 Зарождение Анархистской партии было очень скромным. Она родилась из протеста, который вскоре превратился в ожесточённую борьбу против власти, утвердившейся внутри Международного Товарищества Рабочих. Однако это скромное начало скрывало великий принцип – принцип отрицания власти вообще, во всех взаимоотношениях между членами Общества, и высокий идеал – идеал Общества, основанного на полной свободе личности и свободном обединениии свободных личностей, свободных групп и свободных федераций групп. 




 Партия находила поддержку своим идеям во многих кругах. Она оказалась в согласии с великой работой – критикой власти, которая шла в недрах трудящихся классов. И она оказалась в согласии с мыслью, которая в последнее время занимала всё более и более заметное место в трудах современных философов. 




 Идея росла; она находила поддержку и в философии, и в науке; она развивалась. И как бы мало ни было число анархистов, анархистская идея настолько соответствовала современному прогрессу мысли, что в этот момент мы можем сказать, что она УЖЕ глубоко изменила существующие представления по многим жизненно важным вопросам, связанным с великой борьбой за человеческое освобождение. 




 Представления о соотношении ролей Эволюции и Революции в прогрессе человечества в последнее время полностью изменились. Ни один разумный человек теперь не может противопоставлять Эволюцию Революции – ведь очевидно, что обе являются лишь двумя аспектами одного и того же прогресса. Заторможенная Эволюция вызывает Революцию, а принципы, провозглашённые Революцией, применяются к жизни последующей Эволюцией. Даже некоторые видные дарвинисты теперь признают, что революции были необходимыми частями прошлой органической эволюции. Тем более в человеческой жизни: Революция является необходимой частью человеческой Эволюции. 




 Представления о власти также чрезвычайно изменились. Доверие к ней быстро теряется. Если двадцать лет назад противников власти социал-демократы считали глупцами, то теперь те же самые социал-демократы вынуждены склоняться перед неуважением к власти, которое ощущается в их собственных рядах. Государственные социалисты теперь вынуждены отрекаться от государственного социализма – по крайней мере, в своих программах – и они вынуждены каждый день расставаться с той властью, которую раньше считали необходимым условием успеха Социализма. Социал-демократические группы требуют свободы для каждой из них, и бывшие автократические лидеры обязаны признавать эту автономию групп. Старый аргумент о том, что автономные группы уничтожат друг друга своими распрями, просто показался бы смехотворным, если бы его выкопали из социал-демократических газет двадцатилетней давности и принесли на сегодняшние трибуны. 




 Вы все помните злосчастную воображаемую Коммуну из аргумента авторитаристов, которой отказывали в любой независимости на том основании, что она – как говорили наши противники – будет противиться любому прогрессу остальной нации. Как часто мы слышали об этой фальшивой Коммуне в наших дискуссиях! Теперь этот аргумент показался бы просто смехотворным. Самые авторитарные социалисты вынуждены вписывать муниципализацию собственности в свои программы и признавать свободную Коммуну необходимым основанием свободной нации. 




 В экономике идея полной реконструкции всей системы производства стала общепринятой. Тот, кто стал бы теперь утверждать, что Социальная Революция должна просто состоять в том, чтобы каждый рабочий вернулся в свою мастерскую и там получил свою долю прибавочной стоимости – тот, кто повторил бы теперь эту формулу старого марксизма – просто показался бы призраком из прошлого. Зло, как мы все знаем, не в несправедливом распределении прибавочной стоимости, не в низкой заработной плате и не в продолжительном рабочем дне – а в самой системе наёмного труда, в неверном направлении, которое дали производству при системе наёмного труда, в самой возможности и существовании того, что неправильно назвали прибавочной стоимостью. И по мере распространения этих идей коммунистический идеал завоёвывает почву, и ни один мыслящий человек не содрогнулся бы теперь при мысли о коммунистических Коммунах и коммунистически производящих группах, вступающих в свободные соглашения для ведения таких дел, которые требуют согласия многих групп или многих Коммун. А ведь двадцать лет назад такие идеи просто считались глупостью. 




 В то же время неспособность представительного правления становится всё более очевидной даже внутри самой социалистической партии, не говоря уже о более крупных группах, таких как города, нации и федерации наций; необходимость изъятия из рук Государства тех функций, которые оно присвоило себе, по мере того как власть всё более и более переходила бы в руки среднего класса, становится всё более и более очевидной. Не «ограничение власти», а «упразднение власти» становится теперь общим лозунгом даже за пределами наших кругов.

author: Sue Bolton, Sarah Hathway
title: Socialist Alliance: ‘Stop weaponising shocking attack on Helen Haines MP’
content:
Socialist Alliance condemns the terrible attack on Helen Haines MP and we send our best wishes to her and her family.

This shocking incident had been politically weaponised even before the facts were established; the corporate media and some MPs went looking to find someone to blame.

The Zionists and right-wing commentators were quick to blame the pro-Palestine movement, because the alleged perpetrator — along with the majority of people in Australia — was critical of Israel’s genocide in Gaza. It has become stock in trade for mainstream media to brand critics of Israel as “extremist”.

We now know the alleged perpetrator suffered from poor mental health and that their family was friends with the Haines family.

As pressures mount around housing affordability and the rising cost of living, poorly resourced mental health services, especially in regional and rural Victoria, may contribute to anti-social behaviour.

The 2021 Royal Commission into Victoria’s Mental Health System made 65 recommendations and nine interim recommendations. These largely remain unfunded or not implemented, despite the Victorian Labor government promising to do so.

An independent report earlier this year made 270 sub-recommendations — only 54 have been fully implemented.

Right-wing influencers and the manosphere are also playing a role in influencing a layer of more vulnerable people to take on extreme and conspiracist views.

Data from Women for Election shows that online abuse towards those in elected positions is negatively impacting those in office, those running for office and those considering doing so. Just under 90% of women surveyed reported experiencing online abuse or intimidation connected to their political participation.

No one should be threatened or made to feel fear for themselves or their family members.

This attack on Haines is happening in the context of one woman a week being killed by a current or former partner in Australia. Despite advocacy and mass mobilisations to stop violence against women, misogyny is still pervasive.

Abuse and threats of violence towards women are also on the rise.

Pauline Hanson’s One Nation Party has been aggressively whipping up hate and division. Its scapegoating of vulnerable groups, based on ethnicity, religion, immigration status, gender and ability, as the “cause” of societal problems is part of the political context.

The major parties are contributing to this divisiveness, either through policy or rhetoric. This is being exacerbated by the mainstream media’s clickbait.

As a result, it is not just elected representatives who are being targeted with threats and violence; people are being emboldened by divisive politics to target already marginalised groups with racial, gendered or other violence.

There are solutions, but One Nation doesn’t have them. And while the major parties steal One Nations’ immigration policies, they help fuel the tinderbox atmosphere of fear and hate.

The mainstream parties pander to the extremist right, because it helps them divide and rule.

[Sue Bolton is a Socialist Alliance councillor on Merri-Bek City Council and is the Socialist Alliance candidate for Broadmeadows in the Victorian election. Sarah Hathway is a former City of Greater Geelong Councillor and the Socialist Alliance candidate for Lara in the Victorian election.]

author: Mick Armstrong
title: Hate campaign against Andrews indicates right-wing can’t tolerate even tepid social democracy
content:
Rapturous applause swept One Nation’s campaign launch in Melbourne on 3 October as Mark Nicholson, the party’s lead candidate for the Northern Metropolitan region in the upcoming state election, declared that a One Nation government would jail former Labor premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan “by Christmas”.

This was not just some one-off Trumpian gesture. Visceral hostility to Andrews, denounced by Murdoch’s 

Herald Sun

 and 

Sky News

 as “Dictator Dan”, has for years been a core feature of far-right politics.

Andrews is seen as the devil incarnate, the epitome of a communist leader akin to North Korea’s Kim Jong-Un. He is portrayed as being engaged in a dark “globalist” conspiracy to destroy the Australian way of life, including by giving a treaty to Aboriginal people and destroying important freedoms like the right to spread disease so beloved by anti-vax cookers, White Australia supporters and purveyors of Great Replacement-style conspiracy theories.

Far right hostility to Andrews soared during the COVID-19 crisis when violent fascist mobs, whipped up by enraged small business owners, took to the streets to oppose life-saving public health measures. The fact that Andrews’ pandemic measures were popular and Labor kept winning elections in landslides further inflamed their outrage. How could this “communist” keep winning!!! 

But it is not just One Nation and the far-right fringe for whom Andrews is enemy number one. The Liberal party, the whole of the corporate media and the broader capitalist establishment have sought to demonise him, the way in an earlier era they demonised Labor leaders Gough Whitlam and Jack Lang.

In part this reflects the born-to-rule mentality of the Liberal Party’s traditional wealthy backers. Victoria, the state of Menzies, had once been the jewel in the party’s crown. Now, Labor upstarts like Andrews repeatedly win elections. Intense frustration with the state of the Liberal party, which since the Kennett era seemed utterly incapable of getting its act together, simply made them even more bitter and deranged.

The ruling class, of course, generally prefer Liberal governments over even right-wing Labor governments, because of Labor’s remaining, though much eroded, links to the unions and its working-class voting base. The Liberals are simply their sort of people.

But Andrews, though far from being a radical leftist, was more independent of the corporate media and traditional big business institutions than previous right-wing Labor premiers like Steve Bracks and John Brumby. He was also a more interventionist premier, being much more prepared to use the state to push forward economic development rather than simply relying on the so-called free market. Public service employment substantially rose during Andrews’ first two governments, something the neo-liberals bitterly resented.

During the pandemic, Andrews unapologetically stood up to the hostile media pack in his defence of his government’s health measures during his daily press conferences. This stance earned him the approval, reflected in polls, among the large numbers of people who regularly tuned in. He established an image as the strong leader defending the health of ordinary people against the vested interests who hated the health measures because they impacted on their profits. 

The widespread public support for this stand was reflected in the hash tag #IstandwithDan going viral at the time. At its height, 77 percent of the Victorian population backed his handling of the pandemic and Labor won unprecedented support from university educated white-collar voters in the Liberals former eastern suburbs heartlands.

This inflamed the hostility of the media and in particular the

 Age

, which is commonly seen as more liberal than the Murdoch press.

 

But the

 Age

 is a thoroughly establishment institution and is accustomed to playing a role of king maker—it was central to bringing down the Whitlam government in 1975, as well as the Cain/Kirner state Labor governments and installing Liberal Premier Jeff Kennett in the 1990s.

The 

Age

 became increasingly outraged that Andrews was not at its beck and call and seemed impervious to its criticisms, including of his scrapping the East/West tunnel project, his deals with unions like the firefighters and the CFMEU and his failure to cut government spending and the size of the public service.

The 

Age

 relentlessly campaigned against the Suburban Rail Loop. It attacked the project for not having a proper “business case”: simply building a railway to help workers get off the road and move around the city to see their friends and relatives was simply an abomination against the laws of the capitalist market.

But despite the intense hostility of the media and the broader capitalist establishment, and despite being from the ALP Socialist Left faction, Andrews was in no sense an anti-capitalist or radical. Indeed, as early as his days as gaming minister in the Bracks Labor government in 2006 he had cultivated a relationship with influential business people.

Those relationships deepened after he unexpectedly won the 2018 elections. The Labor right had allowed him to remain leader as they thought he would lose and they could then take back the leadership.

That victory cemented Andrews’ leadership and control over the cabinet. He went on to establish a very close relationship with the likes of billionaire trucking magnate Lindsey Fox, described by Labor colleagues as Andrews’ “go to billionaire”.

Andrews and his wife Catherine were regular guests at luxury dinners at Fox’s cliff-top Portsea compound attended by Fox’s sons, who play a key role in running his empire and a circle of über-rich business figures, influencers and spivs such as promotions guru Michael Gudinski, media figure Eddie McGuire, multimillionaire Gerry Ryan and Luke Sayers, former CEO of big four accounting firm PricewaterhouseCoopers and president of Carlton football club.

Lindsey Fox is close to the former head of the ACTU Bill Kelty, who notoriously became a director of Linfox. He is something of a maverick in the capitalist class and at the height of the COVID-19 crisis publicly defended Andrews, who was being relentlessly attacked by other bosses. Nevertheless Fox, a long-standing backer of Jeff Kennett, Tony Abbott and Cardinal George Pell, is in no sense some “woke” or progressive capitalist.

Andrews cut innumerable deals with billionaire property developers, who will also benefit massively from Labor’s appalling decision to rip down the high-rise public housing towers. And the real scandal about Labor’s Big Build is the enormous profits that major construction companies milked from the public purse.

Andrews’ other hand-outs to business included the privatisation of the Port of Melbourne in 2016, the Land Titles and Registry Office in 2018 and VicRoads Registration and Licensing in 2022 and the Public-Private partnerships to build more toll roads like the West Gate Tunnel and North East Link. 

In retirement, Andrews has been establishing a consulting business with links to China including for mining magnate Andrew Forest’s Fortescue Metals.

The gloss was coming off the Andrews’s government by the end of the pandemic. Andrews eventually caved into right wing pressure and eased restrictions too abruptly, needlessly costing lives. As well, the pandemic led to a massive surge in government debt, in part because of the enormous hand-outs to businesses, at the same time as state revenue started to decline.

Labor comfortably defeated the helpless Liberals under Matthew Guy in the 2022 elections but the signs were there that the tide was beginning to turn against them with their primary vote down 6.2 percent to 36.7 percent. 

Under intense pressure from the establishment to “rein in the debt” Labor moved to the right reversing what had always been a fairly modest reform agenda. The money from property sales that it had relied on began to dry up and Labor was simply not politically prepared to seriously increase taxes on big business or impose a wealth tax to fund vitally needed spending on health, education, public housing and infrastructure in new housing developments.

Nor was Labor ever prepared to mobilise its working-class supporters to defend even the most basic reforms from ruling class demands for cuts. And the union leaders disgracefully refused to fight Labor’s harsh pay caps on public sector workers and the increasing number of job cuts.

In 2023, the Big Build construction projects that had been so vital to Andrews’ image as the leader that “got things done” began to be substantially cut back. Then in September, just days before he stood down as premier, Andrews announced the demolition of all 44 of Melbourne’s high-rise public housing towers—a gift to private developers.

The right-wing shift continued under Andrews’ successor Jacinta Allan, who brushing aside environmental concerns, fast tracked approvals for AI data centres. In late 2025, Allan declared that her government would be “ruthless” about attracting data centre capital investment.

Allan never had anything like the popular support Andrews had as the strong leader who could stare down attacks from the Liberals and the corporate media. So the stepped-up right-wing attacks that cut through more, especially in some of the outer suburbs, which Labor had long neglected and where law and order was more of an issue.

Allan dropped plans to raise the age of criminal responsibility to 14 and introduced tougher bail laws, which disproportionately impact Aboriginal people. Adult time for adult crime was increasingly the reactionary mantra of Allan and her deputy Ben Carroll.

The press whipped-up law and order hysteria which intersected with the relentless 

Age

-led and ABC-backed campaign against the construction union, which discredited the whole Big Build infrastructure project, including important developments like the Suburban Rail Loop which had previously been highly popular.

The sacking of Allan as ALP leader and her replacement by Carroll was a further victory for the right and the financial establishment. The message sent from the big end of town was loud and clear: we control this state. Labor governments are only to be tolerated if they totally know their place. There are to be no more Dan Andrews.

It was also an explicit warning to Albanese: don’t you step out of line and get too full of yourself. Federal Labor’s very modest changes to the tax system were denounced as being too much like Dan Andrews.

Ben Carroll as new Victorian premier is doing everything possible to distance himself from the Andrews era. One of his first measures was to officially scrap the building of a statue for Andrews for having served more than 3,000 days as premier—a project that infuriated the far right.

Carroll has bent over backwards to ingratiate himself with big business and introduced tougher crime, bail and sentencing laws. None of this did anything to appease the bosses, who simply demanded more. Nor did it to do anything to improve Labor’s standing with working class voters fed up with federal and state Labor governments that presided over years of cuts to wages and basic public services.

Labor has simply prepared the ground for the likely election in November of a hard right Liberal government supported by One Nation that will further accelerate the assault on working class living standards and democratic rights. This sharply underlines the importance of building a fighting socialist alternative to Labor and the whole capitalist system; a socialist alternative that will champion the rights of workers and all the oppressed.

That is something that the Victorian Socialists, which are standing in every seat in the Victorian elections, has set as its goal. Join their campaign!

title: Leonardo Caffo - The “enemy” isn’t in the streets. It’s what sends you there
content:
Author

: Leonardo Caffo

Title

: The “enemy” isn’t in the streets. It’s what sends you there




 From France to Albania, from Belgium to Turin, the protests of these days stage a clash between metaphors. Young people (the people) and police officers (the State), equally precarious, face each other as if the other were the enemy. But the enemy stopped living where we look for it long ago. And that is precisely where it organizes the anger, makes it visible and summons it into the street. 




 Let me say this right away, to leave no room for misunderstanding: the young people who have been filling the streets of Europe in recent weeks have every right to do so. This is not a rhetorical concession, one of those premises you write only to take back three lines later. They have reasons to spare: schools falling apart, overcrowded classrooms, a future shrinking like a room whose walls someone moves at night while we sleep. Anyone who dismisses them as vandals, as spoiled children of a prosperity they no longer know, or as puppets of some hidden director, has understood nothing. Or pretends not to understand, which is worse. But precisely because they are right, and precisely because their distress is real, it is worth asking the question nobody seems willing to ask these weeks. Not because it is difficult, but because it is uncomfortable for everyone: for governments, for movements, for newspapers, for commentators. The question is simple. Against whom are they protesting? In favor of what? 




 There is no point asking against 

what

. The what is clear, even too clear: the cuts, the cost of living, the decrees, the war that swallows resources, the idea that school should serve the labor market rather than people, impossible rents. But where does the power that produces all this live, if it lives anywhere at all? Because a protest without an addressee is not an absence of politics: it is a politics someone else is doing in your place, using your body, your time, your anger. 




I. The scene: a Europe that always ends up in the same frame




 Let us look at the images before interpreting them. In France the mobilization began in September in Brittany, in the schools, against staff shortages and the decay of public education, and spread across the whole country. On October 6, according to the Interior Ministry, more than 250,000 people were in the streets; according to the organizers, almost twice that. The toll of weeks of protest runs to thousands of arrests and hundreds injured, among students, teachers and officers. In Lens a fifteen-year-old boy lost a hand after coming into contact with a police grenade. In Brussels, on October 9, unions striking against budget cuts were joined by hundreds of students inspired by what was happening in France. A few dozen masked protesters threw stones at the police; the police responded with tear gas and water cannons; twenty-one people were detained, thirteen of them minors. In Albania, the student protest outside the Ministry of Education on October 13 turned within hours into a revolt against the Rama government: the Ministry of Justice in flames, attacks on public buildings, banks and businesses, 89 injured, 61 of them officers. 




 And then Italy. On October 16 thousands of students marched in every city against the school decree, the cap on foreign pupils in classrooms, the 4+2 model for technical institutes, the cost of living, military spending. In Milan, a river of second-generation young people, born here or arrived as children, forming a shield against those who would like to count them. In Rome, bottles and firecrackers outside the ministry. In Bologna, shields in front of the station. In Turin, stones against officers, water cannons against students, and in between some teachers who placed themselves between the two lines, as their French colleagues had done a few days earlier. You don’t need to be a sociologist to notice that the causes are different, and so are the contexts, and yet the final frame is always the same. A kid in a hood facing a kid in a helmet. The protest is born against something enormous and undefined, a social model, a stolen future, a politics that does not listen. And it ends, with almost mechanical regularity, in hand-to-hand combat between two people who have never met and have no personal reason to hate each other. 




 This frame is the real political subject under discussion today. Not because the clash is the heart of the matter: on the contrary, I argue that it is peripheral. But because that frame is a symptom, in the precise sense the word has in psychoanalysis: a compromise formation that shows and hides at the same time. It shows that there is a conflict. It hides who is really party to it. And the media, who love that frame because it brings in viewers, only amplify its function as a screen. Even the mayor of Turin said so, with unexpected lucidity: there are those who use those images to talk only about the clashes, leaving the problems the young people raise in the background. 




II. Two metaphors facing each other in a mirror




 Let us return to those two bodies. The student in the street is a metaphor: he stands for a generation whose future has been taken away, for a school turned into the antechamber of employment, for an existence that discovers itself precarious before it has even begun. But the police officer is a metaphor too. In fact, if you look closely, he embodies it even better. He is often young as well, almost always from the peripheries and the South, poorly paid for a hellish job that asks him to stand for hours under a hail of bottles to defend a ministry whose minister he will never meet. He too has watched his future shrink; he too is the product of a social model that offers a uniform as the only possible stability. The difference between the two is not one of class. It is one of position: one has been put in front, the other behind a shield.

title: Schplinky Donkanov - Infrastructure of Attack
content:
Author

: Schplinky Donkanov

Title

: Infrastructure of Attack

Subtitle

: To Kill and Sustain

Date

: May 2026







 Whatever is most enduring is ultimately overtaken in the ceaseless transformation of things. 




Roger Ames







 In the cycle of life and death,

 One third are the companions of life,

 One third are the companions of death,

 And one third again are people who, because of their preoccupation with staying alive,

 Move toward the execution ground with each and every step.

 Now why do they do this?

 Simply because of their preoccupation with staying alive. 




 I have heard it said that those who are good at holding on to life

 Do not steer clear of rhinos and tigers when travelling in the hills,

 And do not hide behind armor and shields when entering the fray.

 For the rhino finds nowhere to gore,

 The tiger nothing to sink its claws into,

 And the soldier nothing into which he can lodge his blade.

 How can this be so?

 Because there is not a whiff of the execution ground about them. 




Daodejing, Ch. 50




Coping With the Trouble




 I started writing this zine with one question in mind: “If the state is toppled, where the fuck am I getting my hormones?” Its stupid to think that making a stateless world would force me to detransition. As things currently stand, it’s also true. While there is some infrastructure in this country for drug production, according to the government “80% of the activities required to make the drugs sold in Canada are conducted in other countries”

[1]

. This means that even if the productive infrastructure we have was seized and operated correctly, being cut off from the global corporate-state apparatus would make acquiring the materials to manufacture many medicines difficult, if not impossible. 




 Technology is not neutral. This is as true of bio-tech as it is of tear gas and security cameras. The pathways through which we have developed modern medicine rely on resources found halfway across the globe, extracted through violence and exploitation. Getting beyond this state of affairs asks us to not only destroy what exists here and now, 

we also need to create technology that is aligned with our values and capable of meeting our needs

. Only we can create the structures to do that effectively. And while doing so will not free us, it can enable us to confront this world more effectively and expand what we are capable of as the global supply chain collapses. 




 When I started writing this zine, I wasn’t expecting to try and take a sober look at how climate change is likely to shape our world over the next 25 years. I’m not an expert, I don’t know the future, and frankly, thinking about it too much gives me the scaries. I, like most people, get all weird and wide-eyed and would much prefer to simply crawl into a hole, take a very long nap, and get on with living life as best as we can manage in this hellworld. Unfortunately for us, I don’t think we have that luxury. Continuing to stumble blind and unprepared towards an uncertain future is probably the wrong choice to make. That said, I think that the mind-boggling fear and uncertainty that arises in us when we look too closely is paralyzing and unhelpful. I think we should glance at it just long enough to properly inform our strategies, tactics, and actions, and then go dance and love and fuck and destroy until we come back to the presence of our bodies and can keep moving. My hope is that this zine encourages us to do just that. 




 It seems to me that we have about 25 years to invent answers to many difficult questions before the time and resources we need to create those answers becomes much more scarce. I don’t see this as reason to despair, I see this as fuel for joyous experimentation in living and destruction alongside those I love. I see this as an opportunity to train. An opportunity to cultivate the knowledge and skills that will give us an edge in a changing terrain, and to find pleasure in the novel ways we will find to take our freedom. The way ahead might be murky, but together we can find paths forward that this world has not yet seen. 




 A better world is possible. We choose to make it so. 




Principles for living and fighting




 The point of this zine is to argue that our struggle can develop a stronger offence if we put more energy into developing technologies that align with our values, and support us in adapting to the unpredictable effects of climate change. I believe that we not only need to be capable of hitting the state harder, we also need to be able to meet our needs without relying on state and corporate structures. 




 If technology isn’t neutral, then much of the technology we depend on has capitalist and authoritarian values embedded within them. The way we produce life-saving medicine for instance, depends on tightly controlled infrastructure made possible by fossil fuel extraction and global systems of exploitation. It also gives whoever controls that infrastructure immense power over those who depend on the medicine they produce. When power dynamics are created through the possession of essential material structures, power cannot be redistributed by simply taking control of that infrastructure. In my view, the clearest way to redistribute this power is by creating decentralized infrastructure, enabling people to create multiple lines of access to their medicine, or acquire what they need to make it themselves.

title: StudyCorgi - Anarchist Perspectives and the Sociological Imagination
content:
Author

: StudyCorgi

Title

: Anarchist Perspectives and the Sociological Imagination

Subtitle

: Exploring Complex Ideas

Date

: 15 January 2020

Notes

: Work Cited “Anarchist Perspectives and the Sociological Imagination: Exploring Complex Ideas.” StudyCorgi, 15 Jan. 2020, studycorgi.com/on-anarchist-squints-and-the-sociological-imagination/. Accessed 13 Oct. 2026. 

 This paper, “Anarchist Perspectives and the Sociological Imagination: Exploring Complex Ideas”, was written and voluntary submitted to our free essay database by a straight-A student. Please ensure you properly reference the paper if you’re using it to write your assignment. Before publication, the StudyCorgi editorial team proofread and checked the paper to make sure it meets the highest standards in terms of grammar, punctuation, style, fact accuracy, copyright issues, and inclusive language. Last updated: November 26, 2024.

Source

: https://studycorgi.com/




Introduction




 At first glance, it might seem that the two concepts – the anarchist squint and the sociological imagination – have almost nothing in common. 




 Although both concepts promise to drive humanity to a better future if implemented by people, there is a distinct difference in the main ideas: where sociological imagination aims to teach people to use their own experiences to address large social issues (Mills 5), the anarchist squint refers rather to the use of collective mind in solving global issues (Rathmann 232). 




 However, the fact that the two approaches address the importance of both the individual perspective and the community action allows finding the use for a combination of the two views. This essay aims to provide a broader definition of both the anarchist squint and the sociological imagination and to see the underlying similarities and differences that would allow for the employment of both concepts in ensuring a better future. 




Sociological Imagination




 The sociological imagination is an idea that was first introduced by C. Wright Mills, a prominent American sociologist, in 1959. In his book The Sociological Imagination, Mills describes the concept in depth while also suggesting the possible benefits that the implementation of sociological imagination would entail. 




 The author defines sociological imagination is the perspective that allows the person to view larger historical events and issues through the prism of his or her personal experiences and also to see his life and individual problems in the light of the current historical period (Mills 5). 




 According to Elwell, this was a significant drift from the approach used by the social science at the time, which targeted the development of society into an administratively approved form (par. 2), rather than the shape that would be beneficial for the development of humanity on a global scale. 




 Through the idea of sociological imagination, Mills addressed the structural and historical features of the community that significantly affect the views, values, actions, and motivations of the people who compose this community (Elwell par. 2). 




 According to Miller, sociological imagination involves a capacity to shift from one perspective to another across various religious, national, social, and cultural barriers (7), which makes it is an important tool to address the issues not just within one community, but across the world. 




Anarchist Squint




 Despite the fact that many people perceive anarchism as a socially destructive notion, which is chaotic and unreasonable in its aggressiveness, the anarchist squint, developed by Scott, is yet another viewpoint that could be adopted to improve people’s lives in general, especially in relation to the individual’s freedom of choice. 




 Scott admits that he adopted one of the main ideas that contributed to the development of this concept from a Russian philosopher Mikhail Bakunin’s statement “Freedom without socialism is privilege and injustice; socialism without freedom is slavery and brutality” (xi). 




 And, even though the Russian’s statement implies communistic ideas through the rejection of the “privilege,” Scott’s final concept goes beyond that, creating a framework of vision for the global community with the end goal of achieving a better, freer society. 




 As opposed to the more traditional anarchistic notions, Scott’s anarchist squint does not reject the state entirely: “While he occasionally expresses regret that the state’s elimination is probably impossible, more typically he denies any desire to get rid of the state” (Stone 8). 




 Scott insists that the state is not the only source of social problems and that other factors need to be addressed in the anarchist squint: “Nor do I believe that the state is the only institution that endangers freedom. To assert so would be to ignore a long and deep history of pre-state slavery, property in women, warfare, and bondage” (xiv). 




 Overall, anarchist squint implies looking at the history of various movements and states from the point of view of an anarchist. Scott believes that such an approach would promote “the ideas of mutuality, non-hierarchical cooperation and freedom to learn from one’s own mistakes” (King par. 8). 




Similarities and Differences




 Despite the fact that initially, the two concepts seem to have almost nothing in common, some similarities are indeed fundamental to them. 




 For instance, both the sociological imagination and the anarchist squint are based on adopting a certain viewpoint that emphasizes the connection between large issues and smaller ones, either focusing on an individual or the community. 




 By employing this technique, both concepts promote the empowerment of an individual and stress the influence of every person in society on the issues they intend to address. 




 Another similar idea that is present in both viewpoints is the idea of unity. Scott sees the community as one of the key contributors to freedom: “Forms of informal cooperation, coordination, and action that embody mutuality without hierarchy are the quotidian experience of most people” (Scott xxi). Mills, on the other hand, does not openly proclaim cooperation.

title: Wahono Karyadi & Matsutake - Anarchist Archives: Critique & Self-Critique #1.1
content:
Author

: Wahono Karyadi & Matsutake

Title

: Anarchist Archives: Critique & Self-Critique #1.1

Date

: 2026

Notes

: Anarchist Archives: Critique & Self-Critique—will be written and published periodically—is a space for those running the Archipelago Anarchist Archive to engage in critical reflection.

Source

: Retrieved on October 14, 2026 from https://archive.org/details/@archipelago-anti-authoritarian-archive




 Printed and published (or even unpublished) works—such as books, pamphlets, leaflets, and zines—hold a significant place among anarchists. This is because such media have proven capable of preserving the diverse experiences and thoughts of many individuals; in certain cases, even if there is an intervention targeting these printed materials, their existence will endure—if not be eternal—longer than the lifespans of the individuals who lived through those experiences and produced those ideas. And the individuals who have fully preserved these printed and published words will subsequently receive a benefit, such as having access to revisit past “practices for reaching emancipation” (movements and struggles). 




 That is why, according to Baker (2023) in his study of Spanish anarchist counterculture—or the process of evolutionary change—many anarchist libraries were established to provide access to a comprehensive collection of printed works that had long gone out of print. Unfortunately, the history of the growth of this counterculture—or the process of anarchist evolutionary change—did not proceed smoothly in Indonesia; in fact, it came to a standstill. This was because Indonesia endured a prolonged period of authoritarianism—in its harshest form. The anarchists of the 1920s were exiled to Digul following the 1926 uprising; meanwhile, individuals with (anarcho-)syndicalist leanings who emerged in the 1940s were forcibly removed by Sukarno’s Old Order regime from the factories they had self-managed and were gradually pushed out of the intellectual sphere by the PKI; their very existence became completely untraceable following the 1965 genocide and the rise of Suharto’s New Order regime to power (Bima, 2018). 




 However, this prolonged period of authoritarianism was not unique to anarchists in Indonesia. The prolonged period of harsh authoritarianism—namely, the Communist regimes of Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej (1948–1965; 17 years) and Nicolae Ceaușescu, meant that anarchists in Romania and Indonesia shared—without denying the differences in the impacts of the post-communist era in Romania versus the post-colonial and post-military-authoritarian eras in Indonesia, which created complex distinctions—a commonality in the historical development of their anarchist cultures. This is because when the communist regime came to power, anarchists were marginalized—ranging from having their movements suppressed to being killed—and those who survived had to go into exile abroad or, if they remained in Romania, chose to go completely underground (Anarhiva, 2021). This situation ultimately meant that the anarchists who emerged in Romania during the collapse of the communist regime in 1989 or afterward—the majority of whom were active in the anarcho-punk scene— had only a fragmentary understanding—or none at all—of the anarchists who existed before them, meaning they automatically lacked a collective experience to draw upon when practicing anarchist or anti-authoritarian principles (Tataran, 2026). 




 In line with Adrian Tataran, Ucok (2026) also made a nearly identical point during a discussion of the book Unfinished Nation held at the Bunga di Tembok Library. According to him, before Bima Satria Putra’s book Perang yang Tidak Akan Kita Menangkan was published—long after the Reformation—in 2018, the anarchists who emerged—and just like in Romania, many of whom were also active in the anarcho-punk scene—during the fall of Suharto and his New Order regime and the period that followed had no knowledge of earlier anarchist movements, so it briefly crossed their minds that they were the first generation of anarchists in Indonesia. Consequently, lacking the experience and collective memory passed down from earlier anarchists, these later-emerging anarchists had to start from scratch; in stark contrast, the authoritarian regime—though said to have collapsed—already possessed a bureaucracy, structures, and a military that had been built up over decades, were well-established, and ready to be handed down, making it no difficult task for them to return to the seat of power. 




 Drawing on that experience, Ucok said that it is important to launch an initiative to preserve collective memory, so that gaps in historical memory can be prevented and future generations can learn by looking back at history. This collective memory preservation initiative itself can take various forms, with shared responsibilities; for example—in the context of reading—some may collaborate to document and publish, while others discuss and put it into practice, only to have those insights documented and republished. In my view, in addition to the initiatives to publish, discuss, and put into practice—which many friends have already undertaken—archives efforts are essential for documentation and, furthermore, for the preservation of historical memory itself. 




 *** 




 Archives initiatives, particularly community-driven ones (community archives), have in fact been emerging in large numbers and are flourishing. We can say, broadly speaking, that community archives in Indonesia itself has experienced three waves of growth. The first wave was marked by several community archives that emerged in the post-Reform era through 2010, including the Indonesian Visual Art Archive, Warung Arsip/Radio Buku, and KUNCI. The second wave was marked by the emergence of archives initiatives between 2011 and 2021, including—to name a few—Bebaskan Buku!, Perpustaxaan, Ruang Arsip & Sejarah Perempuan, and Queer Indonesia Archive. Meanwhile, the third wave is characterized by archives initiatives that emerged from 2022 to the present, such as Jogja Sonic Index, Pustaka Taratsa (if they can even be categorized as an archive), Pustaka Langka/Logos, Catatan Nusantara, and Puss in Bed Zine Library.

content:
Author

Title

: Prison, Persecution, and Resistance

Subtitle

: The Case of Miguel Peralta

Date

: January 29, 2026

Notes

: 

Translated from Peltz, Nolan, “Prisión, persecución y resistencia. El caso de Miguel Peralta Betanzos”,

 Avispa Midia

, 29 January

, 2026. https://avispa.org/prision-persecucion-y-resistencia-el-caso-de-miguel-peralta-betanzos/ Part of a series of translations in solidarity with Miguel Peralta from a little corner in Chicago known as Blood Fruit Library

Source

: Retrieved 10/19/2026 from https://www.patreon.com/bloodfruit/posts/prison-and-case-165958672




 Miguel Peralta, a community defender and anarchist, exited the Cuicatlán, Oaxaca prison more than six years ago. His original arrest happened on April 2015, and on October 2018 he was sentenced to 50 years in prison for two charges, one of homicide and another of attempted homicide. 




 After an intense legal battle and political pressure, he managed to appeal the sentence. A year later, on October 14, 2019, after almost a month-long hunger strike, Peralta was finally absolved of all the charges and released from prison. In all, he spend a little under 4 years and six months behind bars due to fabricated charges brought against him. 




 Miguel’s arrest came following a sociopolitical conflict that erupted into violence on December 14, 2014 in the Eloxochitlán de Flores Magón municipality in Oaxaca when the Community Assembly was attacked by a violent armed group headed by the petty warlord Manuel Zepeda Cortés. In the conflict that followed, two people lost their life and many were left injured. This attack, although headed and orchestrated by Manuel Zepeda, was used as a pretext to persecute members of the Community Assembly. Thirty five community members were initially charged in the case number 10/2015, and other charges were brought against other members later. Many community members, Miguel Peralta among them, ended up spending time behind bars and, although they are all free now, the persecution against the community members continues on, for more than ten years now. 




 Miguel’s father, Pedro Peralta, had previously been detained on August 10, 2012 when he was taking part in communal work in Eloxochitlán de Flores Magón, Oaxaca. When he was apprehended, he was beaten and tortured. Pedro Peralta spent nearly three years in the Cuicatlán, Oaxaca prison, even spending some weeks alongside his son behind bars before being released on July 30, 2015. 




 Behind the repression and criminalization in Eloxochitlán, there are direct ties between the local petty warlords and State power, including the weaponizing of the legal system against the community defenders. Local petty warlord, Manuel Zepeda, municipal president from 2011 and 2013, used municipal funds to enrich himself, and also extracted stone, sand, and gravel from the community river, materials that furnished his stores and which he in turn sold to carry out municipal projects. When community members raised their voice against his authoritarianism, the theft of community funds, and the ecological destruction of the community, he resorted to flagrant violence. 




 His daughter, Elisa Zepeda Lagunas, used the 2014 conflict as a political springboard, climbing up the hierarchy of public authority using the vocabulary of victimhood. She placed herself as municipal president in the 2017–2019 term before abandoning the position to run as local deputy for the MORENA political party. Since then, she’s been a local deputy, president of the Oaxaca Congress during the LXIV Congress Session, Secretary of Women under the Salomón Jara government, and presently, serves a second term as a local deputy for the MORENA political party. Thanks to her political contacts and power, she has mobilized the repressive State apparatus against members of the community. 




 Indomitable Resistance




 Miguel Peralta’s criminalization, incarceration, and persecution is the aftermath of his struggle for the autonomy and land defense of his community, Eloxochitlán de Flores Magón. Miguel has been an important voice in the condemnation against natural resource extraction and the petty warlord-ism of the Zepeda Lagunas family. He has also been an important voice in the struggle for the community’s autonomy and self-determination against the power grab of petty warlords and political parties alike. The criminalization against him is a direct outcome of his resistance and, despite this, it has not managed to silence his voice. 




 As a prisoner, Miguel Peralta actively took part in the struggle against prisons, in solidarity with other imprisoned men and women and communities in resistance, and for the freedom of his Eloxochitlán de Flores Magón comrades. Between September and October in 2016, Miguel Peralta took part in intermittent fasts in solidarity with a hunger strike launched by anarchist prisoners in Mexico City condemning the prison conditions and the oppressive role of prisons on society. 




 In October 2018, after his first final hearing, Miguel Peralta went on a hunger strike demanding his complete freedom and declaring his body as a weapon of war against incarceration. in March 2019, Miguel Peralta went on a fast in solidarity with indigenous prisoners in Chiapas who had launched a hunger strike demanding their liberty after being false accused under torture. Later, in October 2019, the day of his second final hearing, he went on another hunger strike that lasted 26 days and ended in his release. 




 Beyond hunger strikes and fasts, Miguel Peralta actively participated in discussions and debates around indigenous autonomy, land defense, and against prisons and prison society, taking part in activities organized outside of prison via recordings and writings. He has released statements and analysis dealing with the anniversary of Ricardo Flores Magón’s murder, October 2

nd

 and the Tlatelolco Massacre of ’68, June 11

th

 and the Day of Solidarity with Marius Mason and All Long-Term Anarchist Prisoners, among other subjects. He also organized activities in jail together with other prisoners, in search of spaces of autonomy and self-organization within a facility that sought absolute control and submission.

content:
Author

: Sea // Fish

Title

: Prison Futures

Date

: 10/20/2026




Introduction




 Across Turtle Island the network of U.S. prisons stretch from edge to edge in a vast network. The proliferation of prisons across the occupied land gestures towards the racial ordering of the settler society’s long project of of colonialism and coloniality. With the advent of European settlers on Abya Yala and Turtle Island two significant constituent elements emerged. That being the confluence of multiple modes of productions in unison around the accumulation of capital by European settlers, these modes took the form slavery, serfdom, and salaried labor. With this was the sociogenic imposition, codification, and reification of race as both a biological and hierarchical ordering (Quijano 2000: 216). This historical process of human ordering—in the productive and ideological forces—is the coloniality of power. Colonialism begets a global, and specifically trans-Atlantic consideration. With the transferring of capital to the European metropoles colonial projects and the coloniality of power cross germinate into local formulations of race, hence the local construals of race require global considerations (Pierre 2013: 1). I argue that people in prison utilize communication with the outside world to challenge their position as colonial subjects under global white supremacy, and in doing so exercise their agency as counter-normative spatial politics. To do so, I trace the writings of Kuwasi Balagoon and Malik Muhammad as they exercises agency under incarceration and counter the stability of inside/outside through action and communications. 




 Understanding and parsing the U.S. prison system requires attending to the colonial context they emerged in. The ethnic cleansing, genocide, and forced serfdom of Indigenous people of Turtle Island/Abya Yala by Europeans transformed the land into the Americas and in doing so capitalism emerged for the first time. Through the violent force of European settlers, the labor of all Others was aligned in the accumulation of capital (Quijano 2000: 219). The forced migration of Afrikan communities to the newly transfigured Americas as enslaved laborers produced, not only the commodities that made the European and settled metropoles wealthy but also, the bottom of stratified racial taxonomy to which Europeans became white, Indigenous peoples Indian, and Afrikan peoples Black (McKittrick 2013: 3; Quijano 2000: 219; Wynter 2003: 309). Intimately bound to the transformation of Afrikan peoples into a racialized as Black population on occupied Turtle Island is the colonial experience of Afrikan peoples in Afrika. Specifically, in the modes of production and the social formulations under European plantocracies. The economic production of “native labor” being that of agrarian serfdom for Afrikan peoples in Afrika racialized as native, African, and Black (Pierre 2013: 24, 40, 50), specifically recalls the modes of production of Afrikan people on Turtle Island post-emancipation as sharecroppers. 




 In Sylvia Wynter’s “Black Metamorphosis”, the transition out of plantation production to sharecropping is marked by this racial and geographic transformation. Wynter identifies that under capitalism, invented by European colonization of Turtle Island/Abya Yala, three zones of labor control existed that of the peripheral plantation economy, the semi-peripheral serfdom economy, and the wage labor economy exclusive to the core (151). It is thus that from the transition of enslavement to post-emancipation labor configurations to which the labor of Afrikan peoples on Turtle Island became native laborers in the colonial configuration shifting from peripheral to semi-peripheral (Ibid.). With this was Jim Crow, the indirect rule built on bifurcated legal constructions of apartheid, was the continuity of slave laws which reified the Black subject position as human Other (153–154). With the transition of Black labor as enslaved chattel labor to native labor the transition from human animal to human Other implicated the Black subject as a contradictory human, one who was now minimally human, but whose labor must be devalued to maintain the coloniality of power (162–163). 




 This important historical transition of productive forces in the U.S. underscores the transition from Plantation Archipelago to the Archipelago of Human Others, in this is the Prison Archipelago (Wynter 2003: 321,329; Wynter 1970s: 372). Through the coloniality of power, the sharecropping mode of production encroached upon the status of human, dominated by Man as white bourgeoise, and thus access to value of human labor. But as Wynter described the Black subject position was implicated by Jim Crow, as indirect rule, to devalue the labor of Black sharecroppers. In doing so the Prison Archipelago’s growing (in numbers of people) and expanding (across land) since emancipation, is constructed as poverty producers rather than capital producers (Wynter 2003: 329). It is through the social relationships developed by 300 years of plantation economy which would emerge with capitalism as global structures of labor and social organizations (Wynter 1970s: 390–391).
