author: Darío Aranda
title: La nueva política contra el hambre se cocina en los comedores populares
content:
Por Leonardo Rossi*




Tal vez un síntoma clave de la degradación social que atravesamos sea la profunda aceleración de 

la indolencia respecto al hambre

 de las otras y otros convivientes de esta Tierra que habitamos. Si bien no se trata de un fenómeno nuevo, sí emergen rasgos diferenciales en esta etapa, con la 

violenta narrativa aplicada desde arriba por el gobierno de Javier Milei

 y con amplias porciones de la sociedad y sus subjetividades impermeables a la problemática. 




Se trata de enormes segmentos que exceden largamente al activismo libertariano. No obstante, en estas líneas se apunta a la contraparte de este escenario: 

las organizaciones que les hacen frente y sí se hacen cargo del hambre del prójimo

. A las estrategias desde las que estas organizaciones enfrentan el actual escenario de violencias múltiples y sus deseos políticos —  “horizontes interiores”, como les llama 

Raquel Gutiérrez Aguilar

—, que anidan alrededor de las ollas comunitarias.




En las últimas décadas, la situación del hambre en la Argentina fue abordada desde diversas políticas en clave asistencial como normalidad y no como paso a un abordaje de fondo. Los picos catastróficos de carencia alimentaria con geografías y segmentos sociales marcadamente diferenciados han sido profusamente analizados en investigaciones académicas, de ONGs, instituciones religiosas y movimientos sociales como el informe 

“Rascar la olla”

 —Fundación Rosa Luxemburgo y CELS— o los trabajos del 

Observatorio de la Deuda Social

, por mencionar algunos.




Si hubo una novedad con el actual Gobierno dentro del panorama de las últimas décadas fue la reivindicación discursiva de la producción política del hambre dentro de las reglas capitalistas y la efectiva concreción de ataques directos a las redes organizativas que soportan la alimentación de sus comunidades en condiciones de extrema precariedad económica.




Por eso, es necesario poner el foco en la potencia política que habita en los comedores barriales, a pesar de los múltiples desafíos existentes, e indagar qué nuevos imaginarios y prácticas se pueden abrir tirando del hilo que convidan las cocineras comunitarias para pensar en abordar el hambre a profundidad y cultivar redes agroalimentarias que logren trascender los cíclicos vaivenes de la macropolítica.




Foto: Plaga Colectiva




Las ollas encendidas, moral feminista-comunitaria




La tarea de las mujeres (abrumadora mayoría) que encabezan los comedores son harto complejas y diversificadas. Si con justa razón tantas veces se apunta a que las docentes deben abarcar trabajos que exceden largamente su rol específico, en el caso de las cocineras se trata de trabajadoras que, muy lejos de abocarse con exclusividad a la cocción de ingredientes, deben gestionar en términos muy concretos la creciente y angustiosa demanda por raciones, caminar horas recolectando retazos de madera de la calle e inventando con qué mantener el fuego encendido bajo las ollas frente a inexistentes garrafas, pedir donaciones —a veces a ocultas porque expone la deficitaria tarea de funcionarios locales, que toman represalias—. También hacer las veces de confidentes y asesorar ante crudos relatos de violencia de género, organizar festejos de cumpleaños que pueden ser únicos para muchas niñas y niños, y sigue la lista.




Si bien suele marcarse que la situación del hambre en el país no ha estallado debido al sostenimiento por parte del gobierno nacional de algunas políticas asistenciales a niveles inflacionarios o por encima de estos, menos se dice de la intensa tarea de estas mujeres a lo largo y ancho de la Argentina. Verdaderas artesanas que sostienen, recrean y buscan potenciar lo que resta de comunidad allí donde todo conspira para su horadación.




Si por apenas algunos días, se decretara una “huelga de ollas apagadas”  —recuperando el proceso de lucha encabezado por mujeres durante la primera mitad del siglo XX en Chile para enfrentar a empresas mineras— de todas las cocineras de comedores populares de Argentina, la situación social de seguro sentiría su cimbronazo. Una acción de protesta en esa clave no es concebible ni deseable, más se quiere trazar aquí una imagen que dimensione la relevancia de este trabajo vital que nace de lo profundamente comunitario en cada barrio y paraje del país. Imaginar de qué modo esos más de treinta mil espacios pudieran, cual una gran olla comunal, traducir su relevancia política y perturbar de modo efectivo la normalidad del poder económico-político es una tarea de imaginación política profundamente desafiante.




En el país existe una valiosa historia de marchas y protestas contra el hambre, y de seguro habrá que crear nuevas narrativas y prácticas para sintonizarla con este presente.  Pese a todos los ajustes, represiones, violencias discursivas y administrativas, las ollas no se apagan porque las sostiene una enraizada “economía moral del pan”.




De ese modo definió Edward Palmer Thompson a esas prácticas en sociedades campesinas pre-capitalistas, donde, más allá de las formas de dominación política por arriba, pervivió en el sustrato social un arraigado entramado comunitario, bajo el cual no era concebible que un coterráneo pasara hambre mientras otros comían abundante a diario o se exportaban granos a otras tierras.




Este reaseguro moral respecto al hambre, entendido como un fenómeno que o bien afectaba a toda la comunidad por igual (frente a desastres climáticos, guerras o plagas, por ejemplo) o bien a nadie dentro de ese tejido social compartido, ha existido con sus variaciones en buena parte de las comunidades humanas desde tiempos remotos. Todas y todos alrededor de la olla o nada. Esta moral fue brutal y sistemáticamente erosionada desde sus inicios bajo las relaciones capitalistas, como parte intrínseca de sus regulaciones sociales.




En América Latina contamos con uno de los capítulos fundacionales de esta dinámica, con las plantaciones coloniales azucareras implantadas desde el siglo XVI. Campos de monocultivos para exportar, mientras se destruía la autonomía alimentaria de las poblaciones locales, y se mantenía en los límites de subsistencia con energía nutricional barata a los cuerpos esclavizados. Bajo esos patrones se fue tornando normal lo que se trata de una excepcionalidad antropológica: habitar sociedades en la que “conviven” de forma impúdica millones de hambrientos y enormes depósitos de mercancías alimentarias, avenidas gastronómicas y puertos rebosantes de granos y carnes listos a ser despachados.




Frente a un escenario actual donde se aceleran graves síntomas pre-existentes de individuación de las sociedades, y donde las tareas de cuidados voluntarios se limitan crecientemente a núcleos familiares cada vez más estrechos, las cocineras comunitarias aún llevan en su subjetividad política el cuidar en una clave comunitaria. “En mi barrio, en mi comunidad más cercana, el hambre del prójimo es un problema que me afecta, y me obliga a cooperar con otras y otros para resolverlo”, razonan.




En condiciones de suma precariedad, atravesadas por el pluriempleo ad infinitum, modulando clientelismos y presiones de los patriarcas del hambre, violencias micro y macro, ahí ponen su energía vital cada día para alimentar cuerpos y sentidos de la empatía humana más elemental. No por acaso, el acto de comunión que es compartir el pan con la otra/otro que carece de comida haya sido puesto en el centro de los ataques iniciales de la crueldad libertariana.




Foto: Plaga Colectiva




De los comedores de la carencia a las comensalidades de la abundancia




Lejos de realizar una reivindicación en abstracto de los comedores, se procura aquí disputar el sentido de los mismos abriendo horizontes de reflexión política. Sin dudas, los comedores de los barrios populares son emergente de situaciones de carencia alimentaria que han devenido espacios crónicos. Frente a este cuadro suele emerger un planteo desde múltiples variantes ideológicas referido a que los comedores deberían desaparecer para que especialmente las niñas y niños coman en sus casas. En muchos casos, los comedores ya entregan raciones para que los hogares las administren. No obstante, en un análisis más profundo es importante no realizar una asociación mecánica entre comer en casa y una mejor concepción de la práctica alimentaria.




Por un lado, comer en el hogar puede implicar muchas veces comer solo, en distracción con otras actividades o situaciones problemáticas o afectados por dispositivos tecnológicos que trastornan el momento alimentario. Si bien varios de estos aspectos pueden también ocurrir en un comedor, el hecho de compartir con un nutrido número de compañeras y compañeros la mesa ofrece un momento concreto de comensalidad que de otro modo en muchas ocasiones no existe.




Menospreciado al extremo en la lógica de la aceleración urbana, el compartir espacio y tiempo de calidad con otras y otros al momento de cada comida —y no sólo ante una celebración o encuentro con afectos— es una práctica nodal del sentido de lo humano. Con decenas de miles de años, el hacernos comensales nos ha ido configurando biológica, cultural y políticamente. Comer en casa con un número en extremo reducido de personas o en soledad es una situación típica de sociedades urbano-moderna-capitalistas y con poquísimas décadas de existencia en la mayor parte de la población planetaria.  




Desde esa lectura, repensar un horizonte donde efectivamente existan comedores comunitarios ya no producto de la carencia sino como espacio creativo de encuentro social y transversal, tal como son los clubes de barrio no sería para nada problemático, más por el contrario es una apuesta política.




Los comedores podrían ser ámbitos pensados desde cada realidad local, con articulaciones sindicales, feministas, de diversos movimientos sociales urbanos y rurales, donde niñeces y adultos se reconecten con las prácticas y saberes agroculturales, gastronómicos y de salud colectiva en peligro de extinción.




Se trataría de ámbitos de alfabetización agroalimentaria, en una clave socio-ecológica, desde haceres concretos y cotidianos. Así los comedores deberían estar orientados a producir y distribuir de forma cooperativa abundancia y diversidad alimentaria desde una concepción de suficiencia. Ésta debe estar acoplada a los requerimientos socio-culturales de poblaciones específicas, y no alineada a regímenes calóricos genéricos pensados de arriba hacia abajo.




Foto: Plaga Colectiva




Pensar la abundancia alimentaria en clave de suficiencia como parte de un horizonte de vida digna es confrontar los excesos impúdicos del régimen agroalimentario del capital, con sus ingentes volúmenes de exportaciones, con sus millones de hambrientos, con sus masivos desperdicios y con toda su ineficiencia hidro-energética a cuestas. La suficiencia debe estar concebida desde las necesidades de comunidades concretas, arraigadas a suelos y cotidianeidades existentes, y no como parte de mega planes que busquen reinventar un gigantismo estatal monocultural.




En todo caso, la estatalidad realmente existente debe tener en materia alimentaria una dinámica cocinada desde el “

subsuelo político”

, diría Luis Tapia, poniendo en un lugar primordial a aquellas sabias que encienden cada día las ollas y la enorme heterogeneidad de entramados comunitarios de los que hacen parte

. 




Sin dudas quedan por fuera de estas líneas infinidad de cuestiones por pensar, discutir, reflexionar y construir para hacer de estos horizontes realidades concretas. ¿Qué rol debe tener el Estado, a qué escala, con qué tipo de mediación? ¿Cuáles son los grados de autonomía necesarios en las organizaciones y cómo construirlos para conservar potencia más allá de las coyunturas de arriba? ¿Qué formas de financiar son pertinentes y viables; cómo trazar líneas entre activismo, trabajo cooperativo y trabajo remunerado en procesos sostenidos a mediano plazo son solo algunas aristas?




Este tipo de cuestiones las venimos escuchando en diversos intercambios por el país, y adquieren múltiples respuestas según geografías, tipo de organización y perspectivas de lo político. Lo que sí se impone de forma nítida es que por un lado hay que poner la resolución del hambre en primer plano de forma urgente, y con acciones vinculantes respecto al Estado y recursos acordes.




No obstante, también surge con fuerza la necesidad de nuevos imaginarios políticos frente a la cuestión alimentaria para dejar atrás, de una vez, el círculo vicioso entre asistencialismo fuerte y asistencialismo débil, ahora con la variante de la crueldad libertariana.




Una nueva agenda frente al hambre del amplio campo popular y de las izquierdas obliga a tomar en serio y aprender del ethos político comunal de las cocineras, hacerlo carne y cultivar una política novedosa que eche raíces profundas, empezando dar relevancia política por ese hecho elemental que desde tiempos remotos ha unido y debe volver a unir a las comunidades, el compartir el alimento en cantidad, calidad y diversidad de forma justa y solidaria. El buen comer en comunidad puede ser una guía para reformular el sentido mismo de lo político, y de los imaginarios sobre la felicidad del pueblo.




Foto: Plaga Colectiva










*Integrante del 

Colectivo de Ecología Política del Sur

 y coordinador junto a Patricia Lizarraga de los talleres de educación popular “Alimento y Política Comunal”, organizados por la Fundación Rosa Luxemburgo.







La entrada 

La nueva política contra el hambre se cocina en los comedores populares

 se publicó primero en 

Agencia de Noticias Tierra Viva

.

author: Valerie Anne
title: ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ Kicked Off Season 23 With a Sapphic Smooch
content:
Grey’s Anatomy came back with a bang. (Well, a smooch. But we’ll get there.) Amelia spent the entire episode getting the cold shoulder from Toni because, as I’m sure you remember, we left them last season with Toni showing up at Amelia’s door to profess her love for her, only to realize a naked Cass was already in Amelia’s apartment.

When we return for season 23(!), Toni is giving Amelia the cold shoulder all day. Amelia desperately wants to talk to her, but Toni isn’t hearing her out. They clash over work decisions, and Amelia starts to get frustrated. And at this point I was afraid the show was ending their storyline. I thought it was going to be a dramatic fight and then back to no wlw relationships on the show. I was thankfully wrong!

Eventually, the day leads Amelia to Toni’s front door, where she apologizes again for sleeping with Cass, and explains it was an emotional reaction to being so sure Toni was about get back together with her ex. She regrets it if it means she would lose Toni. She says she’s truly, madly, deeply in love with Toni and that if Toni is done, she’ll move on, but if not, she really doesn’t want to let what they have died. Toni considers her for a moment but then breaks; she’s still in love with Amelia, and she’s not done. The two kiss about it, and while I doubt their road ahead will be paved with roses and rainbows (especially because Toni’s ex is still in the picture, and goodness knows if/when Cass will return to drop bombs) but I’m glad we at least aren’t done with their story yet. I look forward to seeing what Season 23 will bring for our resident gays; here’s hoping none of them disappear into the parking lot of no return.

+ Olivia Rodrigo dropped a remix of her song “Expectations” with a verse by Chappell Roan in it, plus a music video go to alongside it (my TikTok FYP has been enjoying Chappell in the background singing, “not kissin’ no boy, NO BOY”)

+ Speaking of, Chappell Roan got to DJ and play Pink Pony Club at The Abbey, which inspired the song in the first place

author: Mike Ludwig
title: In Virginia, Racism and Redlining Are Fueling a Flock Camera Backlash
content:
Police in Hampton Roads saturated Black and low-income neighborhoods with Flock-style cameras, a study found.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Local governments in Virginia are under mounting pressure to cancel contracts for surveillance cameras known as automated license plate readers (ALPRs). On October 6, the Henrico County Police Division announced that it would terminate its contract for such cameras after residents shared “legitimate concerns about Flock Safety.” In nearby Richmond, Mayor Danny Avula said on October 13 that the city would cancel its contract with Flock Safety, the most famous purveyor of the cameras, but did not rule out using ALPRs from a different company.

“It is a good first step, but we do need to keep the pressure on the city to not automatically switch to another ALPR vendor,” Richmond Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member Victoria McCullough told Truthout.

DSA activists and residents in Richmond pushing police to ditch the contract have powerful research to point to from elsewhere in the state. In the neighboring Hampton Roads region of Virginia, race and class are the primary predictors of locations where police installed ALPRs, a groundbreaking study found earlier this year.

The study found police were more likely to install ALPRs in majority Black census tracts in each of the nine cities across the Hampton Roads region, an East Coast metroplex with 1.8 million residents and multiple cities, including Norfolk and Virginia Beach. About 80 percent of majority Black neighborhoods contain at least one camera compared to fewer than 40 percent of majority white tracts. ALPR surveillance is also more intense in majority Black neighborhoods, where on average there are four times as many cameras than in white neighborhoods when weighted for population share.

In Virginia Beach, police deployed ALPRs in only five of 76 majority white census tracts (6.6 percent), compared to one of two Black census tracts (50 percent). Black residents of the locality are 7.6 times more likely than white residents to live in a census tract with at least one ALPR. When weighted for the number of cameras deployed in each area, Black drivers in Virginia Beach were roughly eight times more likely than white drivers to be regularly surveilled by Flock-style cameras.

Published in January 2026, the study found a “similarly consistent pattern of disproportionate camera coverage” in low-income areas and concluded that ALPR deployment in Hampton Roads follows historical patterns of housing discrimination, racist segregation, and disinvestment. In other words, police have deployed the cameras so Black and lower-income people are more likely to live under high-tech, AI-powered traffic surveillance than whiter, wealthier people.

Dr. Steven Keener is a co-author of the study and director of the Center for Crime, Equity and Justice Research at Christopher Newport University. He pointed to Norfolk State University in Norfolk, one of only five historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) in Virginia, as an example of the increased surveillance presence. The area in and around the university is heavily saturated with Flock brand ALPR cameras, compared to whiter and higher-income areas of Norfolk, the study found.

“The census tract with the most ALPR cameras surrounds Norfolk State, which is the only public HBCU in the region,” Keener told Truthout in an interview. “The cameras completely encircle the campus, so you can’t enter or exit in a vehicle without being surveilled.”

Of the census tracts with the highest number of ALPRs, nine are located in Norfolk, where the cameras are concentrated in historically Black neighborhoods and near public housing. The ALPR data used in the study was only available because a federal judge ordered police to release the records in November 2025 as part of a privacy rights lawsuit filed by two residents of Norfolk. Keener’s team used the data to map out ALPR locations across Hampton Roads and compare the results to Census data on race and income.

“Economic and social policy failures have led to your life being constantly surveilled,” Keener said of lower-income and Black communities. “They’re still doing racialized surveillance and policing, but instead of having an officer on the corner, they are watching you to criminalize your behavior based on where you live.”

Across east Virginia, police deployed ALPRs near public housing projects where many lower-income Black residents live, reflecting Virginia’s history of redlining and other racist policies, according to Keener. Some housing projects are also surrounded by AI-powered “tsunami cameras” that analyze data on people as well as vehicles by recording “360-degree video in ULTRA-high definition 24/7,” according to one manufacturer. The cameras are operated by the public housing authority but often accessed by police, according to reports.

That type of surveillance reaches beyond the region for which the study had data, Keener mentioned. “A journalist, Samuel Parker, in Richmond found that police were watching people enter and exit their homes, using tsunami cameras to investigate social media posts,” he said.

Keener and his team expect similar results to their study in other parts of the country if transparency advocates are successful in pushing police to release such data. Police typically fight to keep such data under wraps — Richmond has refused to release its data despite public outcry over the technology, citing the potential for vandalism — and Keener knows of no other example of police releasing ALPR location data in the United States.

Modern ALPR systems go far beyond recording license plates at a specific time and location. By capturing images of each passing vehicle and using AI-powered software to turn identifiers such as make, model, dents, and bumper stickers into searchable data points, networks of ALPRs allow police to easily build detailed profiles of an individual driver’s movements or daily routine. The data is often fed into centralized, “real-time” surveillance centers where police use AI and “predictive policing” software.

“Predictive policing is this modern idea that, because we have all this data on where arrests have happened … we can predict where crime will happen and prevent it by focusing resources there,” Keener said. “But there are a ton of false positives where police misidentify places and people.” Other critics say predictive policing technology has proven to be both ineffective and a form of social control that reinforces existing patterns of racist and classist policing.

“We are putting our tools up in a racialized manner, so the data is going to be racialized,” Keener said, in reference to his research on ALPR locations. “It looks clean and without bias, but that is just not the case.”

Predictive policing technology also allows police to launder or “tech-wash” racist policing strategies to appear as if they are based on objective data, when in reality already highly policed communities are oversampled in the data that determines which communities are targeted. The report describes a “self-fufilling prophecy” in which highly policed communities produce the data used to identify targets for heavy surveillance in turn producing more data instructing police to consider these communities as threats.

“These cameras could be very useful tools for doling out fines and fees for expired tags and expired registrations that are in high poverty neighborhoods,” Keener said. “We are constantly taxing the poor in this system, and this is a clear way that the poor are going to be taxed.”

Flush with pandemic-era funding and federal grants, police departments across the country have aggressively invested in other high-tech surveillance technology in addition to ALPRs, including advanced AI-powered drones, without consulting the public. The integration of facial recognition technology with these surveillance tools in New Orleans and other localities has sparked outrage, leading a handful of cities to ban or limit its use by police with exceptions for investigations into violent crimes.

The study cites reams of research on the racial biases inherent to surveillance tech algorithms, as well as the negative economic and mental health impacts people experience when living under racialized segregation and high-tech police surveillance. In interviews with Parker, residents of Richmond housing projects described anxiety about being constantly on camera.

“I think it’s terrifying … it wasn’t by accident that these ALPR cameras got put up without public input,” Keener said.

The surveillance isn’t limited to local police, either. Keener warns that federal agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), are increasingly accessing local ALPR surveillance data through “side doors” despite guardrails established by state and local policymakers.

“Essentially, a side door access is like the federal government, in this case, ICE, getting access [to ALPR data] from friendly [police] departments,” Keener said during a recent press conference. “And that’s the most common way that it’s happening.” Investigative journalists found last year that about 50 immigration-related searches were performed across five Virginia counties between June 2024 and April 2025, despite local governments barring the use of ALPRs for immigration enforcement.

While the federal government could subpoena Flock Safety for the same data, since the company also stores ALPR data for training AI models, using these “side doors” is much easier, Keener said.

As the anti-surveillance fight heats up in Virginia, law enforcement has gone on the defensive in an attempt to continue using controversial ALPR tech. Ramin Fatehi is the commonwealth attorney for Norfolk and came into office promising to reduce mass incarceration. He suggested people are misdirecting their frustration with Big Tech toward Flock-style cameras because ALPRS are far more visible than data brokers working behind the scenes to hoover up and sell personal information online, for example.

“That is what has drawn people’s ire; they can see the [ALPR camera], and that is where they are directing anxieties that are perfectly reasonable in the age of AI,” Fatehi told Truthout. “They are right, but they picked the wrong target.”

Like others in law enforcement, Fatehi claims ALPRs are a “precision tool” for solving car thefts, missing persons cases, homicides, and other felony crimes. He said ALPRs can improve the “clearance rate” for homicide cases, or the percentage of cases considered resolved by an arrest or “exceptional means” such as the death of a suspect, for example.

However, journalists recently used FBI data to determine that the installation of Flock cameras and other surveillance devices in Atlanta, Georgia, did not markedly improve the city’s clearance rates from 2021 to 2025. Last month, CBS News also debunked repeated claims by Flock Safety CEO Garrett Langley that the company’s ALPRs helped police solve “1 million crimes” in 2025, which is not supported by available evidence. Asked about the scandals surrounding ALPRs in other communities, including dozens of cases where cops used the cameras to stalk women, Fatehi pointed to a new Virginia law that took effect on July 1 and restricts how police can access, use, and share ALPR data.

The law limits storage of ALPR data to 21 days — unless police have “reasonable suspicion” that a crime has been committed, a lower legal bar than the “probable cause” needed to make arrests. Vehicles placed on so-called “hot lists” can be closely surveilled for longer than three weeks by networks that can extend far beyond where the driver lives. “The fact that ALPRs are subject to abuse is a different way of saying that police officers are human beings and some of them will break the law,” Fatehi said.

Fatehi also suggested that ALPRs might potentially reduce dangerous interactions between law enforcement and Black and Brown residents. In a recent homicide investigation, Fatehi said police used ALPRs to track down the suspect instead of pulling over dozens of drivers who matched a description. Take the scalpel away, and you “are left with a meat cleaver,” he said.

But Keener disagrees, saying the Virginia law placing “guardrails” on ALPRs has no teeth. Violators among law enforcement face only misdemeanor charges, and enforcement of the law is effectively left up to the same institutions it supposedly regulates.

A report published in early 2026 by the Virginia Crime Commission found dozens of violations of the law by police agencies across the state, including storing data past the 21-day time limit. At least 21 police departments or agencies shared ALPR data out-of-state or with the federal government outside of permitted investigations, and 35 percent had not notified the public about an ALPR privacy policy as required by the law.

Keener said he is frustrated that elected officials keep pointing to the law because they know it’s not working, and some state lawmakers have announced plans to introduce proposals for strengthening the law or banning police ALPRs altogether.

Keener also rejects the idea that police would be forced to pull over more Black drivers if ALPR cameras are taken down. “Either we have ALPR cameras or racist policing? Obviously, it’s a false choice.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

title: Andrea Rodríguez Cabral - Hearts on Fire and Other Texts
content:
Author

: Andrea Rodríguez Cabral

Title

: Hearts on Fire and Other Texts

Notes

: Andrea Rodríguez Cabral’s 2026 complete thesis and other relevant texts. This important work of Anarchist Sociologist takes theories and concepts of people like Pierre Bourdieu, Jeff Shantz & Dana Williams, Joan Scott, Louise Tilly, Temma Kaplan, and others, to focus on the Mexican anarchist women in and during Revolutionary Mexico. A great contribution to anyone seeking to understand the interelation between social structures, individual motives, and female participation impacted by both, through an anarchist lens. Translated by Blood Fruit Library/Malvivientes 2026.

Source

: Retrieved 10/19/2026 from https://www.patreon.com/bloodfruit/posts/hearts-on-fire-171440071




María Brousse and Lucía Norman: Two Women Erased from Anarchist History

[1]




Brousse and Norman were prolific writers, organizers, promoters, and revolutionaries. Their work was part of Mexican anarchist history.




 2022 was, by presidential decree, the Year of 

Ricardo Flores Magón

 in Mexico. His name appeared in official documents, gaining popularity; likewise, there was a push to publish and promote texts that dealt with him. However, little to nothing was said of the two 

women

 who accompanied him in life and whom without Flores Magón would not have been able to develop his revolutionary ideas: 

María Brousse

 and 

Lucía Norman.




María Brousse

, also known as María Brousse de Talavera and María B. Magón, was born in 1867 in Zacatecas and died in 1946. She took part in many revolutionary groups and clubs such as 

Club Reforma, Libertad y Justicia

 and the American Socialist Party. At the same time, she was a writer in some papers cut from 

anarchist

 cloth such as 

Regeneración

 and the Cuban 

¡Tierra!

 María was a shining member in the Mexican Liberal Party (PLM), which she was dedicated to organize, promote, and write for. 




 By 1907 María was the romantic partner of 

Ricardo Flores Magón

 and remained so until his death in 1922. She was persecuted and spied on by the Mexican and American governments due to her participation in PLM; for example, in 1916 she was arrested for a couple of days with the aim of confiscating some PLM documents she had in her possession. In 1918 she was jailed for five months due to her participation in the creation of the Ricardo Flores Magón International Defense Commission. Following the death of Flores Magón, 

María Brousse

 remained active for the remainder of her years, writing in the exiled Spanish paper, 

Tierra y Libertad

. 




Lucía Norman

 was the daughter of Martín Norman and María Brousse. Originally from Los Angeles, Lucía followed her mother’s footsteps and became a PLM journalist. She also fashioned herself after her mother in writing for papers of an anarchist inclination, such as 

Regeneración

 and 

Libertad y Trabajo

. Alongside her mother, in 1907, Lucía protested against the jailing of 

Ricardo Flores Magón

, who took on the role of her adoptive father. She was present in the movements demanding freedom for the PLM political prisoners from 1907 to 1922, which earned her a couple days in prison in 1912. 




 In 1917, 

Lucía Norman

 suffered a nervous attack after her romantic partner, Raúl Palma, was imprisoned. This deteriorated her health leading to the cause of her death in August of 1923, almost a year after the death of her adoptive father, 

Ricardo Flores Magón

. 




Citizens and the Revolution




 Flores Magón was jailed alongside Librado Rivera and Antonio I. Villarreal in the county of Los Angeles, USA in 1907 under orders of Porfirio Díaz. Thanks to the letters rescued and made accessible to the public by Jacinto Barreda Bassols,

[2]

 we are able to know of Flores Magón’s perspective regarding the incarceration. Fortunately, these letters also allow us to peer into the lives of 

María Brousse

 and 

Lucía Norman

 and analyze the relationship they had with Flores Magón. The letter selection mentioned here is from September 1908 to February 1909, and they are included in the 

Correspondencia de Ricardo Flores Magón (1904–1912)

 anthology by Barreda Bassols. 




 The letters between María, Lucía and Ricardo were exchanged in secret, hidden in clothing or food. In a November 22, 1908 letter, Flores Magón wrote the following to María, 







 I received the 

tamales

. I liked them a lot. I searched them, for I had a suspicion, that there would be something but there was none. There are some small containers that are lipstick-thick that may be placed and sealed well inside 

chiles rellenos

. [..] Inside these containers may be placed letters written in small lettering and thin paper.

[3]







 Being able to introduce and sneak the letters was an utter challenge to 

María Brousse

 and 

Lucía Norman

, who tended to write just one letter since space was scarce. These letters contain important information for the organizing PLM, such as the plans for the 1908 insurrection that María managed to smuggle out of prison. Besides this work, María and Lucía took charge in providing Flores Magón with other goods, as evidenced by a November 1908 letter, “The clothes arrived with newspapers and I’ve also received fruit, a cake, and pastries. Thank you. Don’t send me books because they won’t give them to me.” 




The Pen of María and Lucía




María Brousse

 and 

Lucía Norman

 were prolific writers far beyond just letters, and they dedicated heart and soul to PLM’s struggle. In February 1916, Lucía wrote the following in 

Regeneración

, 







 Let us not let others think for us or let them paint anarchy in words of blood and fire. Anarchy is peace, it is love, it is good will [..] Let whoever opposes progress blame themselves for blood and fire, not anarchy. We think with our heads. Anarchy Forward! 







 In November of the same year, María also expressed herself in the following manner within 

Regeneración,

title: Arnavutlukta halkın isyanı mahkemelere yöneldi, Başbakan Rama saldırılarını sertleştiriyor
content:
Arnavutluk'ta yolsuzluk, eğitim harcamaları ve hayat pahalılığına karşı büyüyen protestolar pazartesi günü de sürdü. Başkentte Eğitim Bakanlığı önünde başlayan öğrenci gösterisi, polisle çatışmaların ardından başka bölgelere yayıldı.




Bir grup gösterici İstinaf Mahkemesi'nin kapı ve pencerelerini kırarak binaya girdi. Kosova merkezli haber ajansı KOHA, göstericilerin birkaç dakika sonra binayı terk ettiğini duyurdu. İspanyol haber ajansı EFE ise Arnavutluk'un A2 CNN televizyonuna dayanarak binada yangın çıktığını bildirdi.




Polis, mahkemeye yönelik saldırıyla bağlantılı beş kişiyi gözaltına aldı, 15 kişiyi de aramaya başladı. Gözaltına alınanlar arasında 16 yaşında bir çocuk var.  




Akşam saatlerinde Başbakanlık çevresinde yeniden çatışmalar yaşandı. Göstericiler polise taş, havai fişek ve Molotof kokteyli attı. Polis, göz yaşartıcı gaz ve tazyikli suyla müdahale etti. Özel harekât birimi RENEA da Başbakanlık çevresinde konuşlandırıldı. 




Sağlık Bakanlığı: 310 kişi yaralandı




Sağlık Bakanlığı'nın 19 Ekim saat 21:00'de açıkladığı bilançoya göre, gösterilerin başladığı 13 Ekim'den bu yana 310 kişi yaralandı. Yaralıların 191'i polis, 88'i gösterici, 31'i ise olaylar sırasında bölgede bulunan kişiler.




Pazartesi günü yaralananlar arasında bir çocuk ve iki basın mensubu da var. Bakanlık, hastanelerde tedavisi süren kişilerin durumunu izlediğini bildirdi.




Yüksek Mahkeme ve Parlamento binalarında yangın




14 Ekim'de göstericiler Meclis Başkanlığı'nın idari binasına girmişti. KOHA'nın haberine göre binadan belgeler dışarı atıldı ve bazı bölümleri ateşe verildi. Aynı gün Eğitim Bakanlığı ve diğer kamu binaları da saldırıların hedefi oldu.




17 Ekim'de Yüksek Mahkeme'nin bulunduğu binanın bir bölümünde yangın çıktı. Ancak sosyal medyada ileri sürüldüğü gibi mahkemenin bütünüyle yok edildiğine ilişkin haberler doğrulanmadı.




Polisin müdahelelerde plastik mermi, gaz ve tazyikli su kullanması da tartışma konusu oldu. Reuters'ın haberine göre Polis Genel Müdürü Skender Hita, orantısız güç kullanımı iddiaları nedeniyle 7 polis memurunu görevden uzaklaştırdı. 




1000 akademisyen: “Rama istifa etsin, geçici hükümet kurulsun”




19 Ekim'de yaklaşık bin öğretim üyesi, öğrenci hareketini destekleyen ve Başbakan Edi Rama'nın istifasını isteyen beş maddelik ortak bir bildiri imzaladı.




Bildirinin ilk maddesinde şu çağrı yer aldı:







Başbakan Rama'yı öğrencilerin taleplerini dinlemeye ve ülkenin yatışmasının yolunu açmaya çağırıyoruz. İstifasını ve kurumsal istikrarı, durumun sakinleşmesini ve yurttaşların iradesine saygıyı güvence altına alacak bir geçici hükümet kurulmasını istiyoruz.







Akademisyenler, güvenlik güçlerinden öğrencilere yönelik şiddete son vermelerini istedi ve hukuka aykırı emirleri uygulamamalarını hatırlattı.




Bildirinin göstericilere yönelik çağrısında da şöyle denildi:







Hükümete şiddet uygulamak ve protestoları gayrimeşru göstermek için gerekçe vermemek amacıyla işletmeleri, kamu mallarını ve özel mülkiyeti koruyun.







İmzacılar arasında muhalefetteki Demokrat Parti'ye yakın akademisyenler, milletvekilleri ve eski siyasetçiler de var. Demokrat Parti lideri Sali Berişa'nın kızı Argita Berişa ve damadı Jamarbër Malltezi de bildiriye imza koydular.  




Protestolar Trump'ın damadı Kushner'in kıyı projesiyle başladı 




Günümüzdeki öğrenci hareketinin kaynağında, mayısta başlayan çevre protestoları var.




Donald Trump'ın damadı Jared Kushner'in desteklediği, Adriyatik kıyısındaki Vjosa-Narta sulak alanında planlanan lüks turizm yatırımı, çevre örgütleriyle hükümeti karşı karşıya getirdi.




Çevre koruma statüsündeki alanlarda yapılaşmanın önünü açan düzenlemelere karşı başlayan hareket, flamingoların yaşadığı doğal alanlara izafeten “Flamingo Devrimi” olarak adlandırıldı. 




Avrupa Parlamentosu, haziranda Arnavutluk hükümetinden doğayı koruma statüsünü zayıflatan düzenlemeleri geri çekmesini istedi.




Avrupa Parlamentosu Yeşiller grubundan Hollandalı milletvekili Tineke Strik, 19 Ekim'de The Guardian'a verdiği demeçte şöyle dedi:







Arnavutluk hükümeti Flamingo Devrimi'ni ciddiye alsaydı bugün burada olmazdık.







Strik, Rama hükümetini Avrupa Birliği'nin çevre standartları Tiran'ı da bağlayıcı hâle gelmeden turizm projesinin işlemlerini hızlandırmaya çalışmakla suçladı.




Rama ise çevre kurallarının ihlal edildiği yönündeki iddiaları reddetti. Turizm yatırımlarının ülkenin ekonomik kalkınmasına katkı sağlayacağını savundu.




Hareketin öğrencilere yayılmasıyla talepler genişledi. Eğitim masrafları, üniversitelerin durumu, işsizlik ve yolsuzluk iddiaları protestoların başlıca konuları hâline geldi. 




Rama istifayı reddediyor, öğrencilere yaptırım tehdidinde bulunuyor




2013'ten beri iktidarda olan ve 2025 seçimlerinde dördüncü kez iktidara gelen Başbakan Edi Rama, protestocuların istifa çağrılarını reddetti.




Rama, 18 Ekim'deki açıklamasında gösterilerin hükümetten çok Arnavutluk'un Avrupa Birliğine katılım hedefini tehdit ettiğini ileri sürdü:







Bana meydan okunmuyor, hükümete meydan okunmuyor, hükümet çoğunluğuna ya da seçimleri kazanmış partiye meydan okunmuyor. Meydan okunan bir yol, bir misyondur.







Ardından şunları söyledi:







Arnavutlar çok açık düşünmeli: Bunu mu istiyorlar, şunu mu istiyorlar, yoksa Avrupa Birliğini mi?







Rama, 19 Ekim'de polis yöneticileriyle yaptığı toplantıda, şiddet olaylarına karışan öğrencilerin burslarının ve devlet desteklerinin kesilebileceğini; reşit olmayan göstericilerin yol açtığı zararlardan ise ailelerinin sorumlu tutulacağını açıkladı.




Başbakan ayrıca bazı şiddet olaylarının arkasında yabancı parmağı olduğunu ileri sürdüyse de buna dair bağımsız kanıtlar açıklanmadı, olaydaki tek yabancı Donald Trump'ın damadı olarak kaldı.




İktidar partisinden ayrılan milletvekili göstericilerin yanında




Rama'nın Sosyalist Partisi listesinden 2025 seçimlerinde parlamentoya giren 25 yaşındaki Marjana Koceku da partisinden ayrılarak öğrenci gösterilerine katıldı.




Reuters'a konuşan Koceku, protestocuların daha iyi yaşam koşulları ve siyasal değişim taleplerini desteklediğini söyledi.




Muhalefetteki Demokrat Parti ise geçici hükümet kurulmasını ve erken seçime gidilmesini istiyor.




Avrupa Komisyonu, gösterilerdeki şiddeti kınarken barışçıl protesto hakkının korunmasını ve güvenlik güçlerinin müdahalelerinin orantılı olmasını istedi.




Başbakan Rama'nın ülkeden kaçtığına ilişkin sosyal medyadaki iddiaları asılsız çıktı. Avusturya'ya yapacağı ziyareti iptal eden Rama, 19 Ekim'de Tiran'da polis yöneticileriyle görüştü. Hükümet halen gösterilere karşı önlem almakla meşgul. 




(AEK)

author: Julia Conley
title: Trump Officials Look to Delay Pursuing Defaulted Borrowers Until Midterms Pass
content:
Many Trump voters who have defaulted on student loan payments may soon have wages garnished and benefits seized.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

As the Trump administration makes plans to task private debt collectors with going after millions of student borrowers in default on their federal loans, officials are reportedly pushing for the effort to begin after the midterm elections — as they grapple with the fact that many supporters of President Donald Trump are likely to be affected.

The Washington Sun reported Monday that the U.S. Department of the Treasury is planning to move forward with punitive measures after previously blocking a push by the Education Department and Office of Management and Budget to garnish wages and seize people’s benefits if their loans are in default.

As the Center for American Progress (CAP) said in a report Monday, defaults on student loans have reached record levels, with 9.5 million — or 1 in 5 — borrowers unable to make scheduled payments following the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).

The law eliminated the Saving on a Valuable Education (SAVE) program and forced borrowers into the Repayment Assistance Plan instead, bringing the average annual cost to $2,163 per borrower, according to CAP.

According to the Sun, administration staffers have advised officials to consider the impact that more upheaval for student borrowers — in the form of debt collectors either following through on the earlier wage-garnishing plan or seizing tax refunds and payments — would likely have on Trump voters.

“This is not who you think it is. The demographics are not good for us,” aides told officials last year when they pushed for a delay on the wage-garnishment plan.

An Associated Press analysis in July found that states with the highest rates of student loan defaults were overwhelmingly Republican-leaning, with Mississippi, Louisiana, and Alabama leading the way.

The advocacy group Protect Borrowers also found earlier this year that roughly two-thirds of all defaulted borrowers live in states Trump won in 2024.

Sources in the administration told the Sun that some officials are pushing for a further delay of the debt collection, as they ensure the Treasury Department’s portal for defaulted borrowers is working. The Defaulted Loans Support Center was launched last month with the stated goal of giving borrowers “a simple, streamlined way to understand the consequences of default and apply online to either rehabilitate or consolidate their loans.”

Others want to begin garnishing wages or seize tax payments for the current tax year ending in April 2027.

One source told the Sun that they expect many calls to government agencies “from borrowers saying: ‘What’s going on? How do I make sure this won’t happen again?’”

“It would be politically insane to do this before the midterms — but 2027 probably makes a little more sense to give Treasury time to get contracts [with debt collectors] signed, up and running,” they said.

Democratic strategist Michelle Kinney called on Democratic candidates to “get LOUD” about the reported plan to shield the White House and the GOP from accountability.

“Announced after the midterms” so they won’t be held accountable and will try to blame democrats. Democrats need to get LOUD. This is NUTS. https://t.co/t2VqB1KSaX

Michael Pierce, executive director of Protect Borrowers, told the Sun that if the administration follows through with the plan — as families struggle with rising gas and grocery prices resulting from Trump’s tariff policy and illegal war on Iran — “what comes next will be a catastrophe for families across the country,” who will have “even less money to put food on the table or make rent.”

“Restarting debt collection the moment any political accountability has passed just shows how little interest Trump has in helping working families stay afloat,” Pierce told the Sun.

On social media, Pierce noted that despite its threats against borrowers, the administration and any debt collectors it contracts with must ensure the defaulted debts are valid for collection.

Along with the Project on Predatory Student Lending and the Debt Collection Lab at Princeton University, Protect Borrowers wrote to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week, noting the “mounting evidence that the U.S. Department of Education may not have the data it needs to certify these debts for collection in the first place.”

The student loan books are cooked. Everyone knows it. We (@BorrowerJustice @EdDebtJustice @Princeton_DCL) wrote @SecScottBessent last week, raising serious legal issues. Any collector that follows the law must be raising them to @USTreasury, too.https://t.co/tt009mfYKp pic.twitter.com/5q2jpiPubI

“Certifying that a debt is accurate requires having accurate data on the debt in the first place,” they wrote. “According to industry experts, the default database is rife with incomplete or inaccurate records. Former federal officials described ongoing ‘material deficiencies’ in [the Debt Management and Collections System], such as dummy Social Security numbers, inaccurate loan balances, [and] missing communication records… Collecting on uncollectable debt will illegally siphon money from the most vulnerable borrowers who can afford it the least.”

Marshall Steinbaum, an associate economics professor at the University of Utah, emphasized that defaulted student loan borrowers are “overwhelmingly people whose debts would have been erased” by the student debt cancellation plan by the Biden administration, which was blocked after Republican states and other plaintiffs challenged it in court.

“Congratulations to everyone who blocked that,” said Steinbaum, “on their glorious policy success.”

author: Dan Canon
title: SCOTUS Is Undermining the Rules That Have Kept US Elections Peaceful for Decades
content:
The Roberts Court has dismantled guardrails preventing a president from turning state agencies against political rivals.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Courts can create violence simply by putting words on paper. For anyone who has examined any legal system, this should not be a controversial proposition. Some observers argue that the very purpose of written judgments is to justify acts of violence. But one need not go that far to see the immediate effects: A judicial opinion can cause a death, ignite a civil war, legitimize a coup, or even wipe out an entire culture.

If we accept that basic truth, it should not surprise us that jurisprudence can also fuel election-related violence. In U.S. history, the most salient example is United States v. Cruikshank, an all-but-forgotten Reconstruction-era ruling. In Cruikshank, the Supreme Court held that the federal government could not prosecute the broad-daylight massacre of dozens of Black Republicans in 1873, most of whom were defending political offices duly won by their candidates. After two grueling trials and an unlikely guilty verdict by a Louisiana jury, the Court threw out the convictions.

The immediate consequences at southern polls were shocking, if not surprising. Legal scholar James Gray Pope explains that the ruling “opened the floodgates” for white supremacist violence. Over the next three months, southern whites “ousted Republican officials from twelve Louisiana parishes [and] launched a campaign of terrorist assaults on Republican-controlled towns and cities across the South[.]” The strategy worked: Democrats reclaimed Mississippi and Alabama within two years, despite their sizeable Black electorates.

What harm might result from the opinions of today’s Court, an institution unmistakably captured by a power-hungry executive? In a nation of this size, facing democratic decay this severe, there is no such thing as a safe prediction. But if you’re the gambling type, the smart money is on a spectacularly violent future for U.S. elections, if not in the upcoming midterms, then likely by 2028.

Decades of global research have mapped the root causes of election violence. Where contests are winner-take-all, the stakes escalate. Bloodshed is also more common where governing bodies are weak, districts are gerrymandered to exclude voters, or societies carry deep ethnic divisions. Corruption is another critical barometer. A meta-analysis of 65 studies found that the only consistent institutional predictor of election violence is executive constraint: that is, the degree to which a head of state is checked by independent institutions. The more an executive is reined in, the less likely elections are to turn violent. Conversely, when a leader builds informal networks of patronage and punishment, politics ceases to be a contest of ideas and collapses into a fight for survival.

Once we have a grasp on what causes election violence, we can see the pins set up by this Supreme Court, and how those pins are likely to fall in the next few cycles.

The Roberts Court has a long record of hostility toward voting rights, especially the Voting Rights Act. The project Roberts began in 2013 with Shelby County v. Holder, which gutted the VRA’s preclearance formula, reached its culmination in Louisiana v. Callais, dismantling what remained of the law’s practical effects. This means that southern states, which have tried to suppress Black votes for more than 150 years, will be able to restrict access to polls without meaningful federal oversight. According to Justice Kagan’s dissent, Callais will likely result in “the largest reduction in minority representation since the era following Reconstruction.”

Compounding this exclusion is the Court’s surrender to partisan cartels. In Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), the conservative majority declared partisan gerrymandering beyond judicial reach, locking courthouse doors to citizens living in districts with obviously rigged electoral maps. In states like Texas, gerrymandering insulates incumbents from accountability regardless of how the electorate votes. Worse, even if disenfranchised voters manage to challenge suppression, the Court may simply invoke the Purcell principle, another Roberts Court creation that prohibits judicial intervention close to an election. States are therefore effectively permitted to run unconstitutional elections, forcing citizens to vote under discriminatory rules while litigation drags on.

The terms “patrimonialism” and “clientelism” sound academic, but they describe a political arrangement as old as humanity: Those who display loyalty to the king receive wealth, status, or protection, while those who are insufficiently sycophantic are cut off. In such systems, inequality is the point; the law becomes a personal weapon to reward cronies and bludgeon enemies.

The Supreme Court is all too eager to indulge Trump’s obvious preference for this form of government. It now seems quaint to talk, as pundits did during the first Trump administration, of the Emoluments Clauses or the Hatch Act. While the Roberts Court has steadily chipped away at anti-corruption provisions, legalizing post-hoc kickbacks and naked gratuities, its most aggressive move toward patrimonialism came this year in Trump v. Slaughter. Overturning nearly a century of precedent, the Court erased protections that prevented presidents from firing independent agency heads on a whim. By weakening the nonpartisan civil service, the Court granted Trump the power to staff the federal apparatus with personal loyalty enforcers.

Finally, the Court is busily decimating any and all meaningful checks on the Trump presidency, even outside the hiring and firing of federal employees. In the aptly named Trump v. United States, the conservative majority granted the president broad immunity for “official acts,” placing the executive beyond the reach of the criminal law and barring prosecutors from using internal communications as evidence. By pairing civil-service purges in Slaughter with near-total immunity, the Court has stripped away the guardrails preventing a president from turning state agencies, including the Department of Justice and the military, against political rivals. The once-fringe theory of the “unitary executive” is now nearly realized in full.

Across developing nations, the basic story remains consistent: patrimonialism and the collapse of executive constraints can transform elections into extremely high-stakes survival contests, where the political life of a demagogue is explicitly tied to the lives of his supporters. Former Ivorian President Laurent Gbagbo captured the central message of neo-patrimonial rule on the eve of a disputed election that cost 3,000 lives: “If I fall, you do too.” In Nigeria, where elections determine who controls the state treasury, contests became what President Olusegun Obasanjo explicitly called a “do or die situation.” Hired militias carried cutlasses and guns to publicly terrorize polling stations. India, too, features a first-past-the-post system with weak institutional checks, and has experienced decades of election-related violence as a result, a dynamic that political scientist Rachel Kleinfeld warns is “most like what the United States is experiencing.” Worldwide, between 1989 and 2017 alone, over 24,000 people were killed in election-related events. Many of these deaths may be directly attributed this brand of zero-sum desperation.

Thanks in no small part to the Roberts Court, virtually every risk factor in available global examples now has a U.S. analogue: winner-take-all contests, excluded voting blocs, and an unrestrained executive empowered by the courts to purge bureaucracy and mobilize foot soldiers for an existential clash at the ballot box. Perhaps the United States is different enough that these warning signs will result in nothing worse than a few scuffles. But it is dangerously naive to assume we are immune from the kind of explosive violence documented elsewhere.

Callais, Slaughter, Trump v. United States, and other Roberts Court decisions on voting rights and executive power are not technical footnotes; they are structural shifts. At their best, independent courts channel even the most heated political grievances into nonviolent resolutions. If an apex court abdicates that role by disenfranchising voters, institutionalizing clientelism, and shielding executive lawlessness, it removes the pressure valves that keep democratic competition peaceful. That is exactly what the Roberts Court has done over the last 20 years, and its work now is in danger of coming to a head. If unprecedented violence does not attend the next few U.S. elections, it will be in spite of this Supreme Court, not because of it.

author: Saima Desai
title: Beating burnout in social movements requires strategy
content:
This article 

Beating burnout in social movements requires strategy

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







I recently showed up to a protest for the first time in months, looked around, and thought: “Who the hell 

are

 all these people?” 




Friends I could once rely on running into at protests when I was younger were missing. 




The fact that I hadn’t been to a protest in months was unusual. I’d had a hard season of exhaustion and cynicism, and I felt I was falling out of the loop. In the last few years, I turned 30 and moved back to my hometown, and the once-intense focus on social movements that I had in my 20s was now jostling for attention with work and family. 




The absence of my comrades at that protest seemed to signal that others, too, had burned or faded out of organizing.




It’s a trend that Chris Dixon describes in his new book, which is about sticking around for the long haul in the fight for a better world: “In radical activist scenes especially,” he writes, “people tend to age out by their 30s, if not before.” 




When the manuscript of Dixon’s book came my way, it spoke to my fear of burning or fading out of the movements that have given my life meaning and momentum. (I sit on the editorial collective of Between The Lines Books, and helped select the book for publication; it was released in September 2026.) 




After a few recent boom-and-bust cycles of uprisings — 2020’s Black liberation uprising, the Palestine solidarity protests that kicked off in 2023 — it’s a timely and thoughtful book about building movements with care and commitment.













Dixon (who unfortunately shares a name with a far more famous American crypto bro) is an anti-authoritarian activist and a scholar of social movements. “For the Long Haul: How to Stay in the Fight for a Better World” 

is the latest effort in his lifelong project to understand how social movements are built and sustained.




Dixon grew up in Alaska, and the book opens by describing his decades-long friendship with Ruth Sheridan, an anarchist who was in her 70s when she first came to talk to his eighth grade labor history class. That early curiosity — about how left-wing social movements are built and sustained and the unsung activists who make it happen — showed up in his 2014 book “Another Politics: Talking Across Today’s Transformative Movements,” in which he shared lessons from almost a decade spent interviewing organizers across the U.S. and Canada. 




Now, Dixon has reached back into this same conversational archive to write “For the Long Haul.” 




We meet Bill Stivers, an elder communist Dixon befriended as a teen; Rachel Herzing, the co-founder of prison abolitionist group Critical Resistance; the political prisoner David Gilbert with whom he exchanged letters from jail, and many more. 




These lifelong leftists share their observations about what leads to burnout, the many-headed monster that has long stalked social movements. During this time of totalizing neoliberalism and weakened movement infrastructure, it’s grown especially powerful. These movement veterans counsel us to be patient, open-minded and to “practice being nobody special.” 




Dixon tells the story of Stivers who, at the age of 76, travelled from Anchorage, Alaska to the state of Chiapas in southern Mexico to attend the Zapatistas’ Intercontinental Encounter for Humanity and Against Neoliberalism. It was just a couple years after the militant group’s armed uprising and a young Dixon, more swayed by a European left tradition at that time, looked on with skepticism. But Stivers ended up having the more clear-eyed assessment of this new approach to anti-capitalist struggle. Stivers had cultivated the long view, which helped him avoid cynicism and dogmatism, and encouraged him to keep learning and stay open to new developments.  










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










What I found most helpful about the book was Dixon’s formulation of burnout: he sees it not just as a type of overwork or exhaustion, but as a feeling of defeat that becomes more common because of a lack of strategy. Dixon introduces this idea by sharing a conversation he had with Kim Marks, a direct-action environmentalist and Indigenous solidarity organizer in Oregon: “So much of burnout is about not being effective,” she said, “and so much ineffectiveness comes from not having a plan.” 




Dixon traces the ways that people often burn out of activist groups back to this underlying lack of strategy. When a group promises sweeping change but never decides how to take the first step; when a group gets mired in discussions about internal structure or politics and stops taking outward action; when a few veteran members shoulder a huge amount of work while new ones struggle to find meaningful ways to pitch in; when a group is hastily cobbled together to address a crisis then falls apart just as quickly after an unsuccessful campaign — all of these are instances in which a lack of strategy leaves people feeling defeated, ineffective and worn-out. 




A good plan can pull groups out of these exhausting spirals. This involves mapping the current political landscape, articulating our goals, making agreements about what to do and how to support each other in doing it, and then evaluating our success and learning from our mistakes.  




Dixon writes about the importance of imbuing this strategy-setting with care and intentionality, to “help people to talk frankly about workload, make reasonable estimates of what they can do, and look out for one another’s well-being.”




Previous Coverage

 

Why bravery and heartbreak are essential to organizing




You can find many of these same encouragements — for rest, care and intentionality — in the pages of any self-help book. But the goal of capitalist self-help literature is to create an individual who is independent, sane and productive enough to keep cranking the handle of profit-making machines. 




Dixon’s help is different: it’s not for the individual, but for the collective. At the end of the day, “sustained involvement in movements is fundamentally a collective activity, not an individual one,” he writes. No amount of advice given to or followed by the individual can stop the pattern of burnout and disengagement that’s become endemic in leftist spaces. 




As a result, Dixon focuses on collective care rather than self-care. This can look like preparing food for the picket line, planning for childcare and legal support at the direct action, or tending to hurt feelings after the meeting. He calls care work “a crucial — and too often overlooked — foundation for the long haul.”




For Dixon, care is not just a way to make organizing more pleasant for the people doing it, or a moral imperative if the left wants to keep claiming the high ground. Instead, he sees care as a strategic imperative. When we make our political commitments with care in mind, Dixon writes, it forces us to ask ourselves and each other if what we’re committing to is reasonable and tactical. And when it is, we become more likely to stick around for the long run, and also more likely to win.




Not one of Dixon’s ideas stands without a quote from an organizer, an example from a movement or a reference to a movement scholar’s work. One of the book’s main contributions is its vast bibliography — a full third of the pages are suggested reading and endnotes. 




Dixon’s form of activist research is highly attentive to insights that are gleaned from a person’s own experiences. Like this observation by anti-authoritarian activist Helen Hudson, who draws on decades of organizing with prisoners to form her analysis of how the state uses prison to weaken movements: “Prison isolates the prisoners from support,” she told Dixon, “but also deprives younger generations of radicals from the experience of revolutionaries who have much to teach us.”  
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













Dixon encourages younger readers like me to find these people in our own lives — older activists like Stivers and Sheridan who show us that it is possible and lovely to live an ordinary life of unflagging commitment to the left. 




This is not an organizing manual (though Dixon does recommend a few of those in his suggested readings). Instead, what he gives us is a deep study of left-wing dynamics and some broad strokes toward sustainability. The people likely to get the most from this book are those of us who have already gone through many cycles of boom-and-bust social movement activity, and who are looking for fuel that burns longer and cleaner. 




And it’s by paying attention to Dixon’s rigorous practices of listening and sharing that readers will get the most out of this book — leaving not just with a handful of advice, but with an initiation into a practice.

Beating burnout in social movements requires strategy

Waging Nonviolence

.

title: Lycée Paul Éluard : une vendetta de la police nationale contre les jeunes ? Rassemblement de soutien
content:
Rendez-vous mardi 20 octobre à 11h devant le commissariat de Saint-Denis avenue Jean Moulin.




 

 

 

 




Communiqué des personnels mobilisés du lycée Paul Éluard




Depuis dimanche soir, trois lycéen-nes de Paul Éluard à Saint-Denis ont été arrêté-es dans des conditions violentes et indignes, et un autre a été frappé :




 Deux élèves du lycée, avec d'autres jeunes, ont subi une interpellation violente. Une voiture de police a foncé sur elles et eux à toute allure, ils et elles ont été plaqué-es au sol. Ils et elles sont en garde à vue depuis dimanche soir.

 Un autre élève a été suivi par la police lundi et arrêté. Il s'agit du jeune homme que des officiers de la 

BAC

 voulaient arrêter au lycée jeudi 15 octobre, ce à quoi les personnels se sont opposés. La police avait alors indiqué que ce jeune homme serait convoqué. Il n'en a rien été.

 Enfin, un élève, déjà mis en garde à vue la semaine passée, a été frappé par un policier alors qu'il rentrait chez lui. Il a dû être soigné à l'hôpital avant de rentrer chez lui.




Parallèlement, un membre du personnel du lycée, qui se promenait dans les rues de Saint-Denis, a subi des jets de gaz lacrymogène venant d'une voiture de police, dont les passagers l'ont dévisagé en ricanant.




Ces violences sont cohérentes avec les recommandations du ministre Laurent Nunez, qui a appelé les forces de l'ordre à ne faire preuve d'aucune retenue. Elles témoignent aussi d'un sentiment d'impunité de la police, encore plus marqué que d'habitude. Elles semblent enfin relever d'une vendetta personnelle du commissariat de Saint-Denis, ciblant certains élèves déjà identifiés, mais plus généralement les lycéen-nes de la ville.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Police Violence Increases as 800k Protesters Take to the Streets in France
content:
French leaders condemned the uprising, while the left highlighted escalating police brutality against young protesters.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

On Saturday, France saw its largest nationwide protests in years, as popular outrage over the rising cost of living converged with a month-long student movement against the country’s neglected public education system.

Nearly 800,000 people took to the streets in over 140 cities across France on Saturday, according to France’s major labor union, the CGT. The protests were made up of high school and university students who have blockaded their schools over the past month, demanding better education conditions, as well as labor unions, who mobilized workers in protest of public service cuts, and remnants of the 2018 “Yellow Vests” movement.

Mass protests during the day transformed into riots as evening fell, with multiple city halls and offices set ablaze or otherwise damaged. Police arrested some 2,400 protesters.

French leaders have placed blame on the protesters and the far left, including on the far left political party La France Insoumise (LFI), or France Unbowed. In a televised address Sunday, French President Emmanuel Macron said that the riots were caused by “groups from the far left, joined by a number of delinquents and criminals,” and spoke of police who were injured.

Macron attempted to differentiate between protesters with “legitimate grievances” and those who rioted, while stating that the cost-of-living crisis began because of the war in Iran and its effect on the cost of fuel — for which, he added, France is blameless, as it has not taken part in this war.

But while fuel prices have soared due to the U.S. and Israel’s war on Iran, there are much deeper grievances within France. The underlying causes of the unrest include racism and Islamophobia within France, as well as a decade of austerity policies under Macron alongside the rise of the far-right in the context of an upcoming election.

Marine Le Pen, head of the far-right National Rally party, also blamed “the extreme left” for the protests and riots, and specifically the leader of LFI, Jean-Luc Mélenchon. For his part, U.S. President Donald Trump once again blamed immigration, posting on his social media network Truth Social that France needs to “Close [its] Borders and take control.”

After state officials held crisis meetings on Monday, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced that cities across France would impose partial curfews beginning on Monday night.

But while state media and right-wing leaders blamed the left, it is the police that have undertaken massive violence against protestors over the past month, including on Saturday.

In Paris on Saturday, police used tear gas and stun grenades against protesters even before the start of the demonstrations. John Mullen, an activist living in Paris, wrote that police “beat and injured thousands of protestors” as well as journalists and bystanders, and argued that police violence increased popular anger and led protesters to riot.

Manel ben Boubaker, a French teacher who joined the demonstrations in Paris, explained to Truthout that a “peaceful student-led march” faced “intense tear gas.” She described how police “effectively prevented [a protest] from taking place in and around Place de la République: people were blocked from entering, trapped inside, forced to retreat, and repeatedly tear-gassed in the surrounding streets. The violence was not confined to isolated clashes. It shaped people’s ability to gather, move through the square, and demonstrate at all.”

Left-wing LFI leader Mélenchon also blamed the police for inciting violence. Writing on X, he said that protesters were “calm and joyful everywhere when the police aren’t around.”

Last week, French lawyers and rights groups accused police of inflicting “war-like injuries” on youth protesters over the course of the past few weeks of student movement protests. On October 5, a 15-year-old had his hand blown off by a police stun grenade outside of a school protest, and during Saturday’s protests, a 17-year-old permanently lost vision in one eye after police fired a tear gas canister that hit her in the face.

Rayyan Seriket, a member of the French Student Union Federation, said in an interview on Democracy Now! Monday that Macron is blaming protesters for violence while excusing the violence of the police, whereas police violence is “the main violence, the real violence taking place in France” — underscoring that it is violence against children in particular.

During Saturday’s protests, demonstrators draped a giant yellow vest over the Statue of Marianne on the Monument a la Republique in Paris — on the vest was written “The police mutilate high school students” in French.

Students have also complained that the media has focused on acts of violence against property rather than on their demands. In an interview earlier last week, two unidentified young activists spoke of their demands and not being heard:

When you see 98 percent of news channels’ airtime is devoted to burning rubbish bins and only 2 percent to our demands, of course it makes us angry,” one student said. “We’re not happy, we’re not being listened to, we’re not being heard. And all the funding we’re demanding for schools, for our rights, and so on, they’re spending on repression instead. If they had listened to us from the beginning, maybe this would have already been resolved.

A second student reiterated the reasons for the continued youth mobilization. “We’re short of teachers, classrooms, chairs, social workers … Today, we can clearly see that young people’s mental health is deteriorating rapidly. We’re lacking all these things. This has created what you might call a widespread sense of frustration with the state, and that’s why so many of us are out protesting,” he said.

“I don’t think the movement will lose momentum. We’ll stay mobilized until the very end, until our demands are heard,” the young activist concluded.

More protests have been called for next Saturday, October 24, and unions have called for mass strikes on November 5.

France’s protest movement has caused waves across Europe, with similar youth-led protests emerging in Albania, Belgium, Italy, and beyond, also against austerity measures, neglect of public education, and the growth of far-right parties.
