author: By L. Cam Anderson, Contributor
title: How The Proud Boys Lost Their Name
content:
West Palm Beach, FL – On Sept. 26, the film “American Martyrs” premiered at the Kravis Center’s Cohen Pavilion in West Palm Beach, Florida. 




The subject of the film, presented by the far-right media outlet Gateway Pundit, was the Proud Boys – specifically the “seditious five,” whom a federal jury found guilty of seditious conspiracy to stop the presidential transfer of power for their role in the Jan. 6, 2021 storming of the U.S. Capitol.







The official poster for the film, promoted by Enrique Tarrio and Gateway Pundit on X ahead of its premiere. Note that Zachary Rehl, first on the left in the lineup, is AI-generated.







The five Proud Boys presenting the film were chairman Henry “Enrique” Tarrio, Ethan Nordean, Joe Biggs, Zachary Rehl and Dominic Pezzola. In reality, the actual fifth member of the “seditious five” is Jeremy Bertino, not Pezzola, who pleaded guilty and testified against the others during their trial. 




In August 2025, Bertino appeared on an episode of Tarrio’s Substack podcast titled “Kiss of Judas,” where the “government star witness” allowed the permanently sunglasses-clad chairman to humiliate him for the twelve people who liked the post. Despite this entreaty to re-enter the flock, Bertino did not make the cut as an “American martyr.”




Besides Tarrio, who received a full pardon, the others had the sentences commuted by executive order during President Donald Trump’s first day back in office on Jan. 20, 2025. 




The film premiere, held less than four miles from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago Club, was graced by numerous right-wing characters, including leading “Stop the Steal” figure and former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani, 

QAnon digital warrior

 and former U.S. Army general Michael Flynn and convicted fraudster George Santos.




Led by right-wing media figure Lara Logan, the event opened at 7 p.m. with an open bar that overlapped with a 10-minute window set aside for “prayer, national anthem and pledge.”




After the 80-minute film concluded, the Gateway Pundit presented Tarrio with a Gateway Pundit-branded award created specifically for the occasion recognizing him “as an American Martyr and Hero.”




“It’s not an Emmy,” Tarrio wrote on X two days later. “But it’s so much better.”







[Source: Enrique Tarrio on X]







Despite the obvious connections to the Proud Boys organization, the premiere lacked any of the recognizable branding belonging to what it depicted as a persecuted “drinking fraternity.”




Even on Tarrio’s person, the golden cock and abbreviated name have given way to the branding for his streaming outfit, “War Boys,” which has gained a whopping 700 followers on Rumble since the channel was created in April last year.




And on Tarrio’s merch website – where the Afro-Cuban now in his 40s markets just about any idea as apparel, including a t-shirt reading “Enrique Tarrio Eats Cream Pies” with an AI illustration of Tarrio licking an over-sized cream pie – reveals a distinct absence of Proud Boys related merchandise.







[Source: Enrique Tarrio on X]







Tarrio’s ability to capitalize on Proud Boys merchandising, which once characterized his merch store, hit a setback last year when a D.C. Superior Court judge awarded the brand to a historically-Black church following a years-long legal battle set in the wake of the 2020 Presidential election.




At the beginning of 2025, the Metropolitan African Methodist Episcopal (MAME) church was the only place one could purchase official Proud Boys merchandise, re-branded to signify Black pride, with proceeds going toward the church’s community justice fund.




In April 2025, the church’s hold on the brand was tested on the Hudson Valley Proud Boys, who were sued in the Southern District Court of New York for their continued usage of the Proud Boys branding and merchandising.




The court reached a default judgment against the Hudson Valley Proud Boys, a chapter associated with Tarrio, earlier this year on April 8, awarding MAME $75,000 for trademark infringement and nearly $200,000 in attorney’s fees.




The judgment against the Hudson Valley Proud Boys is only a small part of the church’s pursuit to be fully compensated in the amount awarded by the court, which continues to be a major struggle to this day and sees all related parties continue to be wrapped up in the ongoing court battle.







On the night of Dec. 12, 2020, the streets of Washington were thronged with black shirts and red caps.




Beneath the hazy yellow glow of street lights, the death rattle of the defeated president, who lost his reelection campaign the previous month and was doing everything he could to cling to power, took the form of hundreds of Proud Boys and others, shouting and pushing against lines of armored riot police, looking to fight anything they could vaguely describe as “Antifa.”




That the Proud Boys were violently swarming the capital city’s streets was not completely random. 




“Proud Boys, stand back and stand by,” Trump said during a notorious moment in the first debate of the election on Sept. 29 of that year, in response to a prompt from then-presidential candidate Joe Biden to condemn the Proud Boys, a neo-fascist organization that sprouted in the shade of Trump’s personality cult.




The cryptic statement gained the attention of the national media, occupying a prominent place through the rest of the election.




The four words 

were quickly adopted into Proud Boys marketing and merchandise

, and the cryptic response “exponentially” increased the group’s membership, 

according to Bertino in his testimony before the J6 committee in April 2022.




Their relevance at the debate followed the mass popular uprising across the country, and globe, in response to the Minneapolis Police Department’s murder of George Floyd on May 25, 2020. The Proud Boys, along with other far-right groups, responded to these protests by organizing counter demonstrations that often resulted in street fights, 

advocating in advance on social media for members to carry weapons

.




The looming threat of violence is a core component of the Proud Boys. One month into Trump’s first term in 2017, the Proud Boys functioned as street brawlers in Berkeley, California, during the dramatic culmination of far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopolis’ “Danger Faggot Tour.”




It was March 4, 2017, in Berkeley where Kyle “Based Stickman” Chapman was recorded attacking anti-fascist protesters with a stick and was subsequently brought into the Proud Boys by founder Gavin McInnes to form the group’s paramilitary arm, “The Fraternal Order of the Alt Knights.”




From 2017, to Jan. 6, 2021, the Proud Boys engaged in numerous street battles against left-wing protesters, with some of the most violent appearances occurring during the summer of 2020 following the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in June of that year.




But it didn’t end with fights at Seattle’s Capitol Hill Autonomous Zone. The group maintained a presence throughout the year and took a more visible roll in the lead-up to and the aftermath of the 2020 presidential election. One of the group’s largest showings after the Nov. 14 “Million MAGA March” in Washington, D.C., during that short period before Congress would convene to certify the vote on Jan. 6, 2021, was on Dec. 12, which is when things really began to unravel for the belligerent “drinking fraternity.”




Looking for an enemy to physically destroy that balmy winter night in the nation’s capital, several mostly-masked Proud Boys returned to the writhing mass of Fred Perry polo shirts at the intersection of 11th Street NW and E Street NW – only several blocks from the White House – carrying a massive banner reading “#BlackLivesMatter.”




This banner, stolen from the nearby Asbury United Methodist Church, the city’s oldest historically Black church, would serve as a totem for their abuse.




After posing for pictures with the captive banner, they laid it out in the middle of the road, doused it in lighter fluid and lit it on fire.







The Asbury United Methodist Church’s “#BLACKLIVESMATTER” banner, lit on fire in the middle of the street. [Source: still from News2Share video]







“Fuck Antifa!” members of the neo-fascist paramilitary organization began chanting as a plume of black smoke engulfed the crowd gathered around the spectacle. Many raised their hands in the “OK” gesture, a dog whistle invoking white power.




A senior pastor of the church 

reacted in a statement the next day

, comparing the act to a Klan-style cross burning.




Shortly afterwards, another crew of Proud Boys approached the mass carrying another Black Lives Matter banner, this time in a manner reminiscent of a parade. The banner was stolen from the Metropolitan African Methodist Episcopal Church more than 20 minutes away by foot.







A group of Proud Boys returns with the Metropolitan African Methodist Episcopal Church’s Black Lives Matter banner. [Source: still from News2Share video]







One Proud Boy broke from the crowd to charge them, assuming they were counter-protesters, until another stopped him and presumably explained the odd juxtaposition to him.




“Oh you motherfuckers,” one said in a thick drawl. “We thought we’d gotten something to steal.”




This specific banner was paraded around and stomped on earlier in the night, after several Proud Boys scaled the church’s fences and cut the zip ties securing it in place.




This banner, like the last, was also destroyed, 

according to local news reports

.




The night ended with more than three dozen arrests, multiple stabbings and four churches vandalized. The banner burning was charged by police as a hate crime, and Proud Boys leader Enrique Tarrio took responsibility for the incident in 

an interview with the Washington Post

 roughly one week later.




Two days before the January 6, 2021 attempted insurrection, MAME Church sued Tarrio and Proud Boys International, the parent company of the violent “drinking fraternity.” Tarrio was banned from the city, explaining his ultimate absence from the storming of the Capitol building, where members of his organization played an out-sized role.




Less than one month later, Proud Boys International manager Jason Lee Van Dyke – 

now an instrumental part of the white supremacist outfit Patriot Front

 – moved to terminate Tarrio’s license to use the Proud Boys trademark, citing the Dec. 12 incident as the motivating reason. In a related move, Van Dyke also moved to disband Proud Boys International and to surrender the registration for the Proud Boys trademark.




On June 30, 2023, the Superior Court of the District of Columbia ruled in favor of MAME, granting the church more than $1 million against the Proud Boys, in addition to interest and nearly $2 million in attorney fees.




To get this money, the church filed another action on July 2, 2024, in pursuit of the Proud Boys’ most valuable property: the brand itself. On Feb. 3, 2025, the court reached a default judgment – a familiar pattern later echoed by the Hudson Valley Proud Boys – ordering all of Proud Boys International’s “interests in the trademark ‘Proud Boys’ […] transferred to” MAME, according to court documents.







The Proud Boys brand was not nearly enough to compensate the church, and, since the ruling, Tarrio and his group have paid approximately $7,800 of the more than $3 million owed to the church, according to court documents.




Because of this, the case remains open in the D.C. Superior Court system as the church continues to pursue any money from the defendants that could fulfill their obligation. This includes obtaining a default judgment against alternative fund raising platform GiveSendGo in 2025 and having the D.C. Superior Court place a lien on any funds paid to Tarrio by the U.S. Department of Justice’s Anti-Weaponization Fund or its successor or replacement programs earlier this year.




The Anti-Weaponization Fund was a proposed billion-dollar payout from the federal government to J6ers who Trump pardoned or had their sentences commuted at the beginning of 2025.




“Faced with the Defendants’ unwillingness to engage productively in post-judgment discovery, the Church has been forced to find creative workarounds,” the church wrote in a motion to subpoena third parties in May this year. “The Church must seek discovery from these third parties because the Defendants have either refused to respond to the Church’s discovery altogether or have produced incomplete records that can be supplemented with information from the third party.”




On Sept. 11, 2025, the court ordered Tarrio to turn over for review all Telegram chats with information related to advertising or fundraising activities. Tarrio refused to comply, and a similar request was made the following Oct. 10.




On Dec. 19, it evolved into an order that Tarrio turn over his electronic devices for forensic examination, and on Jan. 27, 2026, following further non-compliance, the court issued a bench warrant against him and found him in contempt of court.




On Sept. 28, the first weekday after the premiere of “American Martyrs”,” Tarrio filed his second motion to vacate the default judgment – the first filed in December 2022 – including the $3.2 million award to the church, accusing the court of “massive fraud” and “near-total denial of due process.”




A significant part of Tarrio’s ploy to escape his and the organization’s legal debts is the Justice Department’s April 21 

grand jury indictment of the Southern Poverty Law Center

, which charged the organization with 11 counts of wire fraud, false statements to a federally insured bank, and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering.




More specifically for Tarrio’s purposes, the indictment against the SPLC identifies several field sources, employed by the organization to infiltrate hate groups. For many in the far right, it was a quick leap from “the SPLC is funding infiltrators” to “the SPLC is directly funding and operating those hate groups.”




Tarrio’s motion relies on a theory that Jason Kessler, the primary face behind the 2017 Unite the Right rally, was one of the informants paid by the SPLC, an accusation Kessler denies.




“If [the informant] is indeed Mr. Kessler […] this means that a fundamental component of this Court’s multi-million-dollar judgment is 

based on manufactured fraud, paid-for by the SPLC

,” Tarrio’s motion reads.




Heidi Beirich, an expert on far-right extremism and the former SPLC executive who oversaw hate group monitoring, cited the Unite the Right rally in her testimony before the D.C. Superior Court against the Proud Boys to portray the “drinking fraternity” as a white supremacist hate group, according to the motion.




On Aug. 12, Beirich was criminally indicted in a superseding indictment against the SPLC on federal charges of financial misconduct in the Middle District of Alabama, a fact that is frequently mentioned in the motion in regards to Beirich.




“Of course an indictment contains allegations only,” the motion reads, relying almost entirely on indictments to build its case against the default judgment. Tarrio’s motion uses the indictment to impugn Beirich’s character and call into question the Proud Boys’ ‘hate group’ label, which played a part in the default ruling against the group.




Tarrio’s motion is undersigned by his newest attorney on the case, Roger Roots, who frequently runs for office in Montana on the Libertarian Party ticket. His website still seems to advertise excerpts from these campaigns, generalized for whatever office he plans on running for in any given year.




“ONE-QUARTER OF ADULT MALES ARE CONVICTED FELONS,” the website reads under a top issues section. “AS I WRITE THESE WORDS IT IS AN ACTUAL QUESTION AMONG POLICYMAKERS WHETHER THERE WILL SOON BE CONCENTRATION CAMPS FOR AMERICANS ON AMERICAN SOIL.”




Roots has also previously represented other Proud Boys, as well as anti-government militant Ammon Bundy and Oath Keepers founder Stewart Rhodes. In a separate case representing Dominic Pezzola – the first J6er to breach the Capitol building, using a stolen riot shield to smash open a window – Roots compared Pezzola’s actions to “desegregation demonstrators who performed sit-ins at Woolworth lunch counters in the 1960s.”




The next court date in the trial is set for Dec. 1 of this year.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Palestinian Youth Helped Save WaPo Journalist Attacked by Israeli Settlers
content:
Jasper Nathaniel recounts how the youth beat settlers back with stones, allowing him and others to rescue Heidi Levine.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Israeli settlers backed by IDF soldiers brutally assaulted Palestinian olive farmers in the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, on Friday. Witnesses say dozens of masked Israeli settlers armed with clubs, sticks, slingshots and guns hurled rocks at Palestinian farmers, set olive trees ablaze and drove people from their fields. Veteran Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, a 64-year-old American, was documenting the attack when settlers began beating her. She suffered stab wounds, a broken rib, four broken vertebrae and a severe hand injury. Levine was wearing a clearly marked press vest and a helmet at the time of the attack. According to the Israeli human rights group Yesh Din, Israeli settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank since September 27, which marked the start of this year’s olive harvest.

“It looked like they were killing her,” says independent American journalist Jasper Nathaniel, who witnessed the attack on Levine and helped intervene. “The Palestinian youth, the shabab, stepped up. They ran out ahead, and they started beating the settlers back by throwing stones at them, which is the only thing that allowed me to then run out front and grab Heidi.” As the journalists and Palestinians retreated into Abu Falah, “The Israeli military jeep that had been standing by the settlers who were attacking us then drives into the village itself, … and they start firing into crowds of Palestinian people.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.

In the occupied West Bank Friday, Israeli settlers brutally assaulted Palestinian olive farmers in the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah. Witnesses say dozens of masked Israeli settlers descended from a nearby hilltop, armed with clubs, sticks and slingshots. Some even had firearms. They hurled rocks at Palestinian farmers, set olive trees ablaze, drove people from their fields.

Veteran Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, an American, was on the scene documenting the attack when settlers surrounded and began beating her. At the time, she was wearing a vest, clearly marked “press” on the front and back, and a helmet. Video of the assault shows masked men surrounding Levine, knocking her to the ground, repeatedly beating and kicking her as she tried to protect herself. They reportedly stole her passport, camera, equipment, wallet and phone. She suffered a broken rib, four broken vertebrae, lacerations across her body and a severe injury to her hand. Levine was taken to a hospital in Ramallah, where she spoke to reporters.

HEIDI LEVINE: Today, I was brutally attacked by — I mean, we saw on the — in the distance, on the hilltop, I would say, at least 50 masked men. I was — I had a 100-to-500-millimeter lens that I could see them masked with slingshots. And when they came running down, I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and my helmet; otherwise, I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times. And then, after like 10 minutes, they, like, tried to get me to stand up, and then pushed me down again and continued to kick me. And I was trying to hold on to my cameras and my pouch, and I had my phone on a string on my neck, that they eventually just broke everything off of me and continued kicking me. And then, the next thing I noticed is I was getting evacuated by my Palestinian colleagues and medical service that rushed me in an ambulance first to the medical center in Abu Falah to check me and then to the hospital here.

AMY GOODMAN: From her hospital bed, Washington Post reporter Heidi Levine went on to say this.

HEIDI LEVINE: One message to their parents: I don’t know how a parent can raise such monsters, really, honestly. I have witnessed their behavior attacking families, and which we recently published a story. And I just am so ashamed that as a parent myself, I cannot understand how a parent can raise such individual monsters. They’re not even humans. And yes, they are Jewish terrorists, and they are giving everyone in the country a horrible reputation.

AMY GOODMAN: That’s Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine speaking from her hospital bed in Ramallah after being attacked by Israeli settlers.

On Friday the Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office issued a statement saying, in part, quote, “The facts surrounding the confrontation near Abu Falah, during which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was allegedly assaulted, remain unclear and are under investigation. … We will not allow disputed incidents to be exploited to demonize the hundreds of thousands of law-abiding Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria,” Netanyahu said.

In response, The Washington Post executive editor, Matt Murray, wrote on social media, quote, “To be clear: Some facts are neither in dispute nor unclear. Our photographer was clearly marked as Press. She was clearly beaten. These are not partisan or risible statements, but indisputable. We urge a thorough investigation and accountability,” said The Washington Post.

In a post on X on Saturday, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called the assault, quote, “despicable act of terror carried out by mass cowards,” unquote.

On Sunday, two days after the settler attack on Heidi Levine, President Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s October 27th election.

According to the Israeli human rights group Yesh Din, settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks against Palestinians since September 27th, which marked the start of this year’s olive harvest. Just a day after the settler attack on Heidi Levine, mass settlers attacked a group of European diplomats from France, Belgium and Poland who were visiting the West Bank village of Taybeh. Earlier today, Israeli police announced they had arrested 10 suspects as part of an investigation into violent incidents in the occupied West Bank.

We go now to the West Bank, where we’re joined by Jasper Nathaniel, who witnessed the attack on Heidi Levine and helped intervene. He’s a journalist covering Israel’s occupation of the West Bank on his Substack, Infinite Jaz. His new piece is headlined “The Palestinians Who Rescued Heidi Levine.” He’s joining us now from the occupied West Bank.

Thanks so much for being with us, Jasper. What happened?

JASPER NATHANIEL: Well, I mean, it’s olive harvest season here in Palestine, and, you know, the olive harvest is supposed to be a celebratory time of year. I mean, in years past, you know, whole families would come out together. There would be these beautiful picnic spreads, and, you know, it was a — there was no rush.

On Friday morning in Abu Falah, there were no women or children. There were just men rushing to pick the olives as fast as they possibly could, because just in the distance, on top of a hill, we were literally watching these settlers, who live in an outpost there that the Israeli government knows about. We watched them put on their masks, pick up their clubs and prepare for the assault. About an hour into the harvest, the settlers started charging down the hill.

And by the way, I should mention, this village coordinated with the IDF to do their olive harvest on that day, under the pretense that they would get protection from the settlers who are living on their land. The IDF didn’t show up.

So, the settlers start charging down the hill. They are all wearing masks. They’re holding, you know, these big clubs, and they’re swinging giant rocks that are — you know, can maim people when they hit them. As that’s happening, the farmers — many of the farmers start to retreat back into the village, but the shabab, or the Palestinian youth, sort of emerge and start protecting the village.

You have to keep in mind that this is not just about the olive harvest. Abu Falah, like in many communities around the West Bank, the olive fields there are the buffer zone between the violent settlers and the village itself. In other words, if the settlers were able to push past the olive groves, they would then be in the residential part of the community. They would be burning homes. They would be assaulting people. And they would basically try to, you know, expand their territorial control into the village.

So, these young Palestinians step up. All they have is rocks. They’re totally outgunned always. And they basically charge back at the settlers. And for maybe 10 minutes, the Palestinians were successfully defending their land with just stones. And then these settlers start setting the olive trees on fire. So, suddenly, there’s smoke in the air.

And then the thing that really changed things was when the IDF finally did show up. They came screaming in in a military jeep, and rather than do something to stop these masked settlers who were assaulting Palestinians on their own land, they start shooting tear gas at the Palestinians who I was with. As that’s happening — so, now there’s tear gas and smoke in the air — a truck full of settlers then speeds in. Settlers in the back, wearing all black, shooting M16s into the air like ISIS, start flying in. So, now there’s machine gun fire, too.

So, it was at that moment that everybody on the side of the village, as in the Palestinians and the journalists who were there and the activists who were there with them, just turn around and run. So, we’re all now just running back towards the village. And that is when Heidi was caught by settlers.

So, basically, once I got far enough out of the cloud of smoke and tear gas, I looked back, and I could just see a — within this massive mob of, like, probably 50-plus settlers, there is a smaller circle of maybe four or five just, like, savagely beating somebody on the ground with their clubs, with their feet, with their fists. I only discovered it was a journalist when somebody grabbed their blue press vest and pulled them up. And for a minute, I thought they were helping them, and then they held them up so that another settler could come and kick her in the stomach and knock her back down. So, we saw that this was happening, and me and a couple other journalists and a group of Palestinians, you know, knew that her life was in danger. I mean, it looked like they were killing her. In the video, you can see them, you know, raining down these blows with these clubs, that certainly could have killed her.

And so, there was really no way to get around the settlers, because they had fanned out across the fields, and they were continuing to throw rocks, and the army was tear-gassing us. And so, the only way to get to her was to go directly through it. And so, once again, the Palestinian youth, the shabab, stepped up. They ran out ahead, and they started beating the settlers back by throwing stones at them, which is what — the only thing that allowed me to then run out front and grab Heidi.

Once I got to her and I realized that it was not what I expected to see — it was, you know, a 64-year-old woman — she was in terrible shape. You know, she could not really stand on her own. She was completely dazed, clearly in agony. And I started trying to lead her out. As I’m doing that, the settlers make another charge towards us. And so, now I’m begging Heidi to run. She’s saying, “Let me die. Let me die.”

And then, just as I’m starting to think, “We might be overrun here. You know, these settlers could potentially catch us, and then I’ll be on the bottom of that pile,” once again, the Palestinian youth created a literal perimeter around us to protect us and to beat the settlers back with stones once again, just to defend two journalists who, you know, in many cases, they had met that day or hadn’t even met at all. And so, that’s when we were able to finally get Heidi to safety. The Palestinian Red Crescent came and met us, picked her up, got her into an ambulance and drove away.

After that, the Israeli military jeep that had been standing by the settlers who were attacking us then drives into the village itself. So, doesn’t arrest or do anything to stop the settlers who have just almost murdered a journalist; instead, they drive into the village, and they start firing into crowds of Palestinian people, hit a 54-year-old man in the thigh with an expanding bullet, shattered his femur. They later accused him of charging at the IDF with a sharp object. The New York Times has photographs that shows he was running away from them with a small plastic rake in his back pocket.

Then, you know, I got to the man who was writhing on the ground in pain. He was surrounded by soldiers who would not let paramedics near him. They were pointing their guns at the paramedics. They were throwing journalists out of the way. I got shoved by the butt of one of their guns. They were trying to demand that the man who they had just shot show him ID, and they said they would not allow him to get into the ambulance until he did. I don’t actually know if he ended up showing him his ID, but eventually the Palestinians were able to get him into an ambulance and drive away.

Sometime after that, I think there was more tear-gassing. The soldiers left. The settlers left. And then, I think, you know, the best — the only positive of this story is that the Palestinians then returned to their olive fields and resumed picking olives.

AMY GOODMAN: Jasper, we just have a minute, and I wanted to know about the U.S. response. You have the U.S. Ambassador to Israel Huckabee calling them “terrorists,” but you have President Trump, after Netanyahu denied the attack was clear — Washington Post refuted what he said — President Trump endorsed Netanyahu for his race for the prime ministership.

JASPER NATHANIEL: I mean, I think we should talk about Huckabee, because Huckabee actually is at a point now where he is willing to call these violent settlers terrorists. He did that six weeks ago when he visited Turmus Ayya, which is the town that I’m in right now. I’m sitting in Turmus Ayya. This is the largely American village where I filmed a brutal pogrom exactly a year ago, in which another old lady was clubbed by settlers. This town, Huckabee visited it because it’s full of American citizens who are being brutalized.

Six weeks ago, he stood in this village in somebody’s home and told the people there that they deserve to live with safety and peace and dignity, and that they were going to crack down on the terrorists that were killing them. This morning, Amy, a couple hours ago, settlers came in from the outpost, burned a home and cracked an American citizen’s skull open. So, that is how much Huckabee’s words count for. In this very town six weeks ago, he promised that they would be kept safe and there’d be accountability. Now he is nowhere to be found. His words are completely empty. People here are once again, you know, being beaten to within inches of their lives. Their homes are being destroyed. And, you know, it’s just — it’s business as usual on the West Bank, which is just, you know, relentless brutalization by the state of Israel, frankly.

AMY GOODMAN: And who’s the American citizen?

JASPER NATHANIEL: His name is Mohammed Sakat, and I know that there are pictures of the wound. It is — I mean, it’s really, really gruesome. His head is split wide open. And by the way, the day before Heidi was attacked, an American citizen in a town called Burqa was also beaten by settlers, almost killed. He has gigantic, deep gashes in his head. His skull was broken. That’s another American citizen, Haitham Taysir.

So, you know, listen, like, the American citizens here, their lives are not worth more than Palestinians, of course. But the fact that, you know, even when American citizens are brutalized, nothing is done — maybe some empty words, but nothing is actually done — I mean, it tells you all you need to know about how seriously the state of Israel is taking their problem of state-backed settler terrorism.

AMY GOODMAN: Jasper Nathaniel, we thank you so much for being with us, journalist covering Israel’s occupation of the West Bank. We’ll link to your piece, Infinite Jaz on Substack, “The Palestinians Who Rescued Heidi Levine,” speaking to us from the occupied West Bank.

Coming up, we look at the assassination of Juan Francisco Solórzano Foppa, a leading former anti-corruption prosecutor in Guatemala. I speak with his mother. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: “Nunca Mas,” “Never Again,” by La Santa Cecilia in our Democracy Now! studio.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

title: Election Officials Fear Trump Has Compromised Cybersecurity Agency
content:
Critics say the administration has undermined an agency key to protecting election infrastructure ahead of the midterms.

Critics say the administration has undermined an agency key to protecting election infrastructure ahead of the midterms.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it.

The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request.

The proposition was shocking to CISA’s career staffers, according to one of the former officials. CISA typically worked to thwart hackers. Moreover, the agency had been directed not to alert the voting machine company if it uncovered flaws, contrary to its standard practices. The request made the CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference.

“My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any [election] results they don’t like,” one of the former officials said. “This goes against everything CISA represents.”

The CISA employees repeatedly told the political appointees that their request was impossible, in part because the agents capable of pulling off such an operation had just been laid off by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative. The appointees eventually stopped pressing CISA.

Though not acted on, the request shows how the Trump administration has tried to use the agency for its own ends while draining it of resources for one of its critical missions: protecting the nation’s voting systems.

In Trump’s second term, his administration has laid off or pushed out more than 1,000 CISA employees, shrinking the agency by about one-third. The president’s 2027 budget proposal would reduce funding for the agency by another $700 million, which could necessitate 900 additional layoffs.

In response, Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation into CISA’s ability to do its job and demanded answers as to why federal funds are not being used to support election security as directed by Congress.

Since Trump signed the CISA Act in 2018, the agency has worked with state authorities and voting machine vendors to help protect election infrastructure from cyberattacks. During Trump’s second term, though, CISA has abandoned much of this work. Several state election authorities said the agency provided them no assistance — and no explanation for its absence — during the most critical planning stages for the upcoming midterms.

“There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as a consultant for CISA. In 2025 and through mid-September 2026 — when the bulk of preparations for the election typically would have been completed — “they were nonexistent. Literally nonexistent.”

While Trump has repeatedly warned that America’s elections are vulnerable to hacking, in some cases repeating disproven claims, experts said his administration is undermining the federal government’s role in helping secure them.

Though CISA re-emerged in September with a last-minute security plan for the election, some state officials told ProPublica they fear that what is left of the agency has been compromised by a conspiracy-obsessed presidential administration. In recent months, in reviving debunked theories about the 2020 election, the Trump administration has declassified troves of records, including sensitive material that state officials provided to CISA. Some state authorities said they no longer trusted the administration enough to share information with CISA, a key to the agency’s success in past elections.

“They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing relationship,” said one former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who now advises state governments on national security. “There’s no fucking way they’re ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.”

A spokesperson for the White House declined an interview request but defended Trump’s handling of election security in an emailed statement. “President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections,” said Lauren Bis.

Bis referred specific questions about CISA’s handling of elections to DHS. DHS and CISA did not respond to interview requests or to a detailed list of questions.

Current and former CISA employees and state election officials describe an agency that has become significantly less equipped to help states fight legitimate cyber threats. State leaders say they have used their own resources to shore up gaps left by CISA, such as paying for sensor technology that can detect unusual activity in election networks. But some services, like intel on foreign actors, can’t be replicated. Some people interviewed said they were worried that Trump and his allies continue to ratchet up rhetoric about voting security, particularly about threats to voting machines. Officials in one large voting jurisdiction said they have met privately with machine vendors to come up with a contingency plan if the federal government seizes their machines or declares them unusable.

“I don’t pay attention to what the president says. I pay attention to what his administration does,” Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said. “And what they’ve done is basically cut us off and left us on our own.”

Defending elections from hackers wasn’t always part of DHS’s remit.

Throughout the mid-1990s and 2000s, a series of cyberattacks rocked the federal government, demonstrating the emerging threat. In 2007, hackers broke into the Pentagon and stole terabytes of sensitive data. The digital heist, by an unknown foreign adversary, was so damaging that one intelligence leader later described it as an “espionage Pearl Harbor.”

Under George W. Bush, DHS underwent a reorganization to more effectively combat terrorism and respond to disasters like Hurricane Katrina. The department dedicated resources under an office called the National Protection and Programs Directorate to help fortify advanced cyber defense systems and important infrastructure. The office’s work ranged from helping secure events like the Super Bowl to protecting chemical plants to issuing cybersecurity warnings to the private sector and the public. In 2018, Trump signed a bill making the office a stand-alone agency, allowing for more federal funding and transforming it into, essentially, the ultimate tech support desk for anything DHS designated “critical infrastructure.” The bill renamed the agency CISA.

Though Trump helped create CISA, he didn’t much appreciate the work the agency did under its old name to expose the extent of Russia’s meddling in the 2016 presidential election. Russian agents had unleashed a massive disinformation campaign, with a Kremlin-backed troll farm creating thousands of social media accounts posing as Americans and promoting Trump, according to bipartisan reports from the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence released before the 2020 election. A dozen Russian military agents were indicted for what the Justice Department described as “a sustained effort to hack into the computer networks of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the Democratic National Committee, and the presidential campaign of Hillary Clinton.”

Trump publicly downplayed this interference, but DHS leadership saw the Russia attack as an escalation. In January 2017, before Trump took office, DHS upgraded America’s elections to the status of critical infrastructure. This placed the polls and all voting technology used in federal elections under the watch of what would soon become CISA.

To carry out this function, CISA needed help. But states and voting machine vendors were wary about sharing data on weaknesses in voting systems, fearing it could be exploited if certain details were to become public. State officials were also reluctant to cede any role in election preparation to the federal government.

Gradually, though, CISA and state election officials negotiated a fragile trust. At its center was a commitment: The sensitive information states and vendors shared with CISA would be kept confidential.

“It took years and years of building trust, of talking to election officials, of hiring people with elections experience who could be validators for the work that CISA wanted to do, before they finally built strong working relationships,” said Derek Tisler, who specializes in election security as counsel for the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan institute based out of New York University School of Law.

Under Director Chris Krebs, CISA hosted penetration testing in which its agents would try to hack into a state’s system to locate weaknesses that could then be patched, along with tabletop exercises simulating a series of potential catastrophes around elections. CISA also offered regular secret-level briefings to secretaries of state to share federal intelligence. And CISA paid for sensor technology that looked for potential malicious online activity on election networks, notifying officials about emerging threats.

“The staffing was there, the expertise was there, the visibility was there, the funding was there,” Macias said.

The consortium shared data as run of the mill as spambots as well as more serious threats. If Virginia caught unusual activity in its system, it could let other states know to be vigilant.

While CISA had prepared for attacks from the Chinese and Russian governments, or lone wolf hackers, few there had expected the threat to elections would come from inside the White House. But when Trump refused to concede to Joe Biden in 2020, claiming the vote had been rigged, CISA became a key component of the guardrails that ultimately led to the election results being certified.

The agency, in a statement co-signed by secretaries of state and voting machine vendors, vouched for the election’s integrity, calling it “the most secure in American history.” When Krebs publicly rebutted claims amplified by the White House as “unsubstantiated” or “technically incoherent,” Trump fired him over Twitter.

As Congress prepared to vote on certifying the election results, it was members of CISA, along with the FBI, who convinced then-Attorney General Bill Barr that the conspiracy theories embraced by the president could be explained by human error, not systemic fraud or hacking.

When Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, his administration immediately started to dismantle CISA. The administrative notices were sent out just a couple of weeks after the inauguration and included the team in charge of dispelling disinformation.

For the employees under the DOGE microscope, work became impossible, said one former senior CISA employee. “Those groups couldn’t even order a pizza.”

DOGE laid off people critical to the agency’s election work, including those who’d worked closely with states. The Trump administration cut funding for the technology that monitored web and election servers, blinding the federal government to breaches it had detected.

When it came time for states to prepare for the 2026 midterms, CISA had disappeared.

On the evening of July 16, in the Black Hills of South Dakota, dozens of election officials and their staffs gathered for a reception near Mount Rushmore. It was the third night of an annual conference for secretaries of state, drawing participants from red and blue states. They’d spent the week discussing state voter roll maintenance and voter ID — issues that at times made for disagreements.

At about 8 p.m., a wave of discomfort swept through the crowd, visible on attendees’ faces as they glanced frequently at their phones, according to people at the event. Any minute now, Trump was going to address the nation on election security. Some at the reception worried he would declare a national emergency, as his allies had urged him to do months earlier, and use it as a pretext to direct the government to seize voting machines.

Then reports on the speech began rolling in, and the mood shifted. The claims Trump was making were unsubstantiated and outlandish. Many had been examined ad nauseam, including by those at the reception, and roundly debunked. The collective anxiety that was palpable moments earlier melted away, as many saw the speech as another attempt to revive disproved theories unlikely to be taken seriously by most voters.

“Everyone just sort of guffawed and put their phones away and went to the bar,” recalled Quinn Raymond, co-founder of VoteShield, a nonprofit that works with states to help monitor voter registration data, who was at the event.

Still, if the speech made little impact, records published by the Trump administration to support the president’s claims damaged the already eroding relationship between CISA and state election officials. The material included raw information states had shared with the agency that was supposed to remain private, such as a log of communications from Election Day 2020 detailing activity being monitored in several states.

“It betrayed the trust of all partners who were willing to share information at the time,” said Geoff Hale, who worked on CISA’s elections team from the agency’s inception until last year. Now he specializes in election security at the Center for Democracy & Technology, a nonprofit that advocates for digital and civil rights.

Bis, the White House spokesperson, denied that the Trump administration broke any agreements in releasing the information. “The release of such information is exactly the sort of transparency news organizations should applaud,” she said. Bis also defended Trump’s speech, saying it had been fact-checked “by the agencies whose evidence was released and did not mischaracterize any information.”

Hale and others said the speech was one of several instances demonstrating the Trump administration’s reckless attitude toward sensitive data collected by CISA. Earlier this year, Politico reported that acting CISA Director Madhu Gottumukkala had uploaded records to ChatGPT, even though DHS had barred its employees from using the unsecure program. A CISA spokesperson told Politico that Gottumukkala had been permitted to use the technology for a “short-term and limited” basis.

Last May, an independent journalist named Brian Krebs exposed that CISA published private data, including passwords, cloud keys and other information, on its public GitHub page, in a folder labeled “Private-CISA.” A CISA spokesperson told the journalist there was no indication that sensitive data was compromised.

Some state election authorities were also alarmed to see the lengths to which the Trump administration went to legitimize the president’s fixation on the 2020 race.

In fall 2025, Missouri election officials produced a memo stating Andrew McCoy Warner, a Department of Justice official and prominent 2020 election conspiracy theorist, had called several clerks asking for access to voting machines. Tulsi Gabbard, then the director of national intelligence, had also led an operation in Puerto Rico to seize election machines. When the private cybersecurity contractor hired to examine the machines, Mojave Research Inc., failed to find evidence supporting claims about 2020, the federal government became “dissastified” with its services and stopped renewing its contract, its CEO later told reporters.

A spokesperson for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence told reporters in August that Mojave’s work ceased because it had completed its contract. Testifying before Congress in March, Gabbard said the seizing of voting machines came at the request of an assistant U.S. attorney in Puerto Rico.

“What happened in the second Trump administration is from almost day one — I mean, literally the first two months — they took all that was built up by Trump 1 and just decimated it,” said David Becker, founder of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonprofit that works with state election authorities. “Election officials lost trust in the federal government.”

It didn’t help that, in his speech, the president mocked CISA’s defense of the 2020 election, calling the statement about it being the most secure in history a “very pat line” concocted as part of a deep-state cover-up. One former career CISA employee described being crestfallen at the Trump administration’s erosion of all they’d accomplished.

“We worked so hard to build that trusted relationship,” said Caitlin Durkovich, former DHS assistant secretary for infrastructure protection and co-founder of the cybersecurity firm Civira Partners. “I don’t know how you put it back together.”

A few weeks after Trump’s speech, the state election officials gathered once more, this time for a video call with Nick Andersen, who had replaced Gottumukkala as CISA’s acting director.

Though the primaries were already under way, this was the first time many had met Andersen, a former cybersecurity adviser to Trump’s White House who had joined CISA a year earlier. Andersen is also a district representative for the Republican Party in Virginia, according to the party’s website. In March, he gave a speech to the Fairfax GOP chapter titled “Fighting Democrat Redistricting.”

Speaking over video in August, the boyish-faced former Marine Corps engineer announced that DHS was preparing to release a plan on how it would work together with state officials to secure the election, according to five people who were present at the video meeting, some of whom shared notes with ProPublica.

Many on the call were stunned at what they perceived as a lack of understanding of election planning. Early voting for the general election was just around the corner. They had spent over a year preparing for the midterms, and there was no more time for ambitious work.

Some peppered Andersen with questions: Where had CISA been when there was still time to make improvements?

Andersen blamed any lapses or perceived breaches in trust on the federal government shutdown in fall 2025, twirling his pen uncomfortably and sipping from a Monster energy drink.

Fontes, Arizona’s secretary of state, was blunt about his feelings regarding working with Andersen and CISA, according to several of the people on the call.

“I told him I didn’t trust him,” Fontes recalled in an interview. “I did raise my voice a little bit, because I’m frustrated — very frustrated — that they would have the temerity to come in, clear the entire deck of competent professionals, stop supporting the states, eviscerate the coordination efforts that they had and then suddenly come in and say: ‘Oh, we’re from the federal government. We’re here to help.’”

Indeed, one recently departed CISA official said attempting to do the agency’s typical election work now would be futile. In previous years, CISA had finished almost all its preparations with the states by Labor Day.

“That ship has sailed,” the official said.

CISA published its security plan for the 2026 election on Sept. 24. The 13-page document describes how, over the past two years, CISA has “recommitted to its statutory mission and remains resolute in strengthening the security of elections.”

State officials said their planning will ensure a secure election, even without help from CISA. Yet they and cybersecurity experts worry that Trump will say the election was hacked if Republicans don’t win in November.

The security plan calls for “leveraging collaborative partnerships” with states the agency has abandoned since Trump took office. Shenna Bellows, Maine’s secretary of state, said she’d welcome that but was skeptical of the agency’s motivations.

“For CISA to promise election officials now, at this point in time, that they are going to be a resource for the 2026 election is too little, too late,” she said.

title: Man Dies in ICE Custody at Texas Jail Operated by GEO Group
content:
The daughter of Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias said staff at the facility wouldn’t “give him his medications.”

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

A 56-year-old Mexican man held at a federal immigration facility in Laredo was found dead in his cell Saturday morning, his daughter and U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Laredo, confirmed to The Texas Tribune.

Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias was found unresponsive by staff at the Rio Grande Processing Center during a security check at around 10 a.m. Saturday, Cuellar said. Staff performed CPR and called emergency services.

Andrade-Covarrubias is the seventh person to die while detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Texas this year — the first being Geraldo Lunas Campos, whose death was ruled a homicide by the El Paso Medical Examiner’s office in January.

He’s also the second to die in an ICE facility in Laredo this year. Felix Alcorta-Rodriguez, a 63-year-old Mexican who was being held at Webb County Detention Center, died on June 19 after being found unresponsive, according to the agency.

The GEO Group, which operates the facility, referred the Tribune to ICE. Officials with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent Sunday and Monday.

Andrade-Covarrubias’ daughter, Estefani Andrade, told the Tribune that her family has not yet been contacted by federal agencies. Instead, she said, they heard about his death on Saturday through the Webb County Medical Examiner, which is performing his autopsy.

Estefani Andrade, 29 and a U.S. citizen, said the family is going to visit the detention facility on Monday to get his belongings.

Andrade-Covarrubias lived in Dallas for decades, had three adult children who were all born in the country and worked as a contractor painting apartments and townhomes, his daughter said. He wanted to eventually return to Mexico and had been travelling back and forth to build a house there, his daughter added.

She said her dad was detained in June at the border after coming back from Mexico by bus. She added that during his months in detention, “he lost weight because he didn’t look the same as when we were doing, like, the video calls with him.”

Cuellar said he planned to visit the facility Sunday afternoon.

“I’ll ask the basic questions: What happened?” he said. “What were the conditions? [Was] there medical? Is there anybody ill? I’m gonna talk to the medical folks there.”

Estefani Andrade said her dad had a heart condition, along with diabetes and high blood pressure. He had medicine with him when he was detained, but she said staff at the center wouldn’t “give him his medications.”

She also said her dad was sick at the detention facility. He had a cough — which she said was concerning since he was hospitalized for COVID-19 in 2021 and that took a lasting toll on his health — and told her that he wasn’t feeling good. He sought help from the facility’s medical staff but he told her that “they would just ignore him.”

She said her dad told her that he felt like medical staff at the center was brushing off his concerns, even when he told the staff that he was having trouble breathing and feeling tightness in his chest.

Estefani Andrade said she is now trying to be strong for her mom, who is devastated.

“When she got the news, she wasn’t all there,” she said. ”It’s hitting her really hard.”

title: Border Czar Homan Confirms Trump Admin Is Looking to Denaturalize Ilhan Omar
content:
Previous inquiries into Ilhan Omar’s citizenship have found no evidence of fraud.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Appearing on Fox News over the weekend, border czar Tom Homan gave the starkest indication yet that the administration is moving forward with plans to “denaturalize” Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minnesota), stripping her of U.S. citizenship status that she’s had since she was 17 years old.

Last week, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided Omar’s residence in Washington D.C., seizing her phone, notebooks, personal computers, and passport. Members of her family have also received subpoenas relating to the investigation. So far, the details of the inquiry have not officially been made public, but sources with knowledge of it say it stems from paperwork Omar’s father submitted when she applied to become a citizen in 2000, at age 17.

Homan appeared to confirm that is the investigation’s focus.

“If you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody. We’ve done it before … And certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen” to Omar, he said on the program.

The border czar left some rhetorical wiggle room, but reiterated that the administration was looking into fraudulent behavior by the Minnesota lawmaker or her family members.

“I’m not going to get ahead of the bureau or HSI, but I’ve been told they have a strong case, and we’ll let the evidence lead where it leads,” Homan said.

A person can be denaturalized, or have their citizenship status revoked, only in extreme circumstances — generally, when evidence of fraud is discovered later on. Several conservative conspiracy theorists have alleged that Omar’s father lied about her age when she applied for citizenship, pointing to evidence that she once changed her birth year from 1981 to 1982 in official records, which would have made her 18 when her application was submitted.

But that change was made to correct another error, Omar maintains, and fact-checking websites have demonstrated there is no evidence that the change was for malicious reasons. For denaturalization to occur, there must be evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that fraud actually happened.

Notably, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) examined accusations of fraud relating to Omar’s citizenship several years ago, and found no evidence to justify moving forward on the matter. But President Donald Trump has targeted Omar for over a decade, including demanding that she and other lawmakers of color “go back” to their own countries after they criticized him in 2019. All four of those members of Congress, collectively known as “the Squad,” are U.S. citizens.

Trump reiterated that demand for Omar during a Newsmax interview this past week.

“I think she hates our country. She is a person that truly hates our country. … I’ve said it many times before, she ought to go back to her own country,” Trump said.

Responding to the raid on her home, Omar blasted the administration, decrying the action as “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”

“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” Omar said, adding: “I will not be silenced.”

Several critics described the raid as outright fascism. But some Democratic lawmakers, including party leaders, have been more muted in their response, including Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-New York), who appears not to have said anything publicly on the matter at all.

Schumer’s silence is a perplexing choice in the eyes of many observers — given its close proximity to the midterm elections, the HSI raid on a lawmaker’s home could easily be cited as additional evidence that a Democratic-controlled Congress is necessary to place a check on such actions by the Trump administration.

title: Who pays the price of peace?
content:
In his work 

The Old Regime and the Revolution

, Alexis de Tocqueville exposes one of the fundamental contradictions of the French Revolution: The monarchy had been overthrown, and the institutions of the old regime had been abolished, yet the centralist tradition of state domination over society persisted within the new order. The regime had changed, but the state’s power to determine social relations remained largely intact.




As Tocqueville demonstrates, therein lies a fundamental danger: Change can perpetuate existing power structures rather than overcome them.




From this perspective, the process currently underway in Turkey concerning the Kurdish question must also be examined. The decisive question is not merely whether the armed conflict will come to an end, but whether the historically entrenched relationship of domination from which this conflict emerged will also change.




After more than half a century of struggle, the Kurdish freedom movement has made historic decisions that fundamentally transform its armed strategy and organizational existence. These decisions cannot be explained by the naivety of a movement unaware of Turkey’s political realities. Throughout its long struggle, the Kurdish movement has come to understand the centralist nature of the state, its security-driven reflexes, and its resistance to democratization. Its insistence on a democratic solution stems not from ignorance of this reality, but from a determination to change it.




However, a movement’s willingness to transform itself offers no guarantee that the state power confronting it will undergo a similar transformation. Today, we are dealing not only with historically entrenched patterns of state conduct, but also with the current regime’s strategy for shaping its own future. The Kurdish question is not separate from this strategy. Rather, it is one of the central issues that the regime seeks to restructure in line with its political and regional objectives.




The transition is not intended to be a solution




The limits of this approach become particularly evident in remarks made by presidential adviser Mehmet Uçum on October 17. Uçum defines the process in unequivocal terms: “This is not a resolution process, but a transition process.”




This is by no means merely a terminological distinction. A resolution requires confronting the historical causes of a conflict, the political demands of the parties involved, and the question of equal rights. The transition described by Uçum, by contrast, is based on ending the movement’s organizational existence, completing the disarmament process in full, and having its completion verified and confirmed by the state. Democratization and a new constitution are designated as subjects for separate negotiations. The idea that they should be made prerequisites for the transition is explicitly rejected.




As a result, the transformation of the Kurdish movement becomes a concrete obligation in the present, while the democratic transformation of the regime is postponed to an indefinite future.




There is a timetable for disarmament, but none for political equality.




Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş has also stated that even after a law is passed, no further steps will be taken until disarmament has been verified and officially confirmed by the state. At the same time, he calls for an end to “separatist language.” Verifying disarmament is an understandable necessity within a negotiation process. However, when the state authority responsible for verification also dictates which political views may no longer be expressed, this goes beyond security-related oversight.




Uçum, for his part, establishes a hierarchy among political actors within Kurdish politics. He determines who should be regarded as legitimate negotiating partners and who should be considered obstacles to the process. This reveals an approach that seeks not only to define the conditions of the transition, but also to determine the boundaries within which Kurdish political representation is permitted to operate.




Who determines the boundaries of what is politically conceivable?




His remarks on the future constitutional debate are particularly revealing: “No one should expect negotiations on the new constitution to be conducted on the basis of ethnic and identity-based political positions.”




Uçum argues that these issues must come to an end not only in practice, but also “in people’s minds.” This is no longer simply about ending the armed conflict. Rather, boundaries are also being drawn around the political demands Kurds may bring into the new phase and the visions of the future they are even permitted to put forward for discussion.




Yet peacefully discussing independence, federalism, autonomy, or democratic coexistence, and advocating corresponding political positions, does not in any way imply a desire to continue the armed conflict. Renouncing armed struggle does not mean renouncing the right to self-determination.




Uçum’s remarks cannot be regarded as a definitive decision by the state. Nevertheless, the approach they reveal is sufficiently clear: The regime seeks to end the conflict while retaining the power to define the political boundaries of the new phase.




The end of armed struggle is not yet a solution




It is precisely at this point that Tocqueville’s critique of centralism acquires particular significance. A centralist state does not necessarily resist change. At times, it directs that change itself and even presents itself as its driving force. However, it resists when change begins to challenge its own structures of domination. The fact that a regime makes the Kurdish question politically manageable in accordance with its own vision of the future does not mean that it has resolved it.




The end of armed struggle does not mean that Kurds have thereby been recognized as a collective political subject. They did not acquire their political existence only with the beginning of the current process. Rather, they have developed their own political will through more than a century of resistance and immense sacrifices. The state’s responsibility, therefore, is not to bring this will into existence, but to cease denying its existence and the rights associated with it.




The measure of a genuine solution cannot, therefore, be the silence of weapons. What matters instead is the recognition of Kurds as political subjects with the right to participate in determining their own future and to make their own decisions.




The state is not content with being merely one of the parties to the peace process. It also claims the role of arbiter, control over the process’s timetable, and the authority to define the boundaries of legitimate political expression. This does not constitute a democratic solution between political subjects on an equal footing.




Who bears the burdens, and who reaps the benefits?




Through historic decisions, the Kurds have demonstrated their willingness to engage in negotiations and assume the far-reaching obligations associated with peace. Yet peace cannot be an agreement in which one side takes concrete and irreversible steps while the other postpones its responsibilities to an indefinite future.




The burdens of peace must be distributed with due regard for historical responsibility and political equality. For the state to confront its policy of denial, recognize the collective existence of the Kurdish people, and provide legal guarantees for that recognition is not a concession it graciously grants in exchange for disarmament, but a necessary prerequisite for a just solution.




This is precisely where the fundamental problem lies: instead of conducting negotiations between political subjects on an equal footing, the conditions of the transition are being determined unilaterally. The consent of a people cannot be secured by dictating which political demands they must abandon.




At this point, the warning issued by Ömer Hayri Konar from Imrali also takes on particular significance. He cautioned that the policies pursued thus far are continuing in more subtle forms. A change in the methods of struggle does not mean that the historical causes from which that struggle emerged have been eliminated.




The end of the conflict could bring Turkey considerable benefits, ranging from security and regional relations to domestic politics and its international standing. However, if the regime appropriates these benefits while the collective rights and political equality of the Kurds remain unresolved, an unavoidable question arises: Who bears the costs of peace, and who reaps its rewards?




Put more pointedly, this amounts to getting off cheaply: claiming the benefits of ending the conflict without changing the historical relationship of denial and domination from which the conflict emerged.




A democratic solution to the Kurdish question and the democratization of Turkey cannot be separated from one another. However, this connection does not justify postponing the recognition of Kurdish rights to an indefinite point within an equally uncertain democratization process. There is therefore no contradiction in defending the negotiation process while simultaneously criticizing the regime’s position. Supporting peace does not mean suspending democratic opposition.




Self-determination is not a favor granted by the state




The Kurds are not waiting for the state to grant them their freedom. Their history of struggle spanning more than a century already demonstrates this. What is expected of the state is that it assume its historical responsibility: acknowledge the policy of denial, the massacres, forced assimilation, and the political order that made all of this possible, and initiate the legal and democratic steps arising from this reckoning with the past.




The state is confronted by a Kurdish freedom movement whose political will has been tested and proven through more than half a century of struggle. This will did not emerge through state recognition, but was forged and sustained in the face of denial and prohibitions, at the cost of immense sacrifices. To assume that the Kurdish freedom movement, after more than half a century of struggle, would submit to the political boundaries imposed by the regime would be to misunderstand both the history and the very foundations of this movement’s existence.




In the same work, Tocqueville describes the confidence that those who carried out the revolution placed in their own strength:




“They were filled with such proud confidence in their own strength that this confidence could sometimes lead them astray. Yet without such self-confidence, a people would never have risen beyond the role of serving others.”




 




This does not mean believing that a people always makes the right decisions, but rather having confidence in its own ability to determine its future, even while recognizing that it may make mistakes along the way. Denial and assimilation are directed not only against a people’s language, identity, and rights. They also seek to undermine its self-confidence. A people is meant to be made to believe that it is incapable of shaping its own future and can exist only within the boundaries permitted by the ruling power.




It is precisely for this reason that Uçum’s demand that political aspirations must also come to an end “in people’s minds” is particularly significant: The aim is no longer merely to determine the boundaries of political action, but also to define the limits of what a people is even allowed to imagine for its own future.




Ultimately, the Kurds can negotiate the conditions, methods, and guarantees of peace. Forms of struggle and political programs may change. However, no negotiation can be made conditional on the Kurds relinquishing their determination to decide their own future. The history of more than half a century of struggle demonstrates that this determination has been sustained not by accepting boundaries imposed by the state, but by resisting them. Throughout history, political orders established to suppress the will of entire peoples have undergone transformation; many have long since become a thing of the past. The measure of lasting peace, therefore, cannot be how far the will of a people can be restricted, but whether political conditions are created in which that will can develop freely.




The patience of the Kurds cannot serve as a guarantee for a democracy whose realization in Turkey has been postponed for a century. Peace does not mean forcing the Kurds to fit within boundaries drawn by the state, but overcoming the system of denial and domination that has imposed those boundaries upon them for a century.
