author: Soraya Kishtwari
title: This Politician Posted a Quote About Palestinian Resistance. Now France Is Dragging Her Through the Courts
content:
For the last three years, Rima Hassan has watched in horror as thousands of people have been killed in her family’s homeland. The French jurist and La France Insoumise (LFI) MEP, who was born stateless in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria, is one of France’s most outspoken critics of both Israel’s genocide in Gaza and the complicity of Europe’s governments.




Now, she could be sent to prison over a post on social media.




In March, Hassan posted a quotation on X/Twitter attributed to Kōzō Okamoto, a member of the Japanese Red Army who took part in a 1972 attack on an Israeli airport in which 26 people were killed.




“I gave my youth to the Palestinian cause,” Okamoto’s quotation read. “As long as there is oppression, resistance will not only be a right, but a duty.”




Far-right National Rally politician 

Matthias Renault

, interior minister 

Laurent Nuñez

 and two French pro-Israel lobby groups reported Hassan to prosecutors for 

apologie du terrorisme 

(the glorification of terrorism) – a criminal offence. 

Hassan denied the charges

 and said her main goal had been to share a quotation about the “philosophy of resistance”, and that she couldn’t be accused of glorifying terrorism for doing so.




Hassan’s trial began on 19 October. If found guilty, she could be sentenced to up to seven years in prison and fined €100,000 under French law. Her situation, she said, is the latest in a series

 of legal and political battles in France over solidarity with Palestine

.




“

People who stand in solidarity with Palestine are labelled as terrorists because it [this label] is the only instrument that allows them to silence concrete opposition and activism,” Hassan told Novara Media ahead of her trial.




This isn’t the first time the French state has brought the full force of its institutional machinery against Hassan. 

22 legal proceedings

 have been initiated against her in the last two years in connection with her political views (six have been closed by prosecutors without questioning, 13 after questioning and three remain open). In September, a separate trial in relation to 

two social media posts from 2025

 was adjourned.




Prior to the opening of the investigation

 into the post in March, police had 

reportedly already been surveilling Hassan

, tracking her movements and monitoring her phone activity. In April, she was taken into custody for questioning in what she describes as a “deliberate attempt” to circumvent her parliamentary immunity. Details of her arrest, including the claim she was carrying drugs, were then 

leaked to the press

 (the drug probe was subsequently dropped).




Hassan’s lawyer, Vincent Brengarth, has 

long maintained his client’s innocence

, alleging the prosecutions are part of a “campaign of judicial harassment aimed at silencing her”. Five UN special rapporteurs have 

raised similar concerns

, warning the French government that Hassan appeared to be facing “political and judicial harassment”.




Hassan told Novara Media she believed that the accusations against her were a “misuse of anti-terrorism laws”.




“The shift is very interesting,” she said, noting how she believes that we’re moving towards a situation in which the accusation of terrorism is directed at “all political opposition”.




Hassan’s case is perhaps the most high-profile of hundreds of cases of alleged 

apologie du terrorisme

 offences in France. 

In October 2023, police arrested trade union leader Jean-Paul Delescaut over a leaflet published following the 7 October attacks (Delescaut was convicted and sentenced, before being 

acquitted on appeal

). In another case, the suspended sentence of a former deputy mayor, Mohamed Makni, for sharing a quotation which described the attacks as “resistance” was upheld by France’s highest court (Makni is now 

challenging the ruling

 at the European Court of Human Rights). B

etween October 2023 and October 2025, 

more than 350 people

 were convicted of the offence in total. While it’s unclear how many were in relation to Palestine, rulings surged after 7 October.




None of this may surprise anyone living in the UK. Since it was banned as a terrorist group in July 2025, those in the UK expressing support for Palestine Action, an organisation which targeted companies

 involved in supplying military equipment to Israel, 

risk up to 14 years in prison. What’s followed, due to huge public opposition to the ban, has been 

a 1,553% uptick in terrorism arrests

 – 94% of them in the year ending June 2026 linked to the proscription.




Dr Eliza Bechtold, a trained lawyer and a researcher at the University of Oxford, studies how modern anti-terror frameworks use over-expansive definitions of “terrorist-related speech” to criminalise political dissent.




“The more we look at it, the more we see how it’s being used by states as sort of a cudgel to silence disfavoured political viewpoints,” Bechtold told Novara Media. “That has profound impacts on public discourse, freedom of association, all of these really fundamental rights that underpin democracies.




“Academics, human rights lawyers, legal advocates have been sounding the alarm for quite some time on these types of offences that punish purely speech, absent the attendant act, and are becoming increasingly attenuated from traditional criminal notions of incitement.”




Bechtold also noted in a 

recent paper

 that “no contemporary example better supports just how concerning this is than the global policing of speech surrounding the war in Gaza” – an 

analysis shared

 by the UN special rapporteur on freedom of opinion and expression. She told Novara Media that while the wider “chilling effect” of prosecutions is hard to measure, their impact certainly 

extends well beyond those prosecuted

.




Palestine is expected to be a key campaigning issue for Hassan’s party, LFI, in the run up to France’s presidential election in April next year.




For those caught between their conscience and the law, Hassan is unequivocal: “Today, for me, they [advocates for the Palestinian cause] are… the heroes of our time: those who make sure that our countries are not complicit, and who target the material and logistical support provided to Israel.”




Hassan’s trial – “the trial of the century for freedom of expression”, 

Brengarth said

 – continues at Paris criminal court.

author: Jolene Banning
title: My ancestors showed me how to grieve
content:
Jolene Banning’s daughter Amber-baa, depicted through the eye of an eagle. Illustration by Jessie Boulard




Content warning: This story deals with child loss and grief. Please look after your spirit and read with care







Three years ago I was hit with a pain so deep that it seared through every fiber of my body. 




Two police officers pulled up in my driveway, driving a dark SUV, wearing dark suits and ties. They came to inform me that my child, my baby, my daughter Amber had died. 




The blow of information left me numb, stunned, separated from myself like I was watching this happen instead of partaking. 




Instantly, I became a member of a club I never wanted to belong to: of parents who have lost their children. Because I know I’m not alone in this rapidly growing group of people. It doesn’t feel natural to bury our children, so young, so beautiful. 




Amber-baa had long, shiny dark brown hair, round brown eyes, thick eyebrows and a million dollar smile — which she should, considering how much I paid the orthodontist. She was warm, caring, and fun to be around. She lit up a room and made sure everyone felt seen. And in the blink of an eye, without warning, I had lost all of that. The silence was deafening. The pain was inescapable. 




Experiencing this kind of loss and grief is not uncommon for Indigenous people. In “Canada,” our communities experience significantly higher mortality rates. Our women and girls are at a 12 times higher risk than the average citizen to go missing or be murdered. 




Violence against us is fuelled by systemic racism, sexism, and colonialism — as outlined in 

Reclaiming Power and Place, the Final Report of the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls

. 




We hear about these losses. Sometimes it makes the news, stats are shared, but then we don’t hear from anyone again. The news has passed, new topics are making headlines. 




Losing my daughter, and losing other important people in my life too soon, led me to want to acknowledge this and share my reality, and I grapple with how we can begin to heal. 




My first loss came when I was only 13. My baby brother was only six months old and died of meningitis after spending a week in the Toronto Hospital for Sick Children. After that, I would go on to lose many of my aunties, uncles and cousins, and grandparents. 




Many lives shut down before they even reached their prime. 




“For these four days, my pain was spread out amongst everyone at the fire.”




When I lost my girl, on April 28th, 2023, there was no way I was sending her on her next journey in a way that was not ours — in a church made of brick and mortar while someone delivered a sermon about finding God and peace. 




So I turned to my Anishinaabek community and found knowledge holders and learners willing to share with me. 




I was told I need to send my girl off with a four-day sacred fire ceremony, something I had never done or even participated in until this loss. 




I called the Elders that I knew, and many people worked behind the scenes to ensure I had enough fire wood, food, and company. Firekeepers attended to the fire and explained which direction to enter, drum groups stopped by and offered songs. 




Every morning, as the sun rose, my dad was there, sharing family stories. Relatives from the north made the trek to offer medicine, condolences and stories of their own.




Another community member, who lost a child, offered to make my daughter a headstone. It’s a simple cross, with her information, and features a painted medicine wheel. 




For these four days, my pain was spread out amongst everyone at the fire.




I also learned during this ceremony that my daughter needed to start her journey and there were ways I could assist her. 




She needed her own bundle with exactly four matchsticks, a copper cup, an outfit made in her colours so our ancestors can recognize her and moccasins — basic and unembellished ones, since our offerings grow in size when they reach the other dimension, realm, Spirit World, and we don’t want her weighed down, unable to walk. 




I was told she will come to a crossing, where she will have to share everything about herself and her journey so far. Then our ancestors will travel across the divide to accept her. Her bundle was packed just right. 




Every day and every night over four days we feasted for her by offering a spirit plate to the land, another to the fire. 




In Anishinaabek culture, we add the prefix -baa onto a name to signify they have passed on.




It was with the love and support of family, community and ancestors that kept me going through that initial service. It was being surrounded by everyone that made the days go by. 




But eventually, the service came to an end and everyone went back home. For the first time since the loss happened, I was completely alone with my thoughts, and all I thought about was my child. 




What could I have done differently? How are her babies going to live without her? How do such little people, babies, process this monumental loss? How do I live again, knowing a huge piece of me is gone? Did I love her enough? 




I decided I needed to go home to my maternal homelands, in Sioux Lookout, where my mom was born, and the land my grandparents came from. I wanted to visit my cousins Shirley and Dennis Anderson. 




Together, they have a world of knowledge behind them. Both Shirley and Dennis were raised on the land,  growing up traditionally, raised in the language. As a young adult, Shirley was working in a thriving metropolis as a model and hairstylist before coming back home to work for her people. 




She and I can spend hours talking about everything from life, love, family, death — you name it — over BINGO or while driving around to garage sales. It was during one of our talks that she asked me to talk to my girl, like I would if she was right there with us.




Shirley brought me to a camp she has on an island on Lac Seul First Nation. It’s a shared space where her son and daughter have camps as well. That summer I had eagles all around me, watching me, talking to me. I even captured it on video and audio recording as we fed one.  




“I felt reassured that our ancestors were guiding me and my daughter.”




While I was in Sioux Lookout, I went to visit a friend in long-term care, Garnet Angeconab-baa (who has since passed on). 




When I first met him, he was suffering from Kennedy’s disease, a degenerative disease that eats away at his body. The last time I saw him, during a film screening in 2019, we talked about the epidemic of missing and murdered Indigenous Peoples. 




We have a connection because the body of my aunt Audrey-baa Anderson was found on the side of the highway in Sioux Lookout in 1972, at the young age of 19-years-old. Not yet an adult. On this visit I told him that I lost my daughter. He told me he could read it on my face before I said anything. 




Garnet-baa told me how he first started talking about his experiences of Indian Residential School, in sharing circles with other students and a social worker. When the sharing was done, he hopped in his car and drove more than a thousand miles before taking a real rest stop at a lake, where he ran into an Elder from his university days. 




The Elder advised him to pick up a rock, and to take each thought, memory, pain, and share it with the rock he was holding. Then, to offer that rock to the water and let the water take it and carry it for you. Garnet-baa asked me to do this.




Not long after that, I went to a women’s healing retreat. The retreat began with a morning introduction to each other, and the Elder in residence. At the end of the first morning’s introductions, as I was leaving, the Elder tapped me on the arm and said: “she made it to the other side.”




Without asking the Elder anything, she offered me this knowledge. During my daughter’s sacred fire, I prayed for her connection to our ancestors and a huge relief came after the Elder shared that information. 




I felt reassured that our ancestors were guiding me and my daughter.




After that, I was more open to attending ceremonies for healing and connection. 




I am someone who’s never grown up with ceremonies but they were always around me, their simple acts always evident, like seeing asemaa (tobacco) laid on the ground where we cut wood, cedar branches hung on doorways or in my grandma’s shoes, ashes from the fire marked on foreheads of children, sharing of moose meat after a good hunting season. 




Our cultural and traditional practices were banned and outlawed for more than 60 years, but it didn’t matter if I had years of experience or not. 




I had to acknowledge that ceremony is something that lives within all of us, and certain practices help aid in that connection. I couldn’t deny it anymore, especially after having experienced it first-hand. I was open, mindful and held blood memory. 




During my time in ceremony I was given the knowledge that love never dies and I felt my daughters love and the love of all my ancestors. It is unwavering, determined, warm and always present even if one person is in this world and the other is not. 




My grief is unharnessed love, at times exploding through tears. But I learned enough about my ceremony; the acts of a sacred fire, the importance of feast plates for both land and fire, medicines and the messages they can carry with asemaa. 




I can take my pain and offer it to ni-mishoomis, grandfather rock, and Gichigami, Lake Superior, because they are strong enough to carry that pain away for me. I can connect and direct that love to exactly where it needs to go, with the ones who need to hear this message most: my daughter’s children. 




They are listening, watching and ready to learn that a mothers love never dies. Our ancestors showed us how. 




The post 

My ancestors showed me how to grieve

 appeared first on 

Indiginews

.

author: Chris Walker
title: More Than $137 Million Has Been Spent on AI-Generated Midterm Ads
content:
The vast majority of ads emanate from GOP campaigns, depicting their Democratic opponents in fictionalized scenarios.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Millions of dollars have been spent on AI during this year’s midterm election campaign, oftentimes through candidates using the technology to depict their opponents in fictional situations, portraying them in negative ways to unsuspecting voters.

According to research from Wesleyan University, over 200 ads have used AI in this election cycle. The ads have totaled more than $137 million in campaign spending.

More than 80 percent of the ads have been produced by Republican candidates or political action committees (PACs) aligned with the GOP. One such ad, featuring Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul (who is running for re-election in New York), features her walking alongside New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. The governor reminds Mamdani, “don’t say affordable” while the two refer to how they plan to govern the state moving forward.

No such statement from Hochul exists, and the video of them walking next to each other in such a way is entirely fictional. The ad doesn’t contain any disclaimer informing viewers that it’s generated by AI.

“It’s the year of the AI election,” Fred N. Davis III, founder of Strategic Perception, an advertising firm based in Hollywood, said to The New York Times. “It’s top of mind for everybody in my business and pretty much everybody in the political business.”

Some candidates who have become the victims of AI advertising are pushing back. Rebecca Cooke, a Democrat seeking to unseat Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R) in a contentious election in Western Wisconsin, sent a “cease and desist” order to him for posting a series of online AI ads he made against her. One of those ads featured fictionalized versions of Cooke and former President Joe Biden, with the former stating that she plans to “take advantage of as much corruption as possible” if Democrats win the elections.

“These defamatory, misleading videos undermine our democratic process and are the exact kind of mudslinging voters are tired of,” the letter said to Van Orden.

Wisconsin law forbids the use of deepfake videos in political messaging, but there is a loophole for federal candidates. The letter takes note of that state statute, telling the Republican lawmaker that he is “violating the spirit of the law.”

Van Orden has continued to produce AI videos. And though he has used Cooke’s image less often, he has now resorted to using an animated duck to refer to her, whose voice sounds eerily similar to the Democratic candidate’s.

For his own part, President Donald Trump has rejected calls for the government to regulate AI, instead touting a non-binding “self-policing” accord that he and several AI companies have signed onto. He has also sought to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” and has made the extraordinary claim that any criticism of the technology is akin to an act of treason.

American voters, meanwhile, would like to see more regulation of AI.

According to a Johns Hopkins University poll published this summer, most Americans back a “right to human” law, which would allow them to opt out of AI interactions if they so desire, including 79 percent who support that concept in health care settings, 76 percent who back it in legal proceedings, and 73 percent who say such a law should apply when AI is aiding in government services.

A recent CNN poll also found that most Americans believe the U.S. government is not doing enough to regulate AI, with 71 percent of respondents expressing that view. Support for regulation is also bipartisan — 85 percent of Democratic-leaning respondents support regulation, while 63 percent of Republican-leaning respondents do as well, the survey found.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Chiara Miraglia
title: CPDP 20th international conference
content:
CPDP (“Computers, Privacy and Data Protection”) is a non-profit platform founded in 2007 by research groups at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel, the Université de Namur, and Tilburg University, later joined by INRIA and the Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research. Today, CPDP is carried by 20 academic centres of excellence from the EU, the US, and beyond. Based in Brussels, CPDP has become a world-leading multidisciplinary conference, convening a global community across research, policy, practice, civil society, and technology to engage with cutting-edge developments in privacy and data protection.

Organiser: 20 academic centres of excellence from the EU, the US, and beyond

The governance of the digital world is fragmented and faces difficult challenges. Technologies that shape our lives develop faster than the means – or even the will – to regulate them for the protection of privacy and other fundamental rights.

What We Owe the Future invites reflection on this contribution. Building on this, it looks ahead to what the future demands of us. What will the next twenty or more years need, and how should we help to build it? What do we owe to those who will inherit the world we shape today? Which principles must endure, which protections cannot be bargained away even when the pressure to relax them is strong, and what responsibilities do the custodians of the present bear towards the future?

The year 2027 marks the twentieth anniversary of CPDP. For twenty years, the conferences have stood at the forefront of efforts to understand and contribute to improving the prospect for governance in this fast-moving digital age. As a community of academics, regulators and policymakers, civil society, industry and legal practitioners, CPDP has cast a bright light on issues, practices and rules, and has offered a forum for debate and the exchange of knowledge across a global landscape. What is worth celebrating is not the annual conference itself, but twenty years of bringing this community together and sustaining it through a period of momentous change.

The people whose lives will extend far into that future should help to design the way forward. CPDP 2027 therefore launches CPDP 20: The Next Generation, which include a team of early-career researchers from across disciplineswho will co-curate the programme and help identify its most pressing questions. This team will identify connections across fields and help to explore issues on the horizon, bringing knowledge and fresh perspectives to bear on developments and their likely consequences that will need to be addressed by policy, governance and other action.

author: Andrea
title: ᐃᓄᑐᖃᓄᑦ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᖓ ᐊᖅᑯᑎᒧᐊᕈᓐᓇᖅᐳᖅ 2027−ᒥ, ᓯᕗᓕᖅᑎ ᐅᖃᖅᐳᖅ
content:
For the English version of this story, please see 

Elder van project could hit the streets in 2027, premier says

.







ᑕᓪᓕᒪᓂ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᐅᔪᓂ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᓂ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᑦ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᓂ ᓂᐅᕕᖅᑕᐅᓚᐅᖅᑐᓂ $1 ᒥᓕᐊᓐᓂ ᐃᓄᓕᒫᓄᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᖏᓐᓂ ᓱᓕ ᐅᖅᑯᑎᒦᙱᓚᑦ ᐊᕐᕌᒍ ᐊᑕᐅᓯᕐᒥ ᐊᖅᑯᑎᒦᓐᓇᑎᒃ ᓯᕗᓪᓕᖅᐹᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᓇᓗᓇᐃᖅᓯᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᑕᐃᒪᐃᑦᑐᒥ ᐱᔨᖅᑎᕋᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥ.




ᑐᓂᓯᔪᓐᓇᙱᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᓇᓗᓇᐃᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᓂᖓᓂ ᖃᖓ ᐱᔭᕇᖅᓯᒪᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᓄᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᖅᑎᑕᐅᓪᓚᕆᖕᓂᖓᓂ, ᓯᕗᓕᖅᑎ ᔮᓐ ᒪᐃᓐ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ “ᐱᔪᒪᓂᕆᕙᖓ” ᑕᑯᓂᕐᒥ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᒃᑲᓐᓂᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ 2027−ᒥ — ᐊᕐᕌᒍᑦ ᐱᖓᓱᓂ ᖄᖏᖅᓯᒪᔪᓂ ᓂᐅᕕᖅᑕᐅᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ.




“ᓄᑖᙳᕆᐊᖅᑎᑕᐅᓂᖓ, ᒫᓐᓇᐅᔪᒥ, ᓱᓕ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᙱᑦᑐᖅ,” ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐅᖃᓘᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᐱᖅᓱᖅᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐅᒃᑐᐱᕆ 9−ᒥ. “ᑭᓯᐊᓂ, ᒐᕙᒪᕗᑦ ᒪᓕᒍᒪᐅᑎᖃᙱᓚᑦ ᐆᒧᖓ.”




ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᖅ ᓄᖅᑲᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ 2025−ᒥ, ᐃᓱᐊᓂ ᓯᕗᓂᐊᓂ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᐅᓂᖏᓐᓂ, ᐱᔾᔪᑎᖃᖅᑐᒥ ᐱᑕᖃᙱᓗᐊᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᓂᖓᓄᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓂ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᔪᒃᓴᐅᑕᐅᔪᓂ.




ᑕᒪᓐᓇ ᐊᓯᔾᔨᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐅᐱᕐᙶᖅ 2026−ᒥ ᒪᓕᒐᓕᐅᖅᑏᑦ ᒫᓐᓇᐅᔪᒥ ᒪᓕᒐᓕᐅᕐᕕᖕᒥ ᐊᖏᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋ $1.25 ᒥᓕᐊᓐᓂ ᖄᒃᑲᓐᓂᐊᒍᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ, ᒪᐃᓐ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ.




ᐸᓯᒥ ᐱᔨᑦᑎᕋᕐᓂᖅ ᓯᕗᓪᓕᖅᐹᒥ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᐅᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ, ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᖃᕐᓂᐅᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᓯᕗᓂᒃᓴᒧᑦ ᐊᔪᙱᓐᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᑎᑕᐅᓂᖓᓂ, ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᐱᓕᒻᒪᒃᓴᓂᕐᒥ ᓕᒥᑎᒃᑯᓐᓂᑦ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᑐᒃᑐ ᑖᒃᓯᓂᑦ.
















ᐊᑕᐅᓯᕐᒥ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᖃᖅᐳᑦ ᐊᑐᓂ ᑕᓪᓕᒪᓂ ᓄᓇᓕᐅᔪᓂ: ᐃᖃᓗᐃᑦ, ᐃᖃᓗᒃᑑᑦᑎᐊᖅ, ᑲᖏᖅᖠᓂᖅ, ᓴᓪᓕᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐸᖕᓂᖅᑑᒥ. ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᓯᕗᓂᒃᓴᒧᑦ ᐊᔪᙱᓐᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᑎᑕᐅᓂᖓᓂ, ᓇᖕᒥᓂᕆᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᑲᒻᐸᓂᐅᔪᒥ, ᓂᐅᕕᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᓄᓇᕗᒻᒥ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᓐᓂ.




ᖁᑉᐸ ᒪᐃᒃ ᓇᖏᖅᐳᖅ ᓴᓂᓕᐊᓂ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᑦ ᐸᓯᖓᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᔪᒥ ᐸᐃᕆᓃᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᑦ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᑦ’ ᖃᒻᒪᖓᓂ ᐅᒃᑐᐱᕆ 9−ᒥ. (ᑎᐊᕆᓐ ᓕᐊᑦᔅ ᐊᔾᔨᖁᑎᖓ)




ᑭᒡᒐᖅᑐᐃᔨᐅᔪᓂ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᐱᓕᒻᒪᒃᓴᓂᕐᒥ ᓕᒥᑎᑯᓐᓂᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑐᒃᑐ ᑖᒃᓯᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐊᑐᐃᓪᓐᓇᐅᓚᐅᙱᓚᑦ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᒃᓴᓕᐅᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐆᒧᖓ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐊᖑᔪᒧᑦ.




ᐊᑐᐊᒐᒥ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᑎᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᕗᖅ ᐱᓕᕆᓂᐅᑉ ᑐᓄᐊᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ, ᐱᔭᕇᖅᑕᐅᒍᓂ, ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᐸᕐᓇᒃᐳᑦ ᑐᓂᓯᓂᕐᒥ ᖃᐃᖁᔨᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᑐᒃᓯᕋᐅᑎᓂ ᓯᕗᓂᐊᓂ ᐃᓱᐊᓂ 2026−ᒥ, ᒪᐃᓐ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ.




ᓱᓕ ᐃᓱᒪᒃᓴᖅᓯᐅᕈᑕᐅᓂᐊᖅᐳᖅ ᖃᐃᖁᔨᓂᐅᔪᖅ ᐃᓄᓕᒫᓅᖓᓂᐊᕈᓂ ᐅᕝᕙᓘᓐᓃᑦ “ᖃᐃᖁᔨᓂᐅᔪᑎᒍᑦ,” ᐃᓚᒋᐊᖅᓯᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ.




ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᐱᓕᒻᒪᒃᓴᓂᕐᒥ ᓕᒥᑎᑦ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᖅ-ᑮᓇᐅᔭᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᐅᔪᒥ, ᕿᓚᒻᒥᐅᔪᒥ ᐊᕿᑦᑐᒥ ᐱᒋᐊᖅᑕᐅᓂᖓᓂ ᐱᔨᑦᑎᕋᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᓂᐅᓚᐅᖅᑐᒥ ᐅᒃᑐᐱᕆ 2025−ᒥ. ᑲᒻᐸᓂᐅᔪᖅ ᑭᐅᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ 200−ᐸᓗᖕᓄᑦ ᐱᔨᑦᑎᕋᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᖃᐃᖁᔨᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐱᓇᓱᐊᕈᓯᐅᑉ ᓄᙳᐊᓂᑕᒫᒥ.
















ᖁᑉᐸ ᒪᐃᒃ, ᑲᑎᒪᔨᐅᖃᑕᐅᔪᖅ ᐸᐃᕆᔩᑦ ᑎᒍᒥᐊᖅᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᓄᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᓐᓂ, ᐊᑐᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᒻᒥ ᐱᖓᓱᐃᖅᓱᖅᖢᓂ ᐃᖏᕐᕋᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᒃᑯᑦ ᖃᒻᒪᖓᓄᑦ, ᓂᕿᑖᕐᕕᖕᒥ ᐊᔪᖅᓴᖅᑐᓄᑦ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᓂᕿᓄᑦ ᓂᐅᕕᕐᕕᓄᑦ, ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ.




ᓄᑖᖅ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᒧᑦ ᐊᔭᐅᕐᕕᖓ ᐊᒃᓱᕈᕐᓇᒐᓚᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᓂᐅᕐᓗᖁᑎᖓᓄᑦ, ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ, ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᔪᒥ ᐸᓯᒥ ᐊᔪᕐᓇᙱᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᒪᔪᕋᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᑎᑭᐅᑎᔪᓐᓇᓕᕋᒥ ᐊᒡᒐᒧᑦ ᑎᒍᒥᐊᕐᕕᓄᑦ ᐃᓄᐊᓂ ᐸᓯᒥ ᐃᑭᓇᓱᐊᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ, ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ.




“ᐱᐅᕐᔪᐊᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑕᐅᓂᖃᖅᖢᓂ,” ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ.




ᐃᓄᑐᖃᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᖅ ᐃᒻᒥᓂᒃ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᕗᑦ ᐱᖓᓱᓂ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᓂ, ᐃᓚᖃᖅᑐᒥ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᓄᑦ ᐸᓯᖓᓂ. ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᐸᓯᐅᑉ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᔭᐅᕐᕕᖓ ᓱᕋᒃᓯᒪᖕᒪᑦ ᐊᑯᓂᐊᓗᒃ, ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᐅᖃᑕᐅᔪᒥ ᐊᐃᓂᐊᖅ ᖁᐊᒐᖅ.




”ᐅᑕᖅᑭᙳᓚᐅᖅᐳᒍᑦ ᓄᑖᒥ ᐸᓯᒥ ᑕᐃᒫᒃ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᔪᓐᓃᓚᐅᖅᐸᕗᑦ” ᒪᐃᒃ ᐃᓚᒋᐊᖅᓯᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ.
















“ᐅᔾᔨᕈᓱᒃᐳᖓ ᐊᑯᓂᐸᓘᓂᖓᓂ ᐅᑯᐊ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᑦ ᓯᕗᓪᓕᕐᒥ ᓂᐅᕕᖅᑕᐅᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ, ᐊᒻᒪᓂᕆᐅᖕᓂᖃᒐᓚᒃᐳᖅ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᑲᖅᓴᙱᓐᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᓱᓕᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᓱᓕ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᙱᓐᓂᖏᓐᓂ,” ᒪᐃᓐ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ. “ᒪᓕᒃᑐᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᑕᑯᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᑐᐊᒐᕐᒥ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑕᐅᓂᖓᓂ, ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᓇᔭᖅᑐᒥ ᑕᐃᔅᓱᒥᖓ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑕᑯᓂᕐᒥ ᐃᖏᕐᕋᓂᖓᓂ ᓄᓇᕗᓕᒫᒥ ᐃᓄᖕᓄᑦ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᓂᐊᖅᑐᓄᑦ ᑕᐃᒪᐃᑦᑐᒥ ᖃᓄᐃᑦᑑᓂᖓᓂ ᐱᔨᑦᑎᕋᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥ.”

title: Gewerkschaften, Sozialabbau und Widerstand: Fast 25 Jahre Theorie und Praxis
content:
Dossier




„… 

Als die größte Klippe für wirksame einheitliche Proteste und den Widerstand gegen die Hartz-Gesetze hat sich die breite Akzeptanz des Leistungsprinzips und der Lohnabhängigkeit als einziger Quelle der Existenzsicherung erwiesen. Dies gilt für die Gewerkschaftsbürokratie gleichermaßen wie für die meisten der (noch?) beschäftigten wie erwerbslosen Lohnabhängigen selbst. (…) Durch diese Propaganda wurden auch die Gewerkschaftsspitzen ins Boot geholt, die ihre oberste Aufgabe schon immer darin gesehen haben, „Menschen in Arbeit zu bringen“. (…) Die Mischung aus der angeblichen Alternativlosigkeit der Lohnabhängigkeit und der Angst vor Hartz IV lässt die Belegschaften weitere Verzichte bei Lohn wie Arbeitsbedingungen hinnehmen, anstatt die erkämpften Standards zugunsten aller Lohnabhängigen hochzuhalten

…“  Bittere Bilanz im 

Artikel von Mag Wompel vom 1. Februar 2005 in der Graswurzelrevolution

Was ist bereits gewerkschaftlich an Protesten geplant?







Bundesweite Aktionskonferenz in Göttingen am Sonntag, den 11. Oktober  




„

Wie auf dem zweiten digitalen Ratschlag am 8. September beschlossen, will der Gewerkschaftsratschlag im Nachgang der bundesweiten Proteste am 21. und 26. September eine bundesweite Aktionskonferenz in Göttingen veranstalten. Wenn weitere Kürzungen und Verschlechterungen unserer Arbeits- und Lebensbedingungen verhindert werden soll, dann können die bundesweiten Aktionen im September nur der Auftakt für weitere Proteste sein. Ziel der Konferenz ist es daher, mit möglichst vielen gewerkschaftlich Aktiven aus unterschiedlichen Regionen und Branchen in den Austausch zu treten und gemeinsam an einer wirkungsvollen Strategie zu arbeiten. Im Zentrum stehen dabei die Fragen: Wie können wir (noch) mehr Menschen in Bewegung bringen? Und wie können wir wirkungsvoll den Druck auf die schwarz-rote Bundesregierung erhöhen? Gemeinsam sollen hierfür die konkreten nächsten Schritte verabredet werden. Was steht in den nächsten Wochen auf dem Spiel und wie schaffen wir es, möglichst vielen Kolleginnen und Kollegen den Ernst der Lage bewusst zu machen?

…“ 

Einladung bei der VKG

 







[Bericht] Bundesweite Aktionskonferenz am 11. Oktober in Göttingen: Ausweitung der Sozialproteste 

 


„

Am 11. Oktober 2026 trafen sich über 200 Gewerkschafter:innen zu der Aktionskonferenz unter dem Titel „Sozialstaat verteidigen – Die Reichen zur Kasse!“ Die Teilnehmer:innen kamen aus verschiedenen Gewerkschaften und Branchen, wobei Mitglieder von ver.di und IG Metall am stärksten vertreten waren. Auffallend war allerdings, dass aus den Betrieben der Automobilindustrie, aus denen in den letzten Wochen kämpferische Aufrufe gekommen sind, kaum jemand den Weg nach Göttingen angetreten hatte.




Da der Aufruf zu dieser Konferenz ausschließlich an gewerkschaftliche Aktivist:innen gegangen ist, war es nicht weiter verwunderlich, dass aus anderen Spektren wie Sozialinitiativen oder Wohlfahrtsverbänden niemand anwesend war. Dementsprechend war die Tagung auf Themen, die für Gewerkschafter:innen unmittelbar relevant sind, wie Rente, Arbeitszeit, Befristungen etc. ausgerichtet. Die vorgesehenen Kürzungen bei Elterngeld, Wohngeld oder Unterhaltsgeld spielten so gut wie keine Rolle, obwohl diese die Beschäftigten auch treffen werden. (…)


Bei der anschließenden Diskussion saßen drei ehrenamtliche Kolleg:innen auf dem Podium: Isa Senff von ver.di, Betriebsrätin bei der Post und Mitglied im Gewerkschaftsrat, Claudia Salvoch, Betriebsrätin bei Lufthansa in Frankfurt a. M. und aktiv bei „Unkürzbar“, und Stephan Rolles, Vorsitzender des Vertrauenskörpers der IG Metall bei Saarstahl in Völklingen. Sie vermittelten einen Eindruck über ihre Arbeit zu den Sozialprotesten in ihren Bereichen. Dabei stach besonders Claudia Salvoch hervor, die die Initiative „#Unkürzbar Rhein-Main“ mit aufgebaut und damit ziemlichen Erfolg hat. Isa Senff legte Wert darauf festzuhalten, dass für sie die Frage der Befristungen sehr wichtig ist und dass dies auch im Betrieb eine große Rolle spiele, weil die Befristungen dort sehr häufig sind und schädliche Auswirkungen auf die gewerkschaftliche Organisation haben. In der anschließenden Debatte wurde ihre Position kritisiert, dass man die Gewerkschaftsführungen bei den Sozialprotesten nicht treiben müsse, weil diese sie eigenständig organisieren würden. In der Diskussion wurde sehr deutlich Kritik geäußert, dass alles viel zu zögerlich sei und auch jetzt keine Perspektive zu erkennen wäre. (…)


Vor allem die beiden AGs zu der Verzahnung von Tarifrunden mit den Sozialprotesten und die AG zu dem Thema „Massenprotest jetzt?! Brauchen wir eine zentrale Großdemo?“ fanden großes Interesse. Dabei wurde deutlich, dass viel Eigeninitiative nötig ist, wenn es Erfolge geben soll. Vor allem die Verzahnung von Tarifrunden mit den Sozialprotesten wird davon abhängen, wie diese Tarifrunden gestaltet werden. Nur wenn diese kämpferisch angegangen werden, wird es eine Möglichkeit der Verzahnung geben. Dazu müssen die Mitglieder entsprechend Druck auf ihre Vorstände aufbauen, damit dies gelingt, so wie es bei Mercedes Untertürkheim und anderen Betrieben gemacht worden ist.




Wie wir zu einer Großdemonstration kommen, spielte eine große Rolle auf der Konferenz und war der auslösende Punkt für diese Konferenz. Es soll durch Ansprachen der Kolleg:innen in den Betrieben und Dienststellen versucht werden, möglichst viele zu gewinnen, die bereit sind, zu einer zentralen Demonstration zu fahren. Dazu werden Listen erstellt werden, in denen die jeweiligen Kolleg:innen eingetragen werden können. Dieses Modell war in Frankfurt a. M. sehr erfolgreich, wo am 26. September auch die größte Demonstration stattgefunden hat. Damit soll Druck auf die Vorstände des DGB und der Einzelgewerkschaften ausgeübt werden, damit eine Großdemo in Berlin zustande kommt. Da noch nicht abzusehen ist, wann das Gesetz zur Rente im Bundestag abgestimmt wird, ist noch kein Datum für diese Demonstration festgelegt worden. (…)


Es wäre wünschenswert, wenn sich solche Initiativen für eine kämpferische Gewerkschaftspolitik vernetzen und über ein gemeinsames Vorgehen in den Gewerkschaften beraten würden.




Dass dabei auch die Aufrüstung eine Rolle spielen muss, um die Gewerkschaften dafür zu gewinnen, endlich deutlich Stellung zu beziehen, muss ein gemeinsames Ziel sein. Ohne die immense Aufrüstung und ihre Kosten zu benennen, wird dieser Protest den Sozialkahlschlag höchstens verzögern können. Es gilt eigene Positionen zu den Sozialversicherungen, zur Steuerpolitik und zur Arbeitszeit zu formulieren und dafür zu kämpfen. Dabei wird es notwendig sein, auch den politischen Streik in die Überlegungen einzubeziehen

.“ 

Bericht von Helmut Born vom 14.10.2026 bei der ISO

„Nicht mit uns!“ – Impressionen und Anmerkungen zum DGB Aktionstag in Berlin!




„

Am Samstag waren12.000 Kolleginnen in Berlin gegen die Angriffe auf ihre sozialen Errungenschaften auf der Straẞe. Es war eine groẞe und kämpferische Demonstration. Was auffiel, aber auch notwendig ist: Viele Teilnehmerinnen vertraten weitergehende Positionen, als die vom DGB offiziell ausgegebene Losung „Hart verdient“. (…)

author: Unknown
title: Koçyiğit: We want to see peace in the budget, in language, and in practice
content:
The Turkish government plans to increase spending on defense and the arms industry by more than 60 percent in 2027. Gülistan Kılıç Koçyiğit, deputy parliamentary group chair of the DEM Party, criticized these budget priorities in light of the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process. While billions are being allocated to the military and security apparatus, funding remains insufficient for social welfare, healthcare, and education, she underlined.




At a press conference in the Turkish Parliament in Ankara, Koçyiğit put the planned defense expenditure for 2027 at 3.454 trillion Turkish lira (nearly 62.1 billion euros). This represents an increase of 60.28 percent compared to the 2026 budget. The planned increase, she argued, contradicts political statements about a peaceful resolution of the Kurdish question.




“We would have liked to see a substantial portion of the budget actually allocated to improving the well-being of the population and covering healthcare and education costs,” the DEM Party politician stated.




‘We want to see peace in the budget, in language, and in practice’




Koçyiğit called for the peace process not to be limited to political statements and negotiations. She stated that a departure from decades of conflict-driven policies must also be reflected in the state’s economic priorities.




“The peace process must also be reflected in economic policy. If there is genuine sincerity here, we want to see all the effects of peace. We want to see peace in the budget, in language, and in practice. We want to feel it in every aspect of life,” Koçyiğit said.




According to the DEM Party, the planned military expenditure is part of a fundamentally misguided budget policy. Koçyiğit argued that the draft 2027 central government budget primarily serves the interests of capital, while the social needs of the population are pushed into the background.




According to the figures presented by Koçyiğit, government expenditure is expected to increase by 44.09 percent and revenue by 44.35 percent. At the same time, the budget deficit is projected to rise by 42.57 percent. She was particularly critical of the growing burden of interest payments.




Koçyiğit pointed out that the public funds earmarked for these payments could instead be used to support farmers, improve healthcare for low-income people, and safeguard the living conditions of pensioners and minimum-wage workers.




Floods hit low-income communities particularly hard




In addition to the budget debate, Koçyiğit addressed the recent devastating floods in Istanbul, which claimed six lives and caused significant economic damage. Low-income neighborhoods were particularly hard hit.




She emphasized that the consequences of such disasters cannot be attributed solely to extreme rainfall, but are also the result of inadequate preventive measures and poor urban planning. These shortcomings, she added, further exacerbate existing social inequalities, particularly in poorer neighborhoods.




Koçyiğit criticized the lack of adequate attention to public infrastructure and the protection of the population, saying: “The floods once again demonstrate how closely social inequality, political priorities, and the population’s vulnerability to natural disasters are interconnected.”

author: Mada Masr
title: State security prosecution summons Mada Masr editor-in-chief for investigation
content:
Lina Attalah, Mada Masr’s editor-in-chief, received a summons today from the Supreme State Security Prosecution to attend a questioning session on Wednesday, October 21. The summons did not say why she is being questioned.




The new investigation, Case 9072/2026, is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr, its journalists and its editor-in-chief in the past six years. The most recent was in August 2025, when the security prosecution released Attalah on LE30,000 bail. She was questioned at the time on charges of “broadcasting false news” and “using a website without a license,” based on a National Security Agency investigation report, in relation to a Mada Masr story on prisoners’ complaints of abuse in detention facilities. 

When 

asked 

why she trusted the sources cited in the story, Attalah said she had abided by professional journalistic standards and had acted in the public interest.

 She also pointed to the legally protected right to inform authorities of events through publication, noting that the outlet presents a full range of viewpoints.

The post 

State security prosecution summons Mada Masr editor-in-chief for investigation

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.

author: Unknown
title: Амеде Дюнуа - Доклад "Анархизм и Организация"
content:
Автор

: Амеде Дюнуа

Название

: Доклад "Анархизм и Организация"

Дата

: 27 августа 1907

Источник

: Anarchisme & Syndicalisme: Le Congrès Anarchiste International d'Amsterdam (1907), с. 155-161




 Четвертое заседание, Вторник, 27 августа. – Утреннее заседание. 




 Около девяти часов заседание открывается. 




 РУДОЛЬФ ЛАНГЕ избирается председателем конгресса, а КРИСТИАН КОРНЕЛИССЕН и Р. ДЕ МАРМАНД – его заместителями. 




 Повестка дня предусматривает обсуждение вопроса: «

Синдикализм и анархизм

»

[1]

. Но поскольку один из докладчиков, товарищ Джон Тёрнер, ещё не прибыл

[2]

, конгресс решает сначала обсудить вопрос: «

Анархизм и организация

». Слово предоставляется докладчику Амеде Дюнуа. 
















АМЕДЕ ДЮНУА.

 – Не так далеко то время, когда большая часть анархистов была против всякой мысли об организации. Тогда затеянный нами проект вызвал бы среди них бесчисленные протесты, а его авторов заподозрили бы в скрытых реакционных намерениях и в авторитарных замыслах. 




 Это было время, когда анархисты, изолированные друг от друга, ещё более изолированные от рабочего класса, казалось, утратили всякое социальное чувство; когда анархизм с его непрестанными призывами к преобразованию индивида представал перед многими как высший расцвет старого буржуазного индивидуализма. 




 Считалось, что индивидуальное действие, «индивидуальная инициатива» способна заменить всё. Изучение экономики, явлений производства и обмена обычно считалось чем-то незначительным, и даже некоторые из наших, отрицая всякую реальность классовой борьбы, соглашались видеть в современном обществе лишь антагонизмы мнений, к которым «пропаганда» как раз и должна была подготовить индивида. 




 Как абстрактный протест против оппортунистических и авторитарных тенденций социал-демократии, анархизм за последние двадцать пять лет сыграл немалую роль. Почему же вместо того, чтобы на этом остановиться, он попытался построить – в противовес парламентскому социализму – идеологию, которая была бы ему всецело присуща? В своих смелых порывах эта идеология слишком часто теряла из виду твёрдую почву реальности и практического действия и слишком часто также в конце концов приземлялась, хотела она того или нет, на пустынные берега индивидуализма. Так и пришли мы к тому, что перестали мыслить организацию иначе как в формах, неизбежно угнетающих «индивида», и стали систематически отвергать всякое коллективное действие. Однако именно в этом вопросе об организации, который нас как раз занимает, совершается знаменательная эволюция. Несомненно, эта частная эволюция должна быть связана с общей эволюцией, которую анархизм претерпел во Франции за последние годы. 




 Смешавшись активнее, чем прежде, с рабочим движением, мы преодолели расстояние, отделяющее чистую идею, которая так легко превращается в неприкосновенную догму, от живой реальности. Мы всё меньше интересовались нашими прежними абстракциями и всё больше – практическим движением, действием: синдикализм [то есть профсоюзное движение], антимилитаризм заняли у нас первое место. Анархизм предстаёт нам гораздо меньше в облике философской и моральной доктрины, чем в качестве революционной теории, в качестве конкретной программы общественных преобразований. Нам достаточно видеть в нём наиболее совершенное теоретическое выражение стремлений пролетарского движения. 




 Анархистская организация всё ещё вызывает возражения. Но эти возражения весьма различны в зависимости от того, исходят ли они от индивидуалистов или от синдикалистов. 




 Против первых достаточно сослаться на историю анархизма. Он вышел путём развития из «коллективизма» Интернационала, то есть, в конечном счёте, из рабочего движения. Следовательно, он не есть недавняя, наиболее совершенная форма индивидуализма, но одна из разновидностей революционного социализма. То, что он отрицает, – это не организация; напротив, это правительство, с которым, как сказал нам Прудон, организация несовместима. Анархизм не индивидуалистичен; он федералистичен, «ассоциационистичен» в первую очередь. Можно было бы определить его так: всесторонний федерализм. 




 Впрочем, непонятно, каким образом анархистская организация могла бы вредить индивидуальному развитию своих членов. Ведь никто не был бы обязан в неё вступать и, вступив, не был бы обязан из неё не выходить. 




 Возражения, выдвигаемые с индивидуалистической точки зрения против наших проектов анархистской организации, не выдерживают проверки: они с тем же успехом обратились бы против любой структуры общества. Возражения синдикалистов более основательны. Остановимся на них на мгновение. 




 Существование рабочего движения с явно революционной ориентацией является сейчас во Франции тем великим фактом, о который рискует споткнуться, если не разбиться, всякая попытка анархистской организации; и этот великий исторический факт налагает на нас известные предосторожности, которых, я полагаю, уже не обязаны соблюдать наши товарищи в других странах. 




 — Рабочее движение, – говорят нам, – предлагает вам почти безграничное поле действия. В то время как ваши группы по убеждениям, – эти маленькие замкнутые кружки, куда проникают лишь верные, – не могут надеяться бесконечно увеличивать свои ряды, – в это же время, напротив, профсоюзная организация не отчаивается в том, чтобы вместить в свои гибкие и подвижные рамки весь пролетариат. 




...

author: Cecília Melo
title: Sem educação, clima ou fome: O dito e não dito na propaganda eleitoral de Flávio Bolsonaro
content:
“A boca fala do que o coração está cheio”, diz o versículo 31 do capítulo 12 do livro bíblico de Mateus. E apesar de a fé ter entrado em cheio na campanha presidencial, a lição não parece ter sido colocada em prática pela propaganda eleitoral do candidato de extrema direita Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). Educação, fome, moradia, mobilidade e clima foram termos que nenhum dos guias de exibição gratuita na TV mencionaram ao longo de sua corrida presidencial. A palavra “constituição”, inclusive, não foi sequer mencionada pelo candidato em 14 inserções gratuitas até o momento.  




Segundo especialistas ouvidos pela 

Agência Pública

, até então, o foco do discurso de Flávio Bolsonaro esteve em provocar comoção nos eleitores, através do medo e projetar força pessoal, através da autopromoção. 




A palavra “Brasil”, por exemplo, é a mais usada pela campanha do ultradireitista, numa frequência mais de 18 vezes superior a termos como “proposta(s)”.

 Embora faça parte do seu slogan “O Brasil vai Vencer”, “Brasil” também é usado conjuntamente a “Brasileiro(s)” e “Soberania” para criar sentido de pertencimento nacional, unidade, identidade coletiva e à defesa da nação. É o que diz a professora e pesquisadora em semiótica da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte (UFRN) Lilian Muneiro.




A responsabilidade pela elaboração do conteúdo dos guias – roteiro, cenário e edição, por exemplo – é integralmente do partido político.

 A legislação garante o espaço na programação de rádios e televisões, comerciais e públicas, para veiculação do guia ou propaganda eleitoral de candidatos a cargos estaduais, federais e presidência durante 70 minutos por dia, distribuídos entre os comerciais da emissora. 




O levantamento da 

Pública

 identificou as palavras mais repetidas por Flávio Bolsonaro nos 14 vídeos de seu guia eleitoral até agora. As peças estão disponíveis no perfil do candidato no YouTube e foram exibidas em rede nacional de 28 de agosto a 14 de outubro. O levantamento também identificou palavras que o candidato não citou, mesmo sendo assuntos de preocupação mundial. 




Para a professora do Departamento de Letras da UFRN e pesquisadora em análise do discurso, Cellina Muniz, a escolha de palavras de Flávio Bolsonaro não deve ser interpretada como coincidência, pois para seu campo de estudos, as palavras que usamos não são só nossas, e carregam uma história. 

A construção narrativa visa projetar uma imagem de si “historicamente associada a regimes tipicamente autoritários. Governos totalitários, de diferentes posicionamentos ideológicos, sempre se pautaram na idolatria da figura mítica de um ‘chefe’ que tenta se afirmar simultaneamente como combatente e como guardião”, avalia.



















O dito…




O termo “medo” aparece duas vezes mais que “esperança” nos guias eleitorais de Flávio Bolsonaro. “Esse discurso tenta comover seu público e construir sua adesão por meio do apelo emocional com a criação de um ‘inimigo’ a ser combatido (as milícias, o petismo etc.)”, avalia a professora Cellina Muniz.




“O Brasil nunca teve tanto medo”, disse o candidato no programa exibido no dia 1º de setembro, se referindo a grupos de facções espalhados pelo Brasil.

 “Comando Vermelho”, “facções”, “PCC” “organizações narcoterroristas” e “milícias” não são termos dos mais recorrentes no guia eleitoral, mas aparecem duas vezes mais que as palavras “democracia” e “paz” na mensagem passada aos eleitores.




Apesar do apelo ao medo, alguns fatos conectam o candidato ao universo que critica. Ainda em setembro, a revista 

piauí

 expôs que em 2023, o senador Flávio enviou emenda parlamentar para o Instituto de Formação Profissional José Carlos Procópio (Ifop), uma ONG sediada na Taquara, reduto miliciano na Zona Oeste do Rio. O pedido partiu de Robson Calixto Fonseca, o “Peixe”, preso e condenado por agir como braço operacional da organização criminosa dos irmãos Brazão, os mandantes do assassinato de Marielle Franco. Peixe é apontado como o elo entre os Brazão e os milicianos da região de Jacarepaguá.




Em sua análise, a pesquisadora de semiótica Lilian Muneiro comentou que os vocábulos sobre segurança produzem juntos um “eixo de sentido associado à vulnerabilidade, ao risco, à necessidade de proteção e ao restabelecimento da ordem.

 Nesse conjunto, também é possível observar a dimensão passional do discurso”, afirma.




As escolhas do que compõe o discurso repetido de Flávio Bolsonaro também ajuda a indicar suas prioridades narrativas. O candidato do PL falou mais em picanha do que em Deus ou saúde durante a propaganda eleitoral. O termo “picanha” foi repetido sete vezes, e superou também os vocábulos “corrupção”, “trabalhador” e “escola”. “A picanha é o símbolo do velho, do que tem de mais velho na política, que a gente não aguenta mais, tem uma diferença fundamental entre o atual presidente e eu”, disse o candidato no vídeo veiculado uma semana antes do dia da votação.




“No conjunto dos termos e expressões que são reiterados na fala do candidato, constróem-se eixos discursivos que focam em uma ideia sem aprofundamento, imediatista, apressada e impregnada de um senso de urgência e de ‘medo’, que não dá conta nem explica o processo de construir um ‘Brasil’, como se um país continental pudesse se resumir a soluções simplistas e genéricas”, avalia especialista em semiótica e professora de ciências do consumo da Universidade Federal Rural de Pernambuco (UFRPE), Jaqueline de Melo.




Outra palavra de grande incidência foi “mulher(es)”, a quinta mais citada. No discurso de Flávio Bolsonaro ela está constantemente relacionada a “mães”, como visto no primeiro programa do guia, exibido em 29 de agosto: “Quando eu aprendi com a minha 

mãe

, que formou a minha visão de como as mulheres são. De como elas lideram de uma forma diferente. Em muitas coisas, muito melhor do que os homens”. “Família(s)” também ganhou destaque, sendo a oitava palavra mais citada.




A recorrência destes termos ligados ao feminino conotam um sentido de proteção, cuidado e à reprodução social, o que sugere uma valorização dos vínculos familiares, falou a pesquisadora Muneiro. Essa valorização não significa necessariamente uma relação harmônica na “vida real”. 




Em junho deste ano, a madrasta do candidato e senadora eleita, Michelle Bolsonaro (PL), publicou em suas redes sociais dois vídeos onde se dizia “apunhalada”, “humilhada” e “maltratada” por Flávio Bolsonaro. “Ele disse que seria melhor eu ficar fora das decisões do partido. Disse que eu havia chegado ontem e não entendia nada de política. Diante dessa humilhação, eu disse a ele que estava tudo bem. Entendi que ele não queria o meu apoio ou que este era insignificante. E então eu me recolhi”, disse a ex-primeira-dama no 

vídeo

, que, semanas depois, fez nova publicação indicando reconciliação com o enteado.



















…O não dito…




Um elemento do discurso que também é campo de estudo para analistas é o silêncio. “O não dito faz sentido também. Temas que são importantes para o cotidiano das pessoas não estão presentes, o que nos leva a entender não serem prioridades”

, opina Lilian Muneiro. Cultura, Amazônia, meio ambiente, mobilidade urbana, moradia e clima são alguns dos termos tradicionais no debate democrático mas que não foram mencionados até agora pela propaganda eleitoral de Flávio Bolsonaro. 




Segundo 

pesquisa

 divulgada em setembro deste ano pela Ipsos, saúde, corrupção financeira/política, pobreza e desigualdade social, educação, mudanças climáticas e ameaças ao meio ambiente estão entre as dez principais preocupações dos brasileiros.




“A pergunta que me faço é: de que Brasil está se falando quando as palavras ‘ladrão’ e ‘bandido’ aparecem mais que as palavras ‘escola’ e ‘trabalhador’? Como é possível mencionar os termos ‘melhor’, ‘mudar’ e ‘futuro’, sem ao menos se referir a um projeto de ‘educação pública’ e de ‘oportunidades de emprego’ e ‘geração de renda?’”

, reflete Jaqueline de Melo. 




As duas vezes em que cita o pai, o discurso de Flávio indica continuidade/referência do governo dele. “[…] gera mais empregos e o consumo aumenta. E o governo arrecada mais, taxando menos. Sem sufocar você. Isso já aconteceu com o Bolsonaro”, disse no programa exibido no dia 3 de setembro. 




O “sufoco”, no entanto, não se limita a questões de tributação, como o candidato faz parecer. No primeiro ano de governo, Jair Bolsonaro 

bloqueou

 R$ 5,839 bilhões de investimento na educação brasileira, o que levou os estudantes às ruas contra o congelamento. No âmbito do meio ambiente, em 2020 a Amazônia Legal teve 276 quilômetros quadrados de área desmatada, um aumento de 10% em relação a dezembro de 2019, segundo dados do 

Sistema de Alerta do Desmatamento

. A gestão Bolsonaro também foi marcada pelo retorno do Brasil ao Mapa da Fome em 2021, de acordo com o 

relatório

 das Nações Unidas e a ameaça constante de direitos. 




Outra ausência notada foi a da palavra “agro”. Embora se diga aliado do Agronegócio, e seja apoiado por figuras do setor, como o presidente da Frente Parlamentar Agropecuária (FPA), deputado federal reeleito Pedro Lupion (Republicanos/PR), o candidato à presidência não fez nenhuma menção ao tema durante a propaganda eleitoral gratuita. 

Os termos “feminicídio” e “racismo” também ficaram de fora das peças de campanha do filho 01 de Jair Bolsonaro.



















…e o mutante




A propaganda eleitoral do segundo turno começou em 9 de outubro e, até agora, dois programas do candidato Flávio foram ao ar: um dia 12, outro dia 14 de outubro, e as palavras trazidas por elas mantêm a tônica do que é dito no primeiro turno. 




De novidade nos roteiros da propaganda eleitoral para a TV há termos curiosos, como “hospital”, ausente em todo o primeiro turno, e menções a programas do governo federal, como o Farmácia Popular e o Bolsa Família. 




O posicionamento é uma clara resposta à campanha do adversário petista, Lula, que prioriza esses mesmos temas e põe em xeque a manutenção do investimento deles em um eventual governo Flávio Bolsonaro. 




Essa estratégia fica evidente quando se percebe que Nossa Senhora Aparecida, 

protagonista da polêmica

, que envolveu sua campanha, sobre a suposta alteração do título de “padroeira do Brasil” para “padroeira dos brasileiros católicos apostólicos romanos”, estava entre os temas do programa exibido no dia 12 de outubro, feriado nacional em homenagem à santa. 




O Farmácia Popular é um dos programas sociais protagonistas destas eleições, sendo usado pelas candidaturas de formas diferentes. A medida foi implementada em 2004 durante o primeiro mandato de Lula, que nessas eleições fala em dar continuidade à proposta. O programa conta com ampla aprovação da população, que, segundo uma 

pesquisa

 divulgada nesta quarta-feira (14) pelo AtlasIntel/Bloomberg, é um acerto para 89% dos entrevistados.




Este programa também esteve na mira dos cortes orçamentários do mandato de Jair Bolsonaro, que em 2022 enviou ao congresso uma proposta que previa 59% de redução nos recursos do Farmácia Popular.

 Em seu plano de governo, Flávio não cita o programa social, mas no programa exibido no dia 12 de outubro, afirma que o Farmácia Popular “continua, claro”. 




Metodologia







Foram identificados os 14 vídeos institucionais que integraram o guia eleitoral de TV para a corrida presencial 2026 do candidato Flávio Bolsonaro;




As peças foram transcritas e analisadas de acordo com a densidade de vocábulos utilizados;




Conectores, artigos, preposições e pronomes foram excluídos do levantamento;




Variações de um mesmo termo, por gênero ou número, foram unidos para melhor refletir o sentido do discurso exibido no guia;




A partir da lista das 106 palavras mais recorrentes, a nuvem de palavras foi criada para representar as prioridades discursivas.

author: Yohannes Woldemariam
title: The New Scramble for Africa
content:
Something important is happening across the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa. Wars that appear local are drawing in actors from increasingly far away. Ports built for commerce acquire military uses. Gold mined in conflict zones travels through international financial centers. Drones purchased abroad alter wars. Governments negotiate with foreign powers while those same powers cultivate armed groups or parallel authorities elsewhere.




Sudan, Libya, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia, Somaliland and Yemen are usually discussed as separate crises. Look more closely and the connections become difficult to ignore. A

 

United Nations investigation

 found that forces aligned with Khalifa Haftar helped move Colombian fighters through Libya to support Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces. Sudanese gold travels toward the Gulf, while

 

Chatham House has documented

 the importance of the UAE to the regional gold economy. In western Ethiopia, a

 

Reuters investigation

 found a large training camp for fighters intended for the RSF, with reliable sources saying the UAE financed the facility and provided trainers and logistical support. 




These are not isolated developments. They point toward a changing system of power around the Red Sea.




What is emerging is not another Berlin Conference. Foreign governments are not openly dividing Africa into colonies, and African governments are not passive spectators. They bargain, invite investment, seek weapons and sometimes use outside powers against domestic or regional rivals. But something more than ordinary diplomacy is taking place.




One striking change is the growing importance of powers once treated as secondary actors in African geopolitics. The United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Israel do not possess the worldwide reach of the old European empires. Yet wealth, military technology, commercial networks and strategic geography allow these middle powers to exercise influence far beyond their borders.




They are also flexible about how that influence is exercised. A government can be the useful partner in one country, a paramilitary organization in another, a parallel authority somewhere else, and a commercial company across several of them. The relationship need not be ideological, and the partner need not even be a state. Strategic usefulness can be enough.




The UAE provides perhaps the clearest example. In Sudan, it has been supporting the RSF.




In Libya, it became an important external supporter of Khalifa Haftar’s eastern forces.

 

Reuters has documented

 earlier UN findings that the UAE helped Haftar’s forces build their air power, while Turkey supplied drones and air defenses to the government in Tripoli.




The Sudan and Libya stories have since begun to merge. The

 

UN Panel of Experts on Libya

 found that Colombian fighters transited through Haftar-controlled territory to support the RSF and described Libya as an operational, logistical and tactical base.




Gold reveals the economic side of the same system.

 

Chatham House

 describes gold as a major driver of Sudan’s conflict. Between 2012 and 2022, according to

 figures examined by Chatham House

, the UAE imported 2,569 tonnes of African gold that African countries themselves did not record as exports, worth approximately $115 billion.




The connection between gold and armed power is not abstract. The

 

U.S. Treasury

 sanctioned UAE-based companies connected to the RSF network. It said AZ Gold purchased Sudanese gold apparently for the benefit of the RSF and transported it to Dubai.




Money, weapons and military support can therefore move toward African conflicts while gold and other resources move outward. The old colonial economy required foreign administrators. The contemporary system does not necessarily need them. Governments, armed groups, mining companies, traders, port operators and financial intermediaries can perform different parts of the process.




A recent

 

Financial Times investigation

 traced a much wider Emirati expansion involving ports, mining, agriculture and infrastructure across Africa. A port can be a commercial asset, logistics hub, source of political leverage and, under different circumstances, military platform.




It is here that the idea of a new scramble for Africa becomes useful.




The old scramble sought possession of territory. The emerging one can operate at a distance. An outside power does not necessarily need to govern the mine, occupy the port or administer the population. It needs influence over the networks through which weapons, money, commodities and political power move.




We might call this long-distance colonialism. I use the term as a question rather than a label for every foreign relationship. Foreign investment is not colonialism. An arms sale is not colonialism. A port concession is not colonialism. The important question is what happens when these relationships accumulate, when investment becomes dependency, military assistance strengthens coercive power, and control over ports, resources or security begins narrowing meaningful sovereignty.




The Red Sea is one of the best places to ask that question because the Red Sea has two sides.




Analysis still tends to privilege the Arabian shore: Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Israel and the Houthis. Yet Eritrea, Sudan, Djibouti and Somalia possess the ports, coastlines and strategic locations without which Red Sea politics cannot be understood. Bab el-Mandeb does not separate these worlds. It connects them.




There is historical precedent. During the Cold War, the United States valued Eritrea partly because of Kagnew Station, its strategic communications facility in Asmara. Declassified

 

State Department records

 described American military assistance to Haile Selassie’s government as the quid pro quo for Kagnew. Haile Selassie understood American strategic interest in Eritrea and used it while Eritrean self-determination was being destroyed.




That history makes Ethiopia’s renewed campaign for the Red Sea especially important. The English word “access” makes the dispute sound almost innocuous. Commercial access to a port and sovereignty over territory are entirely different matters.




Ethiopia itself demonstrated the distinction after Eritrean independence. Under the

 

1993 Transit and Port Services Agreement

, Assab and Massawa were designated as transit ports for Ethiopian commerce. Ethiopian goods moving through them were exempt from Eritrean taxes and customs duties. Ethiopia could maintain offices and warehouses.




Ethiopia therefore does not need to own Assab to use Assab. Commercial access can be negotiated between sovereign states when relations are peaceful and based on trust. Territorial sovereignty is another matter entirely.




The issue became even clearer on October 4, when the leaders of Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia met in New Alamein. Their

 

joint declaration

 reaffirmed sovereignty and territorial integrity, rejected recognition or support for Somaliland, supported Sudan’s territorial integrity and, most importantly, declared that governance of the Red Sea is the exclusive responsibility of littoral states.




Ethiopia was not named. It hardly needed to be.




Addis Ababa answered almost immediately. On October 5, after being sworn in for another term, Abiy again insisted that Ethiopia must obtain an outlet to the sea. Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry argued that changing political boundaries do not erase Ethiopia’s historical connection to the Red Sea and insisted upon its “legitimate interests” and “enduring connection” to it.




The disagreement could hardly be clearer. Four states possessing the coastline say governance of the Red Sea belongs to littoral states. A landlocked state answers that proximity and national interest give it a legitimate place in the maritime order.




But proximity is not sovereignty. Geography can create economic and security interests. It does not create ownership of somebody else’s coastline.




The four states also appear to be moving beyond declarations.

 

Reuters reported

, citing Egyptian and other political officials, that Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia agreed to coordinate military and intelligence efforts if Ethiopia’s conflict reaches its borders with Eritrea, Sudan or Somalia. That understanding does not appear in the published declaration, but it suggests that political coordination is acquiring a security dimension.




The geography explains why. Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia form an African strategic arc stretching from the northern Red Sea through Bab el-Mandeb and into the Gulf of Aden. Sudan connects this system to the RSF war and Gulf competition. Eritrea possesses Assab and a long Red Sea coastline. Somalia confronts the Somaliland question and Ethiopia’s attempt to secure a coastal foothold through its memorandum with Hargeisa. Egypt brings the Nile dispute into the same strategic space.




This response also reminds us that Africans are not passive terrain upon which outside powers compete. But “African agency” should not become another abstraction. We need to ask which Africans possess agency, what they use it for and who pays the price.




That distinction is particularly important in Ethiopia. It would be misleading to describe Abiy Ahmed and the UAE simply as partners pursuing mutual national interests. The UAE has a broad regional strategy involving ports, logistics, minerals, and political influence. Abiy’s political calculus is much narrower. His overriding interest is remaining in power.




Ethiopia is not Abiy Ahmed, and his interests should not automatically be treated as Ethiopian national interests. His government has presided over devastating internal wars, displacement and the militarization of political disputes. Foreign money, weapons, drones, and diplomatic relationships can strengthen the government at the center while ordinary Ethiopians bear the consequences.




This is precisely how the new scramble can work. Outside powers do not need local partners who share their long-term objectives. They need partners who find the relationship useful. An outside power may want a port, minerals, military access or regional influence. A ruler receiving its support may primarily want the resources necessary to remain in power. They do not need the same objective. They only need to find one another useful.




Ethiopia’s Red Sea ambitions also intersect with outside military relationships. France agreed in 2019 to help landlocked Ethiopia rebuild a navy.

 

French government sources

 describe assistance in reconstructing Ethiopian naval capacity and training. There is an irony here. France has been pushed out of parts of West Africa while helping a landlocked government on the other side of the continent develop naval capabilities as that government increasingly asserts a strategic claim to the Red Sea.




Israel represents another variation. In December 2025,

 

Israel became the first country to recognize Somaliland

, despite Somalia’s objections and opposition from the African Union. Somaliland has subsequently acknowledged receiving Israeli military and police training. Israel has also publicly supported Ethiopia’s pursuit of maritime access.




These developments do not prove a single coordinated project among Israel, Ethiopia and the UAE. Their interests differ. But they show how local territorial disputes become intertwined with the ambitions of outside powers.




Turkey represents another form of influence. Turkish drones were among the foreign weapons that altered the earlier Tigray war.

 

Reuters reported

 that Washington raised concerns about Turkish armed drone sales to Ethiopia. Ankara did not need to occupy Ethiopian territory to become consequential. Military technology itself became an instrument of influence.




Russia provides another variation. Wagner developed relationships around mineral extraction and security in Africa, including Sudan’s gold economy, while Moscow has pursued a naval presence on Sudan’s Red Sea coast. Organizations and partners can change while the strategic objective survives.




This is not simply Africa versus outsiders. Saudi Arabia and the UAE compete. Turkey and Israel pursue their own relationships. African governments bargain, resist and change partners. What connects these developments is not a secret alliance but a method of exercising power.




Ports, drones, minerals, military training, diplomatic recognition, investment, paramilitary forces and political relationships can all become instruments within the same geopolitical system.




The African shore becomes even more important when instability affects other maritime routes.

 

Reuters reported on October 5

 that Eritrea’s roughly 1,000-kilometer Red Sea coastline is attracting renewed outside attention as conflict involving Iran raises concern about shipping through Hormuz.




This is why the Red Sea cannot be understood from the Arabian Peninsula alone. Hormuz, Yemen, Bab el-Mandeb and the African shore form one interconnected system. A disruption in one part changes the strategic value of another.




Geography can be a fortune for relatively poor countries. Strategic waterways, ports and coastlines can generate transit revenue, investment and bargaining power. But geography can become a curse when powerful actors decide that strategic value gives them entitlement. A commercially valuable port requires peace, insurance, predictable shipping and trust. A war fought to obtain a port could destroy precisely the economic value supposedly being sought.




The Houthis demonstrate another part of this changing order. They are commonly reduced to an Iranian proxy, although the movement predates contemporary Iranian support and emerged from Yemen’s own history. Yet they have demonstrated how a non-state actor positioned near a strategic chokepoint can acquire international influence vastly disproportionate to its conventional economic power. Geography, missiles, drones, and political organization can compensate for weakness.




Middle powers understand the same lesson. They do not need to dominate everywhere. They need leverage at particular nodes.




This is why long-distance colonialism is worth considering. The question is not whether every unequal relationship is colonial. It is whether apparently separate relationships are accumulating into something more durable: control exercised through networks rather than governors.




Who owns the infrastructure? Who finances it? Who controls the port or airfield during a crisis? Who supplies the weapons? Where do the minerals go? Who profits? Who makes the political decisions? And who bears the danger?




Those questions reveal something the conventional political map hides.




Sudan connects Gulf money and gold to western Ethiopia and Libya. Ethiopia’s confrontation with Eritrea connects its internal crisis to Assab and the Red Sea. Egypt connects Ethiopia’s regional confrontation to the Nile. Somaliland connects recognition politics to ports and military access. Yemen and the Houthis connect the African shore directly to Bab el-Mandeb. Russia seeks access on Sudan’s coast. France trains a navy for landlocked Ethiopia. Israel recognizes Somaliland and supports Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions. UAE networks cross several of these theaters.




Once these relationships are placed on the same map, they no longer look like unrelated crises. They form a connected but fragmented system of finance, weapons, commodities, political survival and strategic leverage.




The old scramble sought possession of African territory. The new scramble can be more flexible. It can seek ports without colonies, minerals without territorial administration, and military influence without permanent occupation. It can work through a president, a general, a paramilitary organization, a corporation or a port operator.




That may also explain why it is easier to overlook. The colonial flag has disappeared. The networks have not.




The decisive question is no longer simply whether foreign powers are present in Africa. They are. The more important questions are what their presence produces, which African actors benefit from it, whose power it strengthens, whose sovereignty it diminishes, and who ultimately pays the price.




The Red Sea has two sides, but the African side is rarely acknowledged.




–




This article was first published by 

Z Network

.

The New Scramble for Africa

 first appeared on 

The Elephant
