title: Dilar Dirik: We are discussing how we can transform life through Jineolojî
content:
Speaking to ANF, Dilar Dirik, who attended the European Jineolojî Conference held in Haelen, the Netherlands, under the theme “The Role of Jineolojî in Building Democratic and Communal Life,” assessed the development of Jineolojî in Europe, its relationship with the women’s liberation struggle, and the role it needs to assume in the new period.




Stating that Jineolojî studies in Europe reached an important milestone with the first conference, held in Cologne in 2014, Dilar Dirik said that over the past 12 years, both the scope of the work and the nature of the discussions had changed.




Dilar Dirik explained that initially the focus was on defining Jineolojî and explaining its aims and mission. Today, however, discussions have moved beyond theory and are increasingly focused on concrete methods for transforming social life.







 







An important transformation has taken place since 2014




Drawing attention to the history of Jineolojî studies in Europe, Dilar Dirik said that the first conference, held in Cologne in 2014, marked an important beginning. She said: “Looking at the history of Jineolojî studies in Europe, we can say that many changes have taken place, particularly since the first Jineolojî Conference held in Cologne in 2014. At the beginning, the main aim was largely to explain what Jineolojî was, define it, and set out its aims, role, and mission.




That period was also important for introducing the world to the existence of a movement waging a struggle for freedom in Kurdistan and to that movement’s socialist paradigm, particularly its ideology of women’s liberation. However, many new developments have taken place in the meantime. Numerous women from different peoples have participated in Jineolojî studies and educational activities. The European Jineolojî Committee has made a tremendous effort in this regard. This work has had a significant impact in various fields.”




We are discussing how Jineolojî can transform life




Assessing the current stage of Jineolojî studies, Dilar Dirik said that the present conference reflects the transformation that has taken place.




Stating that Jineolojî is no longer approached merely as a science that needs to be defined, but has reached a stage at which methods for transforming life are being discussed, Dilar Dirik continued: “I believe this conference also reflects the transformation that has taken place. Different paths and methods are needed for the future of this work. Discussions are now focused more on concrete initiatives. Previously, the emphasis was largely on defining Jineolojî. What is Jineolojî? Why is it necessary? These questions now have an established foundation. Today, the struggle is increasingly about transforming life itself. That is why I believe this conference represents a truly historic step.”




Science must serve to transform life




Drawing attention to the importance of the philosophical and scientific discussions taking place at the conference, Dilar Dirik emphasized that scientific work should not be confined to academia. She criticized the relationship between the existing university system and capitalist, imperialist, patriarchal, and colonial structures, and said that alternative scientific methods need to be developed.




She continued: “It is truly valuable to hold discussions of this kind on philosophy, scientific methods, and the organization of a new mindset. Such discussions do not take place within the system we live in. These are not merely theoretical or academic debates, either. When we look at the universities within this system, we see that they do not work to transform our way of life or create a good and ethical life. They serve capitalism, imperialism, patriarchy, and colonialism. For this reason, efforts to develop a new science and different methods to transform life are extremely valuable. Because that is also the true meaning of science: knowing oneself, understanding life, and making sense of the world.”




Jineolojî is not only 




Dirik said that Jineolojî is important not only for researchers or those interested in the social sciences, and explained that this approach can find expression in everyone’s everyday life. She said: “I believe this conference is important both because of the discussions taking place and because of the issues on which the friends gathered here are focusing. The fact that this work emerges from a militant and revolutionary culture is particularly meaningful for many people who are searching for something. It is the same for me. Jineolojî is not a field that should concern only researchers or people interested in the social sciences. Jineolojî can become something that everyone can put into practice and experience in their own lives.”




Dirik also said that the existing work should not be considered sufficient, and that different perspectives need to be developed and new methods created. She said that war, fascism, and militarism are growing increasingly powerful around the world, and underlined that developing new scientific approaches capable of serving social transformation is vital in the face of these developments. “This does not mean that everything is fine as it is today. Many more changes are needed. There is much we can learn from different peoples and movements. Particularly at a time when war, fascism, and militarism are growing increasingly powerful, the search for new paths, methods, and scientific approaches is a vital necessity. This scientific work must serve not the existing system, but the transformation of the world,” she said.




Need for concrete alternatives




Dirik underlined that the discussions held at the conference must lead to concrete social projects, and said that Jineolojî should not remain merely a theory or paradigm. She added: “I believe that everyone here shares the expectation that the conference and Jineolojî studies should not be confined to the conference itself. This conference can lay the foundations for new discussions, new openings, and new relationships. However, it must not remain merely a theory, paradigm, or idea. It needs to find expression in everyday life through concrete initiatives, such as establishing cooperatives, forming communes, or developing specific projects aimed at transforming the world. Developing alternative economic models can also be part of this work. In this sense, Jineolojî can become an ideology of building an alternative society. Indeed, this is how it was also defined at the conference.”




Dirik said that Jineolojî has the potential to foster new relationships among women from different peoples, and that this work should not remain confined to a narrow circle.




She concluded: “If properly understood, Jineolojî can provide a foundation for developing new, different, and creative relationships with women throughout the world. It can become a practice that does not turn inward or remain confined within narrow boundaries, but instead creates space for creativity. It can provide an important foundation for reorganizing and recreating humanity’s most fundamental values. For this reason, I believe Jineolojî must be developed not merely as an idea, but as an approach that serves to build a different way of life.”

author: Brian Hioe
title: Animal Rights Advocates Call for Referendum on Snare Traps
content:
ANIMAL RIGHTS ADVOCATES are currently campaigning for a referendum to be held on the use of wild boar snares.

In particular, animal rights advocates have long criticized wild boar snares as overly cruel. Such traps use spring-loaded mechanisms to tighten around animals’ limbs when triggered.

Nevertheless, such traps have also been criticized for ensnaring other species, as they do not distinguish. Endangered species such as Formosan black bears and leopard cats had also been killed by such traps, as have cats and dogs, sometimes resulting in their losing limbs if they survive.

Though claims had been made that Indigenous hunters used such traps as part of traditional hunting rights, animal rights groups have generally cited that this was rarely the case, in that Indigenous hunters generally do not use such traps. By contrast, such animal rights advocates state that Indigenous hunters more commonly use traps made from wood, bamboo and vines, and other natural materials. In the past, the Central Election Commission turned down calls for a referendum on the use of wild boar snares on the basis that the referendum was unclear as to whether it pertained to traps used by Indigenous hunters.

Otherwise, such traps are sometimes used by farmers as a means of preventing damage to their crops. Animal rights advocates have called on the government to provide electric fencing, protective netting, or other means for farmers to protect their livestock and crops.

The proposals called for by animal rights advocates are relevant to the use, display, and sale of wild boar snares, as well as their import and export. It is thought that China is a major source of some of the wild boar snares used in Taiwan.

It is unclear as to whether the Central Election Commission will approve the referendum currently called for by animal rights advocates. At the same time, without a major political party endorsing it as an issue, such a referendum is unlikely to gain traction. It is to be seen if either the DPP or KMT, or perhaps even both parties, throw their weight behind the proposal.

One notes that there have been cases of political bipartisanship between both major parties on the issue of animal rights in past years, as seen with politicians of both parties supporting enshrining animal rights in the constitution. Even so, such politicians ultimately did not prove serious about such promises outside of election campaigning, as a result of which neither the KMT nor DPP acted on claims in past election cycles that animal rights would see constitutional protection.

author: Barry York
title: From student activism to Pentridge and beyond: the life of Barry York
content:
Barry York was a leading student radical at La Trobe University at the height of the movement against the Vietnam War. In 1972, along with two other student activists, Barry was arrested and held in Pentridge Prison for his anti-war activity. He recently self-published a memoir of his time in Pentridge as a political prisoner which will soon be available at Red Flag books.

The La Trobe struggle was part of the wider student movement opposing the Vietnam War, conscription and apartheid in the late 1960s and early 1970s. On campus, we challenged the university’s ties to political and economic power, including Chancellor Sir Archibald Glenn’s association with ICI (Imperial Chemical Industries, renamed Orica Limited in 1998), which had contracts with the government linked to the Vietnam War. ICI’s parent company also had links to the munitions and chemicals industries in apartheid South Africa. We opposed La Trobe’s rule barring students suspended elsewhere from enrolling, and questioned its possible cooperation with the Joint Intelligence Organisation. At the heart of these campaigns was a basic question: whose interests should a university serve?

At a mass student meeting in April 1971, attended by about 1,000 people, students endorsed demands for action on these issues. It must be noted that, at that time, La Trobe was a small campus and probably only had about 1,500 students on campus at any time. The campaign involved meetings, leafleting, debate, occupations and demonstrations. In July, students blockaded the university governing body, the Council, inside its chambers. The action had been endorsed at a student meeting, but it prompted a heavy police response and intensified the conflict between student activists and university authorities. Several activists were suspended and a larger number were fined. However, we won two key demands—the Chancellor’s resignation was announced in December, and the exclusion rule was rescinded.

This did not end the dispute though. The university authorities sought to stop the Student Representative Council from using its funds to pay the fines imposed on radical students who had been suspended. The fines totalled $3,000: a substantial amount, equivalent to about $40,000 today. Early the following year, the university sought a Supreme Court injunction barring four student activists from entering the campus. When we defied it, Fergus Robinson, Brian Pola and I were imprisoned for contempt of court. Rod Taylor evaded capture.

We were held indefinitely at Pentridge prison, a notorious high-security prison, without a criminal trial, the right to bail or appeal, or the opportunity to cross-examine witnesses. No fixed sentence was imposed. We would remain in prison until the university authorities asked the court to release us. The case raises lasting questions about freedom of expression, judicial power and the use of imprisonment to suppress political dissent.

That struggle forms the background to my memoir. Pentridge Prison closed in 1997, but the reality of life inside its bluestone walls should not be forgotten. The prison has been transformed into apartments, landscaped gardens, shops and fashionable cafés. Much of its brutality has been softened, repackaged or concealed by the redevelopment.

I wanted to recover that history by describing what it was like to be held at Pentridge as a political prisoner, first in D Division and then in A Division. Through observation and conversations with other prisoners, I also came to understand conditions in B and C Divisions and the notorious H Division, known as “Hell”.

The imprisonment of the “La Trobe Three” as we were called shows how fragile our freedoms can be. In writing the memoir, I also wanted to challenge the familiar, softened account of the youth rebellion of that era. The movement was about much more than sex, drugs, rock’n’roll and counterculture. Opposition to conscription, the Vietnam War and apartheid were central concerns. Many young people took their politics seriously; some sought revolutionary change as well as reform and were prepared to make personal sacrifices. Conventional accounts often leave that commitment in the background.

My political engagement with Pentridge continued after my release. From 1973 to 1976, I played a leading role in the Victorian Prisoners’ Action Committee. We campaigned against brutality and degrading conditions and brought prisoners’ experiences into public debate. We organised demonstrations and spoke at schools and public meetings. In one audacious action, we set up loudspeakers outside Pentridge and broadcast messages of solidarity over its walls, symbolically “unsealing” the prison. My memoir offers a history of the committee. I wanted its work, and the prisoners whose lives it touched, to have a place in the historical record.

There was a deeply personal reason for writing, too. I needed to come to terms with the young man I had been and with the Brunswick in which I grew up for 30 years from 1954: a tough, low-income working-class suburb dotted with factories, textile mills, quarries and boxing gyms. That environment shaped my class loyalties.

Prison brought my political and emotional lives together in ways I could not avoid. An affair of the heart made my incarceration much harder. The pain and uncertainty of that relationship accompanied me into cell 108 in A Division and became part of the story I needed to tell.

The memoir is therefore more than a record of prison conditions and political repression. It is an attempt to understand how family, class, politics, public rebellion and private vulnerability became intertwined—and how Pentridge led me into years of political activism and continued to shape my life long after I walked out through its gates.

Barry York blogs at C21st Left.

author: Robert Narai
title: France’s student revolt
content:
Video footage shows tens of thousands of school students packed into Place de la République in Paris, chanting, “High schools in struggle! Youth on fire! The revolution is on the march!” It’s 6 October, and outside Lamartine high school, students hold placards that read, “More class hours than sleep” and “8am to 6pm, are we students or in police custody?”

“We are protesting because we deserve the right to have a good life”, Lyna tells 

Red Flag

 via text from the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis. She is a 16-year-old 

lycéenne

 (high schooler aged 15 to 18) at Paul-Éluard; her parents are Algerian immigrants. Lyna says many young people like her have lost faith that school will lead anywhere. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s budget proposes €54 billion in public spending cuts and the abolition of 1,588 teaching posts. Combined with police who treat young people from the 

banlieues

 (working-class suburbs) like 

racaille

 (“scum”) and a growing far right, it has created a disaffected layer of young people.

“There are cockroaches and rats everywhere”, Lyna says of her classrooms. “We have classes that go from 8am to 6pm. The police harass us on the streets because of the colour of our skin and the 

banlieue

 we live in. We, the children of the 

banlieues

, are abandoned and neglected.” Yet students in better parts of Paris have joined Lyna. “We know we’re privileged, but we support the other 

lycées

”, a student at a private Catholic school told 

Public Sénat

 at the 6 October demonstration.

“

Lycéens

, and even 

collégiens

 [ages 11 to 15], are fighting above all against the two-tier education system they are victims of”, says Arthur, a student at Lycée Charlemagne in Paris and member of the New Anticapitalist Party–Revolutionaries (NPA-R), via message. “On one side, there is pressure at every level to ‘succeed at school’ or you have no future. But on the other, everyone can see that it’s cash that determines ‘success’. Year after year, the number of students per class keeps rising, up to 35, and students go weeks, even months, without a maths or French teacher.”

How the revolt unfolded

The revolt began on 21 September, when about 200 students at Saint-Exupéry high school in Créteil, south-east of Paris, blockaded their school. Within days, the blockades spread across the Paris region, as students in poor and migrant suburbs linked their own conditions—including Parcoursup (an online platform that allocates places at public universities, which entrenches class and racial inequality)—to decades of funding cuts. Hundreds of thousands of students have since joined strikes and demonstrations against the government of Emmanuel Macron, and the revolt has moved beyond the demand for decent schools into a confrontation with austerity, police violence and racism. On 29 September, more than 300,000 people marched in a public sector strike against the budget, carrying signs reading “70 billion euros for the army, nothing for education”. By 1 October, the Interior Ministry reported actions at more than 1,000 schools.

In each blockaded school, daily mass meetings (“assemblies”) decide the next day’s action, and the disempowerment of ordinary life is turned on its head. Arthur says debating the questions the movement raises gives students ownership over it. “The government sought to break the movement by discrediting high school students as rioters ‘manipulated by La France Insoumise’ [France Unbowed, the left-wing party led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon]”, he says. 

“Some students target the police, and rightly so, which has sparked debate: how can the division sought by the government be avoided? What is certain is that in the assemblies we all agree not to be divided, to denounce police violence, to demand the release of all arrested students, and to say what the placards in Lyon say: ‘The burning of garbage only scares the garbage’.”

And as the revolt spreads to every kind of high school, Arthur asks, “How can we maintain the working-class character of the movement and its demands, which was its initial strength, without it dissolving into a kind of ‘everyone together’ mentality?”

National coordination has emerged across the assemblies: 200 delegates from 71 schools met on 10 October and called actions for 13, 15 and 17 October. “No way our struggle is going to be stolen by others!”, Arthur says.

State repression

The demonstrations have been met with fierce repression from the police. By 8 October, 6,877 people had been held in police custody, 86 percent of them minors. At least 215 students have been injured, including a 14-year-old whose jaw was broken in two places, a 16-year-old who lost an eye and a 15-year-old who lost a hand to a stun grenade. Arthur says the movement is drawing the connection between austerity, police violence and racism. “No way we’re going on studying in ‘prison schools’ where young women are policed on the size of the fabric they wear, out of both sexism and anti-Muslim racism”, he says.

Intensified repression has only galvanised the movement. On 6 October, the third national day of action, organisers counted 450,000 people (the government, 266,000) as teachers, parents and workers marched with the students, chanting “High schools in struggle!” and “The revolution is on the march!” Placards read, “Generation 67 is doing May 68”. (In May 1968, a student revolt that began with clashes with police in Paris drew in up to 10 million workers in a general strike.) 

The 

lycéens

’ determination has drawn in the universities. “It’s not only about ‘defending the little ones’ but joining the mobilisation behind a common program”, says Mathis Aversenq, a university student and NPA-R member in Paris. More than 30 universities were blockaded in early October.

Sections of organised workers have joined the students. Teachers at Paul-Éluard formed a human chain to protect students from police; on 6 October, General Confederation of Labour stewards protected school students in Paris, and striking rail workers helped defend a university blockade in Strasbourg. But union leaders have repeatedly tried to limit the movement’s ability to link organised workers with the students. Most offer verbal support to the student mobilisations but refuse to call and organise strikes.

The government has attempted to placate the movement with concessions: on 6 October, “internal democracy” sessions in place of classes; on 8 October, after a television address by Lecornu, a suspension of police grenades, 3,000 replacement teachers and a small cut to petrol prices. The aim is to wear the movement out into the school holidays, which begin after 16 October.

It has not worked. On 13 October, organisers counted 480,000 people at mass demonstrations all throughout the country. At Le Havre, students marched alongside striking Siemens workers, and in Lyon police beat trade union stewards. Greta Thunberg visited Paul-Éluard in Saint-Denis and told students that “workers, university students and school students must unite”.

A history of attacks … and resistance

The revolt needs to be understood as part of a long cycle of resistance in France: public sector strikes in 1995, which forced the government to withdraw an attack on pensions; a student and union movement in 2006; the Yellow Vests in 2018; the 2023 revolt after police killed a 17-year-old; and strikes of millions in 2023 against raising the retirement age, which Macron defeated using Article 49.3 of the constitution to impose the law without a vote. Yet a new generation has learned from these cycles: unlike the 2006 youth movement, which reacted to a new law, the youth are going on the offensive and demanding more.

Each cycle of revolt has been met by a state that has grown increasingly authoritarian and racist. In his book 

Why Fascism Is on the Rise in France

, Ugo Palheta points to banned demonstrations, criminalised dissent and mainstream migration and security policies increasingly indistinguishable from the far right’s:

“More and more demonstrations have been banned in the last ten years and all dissent increasingly criminalised; Islamophobic laws and decrees have been accompanied by media campaigns targeting Muslims … In today’s France, migrants are systematically hunted down and bludgeoned by the police (on the orders of successive governments) … An ever-wider array of publications … promote a conspiratorial racism (the ‘great replacement’ theory) and calls for the establishment of an authoritarian government able to strike back against minorities and the left.”

Previous presidents Chirac, Sarkozy and Hollande, and now Macron have all pushed emergency powers and targeted “enemies within”, Palheta argues, which has dulled public alarm at the rise of the fascist National Rally.

Macron is the highest expression of this so far. His “separatism” law lets the state dissolve any organisation seen as challenging “Republican values”, and it was used against the Collective Against Islamophobia in France. “Denouncing discrimination was thus said to be tantamount to stirring up discrimination”, Palheta writes. Macron’s camp justified this with the far-right slogan of fighting “Islamo-leftism”, and calls now come from the centre as well as the far right to dissolve France Unbowed and the student union UNEF. (If Marine Le Pen wins next year’s presidential election, the National Rally would inherit this machinery to disband left-wing organisations.)

The revolt has brought that climate into the open. The establishment has cast the suburban youth as “wreckers” manipulated by France Unbowed. Presidential candidate Bruno Retailleau accused the party of “organising the insurrection” and proposed banning it. 

France Unbowed, the unions and the radical left 

France Unbowed has become a target because of its role in the revolt. Founded in 2016 by Mélenchon, it won 7.7 million votes in the 2022 presidential election and has around 70 MPs. John Mullen, a Marxist in the Paris region and party supporter, describes it as a mass reformist organisation with deep roots in social movements. On the one hand, its MPs act as a megaphone for the revolt in parliament and stand up to the police: Mélenchon told MPs to place themselves between police and students, and Saint-Denis mayor Bally Bagayoko was tear-gassed while protecting young people. “If there is one issue which is generally guaranteed to bring reformist leaders to heel, it is that of police violence”, Mullen says, and France Unbowed’s leaders have “radically broken with this politics”.

Yet France Unbowed’s strategy is to win elections and use the state to implement its program: a Sixth Republic, public banks and 831 crowd-sourced measures. On the police, it calls for “the refounding of a Republican police force”, Mullen says, rather than dismantling the apparatus that is blinding teenagers. This reformist strategy means subordinating the movement to the party’s negotiations with the state. 

According to Mathis, France Unbowed and the student unions close to it argue for a more moderate course. “They do not take part in the general assemblies and generally try to break the embryos of coordination”, he says, for fear of losing their monopoly of “representativeness”. And although many members are union activists and help build the student mobilisations, France Unbowed has no systematic intervention in the unions, according to Mullen.

The radical left plays a quieter but more driving role, says Mathis. The radicals want the assemblies to decide and workers’ organisations to call strikes now.

What gives the revolt its potential is that workers have begun to move. On 8 October, TotalEnergies refinery workers struck over pay, with the Confederation of Labour estimating more than 60 percent of staff out in Normandy. 

On Saturday 17 October, a cost-of-living day of action modelled on the Yellow Vests, student unions counted 800,000 people at more than 1,000 mobilisations. In Paris, Confederation of Labour members in red vests, health workers in white coats and young Yellow Vests marched with the students, despite a ban on protests near the Élysée Palace. But Confederation of Labour General Secretary Sophie Binet had said only that the confederation supported it, and some unions stayed away. 

Students can close schools, but only workers can shut down production, and that power could link school cuts, police violence, racism and the military budget. 

The movement is already inspiring others internationally. In Italy, Simone Montori of the High School Students’ Network says “the demands of the French students are our demands”. French students are teaching others how to fight. “The arrival of students feeds the feeling that victory is possible, because the movement keeps spreading”, Mathis says. Whether the organised working class enters the fray, and what politics come to dominate, will determine whether it can win.

title: Εκδηλώσεις την Κυριακή 18/10
content:
>Ο αγώνας των Μαπούτσε για τη ζωή και ενάντια στο κράτος, 19:00 στο λόφο Στρέφη


>Για τον νέο αντιμεταναστευτικό νόμο – 5 Χρόνια Ovradera, 19:00







Εκδήλωση: Ο αγώνας των Μαπούτσε για τη ζωή και ενάντια στο κράτος




Η Machi Miriam Mariñan, σύντροφισσα και πνευματική ηγέτιδα του λαού των Μαπούτσε στο νότιο τμήμα της Χιλής, διεξάγει έναν μακρύ αγώνα ενάντια στις νεοαποικιακές πρακτικές που αφορούν τα προγονικά εδάφη της. Συγκεκριμένα, ενάντια σε εταιρείες εξόρυξης, όπως η δασοκομική εταιρεία Minico. Αυτή η βιομηχανία, σε συμπαιγνία με το χιλιανό κράτος από τη δεκαετία του ’70 και ειδικά από την εποχή της δικτατορίας του Πινοσέτ, πραγματοποιεί τεράστιες μονοκαλλιέργειες μη ιθαγενών ειδών που προκαλούν σοβαρά περιβαλλοντικά προβλήματα, όπως δασικές πυρκαγιές.




Σε αυτή την εκδήλωση, αρχικά θα προβάλουμε ένα σύντομο ντοκιμαντέρ όπου η Μάτσι Μιριάμ Μαρινάν θα μας εισάγει στην κοσμοθεωρία των Μαπούτσε και στις απειλές εκδίωξης από τα εδάφη τους. Στη συνέχεια, θα συνδεθούμε μαζί της μέσω βιντεοκλήσης, ώστε να μας ενημερώσει για τους αγώνες της για τη ζωή και την αυξανόμενη στρατιωτικοποίηση του Γουαλμάπου (προγονικό έδαφος των Μαπούτσε).




Πρωτοβουλία αλλληλέγυης στο λαό Μαπούτσε










Εκδήλωση-Συζήτηση για τον νέο αντιμεταναστευτικό νόμο – 5 Χρόνια Ovradera




Το κοινωνικό Κέντρο Ovradera κλείνει 5 χρόνια λειτουργίας.




Κυριακή 18/9 στις 19:00: Εκδήλωση-Συζήτηση για τον νέο αντι-μεταναστευτικό νόμο – Η όξυνση της επίθεσης ενάντια στους/στις μετανάστ(ρι)ες




“…Ο νέος αντι-μεταναστευτικός νόμος που ψηφίστηκε στην Ελλάδα και ακολουθεί την Ευρωπαϊκή οδηγία, κινείται ακριβώς προς αυτή την κατεύθυνση. Παρουσιάζεται ως μέσο για πιο γρήγορες και αποτελεσματικές διαδικασίες, όμως στην πράξη κάνει την διαδικασία ασύλου πολύ πιο δύσκολη και ενισχύει την παράνομη κράτηση και τις απελάσεις. Η παραμονή σε κλειστά κέντρα όσο εξετάζεται το αίτημα ασύλου, γίνεται βασικός κανόνας, ενώ, παρόλο που οι διαδικασίες εξέτασης του ασύλου επιταχύνονται, αυτό ουσιαστικά οδηγεί σε πολύ πιο επιπόλαιες κρίσεις και άρα αρνητικές αποφάσεις σχετικά με τα συγκεκριμένα αιτήματα, αφού σε καμία περίπτωση δεν υπάρχουν οι απαραίτητες συνθήκες (έλλειψη προσωπικού και υποδομών) για να γίνουν ταχύτερα αυτές οι διαδικασίες. Επομένως, στην ουσία, αυτή η τακτική λειτουργεί ως ακόμα ένα εργαλείο για την γρηγορότερη απέλαση των μεταναστ(ρι)ών που φτάνουν στην χώρα.”

author: Andrea DiP
title: Estudantes voltam às ruas para evitar retrocesso, diz dirigente da UNE Gutemberg Rodrigues
content:
Desde o dia 5 de outubro, universitários têm organizado assembleias e manifestações em apoio à reeleição de Lula em diferentes cidades brasileiras. Uma das entidades que organiza e articula esses atos públicos, com a chamada “brigada de vira-voto”, é a União Nacional dos Estudantes (UNE), principal entidade dos estudantes brasileiros que representa cerca de seis milhões de universitários de todos os 26 Estados e do Distrito Federal.




No Pauta Pública desta semana, Andrea Dip recebe Gutemberg Rodrigues, estudante de História da Universidade Estadual do Rio de Janeiro (UERJ) e vice-presidente da UNE. Ele analisa as manifestações que mobilizam a juventude dentro e fora das universidades e relembra o papel histórico do movimento estudantil na resistência a retrocessos, na defesa da educação pública e na formação de novas lideranças políticas.




“O movimento estudantil provoca e ajuda a formar novas lideranças, mas, acima de tudo, ajuda a mobilizar e organizar a luta no nosso país. […] Por isso, o grande grito de ordem dessas manifestações é: ‘ô trabalhador, olha para cá, estou na rua para o seu filho estudar’, destaca.




Em relação aos protestos de jovens em outras partes do mundo, como na França, que começou em meados de setembro deste ano e continuam ativos, incluindo pais e professores, ele reforça que para discutir o futuro é preciso buscar as raízes dos atuais problemas. “É  importante que [as manifestações] estejam sempre norteadas e muito bem organizadas para apontar, de fato, quem são os verdadeiros culpados por essa crise mundial que vivemos”, avalia Rodrigues.




Leia os principais pontos da conversa e ouça o podcast completo abaixo.























































EP 238


											Por que os estudantes voltaram às ruas? – com Gutemberg Rodrigues							













16 de outubro de 2026


					·
				


				Vice-presidente da UNE analisa as manifestações que tem mobilizado a juventude e os desafios para além das universidades





























































0:00




-:–



















15




15
































































Veja mais episódios desta série










Na semana passada, enquanto os estudantes estavam falando sobre proteger a atual democracia, o Flávio Bolsonaro falou sobre querer mudar a Constituição. O que significa para o movimento estudantil, nos próximos anos, uma possível vitória de Flávio Bolsonaro nessas eleições? Como o movimento estudantil e a UNE pretendem atuar e que desafios vão encontrar pela frente caso esse seja o cenário?




É um total descompromisso do Flávio Bolsonaro com a nossa Constituição, com a nossa democracia, e a resposta para ele já está dada. Primeiro, acreditamos que essas mobilizações são capazes de vencer as eleições, reverter o cenário e reeleger o presidente Lula. Mas o Flávio Bolsonaro que nos escute aqui, não vai ter vida fácil se ele for eleito. No dia seguinte, já vamos organizar manifestações em defesa da nossa Constituição, do nosso Estado Democrático, e das nossas instituições de ensino. E não vai ser fácil, porque ele já está falando em usar, se possível e se necessário, a força para passar por cima, por exemplo, do STF [Supremo Tribunal Federal]. É com esse cenário que a gente está lidando.




Assim como o movimento estudantil resistiu e lutou contra a ditadura militar, seguiremos e a resistência vai ser firme. Os atos já mostram nossa capacidade de mobilização nas ruas e nós vamos lutar para que não tenhamos nenhum retrocesso em tudo aquilo que se conquistou [de] avanços e em tudo aquilo que ainda precisamos conquistar para garantir o direito pleno à educação pública para todos os jovens, o direito de ter acesso à cidade. Para que os jovens de [cidades do] interior também, tenham acesso a uma educação de qualidade, que tenham acesso ao mercado de trabalho.




A gente vai estar na rua para lutar por isso. Não vai ter moleza. Sabemos que é muito mais difícil lutar quando se tem no poder um presidente que não tem apreço pela democracia, mas já tivemos em outros momentos da nossa história, e os estudantes resistiram. Infelizmente, durante a ditadura militar, tivemos a perda de diversas figuras históricas, como, por exemplo, o Honestino, que foi morto pela ditadura militar, e o Edson Luís, aqui no Rio de Janeiro. Mas sabemos que, sem a luta e sem a resistência do movimento estudantil, não será possível, se por um acaso o Flávio Bolsonaro ganhar as eleições, a gente manter o nosso Estado, a nossa democracia e os nossos direitos. Então, ao Flávio Bolsonaro: terá muita luta se você for eleito para que a gente não tenha nenhum retrocesso na nossa educação e, para a juventude no nosso país.




Em São Paulo, as deputadas federais Erika Hilton e Sâmia Bomfim, do PSOL, foram reeleitas com as maiores votações entre as mulheres para o cargo no estado. Assim como outras figuras da nova geração da esquerda, elas começaram e se encontraram na política a partir da participação em movimentos estudantis e universitários. Qual é o papel das organizações estudantis na formação política dos jovens?




São só elas, eu acho que elas são quadros hoje nacionais. A Erika é um fenômeno no país inteiro, tem uma representatividade, é uma figura que tem ajudado, e muito, na disputa das redes sociais a favor da democracia, dos direitos da população, com uma representatividade absurda, em especial entre os jovens, que vieram do movimento estudantil. Hoje são diversos parlamentares oriundos, assim como os que já foram eleitos há muitos anos, que foram de outra quadra histórica do movimento estudantil, como, por exemplo, o [deputado federal reeleito] Lindbergh Farias [PT-RJ], que liderou o movimento de caras pintadas.




Eu acho que o movimento estudantil cumpriu e cumpre, durante toda a história do nosso país, um papel fundamental de resistência, de vanguarda contra os retrocessos e na luta por melhores condições para a educação, para a juventude, por menores igualdades sociais no nosso país. Com denúncias sobre a influência e interferência do capital externo, em especial dos Estados Unidos, em nossos processos democráticos. Então, cumpre esse papel de mobilizador, de organizador das lutas, mas também cumpre o papel de formar novos quadros políticos, e isso tem ficado cada vez mais nítido nos processos eleitorais.




Nisso, a frase do presidente Lula é muito assertiva, [quando ele diz]: ‘Jovem, você que é rebelde, que acha que ninguém na política presta, você é o próximo político honesto. É o próximo político que vai mudar esse país’. Acho que esse sentimento também tem tomado conta das pessoas que estão indo para as ruas e temos muito claro o que nos leva às ruas. Todo mundo hoje pega o celular, grava um vídeo, faz uma fala num ato, chama uma mobilização. Tem muitas mobilizações que estão sendo convocadas de forma espontânea. O movimento estudantil provoca e ajuda a formar novas lideranças, mas, acima de tudo, ajuda a mobilizar e organizar a luta no nosso país.




E existe um respeito muito grande dessa juventude que está indo às ruas com relação a quem está conduzindo as mobilizações com o entendimento de que a gente não pode cair em qualquer armadilha da extrema direita. A gente não representa o que eles querem nos impor, [nos taxando] como baderneiros ou algo do tipo. Nós estamos ali para defender nossos direitos e, por isso, o grande grito de ordem dessas manifestações é: “ô trabalhador, olha para cá, eu estou na rua para o seu filho estudar”. Isso vai ficar marcado na nossa história como o grande grito de ordem dessas mobilizações em defesa da reeleição do presidente Lula.




Há mais de três semanas estão acontecendo manifestações estudantis na França. Começam nos subúrbios de Paris e se espalham por todo o país, e também já inspiraram manifestações em outros países. Existem contatos entre Brasil e França, ou entre movimento estudantil em outros países, e há possibilidade dos movimentos estudantis crescerem mesmo por todo o mundo? Também em resposta às múltiplas crises que temos vivido hoje.




Nós temos acompanhado muito as manifestações que têm acontecido na França, assim como a UNE tem um arco de relação com organizações dos estudantes em diversas regiões do mundo, com foco nos países ibero-americanos e maior ainda na América Latina, por meio da [Organização Continental Latino-Americana e Caribenha de Estudantes] OCLAE, que é uma organização que corresponde aos estudantes da América Latina. A nossa avaliação é que essas manifestações dos estudantes, dos jovens, são fruto de um momento histórico que estamos vivendo, em que a crise do capitalismo está cada vez mais severa e mais impactante no nosso cotidiano.




Isso reflete, seja em relação à infraestrutura da educação pública, mas também e, principalmente, nas questões climáticas. São os jovens que são os mais atingidos em relação às questões climáticas, em especial os jovens que são oriundos das periferias e dos territórios, onde a política pública não chega com tanta eficácia. Então, é importante que essas mobilizações aconteçam. Agora, é importante que elas estejam sempre norteadas e muito bem organizadas para apontar, de fato, quem são os verdadeiros culpados por essa crise mundial que vivemos.




Seja a crise do capitalismo, seja a crise climática, que é fruto do capitalismo feroz, que se torna ainda mais devastador quando entra em crise. Ou, principalmente, as guerras que são fruto de uma falta de orientação no mundo, em que um presidente [Donald Trump] se acha imperador do mundo, que influencia no processo eleitoral de diversos países e fica por isso mesmo. Então, o que tem acontecido nas eleições do Brasil, a nítida influência dos Estados Unidos no nosso processo de eleição, seja por meio da Meta ou até mesmo pelo dinheiro que possivelmente o Trump está investindo na campanha do Flávio Bolsonaro, é uma eleição que vai ditar também um pouco dos rumos da democracia no mundo.




Se o Lula for reeleito, o Lula representa uma figura unânime, uma figura que representa a luta dos países do Sul global para que a gente tenha um mundo multipolar, que a gente não tenha um mundo centrado nas desigualdades, que a gente não tenha um mundo onde poucos podem mandar sobre diversas nações, que é o que tem acontecido com os Estados Unidos, que sequestra o presidente de outro país e julga a partir das leis do seu país. Essas pessoas  não escutam o processo democrático. As eleições do Brasil não estão deslocadas desse processo, que tem acontecido no mundo inteiro, de avanço do imperialismo americano, e a influência, principalmente hoje, das redes sociais que elas têm sobre o nosso cotidiano. O Brasil é uma ponta de resistência no mundo para que esses países do Sul Global possam ter a sua soberania e a democracia preservadas.

author: radical.guide
title: Locking arms on Saturday, policing texts on Sunday
content:
The speaker describes a gap many organizers will recognize: people who lock arms against the riot police on Saturday and, on Sunday, feel the urge to tell a partner who they are allowed to text. Our relationships were shaped by families, movies, the church and colonial scripts long before most of us found anarchism. That conditioning can be unlearned, and the invitation is to notice where we still treat the people close to us as property.




From the "Building an Anarchist World Through Relationship Anarchy" workshop at the 2026 International Workshops, co-hosted with the 20th NYC Anarchist Book Fair.




A Radical Guide is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that builds movement infrastructure, including a global directory of radical spaces, mutual aid programs, and educational resources for people doing liberation work around the world.




The full day: 

https://www.radical-guide.com/anarchist-international-workshops-2026/




#Shorts #relationshipanarchy #anarchism #prefiguration #decolonize

author: Ridah Hassan
title: Manosphere making classrooms toxic
content:
“I had male students threatening to rape the female students consistently. They would play ‘rape marry kill’ and used my own name frequently in their ‘game’.”

“Students saying ‘good girl’ to teachers.”

“Less respect for female staff vs male in behaviour—even with the same approaches they instantly listen to males more. More inappropriate jokes—racism, homophobic and sexist jokes with little consequences. Visible [and] audible dismissal/rejection of female staff to their faces when they appear to take classes.” 

These are quotes from a Monash University report which has cast light on the disturbing sexist conditions faced by teachers and students in primary and secondary schools across the country. 

Duty of Care: Teachers’ experiences of sexism, misogyny and sexual harassment in Australian schools

 is based on the testimony of 2,600 educators and reveals the breadth and depth of the crisis. 

A common theme in the report is the lack of respect male students show female teachers. This includes frequent interrupting, ignoring of instructions, mocking and mimicking, speaking disrespectfully and refusing to accept responsibility when challenged about inappropriate behaviour. Physical aggression and intimidation were also reported, along with threats of more serious physical and sexual assault. Male students frequently make “derogatory comments toward females focusing on appearance and worth”, “jokes about gender roles e.g. the kitchen”, “inappropriate sexualised remarks about female bodies, including specifically about peers and/or staff” and “[making] sexual noises in the classroom” while female staff are trying to teach.

This behaviour is contributing to the burn-out of teachers in a profession already facing shortages due to poor pay and unmanageable workloads. One respondent put it clearly: “Being the front line and bearing the brunt of misogyny is exhausting and erodes self-worth”. According to the report, 77 percent of teachers say that sexism and misogyny have a “negative” or “very negative” impact on their wellbeing, and more than 50 percent of female teachers report that they either “occasionally” or “frequently” consider leaving the profession because of it. And the situation is getting worse—both primary and secondary teachers reported that gendered violence on the part of students had increased significantly in the previous twelve months.

Given adult teachers are feeling undermined, threatened and belittled by male students’ behaviour, the impact on teenage girls should be cause for immediate action. According to the report, “Younger students are comfortable using misogynistic language without thought e.g. calling girls in class a ‘slut’ ‘whore’ because they won’t share a highlighter”, and “Women/girls in class are okay with being treated with misogyny as this is seen as ‘normal’ now. They do not retaliate and internalise, making emotional regulation hard”. Another teacher observed: “Female students are scared to speak out and express their opinions in class with males who chastise them. I am noticing students are very hesitant to participate in discussion these days whereas it used to be female students being quite eager to share ideas and answer questions. Female students appear angrier than in the past as well”.

Male students direct sexist and misogynistic language towards their female peers freely, entrenching a toxic gender divide among students. Again, the statistics bear this out, with 80 percent of respondents agreeing that the behaviour is having a negative impact on student wellbeing. In observing and being victim to male students’ sexism—including constantly disrupting learning and making spaces hostile—girls are being socialised to accept dehumanising language and treatment and to make themselves small targets by withdrawing and accommodating to the selfish and anti-social behaviour of boys. 

And though there are undoubtedly some who are willing to challenge their peers’ appalling behaviour, it is an unacceptable environment for female students to be expected to navigate every day, while at the same time trying to do the actual tasks of deciphering Shakespeare or learning calculus. It is well established that students learn best when they feel safe, supported and respected. This is currently not the case for female students at Australian schools. 

Misogyny and the rise of the ‘manosphere’

Further evidence of the problem of sexism among male students is the frequent cases of particularly egregious behaviour that make the news. Student from 

Scots College

 and 

St Gregory’s College

 in Sydney, for example, are currently facing court for a series of alleged crimes including sexual assault, rape and common assault for two separate incidents in July and August. 

An independent cultural review of St Kevin’s College

 in 2021 confirmed that sexist and misogynistic behaviour and views were “still clearly an issue” at the school. It was commissioned following an incident in 2019 when St Kevins students horrified the public with their 

misogynistic chants on a Melbourne tram.

 In 2020, a scavenger hunt organised by students at the Shore School, one of Sydney’s most elite institutions, was 

leaked

 

and found to contain activities such as “Get with an Asian chick”, “Play porn out loud on public transport” and “Get with a chick which is 3/10 or lower (photo of the chick + the dirty work)”. And in 2024, 

male students at Yarra Valley Grammar

 were suspended when their rating system of female students was discovered. 

As many respondents to the Monash University survey noted, an important driving force of this sexism is the rise of the online “manosphere”. This consists of the open use of misogynistic language, the revival and confident reiteration of conservative gender-stereotypes, the glorification of aggressive and violent masculinity and the dehumanisation and objectification of women. It is readily accessible through various online channels, with algorithms actively targeting boys and young men. More than 87 percent of teachers noted the influence of these ideas on the boys they teach, with one describing how they have to be careful “when discussing issues regarding female contribution to society or feminist ideas so as not to provoke students to make manosphere style commentary”. Many say they face “hostile attitudes toward discussions of women’s rights and social equity” from male students, who deny systemic issues of gender inequality, question the relevance of discussing these topics, and approach them with defensiveness and aggression rather than empathy, curiosity or an openness to learning.

These sexist and misogynistic ideas resonate with boys and young men not just because they offer a sense of power and superiority in a world where feelings of powerless and inadequate are endemic. But also because they are reinforced and validated by the wider organisation of society. 

Women’s oppression under capitalism 

Well before the manosphere existed, capitalism was systematically denigrating women and their contribution to society. Women’s work and intellectual and creative contributions to society is and has long been devalued and belittled. Women are concentrated in low-status jobs and are paid less on every measure in comparison with men. They are dehumanised and objectified in pop culture, advertising and pornography, with their bodies used as props to sell things, often on the basis of making women feel they are ugly, unwanted impositions on the world unless they fix themselves with diet, cosmetics, medication, surgeries. And that they only have value insofar as they are appealing to men. Women’s wants, needs, questions and ideas are a side show in much of public and private life—in the workplace, within their families and relationships, and in popular culture. 

Women exist to be judged, policed, made the butt of jokes, dismissed, controlled and purchased. In this context, it is no wonder young people are susceptible to the extreme sexism and misogyny that is now available to them online. 

The fact that sexism in schools and society is on the rise is connected to an interesting and challenging fact of the situation; views on gender and gendered behaviour are going backward by many measures at the same time that there is an increase in curriculum content to educate children about sexual and romantic relationships, consent, stereotypes, and the reality of the sexual and domestic violence epidemic. This gap between intention and reality highlights the limitation of education programs in the absence of addressing the structural, social and economic roots of women’s oppression. 

This is also why it is not just young people who hold sexist views. A Melbourne University report, 

Misogyny, Online Radicalisation, and Youth Extremism in Australia

 which asked 1,122 young people aged 13 to 17 and 2,307 adults about their views on gender, sex and sexual relationships found similar issues across age groups. For example, about 31 percent of males from each generation surveyed (Gen Z, Gen X, Millennials, Boomers) agreed with the statement: “Attempts to give equal opportunities to women in Australia have gone too far”. A quarter of both Gen Z and Gen X males agreed that: “The husband is the head of the household and the wife should be obedient to him”, and more than 23 percent of Gen Z males and 20 percent of Millennial males responded positively to the statement “Sometimes women bother me just by being around”. 

The right weaponises misogyny

The response to the Monash University report has not been across the board soul-searching about how to combat this epidemic of sexism and support female educators and students forced to contend with such hostility. Rather, the right has seen it as an opportunity to attack teachers and engage in a culture war in which they identify men as the victims. 

Liberal leader Angus Taylor claimed that the Respectful Relationships Education program, which aims to facilitate discussions about respect and gender equality, as well as consent in relationships, is simply teachers “pushing an agenda”. Nationals’ troglodyte Matt Canavan agreed that the program is “anti-boy”. Breaking stereotypes in her own way by proving it's not 

only 

men who are misogynists, Pauline Hanson claimed that teachers are “brain-washing” students with these discussions about sexism, gender-roles, consent and how to navigate relationships. 

Their agenda is to demonise social movements that aim to advance the interests at those at the bottom of capitalism’s pecking order—in this case, women. If women can break free from the box they are put in, there’s no reason that other workers, refugees, migrants and others can’t question and challenge the status quo which oppresses them too. And this is not good for profit-making and strengthening the nation that facilitates it, which is the key concern of the right.

Fighting back

The conclusions of the Duty of Care report’s authors are a far cry from those of the right. Their official recommendations include reference to the pay and conditions of teachers being crucial to redressing the crisis of sexism in schools. If teachers, who are mostly women, were better paid, had better working conditions and if the profession was less denigrated by the media and politicians among others, it would certainly make it more incongruent for students to denigrate teachers in the classroom. 

Other recommendations include facilitating whole-school implementations of Respectful Relationships Education, improving work health and safety requirements in schools, and establishing avenues for compensation if they are breached. It is definitely true that the sexist and misogynistic abuse educators experience at work would not be accepted in most comparable workplaces, and educators should have the right to a safe workplace free from actual or threatened physical or sexual violence. At the moment, schools simply can not guarantee this. More funding for teachers and education support staff, smaller class sizes so complex and challenging behaviours are more manageable, funding for allied health such as social workers and psychologists would all help. More educational and critical discussions about gender and relationships in schools would also be welcome. 

However, we need to go much further. 

The misogyny in schools is an echo of the misogyny that characterises the rest of society, and is being normalised by the far right that is gaining ground at an alarming rate. We need an organised fightback against this. We need a political movement that promotes a vision of society that is contrary to the divisive prejudices the right thrives on—that promotes the common interest between workers, the strength that comes from unity and solidarity with the oppressed, and the power that can back that up when workers stand together and take action. We need to use every instance of resistance to reassert women’s rights, fight for dignity and equality. Women will not achieve dignity and equality in schools or anywhere else as long as profit rules and people are a means to an end. We need a socialist vision and a socialist movement that can offer something completely different.

Ridah is a public school teacher in Victoria

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: Westsiders campaign against AI hub
content:
I met Anthony and Samantha on Holden Road in Plumpton, 40 kilometres west of Melbourne’s CBD. We’ve parked our cars at the Melbourne Renewable Energy hub gate, behind which a huge expanse of land could become home to a hyperscale data centre owned and operated by Syncline Energy. 

The surrounding area is a green wedge, meaning that it should be protected from industrial and urban sprawl. There’s a free-range egg farm, rolling fields, some houses and a few horses. Samantha, who is campaigning against the development, lives five minutes away in Diggers Rest and learned to ride a horse right here. In fact, one we are looking at is called Betsy and is the very same horse. 

A 

petition

 against the AI hub raises concerns about environmental destruction, including “endangered ecological vegetation communities, biodiversity corridors, areas of Aboriginal cultural heritage sensitivity and conservation efforts”.

The Plumpton plan is still awaiting approval from the state government. If it gets it, the site will host a

 

350-hectare AI hub

, which the 

Age

 reports is the size of 175 MCG playing fields. The facility will have a maximum power draw of 2.5 gigawatts, more than the entire output of the Loy Yang A coal power plant. Loy Yang A provides around 

30 percent of Victoria’s power

. It would use more power than every other data centre currently operating combined. 

“It’s such a blatant display of profit over people”, says Anthony, who has also been campaigning against Syncline’s plans for months. 

Their campaign group started after a community meeting of 150 people in Sydenham. “Anthony and Ella produced these awesome pamphlets, so we’ve been doing lots of letterboxing”, Samantha says. “We also hosted an information night [and] we’ve got a day of action coming up. We also attended the Senate inquiry as witnesses.” 

The Senate inquiry held hearings in Yarraville last month. The inquiry has heard from residents, local politicians and data centre CEOs. Local testimonies include stories of monolithic structures bearing down on residents, diesel emissions and pollution, drone surveillance, and concerns about fire risk.

“The Plumpton site will have huge amounts of lithium-ion batteries, and we feel like this hasn’t been assessed or regulated enough”, Samantha says. Lithium-ion batteries can trigger thermal runaway, releasing toxic fumes and a self-sustaining fire. Because data centres need 24/7 power, they often rely on diesel or gas generators. This increases the risk of uncontrollable fires. “The combination of lithium batteries and diesel is a pretty nasty sort of fire”, a member of Fire Rescue Victoria 

told the ABC 

in June

. 

The Plumpton group is one of many across Melbourne, mostly in working-class areas. The wealthy areas of Melbourne are unlikely to be high on the list of potential sites for the centres. In fact, Belinda Dennett, CEO of the data centre lobby group, said she wouldn’t want to live near one. Samantha describes her as “AI in human form”. Anthony is frustrated that communities have no say in whether centres get built. “It’s so clear that the system is not set up for a democratic decision”, he says.

Samantha says those living near the site don’t have much idea what is coming to their doorstep: 

“Last time I checked, there’s about 80 residents around here. And none of these guys knows about it. It will be in full view of their backyards, and they almost don’t want to believe me; they think I’m almost a conspiracy theorist. But it’s going to be built here, and they haven’t been notified”. 

That’s why Samantha and her co-organisers have been hosting outreach meetings, and doing the letterboxing and door knocking. They want to inform their neighbours what is coming to their communities and fight it together. 

According to Samantha and Anthony, Syncline’s CEO is a “schmoozer”. At the Senate hearings, he said his company has done a “bad job” at community outreach. He’s trying to turn that around and convince locals the AI hub will benefit them. 

“He is very good at convincing people that this will benefit them, without explaining how”, Samantha says. Anthony and Samantha feel the campaign has put pressure on Syncline, which is now trying to win support for its plan by claiming it will create new jobs. But those in the campaign aren’t fooled.

They also aren’t fooled by the Labor government’s Sustainable Data Centre Action Plan. The government promises that data centres won’t be built near residential areas and requires them to bring their own energy and water. But on closer inspection, these requirements are easy to get around. If recycled water isn’t yet available, data centre companies can simply submit a “plan with the water corporation to offset interim drinking water use”. For electricity, they only have to invest in new renewable generation and storage. Samantha is furious: 

“None of it’s due to come into effect or be legislated until early 2027. So even though we have been waiting almost twelve months for this plan, we still need to wait until early 2027 for legislation to catch up. And that’s just not good enough when we’ve got the department of planning process fast-tracking the data centre application in as little as 28 days.” 

Locals living close to existing data centres are unhappy too. The plan doesn’t affect centres that have already been built or approved. Anthony sums up the mood: “The west is sick of it. The working class is sick of being taken for granted. But we are stubborn people, and we won’t go down without a fight”.

title: Précautions post-pillage
content:
Tout le monde est au courant, les magasins de la Presqu'ile et de la Guill' se sont tous fait ouvrir hier pendant de longue longue looooongue heures. Une belle démarche de prix libre dans un monde où tout augmente. Le truc évidemment, c'est que ce genre de chose ne va pas sans répression, alors voici quelques tips

 

!




Lors des derniers grands moments de pillages (notamment les révoltes suite à la mort de Nahel), les flics ont écumé les sites de revente pendant une longue période après le mouvement, en quête d'objets récupérés à prix très libre pour être revendus ensuite. Pour éviter ça, éviter de revendre les trucs dans les mois qui viennent, favorisez le don à des proches ou attendez les périodes intenses d'échange et d'achats de marchandises comme Noël, les fêtes de fin d'année ou l'Aïd...




Idéalement, ne traînez pas avec les objets que vous avez récupéré pendant un petit moment, c'est frustrant, on sait, mais vous chérirez d'autant ces objets que les souvenirs qui vont avec si vous ne vous faite pas péter avec

 

!

author: Unknown
title: ABD Başkanı Trump’tan İran açıklaması: “Orada biraz daha uzun kalabiliriz”
content:
ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, 3 Kasım’daki ara seçimler için yürüttüğü kampanya kapsamında Kentucky eyaletinin Highlands Heights kentinde konuştu.

ABD ve İsrail’in 28 Şubat’ta İran’a başlattığı saldırılara ilişkin değerlendirmelerde bulunan Trump, İran’ın nükleer silah sahibi olmasına izin vermeyeceklerini söyledi. Trump, saldırılarla İran’ın nükleer kapasitesini ortadan kaldırdıklarını savunarak şu ifadeleri kullandı:

“Biliyorsunuz, güzel İran İslam Cumhuriyeti’ne yaptığım o küçük gezide, onları perişan ettik. Ama o gezide, nükleer kapasitelerini de ortadan kaldırdık.”

“Orada biraz daha uzun kalabiliriz” diyen Trump, İran'ın silahlarını ortadan kaldırdıklarını ve yeniden silahlanmasını engellediklerini öne sürdü. Trump, “Bunu yapıyoruz. (Silahlar) geri gelmeyecek. (Bu) çok çabuk bitecek” dedi.

Trump, ABD’de artan akaryakıt fiyatlarının İran’a yönelik sürecin tamamlanmasının ardından düşeceğini savundu. Trump, “Bu arada, bu süreç sona erdiğinde, benzin fiyatlarınız da eskisinden daha düşük seviyelere inecek” diye konuştu.

Konuşmasında Rusya-Ukrayna savaşına da değinen Trump, ilk görev döneminde ABD ordusunu yeniden inşa ettiğini belirterek eski Başkan Joe Biden’ın bunun “büyük bir kısmını” Ukrayna’ya verdiğini iddia etti.

Ukrayna’ya sağlanan desteğin karşılığında Avrupa Birliği’nden para istenmesi gerektiğini söyleyen Trump, “Çok fazla verdi. Onlar ödeyeceklerdi. Tek yapması gereken Avrupa Birliği’nden para istemekti. Onlar ödeyeceklerdi, ben de gelip bunu yaptım” ifadelerini kullandı.

ABD’nin Venezuela’dan ekonomik kazanç sağladığını öne süren Trump, “Biliyor musunuz Venezuela’dan ne kadar para çıkarıyoruz? Venezuela’dan yüzlerce milyar dolar para çıkarıyoruz” dedi.

Trump, yönetiminin görevde bulunduğu döneme ilişkin ise şu değerlendirmeyi yaptı:

“Grönland’ı, Venezuela’yı, İran’ın nükleer silaha sahip olmayacağını, iş imkanlarını, her şeyi ekleyin, iki yıldan çok daha kısa bir sürede, ülkemizin tarihinde hiçbir yerde böyle bir iki yıl yaşanmadı.”

Suların temizlenmesi, caddelerin temizlenmesi, zarar ve ziyanların tespit edilip Pazartesi günü hesaplarınıza yatırılması, hayatın normalleşmesi.
