Anthropologists have yet to give up their calipers

Secret history, or shaky historiography?

Occult Features of Occult Features

I have been sitting on this review for quite a while. This short book comes up quite often when combing through anarchist literature on occultism (and vice-versa). With the release of more than a million documents from the Epstein files bringing new relevancy to the issue of conspiracy theories, I think the most fortuitous time to publish it has come. Or went, because I again sat on this review for many months.

Occult Features of Anarchism, by Erica Lagalisse, concerns the alleged roots of classical anarchism (and the wider radical milieu) in Western esotericism and in particular, the late antique Corpus Hermeticum. This is combined with an anthropological analysis of conspiracy theories, loosely (indeed, very loosely) connected through the Masonic tradition.

Lagalisse begins Occult Features with two pastiches in her activist and fieldwork. First, she recounts dissuading a fellow activist from accepting an antisemitic conspiracy theory during an EZLN event in Montreal (pg. 3). Then, she observes Montreal anarchists marginalizing an Indigenous Mexican woman named Magdalena – on a speaking tour organized by the EZLN – due to a combination of gendered and racial prejudice (pg. 6). These events left her deeply changed, and her research interests shifted to the influence of theosophy and Freemasonry on classical anarchism (pg. 8). Through this analysis, she hopes to “illustrat[e] the cosmology of classical anarchism” and thus complicate anarchism's alleged relation to secularity (pg. 11). For Lagalisse, this sort of analysis is central to “a decolonized anarchism that properly challenges gendered power”, in which the modes in which the modern colonial state privatizes religion and gender – while reproducing its own cosmology and patriarchal structure – are studied (pg. 12). Thus her focus on esotericism: “any inquiry into the gender of the modern revolutionary left that digs farther back in history than the union movements of the masculine wageworking proletarian [...] necessarily stumbles upon the institution of Freemasonry, among other clandestine fraternities” (pg. 8).

Her first premise is that anarchism, like all Western political theory, is innately tied up with theology, following from Schmitt and Sahlins – particularly, the dialectic between the immanence and transcendence of God. Utopian socialism, anarchism, and Marxism rely on a “cosmology that is incipient in the Middle Ages, changing and crystallizing in the Renaissance, and gradually given a scientific makeover throughout the Enlightenment and up to the twentieth century” (pg. 18). A crucial point for Lagalisse here is the “shift from the spontaneous millenarian movement to the organized heretical one” which is related to the “dissemination of diverse mystical doctrines” that began in Europe during the Crusades – the Corpus Hermeticum is a “largely unrecognized” source of modern leftist politics (pg. 20). This elite practice of magic was in stark contrast to the Early Modern witch trials, which for Lagalisse, represents the gendered persecution of lay healers, wise women, and other “proper empiricists”, which was occurring as the fathers of science were trying to turn lead into gold (pg. 30).

Freemasonry arises out of this gendered state of affairs. Through their influence on Freemasonry, Lagalisse contends that “while real builders are starving”, elite men are more concerned with worshipping the Grand Architect and deny entry to “Jews, women, servants, and manual laborers” (pg. 40). Freemasonry, for Lagalisse, “is what social movements look like after the witch hunts” (pg. 37). From Masonic lodges come revolutionary brotherhoods, formed by Masons and quasi-Masons like Proudhon, Blanqui, and Bakunin (pgs. 44-50). Masonic influence is apparent even on the level of leftist symbolism, from the “pagan pentagram” (the red star) to the “compass, level, and plumb line of Masonic iconography” (pg. 54). This cabalism was tempered by theosophy, Swedenborgianism, and other esoteric movements, through influential anarchists like Owen, Fourier, and Saint-Simon (pg. 57). The Marxian dialectic, too, is rooted in occultism, through Hegel, who had a deep interest and influence in Hermeticism (pgs. 64-66).

From here, Lagalisse begins analyzing anarchism as a historical object. The “gendered quality” of anarchism is “arguably more fundamental” than its relationship to male worker’s movements but extends back and “articulates with an occult cosmology that is older still” (pg. 79).

The first and most pertinent aspect of any book review is whether or not one should endeavor to read (and of course purchase) said book. Unfortunately, I think the chief issue with Occult Features is its diminutive audience. For whom is this written, if not other anthropologists with a very narrow interest in anarchism as a movement? As an archaeologist (a bit of Ausonia lore for you) and a so-called anarchist I suppose I qualify, but the ultimate pith of her argument is, to be frank, old news to me. I am not white, a secularist, an atheist, or someone who takes 19th century political theory very seriously. Nor am I one to be particularly defensive of the “anarchist” label or movement, or one who is unfamiliar with the history of Western esotericism. I do not need to be told, by a white academic no less, that anarchist theory has historically been dominated by white men of a certain economic standing, and that this patterns much of the anarchist movement today. Indeed this can be said of practically all political movements, and really, all modernity – a point I shall return to.

Despite Lagalisse's description of the work as a “short, accessible work” (pg. 15) with import for radicals, for someone without a background in higher education, her opaque references are unlikely to be decoded. Normally I resent claims like this, as they are often deployed as thought-terminating clichés or ego-maintaining mechanisms, but in this case, it genuinely feels intentionally convoluted. To illustrate this point, towards the back cover, she matter-of-factly states that “the cross-cultural dialogues among heretics during the Crusades happened in the context of complex power relations” (pg. 75-76). In what other context could “cross-cultural dialogues” have happened during the Crusades, or indeed any other point in history, let alone between religious minorities? Besides intellectual posturing, there is nothing of substance in such a sentence, and Lagalisse does not elaborate – it seems a half-hearted attempt to shove another marginalized author into her references, in this case, the great Edward Said. It is not the only time she does this.

Despite the fact Lagalisse recognizes the anarchist “selective fascination with Indigenous cultures and cosmologies” as having an origin in the colonial encounter (pg. 60-62), she makes very sure we all know well that she is referencing Indigenous women like Audra Simpson unlike everyone else (pg. 82-83). This is shown to be plainly fetishistic when she defends a white academic who falsely presents herself as Indigenous American simply because she has applicable theory for her study (footnotes on pg. 83).[1] For Lagalisse, it is good enough that this “hotly debated” academic is “ignored”. Of course, settlers do not claim to be Indigenous to be ignored, but to siphon off the little capital (both social and material) relegated to Indigenous people in academia.

This tokenization is also present in her critique of the treatment of antisemitic conspiracy theories in activist circles. Recounting an incident on an Occupy Wall Street listserv, Lagalisse recounts how some Jewish participants elected to “straighten out” an antisemite rather than excise them from the email forum. This, apparently, is presented as evidence that antisemites should be educated. Her entire account of the discussion is based on Jewish participants vs. non-Jewish participants, though it is unclear how she is identifying each. Perhaps grilling each discussant on their respective ancestry? Indeed, anthropologists have yet to give up their calipers (pg. 96-101).

Lagalisse's apparent lack of self-awareness was a major hurdle when reading this work. She is a white, college-educated Québécoise from Montreal, and at times this is painfully apparent. Lagalisse's “hope that some persons identified as ‘conspiracy theorists’ read [this book] and feel both productively challenged and validated by [her] words” (pg. 110) is foolhardy – at least for the “subaltern” conspiracy theorist she describes as believing in a fraternity of Jewish men who know the secrets of magic and mind control (pg. 3).

This is not only laughable, but ironic, too. Lagalisse levies a very particular critique of anarchism:

...as any anarchist can see, fluency in a particular vocabulary, knowing the names of certain historical figures, and being vouched for by someone “in the know” is all requirement for entry into the anarchist club, as is a commitment to a specific ideological constellation informed by the history of its practice, wherein men's oppression by the state becomes the prototype for power in general (pg. 81).

Lagalisse’s observation lacks all semblance of self-awareness except for scant couple of sentences in the last quarter of the book, in which she notes that “anarchist academics...do want me to be accepted into the club and kindly offer [her] the password” (pg. 87) and that “[i]t is arguably no coincidence that as a university professor [she] may respectably discuss Central Intelligence Agency involvement in drug trafficking, yet a truck driver who says the same thing is often tossed off as a ‘crazy conspiracy theorist’” (pg. 101). She is keen to show her entrance into a club of her own, deploying particular scripts and vocabulary, and fetishizing colonized subjects as ethnographers love to do.

Lagalisse, for her dependence on historical methods, shows a strange silence towards very pertinent topics in medieval and Renaissance history of the Western esotericism, and deep mischaracterizations of others. In short, Lagalisse’s historiography is incredibly shaky, and she does not seem to pay close attention to her sources. She peppers her book with a number of minor factual errors, which range from small issues with her Latin, to incorrectly implying that the attribution of the Corpus Hermeticum to Hermes Trismegistus is a later aberration,[2] to anachronistically transposing a medieval Syriac tract to a context 600 years before its composition,[3] to a pet peeve of mine – claiming that Ramon Llull was “primarily influenced by” kabbalah (pg. 25).[4] Lagalisse states outright that Leo Tolstoy was a theosophist with no supporting evidence, while the sources she cites do not mention theosophy (pg. 59). She authoritatively claims that Hegel was a Freemason, citing Susan Buck-Morss, who makes no such claim (pg. 66).[5] These errors are admittedly small, and sometimes inconsequential, but they do not inspire confidence in Lagalisse’s grasp of this subject or her scholarship.

Other problems with her historiography are more complex. Following the Spanish scholar Alberto Valín Fernández, Lagalisse assumes that the origin of the red star and the circle-A have direct origins in Masonic iconography. She identifies the logo of the Federación Regional Española de la AIT as composed of the Masonic “compass, level, and plumb line” altered such that the compass and level form an A inside of a circle (pg. 54). It is dubious as to whether or not the circle-A can even be considered truly Masonic, in the sense of having a direct origin in Freemason lodges of the 19th century. Why should we accept that the compass, level, and plumb line are emblematic of speculative Masons (initiates) and not operative masons (manual laborers who actually work with stone)? Parsimony dictates that we should assume the simpler hypothesis is the correct one: regardless of the influence of the former, which I am not convinced of, surely the latter were more influential in a labor union?

It is not impossible that Freemasons could have proposed or influenced the iconography of the FRE-AIT. But whether such speculation is relevant or should be accepted as evidence of the Masonic cosmology of anarchism is another question altogether. A much more egregious example of her evidence-free sort of historical reasoning is apparent in her analysis of a zine, circulating in Montreal, which features a prominent circle-A in a Gothic typeface. Lagalisse claims that the icon displayed a “clearly stylized plumb line of Masonic iconography – quite possibly unbeknownst to the zine maker”. She contrasts this with the zine itself, which emphatically rejects “waiting on someone else or some divine force to change shit” (pg. 78). This particular example, however, is merely a coincidence . The angular hairlines and lozenge-shaped finials are ornaments of the blackletter script: there is no shortage of “plumbobs” in Gothic capitals.[6] Lagassile can perhaps be forgiven for failing to recognize this – I only recognize it myself for being involved in Chicano gang culture in my youth, though of course we called it an “Old English” handstyle – however, it should not be forgiven that she takes her ultimately baseless speculation for fact, especially as she attempts to ‘educate’ those without higher education.

Similarly, she claims that the Renaissance and the Enlightenment was “inaugurated” by “the dissemination of diverse mystical doctrines” like “Platonic philosophy, Pythagorean geometry, Islamic mathematics such as algebra, Jewish mystic texts, and Hermetic treatises” from medieval Arabic translation movements (pg. 20). Rather than being “well known” as she claims, it is actually an inversion of the traditional mainstream view – in which new translations from Greek, connected to the fall of the Byzantine Empire in 1453 and the exile of Greek scholars, which inaugurated the Renaissance and moved scholarly culture away from Arabic-based traditions and towards a ‘rebirth’ of classical philosophy from the ‘original’ sources.[7] This is a major lapse in Lagalisse’s scholarship, as the image of the medieval world which she draws from is in many ways constructed by Renaissance scholars who were eager to separate themselves from the ‘Gothic’ past. In the medieval period, for Lagalisse, “man’s wish to ‘operate’ on the world [...] was attributed to devilish inspiration” (pg. 29). There is no attribution for this claim and anyone familiar with medieval science knows this is deeply mischaracterized at best and plainly false at worst.[8]

Most perniciously, she opts for the long-discredited model of the early modern witch trials, in which “‘witches’ were generally no more than lay healers...proper empiricists” and therefore “witch hunts were a gendered class war wherein elite males forcibly took over both the conceptual and practical real of healing from peasant women”. While the “fathers of science” were trying to “turn lead into gold”, women healers were being persecuted as witches (pg. 30). She adopts this model wholesale from Barbara Ehrenreich and Deidre English, the former of whom was her academic advisor and who wrote the introduction to this very book. Lagalisse argues that

After all, as “magic” itself was gaining respect in certain elite quarters, women were being persecuted as witches precisely for practicing “magic,” wherein we may observe that the perceived danger was not “magic” itself but the gender of its practitioner. While men's “operation” on the world was sanctioned, women's equivalent “operation” on the world was targeted as heresy.

To begin, the vast majority of women killed during the Early Modern witch trials simply were not lay healers.[9] The persistent myth with Lagalisse deploys is worrying not only because it is long discredited, but also because it ignores the racial and ethnic prejudice that conditioned the witch trials, something which should have been glaringly apparent to Lagalisse, who bookends Occult Features with discussions of antisemitism. In fact, the Hammer of the Witches, which she quotes, is preceded by the Hammer of the Jews! She is persistent in her use of the term “cabalist” without qualification – that is to say, ample references to mystical traditions of Judaism with little or no discussion of said traditions or why that term refers to secret societies in the first place. Her discussion of Spinoza makes no mention of his Sephardic Jewish ethnicity, only his “diverse and contested oeuvre” and influence on Freemasonry.[10]

Lagalisse argues that during the Enlightenment, the occult sciences were not “disqualified, but came to enjoy an increasingly acceptable, even revered, status due to connected advances in mathematics and related practical pursuits” (pg. 29). However, far from being “increasingly acceptable,” magic was steeply contested and declining during this period, especially, but not solely, in Protestant Europe. In fact it is during this period that occultism sensu stricto comes about, by the excision of “rejected knowledge” from accepted scholarly culture. Renaissance magic, rather than being an elite practice, was largely underground and popular among all classes. It was an atmosphere where Reginald Scot can mention Catholics, Jewish mystics, and mythological figures in a single breath:[11]

By the sound of the words nothing commeth, nothing goeth [...] neither all the conjurors, Cabalists, papists, soothsaiers, inchanters, witches, nor charmers in the world can adde such strength to God’s workmanship, as to make anie thing anew, or else to exchange one thing into another.

It was common for these debates to form along Catholic-Protestant lines and to target Jews in particular, as in the above passage. Lagalisse simply appeals to a singular “Church” which did not exist in the time of the Early Modern witch trials (pg. 31).

Despite ample references to Giordano Bruno – footnotes to the great Frances Yates – she makes no reference to his trial and execution at the hands of the Inquisition in 1600.[12] Instead Lagalisse claims that Renaissance magicians were “consistently passed over” (pg. 32) by demonologists, which is simply false. Though dramatic executions carried out against Bruno were indeed rare, demonologists and inquisitors by no means ‘passed over’ Renaissance magicians: luminaries like Johannes Trithemius, Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, and even Giambattista della Porta were all tried and in some cases had their works condemned and burned. Other magicians themselves were burned. There was often a racial component to trials of Renaissance magicians, like that carried out against an enslaved Egyptian, Sellem Bin al-Sheik Mansurn, in 1605.[13]

In short, Lagalisse collapses an incredibly complex atmosphere into a reductionist model dominated by gender, and to a lesser extent, economic class, ignoring significant and important questions of race, colonialism, and religious identity. In doing this she misrepresents her sources, makes egregious errors, or appeals to the outdated and long-discredited theories of her doctoral advisors.

European occultism has never been a singular body of doctrines: it is a heterogenous body of knowledge synthesized from a wide variety of sources, to appropriate Lagalisse, which “happened in the context of complex power relations”. The historical object of European occultism, as constructed by historians and anthropologists, is largely the trace of actors normally excised from mainstream histories and indeed societies, as ossified in the upper echelons of European literary society. These actors – literary forgers, Mudéjares, folk healers, women, heretics, criminals, Marranos, the enslaved – can still be identified, albeit faintly and distorted, in the practices and writings of European esotericists.

Admittedly, while Lagalisse’s historiography is laughable, this does not necessarily discredit her ultimate point: that anarchism’s gendered, racial, and class character articulates within an occult cosmology that, ‘behind the scenes’ so to speak, still patterns leftist social movements today. However, the real problem with this thesis is one of parsimony and causality. She misrepresents what is actually a universal feature of Western scholarly culture as a unique, or at least disproportionately influential, feature of anarchism. There is not anywhere in the sciences, human or natural, that is not touched by these same ‘occult’ features in ways that are equally as pertinent as in anarchism. Further, it is difficult to claim that anarchism’s gendered, racial, and class character comes from this particular occult cosmology, instead of mirroring the structure of the society and culture it originates in. That is to say, the overall structure of society and culture characterizes both occultism and anarchism, and what Lagalisse portrays as a causal relationship is really a correlation.

In any case these same occult features are ever-present in Lagalisse’s book. At times it is difficult to know whether she intends this, or genuinely does not grasp the irony. In either case, she never explicitly discusses it, even while the back cover describes how “hidden correspondences between anarchism, Renaissance magic, and New Age movements” influence anarchism today. The most obvious is her interpretation of leftist symbolism: Lagalisse sees hidden meaning in stars and circle-As, even when such meaning is clearly mistaken, as with the Gothic “plumbobs”. But her overall method, genealogy, is itself nothing more than a reflection of the Pythagorean golden chain, in which the hidden operation of ancient ideas is transmitted from a prisca theologia down to contemporary philosophers. That this genealogy is meaningful, and not simply a record of irrelevant historical accidents, is necessarily esoteric. I am reminded of the geomantic tableaux, in which astrological correspondences (as divined by points made in the sand) are organized into families and lines of descent, and astrological influence traced through generations.

Indeed what is anthropology if not a continuation of the theological project to identify the precise nature of human being, rooted in the mystical anthropology of Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa, Ratramnus, Hadewijch, and countless others? What of the medieval ethnographers, who tie their reports of far-off races with the occult correspondences of stones? Lagalisse has stayed among us kynokephaloi, you see – she makes sure you know she listens to us, or rather, those who claim to be us.[14] Perhaps, if I were to assent to Lagalisse’s thesis, I could argue that her own racial fetishization and philosemitism is due to being articulated within this occult cosmology, like the great Athanasius Kircher who meticulously studied Chinese, Coptic, and Nahuatl to show how they all preserved the Tetragrammaton; or how Leibniz saw creatio ex nihil in the binary numerals of the 易經 Yijing. I think it is far more pertinent, however, that Lagalisse is simply a white academic.

All this being said, I think that interrogating the esoteric roots of anarchism (or any other field) is enriching and often necessary. However, rather than illustrating what does not need to be illustrated (white men are going to be white men, for better or worse), I think it provides an interesting and productive avenue for unsettling and destabilizing our received histories of thought, in ways which go beyond rigid dualisms. Or something. Really, I just want this fucking review to be finished. I deal with white academics more than enough in my day to day life.

[1] The academic here is Andrea Smith, who falsely claims to be Cherokee and has been routinely taken to task by Indigenous women. In 2015, twelve signed an open letter which stated that Smith and others “reinforce[d] a history in which settlers have sought to appropriate every aspect of indigenous life and absolve themselves of their own complicity with continued dispossession of both indigenous territory and existence.”

[2] “The Hermetica or Corpus Hermeticum is a collection of texts written in the first or second centuries A.D., yet during the Renaissance they were held to be the work of Hermes Trismegistus” (pg. 20). The Corpus was held to be written by Hermes throughout antiquity and the medieval period. In fact the Hermetica and the Corpus Hermeticum are not actually the same thing; the Corpus is a specific selection of texts from late antiquity whereas the Hermetica is much broader. Either way, it was in the Renaissance that the attribution to Hermes was disproven by Isaac Casaubon.

[3] That is, the Emerald Tablet.

[4] There is no evidence that Llull was aware of or influenced by kabbalah, though speculation that he was a kabbalist dates back at least to Pico della Mirandola and the later Renaissance Pseudo-Llullian tradition which attributed countless works on alchemy, kabbalah, and magic to Llull. In any case, his system is by no means “primarily influenced” by kabbalah. Any attempt to identify parallels between the two systems, which are very different, inevitably shows an unfamiliarity with Llull, kabbalah, or both.

[5] Buck-Morss does believe it possible that Hegel was influenced by or familiar with Freemasonry, but does not claim that Hegel was himself a Mason, and these are in fact very different claims

[6] The exact typeface is from Thomas E. Hill's Manual of Social and Business Forms (Chicago: Hill Standard Book Co., 1893) and has no relation to Masonry whatsoever.

[7] One of the seminal studies on the relationship of Eastern Greek Eurrope to Western Latin Europe is Deno Geanakoplos’s Interaction of the “Sibling” Byzantine and Western Cultures in the Middle Ages and Italian Renaissance (330-1600)

[8] See, for example, Albertus Magnus’ Book of Stones.

[9] Purkiss, Diane. The witch in history: early modern and twentieth-century representations. Routledge, 2003.

[10] Last Stone, Suzanne. “Spinzoa's Identity and Philosophy: Jewish or Otherwise?”. Cardozo Law Review 25:2 (2003).

[11] Scot, Reginald. The Discoverie of Witchcraft. William Brome, 1584.

[12] Martinez, Alberto. “Giordano Bruno and the Heresy of Many Worlds”. Annals of Science 23:4 (2016).

[13] Agius, Dionysius A., Alexander Mallett, and Catherine Rider, editors. Magic in Malta: Sellem bin al-Sheikh Mansur and the Roman Inquisition, 1605. Brill, 2022.

[14] The κῠνοκέφᾰλοι kŭnoképhăloi were a legendary race of dog-headed men who were said to live on the margins of the classical world in premodernity. Depictions of such monstrous races are the very earliest origin of anthropology, and figures like Augustine and Ratramnus debated and discussed whether they indeed were men or monsters.

title: Ayazağa’da dere yatağındaki riskli yapılarda yıkım başladı
content:
Sarıyer Ayazağa'da selin ardından dere yatağında bulunan riskli yapıların yıkımına başlandı.

İstanbul’da ve çevre illerde etkili olan sağanak sonrası birçok noktada sel suları hayatı felç etmiş, can ve mal kaybına sebep olmuştu. Selin en fazla etkili olduğu yerlerden biri olan Sarıyer Ayazağa Mahallesi’nde yapılan incelemelerin ardından dere yatağına yapıldığı tespit edilen riskli yapıların yıkılmasına karar verildi.

Bu kapsamda, dere yatağında yer alan ve sel tehlikesi oluşturduğu belirtilen yapıların yıkımına başlandı. Ayazağa Stadı’nda başlayan yıkım çalışmasının dere yatağında yer alan diğer yapılarla devam edeceği öğrenildi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Ross Kirshenbaum
title: Washington State Invests My Pension in Genocide. I’m Demanding Divestment.
content:
Workers across the US are demanding divestment from firms that profit from weapons and surveillance. I’m one of them.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Last month, I joined more than 45 bus drivers, teachers, and government workers to testify before the Washington State Investment Board, demanding responsible investment of our pension funds. I arrived grateful to be surrounded by fellow pensioners who were grounded in a shared commitment to fighting for investments that reflect our values.

Quickly it became clear that the Washington State Investment Board was going to strictly enforce the 45-person speaker limit that it implemented last year after beneficiaries began regularly demanding divestment at their meetings. This meant that my friend, a Palestinian member of my union who had taken off the day to testify, was barred from speaking. I had a minute to speak and yielded my time to him. We would not allow their bureaucratic procedures to silence us. We spoke out because we believe our state’s investments should earn money for our retirement funds without compromising our values.

This mobilization of beneficiaries began with Washington’s Cut Ties with Genocide campaign, launched by Washington for Peace and Justice and Jewish Voice for Peace Seattle. Sitting in an early meeting of the campaign, I was heartbroken to learn that the Washington State Investment Board invests my pension money into companies that enable genocide abroad, surveil and warehouse my neighbors, and contribute to climate chaos around the world. When I began my career as a bus driver in 2016, I was proud to have a pension. Now I felt like my pension was tainted. I could see clearly that my future financial stability was built on the destruction of other people’s futures.

What are these harmful investments? The Washington State Investment Board has invested over $204 million in Lockheed Martin, one of the world’s leading weapons manufacturers. Lockheed Martin produces the F-35 fighter jets that have been crucial to the Israeli military’s genocide in Gaza. These jets have the capacity to carry and detonate 2,000-pound bombs — bombs that destroy whole families, buildings, and neighborhoods in Gaza, leaving behind craters in the earth. In just one horrifying example from 2024, the Israeli military used F-35 jets to drop three 2,000-pound bombs on an Israeli designated “safe zone” in Khan Younis, killing 90 Palestinians and injuring hundreds.

The Washington State Investment Board has also invested more than $73 million in Palantir, a secretive data and AI company whose technology enables mass surveillance in the U.S. and across the world. In March, immediately after the horrifying Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) occupation of Minneapolis, the ACLU reported that Palantir technologies “form the backbone for ICE’s mass deportation regime.” Palantir’s leaders embrace surveillance and provide essential data to Donald Trump’s fascist forces. When the Washington State Investment Board invests in these companies, us pensioners are conscripted into complicity with Israel’s genocide against Palestinians, the mass deportations of our neighbors, and global climate devastation.

As a pension beneficiary, I care deeply about ensuring that our state’s public investments are both moral and profitable. The Washington State Investment Board manages over $230 billion in assets, which include retirement funds of public employee pensions for over 600,000 workers like me. Studies show that ethical investing can generate about the same or even more income than investing in war profiteers and human rights abusers.

The Washington State Investment Board has invested over $204 million in Lockheed Martin, one of the world’s leading weapons manufacturers.

We in Washington are not alone in our call: We’re part of a movement across the country of pensioners demanding that our retirement stop enabling human rights violations.

In Maryland, the Baltimore Teachers Union has joined community allies to demand an end to the Maryland State Retirement and Pension System’s investment in Israel Bonds.

Pensioners in Maine have been involved in a legislative push to get Maine’s state pension fund to divest from corporations and countries enabling severe human rights violations — companies like Lockheed Martin.

Union members in New Jersey are calling for their pension fund to divest from Palantir. Workers and retirees across New York State have been tirelessly advocating for their pension funds to be divested from Israel Bonds as well. And just this week, in a victory for workers of conscience, the New York City comptroller announced he would not reinvest city funds in Israel bonds.

Pension workers campaigning for divestment from Israel Bonds, weapons manufacturers, and other harmful corporations are an essential front in our movements for collective liberation. We are also part of a rich lineage of public sector employees and retirees organizing for human rights. In the movement against South African apartheid, rank-and-file activists with unions such as the UAW and the Service Employees International Union (SEIU) joined community members to demand their pension funds divest from companies doing business with apartheid South Africa.

We believe our campaign is winnable because we have seen the success of divestment campaigns throughout history and across the country, and because the Cut Ties With Genocide campaign already won a major victory this year. In March, the Washington State Treasurer’s Office sold over $62 million in Caterpillar bonds — cutting ties with one of the corporations profiting from Israel’s violence against Palestinians. Caterpillar manufactures bulldozers that the Israeli military uses to destroy homes in the Occupied West Bank as part of a broader campaign of ethnic cleansing. This was a very significant victory for many of us in Washington State, especially because the Israeli military used a Caterpillar bulldozer to murder Rachel Corrie, an activist from Olympia, Washington, more than 23 years ago. With all those who came before us at our backs — like Rachel, like the pensioners that fought for divestment from South African apartheid — we will continue this struggle for divestment.

It was especially meaningful to me that I testified before the Washington State Investment Board during the most sacred week of the year in the Jewish tradition — the Days of Awe between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, a sacred time for reflection and recommitment. I spoke out as a beneficiary of the Washington State pension fund, but also as an American Jew who is vehemently against this genocide being waged with my pension money and in my name. For nearly three years we have watched the Israeli military murder families, students, and journalists. We have watched them destroy hospitals, universities, and waterways. Each of us has the responsibility to do what we can in our communities to stop this genocide. It is through relentless collective action that I believe we can build a more just future for all of us.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Ariana Figueroa
title: Immigrants From Ukraine and Sudan Could Soon Lose Their Protected Status
content:
The Trump administration has moved to eliminate legal protections for more than 1 million immigrants that have TPS.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

More than 100,000 Ukrainians and roughly 2,000 Sudanese immigrants are bracing for the possibility they’ll lose their humanitarian protections by Monday.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has not indicated if he will renew protections for Ukrainians, who first received Temporary Protected Status after Russia invaded their country in 2022, and for Sudanese nationals, who were granted the designation several times, most recently in 2022, because of an ongoing civil war.

The Trump administration has moved to eliminate legal protections for more than 1 million immigrants that have TPS. Of the 17 countries with the designation at the start of the second Trump administration, the only remaining protections are for Ukraine and Sudan, which are set to end on Monday, and Lebanon, which is set to expire Nov. 27.

Mullin is supposed to declare his decision at least 60 days before a TPS designation expires, but he’s made no announcement.

The lack of an announcement would put Ukrainian and Sudanese TPS holders in the same situation as 200,000 Salvadorians, who are still in limbo after DHS did not renew protections set to expire on Sept. 9.

If no decision is made, an automatic six-month extension kicks in. DHS has not confirmed whether the extension is in place, only that Salvadorians have deportation protections and work authorization, for now.

DHS did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment about TPS extension for Ukraine or Sudan.

TPS is granted when a person hails from a country deemed too dangerous to return to because of conflict, natural disaster or another destabilizing event. The Trump administration has sought to wind the program down, especially after the U.S. Supreme Court this summer determined that decisions by the executive branch regarding TPS designations could not be challenged in court.

Immigration advocates say the rationale for providing TPS to Ukrainians has not changed.

“With the war in Ukraine still ongoing and conditions remaining unsafe, the administration should extend TPS for Ukrainians,” Jennie Murray, president and CEO of the advocacy group National Immigration Forum, said in a statement. “Forcing people to return to Ukraine in these circumstances is dangerous and a departure from longstanding U.S. policy.”

If Mullin ends TPS for Ukraine, it wouldn’t be the first time Ukrainians have lost humanitarian protections under the second Trump administration.

Last year, the Trump administration moved to end new applicants for a humanitarian program created by the Biden administration that allowed more than 220,000 Ukrainians to enter the U.S.

The State Department has a do-not-travel advisory, its highest advisory level, for Ukraine and Sudan.

Fraught relations between President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy further complicate the issue as Monday’s deadline approaches.

Trump has grown frustrated with the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war, and has blamed Ukraine for a spike in oil prices, ignoring the effect of his war in Iran.

On Oct. 9, Trump moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Zelenskyy called the decision “a weak decision by strong partners,” according to The Associated Press.

On Oct. 10, Trump told reporters that Ukraine should “get a new leader.”

In an interview with NPR, Zelenskyy said the Trump administration said unless Ukraine stops long-range drone strikes on oil refineries in Russia, it could cut off U.S. intelligence-sharing with Ukraine.

The two leaders have clashed in the past.

In February 2025, during a visit to the White House, the president got into a heated exchange with Zelenskyy, appearing to break with Ukraine and its resistance to Russia’s invasion.

Trump’s relationship with Ukraine was also the center of his first impeachment, after a U.S. House inquiry found the president threatened to withhold military aid unless Ukraine investigated his political opponent at the time, Joe Biden.

The U.S. Senate acquitted Trump in an impeachment trial.

There is a bipartisan congressional push to extend protections for Ukrainians at least until the end of 2029.

In a letter to Mullin and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, 31 senators urged for Ukrainians to be granted an 18-month extension, the longest renewal for TPS holders.

“The ongoing war has caused a humanitarian crisis and damage to critical civilian infrastructure that has left many with limited or no access to heat, electricity or medical services,” the senators wrote. “Ukrainian nationals cannot safely return at this time, and allowing TPS to terminate on October 19, 2026, would risk sending more than one hundred thousand individuals back to an active war zone.”

The Republicans who signed the letter were Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska.

The Democratic senators who signed the letter were Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Michael Bennet of Colorado, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Cory Booker of New Jersey, Chris Coons of Delaware, Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada, Tim Kaine of Virginia, Andy Kim of New Jersey, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, Jeff Merkley of Oregon, Patty Murray of Washington, Gary Peters of Michigan, Jack Reed of Rhode Island, Jacky Rosen of Nevada, Brian Schatz of Hawaii, Adam Schiff of California, Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, Tina Smith of Minnesota, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Mark Warner of Virginia, Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Peter Welch of Vermont, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Ron Wyden of Oregon and Tammy Duckworth of Illinois.

Independent Sen. Angus King of Maine, who caucuses with Democrats, also signed the letter.

A handful of Democratic senators also urged Mullin to extend TPS protections for Sudanese in an Aug. 17 letter.

“The ongoing armed conflict, catastrophic humanitarian crisis, and widespread human rights abuses make the safe return of Sudanese nationals impossible at this time,” they wrote. “TPS for Sudanese nationals in the United States remains both a humanitarian necessity and a prudent policy to ensure that individuals are not forced to return to conditions that continue to threaten their safety and well-being.”

Those senators were Warner, Kaine, Schiff, Van Hollen, Warnock, Booker, Bennet and Duckworth.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: anred
title: Apuntes apurados tras la movilización frente al Congreso: “En algún momento hay que pegar el salto”
content:
El textual del título, “En algún momento hay que pegar el salto”, fue dicho por un estudiante de secundaria (16 o 17 años) que estaba en la marcha frente al Congreso (ver video adjunto). Más precisamente, estas fueron sus palabras, cuando la represión ya se había desatado: “Es lógico tener miedo, pero en algún momento hay que pegar el salto y empezar a combatir, hacer lo que haga falta”. Uno de sus compañeros agregó: “Somos hijos de trabajadores, es importante que peleemos por todos”. Como toda persona medianamente informada, los pibes sabían lo que iba a pasar: el gobierno ordenaría una represión para meter miedo, como parte de su apuesta estratégica que es quebrar la voluntad de lucha del pueblo, desmovilizar. Esta vez, sin embargo, la jornada tuvo su particularidad. Hay elementos auspiciosos, a pesar del fracaso parlamentario en el intento de voltear el DNU 12/70 y la prepotencia gubernamental. Estos son algunos puntos fuertes que no debemos dejar pasar. Por Pablo Solana | Reporte Ancora / Imagen Andres Manrique




1. Conflicto universitario I: no fueron solo marchas.

 La toma del Palacio Pizzurno el 7 de octubre sorprendió al gobierno y envalentonó a los estudiantes. Entraron por la fuerza, mantuvieron una sentada y forzaron a las autoridades a atender el reclamo, todo en medio de un esquema de seguridad desbordado por el efecto sorpresa y por la decisión del grupo que planificó la toma. Con ese antecedente, se llegó al día 15 con asambleas en decenas de universidades, tomas en unas cuantas y no solo de Buenos Aires, vigilias, sentadas y semaforazos en colegios en distintas ciudades. En una lucha encabezada por dirigentes del sector poco propensos a la confrontación, la acción directa por abajo gana espacio.




2. Conflicto universitario II: ya nadie está a salvo.

 Un análisis más o menos compartido hasta ahora decía que el gobierno sabía que no era el mismo costo si reprimía a desocupados o jubilados revoltosos, que si se metía con la comunidad universitaria; que había un factor de clase (media, pequeño burguesa) que de algún modo “protegía” las movilizaciones por la universidad pública. Bueno, eso ya no pasa. A diferencia de las cuatro anteriores, esta marcha fue enfrentada sin contemplación. ¿Cuánto falta para que se animen a reprimir, también, una marcha por el 24 de marzo?




3. La movilización se sostiene a pesar de los gases.

 Ya venía pasando en marchas anteriores, pero esta vez la consistencia de la movilización popular se plasmó en una imagen poco habitual. Además del activismo que resiste, de la “juventud revueltista” que se va forjando en cada enfrentamiento con la cana, en el Congreso esta vez convivió el acto de la Universidad con escenas de enfrentamientos en paralelo, a pocos metros, sobre Hirigoyen y sobre Rivadavia. Los dirigentes de la FUA terminaron el acto lagrimeando por los gases. Si hace un año el Frente de Sindicatos Unidos, Fresu, había instalado un palco casi sobre avenida de Mayo para distanciarse de los revoltosos, esta vez el escenario estuvo lejos de las vallas, pero ocupando el centro de la Plaza. Es saludable la decisión de ocupar el espacio público pese a la certeza represiva, más allá de las críticas a la dirigencia de las Universidades.




4. “Es importante que peleemos por todo”.

 La convocatoria universitaria fue central, pero también estuvo en agenda la defensa de la Ley de Tierras (desdibujada por el paso atrás de la Corte), la Emergencia en Discapacidad, y la posibilidad de voltear el DNU 70/12. Por fuera de las agrupaciones estudiantiles y las columnas universitarias, se vio una cantidad importante de manifestantes que estaban allí “por todo”. El antecedente de la Marcha de la Bronca no es circunstancial: aún no es masivo, pero crece un ánimo de confrontación política en las calles contra el gobierno, que no se ciñe a tal o cual “defensa” reivindicativa puntual.




5. “Empezar a combatir, hacer lo que haga falta”.

 Dicha por un pibe de colegio, la frase debe ser puesta en su contexto y en la perspectiva de largo plazo. Pero la claridad de esa sentencia no se limita al activismo estudiantil que se va radicalizando. El enfrentamiento a la represión es cada vez más organizado. La influencia de la revuelta chilena gana espacio: esta vez se vieron baldes apaga-gases y guantes para devolverlos, a ambos lados de la plaza; también aparecieron músicos trompetistas, no ya en las columnas, sino acompañando al activismo de la resistencia: dando ánimo a quienes combaten. Esa mística legítima y necesaria no alcanza para neutralizar las voces que siguen señalando “infiltrados”, pero son síntomas de vitalidad en la revuelta que sería un error pasar de largo.




Hay más aspectos a analizar: dentro de la revuelta, pegarle a un periodista o romper un banco de plaza a mazazos, resta; apoyar las actitudes de resistencia no implica hacerlo ciegamente, sin el debate sobre aciertos y errores que siempre es necesario. Hubo un conjunto de diputados que intentó acercarse a la movilización una vez caída la sesión; pareció un intento fallido, con el riesgo de quedar como actitud estéril, para las cámaras; podría cuestionárseles el sentido más profundo de prestarse a legislar mientras disparan contra el pueblo, tal vez haya allí otro necesario debate. Estas y otras cuestiones quedan apuntadas, para ir conversando. Para que nos encuentren mejor organizadxs las próximas batallas.

title: Süper güçleri olan 5 hayvan:'Marvel kahramanlarına taş çıkartan canlılar
content:
Hasan Can Bilici [email protected]

Kendi vücut ağırlığının binlerce katına dayanabilen canlılardan kopan uzuvlarını yeniden oluşturabilen hayvanlara kadar doğa, bilim kurgu filmlerini aratmayan yeteneklerle dolu. Bazı canlıların geliştirdiği biyolojik mekanizmalar, insanın teknolojiyle bile taklit etmekte zorlandığı özellikler sunuyor.

Doğada hayatta kalmak, her canlı için farklı bir mücadele anlamına geliyor. Kimi hayvanlar avcılarından kaçmak için olağanüstü hızlara ulaşırken kimileri görünmez olmayı, ölümcül darbeler indirmeyi veya ağır çevre koşullarına dayanmayı sağlayan özel mekanizmalar geliştirdi.

Bu özelliklerin bazıları, çizgi romanlardaki süper kahramanların yeteneklerini andırıyor. Ancak bunlar doğaüstü güçler değil; milyonlarca yıllık evrim sonucunda ortaya çıkan biyolojik uyumların ürünü.

İşte Marvel kahramanlarını aratmayan yetenekleriyle dikkat çeken beş hayvan ve onların bilim dünyasını şaşırtan özellikleri.

title: Yurttaş mevcut siyasetten umutsuz, çareyi ‘halk meclislerinde’ arıyor
content:
Fotoğraf: Elif Ekin Saltık/ Evrensel

Elif Ekin Saltık [email protected]

Saha Araştırmaları Merkezi (SAMER), “Yurttaşların Siyaset Algısı, Alternatif Siyaset Arayışı ve Demokratik Katılım Olanakları” başlıklı araştırma raporunun sonuçlarını paylaştı. 14 kentte 428 kişiyle çevrim içi ortamda gerçekleştirilen araştırma, temsili siyasete yönelik derinleşen krizi, yurttaşların mevcut siyasal işleyişe olan tepkisini ve doğrudan demokrasi arayışını verilerle ortaya koydu.

Araştırmaya göre katılımcıların yüzde 45,1’i siyasi kararların alınma biçiminden “memnun değilim”, yüzde 33,9’u ise “hiç memnun değilim” yanıtını verdi. Mevcut işleyişten memnun olmayanların toplam oranı yüzde 79’a ulaşırken, memnun olanların oranı yalnızca yüzde 6’da kaldı.

Öte yandan yurttaşların yüzde 73,1’i siyasete katılımın sadece sandıktan ibaret olmadığını, seçim dışı yolların da varlığını kabul ediyor. Hak arama yöntemleri arasında ise barışçıl gösteri ve yürüyüşe katılmak (yüzde 36,2), sivil toplum kuruluşlarına katılmak (yüzde 26,2) ve imza kampanyaları (yüzde 21) öne çıktı.

Yurttaşlar, siyasetin yalnızca siyasi partiler ve seçilmişler eliyle yürütülmesini yetersiz buldu. Katılımcıların yüzde 77,3’ü, yerel kararlarda bölge halkının görüşünün doğrudan alınması gerektiğini savundu.

Araştırmanın en çarpıcı sonuçlarından biri ise “halk meclisleri”ne olan destek. Yurttaşların yüzde 84,1’i mahalle ve yerel konulardaki kararların doğrudan halk meclislerinde alınmasını “gerekli” veya “çok gerekli” buluyor. Yurttaşların yüzde 73,9’u, böyle bir meclis ya da toplantı kurulması halinde kesinlikle veya muhtemelen katılacağını beyan etti. Ancak bu güçlü talebe karşın, halkın doğrudan katılımına dayalı bir siyasetin Türkiye’de yaygınlaşma olasılığı düşük (yüzde 61) görüldü. Bu durum, katılım talebiyle siyasetin gerçekte dönüşebileceğine duyulan güven arasındaki uçurumu yansıttı.

Mahalledeki önemli bir sorunun çözümü için yurttaşların inisiyatif alma eğilimi (yüzde 39,7) yüksek olsa da bu durum doğrudan aktif ve örgütlü siyasete tahvil edilemiyor.

Aktif siyasetin önündeki en büyük engeller şöyle sıralandı: Yüzde 15,4 ile “katılımın etkili olduğunu düşünmeme”, yüzde 15,2 ile “baskı ve korku ortamı”, yüzde 14 ile “zaman yetersizliği” ve yüzde 10,3 ile “yeterli bilgi ve donanıma sahip olmama”. Katılımcıların yüzde 26,2’si ise doğrudan siyasete katılmak istemediğini belirtiyor.

Rapor, siyaset mekanizmalarındaki toplumsal cinsiyet ve yaş eşitsizliklerine de ayna tuttu. Kadınların yüzde 33’ü aktif katılım hakları konusunda hiç bilgisi olmadığını veya çok az bilgisi olduğunu belirtirken, bu oran erkeklerde yüzde 11,8’de kaldı. Aktif siyasete katılmak istemediğini belirten kadınların oranı (yüzde 39,3), erkeklerin oranının (yüzde 18,1) iki katından fazla.

Gençlerde ise güvensizlik ve uzaklaşma eğilimi dikkat çekti. 18-24 yaş arası gençlerin yüzde 47,6’sı aktif siyasete katılmak istemediğini belirtirken, halk meclisi veya halk toplantısına katılma isteği gençlerde yüzde 56,3 düzeyinde kaldı. Bu oran, yaş ilerledikçe artış gösteriyor ve 65 yaş üzerinde yüzde 100’e yaklaşıyor.

Araştırma sonucu, halkın karar alma süreçlerine doğrudan müdahale edebileceği demokratik, eşitlikçi, güvenilir ve sonuç üreten mekanizmaların kurumsallaştırılmasına duyulan ihtiyacı ortaya koyuyor. Katılımcıların beklentilerinin ilk sıralarında katılım mekanizmalarının artırılması, siyasi haklar konusunda bilgilendirme ve örgütlenme olanaklarının güçlendirilmesi yer alıyor.

Raporun tamamına ulaşmak için tıklayın.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: İzmir Barosu Olağan Genel Kurulu başladı: 'Hukukun üstünlüğünü savunmaya devam edeceğiz'
content:
İzmir- İzmir Barosu 2026-2028 Olağan Genel Kurulu, Bayraklı’daki Mustafa Kemal Atatürk Spor Salonu’nda başladı.

14.670 avukatın üye olduğu baro yönetiminin belirleneceği genel kurulun ilk gününde avukatlar, mesleki sorunlarını tartışmak ve yeni dönem yönetimini seçmek üzere bir araya geldi.

Dört adayın yarıştığı seçimlerde Çağdaş Avukatlar Grubu’nun adayı Emre Öktem, Cumhuriyetçi Avukatlar Grubu’nun adayı Serhat Sökmen, İzmir Avukat Hareketi’nin adayı Volkan Gültekin ve bağımsız aday Tacettin Çolak yarışıyor.

Genel kurul saygı duruşuyla başladı. Saygı duruşunun ardından oy birliği ile divan seçildi.

İzmir Barosu Genel Kurulu’nun divanı adına konuşan Av. Çetin Turan, baronun hak ihlallerine karşı mücadelesine dikkat çekerek, “İzmir Barosu hukukun her alanında yapılan hak ihlallerinin karşısında çıkmıştır. İnsan, çevre haklarını savunmak İzmir Barosunun görevleri arasına girmiştir” dedi.

Ülkedeki hukuki ve siyasi tabloya değinen Turan, mevcut yönetimin hukuk kurallarına uygun hareket ettiğini söylemenin mümkün olmadığını belirtti. Anayasal güvencelerin fiilen ortadan kaldırıldığını ifade eden Turan, yargı organlarının kararlarının uygulanmadığını, bağımsız olması gereken mahkemelerin görev alanlarını aşarak kararlar verdiğini söyledi.

Sulh ceza hâkimlerinin otomatik tutuklama hâkimlerine dönüştüğünü, yurttaşların yasalar karşısında eşit olmadığını belirten Turan, “Yasalar kimine uygulanıyor, kimine uygulanmıyor. Hukuki güvence kavramı terk edilmiş. Gazeteciler tutuklanıyor, televizyon kanalları kapatılıyor. Avukatlık mesleği günlük geçim sorunu dışında müdafiliğini yapamıyor” dedi.

İzmir Barosunun barışı ve toplumsal değerleri savunduğunu vurgulayan Turan, güncel gelişmeler karşısında baronun söyleyecek sözünün olacağını belirtti. Barışa ilişkin tartışmalara değinen Turan, İzmir Barosunun tek adam rejimlerine karşı çıktığını ve hukukun üstünlüğünü esas alan parlamenter sistemi savunduğunu söyledi.

Turan, “Bu karanlığın elbet dağılacağına inanıyoruz. Gelecekten umudumuzu kesmiş değiliz çünkü haklıyız, tarihsel akışın doğru tarafındayız” diye konuştu.

Dünyanın çok sayıda siyasi dava gördüğünü hatırlatan Turan, Türkiye Barolar Birliği kurucu başkanının 1971’de siyasi davalara ilişkin yaptığı tespiti anımsattı. Turan, “Sokrates’i ölüme mahkûm eden hâkimlerden hiçbiri bugüne kadar ulaşamadı ama Sokrates’in savunması devam ediyor” sözleriyle konuşmasını tamamladı.

İzmir Barosu 2026-2028 Olağan Genel Kurulu’nda açılış konuşmasını yapan Baro Başkanı Av. Sefa Yılmaz, hukukun üstünlüğü, savunma mesleğinin karşı karşıya olduğu sorunlar ve ülkedeki hak ihlallerine dikkat çekerek, “Anayasası olan bir ülkeyiz ama anayasanın hiçbir hakka ilişkin maddeleri uygulanmaz. Anayasal bir ülke değiliz” dedi.

Savunma mesleğinin adil yargılanma hakkı ve adalete erişim açısından vazgeçilmez olduğunu vurgulayan Yılmaz, “Savunma mesleğinin olmadığı yerde adil yargılanma hakkından bahsedilemez, adalete erişimden bahsedilemez. İzmir Barosu her zaman savunma mesleğini önceleyen ama hiçbir zaman hukukun üstünlüğünden ödün vermeyen bir anlayışı hayata geçirmek için çalışmıştır” dedi.

Türkiye’nin uzun süredir ağır bir hukuksuzluk döneminden geçtiğini söyleyen Yılmaz, 2010 ve 2017 anayasa değişikliklerinin bu sürecin önünü açtığını ifade etti. Tek adam rejimine geçişle birlikte hukuksuzlukların ve yolsuzlukların gündelik hayatın sıradan olayları gibi karşılanmaya başladığını belirten Yılmaz, “Artık bu ülkede nefes almak bile zor. Bu ülke dört yanı demir parmaklıklarla çevrilmiş cezaevi” dedi.

Yılmaz, insanların söyledikleri sözler nedeniyle gözaltına alınıp tutuklandığını, hatta neden tutuklandıklarını bilmediklerini ifade ederek, “Hukuksuzlukların temelinde bu tek adam rejiminin olduğunu biliyoruz. Faşizm konuşma yasağı değil, söyleme mecburiyetidir” diye konuştu.

İzmir Barosunun toplumsal olaylar karşısında aldığı tutumun yalnızca yönetimlerin değil, bütün meslektaşlarının katkısıyla oluştuğunu belirten Yılmaz, baronun bugün kamuoyunda sözleri merak edilen bir kurum olmasının bu ortak mücadeleyle mümkün olduğunu söyledi.

Yılmaz, Ankara 2 Nolu Baro Başkan Adayı Gökhan Ağdemir’in 10 gün önce yaptığı, “son iki yıl içinde 70 hâkim ve savcı kazandırdıklarına, tavsiye ettiklerine ve görüştüklerine”ilişkin açıklamasını hatırlatarak, bu konuda suç duyurusunda bulunduklarını belirtti. Tek adam rejiminin bütün kurumlarıyla uygulanmaya çalışıldığı bir süreçte genel kurul yaptıklarını söyleyen Yılmaz, “Elbette direneceğiz. Çünkü İzmir Barosunun geleneğinde var” dedi.

Anayasa Mahkemesi kararlarına rağmen cezaevinde tutulan isimleri de anan Yılmaz, milletvekili Can Atalay’a, Soma’da yaşamını yitiren 301 madencinin ailelerinin avukatlığını yapan Selçuk Kozağaçlı’ya, avukatlık mesleğini icra ettiği için tutuklandığını belirttiği Mehmet Pehlivan’a, Selahattin Demirtaş’a, Osman Kavala’ya ve haksız yere cezaevinde bulunan bütün yurttaşlara selam gönderdi.

Yılmaz, avukatlığın hak ihlallerine karşı söz söyleme sorumluluğunu taşıdığını vurgulayarak, “Avukatlık mesleği, hak ihlaline uğrayan kim olursa olsun o alanda sözünü söyleme zorunluluğu olan bir meslektir” ifadelerini kullandı.
