author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: Govt scrambles to solve fuel crisis without clear end in sight, divided on fava bean import ban; Quintet tries to balance competing political initiatives; RSF continues Blue Nile push; Military sets sights on Darfur
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter

 here

.




The struggling wartime economy took center stage this week in Sudan with a pair of issues at the heart of daily life.




The first is a fuel crisis that has grown increasingly worse in recent weeks as gas stations have become makeshift campsites and prices have skyrocketed. While the government has projected an outward image of assurance, behind closed doors, the wheels are turning to try to bring fuel to the nine states under military control.




The plan has two axes, sources informed of the discussion told Mada Masr. The first is essentially a triage: tighten fuel allocations and movement to where it is needed. Various government bodies have tried their hand at centralizing authority to better streamline decision-making, but Sudan’s fractured executive apparatus has seen more attempts than results.




The second part of the plan would require solving the issue at its source: bringing in new supplies to offset the non-performing domestic oil sector. For this, Transitional Sovereignty Council chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan is holding talks with Saudi Arabia. But as an informed TSF source told Mada Masr, the government cannot commit to a timeline to end the crisis until external agreements are finalized and the necessary financial guarantees are in place.




Alongside the fuel crisis, more potential trouble looms on the horizon, and this one is of the government’s own making. At the beginning of October, the Agriculture Ministry announced it would implement a prime ministerial decree banning fava bean imports in order to bolster domestic production and save foreign currency. In the last two weeks, the move has come in for fierce public criticism, which has been mirrored by criticism from the government and traders, sources in both arenas told Mada Masr.




The concern centers on whether a domestic agriculture sector strained by war and the fuel crisis can realistically carry the burden of producing enough supply of the daily food staple. Government sources told Mada Masr that the process in announcing the decision was flawed, and the Cabinet does not have the required data to ensure the ban won’t have disastrous effects. State-level administrative officials and traders chimed in to argue that the timing of the decision hasn’t given farmers enough time to adjust this season’s production plan to bolster supply.




While a source in Prime Minister Kamel Idris’s office projected confidence that the Agriculture Ministry has the necessary data to back up the soundness of the ban, a source in the ministry said that officials are already discussing contingency plans.




The political front this week saw yet another spin on the merry-go-round of political initiatives. The Quintet — which comprises the African Union, the United Nations, the Arab League, the European Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development — is trying to carefully engage with all competing political initiatives without endorsing any. This comes amid increasing divides between civilian political groups and the preparatory committee leading the government-sponsored internal dialogue over who gets to set its terms and who gets to participate. Both sides of the divide are trying to influence the AU to gain a leg up.




On the military front, the Rapid Support Forces continued this week to push for greater control of the Blue Nile locality of Wad al-Mahi. The military was able to push the advance back in a counteroffensive on October 9.




On the western front, the military launched airstrikes on RSF positions as it looked to translate its control of North Kordofan into a stronger position in West Kordofan to take the strategic city of Nuhud. Control of Nuhud would open the door to North Darfur, on which they already have their sights set, military sources told Mada Masr.




From within Darfur, the military made strategic gains this week, with the joint forces advancing from their remaining garrisons in the north of the region down into West Darfur, where they seized control of the agriculturally rich area of Bir Keleikil.




***




Burhan takes direct control of oil file amid worsening fuel shortages




Crowded gas station in Khartoum, September 27. Courtesy: Nepta Petroleum CO.LTD via Facebook.




The Sudanese government is scrambling for solutions in the face of a worsening fuel crisis marked by long lines at filling stations and growing concerns over everything from trade to markets to the ongoing planting season.




Across the nine states under military control, gas stations have effectively turned into makeshift campsites. People wait for one or two days at a time just to secure a single liter of gasoline or diesel — fuel that now costs around 47,000 Sudanese pounds per liter or as high as 80,000 pounds on the black market.




This crisis has driven up food prices and now threatens the summer harvest season. Thousands of farmers are left waiting for fuel to harvest their crops, while the failure of the winter planting season also looms on the horizon.




The state has not admitted outright that there is a fuel crisis, only vaguely acknowledging it to reassure citizens that everything is all right. However, the flurry of meetings and statements of reassurance are enough to show the frenetic pace of what is happening behind the scenes.




And indeed, officials across different levels of government who spoke to Mada Masr talked about a crisis management plan that has taken different directions in recent weeks. But across all levels, the infighting that has plagued the government in a host of other policy issues has derailed any potential momentum in what is already a steep climb out of a crisis caused by an oil sector that has been brought to halt by the war and a lack of foreign currency.




Now, Burhan is trying to transcend weeks of missteps by taking direct control of the file, making oil procurement the purview of a revived government body under his control and trying to secure a lifeline from Saudi Arabia.  But neither of these moves have borne fruit as of yet, and, thus, there is no timeline for the end of the crisis.




The government cannot commit to a timeline until external agreements are finalized and the necessary financial guarantees are in place, a TSC source told Mada Masr. Its immediate aim is to secure regular supplies for the capital and the states, including the agricultural and service sectors, instead of relying on occasional shipments to keep shortages at bay.




The root of the oil crisis lies in the fact that the war has forced oil fields out of service, leaving Sudan increasingly reliant on imported fuel and putting further strain on its already depleted foreign currency reserves, a senior Energy Ministry official told Mada Masr.




The ministry has been working with the Central Bank of Sudan and other authorities to tackle logistical obstacles, manage strategic reserves and distribute available supplies among the states. Yet the bottlenecks remain, despite the measures taken so far and the TSC’s decision to intervene directly, the official said.




On September 20, the TSC assigned its member, Shams Eddin Kabbashi, to oversee the oil portfolio, in a bid to contain the crisis by tightening coordination between the institutions responsible for imports, financing and supply, the TSC source told Mada Masr.




Kabbashi’s mandate extends to oil contracts, financing mechanisms and the restructuring of institutions in the sector, particularly the Sudanese Petroleum Corporation, the state-owned company dissolved in 2019 before the fall of former President Omar al-Bashir. The stated aim is to bring sovereign and executive institutions under a more coordinated oversight system, allowing decisions on imports and financing to be tracked directly, the source said.




But elevating the portfolio to the sovereign level has not resolved the underlying problems. By the time Kabbashi was brought in, financing difficulties had already mounted, and foreign contracts had been delayed. Importing companies were also struggling to secure the required volumes due to difficulties obtaining foreign currency and bank guarantees, the source explained.




His appointment was supposed to address these failures and align the decisions of the Energy Ministry, the Central Bank of Sudan and financial authorities. So far, however, the response has remained largely procedural — reorganizing import mechanisms and negotiating with suppliers. Until financing and shipping arrangements are completed, new contracts cannot deliver the supplies the market needs, the source said.




Faced with this lack of motion, the Energy Ministry officials and Idris made renewed efforts earlier this month.




On October 9, Energy Minister Moatasim Ibrahim Ahmed 

announced 

additional fuel supplies for production and service sectors at a meeting chaired by Idris. Officials also approved a plan to tackle import challenges and ensure a regular supply flow. The meeting brought together the ministry’s undersecretary, the central bank’s first deputy governor and the General Intelligence Service’s Economic Security Department head.




But the announcement offered little indication of what the plan would deliver in practice. No figures were provided for the additional volumes, their distribution across the country or when they would reach the market.




As the government struggles to ease fuel shortages, 24 importing companies have challenged the rules governing who gets to bring supplies into the country. In a joint memorandum submitted to Burhan on October 6, the companies warned that distortions of competition in the petroleum products market threaten supply and price stability, a source at one of the companies that signed the memo told Mada Masr.




Their complaints focus on barriers to market entry: the 200 kilogram  gold deposit now 

required 

by the central bank for each shipment as collateral and the financing arrangements imposed on overseas purchases, he added. The companies see the rules as favoring a small group of importers, leaving others unable to meet the requirements and compete on equal terms.




They are asking to finance imports using their own resources and other legitimate sources, rather than being restricted to designated channels for obtaining foreign currency, the source said. Greater flexibility, the source explained, would ease pressure on the central bank’s reserves and bring more importers into a market struggling to secure enough fuel.




The source added that the companies are also demanding a transparent system for allocating import quotas, with publicly announced volumes distributed according to uniform criteria. Clear allocations would allow companies to negotiate contracts and secure financing with greater certainty, while giving regulators a way to monitor contracted quantities, incoming shipments and distribution.




To review the rules, the memorandum proposes a TSC committee comprising the central bank, relevant ministries and government agencies and representatives of import and distribution companies, the source said.




But rather than empower private sector actors to succeed where the state has so far failed, Khartoum has been pursuing greater control over fuel imports. In June, the Cabinet decided that the state would import petroleum products directly, tasking the finance and energy ministries, the central bank and the Economic Security Department with carrying out the plan. The move was intended to secure supplies, stabilize the market and ease pressure on the exchange rate. A Cabinet official told Mada Masr that it is not meant to displace private importers but to give the state greater scope to intervene when necessary.




But adding the state to the pool of importers does not fix the problems that have constrained them all: access to foreign currency and bank guarantees and the timely arrival of shipments.




Against this backdrop, the presidency is moving to centralize oversight of the sector through a proposed “supreme oil council” chaired by Burhan and comprising the prime minister, the energy minister and the central bank governor, a second TSC source told Mada Masr. The council’s formation is nearing completion, the source said. It would set strategic priorities and oversee decisions on securing petroleum products in coordination with the Cabinet, while executive agencies would retain responsibility for technical and operational matters under the powers defined in official decrees, he added.




The proposed council would expand sovereign oversight of a sector where economic policymaking, commercial contracts, bank financing and economic security intersect. But it also raises questions about who would ultimately be in charge and how the new body would divide responsibilities with the prime minister’s office and the Energy Ministry, particularly given Kabbashi’s existing mandate to oversee the oil portfolio. The final division of powers remains unclear, as does whether the council would stick to setting strategic priorities or directly oversee contracts and financing.




Meanwhile, the government is trying to bring the Sudanese Petroleum Corporation back into the picture. The state-owned company was dissolved in 2019, with its functions transferred to the Cabinet body responsible for oil and gas, which is now the Energy and Petroleum Ministry. The ministry is working to finalize the corporation’s legal and administrative framework and determine how it would operate alongside the Cabinet and private importers, a source in the Energy Ministry told Mada Masr.




Under the proposed arrangement, the corporation would help expand direct imports, oversee contracts and coordinate supply allocations, though its precise powers and the timing of its return remain unsettled.




Whether reviving the corporation will establish a sustainable mechanism for importing and distributing fuel, rather than simply reshuffle responsibilities among government institutions, remains to be seen.




But its role could prove important if the government succeeds in securing a supply agreement with Saudi Aramco, one of the main avenues it is currently pursuing to ease the shortages.




Talks with the Saudi state-owned energy giant began in 2024 but stalled before resuming earlier this year. They have now reached an advanced stage, with a target for an agreement to be finalized before the end of 2026, the Energy Ministry source said. The proposed deal would require bank guarantees from the Central Bank of Sudan and other financial authorities.




According to the source, a specialized Sudanese entity, likely the Sudanese Petroleum Corporation in coordination with the ministry, would sign the contract and manage deliveries under terms covering quantities, scheduling, financing and payment that are still being negotiated.




An agreement could offer a more reliable way to secure part of Sudan’s fuel needs than the piecemeal imports that have left supplies exposed to financing problems and delays. But the negotiations have yet to produce a signed contract, let alone publicly disclosed quantities, costs or payment terms. And a penned deal would still leave the government with the challenge of securing guarantees, meeting its financial commitments and getting the fuel shipped, offloaded and distributed across the country, the source added.




Saudi Arabia’s recent involvement in Sudan’s oil sector is not limited to the Aramco talks. On September 10, Sudan 

signed 

a memorandum of understanding with Saudi Twaik Group to rehabilitate the Jaili oil refinery, which was forced out of service during the first months of the war, and build a new one in Port Sudan. The projects point to an effort to rebuild Sudan’s battered oil infrastructure, but, for now, they remain at the memorandum stage, with a final agreement and implementation still to come.




The Aramco talks and the refinery memorandum came up again on Thursday in Riyadh. Sudan’s energy minister met with the Saudi assistant energy minister on the sidelines of the International Energy Forum and the World Petroleum Congress, where they discussed avenues to strengthen bilateral strategic cooperation on oil, gas and electricity as well as current arrangements, 

according 

to a statement from Sudan’s ministry.




***




Fava bean import ban proceeds without cross-ministry review, raises supply concerns




Fava bean agriculture in Sudan. Courtesy: Al Ula Press




Despite this fuel crisis that is squeezing farmers and raising the cost of agricultural production, the Sudanese government announced in early October that it was moving forward with a long-postponed ban on the import of fava beans, a staple food consumed daily by millions of Sudanese.




The ban was announced by the Agriculture Ministry on October 2 in a decision that saw it withdraw the issuance of no-objection certificates for fava bean imports from any country. The move was announced as implementing an order issued by Idris in April, which his office presented as giving local producers a boost while conserving foreign currency.




But in the two weeks that have followed the announcement, public, governmental and agricultural and trade sector criticism has pushed back on whether the country is ready for such a move, with many saying it could have negative effects on the availability and price of a vital, daily food.




Despite the criticism, the ban remains in effect. But there are signs of concern over the blowback from the decision.




Agriculture Minister Essmat Qurashy has tried to distance himself from the decision after it drew public criticism. At a 

conference 

on October 7, he said the decision fell under the Trade Ministry’s jurisdiction and that his ministry only suspended the certificates in line with an earlier ban.




A senior official at Idris’s office told Mada Masr that the government remains confident in the decision. Agriculture Ministry estimates show good stocks and a harvest expected to cover market demand, the official told Mada Masr.




But the ministry itself is less confident. Officials are now discussing contingency measures for supply disruptions that could arise while the ban remains in force, an Agriculture Ministry official told Mada Masr. These include a joint review of stocks and consumption by the agriculture, finance and trade ministries; a review of shipments covered by contracts signed before the ban; and transitional arrangements to prevent an abrupt drop in supply.




Officials are also considering fixed import quotas if a supply gap is confirmed. The aim would be to allow imports when necessary while preserving protections for domestic farmers, the official said.




The official did not say whether the proposals have been formalized or when a decision might be made — leaving the government still weighing how to respond if the supply problems the measures are meant to prevent materialize.




Preventing the import of fava beans was first proposed by the Agriculture Ministry in late 2025 to encourage the crop’s cultivation alongside wheat, but its implementation was postponed until domestic production was sufficient to support the country’s demands, a Finance Ministry source told Mada Masr.




That sense changed as millions of Sudanese returned to areas under military control, increasing demand for imported goods to meet their needs.




According to the Finance Ministry source, Idris ordered the ban to be implemented in mid-September. Qurashy then followed suit with the early October decision.




For the Finance Ministry source, the way the ban was rolled out is itself a concern, raising serious reservations within the ministry. A measure affecting a food staple for millions should be preceded by a joint review of production, trade and financial data, the official said, to allow the government to assess the supply and price risks before shutting off imports. No transition period was allotted for importers to settle commitments or for officials to establish whether available stocks could cover demand, he added.




To determine the right time for the ban to be imposed, economic authorities need reliable figures on current inventories, the coming harvest and consumption across Sudan’s states — data they do not have, the source said. Without this data, authorities risk discovering a supply gap only after it begins to push prices up.




That would place an extra burden on low-income households already struggling with rising food, transport and basic service costs, the official added.




The source in Idris’s office defended the ban as part of a wider push to boost domestic production and reduce reliance on imported agricultural goods. Cheap imports, he argued, leave local farmers struggling to sell their crops at prices that cover cultivation costs, particularly as fuel, fertilizer, labor and other expenses keep rising.




The market, however, needs supplies throughout the year, not just a harvest deemed sufficient. Domestic availability depends on harvest schedules and traders’ capacity to store and transport crops, leaving imports to fill gaps when supplies in wholesale markets fall or prices rise, an import-export company source told Mada Masr.




The risks may emerge gradually as traders’ stocks dwindle and replacement supplies fail to arrive in time, the source warned. Prices could start rising even before a shortage materializes, as expectations of tighter supply feed into the market.




Consumers may then turn to other legumes and food products, pushing up demand for substitutes and extending price pressures beyond fava beans themselves, he added.




The ban decision also assumes farmers can in fact ramp up production. In Northern State, one of Sudan’s main fava bean-producing regions, farmers are already grappling with rising cultivation costs and limited access to financing, a state executive official told Mada Masr.




Higher input costs are forcing farmers to weigh how much land they can afford to plant, particularly when financing is scarce or seeds, fertilizers and other supplies arrive late. Those constraints need to be addressed before the growing season begins if production is to expand, the official said.




But that opportunity has already passed for the current season, which began in October, leaving little immediate room for a quick output increase.




Costs also do not end with the harvest, he added. Packaging, storing and transporting crops all eat into farmers’ returns, with higher fuel prices, service fees and inter-state transport costs adding to the burden.




The result is a widening gap between prices farmers sell at and what consumers in cities actually pay, the official said. The import ban could create room for domestic producers, but only if the government can bring down cultivation and marketing costs and ensure crops reach markets consistently, he added.




Imports account for an estimated 15-18 percent of Sudan’s fava bean supply, with the last year sitting at the upper end of that range, according to estimates provided by the Agriculture Ministry official.




That may be a relatively small portion of the market, but imports still help fill gaps when domestic stocks run low before the next harvest, said Al-Awad al-Safy, a crop trader in Northern State. Banning them could shift demand toward locally grown beans and improve farmers’ returns, but it could just as easily push prices higher if domestic supplies fall short or production and transportation costs remain high, Safy said.




***




Quintet engages Sudan’s rival political initiatives




As rival efforts vie to set the terms for Sudan’s political future, the Quintet, the international mediation group on Sudan, is trying to engage competing Sudanese camps without throwing its weight behind any one initiative.




The group, which comprises the African Union, the United Nations, the Arab League, the European Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, is consulting forces with “divergent positions on the existing authorities” as it engages with the dialogue backed by Burhan, an AU official told Mada Masr. The aim, the official said, is to coordinate the various initiatives, not to endorse one or settle on a single design for the political process.




The Quintet met on Monday with a delegation from the Declaration of Principles Forces — the emerging anti-war alliance trying to 

establish 

itself as a new center of political gravity — at the AU headquarters in Addis Ababa. The meeting followed 

talks 

in Khartoum last month between the Quintet and the preparatory committee for the internal dialogue.




The committee is pursuing its own regional outreach. On Tuesday, it received an invitation from Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the AU’s rotating chair, to visit Burundi in what it aims to be consultations on launching the dialogue.




But attempts to coordinate between the initiatives will not, by itself, resolve the dispute over their underlying political terms. While Burhan’s dialogue is being organized under the military-led authorities, the Declaration of Principles Forces is calling for civilian forces to set the political framework, with military actors confined to security and humanitarian matters, a political source who took part in the delegation said.




The alliance, which brings together civilian and armed groups led by Abdel Wahid Nur’s Sudan Liberation Movement and includes the opposition Sumud coalition led by former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok, laid out its proposal during Monday’s meeting, the political source told Mada Masr. Hamdok attended alongside representatives of the Popular Congress Party, women and youth networks, civil society organizations and independent figures.




The proposal links a ceasefire and humanitarian relief to political talks on governance and the reconstruction of state institutions, but the delegation made it clear that military actors should stay out of the political process, the source said.




The delegation also wants the National Congress Party, the Islamic current and affiliated groups excluded from the next phase. That demand stems from the alliance’s view that Sudan’s current crisis is rooted in the struggle over power following Bashir’s fall, the source said. Allowing forces linked to the former regime back into the process, the delegation argued, would provoke opposition from revolutionary forces and threaten the durability of any political settlement.




The alliance is also tying political negotiations to a tougher approach on arm supplies. During the meeting, it backed the United States-led proposal to extend the UN arms embargo beyond Darfur to cover all of Sudan, arguing that continued weapon shipments and funding to the warring parties would make a lasting ceasefire difficult to secure. The delegation called on the Quintet to work with international sanction bodies to explore ways to curb the flow of arms into the country, the source said.




The proposal is already facing opposition at the UN Security Council, where the US draft resolution to expand the embargo has struggled to advance amid resistance from Russia, China and African members of the council. Sudan’s military-led authorities have also staunchly rejected the move, arguing that it would equate the state’s armed forces with a “rebel militia.”




While the Quintet is trying to bring Sudan’s competing political camps closer together and establish a common ground for an organized process, it has no authority over matters such as the embargo, the AU official said, commenting on the delegation’s proposal.




That alone is enough of a challenge for the mediation body, which has for months failed to move the parties toward an internationally backed political track.




The Quintet’s stated position is that any process must be Sudanese-led and Sudanese-owned, preserve the country’s unity and sovereignty and rule out parallel governing structures. In practice, however, that means engaging with forces that reject the dialogue backed by the authorities in Khartoum while trying to coordinate with those same authorities and, at the same time, advance an alternative process under international and regional auspices, the AU official said.




The problem of competing initiatives was central to the delegation’s discussions in Addis Ababa. Building on the Quintet’s September 

meeting 

with the US-led Quad on Sudan — comprising Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Egypt — on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, the delegation called for a coordinating framework bringing together the Quintet, the Quad and the Troika, made up of the US, the United Kingdom and Norway. Without a common framework, the delegation argued, the proliferation of initiatives has allowed political and military forces to engage with different tracks without a clear understanding of how they fit together, the political source who participated in the delegation said.




Yet Sumud itself is now working to establish another political track.




A senior member of the coalition’s executive office told Mada Masr that Sumud is moving toward boycotting the internal dialogue, including by staying out of its preparatory committee and any meetings that emerge from it.




Instead, Sumud is engaging with civilian forces and regional and international actors to “develop an alternative political track grounded in an agreement among Sudanese forces on the principles of the transitional process and linked to humanitarian and security measures to end the war,” he said.




The coalition wants to bring together forces opposed to the internal dialogue and present a common political vision, with civilian forces taking the lead in setting the process’s terms rather than joining one whose political and organizational framework has already been established, the source added.




The coalition, the source said, rejects how the committee has been framing itself as “a purely administrative body responsible for organizing meetings” — a position it has advanced in outreach to civilian forces as it tries to secure enough participation to launch the process. The committee has insisted that it does not determine participation criteria, set the political agenda or dictate the dialogue’s outcomes.




Civilian forces opposed to the initiative fear that joining a committee formed by the existing authorities would lock them into arrangements that would be difficult to change later, confining their objections to the details of the dialogue rather than allowing them to challenge its underlying framework, the senior Sumud source said.




For Sumud, outside backing for the internal dialogue makes no difference and cannot compensate for those structural objections, he added.




The preparatory committee had hoped that its meeting with the Quintet last month would help it secure participation from forces still wary of the initiative, a committee source 

previously 

told Mada Masr.




Now, it is looking to the AU’s current leadership for help. The committee is preparing to visit Burundi for talks with President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the AU’s rotating chair, on arrangements for launching the dialogue, a committee member told Mada Masr.




Burundi’s ambassador to Sudan delivered the invitation during a meeting with the committee in Khartoum on Tuesday, the member said. Talks are expected to cover the steps needed to launch the dialogue, the reasons some political forces remain reluctant to participate and how African institutions could help widen participation and support the process.




The member said the committee wants to establish a clearer role for the AU in the coming period, particularly in providing “political guarantees” and persuading skeptical forces to join the preparatory consultations. But it also wants to maintain the principle that Sudanese parties should set the agenda and determine the outcomes of their own political process, the member stressed.




The initiative rests on the principle that Sudanese should manage the dialogue themselves, with regional and international actors helping to create the conditions for it to proceed. But with the political framework still contested, it is counting on support from Burundi’s presidency to help address concerns that have kept some forces away. It will continue domestic consultations while preparing for the visit, the member added.




An African diplomatic source informed of the Burundian presidency’s engagement on Sudan told Mada Masr that the invitation is part of an effort to expand contact with the parties involved in the political process. Burundi’s presidency hopes to encourage initiatives that narrow differences and help create conditions for ending the war, the source said.




That outreach, however, should not be mistaken for an endorsement of the committee’s initiative, the source stressed. Like the Quintet, the AU is seeking to engage Sudanese political efforts without appearing to privilege one over the others. The diplomatic source said the invitation does not confer an exclusive mandate on the preparatory committee to manage the political process.




AU support will instead depend on whether an initiative can bring more forces into the process and offer political guarantees they can accept, the source added.




The AU faces a balancing act of supporting Sudanese ownership of the political process while coordinating domestic initiatives with the Quintet’s efforts, without allowing them to harden into competing tracks that may prove difficult to reconcile later, the source said.




***




RSF attempts further push in Blue Nile’s Wad al-Mahi, military repels attack




A week after 

capturing 

the Kadalo mountains area of the Wad al-Mahi locality in eastern Blue Nile near the Ethiopian border, the RSF attempted to advance further, attacking a new area in the same locality. The military, backed by local civilians, repelled the attack.




Both sides subsequently began reinforcing their positions ahead of further operations, according to three military sources.




The RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, launched an assault on the Um Darfa town in the early hours of October 9, one of the sources told Mada Masr. The military, supported by Sudan Popular Resistance forces, launched a counteroffensive, repelling the assault and inflicting heavy losses in personnel and equipment, the source said.




Residents joined the fighting, taking up light weapons to defend their town alongside the military, an activist in Damazin, the state capital, told Mada Masr. Their involvement played a significant role in repelling the attack, he added.




But the fighting has continued beyond the frontlines. The RSF has since continued to target the area with drones, the activist said, including a Sunday strike on the main hospital that injured two medical workers and damaged parts of the facility, forcing it out of service.




On Monday, the military 

said 

that it shot down a strategic drone near Wad al-Mahi, saying it had tracked the aircraft crossing into Sudan from Ethiopia.




The military began reinforcing its positions in eastern Blue Nile the day after the attack on Um Darfa, dispatching dozens of combat vehicles carrying reserve troops to the region’s eastern fronts on October 10, the military source told Mada Masr. The reinforcements, equipped with jamming devices and air defense systems, are intended to secure military-held positions and support operations to retake sites captured by the RSF and are also tasked with clearing key positions along the Ethiopian border, the source added.




By Monday, signs of a parallel buildup had emerged across the border. Two military sources told Mada Masr that 40 combat vehicles and dozens of motorcycles had moved from Asosa, in Ethiopia’s Benishangul-Gumuz region, toward Mankush, near the Sudanese border opposite Wad al-Mahi. The sources said the movements could signal preparations for attacks on Abu Gaddaf and Balgwa in the locality, adding that the military had detected them and drawn up plans to counter them.




In the Kurmuk locality, where the RSF deployed additional forces last week, 300 RSF fighters and 50 vehicles also launched an attack on October 9 on Jabal Kadam, to the east of the RSF-held Kurmuk city, one of the military sources said.




The military managed to draw the attackers into an ambush and repelled the assault, he added.




Damazin’s Fourth Infantry Division 

said 

the military’s forces inflicted heavy losses on the RSF in personnel and equipment.




***




Military steps up air campaign in Kordofan as forces prepare for Darfur fighting




As the military presses to consolidate control over North Kordofan and advance into West Kordofan, it stepped up airstrikes on RSF positions across the two states. To push back the military advance, the RSF has repositioned fighters around the strategic city of Nuhud ahead of a possible military push.




The military is now reading its divisions as it looks to take the next phase of fighting to Darfur.




North Kordofan’s Abu Haraz and West Kordofan’s Um Samima, Khawi, Zeleita and Sarif Ankoush came under airstrikes on Wednesday, a military field source told Mada Masr. The raids killed a number of RSF fighters and destroyed 15 combat vehicles, the source added, describing the current operation as an effort to advance toward the edges of Darfur.




The RSF, meanwhile, has moved large numbers of fighters to Nuhud, stationing them along the city’s southern and western outskirts in anticipation of possible surprise attacks, the source said.




Nuhud is the northeastern point in West Kordofan’s strategic triangle, alongside Babanusa and Heglig. Whoever controls the city holds a key staging point linking West Kordofan to North Darfur.




A retired military officer said the RSF may now prioritize fortifying its positions and troops in Darfur over mounting a sustained resistance in West Kordofan, especially that the military has dismantled its core forces in North Kordofan.




The anticipated push westward is also bringing the Sixth Infantry Division back into the Darfur theater. The division endured 18 months of RSF siege in Fasher before the city and its garrison fell in late 2025. It has now been moved from its temporary base in Merowe in Northern State to Khartoum ahead of a redeployment to fight in Darfur.




At a farewell ceremony for the division on Tuesday, the Merowe air base commander told troops they would meet again in Fasher. Deputy division commander Abdel Jabbar Babiker said the force is now heading to the frontlines to retake the city.




A military source told Mada Masr that the division’s troops had undergone intensive training in preparation for deployment. Forces from the 20th Infantry Division in Daein, the 15th in Zalingei and the 22nd in Babanusa have also been repositioned to join the frontlines, the source added.




***




Military repels attack on its positions in South Kordofan’s eastern Nuba Mountains




Fighting broke out in Um Deheilib in the eastern Nuba Mountains of South Kordofan on Sunday, when the RSF and its ally, SPLM-N, attacked military positions in the area, a field source among civilians mobilized to fight alongside the military told Mada Masr.




Clashes lasted around six hours before the military ultimately repelled the assault, leaving dozens of RSF and allied fighters killed or wounded, the source said. The military also suffered several casualties, he added.




The RSF and its allies are seeking to open a new front in the eastern Nuba Mountains, the source said, noting that the military’s 10th Infantry Division in Um Jubeiha has deployed additional troop and logistical reinforcements in preparation.




The same day, SPLM-N artillery fire struck Kadugli, the state capital, killing a mother and her three children, the Sudan Doctors Network 

said

.




***




Military, allies advance in West Darfur’s border areas




Advancing from their strongholds in North Darfur, the military and its allies captured more ground in West Darfur’s border areas this week.




Military troops and fighters from the joint force of allied armed movements set out from Gargira in North Darfur on Wednesday and crossed into West Darfur, reaching Bir Keleikil, where they clashed with the RSF for five hours, a field source with the joint force told Mada Masr.




The forces ultimately took control of the area, inflicting casualties on the RSF and seizing several combat vehicles, the source added.




Joint force fighters 

posted 

videos showing the takeover.




Bir Keleikil lies around 32 km from the Chadian border, in the eastern part of the Jabal Moon locality. One of West Darfur’s most fertile agricultural areas, it also draws herders during periods of drought.




Khartoum-appointed West Darfur Governor Bahr Eddin Karama 

hailed 

the recapture in a statement on Wednesday.




***

Govt scrambles to solve fuel crisis without clear end in sight, divided on fava bean import ban; Quintet tries to balance competing political initiatives; RSF continues Blue Nile push; Military sets sights on Darfur

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.

.







ᓯᕗᓕᐅᕐᑎᐅᓂᖅ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᕙᖕᓂᖅ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᓯᒪᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᐅᕙᓂ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᐅᕙᓂ ᐊᕐᓴᕐᓃᑦ ᑐᔪᕐᒥᕕᒃᒥ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 3-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑕᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᒥᕐᖑᐃᕐᓯᕐᕕᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᑐᙵᓱᒃᑎᑦᑎᔨᐅᖃᑕᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᐅᑯᓂᖓ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᖏᓐᓂ.




ᓄᕗᐊᓕᐊ ᑭᐅᕆᐅ ᑭᙵᕐᓂ ᓄᓇᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᑖᖅᑎᑕᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐆᒥᖓ ᑳᒻ ᐃᐅ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓂ ᓯᕗᓕᐅᕐᑎᐅᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᓵᓚᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᕙᒃᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐊᐅᔭᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᒪᔨᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᔭᐅᓕᖅᖢᖢᓂ ᕼᐋᒻᒪᓚᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕌᓂᒃᑳᖓᑕ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ.




“ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᖅ ᐱᒻᒪᕆᐊᓘᒻᒪ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓄᑦ ᓲᖃᐃᒻᒪ ᖃᓄᐃᑦᑕᐃᓕᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᕈᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᕐᒨᖓᓂᖓᓄᑦ, ᐃᓱᒪᒃᑯᓪᓗ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓯᒪᓂᕐᓴᐅᔾᔪᑎᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᕐᓴᕈᑎᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐃᓅᓯᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᑐᕈᓐᓇᖅᑐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓅᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᕐᒧᑦ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑭᐅᕆᐅ ᕙᐃᔅᐳᒃᑯ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 8-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




ᐅᓇ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓕᒃ 18-ᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑎ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᖅ 40-ᖏᓐᓃᑦᑐᓂ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓕᖕᓂ 5-ᓂ 12-ᓄ 4:00 ᐅᓪᓗᒃᑯᑦ 6:00 ᑎᑭᓐᓇᓱᖕᓂᖓᓂ ᐱᓇᓱᐊᕈᓯᐅᑉ ᐃᓗᐊᒍᑦ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᒃᑯᕕᒃᒥᑦ.




ᑐᓴᕐᓈᖅᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᐅᑯᐊ ᐃᙱᖅᖢᑎ Black Eyed Peas ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᓯᖏᑦ ᐃᙱᕐᑏᑦ ᑐᓴᕐᓈᕈᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᓂᐱᑭᓵᓯᒪᓪᓗᓂ, ᑭᐅᕆᐅ ᑖᒃᑯᓂᖓ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᐅᓪᓗ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᖏᑦᑕᓕ ᐊᓯᐊᒎᖓᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕋᓱᒃᖢᓂ.
















ᐃᒡᓘ ᐃᓗᐊᓂ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᑐᓂᒃ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕋᓱᒃᖢᓂ ᐃᓱᒫᓘᑎᖃᕋᓂ “ᐃᓐᓇᕐᓄᑦ ᐱᒡᒍᓴᐅᑎᐅᓇᔭᙳᐊᖅᑐᓂᒃ.”




“ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᓲᕐᓗ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᖕᒦᖅᑰᔨᓐᓇᕈᓐᓃᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᓱᕈᓰᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᓂ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᕐᓂᕐᓴᐅᓕᖃᑦᑕᕐᒪᑕ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᐅᑯᐊ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓕᐅᕋᓱᒐᑎᒃ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᑦ ᖁᕕᐊᓲᑎᖃᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᑦ ᑭᙵᐃᑦ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓂ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒧᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᓪᓗᑎᒃ.




“ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᔨᐅᕙᒃᑐᑦ ᐆᒻᒪᑎᒋᔭᐅᒻᒪᕆᒃᑐᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖏᓐᓂᒃ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨ ᑐᑭᒧᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᔨᖓ ᐃᐅᕋᓐ ᕌᐱᓐᓴᓐ ᐅᖄᓚᐅᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 8-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




ᖁᓕᐅᓪᓗᑎᒃ (10) ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᑦ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓖᑦ 13-ᓂ 19-ᒧ ᑖᒃᑯᐊ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᒪᓂᒻᒪᐃᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐅᓗᕆᐊᓇᙱᑦᑐᒥ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓄᑦ ᐅᐸᒃᑕᐅᕙᒃᑐᓂ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᕕᕝᕗᐊᕆᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᑖᒃᑯᐊ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᑦ 200 ᐅᖓᑖᓃᑦᑐᓂᒃ ᕚᓚᓐᑕᐃᓐᔅ ᑕᐃᒥ (ᓇᒡᓕᒍᓱᖕᓇᒥ) ᐅᓪᓛᕈᒻᒥᑕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᑦ, ᕌᐱᓐᓴᓐ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.
















“ᐅᑯᐊ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᑦ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᔭᖃᑦᑎᐊᖅᖢᑎᒃ, ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᒌᑦᑎᐊᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᒃᑯᒋᔭᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑲᑦᑕᖅᑐᑦ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. “ᐊᓯᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᔭᐅᑦᑎᐊᓕᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᑦ, ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᐱᕈᖅᑎᑦᑎᕙᓪᓕᐊᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓯᒪᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᕙᖕᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓯᕗᓕᐅᖅᑎᐅᕙᖕᓂᖅ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᖓᓂᖓᓂᒃ.”




ᐃᖃᓗᐃᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᐸᐅᔭᖓᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑐᑭᒧᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᔨ ᐳᕆᑕᓐ ᒪᒃᓂᐅᓪ ᑐᓂᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒥᒃ ᓯᕗᓕᐅᖅᑎᐅᓂᖓᓄᑦ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒧᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᒥ.




ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ, ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᑦ ᕼᐋᑭᖅᑎᐅᓂᑯᕕᓂᕐᒥ ᔪᐊᑎᓐ ᑐᑐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓅᔪᓐᓃᕐᓯᒪᓕᕐᑐᒥ ᐅᑭᐅᕐᑕᖅᑐᕐᒥ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑎᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᔨᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᑯᒥ ᐊᑏᒪ ᕼᐊᓪᓚᕆᒥ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᑖᖅᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ (Hall of Fame) ᑖᓐᓇᓗ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᓵᕐᓂᑰᓪᓗᓂ.




ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᑐᓂᓯᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑎᓄᑦ, ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨᖏᓐᓄᑦ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᕙᒃᑐᓄᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ.




ᖁᙱᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᐃᓚᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ 100 ᐅᖓᑖᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒻᒪᕆᖕᓂ ᐅᐸᒍᑎᓯᒪᓪᓗᑎᒡᓗ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐱᓇᓱᐊᕈᓯᐅᑉ ᓄᙳᐊᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᒥ.
















ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐃᓚᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐅᑯᓂᖓ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐹᔅᑭᑦᐹᓪ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᙱᓐᓂᒃ, ᕚᓕᐹᓪ ᓄᓇᕗᑯᓐᓂ, ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᓵᑯᑯᓐᓂᑦ, ᓄᓇᕗᒥ ᐱᖕᐹᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᓐᓂ, ᐃᖃᓗᒃᑑᑦᑎᐊᕐᒥ ᐅᓇᑕᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᙱᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐹᑦᒥᓐᑕᓐᑯᓐᓂ ᑐᙵᓱᒃᑎᑦᑎᔨᐅᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᖕᒥ ᐃᖃᐃᓕᓴᕐᕕᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 3-ᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 4-ᒥ.

author: Brad Reed
title: Rule Lets Fossil Fuel Companies “Unintentionally” Kill Polar Bears and Walruses
content:
The Trump administration’s rule change was a major priority for the Alaska Oil and Gas Association.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Oil and gas companies will now be permitted to kill polar bears and Pacific walruses off the northern coast of Alaska so long as such killings are “unintentional,” according to a new Trump administration rule.

The US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) on Friday finalized a rule change that would shield fossil fuel companies from legal liability if they engage in the “incidental, unintentional” killing of the animals “during year-round oil and gas industry activities in the Beaufort Sea… and adjacent northern coast of Alaska.”

Under the rule change, which is scheduled to last through 2031, the FWS “will issue letters of authorization” that sign off on the incidental killing of wildlife upon request by oil and gas companies.

As noted by a report in Bloomberg Law, the proposed rule change “drew more than 85,500 public comments, nearly all in opposition,” before the FWS ultimately signed off on it.

The rule change was a major priority for the Alaska Oil and Gas Association, which represents fossil fuel giants and requested the revision in September 2025.

Allowing for the incidental killing of polar bears isn’t the only controversial rollback of environmental regulations made by the Trump administration in recent weeks.

In September, The New York Times reported that FWS had gutted a key provision in the Endangered Species Act by arguing that only the intentional killing or wounding of protected species counts as illegal “harm.”

Last week, it was revealed that the US Department of the Interior is moving ahead with a plan to let fossil fuel companies conduct specific wintertime operations at the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska without undergoing reviews mandated by the National Environmental Policy Act.

Even though the Trump administration has prioritized the development of domestic fossil fuel production by gutting environmental standards, these policies have not translated into the promised cheaper oil and gas prices, which have spiked over the last half year thanks to the president’s illegal war with Iran.

This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

author: Kevin Carson
title: Review. CLR James: Cultivator of the Popular Will, by Matthew Quest
content:
Matthew Quest. 

CLR James: Cultivator of the Popular Will. A Study of the History and Politics of World Revolution

 (Brill, 2026).




As Matthew Quest notes in his appendix, “Top Ten Reasons We Don’t Know More about CLR James,” CLR James is a relatively obscure thinker even among the African-American left. This is doubly so on the left more generally. According to Quest, James’ thought occupies a marginal position on the left primarily because his fundamental orientation — an affinity for direct democracy and workers’ self-management — is fundamentally at odds with the centralized, mass-based politics of the Old Left, whether Marxist-Leninist or Social Democratic. He was hostile to the British Labour Party and Atlee, the US Democratic Party and FDR, and to post-independence African leaders who were lionized elsewhere on the left. He saw nation-states and vanguard parties as mostly destructive rather than helpful, and the history of nationalization by progressive governments as hostile to self-management. James also saw the class reductionism of the dominant currents of the left, with their neglect of racial and anti-colonial dimensions of struggle, as failing to meet the needs of the time.




Quest himself is a perfect fit for intellectual biographer of James, as a historian and critic of national liberation movements in Africa and elsewhere in the colonial and post-colonial world, as well as post-independence governments. James’ central values of direct democracy and self-governance resonate strongly with Quest’s hostility — which come through clearly in these quotes from his Preface — to self-serving establishments, Black, revolutionary, and/or “progressive.”




The search for identity and heritage, in all their proper cultural nuances, for those who have known scars, exploitation, and who are overcoming insecurity, cannot be permitted to be captured by those who define freedom as managing subordinate lives. This is how all who fatefully embrace the state define it. These are the facts of the long duration of post-civil rights, post-colonial existence.




…Hopefully, we have now learned that the challenge to respectability politics without opposition to elite representative government is a fraud….




We are living in an affirmative action empire and ethnically plural police state alongside subcontractors of guilt and activists for the government, funded by the white rich, talking about privilege. We have people lecturing us about the problem of ‘colour blindness’ who are not opposed to the police state; they are explicitly part of the boss class who murder, mass incarcerate, and get out the vote for those who exploit.




* * *




…[W]hen I questioned whether the working people of Cuba actually governed that country, many dedicated revolutionaries, socialists, and anti- imperialists replied that it did not matter. For most insulted by the historical denial of self-determination of conquered peoples and for most organising for some future socialism or communism, it did not matter whether ordinary people directly governed or not. This should shake those who are not Machiavellians to the core. We should not be so thirsty for empowerment that we will accept a half-made or second-hand society as a dwelling to sustain our search for liberation.




…No workers or youth to whom we were introduced asked questions about their contradictions. Surely, ordinary people in Cuba asked these questions but were not featured on the directed tours and cultural events. This raised questions about the democratic content and the political economy of the socialist future and the ethics of those who took part in such projects.




* * *




CLR James famously said: ‘Political treachery is not the monopoly of the white race’. He also said there are Black people who treat Black toilers like ‘colonial trustees’, and while they talk of desiring ‘independence’ and ‘power’ they already live a ‘delightful’ existence at the toilers’ expense.




James’ life (1901-1989) spanned the Russian Revolution, the rise and fracturing of Marxism-Leninism, and postwar national liberation movements, and intersected with them at numerous points.




Born in Trinidad, he lived in numerous countries over the course of his lifetime. His activist career was wide-ranging and global; as Quest writes, “James and his associates worked for an American revolution, a Caribbean revolution, African revolution, and world revolution.” He authored numerous historical works, including 

The Black Jacobins

 on the Haitian Revolution, and a huge volume of political work and occasional writing. Along with Trotsky’s former secretary Raya Dunayevskaya, he co-founded the Johnson–Forest Tendency, a tendency within the Shachtmanite Workers’ Party (the Shachtmanites being a split from Trotskyism which held that the USSR was not simply a deformed workers’ state, the orthodox position, but a new form of oligarchical class system under the collective rule of the bureaucracy). The Tendency was a major formative influence on autonomist Marxism.




Quest sets out to show “for the first time,” in contrast to the neglect of previous scholarly treatments of James, the centrality of direct democracy and workers’ self-management to his life and work. And he does not hide behind scholarly neutral language. “This book is not for the hesitant, the insincere, or pretenders, or those who wish to sustain illusions. For such readers, encountering this work will be like walking on broken glass barefoot.” As he summarizes it:




James’s philosophy of history, as well as his radical journalistic strategies, transcends the material facts of suffering and trauma, and it observes the self- directed liberating activity of ordinary people, sustaining with reverence their character, beyond blind spots, in search of the hidden depth of their creative capacities and repressed strivings.




This book, abundantly documented with primary archival sources (from obscure letters to unpublished manuscripts), illustrates aspects of James’s intellectual history and reveals biographical elements previously unknown. However, it also offers the most comprehensive treatment of James’s political thought to date. It will stand out for the detail in which it explores James’s theorising, strategising, and the internal dynamics of his small revolutionary political organisations and mass party politics.




Indeed, this is a massive book, totaling over 1100 pages. Besides those on his personal and literary life, individual chapters detail his views on the philosophy of history, direct democracy, the progressive welfare state, revolutionary praxis, dialectics, his interpretation of Marxism, the Bolshevik Revolution, the postwar communist regimes of Eastern Europe, Castro, Mao, the Haitian Revolution, Kwame Nkrumah, Caribbean revolutionary politics, Black liberation in the United States.




The chapter “Every Cook Can Govern” is key to James’ approach to everything, as covered throughout the rest of the book. As James states his own philosophy:




…[I]n any society, particularly contemporary society, you have people born and grow up with a tendency to rule. In order to have democracy, you have to oppose those people. That is the problem. It isn’t lack of faith in the democracy itself. But the instinct to rule is because there are a number of people who believe that there must be order and some people in charge. The whole history of humanity tells them that, and that is the problem the ordinary man faces … My idea of socialism is very extremely opposed to the usual. For many people, socialism is the further control by people who are put in authority. For me it is the opposite.




In his chapter on the New Deal, Quest quotes James comparing the state capitalism of FDR, and specifically its conflicts with the CIO, to that of Stalin:




What the American workers are revolting against since 1936 and holding at bay, this, and nothing else but this, has overwhelmed the Russian proletariat. The rulers of Russia perform the same functions as are performed by Ford, General Motors, the coal operators and their huge bureaucratic staffs. Capital is no Henry Ford; he can die and leave his whole empire to an institution; the plant, the scientific apparatus, the method, the personnel of organisation and supervision, the social system which sets these up in opposition to the direct producer will remain the same. Not inefficiency of bureaucracy, not ‘prestige, powers, and revenue of the bureaucracy’, not consumption but capital accumulation in its specifically capitalist manner, this is the analysis of the [American] and Russian econom[ies].




James’ critique of Nkrumah’s Ghana in the 1960s, following his earlier admiration, was typical of his views on the national liberation movement leaders who came to power after independence.




CLR James’s critique of Nkrumah for a high modernism focused on urban construction and big development projects like the Volta Dam (the Akomsombo Dam) is little known in contrast to the fuss over deposing Nkrumah’s chief justice. James argued ‘Nkrumah has been playing around with a fiction called social democracy’. ‘Not the mild Fabianism of Grantley Adams, Norman Manley or Eric Williams’, which Caribbean politicians ‘don’t take too seriously’, James explained Nkrumah was really working too hard to impose modern economic development on Ghana, in a fashion that subordinated workers and peasants. James revealed disappointment that almost all economic activity by the people of Ghana was controlled or engaged in by state power. Ghana had become ‘a totalitarian state: no democracy, no socialism’.




This is no hagiography. Quest is more than willing, when he considers it necessary, to take James to task for inconsistency with his own values. A good example is the chapter on Lenin, in which he criticises him for his admiration of Lenin.




James’s Leninism existed in tension with his politics of direct democracy and workers’ self-management for modern industrial nations – aspects of which appear in his historical narratives of peripheral nations as well. We are partially indebted to his more libertarian socialist writings as a basis for making this criticism. Nevertheless, James’s Leninism and labour’s self-emancipation are not intellectual legacies which can be reconciled uncritically, save for scholars and activists who wish to elevate the banner of labour’s self-emancipation only to discipline and discard working people when they have their opportunity to enter the rules of hierarchy.




Quest’s summary of the significance of James’ philosophy in the Conclusion also sums up his own understanding of the world:




World revolution is not absurd. CLR James and his associates worked for an American revolution, Caribbean revolution, African revolution, and world revolution. And for this reality not to be faced as the unapologetic centre of inquiry into his life and legacies is to carry out a dastardly deed. Especially for those who believe fascism is on the brink, as if an avalanche fast approaching, and barbarism can be found everywhere, it is time to move beyond the thin gruel many offer in the name of historical scholarship and dried-up social movement thinking.




…If the world seems to be breaking up and in crisis, we must remember that it is not 

our

 world that’s in crisis. Just as if the government is in crisis, it is not 

our

 government. Not only is a new world possible, but new types of 

political

 people, different forms of organisation and arrangements of society are feasible and within our reach.




…Those who wish to restore institutions and systems they insisted were fundamentally bankrupt only a few years ago are emblematic of contemporary derangement. False words, banners, and picket signs responding to our accursed lot, necessarily are distributed by those who in fact are in social harmony with a significant section of overseers.




The moment for the socialist-curious (dubious as it always has been) to be enamored with senators, mayors, parliamentarians, and congresspeople condemning oligarchy (rule by the few), while openly collaborating with half the rulers of the world and their blocks of capital, is coming to an end. It is like cheering on those who oppose theocracy wishing to be Pope or the Ayatollah. Something else is required of us.




Quest’s book is a monumental work of scholarship, likely to be a standard resource on CLR James for years to come. It will be valuable to James scholars and the James-curious, researchers of national liberation movements and the left more broadly in the 20th century, and anyone interested in broadening their understanding of politics and society.

title: Resolution der IG Metall Vertrauensleute Mercedes Benz Untertürkheim: „Schluss jetzt. Protest, Widerstand, Streik! Die Bosse wollen Klassenkampf? Können sie haben!“
content:
Dossier




„

Fast kein Tag vergeht, an dem nicht ein Unternehmen ankündigt, zu entlassen oder auf unsere Kosten ,sparen“ zu müssen. Die Krise ist allgegenwärtig. Und die Bosse wollen uns dafür bezahlen lassen. (…) Bessere Politik braucht unseren gewerkschaftlichen und politischen Kampf! Deshalb warten wir nicht, bis uns jemand bittet zu protestieren. Wir fangen damit an! Sich selbst leidtun, auf eine vermeintliche ,Alternative für Deutschland“ hoffen oder Bitten und Betteln bei der Regierung hilft nicht. (…) Wir engagieren uns in unserer Gewerkschaft und verlangen so bald wie möglich, Demonstrationen gegen die Gier der Bosse, gegen die Regierung und für eine bessere Zukunft zu organisieren. Bis hin zum Streik. Und wenn die Gewerkschaftsspitzen sich zieren, dann machen wir das selbst

.“ 

Resolution der Vertrauensleute Mercedes Benz Untertürkheim vom Juni 2026

 

, die weitere Teile in der IG Metall inspiriert hat, nun auch als Petition. Siehe weiteren Widerstand:







20 Arbeiter:innen von Mercedes Stuttgart Untertürkheim fahren nach Berlin um Merz den „Marsch zu blasen“ 

 


„

Die Idee der Kolleg:innen: Warum nicht nach Berlin fahren, wo die Angriffe des Kapitals auf die Beschäftigten von der Politiik gebündelt werden? „Da Druck machen, wo es angebracht ist.“ Speerspitze für die verheerende aktuelle Angriffswelle ist doch Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz. Warum ihn nicht persönlich zur Rede stellen, ihm ordentlich den „Marsch blasen“, was seine Polititk so anrichtet, und ihm die Resolution der Mercedesvertrauenskörper persönlich übereichen? Die Idee war geboren.




Die Aktion




Am 9. Oktober war es soweit. Etwa 20 gewerkschaftliche Aktivist:innen hatten sich einen Tag Urlaub genommen und aus eigener Tasche eine Bahnfahrt nach Berlin gebucht. (…)




Am Nachmittag fand dann ein öffentlicher Protest vor dem Haupteingang des Bundestags statt. Gemeinsam mit Gewerkschafter:innen von IG Metall, Verdi und GEW aus Berlin, darunter auch eine Vertrauensfrau und ein Betriebsrat von Mercedes Berlin Marienfelde. die wir über Nacht vom Forum Gewerkschaftliche Linke Berlin noch ganz kurzfristig mobilisieren konnten. Gemeinsam hieß es hinter einem riesigen Transparent mit der Aufschrift „ohne Streik wird sich nichts verändern„: „Wir sind da, bereit zu kämpfen!“ „35 Stundenwoche“, „Merz muss weg“ und mit ihm seine Politik. „Solidarität gewinnt! Legt die Arbeit nieder! Geht auf die Straßen und zeigen wir Merz und den Bossen, wer hier im Land wirklich die Macht hat!“ Und sie skandierten ganz deutlich angesichts der anstehenden Tarifrunden: „Streik für unsere Löhne. Streik für unsere Zukunft bis dieses System wackelt. Ohne Streik wird sich nichts verändern.“




Um 17 Uhr ging es zum Bahnhof zurück mit dem Zug in den Südwesten der Republik

…“ 

Bericht vom Peter Vlatten vom 15. Oktober 2026 im Forum Gewerkschaftliche Linke Berlin

 

 

 mit Video




Petition: GEGENWEHR JETZT! Den Generalangriff der Bosse und ihrer Regierung stoppen. Für kämpferische Gewerkschaften. Für die Verteidigung unserer Errungenschaften.  




„

In den letzten Monaten haben Wirtschaftsbosse und Regierungsvertreter über die Medien den schärfsten Klassenkampf von oben in der deutschen Nachkriegsgeschichte angezettelt. (…) Mächtige halten Zeit für reif, Tarifverträge und soziale Sicherungssysteme einzustampfen. (…)

 

Wahrscheinlich haben viele von uns zu lange an die „Sozialpartnerschaft“ geglaubt. (…) Sie wollen auf unseren Kosten ihre Krise überwinden und ihre Profite sichern oder sogar ausweiten. Wir dagegen wollen ein würdiges Leben mit guten Arbeitsbedingungen, sozialer Sicherheit, Gesundheit und Frieden. 

Interessengegensatz erfordert Widerstand




(…) Die Angriffe werden nicht aufhören, wenn wir stillhalten. (…) Wenn wir heute zurückweichen, werden morgen nicht nur die nächsten Angriffe folgen. Rechtstendenzen kommen nicht von ungefähr (…) Die Gewerkschaften dürfen sich nicht noch einmal durch Untätigkeit mitschuldig machen. Wir sagen deshalb: Unsere Errungenschaften sind nicht verhandelbar! (…)


Es ist gut, dass ver.di Proteste zur Verteidigung des Sozialstaats organisiert. Es ist gut, dass die IG Metall am 21. September zu einem Aktionstag in der Auto- und der Zulieferindustrie aufruft. Es ist gut, dass der DGB am 26. September bundesweit Demos organisiert. Das alles wird aber nicht reichen. Es können nur erste Schritte in Richtung eines konsequenten Widerstands sein. Wir brauchen Gewerkschaften als wirkliche Gegenmacht…“ 

Petition bei change.org

 

 von Gewerkschafter:innen, Betriebsrät:innen, Vertrauensleuten und aktiven Kolleg:innen mit 130 namentlich genannten Erstunterzeichner:innen (darunter Mag Wompel/LabourNet)







Petition „Gegenwehr Jetzt!“ als Flyer

 

 (4 Seiten DIN A5) zum Verteilen, Einlegen in Betriebszeitungen, Auslegen in Pausenräumen, kulturellen Treffpunkten, … wo immer ihr es für sinnvoll erachtet…




Zur Unterstützung der Verbreitung gibt es auch ein 

Plakat zur Petition

 




Siehe zu den genannten Aktionen das Dossier: 

Gewerkschaften, Sozialabbau und Widerstand: Fast 25 Jahre Theorie und Praxis










[Fotos] Aktionstag 21.09.2026 Mercedes-Benz Werk Untertürkheim – AUFTAKT zu einem HEISSEN Herbst (während Daimler erpresst)

„Sparprogramm“ und Effizienzsteigerung dank E-Auto auch bei Daimler – Leiharbeiter zuerst…

Der Widerstand gegen die Folgen der Profitkrise für die Auto-Belegschaften wächst




Siehe Bericht aus Bawü und Untertürkheim auch in: Gewerkschaftsdemos: Ende der Harmonie.

Widerstand und kein Schritt zurück – offener Brandbrief von Mercedes Vertrauensleuten und Betriebsräten an den Vorstand der IG Metall




„… 

Mitte Juni beschlossen die IG Metall Bereichs-Vertrauenskörperleitungen bei Mercedes Untertürkheim eine Resolution, in der sie die aktuelle Politik der Bundesregierung mit klaren Worten beschreiben. Dort heißt es, mit dem angekündigten Stellenabbau, der geplanten Abschaffung des 8-Stunden-Tags und all den weiteren Angriffen auf unsere Arbeits- und Lebensbedingungen hätten die Bosse und ihr Staat uns, den lohnabhängig Beschäftigten, den Krieg erklärt. Damit sprechen die Kollegen vielen von uns aus der Seele. (…) Umso größer waren unser Erstaunen und unsere Empörung, als wir wenige Tage später den Gastkommentar von Christiane Benner gemeinsam mit dem milliardenschweren BDI-Präsidenten Peter Leibinger und dem Vorsitzenden der IGBCE, Michael Vassiliadis, lesen mussten. (…) Mit dem Kapital gemeinsam die Feder zu schwingen und gleichzeitig uns Mitgliedern die Kampfbereitschaft zu predigen hat mit Authentizität nichts zu tun. Wir fragen uns: welche der beiden Seiten spielt uns etwas vor? (…) Wir sagen es ganz deutlich: Damit spricht unsere Vorsitzende weder in unserem Namen noch im Namen der vielen Tausend aktiven betrieblichen Kolleginnen und Kollegen, die hinter uns stehen. Was uns zusätzlich verwundert: Warum erscheint dieser Kommentar nur wenige Tage nach der Untertürkheimer Resolution? Ist der Gastkommentar als bewusster öffentlicher Widerspruch zu der Positionierung aus unseren Betrieben gemeint? (…)


Wir wollen es deshalb noch einmal klar sagen: Die Unternehmerverbände, die Bundesregierung und wir Beschäftigten verfolgen gegenwärtig offensichtlich sehr unterschiedliche Interessen. Sie wollen auf unseren Kosten ihre Krise überwinden und ihre Profite sichern oder ausweiten. Wir dagegen wollen gute Arbeitsstandards erhalten, soziale Sicherheit, bezahlbaren Wohnraum, gute Bildung, Gesundheit und Frieden. (…)


Wir erleben in unserem Betrieb jeden Tag, dass wir in einer Klassengesellschaft leben. Wir erleben, dass die Interessen von uns lohnabhängig Beschäftigten und die Interessen von Unternehmensleitungen und der Regierung immer häufiger diametral gegenüberstehen. Gleichzeitig sehen wir aber auch die Chance, aus diesen Konflikten gestärkt hervorzugehen. Als Gewerkschaft, die sich nicht alles gefallen lässt. Als Gewerkschaft, die wieder kämpft. Und als Gewerkschaft, die ihre Stärke aus den Betrieben und den Kollegen bezieht. Die Errungenschaften, die unzählige Kollegen vor uns hart erkämpft haben, dürfen wir uns nicht zahnlos aus der Hand nehmen lassen

…“ Der sehr umfangreiche 

am 11. August 2026 im „Forum gewerkschaftliche Linke Berlin“ dokumentierte offene Brief

siehe diesen auch 

als pdf-Datei

Es gibt Fragen, die beantwortet sein wollen. Eine davon ist, wie ernst meint es die eigene Führung damit, den notwendigen Widerstand zu organisieren, um die gegenwärtige Angriffswelle von Kapital und Regierung zurückzuschlagen? Wie ehrlich gehen wir als Gewerkschafter:innen miteinander um?

gemeinsame Erklärung

Fast kein Tag vergeht, an dem nicht ein Unternehmen ankündigt, zu entlassen oder auf unsere Kosten „sparen“ zu müssen. Die Krise ist allgegenwärtig. Und die Bosse wollen uns dafür bezahlen lassen. (…) Das Geld, was in den Sozialkassen durch die Sparmaßnahmen fehlt, flieẞt auch in die Aufrüstung. Unsere Jugend soll wieder für die Profite der Konzerne in den Krieg ziehen. Bessere Politik braucht unseren gewerkschaftlichen und politischen Kampf! Deshalb warten wir nicht, bis uns jemand bittet zu protestieren. Wir fangen damit an! Genau so, wie die Vertrauensleute von Mercedes Untertürkheim! Sich selbst leid zu tun, auf eine vermeintliche, Alternative für Deutschland“ zu hoffen oder Bitten und Betteln bei der Regierung hilft nicht. (…)


Wir sind Kolleginnen und Kollegen aus verschiedenen Volkswagen-Werken. Wir sind Vertrauensleute, Betriebsräte und Vertrauenskörperleitungen. Vor allem aber sind wir kämpferische IG-Metaller. Wir stellen uns dem geplanten Stellenabbau entgegen und lehnen jede weitere Kürzung ab

…“ 

Flugblatt vom 3.8.2026

„

Die Vertrauensleute von Mercedes-Benz Untertürkheim haben vorgelegt. Als IG Metall-Ortsjugendausschüsse Stuttgart, Esslingen, Freiburg-Lörrach, Ludwigsburg-Waiblingen, Reutlingen-Tübingen und als JAV Mercedes-Benz Untertürkheim ziehen wir nach. Fast jeden Tag hören wir: Jobs werden gestrichen, Auszubildende und Studierende nicht übernommen, ganze Werke schlieẞen. Überall soll gespart werden – vor allem auf unsere Kosten. Und nicht nur im Betrieb werden wir angegriffen.


Auch die Politik gibt den Forderungen der Kapitalisten immer weiter nach (…)


Während bei uns gekürzt wird und wir unsere Jobs verlieren, ist plötzlich genug Geld da: für Aufrüstung und Krieg. Auẞerdem wird die Wehrpflicht wieder eingeführt, da wir dieses Elend im Zweifel sogar mit unserem eigenen Leben verteidigen sollen. Aber statt ,,fürs Vaterland zu sterben“, wollen wir:

Doch eins ist klar: Das bekommen wir nicht geschenkt. Denn: die Kapitalisten – und wir? Wir spielen nicht im selben Team.


Die machen Profit. Wir machen die Arbeit. Die werden reicher. Wir sollen verzichten.


Rumjammern bringt nichts. Betteln auch nicht. Und darauf hoffen, dass irgendwer das schon regelt, erst recht nicht. Wenn sich etwas ändern soll, dann nur, wenn wir es selbst in die Hand nehmen und kämpfen.


Deshalb sagen wir: Protest, Widerstand, Streik!


Im Folgenden schlieẞen wir uns den Worten der Vertrauensleute aus Untertürkheim an

…“

title: YRK: We will exercise our right to self-defense against any attack targeting our people and forces
content:
The Command of the East Kurdistan Defense Units (YRK) issued a written statement regarding the latest attacks by the Iranian regime on the Shaho region. The YRK warned that it would fully exercise its right to self-defense if the attacks continued.




The YRK Command’s statement on Saturday reads as follows:




“Recently, our forces have once again become targets of attacks by the Iranian regime. We are sharing information about each attack to ensure that the public is informed of the facts. As we have stated before, we reiterate once again: We will exercise our right to self-defense against any attack targeting our people and our forces.




Since October 13, the Iranian regime has deployed a large force of Revolutionary Guards (Pasdaran), along with heavy weapons and kamikaze (explosive-laden) unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), to the Shaho region. On October 13, the enemy bombed and shelled the Qilbê Plain area using heavy weapons and kamikaze drones.




Furthermore, in the early hours of October 15, the Kela Terzan area was attacked by four UAVs, followed by further bombardment by Revolutionary Guard forces that continued until noon. The regime has increased the number of troops in the region, indicating its intention to continue military operations and attacks against our forces in this area.




We would also like to emphasize that our forces have issued the necessary warnings in response to these attacks. However, this does not mean that our response will always be limited to warnings. If these attacks continue, we, as the East Kurdistan Defense Units, will fully exercise our right to self-defense and respond accordingly.”







Iran’s Revolutionary Guards attack Kurdistan highlands with heavy weapons

The Kurdistan Human Rights Network reported heavy artillery shelling and drone attacks by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on parts of the Shaho Mountains in the Dasht-e Qalb area....
