title: Book Review: Maximum Leverage: From the Street to the Picket Line
content:
Union strength or weakness is often seen only through the light of a strike or lockout. Phil Cohen’s memoir, 

Maximum Leverage: From the Street to the Picket Line

, tells a different story. Union building is on-going, from organizing to win a first contract, to maintaining and strengthening that contract over time, from grievance handling to arbitration, from safety and health to pension rights. And in every situation there is a need to build membership participation, develop and support local leadership, strengthen mutual support, ensure understanding of rights, understanding of power and how to wield it (or lose it). 




Cohen demonstrates as much as he explains how every aspect of the above is at the heart of a union’s ability to improve conditions on the job, improve pay and benefits, and ultimately be able to win on the picket line if it comes to that.




A chapter recalling fighting back against a union-busting attorney during bargaining is emblematic. BTR Sealing Systems in Reidsville, North Carolina—a factory making wiper blades for auto companies—negotiated a first contract with workers after the plant was organized in 1995. Frequent grievances and conflicts with supervisors were part of the reality where both workers and frontline supervisors were unfamiliar with negotiating day-to-day disputes via a contract. Nonetheless, eventually issues were resolved and a working relationship developed between the union and the company.




The developing good workplace environment turned poisonous when the second contract came up and management’s proposal included eliminating the union’s right to file National Labor Relations Board or discrimination charges, eliminating past practice as an argument during a grievance procedure, requiring the union to sign up all members anew at the end of each calendar year, amongst other poison pill provisions. Complicating matters, some union members were pushing for wage demands beyond what the union could win or the company could pay. 




For Cohen, this meant waging a no-holds-barred campaign against management while educating the membership about what would or would not be possible to achieve. He makes clear, too, that while compromises are necessary in any battle, these ought not compromise rights or unity, and that while maintaining a good relationship with managers can be helpful, members’ interests and needs always must come first.




Key in all of this, however, was aggressively resisting management’s assaults, winning improvements in conditions, pay, benefits wherever there was an opening, all while maintaining workplace unity. As Cohen tells a manager who wants him to support an inadequate contract, “One thing you’ve got to understand about me. My goal isn’t to ratify by fifty percent plus one. I’ve got good instincts about a local’s threshold. If I don’t sense a nearly unanimous ratification, I’ll get out in front of the militants and recommend the contract be voted down. A split vote means a divided local for the next three years. I’d rather walk a picket line.” 




Ultimately, none of the company’s anti-union proposals were in the final contract, the union won some wage gains and improved contract language—and strengthened the local’s in-plant leadership.




GO ON THE OFFENSIVE




Similarly, Cohen describes the strategy he employed in 1998 engaging a vastly different workforce when winning a first contract with newly organized Starlite Bedding (a company manufacturing mattresses) in Greensboro, North Carolina, and again when resisting a decertification attempt at a Kmart distribution center in the same city in 2002. Other fights he recounts address potential layoffs and a threatened closure at a textile mill, overcoming KKK influence at a foam manufacturing plant, and resisting concessions at a large clothing manufacturer.




Yet his memoir is not just a recitation of war stories. When describing how he successfully defended a warehouse worker unfairly fired, Cohn explains the difference between non-union “employment-at-will” and union contract “just cause” protections. So too in a chapter on helping a worker at a textile mill (making carpets) get compensation for a workplace injury, he explains how employers try to get around fairly paying workers’ compensation claims.




Although each situation is different, each similarly involves total awareness of the personalities and economics involved, and requires an organizer’s judgement of how to involve local communities, reach the media, and utilize union legal and research resources. Cohen’s approach, even when holding a seemingly weak hand, is to go on the offensive while maintaining realism about the objective, all while never losing sight of the goal—be it a good contract, saving pensions, or ensuring workplace safety.




STAY AGGRESSIVE EVEN UNDER ATTACK




There are good books that explain how unions function, that discuss the role of the NLRB or OSHA, that discuss labor strategy and cite examples of what has or has not worked in the past. What gives Cohen’s book a substance most “how to” or theoretical accounts lack, is that he is writing about his own experience, giving names and faces to vivid personalities with all their quirks and contradictions that is the living reality of a union. Thus readers see the range of experiences that embodies labor organization, in a way no textbook can provide.




One lesson that comes through is to always be aggressive on behalf of the membership—even (or especially) when under attack. Union building for Cohen is rooted in understanding points of strength and weakness on both sides, thereby discovering where the union has “maximum leverage.” 




Cohen’s own life experience informed his practical and moral understanding of where the difference between the boss and workers lies:




Management investigations tend to be little more than an exercise in rubber-stamping previously made decisions. They seldom take time to scratch beneath the surface of what appear to be straightforward incidents, in search of the whole truth. Employees are considered expendable and the impact on human beings and their families isn’t a corporate consideration.




Human resource directors, even the few who actually give a damn, understand that keeping their job depends on maintaining levels of productivity that won’t tolerate distractions motivated by compassion or justice.




’SOUL OF AN OUTLAW’




Cohen became a union activist when working as a bus driver in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, in the early 1980s at a facility where the workers were represented by a do-nothing local. Success there took him on the path to become a union rep for ACTWU (Amalgamated Clothing and Textile Workers Union), on through its various iterations as UNITE, UNITE HERE, and continuing into its current incarnation as Workers United-SEIU. From first to last (the final campaign noted in his memoir was in 2018) it was the culture and the militance of the southern textile workers that he embraced.




Life experience before moving south, however, prepared Cohen for the union organizing to come. On the streets of New York from 1967 (when he was 16) through the late 1970s, Cohen was part of New York’s East Village scene during a time when the counter-culture was collapsing into survival mode, where life was cheap in every sense of the word. 




During those years he frequently drove cabs which, in pre-gentrified times, was considered the most dangerous job around. He washed dishes, lived in and “managed” a hotel for people who fell through the porous cracks of the city. It is a world vividly described in the first section of 

Maximum Leverage

—bringing to mind my own memories of those times and neighborhoods.




Being part of the world with people who were handed a bad deck, every day on the knife’s edge, set the framework for how Cohen approached unionism, as he notes in the prologue: “I always had an instinct for survival and playing the system, sometimes using it to keep other street kids alive or out of prison … I had the soul of an outlaw but was never a criminal. An outlaw ignores the rules in favor of his own code but doesn’t prey upon the weak and innocent.”




Similarly, life where food, shelter, safety were always in question helped shape the convictions that made him a unionist. As he writes, “Living on the fringes of society did far more to shape my views about social justice and how the system really works than any classroom could have.”




Kurt Stand is a longtime labor movement activist and a member of the Democratic Socialists of America.

 Maximum Leverage 

was published by Hardball Press. You can purchase a copy directly from the author at 

fightingunionbusters.org

.

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: As parts of the Nicola River run dry, a father fears what his children will inherit
content:
Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, walks through a dry stretch of the Nicola River on Sept. 18, 2026, a few minutes downstream from his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in the Nicola Valley, in B.C.’s southern interior. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




On this stretch of the Nicola River, Brian Holmes misses the sound of water. 




“This is heartbreaking,” he quietly says to himself as he prepares to park above a kilometre-long stretch where no surface water remains.




In the absence of the river’s flow, birds can be heard in the thick vegetation, their calls occasionally joined by a horse neighing in the distance or a car passing along Douglas Lake Road above.




The 44-year-old Upper Nicola Band (UNB) member and father of two leaves his vehicle and disappears into the bush separating the river from a small ranch below the road, a few minutes downstream from his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in the Nicola Valley, in “B.C.’s” southern interior. 




He re-emerges from the bush and makes his way down a steep slope into the exposed riverbed, where large boulders rise from a channel that should be running with water on this warm mid-September morning.




The Nicola River winds roughly 210 kilometres through syilx and Nlakaʼpamux homelands. It flows from its headwaters on the Thompson-Okanagan Plateau, down through Douglas and Nicola lakes before passing through Merritt, and eventually joining the Thompson River northeast of Lytton at Spences Bridge.




But along this one-kilometre dry stretch between Douglas and Nicola Lakes, just around the corner from the community’s drinking water, the waterway resembles more of a meandering valley of rocks.




“I’ve been looking at it enough that it’s numb to me now. This didn’t happen yesterday. It’s been like this for the last month,” said Holmes.




He said that it’s tough to see dried-up sections of the river, especially “when you know there should be water.”




“It’s supposed to be the major river system in this watershed, but it doesn’t have any water flowing through it over the surface,” Holmes said.




“We’ve seen a little bit of a flow coming out of Douglas Lake, but it’s going to get sucked in by the groundwater now. There is a little trickle, but then it just disappears partway down. Any water that pops up anywhere is all groundwater.”




Just upstream, on a bend in the river, there’s a deep hole in the waterway that Holmes and his friends used as a makeshift natural swimming pool every summer when they were children.




Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, stands near a deep hole in the Nicola River that he and his friends swam in as children, in his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) on Sept. 18, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




“I don’t know if you would swim in it now,” he said, citing health concerns from a buildup of harmful algae blooms in the water.




“I’m hoping by the time (my sons) get to my age, they can enjoy it. If we’re in these (drought) cycles — hopefully we can survive long enough.”




He walks across the dry riverbed, using the boulders as stepping stones, then stops for a moment and looks downstream to where water should be flowing.




Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, walks through a dry stretch of the Nicola River on Sept. 18, 2026, a few minutes downstream from his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in the Nicola Valley, in B.C.’s southern interior. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




“It’s like another world, man. It’s — I don’t know. It just makes me think about missing that sound of water flowing,” Holmes said.




“When you walk down a stream, and there’s no water, it’s like losing a relative, losing a part of you. It’s just hard to explain.”




A few dozen kilometres up the river from this spot, where the stream converges with Chapperon Creek before flowing into Douglas Lake, IndigiNews observed smaller dry patches along the waterway’s surface as well.




A dry patch of the Nicola River, at its confluence with Chapperon Creek northeast of Douglas Lake, on Sept. 18, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




The watershed entered the growing season with little room to spare. In March, “B.C.’s” River Forecast Centre 

forecast seasonal inflows

 to the Nicola River and Nicola Lake at just 40 to 60 per cent of normal, citing low snowpack, dry weather and already-low flows.




By mid-June, the Nicola basin was a Level 4 on 

the province’s drought scale

, the second-highest rating. It remained at that level in mid-July and had reached Level 5, the highest rating, by early August. 




It dropped to a Level 2 as of October, but the concern now extends into another winter. In its 

fall seasonal outlook

, the BC Wildfire Service warned that an intensifying El Niño could bring warm, dry conditions and reduced snowpack to the Interior, limiting the prospect of drought recovery before next summer. 




Holmes described a year in which insufficient snow and precipitation, combined with warm temperatures, left less cold water flowing from the highlands into the watershed’s rivers and creeks.




As flows diminished, some waterways dried up. Elsewhere, he said, nutrients and sediment accumulated in the remaining water, with algae spreading across rivers, creeks and lakes. 




An algae bloom on spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in Upper Nicola Band territory on Sept. 18, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




“It’s pretty tough,” Holmes said of the conditions. 




“Usually, I go out on (Douglas Lake) and get the calm. But now, when I go on the lake, I see the algae, I see the low flow. It just makes it worse. It makes me wonder, ‘What are we doing?’”




For much of September, Holmes, who has served on his community’s council for over a decade, has been “taking some action” by documenting the watershed’s ailing health and posting videos to 

his YouTube page

. 




“I can not sit here and watch it happen, and have my kids not being able to enjoy what we had, what we did when we were kids.”




Bringing awareness to the issue through his videos “is the hope,” he said.




Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, stands near an algae bloom on spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in Upper Nicola Band territory on Sept. 18, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




“The more people that are aware of the situation, the more they can express concern and advocate for more work to be done about it. Or, step in and help,” he said.




“If the land isn’t healing and healthy, then our people aren’t healing and healthy.”




Alongside those effects on the community, Holmes worries about what continued drought and poor water quality could mean for native fish populations, now and in the years ahead.




“We could lose this ecosystem for a whole generation (of fish) — that’s the concern with the kokanee,” he said. “If we don’t do something, they’ll be like the salmon: they won’t be here anymore.”




Spawning adult Kokanee in Quilchena Creek on Sept. 18, 2026, near where the creek flows into Nicola Lake. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




These cumulative impacts, he said, warrant treating the watershed crisis as an emergency.




“If this continues into the winter and into next year, it’s going to be even worse than what we experienced this year,” he said.




“If we don’t think this is an emergency, wait until next year. Everything [in the water] is going to be dead. The fish in the lake will be dead. That’s my worry.”




A dead adult Kokanee near Quilchena Creek by Nicola Lake on Sept. 18, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




‘In my lifetime, I haven’t seen water this low’




Snowmelt and precipitation help replenish the watershed’s rivers and creeks, while dams on lakes such as Chapperon regulate the release of stored water.




But the region didn’t get the snow or precipitation levels that they “really needed” at the beginning of the year, Holmes said. 




He said warm temperatures also brought an earlier spring freshet, the seasonal rise in streamflow as snow melts. Clearcut logging in the highlands has affected the land’s ability to retain water, he added.




“It’s melting earlier. But this year, we didn’t even really have a freshet. Flows came up, but nothing of concern. You could barely tell that they came up.”




Surface waters dried up “pretty quick” by June, he said.




“In my lifetime, I haven’t seen water this low.”




A dry stretch of the Nicola River on Sept. 18, 2026, a few minutes downstream from the Upper Nicola Band community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake). 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Both UNB communities, spaxmn and n̓łq̓iłəml̓x (Quilchena), get their drinking water from wells supplied by groundwater reserves rather than creeks or other surface waters.




Holmes worries that if drought and water scarcity continue into the following year, the lack of surface water flowing through the watershed could begin to affect groundwater availability.




“Because the surface water is no longer there, it starts dewatering the groundwater — there’s less groundwater to take from, because the surface water isn’t replenishing,” he said.




“It’s just a domino effect. If we don’t get more precipitation, more snow, to fill these, it’s going to start impacting our groundwater, which is very important as well.”




Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, looks towards algae and low-water-flows on the Nicola River in his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) on Sept. 18, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




A notice in Upper Nicola Band’s 

Sept. 2 newsletter

 said a water restriction for Douglas Lake residents was lifted on Aug. 25, though it continues to urge conservation. 




He raised a question about the community’s future.




“If there isn’t water here, how much longer can we live here?” he asked.




“That’s part of why our community is out here, because of water.”




‘Now, my kids can’t even go in here’




Holmes said low flows and warm temperatures, combined with nutrients from cattle manure and runoff from wildfire-affected land, have contributed to algal blooms across the watershed’s lakes, rivers and creeks — from Nicola River to Douglas Lake.




An algae bloom on spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in Upper Nicola Band territory on Sept. 18, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




“There’s no flush of the water through the system,” he said. “You actually go into these streams, and there’s so much algae on the rocks and slime on the rocks in the stream, because it’s not flowing enough and the temperatures are too high.”




Warm, slow-moving water and excess nutrients can encourage the growth of cyanobacteria, commonly called blue-green algae. Some produce toxins harmful to people and animals, according to 

Health Canada

. 




At Nicola Lake, 

BC Parks advises

 visitors to avoid contact with suspected blue-green algae and discourages swimming near blooms.




“We’ve had people that got splashed by some algae water and started rashing up from it,” he said.




Water-quality concerns have also changed how community members practice ceremony.




“Now, when we do ceremony, we don’t go in the water anymore – part of the ceremony is going in the water. But because of the quality and the issues that we’re seeing, it’s unsafe to put individuals in there.”




Holmes said community members have been advised against eating kokanee harvested from the watershed because of the blooms, “because you just don’t know how much has accumulated in them.”




“It’s questionable to eat the fish out of here.”




Algae and low-water-flows on Quilchena Creek on Sept. 18, 2026, where the waterway flows into Nicola Lake. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Recreational swimming and fishing “is just no longer,” he said.




“I remember, as a kid coming up in these areas, and it was fine to swim in this in the summertime. There was no concern. Now, my kids can’t even go in here and swim in it.”




A generation of kokanee at risk




On Sept. 18, adult kokanee were spawning in the shallow flows of Quilchena Creek, a tributary of Nicola Lake. Among the fish, IndigiNews observed a dead adult that Holmes said appeared to have died before spawning.




“When it’s super warm, it’s really tough for them to come up through here. It’s a lot of energy being exerted to get through,” he said.




A dead adult Kokanee in Quilchena Creek on Sept. 18, 2026, where the creek flows into Nicola Lake. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Kokanee are a freshwater form of sockeye salmon. While ocean-going sockeye migrate to sea before returning to freshwater to spawn, kokanee remain in freshwater throughout their lives. In this system, Holmes described kokanee living in Nicola Lake before moving into rivers, creeks and other tributaries to spawn.




Adults die after spawning, leaving their eggs to develop in the gravel.




“Their babies will go out in the springtime and then come back, two to three years from now. But if the water stops flowing in this creek, then that whole genetic generation of that fish is gone,” said Holmes.




“If that keeps happening over the next couple of years, we will eventually lose all the kokanee in this lake — at least the ones that spawn in this system.”




Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, walks by a dead adult Kokanee in Quilchena Creek on Sept. 18, 2026, where the creek flows into Nicola Lake, downstream from his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake). 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




For ocean-going salmon returning to the upper watershed, the route passes through the outlet of Nicola Lake, where the Nicola Dam stands. The original structure was built in 1927 and replaced in 1985-86, according to provincial records.




Holmes links the disappearance of those salmon from the upper watershed to the dam and changes in water flow.




“The water stopped flowing. The government said the salmon will figure stuff out; the experts were saying they’ll figure stuff out, so no real action was taken. Here we are, 40 to 60 years later, there’s no salmon in this upper part of the watershed,” he said.




“It’s a similar conversation with the kokanee, that they’ll figure things out. I’m not wanting to take that risk.”




Beyond the spawning grounds, Holmes has been watching for other wildlife along creeks and rivers with little or no surface water. He said the shortage of cold-water flows has consequences throughout the watershed.




“If there’s no water here, then these animals are no longer here, including bears, deer and moose. All the ungulates that rely on it,” he said.




“Even the mice, the snakes. It’s a huge cumulative impact, when you really sit down and think about what needs access to water.”




Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, walks along a low-flowing Quilchena Creek on Sept. 18, 2026, where the waterway flows into Nicola Lake, downstream from his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake). 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




‘We just can’t keep making it worse’




Holmes hopes a proposed fish hatchery at spaxmn could open in 2027. Eggs collected from breeding fish would be incubated and young fish raised at the site before being released into the watershed.




“The genetics from the natural, native fish — you can grow them in a hatchery, because they obviously can’t — they’re not going to survive in these rocks,” he said.




Through the 

Nicola Watershed Governance Partnership

, Holmes said there have also been discussions about increasing water storage to address low flows and water scarcity during drought.




The partnership brings together the provincial government and five First Nations governments: Coldwater, Lower Nicola, Nooaitch, Shackan and Upper Nicola. 




“We’re actually talking about putting a dam here on Douglas Lake. That will hold back water,” he said.




spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in Upper Nicola Band territory on Sept. 18, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




The proposals also include upgrading the existing dam on Chapperon Lake and building one on Pennask Lake to increase storage in the headwaters. The aim is to retain water during wetter periods for release when downstream flows fall.




“I’m not saying it’s going to cure it all. But it’ll help alleviate it, and hopefully get us through this cycle,” he said.




“We’ve done a study through the Nicola Watershed Partnership to identify those sites. Now we just need to go source funding to implement it.”




The partnership’s 

2024 call for a storage investigation

 sought an inventory of existing reservoirs and potential new sites in the Nicola watershed above Merritt, excluding Nicola Lake and its dam, and in the Coldwater watershed. Researchers were asked to assess storage capacity, environmental impacts and downstream effects, then recommend sites for further feasibility studies.




The province has acknowledged difficulties turning earlier research into action. In its 

June 2025 order establishing a water sustainability planning area for the Nicola watershed

, it cited costs, coordination difficulties and limited capacity while responding to seasonal emergencies as reasons recommendations had not been fully implemented.




Work on the water sustainability plan remains underway, according to “B.C.’s” 

2025–26 progress report

.




To address algal blooms, Holmes called for greater efforts to limit cattle access to rivers and streams, protecting waterways from manure and other contaminants. He also wants changes to logging practices to help retain water at higher elevations for longer.




A separate forest-planning process is underway in the region. From May to July, the Ministry of Forests sought public input on the 

tmíxʷ naqscn Forest Landscape Plan

, which First Nations and the province are developing for an area that includes the Merritt Timber Supply Area. Water, watershed health and climate adaptation are among its priorities. The process remains in its second of five phases, identifying and assessing the values that will guide future forest management.




“The water’s sick. We need to give it time to heal. So stay away from it, stay out of it. It’ll do its thing. We just can’t keep making it worse,” he said.




“We have to be conscious of our own use and our own contamination to it.”




Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, walks near spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in his community on Sept. 18, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Recovery could take longer than one winter. In a 

Sept. 21 bulletin

, the province warned that precipitation may first replenish depleted soils and groundwater before reaching rivers, lakes and reservoirs. Restoring water levels could take several years.




While plans and efforts are being made to help the water, Holmes said, “it’s tough to sit here and experience this.”




His sons already send him photographs of the dry riverbed on their way to school.




“I wonder for our children, ‘Is this going to be what they’re going to live with?’ When my kid is my age, he won’t have any kokanee here. And what is he going to eat? Rocks? It’s crazy, right?”




The post 

As parts of the Nicola River run dry, a father fears what his children will inherit

 appeared first on 

Indiginews

.

author: Aaron Regunberg
title: New Documents Expose Exxon’s Attempt to Suppress Damning Climate Evidence
content:
A paper from 1992 shows the oil company anticipating how the melting of Arctic ice sheets could impact its bottom line.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

“Do you believe that statement’s misleading?”

“All the clauses in there are patently false. And I told them so.”

So reads an exchange from the deposition of Joseph Weissman, an ExxonMobil scientist with the company’s former algae biofuels program. The “patently false” statement in question was a corporate press release claiming algae biofuel was a viable solution to climate change that the company would soon be producing at scale. Extensive reporting has already uncovered how ExxonMobil spent nearly half as much advertising its algae research as it spent on the research itself. But testimony like Weissman’s shows just how clearly the company understood that this much-touted project was, in Weissman’s words, a “dead end.” The goal was not to create a viable alternative energy source, but simply, as one internal memo put it, to make consumers “[b]elieve ExxonMobil is committed to helping solve climate change.”

Weissman’s deposition was taken by the Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office as part of its lawsuit against ExxonMobil alleging consumer protection violations. In an under-the-radar filing in April, Massachusetts disclosed this deposition, as well as a range of other documents it had uncovered, to demonstrate the relevance of additional investigative targets that ExxonMobil had been furiously attempting to shield from discovery. These newly released materials cover a range of topics and time periods, from memos on the company’s more recent deceptive advertising campaigns to evidence of its decades-old climate knowledge.

One of the documents is a 1992 paper, “Climate Change Impacts on Northern Offshore Petroleum Operations,” which analyzes how Exxon’s operations in the Beaufort Sea would be affected by its predictions of a “much thinner ice sheet” and other anticipated effects of global warming caused by the use of its products. The upshot for Exxon: “[I]f ice conditions become less severe as predicted, then offshore petroleum operations will become easier and less costly.” Papers like this, demonstrating ExxonMobil’s sophisticated understanding of the realities of global warming, were produced at the same time the company was ramping up its public efforts to, in its own words, “emphasize the uncertainty in scientific conclusions” on climate change in order to prevent the “development of nonfossil fuel resources.”

Needless to say, the contrast between oil companies’ internal climate knowledge and external climate denial is profoundly damaging to the industry. This helps explain why it is going to such extraordinary lengths to attack these climate cases. These corporations are not just afraid of losing these lawsuits; they’re also afraid of the damning evidence the suits will uncover.

This is the skeleton key for understanding Suncor v. Boulder, the high-profile climate case the Supreme Court heard in early October.

Suncor began in 2018, when Boulder, Colorado, sued fossil fuel companies Suncor and ExxonMobil for damages from climate change and the companies’ lies about their role in fueling it. After the Colorado Supreme Court rejected the defendants’ motion to dismiss the case, Suncor and ExxonMobil — likely terrified of what would happen if Boulder were allowed to have its day in court — asked the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene, repeating a request the fossil fuel industry has made again and again in recent years, alongside parallel efforts to lobby Congress and state legislatures to grant it immunity from all climate-related liability.

There is a reason why oil and gas companies are so desperate to stop these cases by any means before they proceed any further. We have likely seen just a sliver of the evidence they have that shows they’ve spent decades knowingly deceiving the public about climate science, climate harms, and their commitment to climate action. How many more reports are they sitting on like the 1992 paper laying out ExxonMobil’s projected opportunities for profiting off a melting Arctic? How many more internal communications like Weissman’s saying that “all the clauses” in a 2018 press release about ExxonMobil’s signature climate solution were “patently false?” The current offensive isn’t just about defeating the cases. It’s also about preventing the public from learning the extent and severity of the industry’s wrongdoing. It’s about fossil fuel CEOs’ profound fear of sitting in front of a jury of 12 Americans and trying to defend their companies’ deceptive conduct — because they know it’s indefensible.

Regardless of how the Supreme Court rules in Suncor, it’s hard to imagine these companies can bury the evidence of their lies and escape accountability indefinitely. Whatever the onetime value of fossil fuels to the economy, their harms now massively outweigh their benefits, particularly since the vast majority of fossil fuel use can be replaced by cleaner, cheaper, safer forms of energy — and this has been true for a long time. Instead of adapting, the industry has clung tightly to a civilization-endangering business model and engaged in a massive deception campaign to do so. Along the way, its conduct has become some of the most harmful and culpable in human history. Eventually, it will be held to account.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Mag
title: Italien: Landesweite Arbeitsniederlegungen vom 11. Oktober 2026 bis zum 10. April 2027 für mehr Gesundheitsschutz, Entlohnung und Arbeitnehmerrechte bei Amazon
content:
„

Die Gewerkschaft ALA (Associazione Libera Associates) hat für die Amazon-Belegschaften in Italien vom 11. Oktober 2026 bis zum 10. April 2027 zu landesweiten Mobilisierungsmaßnahmen aufgerufen. Der angekündigte Zeitraum entspricht nicht sechs Monaten ununterbrochenem Streik: Er erlaubt laut Angaben der Gewerkschaft ein- oder zweistündige Arbeitsniederlegungen zu Beginn oder am Ende der Schicht sowie ganztägige Streiks. Die Gewerkschaft fordert Verbesserungen in den Bereichen Sicherheit und Gesundheitsschutz, Vergütung, Arbeitszeitgestaltung und die Achtung der Arbeitnehmerrechte. ALA weist darauf hin, dass der Aufruf eine Reaktion auf Probleme darstellt, auf die sie bereits seit Langem hingewiesen hat, sowie auf die unzureichende Reaktion auf ihre Verhandlungsforderungen. Das flexible System der Arbeitsniederlegungen ermöglicht es, an verschiedenen Standorten und in verschiedenen Schichten zu intervenieren, ohne eine Unterbrechung der Tätigkeit als dauerhaft darzustellen, die es nicht ist

.“ Aus dem span. 

Beitrag vom 13. Oktober 2026 der Redaktion von Sindicalismo.org

 

 (Amazon gegen seine Beschäftigten: Sieben internationale Konflikte zwischen Streiks, Gewerkschaftsbildung und Entlassungen, maschinenübersetzt), siehe auch die A.L.A. dazu:







ALA-STREIK BEI AMAZON: IM MITTELPUNKT DER MOBILISIERUNG 

Gesundheit, Arbeitsbedingungen, Vergütung, Arbeitszeiten und Achtung der Rechte




„

A.L.A. ruft zu einem neuen landesweiten Streik der Beschäftigten der Unternehmen der Amazon-Gruppe auf, da auf die Forderungen nach Verhandlungen nicht eingegangen wurde und die bereits gemeldeten Probleme weiterhin bestehen.




Die Durchführung des Streiks erfolgt gemäß den organisatorischen Vorgaben der Gewerkschaft, die den Beschäftigten regelmäßig über die offiziellen Kanäle von A.L.A. mitgeteilt werden. Dies gewährleistet ein einheitliches Vorgehen, verhindert Verwirrung durch falsche Interpretationen und schützt jeden Streikteilnehmer rechtlich. (..)




Die Entscheidung folgt auf monatelange Meldungen, Forderungen nach Maßnahmen und gewerkschaftliche Initiativen zu Problemen, die ALA täglich an den Arbeitsplätzen erfasst.




Wir sprechen hier nicht von abstrakten Themen. Wir sprechen von den Bedingungen, unter denen Tausende von Menschen jeden Tag arbeiten

. 

(…) AB DEM 11. OKTOBER STREIKEN WIR. Nicht gegen die Arbeit. Sondern weil die Arbeit diejenigen respektieren muss, die sie verrichten

.“ ital. 

Mitteilung von A.L.A. vom 5.10.2026

 

 – Associazione Libera Associates (maschinenübersetzt)







Siehe zu Amazon in Italien auch:







2026: 

Italienische Gewerkschaften schließen mit Amazon eine Vereinbarung für alle 57 Standorte (Transport und Logistik) ab, die u.a. die Videoüberwachung einschränkt

Die Rebellen von Amazon: Neuer Streik in Vigonza, Italien

Streiken gegen Amazon – geht da endlich was?

Streik bei Amazon nahe Turin – und einige Schlussfolgerungen aus bisherigen Kämpfen in Zeiten von Corona

Ohne DHL, Hermes oder lästige Festangestellte: Amazon Flex international




Dossier: 

Gegen Amazons Spionage-Regiment: Gewerkschaften in Spanien, Großbritannien und Frankreich – und in Winsen – mobilisieren zum Widerstand




Dossier: 

„Haltet das Maul und arbeitet mehr“ – die rücksichtslose Corona-Politik von Amazon ruft immer mehr Widerstand hervor: Weltweit

Erster Tarifvertrag bei Amazon erkämpft: In Piacenza/Italien wird die Neuordnung der Schichtarbeit vereinbart

Italien: Landesweite Arbeitsniederlegungen vom 11. Oktober 2026 bis zum 10. April 2027 für mehr Gesundheitsschutz, Entlohnung und Arbeitnehmerrechte bei Amazon

 erschien zuerst auf 

LabourNet Germany
