author: Darío Aranda
title: Las cuentas no cierran en Vaca Muerta: la fuga de dólares que oculta el relato extractivo
content:
Por Natalia Concina




La explotación de Vaca Muerta permitió el ingreso al país de casi dos mil millones de dólares entre lo que vendió y lo que pidió como préstamo durante 2026. Lejos de quedarse en el país, 

esas divisas volvieron al exterior y le permitieron a las empresas petroleras y de diferentes rubros fugar sus ganancias

. Un nuevo estudio del grupo de investigación EJES confirma que el yacimiento de petróleo no convencional permite hoy sostener la estabilidad cambiaria, pero 

consolida a los sectores de poder concentrado y genera una millonaria deuda a futuro

.




Durante la primera parte del año, las empresas que explotan Vaca Muerta pidieron préstamos por 936 millones de dólares mensuales promedio, una cifra incluso superior a las divisas que generaron por las ventas al exterior de hidrocarburos (que rondaron en un promedio de 754 millones por mes).




Esta inyección de divisas extranjeras es la que garantiza hoy la estabilidad cambiaria, es decir, que el precio de la moneda estadounidense esté más o menos estable. Sin embargo, 

los dólares que ingresan por el endeudamiento privado son un problema para toda la sociedad

 porque —a futuro— utilizarán los dólares que genera toda la economía. ¿Por qué? Porque para cancelar sus deudas la empresas comprarán los dólares disponibles en el Banco Central, que a su vez ingresarán por las exportaciones u otros mecanismo (como podría ser esta de toma de deuda).




En otras palabras, Vaca Muerta permite hoy la “sostenibilidad” del modelo a través de estos dólares de los que se nutren, además de las empresas petroleras, los sectores corporativos más concentrados de la economía local para remitir sus ganancias al exterior, un proceso que se intensificó desde diciembre pasado. 

Una especie de puerta giratoria de dólares

, aunque las deudas quedan.




Foto: Martín Álvarez Mullally




Estas conclusiones son los pilares más importantes d

el informe “

¿A dónde van los dólares de Vaca Muerta”,

 

el tercer estudio realizado por el Enlace por la Justicia Energética y Socioambiental (EJES)”

, una articulación de organizaciones que desde 2024 analiza sistemáticamente los números del yacimiento no convencional en forma crítica, exponiendo sus implicancias ocultas detrás del supuesto boom energético.




“El análisis de los datos del Banco Central de 2025 y lo que va de 2026 permite consolidar dos miradas respecto a Vaca Muerta: por un lado, que su función es traer dólares y no se está pensando en eslabonar un conjunto de actividades económicas a partir del yacimiento; por el otro, que 

lo único que dejará al país son deudas

”, asegura a Tierra Viva el economista Marco Kofman, autor del trabajo.




¿A dónde van los dólares de Vaca Muerta? - EJES




Récord de ventas




En los primeros cinco meses de 2026, el país exportó 314.000 barriles diarios de petróleo, acumulando un total de 3.773 millones de dólares, lo que da un promedio de 754 millones por mes. No sólo se aumentó la cantidad de crudo sino que coincidió con un precio internacional relativamente elevado.




De las diez primeras empresas que comercializan internacionalmente el crudo argentino, hay cinco que exportan más del 50 por ciento de su producción local. Respecto al gas de Vaca Muerta, se vende al exterior sólo entre el cuatro y el cinco por ciento.




Pese a la orientación exportadora, el informe destaca que en los últimos años Argentina disminuyó la importación de hidrocarburos drásticamente, parte por la producción de Vaca Muerta, parte por la crisis en la producción local. En ese contexto, la balanza comercial energética (diferencia entre la compra y la venta de petróleo y gas) es favorable para la Argentina, que pasó de estar en rojo a tener un superávit de 3.000 millones de dólares acumulado sólo en los primeros cinco meses de 2026.




“A este ingreso de dólares por ventas (dólares comerciales), 

se le suman los dólares financieros, es decir los que ingresan por toma de deuda de las empresas

 

que funcionan como un respirador artificial del modelo de Milei 

y le permite que el dólar se mantenga estable, sin tener que devaluar ni poner controles cambiarios”, explica Kofman.




Foto: Depositphotos




El trabajo de EJES explica que de los 22.617 millones de dólares que el sector privado ingresó al país por la vía del endeudamiento, 14.441 millones —casi el 64 por ciento del total— fueron aportados por las empresas energéticas; en los primeros cinco meses del año, ese endeudamiento fue de 936 millones de dólares promedio mensual.







“Este proceso de ingreso de dólares financieros es algo que está pasando por debajo del radar. Pero como llegan se van: hay un montón de actores que se llevan dólares de la economía que son los que están bancando al presidente Milei. Por eso sostengo hace un tiempo que detrás de Vaca Muerta hay una muy sólida comunidad de negocios que involucra no sólo las empresas energéticas sino a todos los sectores que en Argentina tienen capacidad de apropiación de riquezas”, dice Kofman.







Para comprender cómo se da este proceso en la práctica hay que imaginar lo siguiente: cuando una empresa toma una deuda, al Banco Central le figura un ingreso de dólares. Probablemente esa moneda estadounidense nunca se pesifique, porque la mayoría de las operaciones del sector energético son en dólares. Pero el punto es que esas divisas están allí, disponibles para que cualquier empresa (por ejemplo, una empresa alimenticia o metalúrgica) pueda comprarlos y enviarlos al exterior.




Y aquí viene otro dato clave que el trabajo revela: 

la salida de dólares al exterior está batiendo récord en 2026.




Foto: Presidencia de la Nación




Récord de fuga

 de dólares




“Todas las empresas que operan en Vaca Muerta, tengan o no casa matriz en Argentina, están transnacionalizadas, es decir que tienen su estructura jurídica en países con escasa o nula tributación, lo que se conoce como paraísos fiscales”, explica Kofman.




En 

trabajos anteriores

 realizados por EJES, Kofman ya había detallado los diferentes mecanismos por los cuales las compañías logran enviar al exterior sus ganancias en dólares: remitir a sus casas matrices los excedentes generados por las ventas, pagar servicios que contrataba fuera del país e incluso “auto endeudarse”, pedir préstamos a empresas del mismo grupo para luego tomar dólares para pagar los intereses.




Desde el macrismo y 

hasta abril de 2025

, la primera forma —que es el envío de las ganancias a la casa matriz— se vio afectada por lo que popularmente se conoció como “cepo”, que era en realidad un monto máximo. Tras la flexibilización de esta medida, entre diciembre y mayo de 2026, empresas de diferentes rubros —con las petroleras a la cabeza— remitieron al exterior más de 2.000 millones de dólares. Como se menciona antes, la disponibilidad de los dólares para estas operaciones fue posible gracias a Vaca Muerta.




“Argentina está en un récord histórico de exportaciones y, sin embargo, cuando analizamos las cuentas del central, no hay un sólo mes en el que le hayan sobrado dólares, es decir, todos los meses está en rojo. Esto quiere decir que a través de todos estos mecanismo, 

se fugaron más dólares de los que ingresaron

”, señala Kofman.




Foto: Ministerio de Economía




Lo que dejará Vaca Muerta




Como parte de los beneficios del 

Regimen de Incentivo a la Grandes Inversiones (RIGI)

, las empresas no tienen exigencias de contratar proveedores internos, por lo que el eslabonamiento productivo —que en algún momento se consideró que podía suceder a partir de Vaca Muerta— no pasó.




“Si uno mira cómo evoluciona el empleo en Neuquén, es una de las pocas provincias que no perdió puestos de trabajo, pero al ritmo que está creciendo le harían falta 200 años 

para llegar a un cuarto de los dos millones de personas que prometió Federico Sturzenegger

”, sostiene Kofman.




Y añade: “

No deja empleos, no deja dólares, lo que sí está dejando es una comunidad de negocios muy sólida y una deuda de más de 20.000 millones de dólares

. Y la deuda privada es un problema para toda la sociedad porque para pagarla se utilizan los dólares que genera toda la economía”.




El economista deja en claro cuál es la verdadera trampa: “Los dólares que se generan a partir de la actividad de las empresas en Vaca Muerta son producto de un largo eslabonamiento de actividades humanas, sociales y productivas. Sin la educación de los trabajadores, las rutas, la salud; no se podría explotar. Entonces, 

ese esquema de que las empresas tienen derecho de quedarse con los dólares que se producen por las ventas que hacen es una trampa

, porque esos dólares fueron generados por la sociedad argentina. Esas empresas no podrían vender sin toda la infraestructura y sin los trabajadores”.




La entrada 

Las cuentas no cierran en Vaca Muerta: la fuga de dólares que oculta el relato extractivo

 se publicó primero en 

Agencia de Noticias Tierra Viva

.

author: Unknown
title: PFDKê ceza li Amedsporê birî
content:
Lijneya Dîsiplînê ya Futbola Profesyonel (PFDK), biryarên xwe yên derbarê bûyerên ku di maçên hefteya 7an a Lîga Superê de qewimîbûn, eşkere kir.




PFDKê di mijarên, ji ber dirûşmên “kirêt û nexweş” ên alîgirên Gençlerbîrlîgiyê yên di maça Gençlerbîrlîgî-Amedsporê ya ku li Enqereyê hat lîstin de, kartên alîgirên ên li pişta qaleya bakûr, trîbuna rojava û vîpê biryara xwe da. PFDKê xwest hem ev kes werin astengkirin û ketina wan a maçên din bê qedexekirin.




Li gorî nûçeya Ajansa Welat PFDKê 280 hezar lîre cezayê pere li Amedsporê birî. Lijneyê ev ceza wekî “bûyerên li qadê” bi nav kir û cih neda bê ka ev bûyer çi ne. Lijneyê ji ber bûyerên di gelek maçên dawiya hefteyê de qewimîn, cezayên cûda dan tîman.




Maça Mardînspor û Bursasporê




Di Lîga 1emîn a Trendyolê de, di maça ku Bursasporê di 11ê Cotmehê de li qada xwe li dijî Mardîn 1969 Sporê lîst û 2-1 winda kir.




Alîgirên Bursasporê hema hema di seranserê maçê de dirûşmên nexweş berz kirin. Dîmenên van dirûşmên nexweş li ser platformên medyaya dîjîtal bi hezaran caran hatin parvekirin. Bi taybetî dirûşmên nexweş ên li dijî golparêzê Mardînsporê Erce Kardeşler bûn rojev.




Lê belê, PFDKê ji ber bûyerên qadê li gorî xalên 52/2 û 46/1 ên FDTyê (cezarkirina tîmê ya ji ber bûyerên qadê yên ku ji aliyê temaşevan, endamên klûbê an jî futbolvanan ve hatine kirin; avêtina madeyên biyanî bo nav qadê, ketina temaşevanan bo nav qadê, vêxistina meşaleyan hwd. vedihewîne) 140 hezar TL cezayê pereyan da.




Tevî ku dirûşmên kirêt û nexweş ên alîgirên Bursasporê yên di seranserê maçê de ji aliyê her kesê ku maç ji TVyê temaşe dikir ve hat bihîstin jî, nedana cezayekî bi vî rengî careke din nîşan da ku PFDK biryarên çiqas alîgir digire.




(AY)

author: Andrea DiP
title: Por que os estudantes voltaram às ruas? – com Gutemberg Rodrigues
content:
“Estamos na rua contra a extrema direita e, sobretudo, contra o que ela representa de retrocesso no nosso país”,  é o que afirma o vice-presidente da União Nacional dos Estudantes, Gutemberg Rodrigues, nesta entrevista para o Pauta Pública que analisa a volta de estudantes às ruas após o resultado do primeiro turno das eleições presidenciais.




Desde o dia 5 de outubro, universitários têm organizado assembleias e manifestações em apoio à reeleição de Lula em diferentes cidades brasileiras. Na conversa com Andrea Dip, Gutemberg relembra o papel histórico do movimento estudantil na resistência a retrocessos, na defesa da educação pública e na formação de novas lideranças políticas, destacando também a importância de defender direitos já conquistados.

author: anred
title: Argentina, no la entenderías: la marcha que transformó un reclamo universitario en una batalla contra el ajuste
content:
Imagen: Melina Deledicque.




La quinta Marcha Federal Universitaria desbordó su reclamo original y se convirtió en una movilización multisectorial contra el ajuste. Universidades, sindicatos y organizaciones sociales defendieron la educación pública, la soberanía, los derechos sociales y los bienes comunes. Más de 100 mil personas marcharon al Congreso pese a la represión estatal. 

Por Melina Deledicque (trabajadora no docente de la Facultad de Trabajo Social de la UNLP) y Mariano Féliz (trabajador docente de la Facultad de Humanidades y Ciencias de la Educación de la UNLP), para Huella del Sur.







Cronología de una marcha que unió las luchas




Hace un mes, el movimiento universitario resolvió convocar a la quinta Marcha Federal Universitaria para el jueves 15 de octubre en la Plaza de Mayo, frente a la sede del Poder Ejecutivo.




La convocatoria respondió a la negativa del Gobierno nacional a cumplir la resolución dictada por el juez de primera instancia Martín Cormick, que ordena al Poder Ejecutivo aplicar la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario, a casi un año de su aprobación. 

Según el Gobierno

, la ley no está siendo incumplida, sino que se encuentra “suspendida”. Sin embargo, el Poder Ejecutivo desoye el fallo judicial, que dispone la actualización de los salarios docentes y Nodocentes y de las becas estudiantiles conforme a lo establecido por la ley.




Imagen: Melina Deledicque.




Imagen: Melina Deledicque.




Mientras tanto, el proyecto de Presupuesto 2027 contempla partidas aproximadamente un 33% inferiores a 

las solicitadas

 por el Consejo Interuniversitario Nacional (CIN): mientras el Gobierno prevé unos 7,3 billones de pesos para las universidades nacionales, el CIN reclama 11 billones.




El miércoles 14 de octubre, el juez Cormick hizo efectivo el apercibimiento que había dispuesto previamente y fijó astreintes —multas compulsivas— de 100.000 pesos diarios para Diego Santilli, titular de la Jefatura de Gabinete, mientras persista el incumplimiento de la resolución judicial. La sanción recae inicialmente sobre Santilli y podría extenderse a otros funcionarios o incrementarse si el Gobierno no acata la decisión. Sin embargo, el mismo día de la movilización, la Cámara de Apelaciones puso en suspenso la multa.




Imagen: Melina Deledicque.




Imagen: Melina Deledicque.




Todo cambió con la resolución de la Corte Suprema de habilitar el artículo 154 del DNU 70/23, permitiendo la extranjerización sin límites de tierras rurales en Argentina. Si bien, frente al repudio popular, la Corte 

dio marcha atrás

, el clima político ya se había enrarecido.




Estas circunstancias aceleraron la convocatoria de la oposición en la Cámara de Diputados para avanzar en el rechazo definitivo del DNU 70/23. En esa misma sesión se proponía discutir también la prórroga de la Ley de Emergencia en Discapacidad y una ley destinada a aliviar la situación de las familias sobreendeudadas y en mora.




Recordemos que el Senado de la Nación ya había votado la derogación del DNU 70/23 a comienzos de 2024. Ese decreto continúa en el centro de la escena por sus efectos sobre el precio de los alquileres, las tasas de interés de los créditos y las cuotas de la medicina prepaga, entre otros aspectos. En la Cámara de Diputados, la oposición nunca consiguió los votos necesarios para avanzar en ese sentido. Lamentablemente, este jueves tampoco se alcanzó el quórum para habilitar la sesión. 

Varios gobernadores

 aliados del gobierno libertariano blindaron el DNU 70/23, ya que diputados de Tucumán, Jujuy y Santa Fe vaciaron sus bancas, al igual que los gobernadores de Unión por la Patria, Melella y Zamora.




Imagen: Melina Deledicque.




Imagen: Melina Deledicque.




Con ese contexto, la comunidad universitaria decidió que la movilización sería frente al Congreso. De esa manera, en pocas semanas, una marcha inicialmente convocada por el movimiento universitario se transformó en una movilización multisectorial de alcance nacional, con concentraciones frente al Congreso y en las principales plazas de todo el país.




La movilización sumó más de 100 mil personas en CABA (y decenas de miles más en el resto del país)

, y se sostuvo a pesar de un clima inhóspito e incluso un chaparrón intenso al cierre. A la misma se sumaron 

organizaciones de personas con discapacidad, de familias endeudadas, sindicatos combativos —como los integrantes del FreSU, bancarios, aceiteros, camioneros y otros—, e incluso la CGT

.




Como tantas veces, ante el reclamo legítimo para exigir el cumplimiento de la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario, la única respuesta de un gobierno abiertamente autoritario es la represión. Antes del cierre del acto iniciado alrededor de las 15:30 horas, las fuerzas de seguridad salieron a “despejar” la Plaza de los dos Congresos con gases lacrimógenos y carros hidrantes.




Una marcha multisectorial con una prenda de unidad: defender la vida en común




A pesar de que el Congreso no sesionó, podríamos decir que la marcha logró un objetivo superior. Si decimos que articuló múltiples demandas sectoriales, no estaríamos equivocados, pero esa mirada sería insuficiente si no lográramos ver lo que las vincula.




Imagen: Melina Deledicque.




Imagen: Melina Deledicque.




En los hechos, 

a casi tres años del inicio del gobierno de Milei, la movilización convocada unifica a las comunidades agredidas por el programa de austeridad y crueldad del gobierno libertariano.

 La agenda de las organizaciones pone en el centro a quienes se encuentran en situaciones de mayor vulnerabilidad y a quienes sostienen su defensa: 

jubilades, personas con discapacidad, estudiantes y trabajadores universitaries, personal sanitario y familias endeudadas

.




Lo que se puso en juego este jueves es la utopía de construir una sociedad que priorice la reproducción de la vida en todos sus momentos y etapas, en sus formas simbólicas y materiales. 

Lo que esta movilización pone en el centro es el conjunto de los bienes comunes: la tierra y el territorio, el conocimiento como bien colectivo y no mercancía, y el cuidado de la vida de las personas

.




Imagen: Melina Deledicque.




Imagen: Melina Deledicque.




Las luchas van tejiendo un entramado político y delineando un camino de superación radical del plan libertariano de Milei. La pregunta que se abre es si el sistema político, tan fracturado y degradado como el actual, podrá nutrirse de esas energías colectivas para abrir una etapa capaz de sepultar el programa de guerra de las clases dominantes contra los sectores populares.




Será una batalla decisiva, aunque no la última ni la definitiva.




Imagen: Melina Deledicque.




Imagen: Melina Deledicque.




Fuente: 

https://huelladelsur.ar/2026/10/15/argentina-no-la-entenderias-la-marcha-que-transformo-un-reclamo-universitario-en-una-batalla-contra-el-ajuste/

author: Cas Smith
title: Land Forces weapons expo protested in a time of genocide
content:
Around 2000 anti-war activists took to the streets on October 6, in a strong rebuke to the weapons’ manufacturers displaying their wares at the Land Forces International Land Defence Exposition and Western Australian Labor, which welcomed it.

The rally, one of the biggest in recent years, began at Yagan Square near Northbridge, before marching through the city to Elizabeth Quay, close to the Perth Convention Centre.

A “security area” had been set up around the expo venue, which included the Elizabeth Quay train station and several sections of surrounding streets.

A new law, the Land Forces (Special Powers) Act 2026, gave police the “ability to establish checkpoints, cordons, and roadblocks, while also searching people, bags, and vehicles, and issue lawful directions for a 10-day period”, until October 10.

Alongside this, several activists had been told they were banned from the security area, and could face fines of up to $36,000 and three years in prison if they challenged this.

The media coverage of these repressive security initiatives — to which WA Premier Roger Cook had allocated $11.5 million — may have encouraged people to come to the rally, which was hosted by WA Anti-War Collective, Stop AUKUS WA, Nuclear Free WA, Independent and Peaceful Australia Network (IPAN), Friends of Palestine WA (FOPWA), Students for Palestine WA, Right To Protest WA and Extinction Rebellion Western Australia.

It included several creative aspects, including a flash mob dance to the tune of the Temptations’ song “War” and a performance by Drummers for Climate Action.

Noongar Elders Uncle Headley Hayward and Uncle Herbert Bropho gave the Welcome to Country. Adrian Glamorgan (Independent and Peaceful Australia Network and Stop AUKUS WA), Danica Scott (Stop AUKUS WA and Freiends of Palestine WA), Greens MLC Sophie McNeill, Rojin Didari (Students for Palestine WA) and Berlin Guerrero (Migrante and International People’s Struggle) addressed the protest.

Sam Wainwright (Stop AUKUS WA), who MCed the rally, said Labor’s decision to roll out the red carpet for weapons manufacturers indicated his priorities.

“[Land Forces] comes in the context of a worldwide increase in military expenditure, including a 50% increase in military expenditure by Donald Trump. It comes in the context of the genocide in Gaza, and a climate emergency,” Wainwright said.

“It poses the question: What is the real response of our rulers to what are known as the ‘poly crises’ of capitalism. Is it not repression at home and war abroad?”

It was particularly horrific that weapons used in Gaza would be on display at the exhibition, Wainwright added.

“For the last three years, we have begged this federal government to stop sending arms to Israel and to cancel bilateral military ties, because it’s the one thing you’d do if you were serious about stopping the genocide.

“Labor won’t, because it has committed to making Australia one of the 10 major weapons exporters in the world. Roger Cook has said he wants to make weapons exports the number two industry in WA. The place of Israel in the military industrial complex means deepening bilateral military ties with that state.”

Elbit Systems and Rafael were among the Israeli weapons companies featured at Land Forces, alongside Lockheed Martin, which constructs the F-35 fighter jets used in much of the destruction of Gaza.

author: Ash Sarkar
title: A Motion, a Meltdown, and an Andy Burnham-Shaped Opportunity
content:
They’re calling it the E motion heard around the world, as the fallout continues from the Green party’s ‘Zionism is Racism’ policy, passed at its conference earlier this month.




The motion has dominated the headlines since making it onto the agenda for autumn conference, eclipsing what the leadership had hoped would be the party’s trademark rent controls policy. It kicked off a briefing war, led by GPEW stalwart and second referendum-enthusiast Caroline Lucas. It also prompted 

pointed queries

 from the Equalities and Human Rights Commission.




And now, unwilling to let a good crisis pass him by, prime minister Andy Burnham has piled in, 

ruling out any future coalition

 with the Greens while the policy remains in place. Supporters of the motion may greet this news as a strategic win – distance from Labour cements the Greens’ status as an insurgent, anti-establishment force. But there are rumblings of discontent amongst parts of the Green party of England and Wales.




It’s no secret that Zack Polanski (while publicly supportive of the argument that Israel’s displacement of, and genocide against, the Palestinians is the result of racist ideology) needed this motion like he needed a hole in the head. He was careful to neither unequivocally back nor deride the motion, and warned that it may “create a distraction” by putting Green members and pro-Palestine activists in a position of being attacked.




Whatever the virtues of the motion were, and still might be, Polanski was proved right on this latter point. The days leading up to his unsuccessful attempt to become the MP for Holborn and St Pancras were a storm of negative media coverage, in which he was forced to defend his party against accusations of being a threat to Jewish people. It would be wrong to characterise the byelection loss as a direct result of the ‘Zionism is Racism’ motion. But it didn’t exactly help his efforts to get elected either.




What followed were the first stirrings of Green infighting. For those steeped in the factional bloodletting of Labour party politics, this is all fairly tame stuff: Lucas, the night of the count, 

failing to shut down talk

 of Polanski stepping down, Ellie Chowns 

calling on her leader to “step up”

. But while the Greens might put the ‘civil’ in civil war, this level of publicly-litigated internal division is new for the party.




What’s more, local Green parties and councils have had to manage the reactions of a significant number of Jewish residents and organisations. Haringey council, led by the Greens, found its attempts at overture 

knocked back

 by one local synagogue. “We take it from both the tone and the content of your email that you are deeply embarrassed with the decision taken by your party,” wrote Highgate United Synagogue. “[Your] embarrassment is not enough. If you really want us to feel you do not agree with the racist and genocidal implications of your party’s policy, the least we can expect is for you to publicly resile yourself from that policy and commit yourself and your party colleagues to reverse that policy.”




Enter one Andrew Burnham. Though the early months of his premiership have been marked by his attempts to mend fences with voters alienated from Labour by the party’s moral turpitude on Palestine, the temptation to kick his progressive rivals while they’re down was seemingly too much to resist.




Condemning the motion in the House of Commons at this week’s PMQs, 

Burnham thundered

: “It is wrong, it is antisemitic, and this side of the House will have nothing to do with it.” Polanski, in a statement, hit back, pointing out that he’s the only Jewish leader of a political party and himself a victim of antisemitism – while the prime minister “arms a genocide and locks pensioners up for opposing it”.




Westminster grandstanding has since filtered down to local governance. Yesterday, Labour issued an ultimatum, saying it would scrap any power-sharing deals with Greens in local authorities unless local Green electeds reject the ‘Zionism is Racism’ motion passed by members at conference. According to the New Statesman, such agreements prop up 

more than a dozen local authorities

, including in Bristol. Nice gauntlet you’ve got there, shame if anyone threw it.




Perhaps Alanis Morissette might have something to say about a devolution-loving prime minister imposing the will of the Westminster government on local authorities the minute he thinks it’s advantageous to do so. It’s worth pointing out that it has every chance of backfiring on the Labour party – there are few voters who want to see local government dysfunction inflicted in the name of protecting Israel’s state ideology. Labour lost votes over Gaza, and it might prove unwise for Burnham to remind people of that particular issue.




But we’re at a moment where the interests of Green electeds, and some Green activists, are at odds. The May 2026 breakthrough was powered by thousands of Green members – doorknocking, canvassing, leafleting, and getting out the vote. But that very achievement, getting Greens into councils where they might advance the eco-socialist cause by delivering for voters, is easily imperilled by that selfsame membership attempting to remodel the party in their image. That’s a tension: and one that Burnham is determined to exploit.




You can see how this puts Polanski in an invidious position. On the one hand, there’s making and protecting electoral gains, and establishing the Green party’s credibility by governing effectively. On the other, there’s standing with his members when they’re under ferocious attack by the British establishment (even if he’d rather not have picked this particular battle). But perhaps the looming interest of the EHRC, who wrote to the Greens citing the “many Jewish people [feeling] vulnerable” as a result of the motion, might hint at a way out.




Should the Greens face legal challenge, or EHRC investigation, the tactical case for reintroducing the amendments aimed at protecting Jewish members within the party gets stronger. If Polanski backs it wholeheartedly for spring conference, he might just find a way of mitigating the attack lines on antisemitism – and get back to the things he’d much rather talk about.

author: groundxero
title: No Bonus, Unpaid Wages, Missing PF Dues: Thousands of Tea Workers Take to the Streets in North Bengal
content:
More than a hundred tea estates in North Bengal reportedly missed the 5 October deadline for payment of the 20% annual bonus. Thousands of workers across Merico-Sammelan gardens in the Dooars are protesting unpaid bonuses, outstanding wages and provident fund dues, even as the state government’s assurances and meetings yield little.




 




Groundxero

 | 16 October 2026




 




On the morning of Shashthi, as people across Kolkata throng Durga Puja pandals, women tea garden workers in North Bengal are taking to the streets to fight for a bonus that should already have been in their bank accounts. Workers, led by women workers from Hantapara, Gayerdanga and Dumkipara tea estates marched towards Madarihat to demand payment of their bonus. Workers at Birpara are preparing similar protests, while others staged demonstrations outside factory gates and approached the police.




 




Their immediate demand is straightforward: payment of the full 20% annual bonus. But the protests expose a much wider crisis of unpaid wages, withheld provident fund contributions, unpaid gratuity, and the continuing impunity enjoyed by tea garden owners.




 




At the centre of the current confrontation is the Merico Agro Industries and Sammelan Tea & Beverages group, which controls 12–13 tea estates employing nearly 10,000 workers, the vast majority of them women. The management has sought to persuade workers to accept a bonus of just 10%. The workers, led by the Paschim Banga Cha Majdur Samiti (PBCMS), have refused to settle for half of what they are demanding.




 




The West Bengal government had set 5 October as the deadline for payment of a 20% bonus to tea garden workers. Yet, according to available reports, only 170 of the Dooars’ 285 tea gardens had paid bonuses by 10 October. More than a hundred estates had reportedly failed to pay workers even a single rupee.




 




The failure is particularly revealing because the change of government in West Bengal was accompanied by the BJP’s promise of a new political and administrative dispensation. For tea garden workers, however, the much-publicised ‘double engine’ government appears to be running along the same tracks as its predecessor: false assurances for workers, impunity for defaulting employers, and little effective action to compel payment.




 




Last year, the Trinamool Congress government had also advised employers to pay a 20% bonus. This year, the BJP government issued a similar directive, setting a deadline of 5 October. But an advisory, however emphatically worded, is no substitute for enforcement. Employers continue to delay and withheld payments while workers lose wages, spend days in demonstrations and struggle to meet their basic needs.




 




Pay slips issued but no payment made 




 




The confrontation at Bagrakote Tea Garden illustrates the gap between management promises and workers’ actual experience. After the bonus remained unpaid, workers went on strike and blocked the Siliguri–Dooars national highway at Meena More. Following the mobilisation, the management issued a notice promising payment of the 20% bonus by 13–14 October.




 




Both dates passed without the promised payment.




 




On the night of 14 October, owner Surajit Bakshi telephoned PBCMS leaders and reportedly asked them to persuade workers to accept a 10% bonus, saying that this was all he had managed to arrange. The union refused to endorse the proposal, maintaining the workers’ demand for the full bonus.




 




On 15 October, garden managers distributed pay slips promising a 20% bonus. Workers waited for the money to arrive in their bank accounts. Managers waited for funds to become available. Police stood guard over the managers, while rumours circulated among workers that payments had been made in neighbouring areas.




 




By 10 pm, according to PBCMS, not one of the approximately 10,000 workers employed across the Merico-Sammelan group’s gardens had received any money.




 




The episode captures the absurdity of a system in which paperwork and promises can be produced on schedule, but the payment of workers’ dues remains indefinitely negotiable. The workers are expected to trust pay slips, wait through successive deadlines and accept management’s financial difficulties as an excuse. Their own financial difficulties, and their rightful dues, meanwhile, receive little consideration.




 




Labour department calls meetings without accountability




 




The labour department’s handling of the dispute has added to workers’ frustration. According to PBCMS, one meeting was cancelled on the grounds that management representatives were busy arranging bonus payments. No payment followed. At another meeting, union representatives reportedly waited for six hours without any meaningful discussion. The proceedings eventually deteriorated into shouting and the breaking of chairs, with BJP-affiliated union leaders allegedly abusing their own MLA, Puna Bhengra.




 




For workers already waiting for their dues, such meetings mean another day lost without a resolution. The spectacle of official consultations cannot conceal the absence of effective intervention.




 




The crisis is not confined to the annual bonus. PBCMS alleges that almost all the Merico-Sammelan gardens owe workers three to four fortnights’ wages, last year’s leave allowance and 10% of last year’s unpaid bonus. The union also alleges that provident fund (PF) contributions deducted from workers’ salaries have not been deposited into the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (

EPFO

) accounts since June 2023—an action unions label as criminal breach of trust. Retired workers are reportedly dying without receiving their gratuity.




 




Meanwhile, factories have shut, gardens have deteriorated and green leaves are reportedly being sold through brokers. The conditions raise serious questions about the management of these estates, the protection of workers’ livelihoods and the government’s willingness to hold employers accountable.




 




Workers suffer for the owners’ impunity




 




Workers are mobilising across the Dooars and North Bengal, with protests reported at Dumkipara, Lankapara, Hantapara, Nagaisuri, Garganda and other gardens associated with the group. Women workers have been at the forefront of the mobilisation, marching towards Madarihat and organising demonstrations at factory gates. Workers in Birpara have also been preparing to join the protests.




 




Their determination exposes the unequal balance of power in the tea industry. Workers whose labour sustains the plantations must organise, march and confront the authorities to secure payments that are already due to them. Employers, by contrast, appear able to delay and even withheld payment even after announcing deadlines and issuing written assurances.




 




The reports of prolonged non-deposit of provident fund contributions are particularly grave. The government must also address the reported non-payment of wages and gratuity. Issuing advisories and convening meetings will not resolve the crisis unless the authorities ensure that employers meet their obligations and face consequences for violations. The failure to secure payment by the announced deadline demands an explanation of what enforcement measures, if any, have been taken.




 




PBCMS has demanded immediate payment of the full 20% bonus, all outstanding wages, leave allowance and gratuity, the deposit of every rupee deducted towards provident fund contributions, and legal action against those responsible for violations.




 




These are not extravagant demands. They concern workers’ earnings, statutory entitlements and economic security. The government must move beyond assurances and take effective steps to ensure that workers receive what is owed to them.




 




As people in Kolkata sip tea between visits to Durga Puja pandals, the workers who produce that tea are fighting to obtain their own unpaid dues. The contrast is stark: the festive economy depends on workers’ labour, yet thousands of them face the prospect of celebrating the festival season without money that should already have been paid.




 




The Government has changed but the ‘Acche Din’ of tea garden owners appears remarkably secure. The BJP’s ‘double engine’ government now faces a simple test: will it enforce workers’ rights, or will it let garden owners to continue with their illegal exploitative labour practices, while its engines runs smoothly — in the service of employers!




 




Workers cannot pay their bills with government advisories, feed their families with pay slips or retire on false promises. Unless the workers’ united struggle force authorities to compel employers to pay, the change of government will mean little to the thousands of women and men whose labour sustains North Bengal’s tea gardens, and its economy.

author: Sam Bright
title: Reform Figure Behind ‘Shocking’ Grenfell Comments Still Involved in Party
content:
A former housing executive fired by 

Reform UK

 for making “shameful” comments about the 2017 Grenfell Tower tragedy still claims to have a role in the party, DeSmog can reveal.




Simon Dudley, a former chair of Homes England, was removed as the party’s housing spokesperson for making – 

in the words

 of Reform leader 

Nigel Farage

 – “shocking” and “deeply inappropriate” comments about the disaster.




In an interview with Inside Housing in April, Dudley said the deadly blaze, which led to the deaths of 72 people, was a “tragedy” but that “everyone dies in the end”. He claimed that rules introduced in the wake of the fire to improve safety standards were examples of “regulation which is not working”.




Dudley was roundly criticised for his remarks, including by groups representing Grenfell survivors and next of kin. The then prime minister Keir Starmer called the comments “shameful”.




However, despite being sacked as Reform’s housing spokesperson, Dudley still appears to work with the party.




He 

introduced

 Reform’s deputy leader and housing chief 

Richard Tice

 to business delegates at the party’s annual conference in September, and chaired a question and answer session following Tice’s speech.




A post from Simon Dudley on LinkedIn about his involvement in Reform’s 2026 annual conference. 

Credit: 

Simon Dudley / LinkedIn




According to a transcript, Tice 

thanked

 Dudley for his “generous” introduction, after which Tice presented Reform’s sweeping policies to 

deregulate

 the planning system.




While Dudley’s exact role in the party is not known, his social media profiles – including his up-to-date 

LinkedIn CV

 – continue to list him in a ‘Housing and Infrastructure’ position at Reform.




He’s also a keen party activist who has 

accused

 the Conservatives of copying Reform’s ideas and who 

campaigned

 for Farage in this summer’s Clacton by-election.




Neither Reform nor Dudley denied that he is still involved in the party when approached by DeSmog for comment.




However, Dudley’s continued involvement contrasts starkly with Reform’s response to his remarks in April.




“He’s under Richard Tice’s department, Richard appointed him housing spokesman given his depth of experience in developing new towns,” Farage said at the time. “But the comments were deeply inappropriate, they were frankly rather shocking to many people, and Richard has dealt with it.”




In response to the backlash in April, Dudley said that “Grenfell was an utter tragedy and quite rightly prompted a wholesale review and tightening of fire regulations.”




He added: “I said it was a tragedy in my interview with Inside House [sic] and in no shape or form am I belittling that disaster or the huge loss of life. It must never happen again. I reiterate that, and am sorry if it was not sufficiently clear.”




A new undercover investigation due to be released by ITV in full on Sunday 18 October shows Reform councillors making a number of sexist and racist comments. One Reform councillor from south London is 

filmed

 saying that King Charles should be decapitated because he is secretly a Muslim. 







A 

version

 of this article was also published by The New World. 







Reform’s Deregulation Agenda




The Grenfell Tower fire on 14 June 2017 was one of the worst tragedies in modern British history. Just before 1am, a high-rise fire broke out in the 24-storey block in Kensington, London, which spread rapidly due to the highly combustible cladding that had been installed on the building a year earlier.




The government has subsequently introduced new fire safety rules, particularly in relation to high-rise blocks, to prevent another similar disaster.




However, Reform initially echoed Dudley’s remarks about the new regulations being too onerous. Speaking in April, a party spokesperson said: “Simon’s comments on Grenfell reflected his broader point that the regulatory pendulum has swung too far in response to the tragedy. As he explained, there is a fine balance between over-regulation – which can slow the delivery of new homes – and ensuring that more homes are built safely without too much red tape.”




A post from Simon Dudley on X about his involvement in the August 2026 Clacton by-election campaign. 

Credit: 

Simon Dudley / X




This conforms to Reform’s deregulation agenda, which would reduce the taxes and laws applied to major corporations, potentially benefitting some of the party’s 

biggest donors

.




Reform has supported more permissive rules for the crypto, finance, and housing industries – all of which have contributed substantially to the party’s coffers – with Farage 

promising

 a “bonfire of business regulation” if he becomes prime minister.




This also applies to the oil and gas industry. Reform, which has accepted 

more than £24 million

 from fossil fuel interests, has said it would scrap the windfall tax on fossil fuel profits, end the ban on new North Sea drilling licences, and ditch the moratorium on fracking for shale gas.




Senior Reform figure 

Andrea Jenkyns

, the mayor for Greater Lincolnshire, 

has said

 that she would “turn the countryside into Swiss cheese” through the mass expansion of fracking across the UK.




The party, some of whose senior figures 

frequently deny

 the science of climate change, would dramatically increase the production of fossil fuels in the UK and reduce state support for renewable energy – despite the 

impact of high gas prices

 on the cost of living, and the growing frequency of climate-induced extreme weather events.




The post 

Reform Figure Behind ‘Shocking’ Grenfell Comments Still Involved in Party

 appeared first on 

DeSmog

.

Συζήτηση – ενημέρωση για τη δίκη του αγωνιστή Κ.Α. και μπαρ οικονομικής ενίσχυσης




Λέσχη Εργαζομένων και Νεολαίας Βόλου




Την Τρίτη 20 Οκτωβρίου θα διεξαχθεί στο εφετείο της Λάρισας η δίκη σε 2ο βαθμό του αγωνιστή Κ.Α., που διώκεται για τη συμμετοχή του στη μεγάλη διαδήλωση ενάντια στην καύση σκουπιδιών τον Ιούνη του 2020 έξω από την ΑΓΕΤ.




Αν και πρωτόδικα η διωκτική σκευωρία κατέρρευσε με πάταγο, καθώς το δικαστήριο έκρινε αθώο τον Κ.Α. για το κακούργημα της χρήσης εκρηκτικών υλών και για τα πλημμελήματα της οπλοχρησίας και της πρόκλησης βαριών σωματικών βλαβών, τον έκρινε όμως ένοχο για τα πλημμελήματα της διατάραξης κοινής ειρήνης, της βίας κατά υπαλλήλων και της οπλοκατοχής, καταλογίζοντας του την ποινή των 3,5 χρόνων φυλάκισης.




Με ακραία εκδικητική κατεύθυνση εισαγγελέας και δικαστές εξάντλησαν τα ποινικά όρια για τις εν λόγω κατηγορίες, αρνούμενοι να δεχτούν οποιοδήποτε ελαφρυντικό, αδιαφορώντας πως στην ακροαματική διαδικασία δεν αποδείχτηκε καμία από τις πράξεις που καταλογίζονταν.




Η πρωτόδικη απόφαση αποτύπωσε τη σαφή κατεύθυνση του αστικού συστήματος να καταδικάσει ανθρώπους των κινημάτων και να τους εμπλέκει σε πολύχρονους και πολυέξοδους δικαστικούς αγώνες, για να φρενάρει τη λαϊκή απαιτητικότητα.




Ταυτόχρονα η απειλή φυλάκισης του Κ.Α. διεκδικεί να ολοκληρώσει την τρομοκρατική εκστρατεία που κορυφώθηκε στην πόλη του Βόλου με τον βασανισμό και την κρατική δολοφονία του Βασίλη Μάγγου. Τα επιχειρηματικά συμφέροντα ζητούν αίμα και διώξεις για να στεριώσουν.




Στα πλαίσια αυτά την Παρασκευή 16/10 στις 21:00 στο χώρο της Λέσχης εργαζομένων και νεολαίας, θα διεξαχθεί συζήτηση – ενημέρωση για τη δίκη του αγωνιστή Κ.Α., με συμμετοχή και του ίδιου, και θα ακολουθήσει μπαρ οικονομικής ενίσχυσης για τα δικαστικά έξοδα.




Δε θα μας δικάσουν οι δολοφόνοι της ΑΓΕΤ – Lafarge




Η αλληλεγγύη το όπλο μας




Ότι έχουμε είναι ο ένας την άλλη.

author: Joshua Carroll
title: Councils Face Upheaval After Labour Threat to End Coalitions With Greens
content:
Labour’s threat to end local power-sharing agreements with the Greens in response to its ‘Zionism is racism’ motion could lead to disruption at councils across England and Wales. 




Bridget Phillipson, Labour’s chair, said on Thursday that Greens working in coalition with the party in local councils must “make clear that they reject” the motion. Otherwise, she said, “Labour will bring any such local arrangement to an end”.  




She also echoed a claim by prime minister Andy Burnham that the motion is “antisemitic”. In response, the Greens accused Labour of conflating criticism of Israel with antisemitism.




Between 17 and 19 councils could be affected if Labour ends the agreements, according to various media reports. They include Sheffield City Council, which is at “risk of collapse” if Labour ends their coalition with the Greens, the 

Yorkshire Post reported

. 




Wealden Council, which is led by Green party deputy leader Rachel Millward, may also be affected. The council is dominated by the Greens and Lib Dems, with Labour providing two councillors to give the alliance a slender majority. Before Labour joined, the alliance led the council without a majority. 




Millward has already publicly opposed the motion. Green leader Zack Polanski did not vote and has said he wanted amendments, including one aimed at reassuring people within the party who attend Zionist synagogues. Members, not leaders, passed 

the motion

 by 1,022 votes to 813 at their annual conference on 4 October. 




The motion says Zionism calls for “an ethnonationalist Jewish state” and has led to the “dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians” while creating “racial hierarchies”. 




A Green party spokesperson said in a statement: “For the Labour government to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism is disappointing and wrong. Trying to tell local parties what to do and who they can work with is undemocratic. Whilst Labour continue to try to meddle in our internal democracy, arm a genocide and lock up protesting pensioners, we will not take lectures from them.” 




Speaking during prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, Burnham ruled out a national coalition with the Greens because of the motion. 




Polanski 

hit back at Burnham’s statement

“A Labour government who apologised over their actions over Gaza is demonstrating that it was all performative. Andy Burnham still stands with Israel whilst it kills innocent people,” he said.

author: Author and Editors
title: Who Gets to Turn Numbers into Evidence?
content:
Turning numbers into evidence is a form of labour – and in the Global South, that labour is unevenly distributed.




1. Who Gets to Question the Numbers?




By the end of 2018, India’s National Sample Survey Office had completed its 2017–18 Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) – the government’s own instrument for measuring employment. The report was not released. Weeks later, a version leaked to the press showed unemployment at 6.1%, its highest level in forty-five years. Two members of the National Statistical Commission, which had approved the report, resigned over its withholding.

1

 The immediate dispute was not over a mathematical error in the figure, but over whether the public would be allowed to see it.




The PLFS controversy showed how much political weight a number can carry. Numbers are central to public debate: debt ratios, growth rates, unemployment rates, poverty lines, price indices, and export values help decide whether an economy is ‘recovering’, whether workers are ‘employed’, and whether public spending is treated as ‘affordable’. But withholding a number is only one way to control its political meaning. Numbers can also obscure reality through the definitions, classifications, comparisons, and formats that make them appear neutral.




Unemployment rates are a good example of what numbers can reveal and obscure at the same time. An unemployment rate is never a simple head count of the jobless. It is a ratio between those classified as unemployed and those counted as part of the active labour force. That ratio depends on definitional boundaries: who qualifies as employed, who is actively seeking work, who has stopped searching, who is immediately available to work, and which forms of informal or unpaid labour fall outside the metric.




The rate can fall because employment has genuinely expanded, but it can also fall because discouraged jobseekers stopped searching, because precarious informal work is counted as employment, or because underemployment has been swept into a different statistical bucket. On its own, the number cannot tell us which underlying social process it records.




These examples point to a deeply political problem. Accuracy is only part of it. The deeper question is who has the power to interrogate a number. Who can probe its definitions? Who has the means to audit the denominator, distinguish a count from a rate or an index, or tell a nominal value from a real one? Who can trace a polished indicator back to the realities of labour and class, gender and region, debt and the world market?




These questions have real-world implications that affect the lives of billions. International Monetary Fund (IMF) surveillance and its formally voluntary data-dissemination standards shape the formats through which states report economic data; World Bank lending has financed and shaped the development of national statistical systems; the United Nations’ System of National Accounts defines the international standards for measuring gross domestic product (GDP); and sovereign credit ratings from Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch influence borrowing costs through methodologies whose final judgements are not fully open to public scrutiny.

2




This concentration of statistical authority leaves researchers in the Global South in a bind. They may ask how sovereign debt constrains public spending, or how commodity prices bind national production to an unequal world market. But the data through which they must answer those questions are often organised elsewhere, sometimes by the very institutions and standards they seek to interrogate. The pattern is not new. Raúl Prebisch’s account of core–periphery terms of trade

3

 and Walter Rodney’s account of colonial economies organised for extraction

4

 point to an older problem: economic domination shapes not only the movement of commodities, labour, and capital, but also the terms through which those movements are counted, compared, and understood. The question today is how that older problem reappears in datasets, indicators, metadata, and institutional standards. Nor does the Global South confront this problem from a single standpoint. A finance ministry technocrat, a business lobby, and a union research department do not approach IMF numbers with the same interests. The question is therefore not only where statistical authority is located, but whose interests its categories and measures serve.




For researchers, movements, and public institutions that have long had to rely on metrics pre-packaged by dominant institutions, the challenge is not simply a lack of data but unequal power to turn raw numbers into evidence. The emergence of AI tools changes this terrain by lowering the cost of that work. But AI’s political significance can only be understood by first looking at the labour that comes before analysis: the choices, checks, and transformations that decide what a number can be made to show.




2. Numbers Are Not Evidence Until Someone Makes Them Evidence




Quantitative research is often imagined as a linear process: the data exist, then they are cleaned, analysed, visualised, and interpreted. This sequence feels intuitive, but it starts too late. Much of empirical inquiry happens before formal analysis begins, in the laborious effort to determine whether a given figure can answer the question in front of it.




A cell value in a table is not yet evidence. It becomes evidence only when connected to a specific research question, a rigorous definition, a unit of observation, a standardised measure, and a basis for comparison. A number may be valid inside its own statistical system and still fail to answer the political question being asked. Recognising when a national total hides deep distributional disparities, or when a trend in money terms hides a change in what that money buys, is part of the conceptual work of quantitative inquiry. So is seeing when a formal head count of workers leaves out labour that is socially necessary.




This connective labour – the work that bridges raw figures and substantive claims – is measurement work. It is the labour of transforming raw administrative or statistical outputs into evidence. Its inputs might be a PDF table, a brief metadata note, or an isolated time series. Its outputs are explicit variables, verified transformations, documented sources, and defensible comparisons.




The term is specific to data, but the kind of translation it refers to has a longer history. Bowker and Star showed that classification systems are built through political and institutional labour.

5

 Marx showed how capitalism translates different kinds of concrete labour into abstract, exchangeable value.

6

 Measurement work names a related translation: the process by which raw figures are made into evidence that can circulate as public truth.




Naming this labour matters because it reframes the primary question from ‘do we have the numbers?’ to ‘what has been done to make these numbers usable as evidence?’




GDP, for instance, can be expressed as an absolute level, a year-on-year growth rate, a per capita value, a nominal series, or a deflated real index. A poverty line can make material deprivation visible, but where it is drawn also decides how many people count as poor at all. A consumer price index captures inflation, yet its political implications diverge dramatically depending on whether the focus is on food security, fuel costs, real wages, or basic household survival. These are not minor technical adjustments. They decide which parts of social life a number can show, and which it leaves out.




Take the World Bank’s ‘Pink Sheet’ on commodity prices.

7

 The downloaded annual workbook is a complex file containing multiple sheets: nominal prices, real prices, price indices, and weight structures. A researcher studying agricultural dependency has to choose which version of the price to use. Should they track the price as it appeared at the time, or adjust it to show its purchasing power across years? Which commodity and unit of measure fit the question? This selection is measurement work. It can make the same decades look like recovery – or like a long decline in what those prices could actually buy.




Similarly, a basic GDP growth series can support very different, even contradictory, arguments depending on how it is handled. While a raw annual rate highlights short-term volatility, a three-year moving average smooths out short-term fluctuations to expose cyclical trends, and a five-year average makes longer trends easier to see (Figure 1). The underlying data remain the same, but the choice to aggregate or smooth them is a conceptual intervention. Without the technical capacity to construct these alternative measures, a research team is forced to inherit the version used in official press releases to frame national performance.







Figure 1.

 Real GDP growth, read as the annual rate and three- and five-year moving averages (illustrative constructed series, per cent per year; not any specific country).







None of this makes statistical metrics meaningless. It means their authority rests on the chain that connects a raw value to a public claim.




Yet this chain is deeply unequal. Well-funded institutions can spread the pre-analytical labour across dedicated data teams, advanced software pipelines, and robust documentation systems. Researchers, social movements, and public agencies in the Global South often have to carry the sequence themselves: locating raw files, auditing sources, deconstructing tables, writing code, validating totals, and defending their findings in public debates.




This division of labour determines which questions can be asked in the first place. If researchers cannot verify the construct behind a number, an inquiry may never progress to formal analysis. If a spreadsheet cannot be reshaped into structured evidence, the patterns inside it may remain locked away from public debate. When only a handful of well-funded organisations can perform this translation at scale, they retain the power to define economic and social reality through numbers.




Measurement work is a cornerstone of quantitative research capacity. It is not a preliminary chore, but one of the conditions that make empirical inquiry possible.




Yet this foundational labour is routinely erased. The polished indicators in global databases appear as finished facts, with the decisions behind them pushed out of view. This erasure creates two barriers. It discourages researchers from interrogating official statistics, and it leaves them without practice in handling raw administrative data. Often, the numbers exist, but they arrive in formats that are hard to question. A table may be easy to read and still be difficult to check, compare, or reuse.




3. A Readable Table Is Not Yet Data




The gulf between a presentation table and an analysis-ready dataset is visible in a typical worksheet on labour-force indicators (Figure 2). The sheet looks orderly: the two sexes run across the top, sectors down the left, and three related blocks – labour-force participation, work, and unemployment – are stacked one under another. A researcher can read it and a spreadsheet program can display it. But tools such as R, Python, or SQL cannot safely treat it as data, because the meaning of each value is carried by position, formula, and block order rather than by explicit variables.







Figure 2.

 Labour-force indicators by sector and sex, India PLFS 2017–18 (presentation worksheet; usual status – principal plus subsidiary activity; persons aged 15 and above; rates in per cent).

8







In the example above, the labour-force participation rate, the worker–population ratio, and the unemployment rate appear in matching positions across separate blocks. To understand how they relate to one another, the reader has to follow the layout and formulas by hand. That may be enough for one careful reading, but it is not enough for analysis that another researcher can repeat and verify.




An analysis-ready dataset has to be organised differently. The meaning of each number must be built into the dataset itself: the sector, sex, measure, unit, and value should appear as explicit fields, not as clues scattered across the layout. Definitions and formulas should travel with the measure as metadata, rather than be inferred from where a number sits in the grid. The question shifts from ‘can I see the right number near the right label?’ to ‘can another researcher check, group, compare, and reproduce the record without guessing?’ Reshaping the sheet into that form (Figure 3) turns a human-readable layout into machine-checkable evidence.







Figure 3.

 From workbook layout to an analysis-ready long table, India PLFS 2017–18 (usual status – principal plus subsidiary activity; persons aged 15 and above; rates in per cent; data and definitions as in Figure 2).







Once the measure is explicit, the evidence chain can be verified and inspected. Code can test whether totals add up, whether categories repeat consistently, whether rates match their inputs, and whether cases are missing. The record that travels with the dataset – source, layout, definitions, formulas, exclusions, checks – lets another researcher trace each step.




Without that structure and record, a chart may look polished while resting on a number whose meaning was guessed from its place in the table. The evidence cannot be independently checked or reliably reused beyond the person who cleaned it. The same opacity recurs across government reports, international databases, survey summaries, commodity-price sheets, and statistical PDFs – wherever the conditions that make numbers usable as evidence are hidden in layout, metadata, definitions, and institutional practice.




4. AI Lowers the Cost of the Work before Analysis




In this context, AI matters because it lowers the cost of pre-analytical labour. It is most useful for researchers who have a clear question, understand the statistical constructs, and can judge the political stakes, but lack years of formal training in data engineering.




For resource-constrained research teams, a major bottleneck is the difficult transition from a published table to a dataset that can be searched, checked, and analysed. Researchers have to identify the implicit variables, write the code that reshapes the table, verify the formulas, and record where each value came from. Many promising inquiries are abandoned at this stage not because the question is weak, but because the path from source format to evidence is too costly.




AI can help at several points in this transition, so long as each step remains open to human inspection.




Reading the Layout.

 AI can reduce the friction by helping researchers map the structure of the source data. A researcher can describe a table in plain language – quarters across columns, age cohorts down rows, sex categories repeated under each period, and measures stacked in blocks – and ask the system to propose a structure: period, age group, sex, measure code, unit, and value. The point is not to outsource the design, but to get a first draft that can be inspected, corrected, and finalised faster than starting from a blank script.




Drafting the Code.

 AI can help turn the researcher’s plan into a first working script. A researcher can explain what needs to happen to the table: move repeated headings into their own columns, combine related tables or lookup lists, remove footnote markers and other recurring text patterns, make labels consistent, turn numbers stored as text into usable values, or record where the original figures came from. The script still has to be checked against the source. But AI can lower the barrier between knowing what needs to be done and being able to run the code that does it.




Running the Checks.

 AI can also help with verification. A researcher can ask it to generate validation checks: Do sex categories add up to the listed totals? Do regional sub-aggregates reconcile with national aggregates? Does a rate match its numerator and denominator? Were any rows dropped during the reshaping process? These checks are the primary way in which a small team can prevent an empirical claim from drifting away from its material grounding.




Documenting the Work.

 AI can help turn a messy, interactive data-cleaning session into a structured record of the work: which sheet and cell ranges were read, which rows were excluded, how variables were renamed, what assumptions were made, and which validation tests succeeded. That record can be written in plain Markdown, JSON, or any other format the team can review. Without it, the analysis remains an isolated craft. Researchers are forced to reconstruct the same steps again, while institutions with stronger data-management systems retain the authority to define the mainstream narrative.




Diagnostic visualisations extend the same logic. Line charts, bar charts, and histograms can reveal structural breaks, duplicated periods, missing categories, or unusual outliers while evidence is still being made, before a claim has been written around a mistaken pattern.




One political caution belongs here: cleaning sensitive administrative data with a foreign AI tool can make those data newly legible to the company running the model, depending on its retention practices. The same act can build research capacity and open a new point of extraction.




Taken together, these steps place AI inside the measurement workflow rather than above it (Figure 4). AI can lower the cost of moving from a source to a structure, a set of checks, and a record. But the work that gives numbers public meaning – confirming the source, checking definitions, and interpreting the result – stays in human hands.







Figure 4.

 Where AI enters the measurement workflow (schematic; no data).







AI can automate parts of the quantitative workflow, but it cannot replace quantitative research as a whole. Nor does it make programming obsolete. The political opening is that researchers can spend less time fighting syntax and more time on statistical definitions, conceptual design, and political-economic interpretation.




In practice, this means that local research teams, trade unions, and regional public institutions in the Global South can now transform dense, poorly formatted administrative reports into auditable databases that others can inspect, reuse, and contest. This extends the Bandung Circuits’ 

AI for Social Science (AI4SS)

 framework into the terrain of measurement, applying its concern with research sovereignty to the work of turning numbers into evidence.

9




5. AI Cannot Replace Judgement




Making data preparation easier is not the same as replacing intellectual judgement.




An AI system can reshape a file without comprehending its substance. It can infer a tabular layout without knowing whether a given value is a numerator, denominator, total, rate, share, or index. It can produce a clean dataset from a flawed premise. It can accelerate research, but it can also accelerate structured error.




The core principle remains: AI can transform the file, but the analyst must verify what the file actually represents.




Verification is where statistical definition, economic interpretation, and political responsibility converge. Researchers must still decide what activities qualify as labour, which denominator belongs to a rate, whether historical categories remain comparable over time, whether a nominal series must be adjusted for inflation, and whether a chosen price index genuinely addresses the research question. They must also ask whether an official indicator obscures informal work, unpaid care, ecological degradation, or class distribution.




The same limit appears in research on informal work. An AI system can isolate categories such as self-employment, own-account work, or contributing family labour. But it cannot determine whether a category is best understood as an independent livelihood, disguised wage labour, a household survival strategy, or a position of acute subordination within a broader chain of extraction. Translating a statistical category into a concrete social relation requires political-economic judgement. No machine can assume responsibility for how researchers interpret class, value, dependency, or exploitation.




AI can recommend validation checks, but it cannot discern which discrepancy matters politically. A small mismatch in a total may be a rounding issue; a denominator that quietly excludes migrant workers may change the social meaning of the entire rate. AI can render a chart, but it cannot take responsibility for the public claim attached to it.




Using AI responsibly does not mean outsourcing judgement to an algorithm. It means embedding the machine within a disciplined research workflow – checking sources, reconciling totals, documenting each step – and interpreting the result politically. The more powerful these computational tools become, the more clearly researchers must understand their limits.




6. From Data Access to Research Capacity




By this point, the problem is no longer only whether data can be accessed. It is whether researchers have the capacity to turn those data into evidence that can be tested and defended. A dataset may be public and still be politically unusable if researchers lack the time, tools, concepts, and institutional support to work with it. What matters is who can sustain the whole chain: formulating the question, structuring the data, validating transformations, interpreting results, and carrying findings into public debate.




If knowledge production has its own ‘means of production’, then quantitative inquiry is no exception. It requires data and software, statistical concepts and economic theory, infrastructure and documentation – and, above all, institutional time. We call this broader ensemble of conditions the means of quantitative inquiry. It is not a single software package, but the collective capacity to interrogate numbers. Measurement work is a foundational, yet often hidden, layer of this capacity, the point where the structural conditions of quantitative inquiry first become labour.




The central change is not in the questions researchers ask, but in the resources required to answer them with evidence. By lowering that resource threshold, AI can change who builds and defends an evidence base. The first shift is in wider access to materials. A research team that once stopped at a scanned PDF table can now build an auditable database. The second is in deeper access to statistical constructs. A civil society researcher who once had to accept a pre-packaged external indicator can now dismantle and examine its numerator, denominator, and measurement logic. The third is the capacity to build an evidence base of one’s own. A local public institution that once passively consumed international classifications can now test whether those frameworks align with its mandate and build rigorous counter-evidence when they do not. The United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean shows what that third capacity looks like when sustained at an institutional scale. Prebisch directed it from 1950 to 1963, and it has produced alternative development statistics for the region for nearly eight decades.

10




This is, fundamentally, a question of methodological sovereignty. It does not mean that every institution should invent its own statistics or ignore comparability. It means having the capacity to examine inherited measures, test whether they answer local and regional questions, document alternative choices, and make those choices accountable to public argument. For a graduate student, this may mean reproducing an official chart instead of simply citing it. For a union, research institute, or public agency, it may mean maintaining an alternative evidence base that can survive public scrutiny. Kerala’s People’s Plan Campaign, launched in 1996, is a working example of that balance. Local bodies gathered their own data and set their own development priorities, within a common planning framework that kept plans comparable across the state – and the decentralised planning it built continues under the Kerala State Planning Board.

11




Methodological sovereignty matters most where statistics decide a country’s future. In Pakistan – as Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research documents in dossier no. 69, 

How the International Monetary Fund Is Squeezing Pakistan

 – the IMF has made its lending conditional on austerity: removing electricity, gas, and fuel subsidies, raising interest rates, and letting the market set the exchange rate.

12

 The Fund justifies these conditions through an aggregate assessment of debt sustainability. Its judgement of what is ‘sustainable’ reaches the household as the price of cooking gas and electricity. To show how that burden is distributed, local researchers and trade unions need the capacity to work with household survey microdata, reweight price indices according to local consumption patterns, and estimate the effects of the proposed cuts on different groups, particularly working-class households. Owning the means of quantitative inquiry allows researchers to do more than react to the IMF’s claims: they can challenge its arithmetic with evidence that withstands technical scrutiny and equip unions, movements, and governments prepared to contest its prescriptions.




What AI changes depends on who deploys it. In the hands of dominant institutions, it can produce the same pre-packaged indicator narratives at a faster rate. In the hands of scholars, trade unions, social movements, and public agencies in the Global South, it can widen who is able to build and defend an evidence base. That wider access does not mean lower standards. It requires clearer definitions, more traceable data lineages, more reproducible transformations, more explicit verification protocols, and more responsible interpretation. The objective is not to bend numbers to a predetermined narrative, but to let more researchers check what the numbers can and cannot say.




7. Who Sets the Terms of Counting?




Rigour matters because numbers carry power in public life. But not everything of value should be turned into a metric. Some relations of solidarity and subsistence resist counting, and should. The narrower claim is that whoever sets the terms of counting holds real power, and that power should not sit only in the North. That is the test to hold AI to as well: not AI thinking for researchers, but more researchers gaining the conditions to think with numbers.




Who gets to interrogate the numbers? Who gets to turn numbers into evidence? Who gets to use that evidence to challenge frameworks arranged by others? In the Global South, methodological sovereignty begins there: in the capacity to question inherited numbers, defend the evidence built from them, and mobilise it for political and social emancipation.

[1]

 

Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2017–18

.




[2]

. On World Bank financing to build or reform national statistical systems, see the World Bank’s Statistical Capacity Building Program (STATCAP), 

worldbank.org

. On sovereign rating methodologies – which combine institutional, economic, external, fiscal, and monetary assessments into an indicative rating level, allow specified supplemental adjustments, and leave the final determination to a rating committee – see S&P Global Ratings, 

Criteria | Governments | Sovereigns: Sovereign Rating Methodology

, 18 December 2017.




[3]

The Economic Development of Latin America and Its Principal Problems

 (Lake Success, NY: United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America, 1950).




[4]

How Europe Underdeveloped Africa

[5]

, Volume I (1867), especially Part I on the commodity and the value-form.




[7]

,

.




[8]

 All three blocks use PLFS 2017–18 values in usual status – principal plus subsidiary activity (the survey’s ‘ps+ss’ basis) – for persons aged 15 years and above: labour-force participation rate (Statement 8), worker–population ratio (Statement 11), and unemployment rate (Statement 32 and Appendix Table 18, ‘age groups: 15 years and above’).  (2019),

[9]

 See also ‘A Systematic Method for Controlling AI Writing Style’,

.

biblioguias.cepal.org

.
