author: Soreti Kadir
title: Finfinnee is the Third Space
content:
At the end of 2010, I took a trip to Ethiopia to visit my family. At the time, my parents worked in Bole, the commercial centre of Addis Ababa. Being only 16, my movements were more or less regulated by my parents, which meant that I would travel with them into the city each day, after which it was the extent of my curiosity and creativity (and pocket money) that determined what I did until evening, when I would head back to our house on the outskirts of the city. Slowly, interactions with the staff at a nearby cafe, just a few hundred meters from the building where my family worked, became routine. 




Over the two months that I was in Ethiopia, with much of this time spent in Addis Ababa, we spent most of our lunch breaks together, hanging out on the steps of the cafe, sharing stories to pass the time. One day, the conversation of our relationship to ‘Ethiopia’, as a national identity, came up. It’s important to note that I was raised in the Oromo diaspora, a community that, in the years my mother and I migrated to Australia, was made up mostly of political refugees who fled the country after the adoption of the “Transitional Period Charter of Ethiopia” and the official establishment of a transitional government. 




This eventually led to the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) monopolizing power within the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), a process that resulted in the isolation of those seeking political power within the EPRDF through the ballot. Given the size and economic importance of the Oromia region, it was the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), amongst others, that became a key target of political violence, creating political communities in exile exactly like the one that I grew up in.




I inherited a different definition of Ethiopia, coloured by memories and experiences of violence and displacement that informed my relationship to the state as a place of unbelonging for those who shared my identity. The day that the conversation with these two new friends wandered into political territory, we all engaged passionately, striving to reflect the extent of both our personal experiences and hopes for our country. They found my reflections to be overly nostalgic and antagonistic towards the country’s future.  Unconcerned for the good of the future. I found their insistence that we shared a national identity to be inaccurate and offensive. We agreed on little, and I found it exhilarating. 




That evening, I was restlessly anticipating the opportunity to tell my mother about what I thought was the most exciting experience of my trip to date. In recounting the story, I almost gave my mother a heart attack. Angry, afraid, and in shock, my mother warned me sternly against ever engaging in such conversation in public again. She asked me many questions about who these men were, how I knew them, and if we’d ever had such conversations before. What I was blind to, and what was the daily lived experience of my parents, was that Addis Ababa, primarily but not exclusively, was a heavily surveilled city, the State looking for the people doing exactly what I found myself doing that day – discussing the political reality of our country. Thereafter, I was careful, out of curiosity more than fear (being 16 with a high risk tolerance will do that), and refrained from fully-fledged conversations, opting for quiet enquiry when the opportunity presented itself. Although our conversation never veered down the road of politics again, I continued to visit my friends every day and remember rushing to say a heartfelt goodbye on the day I was due to fly back to Australia. 




For this piece, I will centre the discussion on Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, as opposed to extending the conversation to other parts of the country which exist with their own nuances and political realities, requiring more space for analysis than I have here. I share the introductory anecdote to forward the idea that, in Ethiopia, to nurture spaces of connection, community-building, and care, we must first invest in collective repair of the damage wrought by decades of state surveillance that has defined the range and breadth of relational life the city space can hold, and from the legacy of what can only be defined as settler colonialism. ‘Where’, figuratively and literally, can this process of repair take place? I argue that it must take place in Finfinnee, geographically the same location as Addis Ababa, but sociologically and historically, different, and with a capacity unique unto itself to ground and lead us to new political possibilities.




In 1886, Menelik II conquered the lands that were then known as Finfinnee and were primarily inhabited by the Tulama Oromo. As it took on its new identity as the “new flower” (the meaning of Addis Ababa), as both a military barracks for the expansion of Menelik’s empire and as the accumulation point for capital extracted throughout the process of the Ethiopian state’s consolidation, Finfinnee lost something, an essence. Regaining connection with it, not just for the Oromo, but for all who inhabit the Ethiopian state, is vital if we are to become free of cyclical violence, political domination and mass poverty. Fundamentally, this perspective is concerned with the functions that Finfinnee held space for, which were specific to the Oromo’s indigenous ways of organising society and were destroyed to make room for the functions of the modern nation-state’s capital city. Historically, Finfinnee was the convergence point for the five Gadaa assemblies, representing the centre of the loose confederation of diverse Oromo clan groups. This site of togetherness was activated not only for lengthy discussion and dialogue, unrestrained by time and space, taking months if needed and housed only by the branches of the sycamore tree (known as the Odaa) that the meetings would take place under, but, moreover, Finfinnee also provided a place for collective connection with the natural world and the Creator.

Every year, the Oromo would converge in the millions to express gratitude for the change of seasons, for livelihood, and for collective life. This celebration, 

Irreechaa

, was banned under EPRDF rule, and although it was brought back by the current ruling party, what we now have is a pacified, desecrated, and heavily militarized version of the rite. This is because it was brought back to 

Addis Ababa

, not to 

Finfinnee

. If the return of 

Irreechaa

 had been to Finfinnee, rather than being performed as a plasticized event that seems to exacerbate ethnic animosities each year, it would serve as the site of dialogue and togetherness that it is meant to be.




In Finfinnee, the idea of a neighbour going without while your home is full is difficult to embrace. In Addis Ababa, your conditions and survival depend on whether or not you can successfully sell your labour. In Finfinnee, the idea of war as a solution, before all means of peaceful reconciliation are tried, even if these discussions take many months, would be an affront to what it means to inhabit the land. In Addis Ababa, war is a means to consolidate power and make those in the business of war richer. Finfinnee is governed by an entirely different set of ideals from those of Addis Ababa, and this suggestion that we find our way back to these ideals is neither archaic idealisation nor is it the fruit of exclusionary nationalism with which many associate any discussion of Finfinnee vs Addis Ababa. Rather, for the city to make way for healthy public life to emerge, it has to lose grip on its identity as a centre of surveillance and as a place that offers itself as dignifiably livable for only the political and economic elite.




The song 

Abba Bootii

, meaning “Father of the gumboots”, by Jaalee Amantee, uses both lyrics and the music video to make intriguing and poignant commentary on the social and economic reality of this question of Addis Ababa vs Finfinnee. The gumboots, worn traditionally by male farmers and usually accompanied by a dress shirt, pants, jackets, a woollen vest, a baseball cap, and a traditional white cotton blanket draped across the top half of the body, are an aesthetic commonly associated with farming communities on the outskirts of Finfinnee, the traditional lands of the Tulama Oromo. In the chorus of the song, the artist says, 

“Sii ga’eera tufiin biyyaa kan keetii,”

 “You’ve had enough of the disdain that your country shows you,” and then goes on to say, 

“Fiigii Finfineeti,”

 meaning, “Onward to Finfinnee.” In the music video, we see a man intended to represent the Oromo who have embraced the aesthetics of modernity, stepping out of a car, dressed in semi-casual clothes. He sees mannequins dressed in the 

Abba Bootii

 aesthetic and proceeds to go and take selfies with them. As the chorus begins, the mannequins come to life and use their 

shimala

 to chase the man through the city, where he tries to escape by hiding behind different people, each of these people transforming into who all reflect to him the 

Abba Bootii

, played by Jaalee himself. Eventually, the man ends up on land being ploughed by a man (also Jaalee) with an ox, where he faces off with the mannequins, the cityscape visible in the background.  A 

shimala

 is a long stick that is commonly associated with both farming and self-defence practices among the Tulama Oromo. The act of taking a selfie with the mannequins, who are also wearing black masks to further symbolise erasure, and the ensuing confrontation, we can interpret as Jaalee’s attempt to return agency to the wearer of the gumboots in an Addis Ababa social and political environment where the way of life of those who work the land is subject to objectification and erasure.




Although this song is specific to the story of the northern Oromo farmers’ relationship to Addis Ababa and their relationship to the “modern” Oromo, we can apply the message of the song to help us further the analysis we make here. Acceptance and inclusion within the realm of Addis Ababa is conditional upon one’s ability to perform modernity, and this is not just limited to what one wears, but it also includes what one thinks about the state project. What this song implies is that the aesthetic one chooses to adorn in Addis Ababa indicates to the surveillance systems how close or how far they may be from complying with the logics of capital and the state. It is not only the Oromo who would be subjected to this assessment in Addis Ababa; rather, any person representative of the majority subsistence farming class of Ethiopia would be eyed with caution in Addis Ababa, for their rejection of Addis Ababa would be a threat that, if it grew, could collapse the state entirely.




If Addis Ababa must fence itself off from the historic and contemporary realities that created and sustain it to safeguard its survival, then it must remain perpetually alert to any signs of the return to Finfinnee, which is as much a place as it is a political reality and mindset. Finfinnee is the site within Ethiopia where a multi-national class revolution becomes a possibility. It provides the depth of recalibration needed for us to re-enter the communion of person-to-person dialogue, to extend mutual care and solidarity, and to remember a relationship to land that goes beyond extraction. Finfinnee 

is

 the third space. 




The post 

Finfinnee is the Third Space

 first appeared on 

The Elephant

.

author: CNT Villaverde Alto - Comarcal Sur de Madrid
title: Llamamiento de la Mesa Sindical de Madrid a la construcción de Comités Unitarios para la Huelga General del 11N
content:
Para construir la huelga general desde abajo:




Impulsemos comités unitarios por la huelga general en todos los centros de trabajo, centros de estudio, barrios y pueblos de Madrid.




Esta huelga general 

nace de la lucha y la exigencia popular en las plazas y en las calles

, que ha logrado que todas las organizaciones sindicales se sumaran a la convocatoria.




Desde la 

Mesa Sindical por la huelga general

 hemos entendido desde el inicio que las garantías de éxito del 11N y de continuidad de esta lucha es que seamos capaces de 

organizarla desde abajo, en cada centro de trabajo, en cada centro de estudio, en cada barrio y pueblo

. Esto exige la articulación consciente, democrática y solidaria de comités unitarios por la huelga general.




Por ello, 

hacemos un llamamiento a todas las organizaciones sindicales, sociales, juveniles, políticas y a todo el activismo

 a la conformación masiva de comités unitarios, en la que, 

de forma democrática y asamblearia, construyamos espacios de debate y organización no excluyentes y con capacidad de tomar decisiones colectivas

.




Son ya muchas las iniciativas que se están poniendo en marcha. 

Saludamos ese empeño y esperamos y deseamos que ese espíritu unitario, participativo y democrático prevalezca en todas partes

.




¡Organicemos una gran huelga general activa y combativa el 11-N! ¡Continuemos la lucha y la organización después del 11N, gobierne quien gobierne!

Llamamiento de la Mesa Sindical de Madrid a la construcción de Comités Unitarios para la Huelga General del 11N

author: Joseph Lee
title: Long after the Maui fires, toxic metals linger in residents’ bodies
content:
In August of 2023, a series of wildfires broke out across Maui, killing more than 100 people, destroying thousands of homes, and causing billions in damage. Noelani Ahia, who is Kanaka Maoli and co-founder of Maui Medic Healers Hui, helped mobilize nearly 600 volunteers in Lāhainā, including doctors, nurses, and therapists. 




Three years later, the housing and health crises remain acute. Maui Medic Healers Hui runs a free clinic, but Ahia wishes it had 10 more to address the community’s needs. “The fire may be out, but the catastrophe is not over by any stretch of the imagination,” she said. 




The devastation extended well beyond the lives lost and buildings destroyed. Research published last year by researchers with the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, found that 

more than 1 in 5 residents

 had reduced lung function.




Now, new research from the same project has 

found elevated levels of toxic metals

 in the island’s residents months after the fires, with higher exposure associated with impaired lung function. The findings offer further evidence that 

the health consequences of catastrophic wildfires

 can persist long after the flames are extinguished and the smoke clears.




“What we consider and sometimes look at as a one-time event isn’t really one-time anymore,” Alika Maunakea, who is Kanaka Maoli and co-director of MauiWES, told Grist. 




Researchers don’t yet know how much of the contamination came from the fires and how much was already present in the environment. That distinction matters as wildfires increasingly race through towns like Lāhainā and cities like Los Angeles, where burning 

homes, cars and infrastructure can leave contaminants

 that 

people encounter for months

 or years afterward.




Community members hold hands in a prayer circle at a “Lāhainā Strong” gathering in October 2023.
 

Mario Tama / Getty Images




“We have traditionally thought about wildfire exposure primarily through the lens of smoke,” Maunakea said in a press release. “But when an entire community burns, we are dealing with a much more complicated exposure environment.” Researchers must also understand what contaminants were already present, what the fire may have released, and what entered residents’ bodies, he said.




The research, which studied 1,400 adults across Maui six to 18 months after the fires, measured 24 metals in urine samples. It found that participants had higher concentrations of several metals than people in a nationwide health survey conducted before the fires. That included 2.2 times as much arsenic, 2.3 times as much barium, and 3.8 times as much manganese. Antimony, which is used in flame retardant materials and has been previously 

linked to lung irritation, stomach pain, and other symptoms

, was found at levels nearly 40 times higher.




Because the researchers lack comparable data from before the fires, they could not determine how much of the metal exposure resulted from the disaster. Maunakea told Grist answering that question is the next step for the project, which has received a $3.6 million grant from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences. That work will include investigating whether and to what degree past agricultural and industrial activity contributed to the contamination.




“It’s important to realize that these are all part of settler colonialism,” Ahia said. “So what we’re looking at is confounding factors that are to the detriment of the health of our local people.”










Read Next




























Two years after a wildfire took everything, Maui homeowners are facing a new threat: Foreclosure













Anita Hofschneider

 



















Decades of plantation agriculture altered water systems, introduced herbicides, and displaced native plants, leaving a legacy on the islands that is still felt today. Disasters like fires and storms can compound those ongoing environmental problems. 




“If we begin the story when the fire starts, we miss the decisions that shaped the landscape and the community’s ability to respond,” said Katie Kamelamela, who is Kanaka Maoli and an assistant professor at Arizona State University based in Hawaiʻi. “Micro climate change acts on places already shaped by histories of land ownership, water diversion, development, and unequal access to resources.”




Kamelamela said true recovery must look beyond the fire. “I want recovery to be measured by whether people can remain in their communities, care for ʻāina, and pass on their knowledge and practices in place,” she said, using the Hawaiian word for land, which carries deeper meaning and relationship than property or mere place. “Rebuilding should not recreate the same conditions that left people at risk. Caring for ʻāina and caring for people need to be funded and planned together.”




Maunakea said the multitude of intersecting pressures is one reason why he wanted to pursue this research. As climate change continues to accelerate, longstanding issues facing Native Hawaiians like housing, the harms of tourism, and the legacy of plantations can amplify problems. “We worry that disasters like this that we experience on Maui, as well as the floods and other storms that we’re experiencing now, is just going to continue widening the gaps in health disparities that already exist in those populations,” he said.




Moving forward, the project will not just identify health risks but also help residents respond to them. Study participants receive their results, discuss them, and meet with health professionals. “People now know that there’s these types of potential hazards, and what to do about them is a big concern,” Maunakea said. “We still don’t have all the answers for sure, but we are taking the next steps to get a better picture and inform our community around it.”




This story was originally published by 

Grist

 with the headline 

Long after the Maui fires, toxic metals linger in residents’ bodies

 on Oct 16, 2026.

author: CNT Iruña
title: Sorpresa sería que aguantáramos
content:
Cada vez que sale una estadística sobre bajas, la misma historia. Que si faltamos mucho, que si el estrés y la ansiedad se disparan, que la gente ya no aguanta nada. Y ni una vez se preguntan por qué. Pues lo decimos nosotras, que lo tenemos claro: es que nos han dejado a media plantilla y nos piden el trabajo de una y media. Es que te escriben a las diez de la noche y más te vale contestar. Es que los objetivos están puestos para que no los cumpla nadie. Es que con estos contratos no llegas a fin de mes, y encima vives con el miedo al despido pegado al cuerpo, todo el día, hasta cuando duermes. Así que no me digas que es sorpresa. Sorpresa sería que aguantáramos.




Y cuando por fin alguien se cae, la empresa se encoge de hombros y le cuelga el cartel de absentista, como si fuera un defecto de fábrica. Años culpando al que enferma para no tener que mirar lo que enferma. Ya está bien, ¿no?




Una baja por salud mental no es un capricho, por mucho que lo piense algún jefe. Y algún compañero, que también los hay, no nos vamos a engañar. Es parar antes de romperte del todo. Y tienes todo el derecho a hacerlo sin pedir perdón a nadie. No somos máquinas. Nuestra vida vale más que los beneficios de cuatro. La salud no se regatea ni se agradece como si fuera un favor personal del jefe de turno. Es un derecho que costó décadas de lucha, y no vamos a dejar que nos lo vayan recortando por la puerta de atrás. Si media plantilla acaba quemada, el problema no son las personas. Es una empresa que te gasta y te tira, como si fueras material fungible.




Así que sí, cuidarse también es político. El que se coge la baja no le falla a nadie. Y la culpa, esa que te meten, sirve para una cosa: para que te calles. Pues va a ser que no.




¿Y ahora qué? Pues lo de siempre, lo que ha funcionado toda la vida. Cubrirnos entre compañeras cuando una no puede más. No dejar sola a la que se cae. Cortar el cotilleo de quién está de baja y por qué, que bastante tiene ya. Y plantarnos juntas en el curro para exigir plantillas completas, ritmos que aguante un ser humano y desconexión de verdad, no la del convenio que nadie respeta. Derechos laborales no nos han regalado ninguno. Todos se han arrancado peleando. Este también.




La entrada 

Sorpresa sería que aguantáramos

 se publicó primero en 

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

author: Unknown
title: Torino: incursioni della polizia dentro le scuole occupate
content:
Di seguito il comunicato pubblicato dall’

Assemblea Studentesca

 delle scuole di Torino in merito ai fatti degli ultimi giorni. 




La quasi totalità delle scuole torinesi è in occupazione a partire dalla settimana scorsa con l’intento di scendere in piazza tutte unite. Licei e istituti tecnici da giorni sono l’epicentro della lotta studentesca contro la riforma Valditara, il razzismo istituzionale, la guerra, la spesa per le armi, per chiedere urgenti fondi per ristrutturare le nostre scuole, contro le scuole trasformate in caserme e lo strapotere dei presidi.




In migliaia stiamo affermando i nostri diritti e soprattutto che vogliamo contare! Che come studenti e studentesse vogliamo potere decisionale sulle nostre vite e sulle nostre scuole.




Il Governo Meloni e il Prefetto di Torino ci attaccano senza rispondere alle nostre rivendicazioni, cercando di dividerci tra “buoni e cattivi”. Minacciano di intervenire contro le occupazioni e i nostri cortei. Rispondiamo che siamo uniti più che mai è che la nostra lotta è compatta! 




La lotta studentesca in maniera spontanea ha assunto anche forme nuove. Se una parte degli studenti vede nelle strutture scolastiche un obiettivo da colpire la colpa è di chi le ha fatte diventare delle caserme, di chi le ha rese fatiscenti, di chi le ha definanziate per anni, di chi ha fatto finta di non vedere che il razzismo istituzionale era sempre più forte. 




Invece di chiedersi perché alcuni studenti arrivino ad odiare le proprie scuole, i propri banchi, i propri professori, ci si inventa fantomatici “infiltrati” a cui dare la colpa. Si guarda il dito e non la luna. Noi invece siamo consapevoli che dietro a questi comportamenti spontanei c’è la voglia di contare, di farsi sentire, di urlare che esistiamo. Dirigenti scolastici, professori, Prefetto e Ministro dovrebbero chiedersi perché, invece di invocare manette e strette repressive. 




Il nostro movimento è fatto di rifiuto e contrapposizione, ma in questi giorni di vita comune e occupazione, sta generando proposte concrete per una scuola diversa da quella che il sistema ci obbliga a vivere. Laboratori, assemblee, dibattiti sono la fucina in cui un mondo che vogliamo nuovo e collettivo sta nascendo, questo è quello che fa più paura al potere, scoprire che chi si pensava passivo e alienato invece ha vita, idee, voglia di mettersi in gioco. 




Dalla Francia gli studenti ci hanno invitato a muoverci insieme e lo abbiamo fatto, scoprendo che la nostra città può essere un esempio per tante altre in Italia. Molti giornalisti benpensanti nelle settimane scorse guardavano  raccontavano con ammirazione le mobilitazioni al di là del confine, ora che sono arrivate a casa loro e le hanno sotto il naso le oscurano e le criminalizzano. La rivolta per loro va bene solo se la fanno in altri paesi per poi dirci che noi non siamo maturi, che qui è diverso. Bene, ora che la prateria si è incendiata anche qui dovranno farsene una ragione. 




Alle minacce del Prefetto contro le occupazioni  rispondiamo compatti che le difenderemo, a testimoniarlo ci sono le montagne di banchi e cassonetti che sbarrano gli ingressi. Diciamo che gli arresti di oggi contro gli studenti del Levi e di Giaveno sono assurdi e criminali.




I presidi ci parlano di “esterni” come se le nostre occupazioni fossero fatte da infiltrati. Questi fantomatici “esterni” non sono altro che studenti e studentesse che da scuola a scuola si danno man forte a vicenda, creano legami e solidarietà. Chi ha deciso che non possiamo confrontarci fra scuole diverse? Forse si arrabbiano tanto perché per una volta la scuola è aperta a chi decidiamo noi e non loro, è la frustrazione di chi vede il proprio potere vacillare.

author: Santana Simiyu
title: A baby died following FGM in The Gambia. Why did the case end in acquittal?
content:
16th October 2026










A baby died following FGM in The Gambia. Why did the case end in acquittal?
















By Santana Simiyu
















14 min read



















News and Insights




End harmful practices




Africa


























































Nairobi, Kenya, September 30, 2026: 

In May 2026, The Gambia’s High Court acquitted three women prosecuted in connection with the death of an infant following female genital mutilation (FGM). The Court found that the child had died from injuries sustained during FGM, but in her ruling, Justice Janneh upheld a “no case to answer” submission by the defence on the grounds that the prosecution had failed to produce legally admissible evidence establishing the criminal responsibility of the accused. 




The case did not turn on whether FGM had taken place or caused the child’s death, but on whether investigators and prosecutors had gathered and presented sufficient admissible evidence to prove who was responsible. The judgment raises an important question for The Gambia: what does it take to turn laws prohibiting FGM into effective accountability?




Rule of law cannot be selective

 




When news spread that a one-month-old 

girl had bled to death following FGM

 in Welingira, in The Gambia’s West Coast Region, the public was understandably outraged. In such cases, people often expect courts to deliver justice by securing convictions. Yet the outcome of 

The State v. Fatou Camara and Others 

reminds us that the legitimacy of the criminal justice system depends not only on the outcome of a case, but on whether every stage of the justice process, including investigation and law enforcement, adheres to the rule of law. 




The state filed four charges: 

performing FGM, conspiracy to commit a felony, aiding and abetting the procedure, and failing to report the act. The

 three accused pleaded not guilty, placing the burden on the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The prosecution called ten witnesses and submitted evidence to support its case. 




The High Court did not dispute the medical evidence that the child died from injuries consistent with circumcision. Nor did it question the seriousness of FGM. Rather, the court insisted that criminal responsibility must be established through legally admissible evidence, and it correctly observed that the strength of a criminal case is measured not by the number of witnesses but by the quality and admissibility of the evidence they provide.




The court’s insistence on admissible evidence should not be dismissed as a mere procedural technicality. It reflects a foundational principle of the rule of law that courts must follow due process and conduct a fair trial. This requires the State to prove criminal responsibility through lawful and reliable evidence before it can convict a person and deprive them of their liberty. A justice system that relaxes evidentiary standards because an offence is particularly grave does not strengthen justice. It weakens it. Ensuring justice for survivors of severe human rights violations like FGM thus requires every actor in the criminal justice chain to ensure that these standards are met so that the burden of proof can be discharged.




The judgment is an institutional critique




Perhaps the most significant aspect of the judgment is not the acquittal itself but the court’s observations regarding the investigation. Rather than merely concluding that the prosecution had failed to establish a prima facie case, Justice Janneh identified concrete investigative deficiencies that undermined the prosecution from the outset. 




Several police witnesses admitted they never visited the scene where the alleged offence occurred. Others testified that their evidence was based largely on information received from colleagues rather than on their own investigative work. Material witnesses were apparently not identified or interviewed, and little effort was made to gather physical or circumstantial evidence capable of independently linking the accused persons to the offences charged.




These were not isolated oversights. Collectively, they reveal systemic weaknesses in how the police and prosecutors investigate FGM cases. The court’s criticism extended beyond the conduct of individual officers. It raised broader institutional questions about investigative capacity, training, supervision, and compliance with statutory procedures in cases involving vulnerable victims.




When criminal investigations fail, justice fails




The evidence established that the infant died from injuries sustained during female circumcision. What it failed to establish was the criminal responsibility of the accused persons through legally admissible evidence.




That distinction matters.




The acquittal was not the inevitable consequence of an inadequate legal framework. Nor was it evidence that prosecutions are inherently difficult under the 

Women’s (Amendment) Act, 2015

, which bans and criminalises FGM. It was the consequence of gaps and failures in the investigative process.




The cost of procedural non-compliance in criminal investigations




Perhaps the clearest example of procedural failure was the treatment of the alleged confessional statements. The investigating officer acknowledged that no independent witness was present when statements were taken. 




The court observed this breached mandatory safeguards in Section 31 of the Evidence Act, which are intended to ensure statements are given voluntarily and without coercion. Because this procedure was not followed, Justice Janneh ruled the statements couldn’t be admitted as evidence. 




Significantly, the judge remarked that compliance with the statutory requirements would have enabled the court to consider evidence that may have been critical to determining the criminal responsibility of the accused.




This observation should not be overlooked. The court was effectively saying that the prosecution’s case was defeated by the failure to follow the law.




A judgment that speaks to institutions, not just individuals




The judgment therefore exposed an uncomfortable reality: legislation alone cannot secure accountability. This echoes Equality Now’s report, 

Towards Justice: Global Challenges and Opportunities in Litigating Cases of Female Genital Mutilation

, which concludes that while laws against FGM are crucial, they must be backed by effective, adequately resourced enforcement. 




Numerous jurisdictions have criminalised FGM. Yet prosecutions remain rare, with legislative gaps and inadequate implementation impeding justice. Reporting rates remain low due to factors including stigma, threats and community pressure, with inadequate protection for survivors and witnesses, and under-resourced law enforcement creating barriers. Shortcomings in investigations and evidence gathering prevent cases from progressing and cause prosecutions to fail in court. Even when convictions are secured, lenient sentencing can fail to reflect the seriousness of offences. 




Viewed in this light, 

The State v. Fatou Camara and Others

 is about far more than the acquittal of three accused persons. It is a judgment about the lack of institutional accountability.




It reminds investigators that they cannot neglect crime scene management. It reminds prosecutors that they cannot build cases on hearsay or improperly obtained confessions. It reminds governments that criminalising harmful practices must be accompanied by investment in investigative capacity, forensic expertise, and continuous training for law enforcement officers.




Without those institutional reforms, even the strongest legislative protections for women and children risk becoming difficult to enforce.




The Gambia’s anti-FGM law is threatened by a Supreme Court challenge 




FGM is an internationally recognised form of gender-based violence and a fundamental violation of the rights to health, bodily integrity and freedom from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. When FGM results in death, it violates the right to life. 




The Gambia has ratified international and regional treaties that require States to eliminate harmful practices, such as the

 

Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW)

, 

the

 

Maputo Protocol

, and

 

United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child

, which requires States to protect children from all forms of physical or mental violence, injury or abuse, and recognises FGM as child abuse.




While The Gambia has a legal framework criminalising FGM, its full potential in preventing and eliminating the practice has yet to be realised, given ongoing gaps in implementation and enforcement. The law is now under threat from a constitutional petition filed with the Supreme Court, 

Almamy Gibba and Seven Others v. Attorney General

,

 which 

seeks to have provisions criminalising FGM struck down on the grounds that it infringes upon the rights to cultural and religious freedoms, equality and 

family life

 protected under the Constitution. Repealing these provisions before the law has been fully implemented and enforced would risk weakening an important legal safeguard against FGM before its potential impact has been fully realised. 




The case is part of a global pushback against women’s rights, documented in Equality Now’s brief,

 

Words & Deeds: Strategically defending the rights of all women and girls in an era of backlash

. Efforts to advance gender equality are facing mounting and organised resistance, while hard-won legal protections are increasingly being challenged. But regression is neither inevitable nor irreversible.




If the Supreme Court declines to uphold the law, this could place women and girls in The Gambia at greater risk of FGM and further undermine survivors’ access to justice.  The decision could undermine advocacy calling for FGM to be explicitly criminalised in Liberia, Mali and Sierra Leone. And successfully invoking cultural or religious justifications to challenge laws protecting women and girls would set a regressive precedent and risk emboldening anti-rights actors seeking to weaken legal rights elsewhere.




The Gambia FGM case highlights why effective investigations are vital 




The enduring lesson of 

The State v. Fatou Camara and Others

 is not that the law failed to protect a child. Rather, it is that the criminal justice system can only be as effective as the investigations upon which prosecutions are built.




The High Court affirmed the rule of law by refusing to substitute suspicion for proof. At the same time, it issued a clear warning that investigative shortcomings can frustrate accountability, even where the occurrence of a serious crime is medically established.




If there is a reform agenda emerging from this judgment, it is not the need for new offences or harsher penalties in The Gambia. The law that criminalises FGM must remain. What else is needed is a corresponding investment in investigative professionalism, evidentiary compliance, and prosecutorial preparedness. Only then can the promise of the law be translated into meaningful justice while preserving the constitutional guarantees that protect every accused person.




END




Santana Simiyu

 is an advocate of the High Court of Kenya and Legal Advisor at Equality Now, where she focuses on ending harmful practices, including female genital mutilation and child marriage. She has experience in legal and policy advocacy at the national level, including engagement with regional human rights mechanisms. Her work includes strengthening legal and policy frameworks, supporting accountability for violations of women’s and girls’ rights, and advancing the implementation of human rights standards across Africa. Santana holds an LL.B. from the Catholic University of Eastern Africa and a Postgraduate Diploma in Law from the Kenya School of Law.

mkwambai@equalitynow.org

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: On liberal opportunism and the “purity” smear
content:
Photo from Naga City Tourism Facebook page

Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic.

Why did former Vice President and now Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo roll out the pink carpet for the Zionist war machine? When Robredo hosted Israeli Ambassador Dana Kursh for an official courtesy visit, she was not merely performing the routine gestures of local hospitality. She was actively welcoming and legitimizing representatives of the US-Israeli genocidal apparatus. This intervention centers an anti-imperialist analysis to dismantle the liberal apologetics surrounding this act. Rather than an isolated error in judgment, this diplomatic encounter exposes the persistent, foundational tension within the Philippine political landscape: the contradiction between liberal reformism and anti-imperialist national liberation.

Dismissing progressives’ critique of Robredo’s hosting of the Israeli envoy as mere “political purism” is politically and morally impoverished. The underlying mechanism demands a total, systematic critique. To understand why her defenders deploy the “politics of purity” accusation, and why that defense completely falls apart when examining real power dynamics and economic interests, we must lay bare both the liberal class position and the ideological sleight of hand at work.

To make sense of Robredo’s pivot toward imperial hospitality, we must look directly at the liberal class position. Her stance is neither an accidental misstep nor a personal failure of political intelligence but the direct expression of her class character and political alignment. Liberal reformism in the global periphery operates strictly within the legal, institutional, and geopolitical framework dictated by US imperialism.

While Robredo served as a focal point against the overt state terrorism of the Marcos-Duterte dynasties, her opposition was strictly intra-class—a feud over how to manage the neocolonial state, pitting rule-of-law decorum against autocratic violence.

Because her political legitimacy rests upon acceptance by the global capitalist order, her opposition stops at the border of imperial interest. When forced to choose between international solidarity with an anti-imperialist national liberation movement and alignment with the Washington-Tel Aviv axis, liberal reformists invariably side with the imperial core. They cannot critique the drain of value, the extraction of labor, or the military hegemony of US imperialism because their entire political project depends on remaining within that very apparatus.

This structural subservience explains why defenders deploy the “purity politics” weapon whenever that alignment is exposed. Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic. From a materialist standpoint, this argument relies on three ideological fallacies:

First, it replaces a materialist baseline with ideological absolution. Opposition to active genocide, ethnic cleansing, and imperialist aggression is not a performative or elevated ideological standard; it is the absolute baseline of human solidarity and anti-imperialist struggle. Labeling principled opposition to mass slaughter as “purity” redefines baseline morality as an unreasonable demand, attempting to pass off complicity as pragmatic maturity.

Second, it operates on the logic of liberal idealism, which treats political stances as abstract moral choices made in a vacuum. Political actions reflect concrete class interests. Shielding a public figure from accountability for legitimizing a settler-colonial state serves a specific political function: it conditions the middle forces to accept imperial violence as a routine, acceptable feature of global diplomacy.

Third, it trades scientific alignment for unprincipled unity. Transformative praxis distinguishes between principled unity—built on anti-imperialist struggle and mass interest—and unprincipled unity, which colludes with reaction to preserve electoral coalitions. Demanding that the progressive movement remain silent on international solidarity to protect a liberal politician’s image trades human rights and anti-imperialist consciousness for temporary electoral expediency.

This dynamic reveals the distinct role of the middle forces—segments of the middle-class progressives and social-democratic elements whose reactions betray a deep-seated fear of losing mainstream respectability. For these forces, Robredo represented a comfortable alternative to overt tyranny, allowing them to feel progressive without questioning the Philippines’ neocolonial subordination to the US.

When Robredo acts as an agent of normalization for foreign atrocities, it shatters the illusion that liberal reformism can deliver liberation. The attempt to police the speech of critics via the “purity” label is a desperate move to protect that illusion and avoid confronting their own complicity.

Striking at liberal opportunism on Palestine is not an exercise in academic gatekeeping or moral perfectionism; it is an essential task of political education. Genocide is the ultimate expression of imperialist violence, and no movement can claim to defend freedom at home while remaining silent on liberation abroad. We must not allow the hegemony of liberal ideology to confuse anti-imperialist principles or frame Palestine as an optional advocacy.

Ultimately, we are forced to return to the question of Leni’s pink carpet. Just days after her polite handshake in Naga City, the world watched as former ICC judge Navi Pillay—who headed the UN Commission that explicitly ruled Israel guilty of committing genocide in Gaza—was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.

This timing leaves liberals and their apologists with a sharp dilemma. Could someone operating strictly within liberal political interests alter their course when the very international institutions they revere formally name and condemn genocide? It leaves them with only two real possibilities: either we confirm the classic Marxist formulation—that in times of crisis, liberalism unmasks itself to reveal its underlying affinity with fascism and imperial violence—or liberal figures like Robredo must stop being tone-deaf, abandon their electoral opportunism, and recognize the real balance of forces today. Across the globe, from international tribunals to the streets, the peoples of the world are standing firmly for Palestine. Any continued alignment with imperial genocide is not pragmatic diplomacy but a moral and political dead end.

author: CNT Santander
title: Ni alquileres abusivos, ni sueldos de miseria
content:
La huelga es la mejor herramienta que tiene la clase trabajadora para conquistar derechos al sistema capitalista. Las mejoras laborales, las libertades y los avances sociales son fruto de la organización, la solidaridad y la lucha colectiva. Cuando nos unimos, tenemos la capacidad de detener la maquinaria que se alimenta de nuestro esfuerzo.




Desde CNT Santander nos unimos a la llamada del Sindicato de Inquilinas y el 11 de noviembre saldremos a la calle para reivindicar nuestros derechos como clase trabajadora.




Es por todo ello que:







Revindicamos un 

incremento salarial

 en todos los sectores, incluido el salario mínimo interprofesional, que nos permita poder asumir los costes de la vida sin sentir que nos ahogamos, sin incertidumbre ni pánico.




Necesitamos la 

reducción de la jornada laboral máxima

 a 30 horas semanales, sin merma salarial, de manera progresiva.




Lucharemos por 

un incremento de las pensiones públicas

, tanto contributivas como no contributivas.







La vivienda no es un lujo para especular, es un derecho innegociable que ha de ser respetado. Ninguna persona debería elegir entre pagar el alquiler, llenar la nevera y/o encender la calefacción este invierno. Ninguna familia debería vivir con miedo a perder su hogar mientras existen viviendas convertidas en mercancía para la especulación de los fondos buitre.




Exigimos una vivienda digna y asequible para todas las personas

, que se intervengan y regulen los precios, que no haya que destinar más del 30% a este fin, necesitamos que se ponga un límite a los alquileres abusivos que desestabilizan las economías familiares, la 

protección social frente a los desahucios

 y unas 

medidas directas y efectivas

 que pongan las necesidades humanas por delante del beneficio privado, sobre todo las de las personas más vulnerables.




Reclamamos una 

estabilidad en el empleo

 para no vivir con inseguridad, para poder tener planes de futuro y también una 

estabilidad en el arrendamiento de la vivienda

. Precisamos 

contratos de alquiler indefinidos

, no interrumpidos con la llegada del turismo masivo y acabar con la expulsión temporal.




¡A LA HUELGA GENERAL!

CNT Santander

.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: 2023 Operation Al-Aqsa Flood as resistance vs US-Israel
content:
“We cannot condemn the genocide in Palestine without also condemning the imperialist United States.”

Filipino activists remembered the Operation Al-Aqsa Flood three years ago as the day Palestinians amplified their stand against imperialism.

Led by the International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines, Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), and the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), activists marched on October 7 to the US Embassy to remember the historic operation against Israeli occupation after decades of Palestinian oppression.

Carrying the Palestinian flag and placards with images of slain journalists in Gaza, they marched along Kalaw Avenue in Ermita, Manila to condemn the Israeli attacks despite the ceasefire that supposedly took effect on October 10, 2025.

During the program, Amirah Lidasan, secretary-general of Moro Christian People’s Alliance and co-chairperson of Sandugo Movement of Moro and Indigenous Peoples for Self-Determination, said, “Gaza is not the land of another people. Gaza belongs to the Palestinians who are struggling.”

In 2025, US President Donald Trump introduced the Gaza peace plan, also known as the “Board of Peace,” which saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza. It also includes an agreement to end the war.

According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, Israeli attacks since the October 7, 2023 Operation Al-Aqsa Flood have killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children. The actual death toll may be higher, as official records rely on documented deaths and do not account for those still missing or buried under the rubble.

Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) Chairperson and former Bayan Muna Rep. Teddy Casiño highlighted the US role in Israel’s attacks on Palestine by continuing to provide unconditional financial and military support

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) rely heavily on imported arms from the US which accounts for 69 percent of Israel’s weapon imports from 2019-2023.

“We cannot condemn the genocide in Palestine without also condemning the imperialist United States. Not only has Israel committed genocide in Palestine, but the United States has also attached Venezuela, Iran and Yemen, and is now there is possibility to attack Cuba,” Casiño said.

On January 3, the United States abducted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his spouse, Cilia Flores, following months of US strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific that reportedly killed more than 100 people.

The Trump administration’s actions, which critics have condemned as violations of international law and Venezuela’s national sovereignty, reflect what the progressive groups describe as a longstanding pattern of US imperialism.

Despite the controversy surrounding the operation, the Trump administration insisted on its intention to “run the country,” further raising concerns over Venezuela’s sovereignty and the Venezuelan people’s right to self-determination.

Rev. Alan Sarte, secretary-general of the Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association stressed the determination of Palestinians to continue fighting for their freedom, calling on people around the world to oppose imperialism and defend national sovereignty.

“We will ensure that on the day of Donald Trump’s arrival, he is met by a massive protest from the Filipino people,” said Kilusang Mayo Uno Secretary-General Jerome Adonis. (AMU, DAA)

author: Oyunga Pala
title: When Baba Died: One Year Later
content:
Last October, two weeks before Baba died, I was returning to Nairobi after a two-year hiatus. The last time I was home was during the first-year memorial of my sister, Nyangi, who was now the prominent character in my book.




Home had changed in many ways, yet it had not, in a kind of same old but different way. The vibe was familiar, the actors younger, the pace faster. Roads once familiar were now dwarfed by high-rise towers sprouting around the city like wild mushrooms. The expressway from the airport straddling the city dominated the cityscape, a marker of a city in a hurry to grow up.




I used to wonder whether I would change. Would I be like the other diaspora Kenyans I had seen who lost all sense of belonging after just a few miserable winters abroad, and began to look down on their own? Stepping away seemed to have had the opposite effect on me.




This notion of belonging was immediately tested as I faced my former public self. When I announced that I had published a book and would be going on a book tour, the reception was warm. I was reminded of how big 

Mantalk

 was, the weekly national column in the Daily Nation that I laboured over for a decade and that has now become part of the country’s cultural landscape, a reference point to a bygone era, for many stuck in nostalgia. I was no longer the Mantalk guy. I had traveled far both within and without. I had grown up, but to many of my readers, I was still that guy, who showed up every Saturday, a mysterious figure who ruffled feathers. The man some female readers used to love to hate.




I had been part of several life journeys unwittingly. And like all fans of urban culture, I was a mascot for those bygone times. Yet here I was, older, perhaps wiser, certainly a lot humbler. I had just poured my soul into a book that detailed my own journey away from the glam and fame of the national spotlight and delved into trying not only to make sense of my unresolved grief but also the grief of a nation. The shift in persona was stark: From a young man who used to critique modern rules of chivalry to one sharing lessons on how to navigate the profound loss that follows the death of a loved one.




To reach these moments of connection, I first had to navigate the city itself. My first stop the night after my arrival was the Prestige Bookshop and Nairobi traffic- well, what has changed? The roads remained clogged, and nothing quite captures Nairobi’s class dynamics as the expressway, raised above, smooth and scenic, with arresting views of flashy high-rise buildings obscuring the reality of chaos that rules just underneath it, bottleneck traffic, matatu madness, and boda bodas that now make matatus appear quite tame. It became a metaphor in hindsight of how we process grief: stoic and contained on the surface, but underneath the facade, a bubbling volcano waiting to erupt.




I remember Prestige bookshop from another time, when the city centre was a little more serene, and Mama Ngina Street still had a taste of the bourgie back when 20th Century Plaza, the Hilton hotel and the International Life House were iconic landmarks in the city centre. Yvonne Adhiambo Owuor was launching her second novel, The DragonFly Sea, in the small bookshop. The shelves had been pushed to the side to create space for the fans, and I was the MC of the day, here to celebrate one of Kenya’s finest novelists. I looked at the bookshop now, wondering how we had pulled it off, for there seemed to be hardly any room to swing a cat.




When the people started to come through, I knew this was going to be special. Odd that despite 28 years of a public writing life, I had never signed an autograph. I remained struck that people would endure Nairobi traffic to meet over a book and demand my bad handwriting on their personal copies.




I didn’t know what to expect as a new world and role began to unfold for me. Lost connections revived. People I had gone to school with, names I hadn’t seen or heard from in years. Friends, family, acquaintances, total strangers, with entwined pasts and reminders of a time once spent in communion; between the firm handshakes and tight embraces, it took me a minute to realise what was happening.




I was being honoured and celebrated. When I went to Ukombozi Library to donate a copy of my book, I met Ogutu, who told me how the story of my father’s funeral process was also his story. At the United Kenya Club, I met Clifford Derrick, who had just buried his mother, and the book triggered his own spontaneous reflections on his moment of loss. At Nuria bookstore on Moi Avenue, I found my old schoolmate Omenge Nyamato, who was still grieving the recent loss of his mother, and he confessed my book would be a guide through grief that he was no longer interested in suppressing. I spoke to a man called Rollex, who pointed out that it was the death anniversary of his father and he wanted a particular chapter signed in dedication to his memory.




The collective sharing continued in Kisumu when I arrivedat the Text Book Centre at the United Mall. I met Sharon who told me that she had just gone through a season of loss, family members who had seemingly died in pairs, as if calling out to each other from the other side and it did not make sense until she found a page in 

Strength and Sorrow

 that precisely spoke to her unique grief. The next day in Kisumu I met a smart young man called Akal from Lolwe bookshop who filled a room with eager listeners, joining me in a conversation about death and funerary practices.




What had death taught us, and what was it continuing to teach us?




All the people I met had either recently gone through loss, were trying to make sense of a death from the past, or had come to the realisation of the inevitability of our mortality and were seeking the language to understand it. I realised that I was not just selling a book. I had opened the space for something deeper, through mere presence and perhaps holding a mirror to parts of themselves that they could not see or had forgotten existed.




In the various book stops I made, the meet-and-greets turned into spontaneous grief circles, and I found myself counseling strangers who found resonance in my reflections on loss. Together, we could broach pains that they were afraid to touch for fear of what would erupt.




I was here to hold space for people dealing with complicated and conflicted losses, the unresolved, the forgotten, and to share pathways for people looking back to fetch what had been lost. I was no longer that spirited young man who was grappling with the challenges of modern masculinity. Life had reconstructed me, and now I had returned almost in the mode of a death Douala.




Then, just as I concluded the book tour, this shared human inevitability was amplified on a national stage.




The second chapter of 

Strength and Sorrow,

 titled “Baba’s Gone,

”

 is dedicated to my own father.




The first line reads…




When Baba died, I became numb.




He had died of a heart attack….




Then, a national father figure, the one, the country fondly called Baba, the former Prime Minister of the Republic of Kenya and perhaps its most consequential leader, Raila Amolo Odinga, had died.




The same sinking feeling returned. I was numb.




As the phone calls started to come through, I recognized the emotion immediately.




It was…Shock!




My cousin described it precisely.




“I don’t know how I am feeling”.




I remember only ten days prior, sitting at the back of a boda, and just as I arrived at the city centre near the University Way, adjacent to the Uhuru Highway, I encountered a most unusual sight. A flight of bats had covered the sky above. I thought about this moment for a long time afterwards.




It seemed ominous. A bat is a creature that flies like a bird, active at night so its flight during the day is an anomaly. I immediately thought there must be some symbolic resonance to this sight. In esoteric traditions, the bat is a symbol of death and rebirth.




When I received the shocking news of the death of the Baba of the nation, Raila Odinga, I thought of those bats again and of the connections to the story of my father.




When Baba died, I became numb.




He died of a heart attack at eighty years of age. He collapsed in a modest clinic in Kerala India, one morning after his routine walk. They said his bodyguard and personal doctor tried to revive him with CPR and that his last-born daughter was there to hold him as he took his last breath. At my age, I had witnessed the passing of many national figures, but I’d never imagined that this one would feel so personal.




Baba had spent five decades as a political engineer, engineering a new vision for a better Kenya. He rose to the apex in his political career as the symbol of democratic reform and even though he was never elected president, he was the beloved people’s president. An elder statesman and a master bridge builder.




He first came to my attention as a political prisoner in the 80s, spending a total of 8 years in harsh detention conditions and surviving it to move out of his father’s shadow and build an illustrious career in political defiance, before becoming the ultimate pragmatist who always pulled the country from the brink with recurring political handshakes. His life was never quiet despite his advanced age and he continued to build, mentor, and raise the political consciousness of the nation.




He was the man everyone thought to call when the nation itself was burning.




Over the years, I had learnt how to see him as a man and not just as a political figure. He embodied the hopes of my generation, and he was the last of our second liberation heroes who remained relevant straight to our adulthood. Baba was a constant of our political reality, and for my parents’ generation who revered him, he stood like a lighthouse.




Baba was a complex character, and I didn’t always understand his political motivations. He broke my heart many times, but I never stopped admiring his ability to stay relevant and his impeccable sense of occasion. Baba embodied all our political disillusionment and hurts, our historical wounds of exclusion, the ethnic prejudice, and the elusive yearning for a just future.




Now, the biggest tree in the homestead had fallen, and the people were discombobulated.




When the news of Baba’s death arrived, I worried about how the country would react. He had died abroad, and the announcement came that Baba had to be buried in 72 hours. I had never felt such a seismic shift in the political atmosphere and my world was spinning, all I could see was darkness.




I knew my tears for Baba would come, and I braced for the tension of the wake. This was no time to be stoic, for our symbol of stoicism had breathed his last.




I watched the hysteria take over as his body arrived from India. Mourners overran the airport; unruly grief was on display, which degenerated into chaotic scenes at Kasarani Stadium, where the body was taken for a public viewing. I watched in dismay at the government’s irrational response of tear gassing and firing shots to contain overwhelmed mourners. It was heavy to bear.




The trigger-happy security forces, the ethnic profiling, the lack of empathy, and the denigration of the ordinary citizen’s grief.




I remember watching the next day as his body lay in state in Parliament, as the country’s political class got a chance to pay their last respects. I watched their faces, caught the performance, the bewilderment, the genuine grief that bared itself. He lay there, draped in an orange sash and black suit, an odd sight for a man remembered for his boundless energy. The ordinary people who truly loved him held nothing back when his remains were wheeled to Nyayo Stadium in Nairobi and later to Mamboleo Grounds in Kisumu. I thought about the millions watching it on livestream around the country and the world. We were all escorting Baba, united in our grief.




The country was steeped in pensive mourning in the days leading to his final interment in Bondo. That spirit combusted the moment the body arrived in Kisumu, where Baba was met with the deafening wailing of multitudes, crying out for a glimpse of 

Raila, Agwambo, Jakom, Tinga, Wo Nyalego, Wuod Mary.




It was in Kisumu, after the moving 

sigweya,

 the funeral dirge by the Luo elder Ajiki Koth Yamo, that my tears for Baba finally arrived, rolling freely down my cheeks. I knew then I wasn’t weeping alone; the elder’s sonorous chant was the nation’s permission to grieve.




I remembered the date of the state funeral was set for Sunday, four days after his death. The burial date would be on the 19th day of October, in Kang’o ka Jaramogi, in his ancestral homeland in Bondo where he would be laid next to his father’s mausoleum.




Funerals are also history classes, sites of memory where forgotten branches of the national family tree are traced. In the shadow of the coffin, the country revisits the archives of its pain and is forced to confront the unfinished lessons of its struggle and reform. Many were given a proper introduction to Baba’s extended national family and political networks that consisted of multiple generations, all claiming an intimate association.




I found it mildly amusing but mostly sad that the political class used the stage to immediately begin carving up the power vacuum, reasserting old rivalries and desperately laying claim as the rightful custodians of Baba’s legacy.




I knew the spectacle would soon be over and that the real mourning would begin after the cameras moved on and the flags went back up. First comes the shock of the loss, followed by the frenzy of the funeral, and once the deceased is buried under concrete, the second wave of grief kicks in after the adrenaline rush and numbness wears off.




Only then can one grasp the magnitude of the loss as the weeks, months, and years unfold. The listlessness and disorientation follow you everywhere, and the triggers erupt. The true grief work, the task we so love to avoid, can only begin then.




I knew this grief so well. It’s the kind that bangs on your door demanding entry, and when you claim that there are no chairs for it to sit in this house, it answers back coldly. 

“I brought my own stool.”




This was the silence of absence, the helplessness that dominates the thoughts of life after. For us, Baba was that parental figure whose death had never been factored into our reality. The signs could be right in front of you, but for a loss of this magnitude, you are never ready.




Chalgi ngero, thoo wuod Odinga, Chalgi ngero




The night before he was buried, I had my curated Baba playlist on repeat. Coster Ojwang, Musa Juma, Lady Maureen, Emma Jalamo, Prince Indah. I found myself clinging to the refrains, which served as an endless dirge. I needed the music to bear me through the darkness, finding my solace in the song, in the words I couldn’t, wouldn’t stop singing, resisting all attempts to return to normalcy.




How could they understand? We weren’t mourning a politician. This man had transcended that label. They knew him as the Right Honorable Raila Amolo Odinga, the party leader, Agwambo the Enigma, Tinga the Force, Jakom the General, Baba the Patriarch. But he was also Amolo, a human with all his fragilities.




The one who embodied our essence, 

kitwa,

 our nature. He was the epitome of sacrifice, yet he was the special one because he had been tried and tested like no other. He always rose again from the ashes like a phoenix, with that cheeky smile and sparkle in his eye. Amolo was a man whose humanity mirrored our highest hopes and deepest struggles, one who took his personal pain and forged it into purpose. He was our grief alchemist who turned suffering into a source of strength.




I met Amolo in close proximity twice, and both times were rather late in my life. The first time was at the United Kenya Club foyer in Nairobi. I stopped him on his way to the bathroom to share news of my cousin Adhiambo’s passing, knowing his acquaintance with her mother, my Aunty Raduodi. Raila had an incredible grasp of Luo genealogy, and all you needed was to mention a name, and he could trace your ancestry. He paused, remembered a moment from the past, and asked me to pass his sympathies. Just two men, talking briefly, sharing loss.




I stumbled into him the second time in my own village while visiting my cousin Bill Okwirry during Christmas. There was Amolo, amidst friends and family, listening to loud music, sharing laughter and whisky. It was an image of stunning normalcy for a man who, just months before, had suffered a humiliating election defeat after his fifth attempt at the presidency.




I met Amolo as Baba at many other funerals, and it was on those stages that I realised that he was also a historian and griot. At my late uncle Okeyo’s funeral, he arrived halfway through the ceremony, momentarily disrupting the proceedings. When he was given the mic, he regaled everyone with a history lesson, posing questions that reminded us of our shared ancestry.




“Who are these people called the Abasuba? Where did they come from?




This was a uniquely fatherly trait; he was a constant reminder that we are all family.




The true warrior dies on the battlefield. Death found Baba on the go. Even at eighty, he had refused to slow down. Now he rests, the storm has passed, and we continue to assess the loss.




This reckoning takes time, certainly years. You cannot know what you have lost until you have walked through the aftermath because that is when the real, inner pain is revealed, the kind that lingers despite the course of time because that love has nowhere to go.




His physical presence has left us; the 

Mbii

, his inner force, is now subject only to archive and memory. For his presence, our eyes search again.




Where do we find another, like him?




Lowo otero Amolo maa nyocha wa hero!




Baba was our crucible holding together our searing contradictions: the purity of a singular political dream against the murk of political pragmatism, and he was able to hold those contradictions without shattering.




In a recent paper, written by Bishop Francis Omondi, of the Anglican Diocese of Garissa, I found the language to express what I was struggling to explain. Omondi’s paper is on the legitimacy of Baba’s leadership and he opens it with a question that had shadowed Raila all his life: how did a man who never became president remain one of the most influential political figures in Kenya?




Omondi’s answer is insightful. He writes that Raila’s authority 

“emerged from sacrifice. Not from the exercise of power. But from resistance to the abuse of power”.




Presidents come and go, and power won at the ballot box rises and falls with each election, but power born of sacrifice finds its place in the collective memory of a people. Baba may have lost elections, but he never lost the people.




Omondi traces this legitimacy to three sources. The first is resistance in detention, and the price that Raila paid in his own body for opposing dictatorship. Then came reform, captured by the long fight for a new constitution and devolution, a gift that many have forgotten was bitterly fought for. And lastly, perhaps the most controversial, came the consensus, what we remember as handshakes, coalitions and reconciliations that pulled the country back from the brink of disaster. Those handshakes broke many hearts, mine included but Omondi reads them as part of a longer quest for inclusion and stability in a country too often at war with itself.




So one year on, we continue to grieve. His absence still weighs heavily. Depression might come knocking for some, as they come to terms with how dependent they were on the charisma of a single individual.




But we also celebrate because his spirit has finally been liberated from the limits of an earthly existence and all that he represented has been unleashed. This is a generational gift and his story will carry the nation through new seasons of trials. Like Winnie Mandela, he multiplied and we have to grow up and embody what he stood for.




There is no saviour coming. The desire is for another Baba but that same strength now belongs to the collective, who must find the power for their own becoming. Baba’s life’s work is incomplete: his legacy is a call to a generation to complete the work he started.




I return to my playlist, to Coster Ojwang’s tribute to Raila.




Baba’s gone and he is not coming back.




The brave one has left us.




Mayoo wee! Amolo osenindo




Chalgi ngero, thoo wuod Odinga, Chalgi ngero.




References:







Ojwang, Coster (2025) Raila Odinga,
















Omondi, Francis (2026). Resistance, Reform, and Consensus: Raila Odinga’s Leadership and the Evolution of Political Legitimacy in Kenya. figshare. Journal contribution

. https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.34335738

title: Αντιφασιστική διαδήλωση στο Περιστέρι, Παρασκευή 16/10, στις 19:00
content:
Αφίσες/Καλέσματα:




Προλεταριακό Αντιφασιστικό Μέτωπο Δυτικών Προαστίων




ΑΝΤΙΦΑΣΙΣΤΙΚΗ ΣΥΓΚΕΝΤΡΩΣΗ




ΠΑΡΑΣΚΕΥΗ 16 ΟΚΤΩΒΡΗ στις 19:00 πλατεία δημαρχείου (μετρό Περιστέρι)







ΦΑΣΙΣΤΕΣ ΤΟ ΜΕΛΛΟΝ ΣΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΡΟΔΙΑΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΟ




Η Δολοφονική επίθεση με μαχαίρι στον αντιφασίστα στην Ελευσίνα και η επίθεση με μπογιές και σπρέι στο στέκι της Αριστερής Κίνησης Περιστερίου θα απαντηθούν κοινωνικά και μαχητικά.




Καλούμε όλο το αντιφασιστικό κίνημα σε πλήρη συσπείρωση και μαχητική θέση ενάντια στους μαχαιροβγάλτες νοσταλγούς των ναζί.




Ο φασισμός δεν πέφτει από τον ουρανό. Γεννιέται μέσα στις αντιθέσεις της καπιταλιστικής κοινωνίας και αποτελεί την πιο ακραία και αντιδραστική μορφή υπεράσπισης της εξουσίας του κεφαλαίου. Όταν η κοινωνική οργή μεγαλώνει, ο φασισμός επιχειρεί να της δώσει άλλο στόχο. Να στρέψει τον εργαζόμενο ενάντια στον μετανάστη, τον φτωχό ενάντια στον φτωχότερο, τον έναν καταπιεσμένο ενάντια στον άλλο. Ο ρατσισμός και ο εθνικισμός είναι τα όπλα του για να διασπά την εργατική τάξη και να κρύβει τον πραγματικό ταξικό αντίπαλο.




Γινόμαστε εκ νέου μάρτυρες του ίδιου φαινομένου, σε μια εποχή πολέμων, ακρίβειας, φτώχειας και ανασφάλειας, η ακροδεξιά προσπαθεί ξανά να δηλητηριάσει την οξυμένη κοινωνική οργή με ρατσισμό, εθνικισμό και μίσος. Προσπαθεί να πείσει τον εργαζόμενο ότι για τη ζωή που του στερούν φταίει ο πρόσφυγας, ο μετανάστης, ο διαφορετικός. Να μετατρέψει την αγανάκτηση σε τυφλό μίσος και να αφήσει στο απυρόβλητο τις πραγματικές σχέσεις εκμετάλλευσης και εξουσίας.




Δεν υπάρχει πιο ειρωνική συγκυρία που να αποδεικνύει του λόγου το αληθές όταν την επόμενη της φασιστικής δολοφονικής επίθεσης στην εργατούπολη της Ελευσίνας δολοφονήθηκαν μερικά χιλιόμετρα πιο κάτω, ξανά από εργοδοτική αμέλεια, δυο εργάτες στην Motor Oil στους Αγίους Θεοδώρους. Το έγκλημα αυτό είναι ένα από τα πολλά των τελευταίων χρόνων και οι δύο εργάτες που έχασαν την ζωή τους είναι 2 από τους 142 (ΟΣΕΤΕΕ), μέχρι τώρα, εργαζομένους που έχασαν την ζωή τους εντός του 2026. Δεν είναι, λοιπόν, καθόλου τυχαίο ότι τέτοιες φασιστικές επιθέσεις πραγματοποιούνται σε ανθρώπους που μάχονται για έναν πιο δίκαιο κόσμο ή σε συλλογικότητες που επιδιώκουν να περιγράψουν μια άλλη κοινωνία χωρίς εκμετάλλευση ανθρώπου από άνθρωπο. Όπως δεν είναι τυχαίο ότι αυτά συμβαίνουν κατά βάση σε περιοχές που διαμένουν ή εργάζονται τα φτωχότερα κοινωνικά στρώματα, όπως είναι η Ελευσίνα, με βιωμένη την εργοδοτική αυθαιρεσία και την εγκληματική αμέλεια με σωρεία εργατικών ατυχημάτων και δυστυχημάτων.




Γι’ αυτό η αποφυλάκιση του Ηλία Κασιδιάρη και η δηλωμένη πρόθεσή του να επιστρέψει στην πολιτική δράση, δεν μπορούν να αντιμετωπίζονται με αδιαφορία. Η Χρυσή Αυγή δεν ήταν απλώς ένα ακροδεξιό κόμμα. Ήταν μια ναζιστική οργάνωση με τάγματα εφόδου, ξυλοδαρμούς και δολοφονικές επιθέσεις. Δεν ξεχνάμε τους Αιγύπτιους αλιεργάτες, τους συνδικαλιστές του ΠΑΜΕ, τον Σαχζάτ Λουκμάν. Δεν ξεχνάμε τον Παύλο Φύσσα. Και δεν πρόκειται να αφήσουμε τη μνήμη αυτών των εγκλημάτων να ξεθωριάσει για να παρουσιαστούν ξανά οι ίδιοι άνθρωποι και οι ίδιες ιδέες ως κάτι «καινούργιο» ή «αντισυστημικό».




Απέναντι σε αυτή την απειλή δεν χωρά εφησυχασμός. Ο φασισμός δεν αντιμετωπίζεται με σιωπή και αναμονή. Αντιμετωπίζεται πολιτικά και μαζικά, στους χώρους δουλειάς, στις σχολές και στις γειτονιές, με οργάνωση, ταξική αλληλεγγύη και συλλογική δράση. Η αντιφασιστική πάλη δεν είναι τελετουργία μιας επετείου. Είναι καθημερινό μέτωπο απέναντι στο φασισμό, στον ρατσισμό και στις κοινωνικές συνθήκες που τους επιτρέπουν να σηκώνουν ξανά κεφάλι.




ΦΑΣΙΣΤΕΣ ΘΑ ΠΕΡΑΣΟΥΜΕ ΑΠΟ ΠΑΝΩ ΣΑΣ







 Αριστερή Κίνηση Περιστερίου




 ΟΙ ΝΑΖΙ ΔΕΝ ΕΧΟΥΝ ΘΕΣΗ ΣΤΙΣ ΓΕΙΤΟΝΙΕΣ ΜΑΣ




[ 

 ΑΝΤΙΦΑΣΙΣΤΙΚΗ ΔΙΑΔΗΛΩΣΗ ΣΤΟ ΠΕΡΙΣΤΕΡΙ ]




 Παρασκευή 16/10 στις 19:00, στην πλατεία Δημαρχείου







 Την Πέμπτη 8/10, νεοναζί έστησαν ενέδρα και μαχαίρωσαν αντιφασίστα στην Ελευσίνα.




 Το βράδυ της Δευτέρας 5/10, φασιστοειδή γέμισαν την πρόσοψη του στεκιού της Αριστερής Κίνησης Περιστερίου με ναζιστικά σύμβολα.




 Τις τελευταίες μέρες, φασίστες βάφουν τα σχολεία των δυτικών προαστίων με σβάστικες.




Οι ναζί μαχαιροβγάλτες κλιμακώνουν την προσπάθειά τους να επαναφέρουν στους δρόμους τα τάγματα εφόδου, και αυτό δεν είναι τυχαίο. Συμβαίνει παράλληλα με την υπερπροβολή της αποφυλάκισης Κασιδιάρη από τα ΜΜΕ, αλλά και με το σταθερό άνοιγμα της κυβέρνησης Μητσοτάκη στην ακροδεξιά.




 Καλούμε όλο τον κόσμο της πόλης να σταθεί απέναντι στο τέρας που θέλει να πατήσει το πόδι του στις γειτονιές μας !




 Την Παρασκευή 16/10 στις 7 το απόγευμα διαδηλώνουμε μαζί στην πλατεία Δημαρχείου Περιστερίου!




 Ο φασισμός δεν έχει θέση στην πόλη μας!







☆ Δυτικός τομέας Ρουβίκωνα







 Την Πέμπτη 8/10, νεοναζί έστησαν ενέδρα μέρα μεσημέρι και μαχαίρωσαν, παρολίγο θανάσιμα, αντιφασίστα σύντροφο στην Ελευσίνα.




 Το βράδυ της Δευτέρας 5/10, φασιστοειδή γέμισαν την πρόσοψη του στεκιού της Αριστερής Κίνησης Περιστερίου με ναζιστικά σύμβολα.




 Τις τελευταίες μέρες, φασίστες βάφουν τα σχολεία των δυτικών προαστίων με σβάστικες.




Κάθε επίθεση είτε σε χώρους του κινήματος είτε σε συντρόφους και συντρόφισσες δεν θα πρέπει να μένει αναπάντητη.




Εδώ και αρκετό καιρό, οι φασίστες έχουν αρχίσει να διεκδικούν όχι μόνο την επάνοδό τους στην πολιτική σκηνή, αλλά και την εδραίωσή τους στον δρόμο. Αποτελεί, λοιπόν, καθήκον κάθε αντιφασίστα και αντιφασίστριας, και του ριζοσπαστικού κινήματος συνολικά, αυτά τα φαινόμενα να τα κόβει από τη ρίζα.




Τσακίζουμε τον φασισμό και το σύστημα που τον γεννά!




ΜΑΧΗΤΙΚΟΣ ΑΝΤΙΦΑΣΙΣΜΟΣ ΕΝΑΝΤΙΑ ΣΤΟΥΣ ΠΑΡΑΚΡΑΤΙΚΟΥΣ ΦΑΣΙΣΤΕΣ

title: Rojnameger Bahadir Ozgur bi şerte kontrol edlî serbest bû
content:
Nivîskar û bernamegerê Halk TVyê Bahadir Ozgurr duh(15ê Cotmehê) hatibû desteserkirin. 




Rêvebera Weşanê ya Giştî ya halktv.com.tryê Bengu Şap Babaekerê agahiya desteserkirinê li ser hesabê xwe yê Xê bi gotinên “Bahadir Ozgur tê desteserkirin” ragihand.




Ozgur îdîaya ku “nihêniya lêpirsîna fonê binpê kiriye” hat desteserkirin. Lêpirsîn ji aliyê Serdozgeriya Komarî ya Stenbolê ve tê birêvebirin.




Ozgur piştî karûbarên li Emniyetê îro ji bo Edliyeyê hat şandin. Dozgeriyê bi daxwaza şertê kontrola edlî û qedexeya derketina derve Ozgur sewqî dadgehê kir.




Dadgehê jî xwest ku Ozgur heftê de 2 caran li emniyetê îmzeyê bide û derketina derveyî welat lê qedexe kir û serbest berda.




Rojnameya Evrenselê nivîsî ku polîsan Ozgur birine Emniyeta Vatanê. Rojnameger Hakki Ozdal jî gotiye ku îfadeya Bahadir Ozgur a li emniyetê bi dawî bûye û dê di saetên sibehê de bibin adliyeyê.




Her weha hesabê Xê ê Bahadir Ozgur ku 163 hezar şopînerên wê hene (@bahadir_ozgr) hat astengkirin. Ev hesab hîn ji aliyê platforma Xê ve ji bo bikarhênerên li Tirkiyeyê nehatiye reş kirin.







Lîsteya di lêpirsînê de kiribû nûçe




Bahadir Ozgur di nûçeya xwe ya 13ê Cotmehê de diyar kiribû ku Serdozgeriya Komarî ya Stenbolê lîsteya tedbîrê ya mal û mulkên 141 kesan ku di nav wan de wezîra berê Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya û hevjînê wê İlyas Kaya jî hene, ji saziyên peywendîdar re şandiye.




Ozgurr nivîsîbû ku serdozgeriyê di 13ê Cotmehê de nivîseke nû şandiye û ragihandiye ku navên 29 kesan di lîsteyê de ‘bi xeletî’ cih girtine û diyar kiribû ku di nav van kesan de Enver Çevik û Kemal Akkaya jî hene.




Serdozgeriyê ragihand ku wan ev rewş bi nivîseke nû rast kiriye û tedbîrên li ser mal û mulkên 109 kesan berdewam dikin.







(VC/AY)
