title: Antifaschist Gino stellt sich in Hannover
content:
Am heutigen Donnerstag, 15. Oktober 2026 stellte sich Gino um 18 Uhr selbstbestimmt in Hannover den deutschen Behörden, die ihn im Rahmen des sog. Budapest-Komplexes per Europäischem Haftbefehl gesucht hatten. Vorgeworfen wird dem Antifaschisten, Anfang 2023 an körperlichen Auseinandersetzungen mit Nazis in Budapest beteiligt gewesen zu sein. Gino, der in Italien aufgewachsen ist, lebte zuletzt in Frankreich, wo die Justiz 2025 seine Auslieferung an Ungarn abgelehnt hatte. Am 30. September 2026 hatte das Pariser Kassationsgericht jedoch einem deutschen Auslieferungsersuchen stattgegeben, woraufhin sich der Aktivist heute in Deutschland stellte. In Kürze soll Gino nach Karlsruhe verbracht werden, wo die Haftprüfung am Bundesgerichtshof stattfindet.

Die Verhaftung ist Teil des sog. Budapest-Komplexes, einer internationalen Kriminalisierungswelle gegen Antifaschist*innen, die hauptsächlich von Ungarn und Deutschland forciert wird. Auslöser sind mehrere Vorfälle am Rand des NS-verherrlichenden Großevents „Tag der Ehre“, des europaweit größten Nazi-Vernetzungstreffens, das jedes Jahr in Budapest stattfindet. Anfang Februar 2023 kam es dort zu körperlichen Auseinandersetzungen zwischen Antifaschist*innen und Nazis. Das nahmen die ungarischen Behörden zum Anlass für eine internationale Verfolgungsoffensive gegen die antifaschistische Bewegung, wobei die deutschen Repressionsorgane engagiert Schützenhilfe leisten. In Ungarn drohen bis zu 24 Jahre Haft unter folterähnlichen Bedingungen, doch auch in Deutschland laufen offen politische Gerichtsprozesse gegen Beschuldigte. Ein Höhepunkt der deutsch-ungarischen Komplizenschaft in diesem Repressionskomplex ist der Fall von Maja: Die non-binäre antifaschistische Person aus Jena wurde im Juni 2024 von den deutschen Behörden offen rechtswidrig an das queer- und trans*feindliche Ungarn ausgeliefert und sitzt seither dort unter unmenschlichen Bedingungen in Haft. In einem Schauprozess verhängte die ungarische Justiz am 30. September 2026 vor dem Berufungsgericht sieben Jahre Haft unter schwersten Bedingungen.

Zu den Beschuldigten zählt auch Gino, der in Mailand aufwuchs und später in Finnland lebte, aber einen albanischen Pass hat. Vor den Verfolgungen im Budapest-Komplex floh er nach Frankreich, wo die Justiz über das ungarische Auslieferungsersuchen per Europäischem Haftbefehl befinden musste. Im April 2025 lehnte das Pariser Berufungsgericht ab, Gino an Budapest zu überstellen. Dabei verwies es auf die katastrophale Menschenrechtslage, insbesondere die drohende Folter, und auf die fehlende Rechtsstaatlichkeit in Ungarn.

Im Rahmen der deutsch-ungarischen Zusammenarbeit bei dieser Verfolgungsoffensive verlangte daraufhin Deutschland mit einem eigenen Europäischen Haftbefehl Ginos Auslieferung. Zur Begründung verweist die Bundesanwaltschaft darauf, dass in Budapest auch zwei Nazis mit deutscher Staatsangehörigkeit verletzt worden seien. Deshalb wolle sie den Antifaschisten vor ein deutsches Gericht stellen – anhand der mehr als fragwürdigen Ermittlungsergebnisse der ungarischen Polizei.

Am 30. September 2026 hatte das Pariser Kassationsgericht dem deutschen Auslieferungsgesuch stattgegeben. Dabei ist die Verfolgung in Deutschland enorm, denn wegen der eigentlich banalen Körperverletzungsdelikte vor mehr als dreieinhalb Jahren drohen bis zu zehn Jahre Haft in einem politischen Prozess. Vollkommen ausgeblendet hatte die Pariser Justiz dabei zudem das hohe Risiko, dass die deutschen Behörden sich nur zum Handlanger Ungarns machen könnten, indem sie Gino an Budapest ausliefern und so das Pariser Urteil von 2025 umgehen.

„Ginos sofortige Verhaftung am heutigen Tag ist ein weiterer Höhepunkt in der deutschen Kriminalisierung von Antifaschist*innen im sog. Budapest-Komplex. Er hat sich freiwillig und selbstbestimmt den Behörden gestellt. Es gibt keinerlei Anlass, ihn in Untersuchungshaft zu nehmen!“, erklärte Hartmut Brückner vom Bundesvorstand der Roten Hilfe e. V. „Nun muss es in jedem Fall darum gehen, eine drohende Auslieferung an Ungarn zu verhindern. Die dortige Situation von Maja zeigt, dass auch unter Péter Magyar die unmenschliche Behandlung und Folter von Antifaschist*innen weitergeht und politische Schauprozesse an der Tagesordnung sind.“ Ergänzend bekräftigte er: „Wir stehen an der Seite von Gino und allen anderen verfolgten Antifaschist*innen und fordern die sofortige Freilassung. Wir sind alle Antifa!“

author: Ed Wanderley
title: A misoginia de diálogos de Vorcaro e CEO que expôs atrizes: “Mulher não pode fazer isso”
content:
Com a boca vermelha e a pele totalmente pintada de verde, Deborah Secco adentrou o Baile da Vogue de 2024, no Copacabana Palace, alternando entre sorrisos fartos e carão carregado nos olhares sensuais, um combo recorrente que já virou tradição no evento, no qual é convidada de destaque. A atriz encarnava um ser extraterrestre de roupas curtas, brancas, com direito a um bebê alien a tiracolo, no estilo carnavalesco típico da celebração, uma das grandes apostas publicitárias da Vogue Brasil e da Editora Globo nas semanas que antecedem o Carnaval.




Mas enquanto posava para os fotógrafos de dezenas de publicações e curtia a festa com sua tradicional animação, Deborah, que dividia o espaço com a nata executiva do Grupo Globo, estava desavisada do julgamento de alguns dos presentes mais relevantes do evento. 

“Eu só olhava pra bunda dela rs”. As palavras são do então diretor-geral de mídias impressas e rádios da Editora Globo, Frederick Kachar, para o dono do Banco Master, Daniel Vorcaro, horas depois. “Mas tava muito feia kkk”, rebateu o banqueiro. “Concordo que a fantasia era broxante”, completou Kachar.

 “Tá doido, mulher não pode fazer isso”, disparou Vorcaro.




Os diálogos fazem parte de um conjunto de mensagens interceptadas pela Polícia Federal (PF), entre outubro de 2023 e julho de 2025, cujo vazamento ganhou força nesta semana e levou à demissão do executivo de mídia nesta quinta-feira (15). Em nota, o Grupo Globo não menciona o conteúdo misógino das mensagens como um dos motivos da demissão, mas sim a preservação da independência editorial da Editora Globo.




Nota na íntegra




Grupo Globo comunica desligamento de Frederic Kachar e reforça independência editorial de seus veículos.




O Grupo Globo comunicou hoje o desligamento do diretor-geral de Mídia Impressa e Rádio, Frederic Kachar. O conteúdo das conversas privadas mantidas com Daniel Vorcaro entre outubro de 2023 e julho de 2025, às quais a empresa teve acesso ontem, revela uma relação inadequada do executivo com um anunciante.




A Editora Globo reforça seu compromisso com a ética e a transparência e reafirma a absoluta independência editorial do jornalismo de seus veículos, premissa essencial de sua atuação. O protagonismo da cobertura crítica, isenta e independente que tem feito do caso Master é a demonstração concreta do compromisso inegociável de seus veículos com os Princípios Editoriais do Grupo Globo.




A empresa reconhece os 29 anos de dedicação de Kachar ao desenvolvimento de seus negócios de mídia e informa que o nome de seu substituto à frente da Editora Globo e do Sistema Globo de Rádio será divulgado em breve.




Comunicação Globo

Rio de Janeiro, 15 de outubro de 2026

Mais informações: 

https://imprensa.globo.com/







Além de comentários objetificando atrizes ligadas ao próprio Grupo Globo, o conteúdo revela comentários machistas e convites mútuos para festas com mulheres, discrição “sem celular” e encontros descritos como idas à “Ucrânia”.




Um baile de machismo




“Muita mulher pro crime e só gay. Elas tavam dando em cima mesmo acompanhado”, foi assim que Fred Kachar descreveu o ambiente do evento da revista até então sob sua responsabilidade. E completou: “Me fodi. Minha ex foi e marcou em cima”. A ex em questão é a atriz Monique Alfradique, que também chegou a se envolver com Daniel Vorcaro meses depois. “No final não teve jeito. Marcação cerrada”, escreveu ainda. Alfradique não quis se pronunciar sobre os conteúdos das mensagens até a publicação desta reportagem.




“Deborah secco tava pra jogo”, escreveu Kachar. O executivo da Globo ainda relata que a atriz seria madrinha do camarote do Grupo no Carnaval do Rio de Janeiro e teria dito querer “curtir solteira” nos festejos. “Relação aberta. Preciso de uma dessas”

, escreveu Kachar. “Todos nós”, respondeu Vorcaro.




A assessoria de Déborah Secco repudiou a associação indevida do nome da atriz a comentários de teor machista, desrespeitoso e irresponsável, disse que a atriz não conhece Daniel Vorcaro e que sua relação com Fred Kachar sempre foi estritamente profissional. “Tiveram encontros em trabalhos, onde foram fotografados, sem qualquer vínculo entre eles”. A equipe da atriz também destacou que os comentários que se tornaram públicos diz respeito a um evento “onde ambas estavam trabalhando”.




“É inadmissível expor a imagem e a reputação de uma mulher com base em uma narrativa que não corresponde à sua realidade. Também é lamentável a forma como mulheres foram mencionadas, em comentários que não devem ser tratados com naturalidade nem usados para alimentar especulações”, diz a nota.




Leia a nota na íntegra




Diante das informações divulgadas, a assessoria de Déborah Secco repudia a associação indevida do nome da atriz a comentários de teor machista, desrespeitoso e irresponsável.




Déborah Secco não conhece Daniel Vorcaro. Sua relação com Fred Kachar sempre foi estritamente profissional, tiveram encontros em trabalhos, onde foram fotografados, sem qualquer vínculo entre eles.




É inadmissível expor a imagem e a reputação de uma mulher com base em uma narrativa que não corresponde à sua realidade. Também é lamentável a forma como mulheres foram mencionadas, em comentários que não devem ser tratados com naturalidade nem usados para alimentar especulações.




A assessoria repudia qualquer tentativa de envolver a atriz Déborah Secco nesses acontecimentos. Sua trajetória, construída ao longo de anos de trabalho, merece ser tratada com responsabilidade e respeito.




Também é importante esclarecer que o comentário de teor machista e misógino surgiu a partir da presença de Sabrina Sato e Deborah Secco no Baile da Vogue 2024, onde ambas estavam trabalhando. Algumas publicações, no entanto, vêm apresentando os fatos de forma descontextualizada, dando a entender que elas estariam em uma festa com Daniel Vorcaro e Fred Kachar, o que não corresponde à realidade. Daniel Vorcaro, inclusive, não estava

presente no evento.






















O banqueiro reagia às impressões do amigo, cuja relação seria uma “

amizade que supera negócios

”, mas não esteve presente no evento de 2024, em que suas empresas figuravam como patrocinadoras. A tabela com o orçamento para patrocínio em 2025, compartilhada no WhatsApp, considerava reajuste sobre os valores do ano anterior, que supostamente somaram R$ 1,7 milhão no Baile da Vogue e no Carnaval em 2024.




Outra artista citada no contexto da festa e de que estaria “pra jogo” foi a apresentadora Sabrina Sato. “Sabrina [Sato] também. Aniversário dela.”, disse Fred Kachar em relato para o banqueiro Vorcaro. “Soltinha”, resumiu o executivo sobre a profissional que estava em uma festa carnavalesca.




Sabrina Sato disse nunca ter tido contato com Daniel Vorcaro e relata que encontrou Kachar apenas em uma premiação de revista, quando foram fotografados, mas nega qualquer vínculo entre eles. “É inadmissível expor a imagem e a reputação de uma mulher com base em uma narrativa alheia à sua realidade.

 O respeito à dignidade das mulheres não é uma concessão. É um direito. E comentários desta natureza não podem ser tratados com naturalidade, reproduzidos ou utilizados para alimentar especulações”, afirmou em nota à 

Pública

.




Nota na íntegra




Diante das informações divulgadas, a assessoria de Sabrina Sato repudia a associação indevida do nome da apresentadora a um comentário de teor machista, desrespeitoso e irresponsável.




Sabrina nunca teve qualquer contato com Daniel Vorcaro e encontrou Fred Kachar apenas em uma premiação de revista, ocasião em que foram fotografados, sem qualquer vínculo entre eles.




É inadmissível expor a imagem e a reputação de uma mulher com base em uma narrativa alheia à sua realidade.




O respeito à dignidade das mulheres não é uma concessão. É um direito. E comentários desta natureza não podem ser tratados com naturalidade, reproduzidos ou utilizados para alimentar especulações.




Qualquer tentativa de envolver Sabrina nesses acontecimentos é repudiada. Sua trajetória, construída ao longo de anos de trabalho, merece ser tratada com responsabilidade e respeito.






















Não é sobre fama, nem sobre desejo




A 

Agência Pública

 questionou o grupo Globo se denúncias foram feitas ao compliance da companhia quanto à relação de atrizes e outras artistas e sua relação com figuras de poder como Kachar na dinâmica corporativa da empresa, mas não obteve resposta até o momento.




“O que mais me chama a atenção nesse episódio, para além da gravidade do conteúdo das conversas divulgadas, é a relação entre poder, comportamento e silêncio. Quando alguém ocupa uma posição de influência, suas atitudes têm consequências que ultrapassam as relações individuais”, resume a psicóloga organizacional e fundadora do Instituto Internacional em Segurança Psicológica (IISP), Patrícia Ansarah. O IISP atua na prevenção de riscos psicossociais, de assédio, de sobrecarga e de violência organizacional.




Segundo Ansarah, quando comportamentos machistas e misóginos são naturalizados, minimizados ou protegidos por relações de poder, perpetuamos uma cultura patriarcal que legitima a desigualdade e a reação da sociedade a esse tipo de episódio vivenciado pelas atrizes do Grupo Globo ajuda a definir o que é tolerado, o que pode ser questionado e quais são as consequências para quem decide reagir.




“Em uma sociedade marcada por profundas assimetrias de poder, discordar, impor limites ou denunciar comportamentos abusivos pode ter um custo muito alto. E isso se torna ainda mais grave para as mulheres, que, historicamente, enfrentam barreiras para serem ouvidas, levadas a sério e protegidas quando decidem denunciar.

 A escolha entre expor publicamente uma violência e se preservar, neste contexto, é fácil: o silêncio predomina.”




A manifestação do economista Fred Kachar a respeito de mulheres, no entanto, não se limitava a famosas de seu convívio no Grupo Globo. Em 19 de janeiro de 2024, semanas antes do Baile da Vogue sobre os quais os comentários machistas foram feitos, o executivo e o banqueiro discutiam a proposta de patrocínio do Banco Master para o período carnavalesco quando Kachar perguntou se Vorcaro iria à Sapucaí. Vorcaro disse que precisava “fugir esse ano” e brincou que só Kachar conseguia “passar ileso tanto tempo” no Carnaval. Ao que o ex-diretor-geral da Globo respondeu: “Ileso nada. Três ex minhas nesse ano. Vou pôr um tatame na pista. Só vou ligar o foda-se. Todas achando que estão comigo. E eu vou fingir demência.”



















Preocupação apenas com “indiscrições”




As mensagens vazadas entre Kachar e Vorcaro registram ainda convites do banqueiro para eventos restritos. Em 7 de fevereiro de 2024, o banqueiro disparou: “Bora hoje, que vai ser animado. Tem dois oligarcas russos indo e plantel [equipe]”. Vorcaro continuou descrevendo que seria no bairro dos Jardins, em São Paulo, em “lugar fechado, só convidado”. Kachar não teria comparecido. Dois dias depois, o banqueiro escreveu: “Seu bolo tá anotado. Perdeu”.




Os encontros do gênero passam a ser mencionados com expressões de guerra nas semanas seguintes. Em 12 março de 2024, Vorcaro disse que o plano da noite seria um “ataque soviético”. Mais tarde, Kachar perguntou se ele já estava “na Ucrânia”. Dias depois, o executivo quis saber se haveria “guerra na Ucrânia nessa semana”

. “Tem hoje. Bora?”, respondeu o banqueiro, informando que começaria às 23h. Em maio, Vorcaro disse que as festas aconteciam “toda terça”.




Em 15 de maio de 2024, em Nova York, na semana do prêmio Personalidade do Ano da Câmara de Comércio Brasil-Estados Unidos, Vorcaro disse que não iria a outro evento da programação e escreveu: “Fechei um lugar. Sem celular. E sem risco. Pra verdadeira festa rsrs”. Kachar respondeu: “É nessa que eu vou! Posso, né?”. “Óbvio. Convidado de honra”, disse o banqueiro. O executivo da Globo chegou ao local perto da meia-noite.




No dia seguinte, Kachar agradeceu o convite: “Será que alguém anotou a placa do caminhão que me atropelou rs?” e disse ter ido embora às 0h45. Vorcaro contou que chegou às 4h e acordou às 7h. “Ídolo. Se eu faço isso saio de ambulância do quarto”, escreveu Kachar. O banqueiro completou: “Só que fiz isso 3 dias seguidos. Ainda com a Fabíola me esperando no hotel kkkk”. O executivo respondeu: “Não acredito. Ela veio? Ídolo máximo, então. Isso eu jamais consegui” e depois conclui: “Eh um accomplishment [realização marcante]”.




Kachar e Vorcaro foram procurados pela 

Pública

, mas até o momento não se pronunciaram sobre o caso. Em caso de manifestação, este espaço será atualizado.

author: Daniel Hunter
title: How Vermont shut down ICE
content:
This article 

How Vermont shut down ICE

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







After Operation Metro Surge, the Trump administration moved to rein in the Bovino-style spectacle with its made-for-TV arrests. In an attempt to avoid another public outcry, Immigration and Customs Enforcement has quietly settled into a new rhythm.




Arrests have still increased month after month, reaching 

a record high

 of roughly 51,000 people taken into ICE custody in August. This is part of a new surge — carried out in hospitals, courthouses and airports — with an intent to stay off the nightly news. As 

The

 

New York Times

 

reported

, this phase is “captured mostly by grainy security camera footage, through cracked blinds and from behind closed doors.” 




This phase is also backed by a dragnet of data. At airports, ICE has been 

running name matches with TSA to detain people

 at check-in counters and gates. It has found a backdoor into the country’s license-plate cameras: Records show local and state police 

ran more than 4,000 immigration-related searches

 on Flock’s camera network in a single year. (Yet another reason 

Flock cameras should not exist

.)




Perhaps surprisingly, much of the tech infrastructure driving ICE’s new surge is headquartered in … Vermont. The town of Williston, outside Burlington, is home to both ICE’s 

Law Enforcement Support Center

, which houses the agency’s national tip line, and ICE’s National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center, or NCATC, its social-media surveillance hub. 










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










As ICE tries a new approach, this new phase of resisting ICE requires moving to more offense — and the people of Vermont are offering us some clear lessons. 




Vermont resistance




Resistance started with the fight over flights. Early in Trump’s second term, activists 

documented

 ICE moving detainees onto commercial flights out of Burlington’s airport — more than 450 people as of mid-July 2025, by their count. They showed up in airports as witnesses and disruptors, sometimes aided by empowered flight attendants. They forced an ICE retreat: organizers say 

ICE hasn’t moved detainees through the airport in more than a year

.




More recently they’ve gone after the hard infrastructure. Sit-ins at the White Cap Business Park in Williston, where the NCATC facility is located, have led to arrests for allegedly blocking the entrance to the ICE offices, including 

11 people in February and 13 in July.




After those arrests came some unusual twists, which speak volumes about the courage it takes to refuse unjust orders and to continue protesting in the face of repression.




Complicity and noncooperation




Responses to authoritarianism are as old as a time — many of the same dynamics from Vermont show up in the ancient story of Pharaoh and Moses.




Undeniably the most powerful person in his land, Pharaoh was the ultimate authoritarian. His big trick was taking beautiful work and turning it evil. Take the work of midwives, whose job is to usher life into the world — he turned that work into ugliness by ordering the Hebrew midwives to kill every newborn boy. 




But we all have a choice. And famously, several of the midwives refused. Their act of noncooperation with an unjust order is the reason Moses lived.




We are living through a moment when institution after institution is being turned toward evil. Some, like the Department of Justice, were already a mixed bag. But now it is being turned against the very logic of due process it claims to serve, as we’ve seen recently with the 

criminal indictment of whistleblower Cassidy Hutchinson

. Other institutions, like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, are being perverted, with 

great resistance from insiders

 who cling to the key values that these agencies were founded on.




Previous Coverage

 

The movement to defend the Minneapolis 15




In Vermont, the local prosecutor, Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George, faced her own choice. When asked to 

bring charges

 against the protesters who held the sit-ins, she repeatedly declined, citing limited resources. That makes sense: No one was harmed, and the protesters have a strong necessity defense — the argument that they were preventing an even greater harm. Every minute that ICE isn’t taking part in abducting people is good for the country.




Then came a bizarre turn of events. The state’s public safety commissioner 

directed state police to send the cases to Vermont’s Attorney General Charity Clark

, bypassing normal procedure and upending the traditional role of the attorney general. Clark, a Democrat, decided to charge the protesters with trespassing.




In an 

op-ed

, she said her hands were tied: “Justice must be blind or our system will fail.” Back to Pharaoh: This is a bit like a midwife in the next town over raising her hand to say, “I’d like to kill Moses, because that’s what the law dictates.”




Protesters recently unearthed relevant Vermont history — a model of state-level noncooperation. After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, which ordered cooperation with slave catchers, Vermont passed a state statute known as the Habeas Corpus Law. It effectively nullified the federal law, and went so far as to 

require

 state attorneys to defend anyone accused of being a slave, with full representation before a judge and a jury. The entire practice of nullification was deemed highly escalatory — so much so the federal government threatened military invasion — but due to the state’s resistance, throughout Vermont there was effectively no participation in the Fugitive Slave Act.




As in that case, the pressure from the federal government has continued. One week before a planned week of direct action, the federal government suddenly charged five people from the earlier protests with 

obstructing access to a federal facility

 (punishable by up to 30 days in prison or a $5,000 fine), likely hoping to deter further escalation.




We all have a choice: complicity with Pharoah or noncooperation. Despite the threats and new legal challenges, the protesters in Vermont chose the riskier, more liberatory path.




A funeral, a guerrilla garden and a sit-in




The week of direct action went on as planned, beginning with a funeral. On Oct. 5, more than 30 clergy led a procession of a hundred or so mourners who walked behind a hearse to the White Cap Business Park, singing “Amazing Grace.” They carried 95 paver stones, each representing a life taken by ICE — directly or from complications while detained — and placed them one by one in a handmade coffin of Vermont pine. The action echoed the 

Stolen Neighbors Quilt

 created in Minnesota, which remembers people who were deported. Here, names of those killed by ICE were read out. Then, in front of the doors of the spy center, the coffin was nailed shut. 




A crowd gathers in Williston, Vermont on Oct. 5, behind a coffin filled with paver stones representing lives lost to ICE. (Shut Down ICE VT)




Rev. Marybeth Redmond 

said

 at the vigil, “I have walked alongside Vermonters struggling to survive, and I have never seen our immigrant neighbors so hunted, so afraid and so alone.”




In the end, it was a symbolic act. Security scattered the stones, and the property manager and others were seen taking crowbars to the coffin. But it was only the beginning of the week.




The next action was a garden. Because what would you expect from Vermont? Rather than using just their bodies to get in the way, about 40 protesters 

arrived at sunrise with pots, planters and bags of soil

. 




They affixed the boxes to the pavement with construction adhesive, painted and chalked them with flowers, insects and slogans, flew a rainbow kite, and by mid-morning, had gotten a full dance party going. The action blocked the road to 188 Harvest Lane, which houses 

ICE’s national tip line

.




They were also highlighting the environmental violence of ICE’s data intensive operation. Gardener Isaac Petersen said, “ICE’s surveillance technology is extremely energy-intensive, much of it powered by AI and data centers. It harms our communities directly by targeting our neighbors.”




State and local police moved some barriers, but largely left the garden alone, which blocked the road for most of the day. ICE’s parking lots were nearly empty all day, and the rumor was that ICE was told to avoid coming into the office.




Protestors hang handwritten “tips” outside the ICE office housing the agency’s national tip line. (Shut Down ICE VT)




Each day escalated from the day before. By Thursday, protesters went right up to the front entrance of the Harvest Lane facility. Dozens had arrived before 8 a.m. to deliver handwritten note cards with “tips” encouraging ICE employees to find other jobs. The protesters started by taping those messages to the windows and doors. Then they hauled out a rug, a couch, a coffee table and a fold-up mattress — a makeshift living room — and sat down, singing and playing music, effectively shutting the place down. 




Much of this has been intergenerational. Vermont protesters have 

ranged

 from people in their early 20s to an 83-year-old from Bethel and 85-year-old from Sharon.




Some of those sitting at the entrance this week had taken part in earlier acts of civil disobedience, and several now face charges brought by Clark. 




Organizers say the ICE facility was effectively shut for much of that week, its parking lots empty. Police interference was minimal: At one point, officers came over only to remove the items protesters had used to block a surveillance camera, then returned to their cars. As the organizers said in their press release, “ICE employees went home rather than face Vermont’s week of bold, decisive action.”




What you can do 




The 

week of action

 was only one moment, and organizers hope others will organize their own — aimed at different pieces of ICE infrastructure. There are 

other flash points around the country this month

, too, in Austin, Minneapolis and Arizona.




As for Shut Down ICE VT, 

the group behind the week of action

, they plan to keep going. One simple way to support them: 

Call the tip line

 that ICE runs out of Williston to encourage neighbors to turn each other in. To disrupt its activity, the group is encouraging people to 

call 866-347-2423

 and tell whoever picks up all the different ways ICE could be making a better world. According to organizers, this tactic has been so successful the lines are clogged — one person was on hold for 2 hours and 18 minutes until her phone died. (This tactic was used in the early 

DOGE days

.) Instead of doing Pharaoh’s bidding: What are the beautiful things you could be doing with your life? It can be a bit of a daily ritual.
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













Because here, in the end, is Pharaoh’s trick: He changed the meaning of what was legal. He didn’t simply say, “You must obey me.” He said that if you refused, you were the one breaking the law.




But we should remember whose side the law has so often taken. The law stood against enslaved people seeking freedom. It stood against women having control of their own bodies. It stood against trans people claiming full autonomy. The law, by itself, is no defense against injustice — and must not be turned into an instrument of oppression.




Sarah George declined to prosecute protesters for a reason. By stepping in to take up the case, Charity Clark has signaled a willingness to participate in the repression. The people shutting down ICE in Vermont are on the right side of history. Let’s find ways to join them.




This article 

How Vermont shut down ICE

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Students Say Cornell Banning Frat Parties and Adding Investigators Insufficient
content:
“Nowhere among these measures is the institutional change that students demand,” said Students for a Democratic Cornell.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Cornell University has suspended parties and social events at fraternity houses for the remainder of the academic year, and will work with state police and their sexual assault investigators on future cases.

The changes came in response to outrage over a gang rape at the university in 2024 that has brought national attention to the issue of sexual violence on college campuses and the failures of administrations to address the problem.

Cornell’s President Michael Kotlikoff announced these changes on Tuesday, after weeks of protest against the administration’s mishandling of the 2024 case that have escalated into calls for Kotlikoff’s resignation.

In 2024, a Cornell student, known by the pseudonym Jane Doe, reported that she had been drugged and raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity on campus. Her case was initially dismissed by the district attorney after university police “summarized” her complaint while omitting mentions of sexual violence and drugging. In mid-September, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the university, the Chi Phi Fraternity, and the 7 men. Weeks later, NBC reported on court documents and text messages revealing conversations rife with the language of rape culture among the fraternity brothers. Subsequent reporting on the university’s mishandling of Jane Doe’s case prompted protests at Cornell and the reopening of her case by the district attorney.

“I have spent the past weeks listening to students, faculty, staff, parents, alumni, and trustees, who have shared their feelings of deep connection and sympathy with Jane Doe, anger and frustration that this could happen at Cornell, and outrage at the broader prevalence of sexual violence against women in our society,” Kotlikoff wrote in his announcement Tuesday.

In addition to suspending fraternity parties and working with New York State police “trauma-informed criminal investigators,” Koltikoff promised more staffing to support students who come forward with complaints of sexual assault.

But students at Cornell have called these measures insufficient.

Students for a Democratic Cornell (SDC), which organized a protest on campus on October 5 that was attended by thousands of students and faculty members, said that the measures demonstrate a refusal “to make institutional change on sexual violence.”

In a press release shared with Truthout, SDC explained that “Nowhere among these measures is the institutional change that students demand; specifically, there is no mention of reforming Cornell’s corrupt judicial system or an independent investigation not led by the Board of Trustees.”

The group contends that these measures allow the university to skirt the blame for its part in mishandling the 2024 case as well as its role in creating a “campus-wide epidemic” of sexual violence at Cornell.

Saya Taylor, a member of SDC, explained that the group “will continue to push until all of our demands are met – not just a select few that allow the administration to place blame on other parties.”

While the SDC does not view limiting fraternity parties as a useful measure in combatting sexual violence, other groups disagree – as was clear in the chants and slogans calling for banning frats entirely during the October 5 protest.

Kaori Quan of Cornell’s Graduate Student Union (CGSU) told Truthout that the barring of fraternity parties for the remainder of the academic year does not go far enough. “Stopping frat parties for a year does not address the systemic issues on campus that perpetuate rape culture,” she said, “namely, the intertwined nature of donor money and Greek life.”

“Until Greek life is off our campus entirely, Cornell will continue to prioritize the money it brings in over the health and safety of both students and workers.”

Referring to Cornell’s plan to work more closely with state police and investigators, Quan added that “so long as there is money in protecting Greek life, the campus police and the investigators they work with will answer to university administrators, not the students they supposedly protect.”

“CGSU’s stance is that working more closely with state police will do more harm than good,” Quan also told Truthout.

Police are most often found to be counterproductive, if not harmful, to victims of sexual violence. In a 2024 survey in the U.K., 73 percent of survivors of sexual violence said that their attempts to report the assault to the police worsened their mental health due to their treatment by law enforcement, with significantly worse treatment of Black survivors and survivors of color. A local 2026 report found that police sexual violence in New York City is widespread and rarely punished, and suggests non-carceral forms of intervention are needed.

Quan reiterated the CGSU’s demands for “the resignation of all administrators involved in the handling of Jane Doe’s case,” particularly Kotlikoff, “the expulsion of the Chi Phi brothers who raped her, the banning of IFC Greek life from campus, and an entirely new democratic judiciary system.”

“Koltikoff’s response does not meet any of these demands. It does not even qualify as an apology for the harm he and his administration have done,” she concluded.

University groups are undeterred in their campaign for structural changes at Cornell.

Taylor said SDC’s efforts will continue “to put pressure on the administration by working with the coalition we assembled with over 25 organizations on campus.” In addition to a seven-hour sit-in on October 10, the group has co-organized installations on campus about sexual violence – and is planning an action for Friday, October 16, when Cornell University trustees will be on campus for their annual summit.

Faculty, too, have been organizing, propelled by the students’ protests. On October 7, two days after the mass protest organized by SDC, Cornell faculty issued a resolution that it has “no confidence” in the administration’s ability to “effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell.” The resolution has been signed by over 100 faculty members.

On Wednesday, faculty members held the first of two debates on the no-confidence resolution, which will be voted on at the end of October. Several professors called on Kotlikoff to resign, though the president continues to state that he will not do so.

The case has also reinvigorated discussions about the problem of sexual violence at universities beyond Cornell. In October alone, students at George Washington University, Brown University, Harvard, UCLA, Columbia, and the University of Minnesota, among others, have protested their own university’s responses to rape accusations, against rollbacks to Title IX, and to call for an end to sexual violence.

author: Christopher Cartwright
title: As Resistance to Flock Cameras Grows, Another Surveillance Network Is Spreading
content:
Fusus software is being used in at least 324 US communities, with nearly 624,000 cameras connected to a Fusus network.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

More than 28,000 cameras in Atlanta are integrated into a “real-time crime center,” allowing police live access to many of their video streams. In Hawthorne, California, the city surveillance network includes more than 3,700 cameras. And in Seat Pleasant, Maryland — a town of 4,500 — police have access to one integrated camera for every three residents.

These communities are among hundreds in the U.S. that have adopted Fusus, a surveillance platform that allows police to watch live camera networks in their jurisdictions. While local resistance to Flock Safety automated license plate readers has swept the nation — including vandalism of cameras, cities canceling contracts, and a recent national week of action organized by the group DeFlock — the Fusus software has continued to spread.

Owned by Axon, the company behind Tasers and body-worn cameras, Fusus enables police to link security cameras, automated license plate readers, doorbell cameras, police dash cameras, drones, and body-worn cameras to a central hub that can use AI, according to the company’s website. The software’s distinction is its ability to integrate privately owned cameras from individuals, organizations, and businesses, whose participation the company encourages through its voluntary Community Connect program.

A Prism analysis of public information obtained from Axon’s website and the Fusus application programming interfaces (APIs) shows that the software is being used in at least 324 U.S. communities, with nearly 624,000 cameras connected to a Fusus network. These range from rural areas — such as Plaquemines Parish in Louisiana and Artesia, New Mexico — to major cities, including Dallas, Seattle, Miami, and New York City.

Privacy advocates and community organizers say this integrated system rapidly expands the reach of police power. Ed Vogel, a co-founder of Southerners Against Surveillance Systems and Infrastructure, argued that the Fusus business model inherently encourages additional surveillance.

“Anyone who is concerned about Flock safety and license plate readers should be equally concerned with Axon and Fusus,” he said. “Fusus is a tool that invites the police to build out a surveillance apparatus in order to optimize the technology. Because it’s a software that integrates a variety of surveillance tools into it, in order to make the most of it, the police want to and will try to acquire more technology so that they can integrate more tools.”

Data obtained from the APIs include the number of registered, integrated, owned, shared, and subscribed cameras. Registered cameras are those submitted to a police-maintained database. This doesn’t give law enforcement live access to each camera feed, but allows them to create a network map for future investigations. Integrated cameras are those that give police live access, and Axon’s Fusus manual says police can share these video streams with other law enforcement agencies.

Axon did not respond to multiple requests for comment or clarification on the definitions of owned, shared, and subscribed cameras. On its website’s FAQ page, the company says Fusus “promotes ethical policing by improving the accuracy of suspect identification, helping reduce reliance on potentially biased eyewitness accounts.”

In May 2023, the Electronic Frontier Foundation reported that nearly 150 jurisdictions used Fusus. That number has more than doubled since, according to Prism’s analysis of Fusus API data.

Georgia leads the nation in integrated cameras, with more than 275,000. An Axon-run website urging people to register and integrate cameras into the Atlanta police system, called Connect Atlanta, shows that the city has 29,855 integrated cameras, the most of any Fusus network, as of Oct. 15. Sandy Springs, Georgia, has the second-most at 16,415.

The Illinois State Police, the only state agency publicly reporting that it uses Fusus, has integrated more than 4,100 cameras. Three public universities — the University of Illinois, the University of Missouri and the University of Arizona — also use the technology.

Major Nathan Swyers, who leads the intelligence unit for the Dallas Police Department, wrote in a statement to Prism that the department has about 1,500 cameras integrated and viewable within Fusus, and over 4,000 registered cameras throughout the community. “Having this tool makes the citizens and the officers of Dallas safer,” Swyers added.

The Illinois State Police and police departments for Atlanta; Sandy Springs; Memphis, Tennessee; and Orlando, Florida, did not respond to requests for comment on how they use the technology.

Vogel suggested that the growth of Fusus, along with Flock and other surveillance technology, shows that people need to focus on the larger debate of surveillance in their communities.

“We need to focus our organizing around surveillance apparatus and not a specific technology or equipment,” he said. “And we need to focus it on the infrastructure, like real-time crime centers.”

Information on organizations and businesses that link their cameras to Fusus is limited. In Dallas, Axon stated that nearly 40 organizations have partnered with the police department. These include the American Airlines Center, QuikTrip, the Jewish Federation of Greater Dallas, and the Catholic Diocese of Dallas, according to a press conference held earlier this year. Those businesses and organizations did not respond to requests for comment.

Axon touts the voluntary nature of the Community Connect program. Yet Ginny Welsch, a member of the Nashville Metro Council in Tennessee who opposed the city’s proposed adoption of Fusus, said that that framing twists the argument.

“I don’t think anybody’s looking at the fact that individual citizens shouldn’t be able to opt me in to being surveilled, and that’s what they’re doing when they have this thing,” she said. “My neighbor gets to say, ‘Yes, I’m in,’ and then suddenly I’m part of this big surveillance system with them. You’re opting me into something that we don’t want.”

Every camera linked to a Fusus system needs to connect to a device sold by Axon. The annual subscription fee is $150, and hardware costs begin at $350, with higher prices for additional storage and the inclusion of built-in AI.

While Axon says the system doesn’t use facial recognition technology, it simultaneously highlights the AI capabilities. The AI analyzes the video streams, allowing police to identify vehicles, people, and objects or send alerts when certain unspecified criteria appear on camera.

According to a 2023 news report, all of the roughly 620 integrated cameras in Memphis had AI capabilities. There are now more than 3,000 integrated in the city, according to the API data.

Despite growing use of the technology, pushback is mounting.

In May, the City Council in Asheville, North Carolina, voted 6-1 to approve a Fusus contract despite significant opposition. Resident Steve Cooperman said the council ignored warnings from locals and instead relied on the story being told by police and technology companies.

“When they were presented with people who aren’t paid to do this work, who’ve done extensive research, they were very dismissive of those folks,” he said.

Nashville, Tennessee, has fully resisted implementing Fusus. Welsch — who represents Nashville’s 16th District — said the city used the software without council approval until 2024, when a renewed contract was voted down. In 2025, the council approved legislation that added some restrictions should Fusus be approved, but a contract has yet to come back for a vote.

Kelly Chieng, a local community organizer, highlighted guardrails as something that “makes people have a false sense of security.” In her opinion, pushback was successful in Nashville because groups have created firm demands and resisted compromise.

“People should resist the inevitability of this stuff, because we’re seeing stuff coming down. I don’t think we should stop at guardrails or regulation,” she said. “I think we need to keep pushing.”

title: İstanbul: Selde can kaybı 4'e yükseldi, 5 kişi de kayıp
content:
İstanbul Valisi Davut Gül, 15 Ekim akşamüstü yaptığı açıklamada 3 kişinin yaşamını yitirdiğini, 5 kişi için kayıp başvurusu yapıldığını bildirdi. Gül'ün açıklamasının ardından Beykoz'da işçi Faik Şentürk'ün ölüm haberi geldi. 




Vali Gül, kurtarma ve sağlık çalışmalarına ilişkin şu bilgileri paylaştı: 







“7 hemşehrimiz tedavisi bittikten sonra taburcu oldu, 5 kişiyle ilgili kayıp başvurusu yapıldı. Arama çalışmaları devam ediyor.”







Gül, kentin normalleşmeye başladığını, hasar tespit çalışmalarının sürdüğünü ve zarar gören yurttaşlara ödemelerin en geç pazartesi günü başlatılacağını söyledi. 




84 yılın yağış rekoru kırıldı, 3 bin 50 kişi kurtarıldı




İçişleri Bakanı Mustafa Çiftçi, İstanbul'da yağışın bazı bölgelerde metrekareye 

272 kilograma

 ulaştığını açıkladı. İstanbul Valisi Davut Gül ise kentin 1942'den bu yana kaydedilen en yoğun yağışla karşı karşıya kaldığını söyledi.




Vali Gül'ün akşam saatlerinde verdiği bilgiye göre selde mahsur kalan 3 bin 50 kişi kurtarıldı. Kurtarılmayı bekleyen kimse kalmadığını belirten Gül, kayıp başvurusu yapılan 5 kişinin aranmasına devam edildiğini bildirdi. 




İstanbul'da 16 Ekim Cuma günü de okullarda eğitime ara verilecek. Erdoğan, sağanağın devam edeceğine ilişkin tahminler nedeniyle yurttaşlardan resmi uyarıları izlemelerini istedi. 




838 sigortalı hasar ihbarı




Türkiye Sigorta Birliği (TSB), 15 Ekim itibarıyla İstanbul'da sel ve su baskınları nedeniyle sigorta şirketlerine 838 hasar ihbarı yapıldığını açıkladı. Bunların 776'sı yangın sigortası, 62'si kasko kapsamında kaydedildi.




TSB Başkanı Ahmet Yaşar, Bursa, Kocaeli ve Yalova'daki başvurularla birlikte toplam ihbar sayısının 897'ye ulaştığını belirterek şöyle dedi:







“Bunlar, henüz ilk bildirimler. Önümüzdeki günlerde yeni ihbarların gelmesi ve ekspertiz çalışmalarının ilerlemesiyle hasarın gerçek boyutu daha net ortaya çıkacaktır.”







İstanbul Valisi Davut Gül de hasar tespit çalışmalarının sürdüğünü, selden zarar gören yurttaşlara yapılacak ödemelerin mümkünse cuma öğleden sonra, en geç 19 Ekim Pazartesi başlayacağını bildirdi.




Barajlarda bir günde 7,16 puan doluluk artışı




İstanbul Su ve Kanalizasyon İdaresi'nin (İSKİ) 15 Ekim saat 09.14'te yayımladığı verilere göre, bir gün önce yüzde 38,06 olarak ölçülen kente su sağlayan barajlardaki ortalama doluluk oranı  yüzde 45,22'ye çıktı.




Elmalı Barajı yüzde 100 doluluğa ulaşırken, doluluk Istrancalar 'da yüzde 84,2, Alibey'de yüzde 68,13, Darlık'ta yüzde 67,74 ve Ömerli'de yüzde 62,17 seviyesine yükseldi.




Diğer barajlardaki doluluk oranları Terkos'ta yüzde 34,64, Büyükçekmece'de yüzde 29,02, Sazlıdere'de yüzde 27,47, Kazandere'de yüzde 8,28 ve Pabuçdere'de yüzde 3,41 olarak kaydedildi.




Yağış öncesinde Elmalı Barajı'nın doluluğu yüzde 77,79 olarak  ölçülmüştü.




Elmalı Barajı tamamen doldu: Taşkın tehlikesi var mı?




Elmalı Barajı'nın yüzde 100 dolması, barajın yıkılma veya denetimsiz taşma tehlikesi altında olduğu anlamına gelmez. Barajların olağan su tahliye sistemleri bulunuyor. Ancak güvenliğin değerlendirilmesi için doluluk oranının yanında baraja gelen su miktarı, dolusavak kapasitesi ve aşağı havzadaki akış koşullarının da bilinmesi gerekiyor.




(AEK)

author: Amy Goodman
title: Regulation Should Target AI’s Current Harms, Not Superintelligence Possibilities
content:
A mix of science fiction and delusion distracts from the real harms that we’re seeing, says tech journalist Paris Marx.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

We speak with tech journalist Paris Marx about his new book, Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires. In the book, Marx exposes the deceptive ways tech companies are taking resources from vulnerable communities in order to build massive AI data centers. “We have seen the tech companies that, back in 2019, 2020, wanted us to see them as climate leaders … completely throw their targets out the window in order to pursue generative AI and this data center buildout,” says Marx. He notes that after failing to connect to electrical grids in the locations where they were building data centers, some AI companies have pivoted to building “on-site gas plants,” further increasing dependency on fossil fuels.

Tech companies “want us to believe” that AI models are “starting to become so powerful that within 10 years they could decide that they want to wipe out humanity or a significant chunk of humanity,” says Marx. “That is a mix of science fiction and delusion … and it is also a very effective way to distract from the real harms that we’re seeing from these generative AI products.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now! I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: With the midterms less than three weeks away, we continue to look at how AI data centers have emerged as a political flashpoint.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re joined now by the Canadian journalist Paris Marx, host of the award-winning Tech Won’t Save Us podcast, writes the Disconnect newsletter, author of the new book Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires. He’s joining us from St. John’s, Newfoundland.

And we just talked to Justin Pearson, taking on Elon Musk’s xAI data centers in Memphis. In fact, though, the largest concentration of data centers is in northern Virginia, as you write about. And Nermeen and I are speaking to you from New York, which has the only state moratorium on the building of data centers. Can you give us — can you put that battle in Memphis in the global picture? Why northern Virginia, for example, is there this massive concentration of data centers? It’s not one of the poorest areas in the country.

PARIS MARX: No, certainly not. It’s much more for historical reasons, right? Because a lot of that early work on the internet was happening in northern Virginia, you know, obviously, a lot of military spending that went into that. And, of course, for that reason, a lot of infrastructure, a lot of, you know, fiber infrastructure, connectivity infrastructure, data centers, certainly, over time, were built out in that area. And that, you know, kind of — that legacy continues to this day.

And so, you know, the people who live there in northern Virginia have really felt the effects of all of these data centers having been built out. And especially, you know, they have had data centers for a long time — right? — but one of the things I try to get to in the book is really the shift from data centers as they used to be, you know, in industrial areas, maybe not so much larger than other tenants that would be in those, you know, kind of industrial parks and things like that, to the hyperscale data centers that are just on a whole other scale. You know, the resource demands are just immense, as, of course, you know, Representative Justin Pearson was just talking about in Memphis, where they have really been feeling this firsthand. And I think, you know, because Elon Musk was involved, this really brought it to the attention of a lot more people, seeing the effects that come with one of these major data centers. But, obviously, in northern Virginia, people are feeling a lot of that.

But as we have seen this significant escalation in the construction of these hyperscale data centers, particularly in the past four to five years, and certainly since the generative AI boom really started to take off in 2023, we have seen not just many more communities in the United States seeing data centers planned or being constructed next to them, and feeling, you know, what comes with that, whether that is the increases in their electricity prices, the pressures on their water system, or just, you know, kind of the noise and light pollution that can come from living next to one of these infrastructures, but many more communities around the world are feeling that, too. And I think that’s part of the reason why we’re seeing this kind of collective backlash, you know, throughout the United States, but in many other parts of the world, against these data centers.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: So, Paris, let’s just — you know, to give people a sense of the scale of these data centers, there are 3,000 — more than 3,000 operational data centers in the U.S. now and about 1,500 that are being planned. So, why don’t you explain, if you could, why? Why so many, and why so quickly?

PARIS MARX: Yeah, absolutely. So, you know, we need data centers to process the types of things that we do online, you know, the digital services that we use. You know, of course, I’m connected to you digitally. That is likely going through a data center somewhere, right? So, it’s not to say that we need absolutely no data centers; we need to get rid of them all. I think there have certainly been benefits from the digital technologies that have arisen over the past few decades. But we have seen this continued escalation in the amount of computing power that the tech companies and the tech industry are demanding, right? And they make the products that they’re offering to people more computationally intensive.

And so, the real reason, you know, one of the key reasons at least, that we have seen this significant escalation over the past few years in the construction of data centers, because we really saw this start to take off in 2023, 2024, which is why it has become such a political flashpoint over the past 12 to 18 months, is really because of generative AI — right? — because of the chatbots and image generators that companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, but also Google, Microsoft, Amazon, have been pushing for the past few years, because, you know, for regular people who are not really into the technical side of things, it might just be like, “Oh, OK, this is a new service that these companies are offering,” but the reality is that these are much more computationally intensive than what, you know, these companies were offering before.

It takes a lot more computation to kind of create, you know, kind of a text response to a prompt that you’re putting in, or to generate an image or a video based on some prompts that you’re putting into the system. And that has meant they have needed to build so many more data centers so much more quickly and make those data centers even larger than they have in the past, which, again, is why so many people are, you know, seeing data centers arrive in their communities, just because these tech companies are looking for so many places to be able to locate them, places that are willing to, you know, have them become their neighbors. And they’re finding that increasingly a lot of communities are saying no to that.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: Well, one of the chapters in your book, Paris, is devoted to the climate impacts, which we heard about earlier from Justin in Memphis. So, the question — you know, obviously, America, the U.S., has exponentially more data centers than any country in the world. Now, China, which is also building, you know, massively data centers, though, again, nowhere near the number of what the U.S. has, they have been attempting to employ renewable energy to diminish the climate impacts of these data centers. In your research, do you see any indication that these tech companies are looking for more sustainable sources of energy?

PARIS MARX: Not in any significant way, right? Like, if you listen to what the tech companies say, they will certainly tell you that they’re investing a lot of money in renewable energy. You know, in the past, you know, last year in particular, they made a big push into nuclear energy, which, obviously, is very debatable whether it can be considered clean. But in their ledger, they would claim it is — right? — which is part of their way to say, like, you know, “Look, we’re trying to do this efficiently. We’re trying to do this sustainably.” And, you know, they will certainly talk about how they will reduce kind of the intensity of water use at a data center — right? — so, you know, kind of the total quantity that a data center itself will use. But then, when you look across the total number of data centers that they’re building out, their water use and their electricity use, as well, is just absolutely soaring.

But the real story here, if you think about the climate impact, is really their dependence on fossil fuels and their dependence on natural gas, in particular. And so, you know, in kind of ’23, ’24, we saw this real push for them to try to get connections to the grid in the various places where they were building out these data centers, right? But in many of those places, they have now exhausted those connections, right? The demand on the grid was so great that it became much more difficult to connect a data center in the kind of amount of time that they would need to connect it for it to come online to, you know, benefit their generative AI ambitions.

And so, what we’ve seen over the past year is a real pivot toward building on-site gas plants. You know, obviously, when we look at Memphis, there was the use of a lot of generators on site in order to power the data center. We have seen other data centers using that model, as well. But now, of course, increasingly they’re moving toward actually just building dedicated gas plants for the data centers, such that there was a report out recently that it’s something like 189 gigawatts of new gas capacity is in the pipeline in the United States just to power these data centers, which is just staggering to imagine, right?

You know, we have already seen our governments roll back on their climate ambitions. We have seen the tech companies that, back in 2019, 2020, wanted us to see them as climate leaders and, you know, as though they cared about climate change and taking action on that, completely throw their targets out the window in order to pursue generative AI and this data center buildout, regardless of the consequences that come of that. And, of course, you know, those are consequences that will be felt by everybody through, you know, how it’s going to make climate change worse. But again, as Representative Pearson was saying, we also see very clearly the local impacts of local air pollution on the people who live next to these data centers, as the people in Memphis are feeling, but also in many other communities where this is happening.

AMY GOODMAN: Paris Marx, I want to ask you about your critique of the legislation Senator Bernie Sanders is putting forward, certainly seen as an AI critic, a deep concern about what’s happening, and what’s happening so fast. Senator Sanders and Congressmember Greg Casar announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act to stop AI oligarchs from building machines humans cannot control. It would permanently ban the development and deployment of superintelligent AI and temporarily pause advanced AI development until a federal regulator has established safety rules. They would also direct the U.S. to pursue international agreements to prevent superintelligence from being developed anywhere in the world. You are critical of this approach.

PARIS MARX: Yeah, absolutely. You know, I certainly welcome Senator Sanders’ work on the data center moratorium and trying to move that forward on a national level. I think that’s very important. And, you know, even when we look at the kind of superintelligence legislation and, you know, the discussion of kind of limiting or rolling back the further development of these AI models, I would also be on board with that, as well, but probably not for the same reasons that are being laid out in this legislation.

And so, to me, this feels like a response to these narratives that we have had for the past couple months now about, you know, the power and the threat that these AI models can pose to humanity. Right? You know, we have seen these tech companies and people who work at them come out and talk about how they feel or they believe — and, you know, they want us to believe, as well — that these models are getting to a place that they are starting to learn on their own, and they’re starting to become so powerful that within 10 years they could decide that they want to wipe out humanity or a significant chunk of humanity, and that is a real threat to, you know, our collective species, right?

And to me, quite frankly, I feel that that is a mix of science fiction and delusion on the part of the people who are running these companies, and it is also a very effective way to distract from the real harms that we’re seeing from these generative AI products, from the chatbots and image generators today. You know, for me, I think that, you know, kind of this future-focused stuff is an attempt to make sure that regulation is not targeting the things that people are actually feeling and that would actually restrict what the chatbots and the AI companies are doing right now, and, you know, rather, having the discussion being about something that might happen 10 years down the line, that I would argue is actually very unlikely and doesn’t reflect how the technology really works.

You know, what I would like to see, from a regulatory perspective, is not this focus on the superintelligence stuff, but, you know, the effects that — you know, as we’re seeing more reports, the effects that dependence on chatbots can have on people’s mental health, where we see them have mental health spirals because they have become dependent on these technologies; you know, the kind of deepfake crisis that we have seen, and really saw very clearly on Elon Musk’s platform and with the Grok chatbot at the beginning of the year; the questions about what dependence on chatbots and use of chatbots means for people’s ability to learn, to think critically, to kind of have these cognitive skills and to develop them properly.

You know, we can even go beyond that to the environmental impact of the data centers themselves, or, you know, the various other ways that we have seen chatbots used for people to try to harm themselves or to harm others — of course, in the case that we’re seeing here in Canada, where the shooter out in British Columbia earlier this year, in one of the worst mass shootings in our history, was actually using ChatGPT for eight months to help plan violent scenarios in that attack in particular, right up until the morning of the attack, when the shooter asked the chatbot what time school shootings tend to occur, and then, of course, went to carry out that act of mass violence.

And so, these are the things that I think that regulation should really be targeting, not these kind of more fantastical ideas of superintelligence that, you know, I think are really the product of kind of delusional and deceptive tech people.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: So, Paris, would you say that there is a distinction between your critique, which is a political economic critique of the technology, in addition to, of course, these horrifying incidents that you’ve recounted of present-day harms, and the scientific and technological potential of this, say, generative artificial intelligence? Or do you think even that potential that has been touted to us is misleading or an exaggeration?

PARIS MARX: Yeah, in my view, I do think the potential is severely overstated. You know, I think that when we look especially at how the tech industry tends to operate, it it operates on exaggeration — right? — in order to drive investment, in order to drive hype cycles, to get people interested in its products, to, you know, get a lot of media attention on what it’s doing, which is not to say that, you know, at the end of a shakeout — of course, there’s a lot of talk of whether there is an AI bubble and whether there’s overinvestment into generative AI and into data centers right now, and what might happen when there is a kind of market correction, you know, in that sector.

And I think that what we’ll find is that a lot of the places where the tech industry said that generative AI would be useful is actually not going to pan out in the long run. I think that there will certainly be some instances where, you know, certain sectors, certain companies find that it’s useful to use generative AI products. And even then, I think their use of the products will look very different than what we have today. You know, there’s obviously a big reliance and push to use centralized tools like ChatGPT or Claude from Anthropic, but, actually, I think we’ll see much more kind of use of the open-weight models, the kind of smaller models that are targeted to certain use cases that are obviously also less resource-demanding, which I think is how things are going to shake out.

But even then, I would say that, you know, I think that the usefulness of generative AI as a technology has been overstated. I think that the pursuit of it comes out of certain kind of ideological ideas that the tech companies have. You know, they want to build this, you know, kind of human brain within the computer, and to do that, you need larger and larger models. But that’s not necessarily the best way to actually develop AI for, you know, kind of benefiting the public, right? And one of the things that I took away from Karen Hao’s work, who I know you’ve had on the show, as well, and her book, Empire of AI, is that there are a lot of other ways you can approach AI, right? But a lot of the money that goes into AI development right now is focused on generative AI rather than these, you know, many other techniques or approaches that could actually be much, much better for the public, you know, be using far less resources, but the industry is not very interested in that right now.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: And finally, if you could talk about — because it seems to me that a number of people in the medical profession are very hopeful about the changes that generative AI will make possible in many, many different fields, and already, you know, the discovery of Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which is considered one of the most significant scientific achievements in the history of artificial intelligence. We have 30 seconds. Your response?

PARIS MARX: I am quite skeptical of many of these claims. You know, I think that we have, actually, a history of thinking that new technologies are going to make big changes in medical advances, and then they don’t deliver. And I would just point to, you know, in Canada, the auditor general in Ontario looked into these AI medical scribes, you know, the tools that transcribe conversations between patients and doctors, and found that in over half of cases, they were inserting false information, recording the wrong drugs, you know. And if this is kind of the basis of, you know, how — a patient’s medical history, that can really have some significant effects on, you know, how they are treated going forward, if their medical file is filled with false information about their history. So, again, I’m a bit skeptical on that point, as well.

AMY GOODMAN: Paris Marx, we want to thank you so much for being with us, author of the new book Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires, host of the award-winning Tech Won’t Save Us podcast. He writes the Disconnect newsletter.

A very happy birthday to Juan González! Tomorrow, on Friday, I’ll be at the Woodstock International Film Festival moderating a panel at 2:00. On Monday, at the Eileen Norris Cinema Theater at USC, the University of Southern California, we’ll be screening Steal This Story, Please!, about Democracy Now! And on October 26th and 27th in Colorado, first at CU Boulder, then at Fort Collins. Check our website, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.
