Hello comrades, warm greetings from Bandung to Bristol.

We introduce ourselves as prisoners from what is known as the “Chaos Star.” This correspondence carries fragments of memory from years marked by chaos, surveillance, and arrests. We send this message from behind the bars of a prison in—so called—Indonesia. We are currently serving sentences related to the August 2025 unrest, the pipe bomb attack on a police post in December 2024, and the destruction of Bank Hana during the anti–TNI Bill protests in March and May Day 2025.

The unrest last August became the largest manhunt against activists and anarchists since 1998. This year, 703 political prisoners—although we reject that label—are still undergoing legal processes or are detained. We prefer to be called Anarchist Prisoners rather than Political Prisoners. This is an issue we want to critique. The label “political prisoner” places us within certain relations of power: we are framed as symbols of resistance, victims or survivors of a regime, or tools for legitimizing particular political agendas. Instead, we are Anarchist Prisoners. We reject the very foundation of politics itself. Our emphasis is on the autonomy of the subject and individual disobedience, without serving any project or representation tied to political agendas. By using the label Anarchist Prisoners, we assert a distance from the language of power and maintain a position outside the political field that seeks to regulate, define, and justify everything.

Anarchists in Indonesia are facing an extraordinary storm. More than a dozen anarchists have been detained, tortured, and the state is attempting to discipline us by spreading fear. But to us, that is nothing—because we are the storm itself, the disaster made flesh for them. Among us are comrades from Black Bloc Zone, Indonesian Anarchist Black Cross, Contemplative, Katong Press, and many others.

They—our comrades—have appeared like a storm wrapped in fire. Some of us see this moment as a culmination, yet it is neither a beginning nor an end. We gather every flame around us, the flames the state has tried to extinguish.

How many times must we say this: “We can live without the state!” To hell with society! Society is the most perfect tool the state has to preserve itself. We truly, deeply hate society. We believe the dawn of hunger will arrive sooner than expected, marking the beginning of the collapse of the state. To those of you out there: endure, and gather every spark you can find. And to those behind bars—or those who feel imprisoned—you are not alone. Fight! Fight! To hell with winning or losing; what matters is that our eyes remain burning bright in every struggle we face.

One of the starting points that drew us into direct conflict with the state began at the end of 2024. At that time, there was an international call known as Day 1312, understood by some groups as a day of critique against the institution of the police.

On December 13, 2024, there was a global call to action for 1312—an anti-police day, or A.C.A.B (All Cops Are Bastards). One such action took place in Bandung, in front of the Bandung City Police Headquarters. It is no secret that various forms of violence and abuse of power by state apparatus (read: the police) have resulted in human rights violations, one of the most intolerable being the taking of lives. The Commission for the Disappeared and Victims of Violence (KontraS) recorded 602 incidents of violence involving members of the Indonesian National Police (Polri) from July 2024 to June 2025. From the Kanjuruhan tragedy, to Randi and Yusuf, Afif Maulana, Gamma, Affan Kurniawan, to the most recent, Arianto Tawakkal—killed by the police.

As an informal group that condemns all forms of state brutality and pursues theory and practice—through trial and error—of direct action methods to strengthen individuals in reclaiming control over their own lives and using that power to fulfill their own aims, on December 13, 2024, we intended to take part in the 1312 call. However, on that day we were unable to join due to unavoidable circumstances. Eventually, we decided to carry out a direct action on another day—an action conducted individually, separate from demonstrations involving large crowds.

On December 17, 2024, at 02:00 WIB, we planned a spontaneous direct action to throw Molotov cocktails and a pipe bomb at the Letter U Gentong Police Post in Tasikmalaya. After carrying out the action, on December 18, 2024, Naufal and I deliberately fled to East Java, to Jombang and Tulungagung, for several days after seeing news reports that an unknown individual had attacked and burned the police post. The case became serious as Indonesia’s Densus 88 counterterrorism unit became involved in the investigation and crime scene processing. This forced us to ensure we left no trace; in fact, there was no CCTV directly at the police post. The chronology reported in the news was far from the actual facts, which allowed us to breathe a little easier—before a similar action occurred in Makassar.

In January 2025, I received an invitation for a collaborative project from Blessed is the Flame, an anarcho-nihilist/individualist group from Greece, aimed at spreading anarchist propaganda and practices of rebellion internationally. I responded by sending a communique claiming responsibility for the burning of the Letter U Gentong Police Post in Tasikmalaya, as an act of solidarity with Nikos Romanos, Alfredo Cospito, and all anarchist prisoners / FAI–IRF prisoners worldwide.

THE BEGINNING OF SURVEILLANCE AND THE MANHUNT!

On March 31, 2025, the police arrested three of our comrades (MRP (19), MS (19), FSD (18)). The arrests followed a Molotov attack on Traffic Police Post 705 at the intersection of AP Pettarani Street / Sultan Alauddin, Makassar, South Sulawesi. This action was a form of resistance against increasingly oppressive government policies, including the revision of the TNI Law, which expands military control into civilian life—a regressive step that deepens repression.

That night, March 22, 2025, our three comrades approached the post with full awareness that the state only understands the language of real resistance. Molotovs were thrown, flames rose, and within moments the police post became a symbol that people will not remain silent in the face of repression. It did not take long for the authorities to respond. With all their resources and surveillance networks, the police quickly hunted down those responsible. The arrests were carried out systematically, using monitoring technology and their information networks. Our three comrades were eventually captured, handcuffed, and taken in for interrogation.

From March to May, we felt constantly surveilled by police intelligence. Wherever we went, we were watched. On September 4, 2025, we were arrested by Indonesia’s Densus 88 counterterrorism unit along with several police officers at our respective Homes.

The case later known as the Gentong incident was only a small spark within a much broader landscape of conflict. After that, life continued under the shadow of surveillance. We realized the state never truly forgets, and that every event leaves traces that will one day be used again. While some individuals were already on the radar, the situation outside continued to evolve.

At the beginning of the following year, the government pushed forward the revision of the TNI Law. For many, it felt like a step backward—an attempt to reopen space for the military to further penetrate civilian life. Anger that had been scattered began to converge in the streets. Demonstrations erupted across cities, and the social conflict produced by the existence of the state became visible once again.

We claim responsibility for the burning of two Bank Hana ATMs, a Bank Hana office building, a capitalist-owned advertising videotron, and a vehicle belonging to the Indonesian National Armed Forces. These acts took place after demonstrators occupied public space following protests against the ratification of the TNI Law, in Bandung, West Java, on the night of Friday, March 21, 2025. The demonstration in front of the Regional House of Representatives (DPRD) was not ignored by riot police, even as Molotovs, propane gas, stones, and firecrackers were thrown toward the building. In the end, we chose direct action by carrying out burnings at several points mentioned above.

Opposition to the TNI Bill revived long-standing fears about the militarization of civilian space. When students and various groups took to the streets to reject the bill, they faced not only security forces but also the logic of a state always ready to respond to disobedience with repression.

Some time later, as the calendar moved toward May 1, the tension had not subsided. May Day became another space where anger against state control, labor exploitation, and increasingly rigid power once again converged in the streets.

A total of 24 demonstrators, including students and student journalists, were arrested during the May Day protest on May 1, 2025, in Semarang, six of whom were briefly detained as suspects. They were accused of resisting officers and damaging Facilities.

May Day in Bandung left a trail of arrests and unresolved tension. For many, the detention of demonstrators served as a reminder that taking to the streets always means confronting forces ready to suppress it.

Months later, the tension did not disappear—it accumulated beneath the surface. By August 2025, this buildup of social anger finally erupted more widely, making the unrest the peak of a chain of conflicts that had been visible since the early-year protests.

In the end, nothing is ever truly finished. What you call “order” is only a temporary pause in a conflict that continues to pulse beneath the surface. The state may detain bodies, but it can never fully tame the will that refuses to submit. From Gentong, to the streets during the TNI protests, to the August eruption—these are not separate series, but the same pulse in different forms.

We offer no hope, nor do we promise victory. What exists is the slow approach of destruction, and the choice to keep burning within it. If this world is built on control, fear, and obedience, then let it collapse along with all the illusions that sustain it. From behind these bars, we ask for nothing—except one thing: never stop.

Before we close this correspondence, we would like to include a quote from a communiqué we sent during the early days of our imprisonment:

Because what we fight for is not freedom as defined by legal pamphlets or moral values that shift with every press conference. This is a freedom that does not fit within articles of law, does not sit comfortably in courtrooms, and cannot be stamped shut by the state.

Out there, people fall to accidents, addiction, and work-related illnesses legalized by economic necessity. Others die slowly from boredom and isolation, drowning in obedient routines praised as stability. Amid the ruins after August 29, we chose to stake our lives on a leap—without safety nets, without promises of compensation. Nothing is more honest than that choice.

Maybe today we lost a round. But the war over meaning is not over. Our gaze remains forward—and still burning!

Greetings. I am a detainee in what is being called the “Chaos Star” case. I was arrested in Makassar on September 23rd, 2025, by West Java Regional Police, along with dozens of counterterrorism units from Densus 88.

I have been accused of being the mastermind behind the spontaneous uprisings that took place between August and September last year across several cities in Indonesia, particularly Jakarta and Bandung. The authorities also accuse me of inciting acts of vandalism, and of orchestrating a bombing at a police post in West Java in December 2024.

When I was arrested, I was interrogated and tortured throughout the night. They tried to force access to my personal email and questioned me about my friends and their alleged involvement. When I refused to cooperate and chose to remain silent, the officers wrapped a plastic bag over my head to suffocate me, and beat me. This happened several times.

After I was transferred to the West Java Police headquarters, they deliberately tried to isolate me with a state-appointed lawyer so they could claim a legal basis to continue interrogating me, even though I insisted on my right to remain silent.

I believe this arrest is highly political. It serves to protect their image after last year’s unrest, by creating a scapegoat for the fragility of their political system. The events of last year showed that ordinary people can disrupt the state’s control, even if only for a few days.

I cannot deny that the rapid spread of information through technology played a major role. Without platforms like YouTube, Instagram, WhatsApp, or TikTok, such spontaneous uprisings would have been much harder to organize. But this is also the contradiction: the same technology enables authorities to quickly track, identify, and arrest those involved. Through informants and social media activity they build their narrative, and thus accusing anarchists of being the main culprit, especially the so-called egoist and nihilist circles.

They pressured me to falsely implicate my friends using fabricated evidence and testimony. I refused to co-operate.

For the destruction of techno industrial Civilization

My Friends and brothers and sisters, inside and outside these walls, Peace be upon you.

I’m writing this letter to let you know that, God willing, I’m doing alright. A while ago I came down with a mild fever, but alhamdulillah, I’m still holding on, still under His grace and protection. I hope all of you are safe, healthy, and kept well. Aamiin.

I’ve lost count of how many letters failed before this one finally made it out. There are barely any writing supplies in here, and when there are, they never last long. Even now, as I write this, I’m still being kept in quarantine. I don’t know for how much longer. Though honestly, I don’t expect anything from being moved to another block. To me, it’s all the same. The only thing I truly want, the only thing I keep hoping for, is FREEDOM. I want to go home. I want to eat my mother’s cooking again. I want to sit with my family.

I’m writing this in a hurry, with very little to work with, so forgive me if my words feel scattered. Prison really does cripple part of the mind.

Recently, I got to see the outside world again, if only for those weekly court hearings. I was unbelievably happy. Emotional, even. Hehe. I got to meet old friends and new ones too. Thank you for coming, for standing in solidarity with me. I love you all.

I also heard that my brother Albi, who was being detained in Bandung, has finally been released. Alhamdulillah. It made me incredibly happy. I pray the others still locked up will soon breathe fresh air again too.

UNTIL EVERYONE IS FREE. UNTIL EVERY PRISON IS FLATTENED TO THE GROUND.

I’ve been imprisoned over the same case again. The moment I got out, ACAB—or what I call a disease—came to pick me up immediately. They traveled all the way from Surabaya just to carry out another ridiculous assignment. I’m sure they got something in return for arresting me. Who knows what. Things like this only make me trust the state even less. The state was never worthy of trust to begin with. LIARS! They will never hesitate to hunt down people who dare to say “no” to them. And maybe, in the end, it only ends with death.

While being held in quarantine, I’ve been trying to survive as best as I can. Life in here is deeply miserable. And it makes me wonder: since when did saying “no” to the state become forbidden? Since when does refusing obedience turn someone into a terrorist, a communist, a traitor, or whatever label they use for people who step out of line? Now let me ask another question: how could dissent not exist, when people are still capable of seeing, hearing, and feeling for themselves?

Look back for a moment—the events in Pati, where people rose against corrupt leaders who challenged and oppressed their own communities. Then the uprisings in August, when masses of protesters were arrested indiscriminately, dragged away like animals. And so many other incidents after that. Wasn’t all of this cultivated by the state itself?

In the middle of economic collapse, widespread poverty, and the looming threat of war, people eventually want only one simple thing: to eat, to survive, not to starve. And when desperation grows deep enough, people begin turning on one another. Killing one another. Consuming one another. Social war becomes inevitable.

The state is not separate from this. It is the hand directing the performance from behind the curtain. Just think about it: people who take their anger to the streets are arrested and charged with destruction, vandalism, disorder, and whatever else they can invent. Then society is split apart into endless sides, pro and contra everywhere. Even those who merely express solidarity online are hunted down and arrested without hesitation. And somehow they are the ones accused of creating chaos and causing harm.

Alright then, let me ask again: who destroyed the forests of Kalimantan, Papua, and countless other islands to turn them into endless palm oil plantations? Who murdered the mountains by drilling into them and extracting their steam, poisoning the water and leaving behind salt, contamination, and ruin? Who built the nickel projects in Sulawesi and drove Indigenous communities off their own land? And Lapindo, the drilling disaster that drowned entire villages and buried lives that can never be recovered, who was responsible for that? Papuan mothers shot at for defending their autonomy. Honestly, there’s so much destruction I couldn’t possibly name it all.

And after all that devastation, what happens? Are the people responsible ever arrested? Ever punished in proportion to the damage they caused? Is there restoration? Can they ever return those places to what they once were? CAN THEY BRING ANY OF IT BACK? No! Because all of it was protected, funded, and planned by the state itself. The contradictions never end. I could go on forever talking about them. But the rest, I think, you can already see and understand for yourselves.

Lastly, I want to thank all of you—my family, my friends, my brothers and sisters. Forgive my terrible handwriting, and forgive me too if these words don’t sound revolutionary enough. Hehe. We’re only separated for a little while. Hopefully one day we’ll meet again under kinder circumstances, in a better time than this. Until then, take care of yourselves. Be more careful out there. I think the road ahead is still very long. Peace be upon you.

Komar Medaeng Prison, Surabaya April 29, 2026

Yogyakarta Regional Police was visited by students and residents of Yogyakarta. The crowd demanded the release of ALL remaining detainees from the August 2025 uprising. Hundreds of students and residents held a protest in front of the Yogyakarta Regional Police Headquarters on Tuesday (February 24). The demonstration was sparked by anger over the death of a 14-year-old student in Maluku, assaulted by members of the Mobile Brigade Corps (Brimob).The protesters marched from UPN to the Regional Police Headquarters without any written demands or a stage. The protest was described as spontaneous and an expression of disappointed anger. Observations on the ground revealed that the fence on the east side of the Regional Police Headquarters had collapsed. Officers stood guard behind barbed wire to prevent the crowd from entering the police station area. Several police were injured. The people set fires at the police compound, launched fireworks and clashed with police and denounced the police-terror and the Prabowo regime.

Revenge for the prisoners, the tortured, the killed and the disappeared.

Destroy all states — Destroy all police and jailers.

We must ensure our comrades aren’t alone! Send letters of solidarity, love, and rage. Out of the approximately 650 people still detained (either imprisoned or awaiting court decisions) from the August 2025 insurrection, here are two anarchist prisoners who can read English.

Adit: Aditya Nur Cahya Jl. Jakarta Lapas Kebon Waru Kec. Batununggal Kota Bandung West Java 40272 Indonesia Komar: Muhammad Ainun Komarullah Jl. Letjen Sutoyo Komp. Kehakiman Medaeng Kec. War Kabupaten Sidoarjo East Java 61256 Indonesia

author: Maira Escardovelli
title: Fim da escala 6×1 é a maior mudança na jornada do trabalhador brasileiro desde 1988
content:
O Senado Federal aprovou nesta quarta-feira, 14 de outubro, a Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) que determina o fim da escala 6×1, que estabelecia seis dias de trabalho, com somente uma folga por semana. O novo texto constitucional prevê a redução gradual da jornada de trabalho semanal de 44 para 40 horas, sem redução salarial. Desde a promulgação da Constituição Federal de 1988 que a jornada de trabalho no Brasil não sofria uma redução. Foi a Constituição da redemocratização do país que diminuiu para 44 horas a jornada máxima de trabalho semanal que era até então de 48 horas.




A chamada “PEC do fim da 6×1” é uma das principais bandeiras de campanha para a reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. 

A votação teve 75 votos favoráveis e apenas um contra, o do senador Hamilton Mourão (Republicanos-RS), ex-vice-presidente no governo de Jair Bolsonaro. No fim da votação dos dois turnos, os senadores aliados ao governo chegaram a entoar um dos jingles mais famosos da campanha à reeleição de Lula.




A votação em dois turnos no mesmo dia foi viabilizada a partir do requerimento apresentado à Mesa Diretora pela líder do governo no Senado, Teresa Leitão (PT-CE), que conquistou a assinatura de 56 senadores para aprovação do pedido. Partidos de oposição ao governo, como Progressistas (PP) e Partido Liberal (PL), liberaram suas bancadas para votação da PEC. A bancada do Republicanos votou a favor da proposta.




Líder do PT no Senado, Teresa Leitão foi a articuladora da votação da PEC em dois turnos




“Sim, principalmente pelas trabalhadoras, mães atípicas, que serão as mais beneficiadas”, afirmou a senadora Damares Alves (Republicanos-DF), durante a votação. O apoio às mães atípicas é uma das principais bandeiras defendidas pela ex-primeira dama Michelle Bolsonaro, que ocupará uma cadeira no Senado Federal no próximo ano.




Na abertura da sessão desta quarta-feira, o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), destacou que cumpriu com sua palavra ao pautar a discussão da PEC. “Nos últimos meses e semanas, afirmei publicamente que a proposta seria pautada depois das eleições. 

Assumi esse compromisso para que cada senador e senadora pudesse decidir, passada a disputa eleitoral, com liberdade, consciência e convicção. Hoje, nesta sessão deliberativa, cumpro a minha palavra”, declarou Alcolumbre. “Para quem acorda cedo, pega ônibus lotado, cumpre sua jornada e volta para casa no fim do dia, essa é uma mudança gigantesca”, completou.




Em suas redes sociais, o presidente Lula também comemorou a aprovação. “É oficial: a escala 6×1 acabou! Hoje é dia de comemorar uma conquista histórica de milhões de trabalhadores e trabalhadoras. O fim da 6×1 é mais do que uma mudança na jornada. É mais tempo para viver, descansar, estar com a família, acompanhar os filhos crescerem, cuidar de si e aproveitar a vida. Quem trabalha tanto para construir o Brasil também merece ter tempo para viver”, declarou a postagem do presidente na rede social X (antigo Twitter).




Mesmo ausente no Senado, o candidato à Presidência Flávio Bolsonaro também votou, de forma online, a favor da PEC que põe fim à Escala 6×1. Até a última terça-feira, 13 de outubro, o candidato evitou se comprometer com a votação da proposta e defendia como alternativa ao fim da escala 6×1, a inclusão na Constituição do regime de pagamento por hora trabalhada. A mudança ocorreu depois de uma visita ao pai, o ex-presidente, Jair Bolsonaro, que está em prisão domiciliar, condenado pela tentativa de golpe de Estado.




Flávio Bolsonaro não se manifestou nas redes sobre o assunto e preferiu publicar um vídeo, na noite desta quarta-feira, defendendo a redução da maioridade penal.




O caminho até a aprovação da PEC




A votação foi pautada após ter sido aprovada em dois turnos pela Câmara dos Deputados no dia 27 de maio deste ano. Na ocasião, o presidente da Casa, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), determinou a discussão pelo plenário no mesmo dia em que o parecer do relator, o deputado Leo Prates (Republicanos-BA), foi aprovado na Comissão Especial sobre o tema da Casa Legislativa por 34 votos favoráveis e 4 contrários. Já no plenário, a aprovação do texto veio com 472 votos a favor e 22 contra, no primeiro turno e 461 a 19, no segundo turno.




Apesar de ter sido aprovada pela Câmara em maio, a PEC só voltou a ser discutida no Congresso Nacional cerca de quatro meses depois. A demora inspirou a oposição e o Centrão a 

desenvolver a proposta

 de substituir o fim da jornada 6×1 pelo regime de trabalho pago por hora em junho deste ano, como mostrou a Agência Pública. O acordo para retomar a tramitação da PEC ocorreu já no segundo semestre entre o presidente Lula, Alcolumbre e Hugo Motta. Os três se encontraram em 27 de agosto, no Palácio da Alvorada, e indicaram o avanço na tramitação de propostas de interesse do governo, entre elas as PECs da Escala 6×1 e da Segurança Pública, que estavam paradas na Casa Alta.




A reunião ocorreu após meses de afastamento entre o governo federal e Alcolumbre, iniciados quando o Senado rejeitou a indicação por Lula de Jorge Messias, Advogado-Geral da União, a vaga de ministro no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF).




Já como resultado do acordo, na última semana de atividades do Congresso, antes do recesso eleitoral, durante o chamado esforço concentrado, as duas PECs foram deliberadas e aprovadas na Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) do Senado. O relator da PEC sobre a jornada de trabalho na CCJ, senador Omar Aziz (PSD-AM), rejeitou todas as emendas apresentadas e não alterou o texto da proposta, como parte da estratégia do governo para que a PEC continuasse caminhando na Casa. Se o relatório fosse alterado por Aziz, a proposta deveria voltar à Câmara para ser novamente analisada pelos deputados.




Aprovada de forma simbólica, apenas quatro senadores registraram seus votos e se posicionaram contra a proposta na Comissão: Hamilton Mourão (Republicanos-RS), Jaime Bagattoli (PL-RO), Rogério Marinho (PL-RN) e Tereza Cristina (PP-MS).




Proposta de pagamento por horas trabalhadas




O senador Rogério Marinho, que também é coordenador da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) à Presidência da República, apresentou em maio uma PEC que flexibiliza a jornada de trabalho. No lugar do fim da escala 6×1, a proposta defende que o trabalhador possa escolher entre o regime previsto pela Consolidação das Leis do Trabalho (CLT) ou o pagamento por horas trabalhadas, em um regime flexível determinado a partir do acordo entre patrão e empregado. Benefícios como FGTS, férias e 13º salário também seriam pagos proporcionalmente.




Senador Rogério Marinho (PL-RN) é autor da PEC que pretende criar no Brasil o regime de trabalho com pagamento por hora




Apesar de ter afirmado nesta terça-feira, dia 13 de outubro, que votaria no plenário a favor do fim da escala 6×1, Flávio Bolsonaro apoia a PEC apresentada por Marinho. 

Não à toa, o líder do Partido Liberal (PL) na Câmara dos Deputados, o deputado Sóstenes Cavalcante (PL-RJ), afirmou, antes do início da sessão de votação que pode acabar com a escala 6×1, que Flávio deve caminhar com a tramitação da PEC que flexibiliza a jornada de trabalho.




“Queremos redução da jornada de trabalho e liberdade para o trabalhador. Como o governo só quer fazer demagogia eleitoral, votamos o fim da jornada 6×1 e ano que vem aprovamos o pagamento por hora trabalhada”, declarou Sóstenes. A jornalistas, o líder do partido no Senado, Carlos Portinho (PL-RJ), afirmou, também, que o PL vai trabalhar no próximo ano, em um possível governo de Flávio, para mudar o que for aprovado na PEC da 6×1.




Durante a votação, a senadora Teresa Leitão, líder do governo no Senado, chamou atenção para a estratégia da oposição de mudar a pauta. “Tem votos que estão vindo agora [para a PEC do fim da 6×1] para Flávio melhorar na eleição, mas depois esses votos vão mudar na posição de uma nova PEC”, afirmou em referência a “PEC das horas trabalhadas”, de Rogerinho Marinho.




Quando a PEC do fim da escala 6×1 ganhou força?




Apesar de propostas para reduzir a jornada de trabalho terem sido apresentadas no Congresso Nacional desde 1990, a luta pelo fim da escala 6×1 alcançou maior popularidade somente nos últimos três anos, após a repercussão de uma petição pública online organizada pelo Movimento Vida Além do Trabalho (VAT), liderado pelo atual vereador e deputado federal eleito Ricardo (Rick) Azevedo (PSOL-RJ).




Vereador Rick Azevedo foi o fundador do movimento Vida Além do Trabalho (VAT) que inspirou a proposta de fim da escala 6×1 no Brasil




Em 2023, antes de entrar na carreira política, Azevedo trabalhava como caixa em uma farmácia no Rio de Janeiro, quando publicou vídeos no TikTok compartilhando sua rotina, com seis dias de trabalho e apenas um de descanso. “Eu não tenho filho, não tenho marido, sou sozinho e não consigo fazer as coisas, imagina quem tem tudo isso e casa para cuidar. A pessoa se doa para a empresa seis dias na semana e só tem um dia para folgar, isso para ganhar um salário mínimo”, declarou em uma das publicações.




Com a viralização dos vídeos, ele criou grupos nos aplicativos de mensagens instantâneas WhatsApp e Telegram que impulsionaram o movimento. 

Depois de ser catapultado a uma vaga na Câmara Municipal do Rio de Janeiro, Rick Azevedo chega à Câmara dos Deputados em 2027, após alcançar mais de 190 mil votos nas eleições deste ano.




A jornada de trabalho pode inclusive impactar no direito ao voto, conforme a Agência Pública mostrou 

nesta reportagem

. Depois de acompanhar as dificuldades dos trabalhadores que encaram a escala 6×1 para votarem nas eleições de 2022 e 2024, o Ministério Público do Trabalho (MPT) do Rio Grande do Sul obrigou um grupo de empresas a garantir que os empregados tivessem tempo de votar no primeiro turno das eleições deste ano.




A petição “Por um Brasil que vai além do trabalho: VAT e Ricardo Azevedo na vanguarda da mudança” atingiu quase três milhões de assinaturas, chegando a ser citada pela deputada federal Erika Hilton (PSOL-SP) 

na justificativa da PEC 8/2025

, apresentada por ela e outros parlamentares. A proposta previa o modelo 4×3 de jornada de trabalho.




No texto, Hilton afirma que a alteração “reflete um movimento global em direção a modelos de trabalho mais flexíveis aos trabalhadores, reconhecendo a necessidade de adaptação às novas realidades do mercado de trabalho e às demandas por melhor qualidade de vida dos trabalhadores e de seus familiares”.




A proposta da deputada ganhou tração na Câmara e passou a tramitar junto à PEC 221/2019, de autoria do deputado Reginaldo Lopes (PT-MG), que defendia a redução de 44 para 36 horas semanais de trabalho. “Todos tentaram impedir que a nossa matéria desse andamento, quando ela foi protocolada na Câmara. Na própria Câmara houve inúmeras tentativas de obstruir, colocar emendas, mudar o tempo de transição que havia sido proposto. Todas as manobras regimentais foram usadas, mas nós conseguimos aprovar com um quórum altíssimo de deputados”, declarou a deputada a jornalistas nesta quarta-feira, 14 de outubro, durante a sessão da 6×1 no Senado.




Deputada federal Erika Hilton (PSOL-SP) esteve no Senado e acompanhou a votação da PEC que altera a jornada de trabalho




“Os trabalhadores estão aguardando pelo fim da escala 6×1. E nenhuma manobra feita pelos aliados do Flávio Bolsonaro, inclusive já há apresentação de requerimento para tentar aprovar a PEC das horas trabalhadas [referência a PEC apresentada por Rogério Marinho], e emenda tentando mudar o tempo de transição, mas todas elas também serão derrotadas”, completou.




Com maior projeção após a defesa do fim da escala 6×1, Hilton foi reeleita no pleito de 2026 com mais de 1,5 milhão de votos, alcançando a marca de mulher mais votada da história na Câmara dos Deputados.

title: Ankara-Bakü başörtüsü krizi: Bahçeli egemenlik vurgusu yaptı, Aliyev İsrail Cumhurbaşkanıyla görüştü
content:
Azerbaycan Cumhurbaşkanı İlham Aliyev'in başkanı olduğu Yeni Azerbaycan Partisi (YAP), okullardaki başörtüsü yasağına karşı çıkan Erdoğan'ın başdanışmanlarından Oktay Saral'ı ve AKP milletvekillerini hedef aldı.




Aliyev 13 Ekim açıklamasında Ankara'yı Azerbaycan'ın içişlerine müdahale etmemeye çağırdı. Bir gün sonra MHP Genel Başkanı Devlet Bahçeli, Türk devletleri arasındaki ilişkilerin egemenliğe ve iç hukuka saygı temelinde yürütülmesi gerektiğini açıkladı.




Bahçeli, 14 Ekim'deki yazılı açıklamasında, “Her bir Türk Cumhuriyeti kendi içinde müstakil ve egemen bir devlettir” dedi. Türk devletleri arasındaki işbirliğinin “karşılıklı saygı, eşitlik ve ortak menfaatler” temelinde geliştiğini belirtti; 30 Ekim'deki Türk Devletleri Teşkilatı zirvesinde Cumhurbaşkanları Erdoğan ve Aliyev'in buluşacağını hatırlattı.




YAP: “Bir millet, iki bağımsız devlet”




YAP'ın 13 Ekim açıklaması, iki ülkenin ilişkilerinde sıkça kullanılan “Bir millet, iki devlet” formülüne ayrı bir yorum getirdi:







“Bu ilke, bir devletin diğerinin içişlerine müdahale etmesine veya kendi siyasi ve ideolojik yaklaşımlarını dayatmasına hiçbir biçimde dayanak oluşturmaz.”







Açıklamada Türkiye'deki bazı iktidar yanlısı medya kuruluşlarının Azerbaycan hakkında “gerçeğe aykırı, taraflı ve karalayıcı” yayınlar yaptığı öne sürüldü. Saral'ın ve AKP milletvekillerinin sözleri “popülist ve sorumsuz” olarak nitelendirildi.




YAP, başörtüsü gibi hassas konuların Azerbaycan'a siyasi baskı amacıyla kullanılmasını reddederek Erdoağn'ın Genel Başkanı olduğu "AKP iktidarını" uyardı:







“AKP iktidarını bu zararlı siyasetten kaçınmaya çağırıyoruz.”







Parti, İslam dünyasında hiçbir devletin diğer Müslüman halklara iradesini dayatma veya kendisini üstün görme hakkı bulunmadığını savundu. Bu arada, Türkiye'yle tarihsel dostluğu ve ortaklığı sürdürme isteğini de bildirdi. 




Yasak metninde “başörtüsü” sözcüğü yok




Azerbaycan Bakanlar Kurulunun 21 Eylül'de değiştirdiği devlet okulu kıyafet kuralları, üniformanın bütünlüğünü bozan veya laik eğitim ilkesine aykırı görülen ek kıyafetleri yasaklıyor.




Kurallarda başörtüsünden açıkça bahsedilmese de, uygulamada başörtülü öğrencilerin ve öğretmenlerin okula alınmadığına ilişkin tanıklıklar ve görüntüler yayımlandı. Ekim başında öğretmenlerin kıyafetlerine ilişkin yeni düzenlemeler de yapıldı.




Azerbaycan İçişleri Bakanlığı, protestolar sırasında kamu düzenini bozdukları gerekçesiyle 37 kişinin gözaltına alındığını açıkladı. Buna karşılık, yeni kurallara karşı ders boykotları ve gösteriler de devam etti. 




Bakü'de 23 yıldır İngilizce öğretmenliği yapan Gülşen Aliyeva, El Cezire'ye hem kendisinin hem kızının başörtüsü nedeniyle okula alınmadığını anlattı:







“Dini inancımın çalışmama engel olmasına meydan verilmeden görevimi yapmak, öğrencilere ders vermek ve mesleğimi sürdürmek istiyorum.”







Aliyeva, çalışma ve eğitim haklarını aramak üzere yetkili makamlara başvuracağını söyledi.




Milli Meclis İnsan Hakları Komitesi Başkanı Zahid Oruj ise “Okul dışında başörtüsü takılması yasak değil” diyerek düzenlemenin amacının eğitim ortamında ortak kıyafet kurallarını korumak olduğunu savundu.




Muhalefetteki REAL Partisi Başkanı Natiq Caferli, öğrenciler için uzlaşma aranmasını isterken şunları söyledi:







“Öğretmenler yetişkindir; nasıl giyineceklerine kısıtlama getirmek yanlış bir yaklaşımdır.” 







Ankara'da aynı cepheden farklı sesler




Cumhurbaşkanı Başdanışmanı Oktay Saral, 12 Ekim'de X hesabından “İnancı gereği başını örten bir öğrenciyi okul kapısında bırakmak hangi vicdana, hangi adalete sığar?” diye sordu.




“Başörtüsü engel değil, inancın gereğidir.”




Saral, Bakü'den kararını geri almasını istedi. AKP milletvekilleri de yasağa itiraz etti. 




AKP Sözcüsü Ömer Çelik, 7 Ekim'de Türkiye ile Azerbaycan'ın arasına girilmesine izin vermeyeceklerini söylemişti. MHP lideri Bahçeli 14 Ekim açıklamasında iki ülkenin kendi iç hukukuna saygı vurgusu yaptı. Cumhur İttifakı'ndan Saral'ın, doğrudan geri adım çağrısına karşılık Bahçeli'nin Azerbaycan'ın egemenliğine saygı vurgusu belirgin eğilim farklılıklarını yansıttı. 




Bahçeli'nin açıklamasına göre Erdoğan ve Aliyev'in 30 Ekim'de Ankara'daki Türk Devletleri Teşkilatı zirvesinde görüşmesi bekleniyor. 15 Ekim'de Bakü'de yapılacak Asya'da İşbirliği ve Güven Artırıcı Önlemler Konferansı zirvesinde Erdoğan'ı Dışişleri Bakanı Hakan Fidan temsil edecek. 




İsrail neden başörtüsü açıklamasında yer aldı?




YAP, Türkiye'den gelen eleştirilere yanıtında Azerbaycan-İsrail ilişkilerini savunmaya da geniş yer ayırdı:







“Azerbaycan Cumhuriyeti, İsrail'le uluslararası hukuk ve karşılıklı çıkarlar temelinde normal devletlerarası ilişkiler yürütüyor.”







Parti, başkenti Doğu Kudüs olan Filistin devletini içeren iki devletli çözümü de desteklediğini ifade etti. 




Aliyev, başörtüsü konusunda Türkiye ile anlaşmazlığın gündemde olduğu 14 Ekim'de Bakü'de İsrail Cumhurbaşkanı Isaac Herzog'la görüştü. 




Azerbaycan'ın İsrail'le enerji, savunma ve güvenlik alanlarındaki ilişkileri uzun süredir devam ediyor. YAP'ın açıklaması, Türkiye'deki iktidar çevrelerinin bu ilişki üzerinden yönelttiği eleştirileri de reddediyor.




Azerbaycan basını ayrıca İran'ın Sahar Azeri televizyonunun Türkiye'de çekilen protesto görüntülerini Bakü'deki gösteriler gibi sunduğunu ileri sürdü. 




Laiklik ve din özgürlüğü aynı tartışmada




Azerbaycan Anayasası'nın 7 ve 18'inci maddeleri devletin ve eğitimin laik niteliğini, 48'inci maddesi vicdan özgürlüğünü güvence altına alıyor. Hükümet okul kıyafeti kararını laiklik, eşitlik ve hukuk devleti ilkeleriyle savunuyor.




Azerbaycan'daki Toplumsal Araştırmalar İçin Hoşgörü Derneği Başkanı Azer Reşidoğlu ise kuralların anayasaya uygun olmadığını savunarak etkilenenlerin mahkemeye başvurmasını istedi:




“Hakları ihlal edilenler, barışçıl ve yasal yollarla topluca haklarını aramalı.” 

Al Jazeera




Bakü'nün yeni bir uzlaşma veya yasağın uygulanmasında değişiklik kararı aldığına ilişkin herhangi bir gelişme olmadı. Türkiye-Azerbaycan ilişkilerinin resmi boyutu kapsamında savunma ve enerji işbirliği alanındaki işleyiş de bu tartışmalardan etkilenmeksizin sürüyor. 




(AEK)

author: April Holcombe
title: Chinese youth in a very shit time of their lives
content:
Certain quarters of the internet are filling with content lauding contemporary China as an advanced, anti-imperialist, even socialist society. Its unrivalled high-speed rail network and its continued use of Communist jargon have encouraged some disillusioned Western youth to declare themselves in “a very Chinese time of my life”.

State-of-the-art infrastructure and Communist iconography have obvious appeal to a section of people living in decaying, imperialist and increasingly far-right-controlled Western capitalism. But there is a big difference between Instagram China, a Potemkin country showcased by influencers at the invitation of the tourism bureau and marketed to disillusioned Western youth, and the real China, a nuclear superpower ruled by bureaucrat-businessmen.  

Young Chinese people on social media—students, workers and the unemployed—use a very different kind of language than influencers do. Theirs is the language of alienation, exploitation and oppression in a society every bit as capitalist as our own.

“Involution”: an obscure word for a common problem

Ever heard of “involution”? Me neither. This obscure academic term, translated into Chinese (内卷 

neijuan

), has entered common parlance among young people trapped in the country’s hypercompetitive economy. Literally meaning “inwardly curling”, anthropologists repurposed the term to describe activities that increase in complexity but lead nowhere. Chinese youth decided it captured their social predicament: instructed to work ever harder to stay ahead of their peers, they end up doing much more without being any better off.

Neijuan 

describes many things: the gruelling hours at Big Tech companies; the notoriously competitive university entrance examinations; the apps pushing food delivery workers to ride ever faster; and the impossible social media-influenced beauty standards. The second character is now used as a standalone verb, meaning “to work or try too hard”.

Many young people who reject the 

neijuan

 rat race opt instead to “lie flat” (躺平 

tang ping

), a vibe somewhere between “quiet quitting” and “bedrotting”. The Ministry of State Security finds it deeply disturbing that anyone would want to lie flat, claiming in a Douyin (like TikTok) video that “an unnamed overseas organisation heavily funds ‘lying flat’ influencers, mass producing short videos promoting ‘anti-involution equals anti-exploitation’”.

Successive surveys show scepticism and pessimism rising sharply. In 2014, 62 percent of 10,000 respondents agreed that “effort is always rewarded in our country”; only 28 percent agreed a decade later. One-fifth blamed “the unfair economic system” for poverty in 2014; more than one-third did a decade later. Two-thirds agreed their families’ lives would improve from 2014-19, but less than half thought so for 2023-28.

“Graduation means unemployment”

University degrees once guaranteed well-paid government or tech jobs, providing the Communist Party’s dictatorship with a large, stable base of middle-class support. But now, often, “graduation means unemployment” (毕业即失业 

biye ji shiye

). The gradual slowdown in economic growth has intensified competition for entry-level positions (more than 600 people, for example, applied for one basic Beijing office job in November 2025). Stable employment has given way to job flux. “I have family members who, since the early 2000s, never lost their jobs”, labour researcher Kevin Lin told 

Red Flag

. “Last year, my cousin was laid off for the first time. Then he struggled to find another job, got laid off again, and is on to his third job.”

Unemployment is roughly twice the official figure of 5.2 percent, according to estimates by economist Li Daokui. “There are roughly 24 million long-term discouraged unemployed people, which is highly unfavourable for social stability”, the Tsinghua University academic told the China Macroeconomic Forum in July. The youth unemployment rate, officially hitting 17.9 percent that same month, has not included students since it soared past 25 percent in 2024, and hides a vast pool of underemployed youth working as little as one hour per week.

For the first time, the Communist Party’s most recent five-year plan includes no job-creation target. On the other hand, the government has a very clear target of 70 percent AI adoption across key industries by next year, inciting fears of layoffs among many IT workers. “I still can’t shake the feeling that I’m getting closer to being replaced”, one data engineer told Reuters in June.

Those on the breadline will be lucky to get crumbs. Fewer than one-quarter of registered urban unemployed received any government income support, a 2024 assessment by the Chinese Association of Social Security found. President Xi Jinping is a vocal opponent of expanding the safety net, warning in a 2021 address that providing “excessive guarantees” to the working class risks “falling into the trap of ‘welfarism’ that encourages laziness”. 

Working like “oxen and horses” 

Today’s young graduates are increasingly forced into work with app-based employers such as Meituan (food delivery) or Didi (ridesharing). On the eve of this year’s university entrance examinations, an official Communist Youth League social media account joked: “If you don’t get in [to university], you’ll be delivering food in four days. If you do get in, you’ll be delivering food in four years”.

Meituan has turned

 neijuan 

into a fine art, shaving down the allowable delivery time to reward only the fastest riders, increasing traffic accidents and deaths. “Even flying is not quick enough”, one rider told Chinese magazine 

Renwu

. Others complained of being forced to work through typhoons and described the unbearable agony of waiting for elevators as the delivery clock ticked.

More than 250 million workers in the gig economy lack a formal labour contract, according to National People’s Congress Standing Committee member Zheng Gongcheng, which means they have no access to vastly superior employment-based health insurance and pensions. They say they are treated more like oxen and horses (牛马 

niuma

).

In his 2026 memoir 

I Deliver Parcels in Beijing, 

Hu Anyan described what that meant for him when he developed viral pneumonia. “Since I was still a contract worker, it cost me 50 yuan [the Chinese currency] just for the registration fee, every day that I went to hospital for liquids”, he wrote. “This single period of illness set me back some 3,000 yuan, which was what I earned in half a month.”

The government occasionally voices “concern” for delivery riders. But those concerns would be more credible if it hadn’t imprisoned worker activist Chen Guojiang. An administrator of a WeChat group with 14,000 fellow riders, Chen was arrested twice for attempting to organise nationwide strikes. While he languished behind bars for 10 months in 2021, Meituan’s billionaire founder Wang Xing attended lavish celebrations for the Communist Party’s centenary. 

China is suffering from the kind of contradiction only capitalism can come up with: rising levels of overwork alongside growing underemployment. Despite public outcry about the tech sector’s 996 regimen (9am to 9pm, six days per week), and a 2021 court ruling against it, the regimen remains standard. Baidu (akin to Google) head of public relations Qu Jing told workers that 996’s health effects were not her concern. “I’m not your mother. Don’t expect weekends off”, she said in a May 2024 video posted to Douyin, provoking public fury which forced her resignation but has not stopped China from clocking its longest average working week in more than 20 years.

Government suppression of workers’ democratic rights helps bosses rule with the same impunity in the workplace. In August, an office worker called Yang was hospitalised with rhabdomyolysis, an extreme muscular breakdown, after her manager reportedly forced her to perform 200 squats for missing a sales target. “Our objective is to make money, and that definitely requires a certain amount of pressure”, the manager in question later told news reporters.

“No husbands and no babies protects your peace”

Beyond the economy, sexism is a major issue animating young people. With women’s education levels and workforce participation at record highs, the expectation of equal treatment and opportunities rubs abrasively against the continued reality of oppression. Women in China face all the same sexual harassment, workplace discrimination, gender pay gap, online misogyny, impossible beauty standards and conservative “family values” that are pissing off so many women in the West. 

Hong Kong-based socialist Lam Chi-Leung told 

Red Flag

 that anti-sexism began taking an organised form in the late 2000s and early 2010s, mostly by liberal university students and professors. “It was not quite a movement, but it was a public struggle”, Lam said. “There were actions on the street, around public toilets, on campuses, on the subway.”

After a hard government crackdown in 2015, with the closure of dozens of NGOs and the high-profile arrests of five feminist activists, public acts of anti-sexism declined but the mood deepened. “In 2018 and 2019, the #MeToo movement [a US-based campaign bringing to light sexual violence by powerful men] spread to China very rapidly. Attention on the Chinese internet was extremely high”, Lam said.

When women publicly accused high-profile figures of misogyny and sexual assault, China’s ruling class bristled at their nerve. Tennis player Peng Shuai disappeared for years after accusing former Vice Premier Zhang Gaoli of rape. #MeToo was banned from social media, prompting netizens to talk instead about “rice bunny” (米兔, pronounced 

mitu

).

With China experiencing an ageing population and plummeting birthrates, the government is dialling up the pressure on women of childbearing age. This year, the 13 percent value-added tax was applied to condoms and other contraception products for the first time. Some local governments have taken to cold-calling women and asking when they last had their period.

The more the government is seen to press the issue, the more bitter the resistance. Among radical feminist currents, opposition has hardened against ever becoming a “marriage donkey” (婚驴 

hunlu

) or raising children. “No husbands and no babies protects your peace”, they say (不婚不育保平安 

buhun buyu baoping’an

). For those who still want to have children, the costs remain prohibitive. China is one of the world’s most expensive places to raise a child, according to 2024 data from the YuWa Population Research Institute in Beijing. 

Much like in the US, South Korea or Australia, women face a sexist backlash from misogynists, online and offline, who blame them for dating troubles and employment struggles. The most aggressive trolls call women’s rights ideology an unpatriotic, foreign import designed to weaken China from within, highlighting that modern-day Chinese nationalism is run-of-the-mill right-wing chauvinism, not progressive anti-imperialism.

In Lam’s view, President Xi is hostile to feminist sentiment not because he is all-in on the manosphere, but because it publicly airs discontent. “The general dissatisfaction of the masses is very great. In this context, President Xi thinks anything that might stir up social conflict is dangerous”. In the eastern province of Zhejiang, the provincial publicity authority has even advised female stand-up comedians against “stirring up gender antagonism” as some take to the stage to complain about mediocre men or abusive ex-husbands. 

There’s no slang yet for “rising up”, only lying down

The potential for all this discontent to explode into mass struggle is always present, but several factors mitigate against it in the current moment.

First, Chinese people are not yet experiencing a sharp decline in living standards akin to the austerity inflicted on North America and Europe after the global financial crisis or during the post-COVID sovereign debt crises that have swept the Global South. The dramatic slowdown in China’s real wage growth is offset by near-zero price inflation for most consumer goods. 

Kevin Lin compared the situation to that of its neighbour. “In India, it is really a question of survival. If your wages are not going up, you may have to cut down your meals”, he explained. “I don’t think we’re seeing that in China. Of course, the challenge is if you want to buy a house.”

The A$26 trillion elephant in the room is China’s property market slump since 2021. The government prevented a broader economic crisis, but appears to be at a loss for ways to revive construction. Prolonged stagnation could feed its own kind of desperation, since price deflation worsens mortgage debt and encourages working-class and middle-class households to cut or defer discretionary spending.

Second, state surveillance, censorship and harassment make political organising extraordinarily difficult. The brutal 2019 crackdown on socialist students clearly demonstrated the stakes. 

After workers at Jasic Technology Factory in Shenzhen were sacked and arrested for starting a unionisation petition in June 2018, dozens of Maoist-leaning activists converged from across the country to form the Jasic Workers Solidarity Group. City authorities quickly expelled them and a nationwide manhunt of all known JWSG activists and associates ensued. 

Ten months later, police were still dragging students out of Beijing University classrooms and toilet cubicles to interrogate, threaten and torture them. Marxist Studies campus clubs were purged of the left and reorganised under the leadership of the privileged children of elite party bosses.

Another challenge is that China is an enormous country ruled by a sprawling, relatively decentralised apparatus, which makes big-picture political consciousness harder to develop. It is simpler, and safer, to blame corrupt local officials or lawbreaking bosses than to criticise the entire system of party-state capitalism.

The COVID-19 pandemic provided a rare case in November 2022 of a nationwide issue pitting unrest squarely against the central government. What began with calls to end harsh lockdowns snowballed into the White Paper protests, so called because participants held up blank pages to symbolise what they could not say. The protests, which for the first time in generations swept the campuses, included open chanting for press freedom and President Xi’s resignation. 

“The people involved in the protests, of course, were talking about democracy, authoritarianism, freedom of speech”, Lin said. “Underlying that was a kind of economic insecurity: most of the protesters involved are college graduates who feel their lives are stuck.”

Lam said that no lasting organisation emerged from the short-lived 2022 protests, although a small layer of students were pushed to the radical left. Lin noted greater interest in anarchism among the activists he has recently spoken with. Within more coherent left tendencies, Maoism is the dominant oppositional current, which makes things difficult for the much smaller but more principled collections of Trotskyists, against whom Maoists are notoriously hostile. But budding young Trotskyists are using encrypted online forums to share ideas.

Since none of these forces is yet in any position to shape politics, the question remains whether future youth protests aim merely for Western-style liberalism or set themselves much more boldly against capitalism. On this score, recent conversations in China have given Kevin Lin hope. “There are fewer illusions in the Chinese system”, he said, “and there are also fewer illusions about the US government, what the West can deliver, or what life in America looks like”. 

Radicalising Western youth should take heed. Instead of exchanging one set of ruling-class lies for another, we need to build a truly internationalist opposition to capitalist exploitation everywhere.

author: Unknown
title: Ilya Kharkow - I destroy the sense of all insults
content:
Author

: Ilya Kharkow

Title

: I destroy the sense of all insults

Date

: 06/03/2024

Source

: https://questionmark.lgbt/i-destroy-the-sense-of-all-insults/







Marilyn Monroe once said that love and work are the only worthwhile things in life. Trying to combine them, I invented sex.







What do our readers need to know about you?




 My name is Ilya Kharkow. I like polo shirts, anarcho-individualism and PrEP. I’m a writer from Ukraine, but I don’t consider myself a Ukrainian writer. I can only be presented as a rights activist if we are talking about the rights of guys during wartime. But when we talk about me as a gay guy, what is important to me is not rights, but privileges. 




 Today I’ll talk about this in more detail, because 

I want people to come to me not only for revolution, but also for eroticism.




What do you mean?




 The thing is, I’m not a genre writer. Not only do I dislike government restrictions, I also don’t accept restrictions in literature. 

I perceive books as real life, and therefore I try to cram real life into a book with all its unshaven armpits, smells, and stains.




 Most books today are repetitions of well-working schemes. But it’s boring. This has nothing to do with art. A book is not a plot, but an experience and impressions. And I know that experience doesn’t always smell good. 




My goal as a writer is not just to sleep with a young astronomer, but to drag the reader into my bed and make him enjoy someone else’s awkwardness

. Allow the reader to study our moles instead of constellations through the astronomer’s remarks. 

This way I turned sex into my job, but did not become a prostitute.




Can you give an example from your work when you invite the reader into someone’s bed?




 Right after I left Ukraine, I went to a flea market. There I bought an American half dollar coin with Kennedy’s elegant profile on it. I literally fell in love with this profile, and the seller noticed it. 




 I wanted to buy this coin, but I didn’t know what to do with it. Coins can be so beautiful, but if they cannot be spent, they are worthless. The seller advised me to keep the coin in my pocket until I met someone I really like. 




 And then a year ago I gave the coin to an unexpected person. I accidentally met a guy in exile with whom I had been planning a date for 5 years. 5 damn years! Then we spend 3 days in a rented apartment. To get into our bed and find out exactly what happened there, you should read my short story. In this case, for you the title of the story is the code for the door to our bedroom. It’s called ZODIAC DECADENCE IN MY PANTS. 




How did you started writing?




 I don’t remember what came first: masturbation or passion for literature. I think at the same time. 




Masturbation is a great scam

. At first, erotic fantasies involve you in this process, but as soon as it is over, the guy immediately finds himself thrown into a hostile, uncomfortable world. The leap from warm fantasies to a hostile world occurs in a second. I remember that I started writing in order to prolong a pleasant moment for at least a few pages. 




And how can a gay writer prolong pleasure in Ukraine today?




 Firstly, I live in Portugal, not in Ukraine. Secondly, 

I don’t consider myself either a Ukrainian or a Ukrainian writer

. I must repeat this, because in Ukrainian literature there have been several cases of appropriation of writers of a foreign culture. Even if they wrote anti-Ukrainian works, such as Mikhail Bulgakov. Even if they didn’t write in Ukrainian like me. 




 And yet, I’d say that 

today in Ukraine it’s dangerous not only to be a gay writer, but also to have any position that differs from the official one

. Local patriots pay 1,500 hryvnia for public humiliation on camera of those who speak freely. 1500 hryvnia is approximately 35 euros. With this money you can buy 2 solid books in Europe, or you can order the humiliation of a Ukrainian guy. 




Are you afraid for your life?




 When I was in Ukraine, I could have died from Russian missiles. When I tried to leave the country, I could have died at the hands of the Ukrainian military, who catch guys on the street and forcefully send them to war. 

Over the past 2 years, I have imagined my death so often that I am tired of dying.




 Moreover, it is not patriots who constitute the main danger for me in exile, but the Ukrainian government. Ukrainian officials periodically appeal to European countries with a request to deport the guys, so that Ukraine will force us to choose: prison or war. 




Are there topics that you basically don’t write about?




 Of course, everything that is usually written about does not interest me. 

But everything that causes embarrassment or bewilderment is the subject of my study.




 That’s why I find talking about penis size wonderful. Sexually transmitted diseases? I will be happy to write a couple of paragraphs about this. But only in the context of analysis, because analysis is the path to perfection. Analysis is a wrinkle cure for your inner child. Does it make you horny? For now it shouldn’t. 




Other than penises, what else do you enjoy writing about?




 In fact, I’ve been writing too much about war lately. I wrote about human rights, and in particular about the right of guys to refuse military service. But I don’t want war to become my main topic. 




...

author: Priya T.
title: Eugene Debs—the socialist who won a million votes
content:
Eugene Debs was the most popular and beloved socialist leader in United States history. Famed for exceptional speechmaking, the Socialist Party of America raised $20,000 to buy a train for Debs’ inaugural run for president in 1906. The “Red Special” carried Debs across the country to hundreds of meetings, from the union halls of mining towns to a mass gathering of more than 10,000 workers at New York’s Madison Square Garden. 

A lifetime of struggle, and the lessons born from bitter defeats, transformed Debs from a trade unionist and Democrat to a socialist committed to building a working-class party. 

Debs was born in 1855 in the small town of Terre Haute in Indiana. At fourteen, he started working on the railroads. Railways were central to the industrial expansion going on in the United States at the time, connecting major cities and transporting commodities between them. Capitalists employed gangster violence against unions, keeping working conditions dangerous and wages pitiful. Ray Ginger, in his famous 1949 biography of Debs, writes that in his fifth year on the railways, a friend and workmate of Debs fell under a train and died. Worried he’d meet the same all-too-common fate, Debs returned to Terre Haute shortly afterwards. 

While working at a grocery store, Debs took an administrative role at a trade union, the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers. Initially, his attitudes were relatively conservative. He supported the system of craft unionism that dominated the United States, where workers were organised by trade. Railway engineers, firefighters, drivers and conductors might all be in different unions, working on the same train. Debs also viewed strikes as messy actions of last resort, writing in 1880 that while the Brotherhood sympathised with the “deluded and miserable wretches” who engaged in strikes, they believed in “a different way of settling difficulties between employer and employee. We believe in arbitration”. 

Over time, Debs became fed up with craft unionism and turned against it. The various brotherhoods did not support each other. Scabbing during strikes was common, as brotherhoods wanted to advance their own section’s interests, even at the expense of other workers. Debs encountered sectionalism as a barrier to organising the engineers. He began to believe that if unions remained divided, working conditions on the railways would never improve.

Although it caused considerable internal strife, Debs tried to amalgamate the brotherhoods to form a larger union covering the entire industry and all the trades within it. This industrial unionism approach was widespread among socialists at the time. Debs was particularly inspired by the Western Federation of Miners and its leader, “Big” Bill Haywood. 

In 1893, Debs helped form the American Railway Union as an industrial union. It was exceedingly popular, with thousands of workers joining in the weeks following its establishment, many of them young and previously unorganised. The overwhelming enthusiasm for the ARU seemed to vindicate the approach of industrial unionism. 

But as president of the ARU, Debs’ politics were contradictory. In 1894, he argued that if workers achieved vast industrial organisation, striking “would be remanded to the chamber relic of the past. An era of good will and peace would dawn”. This perspective was simultaneously militant and limited. Debs advocated working-class unity, but believed that class interests could be reconciled.

The 1894 Pullman dispute, later known as the “Debs Rebellion”, changed everything. Workers at the Pullman Factory, outside Chicago, were impoverished. The company owned all the town’s housing. After years of work, many were indebted to their employer because of extortionate rents. A proposed wage cut pushed ARU members to launch a wildcat strike, which expanded into a national boycott of all Pullman goods. The dispute was seminal; at its height, more than 100,000 workers stopped work to respect the boycott, and rail transportation came to a standstill in much of the country. 

In response, Chicago’s mayor and President Grover Cleveland, both Democrats, intervened, issuing an injunction against ARU leaders speaking about the dispute and sending in federal troops to break up the strikes. The broader labour movement, including the conservative American Federation of Labor, had refused to support the ARU and scabbed extensively. Without the necessary solidarity, the strike was isolated and ended in terrible defeat. Thousands of ARU members lost their jobs, and Debs was jailed for contempt of court.  

The Pullman dispute stayed with Debs for the rest of his life. In a 1902 article, 

“How I became a Socialist”

, Debs said that after the Pullman dispute, he felt naive for believing that industrial organisation alone could alleviate the ills of capitalism. That approach, he concluded, underestimated how vigorously the capitalist state would fight for the ruling class: “In the gleam of every bayonet and the flash of every rifle 

the class struggle was revealed

”, he wrote. 

Debs also became oppositional to the Democratic Party. He had served one term as a local politician in Terre Haute with the Democrats and had backed Cleveland three times. Now, Debs declared: “I have been a Democrat all my life, and I am ashamed to admit it”. 

In prison, Debs began contemplating socialism. The socialist Victor Berger visited with a copy of Marx’s 

Capital, 

although Debs was more impacted by his practical experience of struggle. Initially, Debs flirted with utopian socialism, floating a plan to find a rich benefactor to establish a socialist colony in the American West. When this proved unviable, Debs returned to Marx, and Marx’s argument that workers—by virtue of their unique position within capitalism—have the ability to overthrow the ruling class and create a new type of economy based on abundance and democracy.  

In 1901, Debs helped form the Socialist Party of America. It was a step forward: a party that clearly advocated socialism and sought to represent workers’ interests independently of the Democrats and Republicans, who represented different wings of the capitalist class. But from the outset, the Socialist Party was divided over fundamental goals and objectives. 

Debs was committed to abolishing capitalism. He did not believe that socialism could be legislated through parliament, famously saying: “Voting for socialism is not socialism any more than a menu is a meal”. The Pullman dispute left Debs disgusted with politicians (he called them “misrepresentatives of the masses”), conservative trade union organisers, and the whole concept of change from above. He stressed that socialism could only be achieved through workers emancipating themselves, a view he articulated in 1906: 

“If you are looking for a Moses to lead you out of this capitalist wilderness, you will stay right where you are. I would not lead you into the promised land if I could, because if I could lead you in, someone else could lead you out. You must use your heads as well as your hands and get yourselves out of your present condition.” 

A right wing in the Socialist Party, represented by figures such as Victor Berger and Morris Hillquit and known as “sewer socialists,” limited its vision to relatively minor reforms and strove to have the government legislate them. They did not advocate for worker militancy, substantially agreeing with the approach of the conservative union bureaucracies of the American Federation of Labor, which had repeatedly sold out workers in alliances with capitalists. Berger also held openly racist attitudes, whereas Debs had opposed the practice of organising trade unions on a segregated basis, and refused to speak in front of segregated crowds. 

The moderate reformists knew Debs had a more expansive vision of socialism than they did, and they opposed it. But they allowed Debs relatively free rein to say what he wanted in public, as his enormous talent as a writer and orator was essential to building the party, and no figure could match the reputation Debs held as a leader. 

While freely advocating his views in lectures and articles, Debs did not fight to win the Socialist Party over to his left-wing perspectives. In fact, Debs largely stayed out of shaping the party’s internal politics, viewing himself primarily as a mass leader. Debs attended the first convention of the Socialist Party but never returned for the rest of his life. As a result, the party apparatus largely fell into the hands of moderate reformists. 

Debs became the most prominent and indispensable spokesperson for a party whose leadership he frequently conflicted with. Having edited a variety of union magazines, Debs took over as editor of the Socialist Party’s 

Appeal to Reason

, building it to a readership of 600,000 at its height. Although he had no desire to be a politician, Debs was so popular among party members that they repeatedly conscripted him to run for president. Believing that elections were an opportunity to educate workers in socialism, Debs campaigned relentlessly and effectively. The Socialist Party received between 400,000 and nearly 1 million votes on the occasions Debs stood for president. In 1912, he received 6 percent of the total votes cast across the country. 

The stance for which Debs is most remembered came towards the end of his life: opposing World War One. Millions of US workers were conscripted to fight in the conflict, and hundreds of thousands died. Debs, with the rights of the working class as his political compass, argued that patriotism and nationalism disguised the profit-mongering interests of capitalists that drove the war, declaring in 1918 that “the master class has always declared the wars” while the working class “fight all the battles ... make all the supreme sacrifices ... freely shed their blood and furnish the corpses”. 

The limited civil rights workers had enjoyed in peacetime were rolled back, with all criticism of the war effort criminalised and strikes labelled “unpatriotic”. Several socialists had been imprisoned for opposing the war. Debs realised that he too needed to go to jail for this cause, conceiving that this act would animate workers to stand against imperialism. 

In Canton, Ohio, in 1918, at age 63, Debs addressed thousands of workers for two hours about the crimes of the war. He knew full well that this would lead to his imprisonment, saying: “I would rather a thousand times be a free soul in jail than a sycophant and coward in the streets”. He celebrated the 1917 Russian Revolution and viewed it as the beginning of a worldwide revolution that he hoped would spread to the United States: “Socialism is a growing idea; an expanding philosophy ... It is as vain to resist it as it would be to arrest the sunrise on the morrow”. 

With that, Debs went to jail for three years. While imprisoned, the Socialist Party stood him for president again, and Debs won nearly 1 million votes from his cell, demonstrating widespread sympathy for socialism and opposition to the war. At the war’s end, President Woodrow Wilson refused to grant Debs amnesty. 

Imprisonment took a toll on Debs’ health and optimism. He lived only five years after his release. Although he maintained his opposition to the war, and desired to speak and tour, he spent much of his time in hospitals or at home. 

The post-war years were trying. The Socialist Party was collapsing. Moderate reformism dominated the party. But Debs stayed a member. Despite supporting the Russian Revolution, Debs refused to throw his weight behind the new Communist Party. Given his prestige and authority, had Debs chosen to support the new party, it may have helped unify a new socialist layer among US workers. 

Whatever his shortcomings, Eugene Debs was a committed and radical socialist, and his life was dedicated to the struggle of workers. Passionate, self-sacrificing, and brave, Debs embraced socialist principles after his experience of workers’ struggle and became someone who embodied them.

title: Ilya Kharkow - How to Ruin Statistics
content:
Author

: Ilya Kharkow

Title

: How to Ruin Statistics

Subtitle

: A Lesson from Ukraine

Source

: https://voidnetwork.gr/2026/07/07/how-to-ruin-statistics-a-lesson-from-ukraine-by-ilya-kharkow/




“Statistics likes to talk about people in large numbers, because that way it can’t see their faces.”




EXCAVATOR




 No one looks at an excavator and thinks: 




 “What a shame it’s not destroying anything right now.” 




 But the moment I refused to take part in a war, people suddenly appeared who were convinced I was wasting my life. 




LANGUAGE




 I’m tired of having to justify the fact that I was born in Ukraine and consider Russian my native language. I grew up in a Russian-speaking mining town in eastern Ukraine. It wasn’t a political statement. It was my life. 




 Before becoming president, Ukraine’s current president played a president in the popular Ukrainian TV series 

Servant of the People

. The show was in Russian. If most Ukrainians had spoken Ukrainian back then, the show probably would have been in Ukrainian too. But for some reason it wasn’t. Neither were most of the films, music, books, TV programs, and everyday conversations I grew up with. 




 Some people see language as proof of loyalty. I see it as a tool. A hammer doesn’t become guilty because someone used it to hit another person. Language doesn’t either. 




DUTY




 Talk of duty begins precisely where volunteers run out. 




 No one asks a hammer whether it wants to drive nails or crack skulls. Its value is measured solely by its usefulness. Conversations about a man’s duty to his country often work the same way. 




 If I am expected to pretend to be a tool, then let me be neither a hammer nor a rifle. I’d rather be somebody’s vibrator. 




UNITY




 On the first day of the war, I boarded a bus from Kyiv to Lviv. Back then, every missile seemed to be flying not just toward the city, but directly at you. At least that’s how it felt. 




 Somewhere along the way came the news that men were no longer allowed to leave the country. A strange feeling. That morning you had still been a person. By evening, you had become a prohibited category. 




 Then soldiers pulled me off the bus. They forced me to sign a document stating that I was volunteering for military service. Later, friends explained that such a thing couldn’t possibly have happened. Later, women on the street politely reminded me that all men were expected to report to the draft office. Later, taxi drivers stopped asking for my destination and started asking: “The draft office?” 




 TV talked about national unity. In reality, the world was losing its mind faster than a morning erection appears. I’ve already used some of these stories in my fiction. The rest are still too dangerous to publish. 




 Everyone kept saying the war would be over in a few days. Four years have passed. No, the last missile won’t change anything. Some wars end before they begin. Others continue long after the ceasefire. 




BORDERS




 There it is again: another well-fed, comfortable person talking about the importance of borders. It’s strange hearing that from people who cross dozens of invisible borders every day. 




 The border between work and home. 




 The border between a friend and a lover. 




 The border between a child and an adult. 




 The border between the person you were a year ago and the person you are today. 




 Everything good in my life began with breaking someone’s rules. So whenever I hear that borders are sacred, I remember that love, emigration, and growing up begin with crossing them. 




NATURE




 I’m tired of hearing that sex between men is unnatural. That we should look to nature for guidance. Fine. Let’s take a look at what nature actually has to offer. 




 As a child from a broken home, it pains me to write this, but nature is not particularly sentimental. A cuckoo chick dropped into another bird’s nest throws the other chicks out to monopolize the attention of its foster parents. Nobody calls that unnatural. 




 I’ve been on many dates. Some of them were terrible, but none of my partners ever tried to eat me afterward, as female praying mantises and some spiders do. 




 Ducks evolved complex reproductive anatomy to protect themselves from gang rape. 




 Maybe we shouldn’t look to nature for moral guidance in every situation. Maybe we should just make love. 




 If morality is determined by nature, then infanticide, cannibalism, and group violence must also be considered natural. 




 Fortunately, people usually build ethics not on what exists in nature, but on consent, freedom, and the absence of harm. That’s why the argument that something is “unnatural” tells us nothing about whether it is good or bad. 




 And if my sex life is still your strongest argument against me, perhaps you’ve simply run out of arguments. 




OBSERVATION




 No important story in my life has ever started with: 




 “I followed all the instructions.” 




THE FACELESS MAN




 States love faces. Faces are easy to hit. Easy to photograph. Easy to paste into documents. 




 I met the Faceless Man in Romania. He was trying to sell an old book. What interested me wasn’t the book itself, but the description. It read: 




 “They say the illustrations in this book were drawn by Satan himself.” 




 Naturally, I didn’t believe it. But I became curious about the kind of person who would advertise a book that way. That’s how I found the Faceless Man. 




...
