title: Childfree – Ein pro-choice Rollenspiel
content:
Childfree ist ein LARP darüber, dass dein Körper nur dir gehört. Darüber, sich zu ermächtigen, lebensverändernde Entscheidungen zu treffen und den eigenen Träumen und Projekten zu folgen. Es ist ein LARP über die Entscheidung, eine Schwangerschaft abzubrechen.




Es ist uns eine große Freude, unsere Ausgabe des Rollenspiels „childfree“ von Axiel Cazeneuve vorstellen zu dürfen. Wir hatten dieses Spiel im Jahr 2023 auf Französisch und Englisch herausgebracht. Zwei Jahre später haben unsere Freund*innen von 

LarpPunk

 es ins Polnische übersetzt, und nun hat das autonome Gesundheitskollektiv Geko aus Bern es ins Deutsche übersetzt.


Die Möglichkeit, frei über den eigenen Körper zu verfügen, ist nach wie vor ein umkämpftes Thema – und wird es wahrscheinlich auch bleiben, solange Einzelpersonen, Institutionen oder Nationen sich die Macht über andere anmaßen. Mit dieser Neuauflage möchten wir uns solidarisch mit all jenen zeigen, die für den freien Zugang zu Schwangerschaftsabbrüchen kämpfen, sei es durch den Kampf gegen 

Abtreibungsgesetze in Polen

 oder durch die Entwicklung von I

T-Sicherheitstools zum Schutz von Pro-Choice-Aktivist*innen in Brasilien

.




Wie alle unsere anderen Produktionen kann „Childfree“ zum freien Preis bestellt werden, und eine PDF-Version steht auf unserer Website kostenlos zur Verfügung. Um das Spiel in gedruckter Form zu bestellen oder bei der Verbreitung und Übersetzung dieses Spiels mitzuhelfen, kontaktiere uns bitte unter evasions@riseup.net.




 

 

 

 

 




Einleitung Von Axiel




„Childfree“ ist ein Live-Action-Rollenspiel – die Teilnehmenden schlüpfen physisch in Rollen, um gemeinsam eine Geschichte zu erzählen, ohne dass ein Publikum anwesend ist – für 5 bis 7 Personen, das in insgesamt vier Stunden gespielt wird. Es befasst sich mit Abtreibung, genauer gesagt mit dem freiwilligen Schwangerschaftsabbruch und bietet den Spielerinnen die Möglichkeit, einerseits die gesellschaftlichen Zwänge im Zusammenhang mit Schwangerschaft oder Abtreibung und andererseits die Individualität der schwangeren Person zu verkörpern. Der flexible und nicht-direktive Rahmen des Spiels ermöglicht es den Spielerinnen, verschiedene Situationen zu entwerfen und vorzuschlagen. Das Geschlecht der schwangeren Person, die Details ihres Lebens, der rechtliche Kontext … all dies bleibt ganz den Spielenden überlassen, die dabei durch die Spielunterlagen unterstützt werden, die so klar und einfach wie möglich gehalten sind. Die Entscheidung, die Schwangerschaft abzubrechen oder fortzusetzen, liegt natürlich ebenfalls bei der schwangeren Rolle (und somit bei der Person, die sie spielt). Indem ich eine Erfahrung biete, die vollständig von den Teilnehmenden gemeinsam gestaltet wird, wollte ich ein wenig von dem weitergeben, was ich durch einen freiwilligen Schwangerschaftsabbruch gelernt habe, sowie das Gefühl der Befreiung, das damit einherging.




Ich habe dieses Spiel 2018 geschrieben: Anlässlich der Veröffentlichung der Ausgabe durch Projet Évasions möchte ich auf meine persönliche Erfahrung zurückblicken und darauf, was mich zum Schreiben motiviert hat.




 

 

 

 

 







Ein Spiel mit wunderschönen Illustrationen von Nemo




Erfahrungen mit einer freiwilligen Schwangerschaftsunterbrechung in Frankreich im Jahr 2017




Anfang 2017 blieb meine Periode eine Woche aus. Da das ungewöhnlich war und ich zudem starke Schmerzen im unteren Rücken und in der Brust hatte, ging ich los, um einen Schwangerschaftstest zu kaufen. (Auf dem Weg dorthin machte ich einen Abstecher in den Laden um die Ecke, weil ich Heißhunger auf Fruchtgelee hatte. Als ich die einsame Pappschachtel auf dem Förderband vorbeiziehen sah, fragte ich mich, ob es sich wirklich lohnte, den Test zu machen).




Natürlich war das Testergebnis positiv. Als ich die beiden Striche erscheinen sah, versuchte ich zu weinen. Ähm … Nein, das klappt nicht. Ich versuchte zu lachen. Nein. Also griff ich zum Telefon – es war, glaube ich, ein Montag, gegen Mittag – und rief beim „Planning Familial“ an (ein Netzwerk aus Vereinen und aktivistischen Gruppen, das in Frankreich Dienstleistungen im Bereich der sexuellen Gesundheit anbietet). Folgendes habe ich wörtlich gesagt:




– „Hallo, ich habe mir vor neun Monaten bei Ihnen eine Spirale einsetzen lassen, ich habe gerade einen Schwangerschaftstest gemacht und er ist positiv.




Stille.




– Oh Scheiße. Können Sie in zwanzig Minuten vorbeikommen?“




Ich sprang in mein Auto, das mein Partner fuhr, und innerhalb einer halben Stunde waren wir im Planing-Familial 31 (die Nummer der Fachabteilung) Büro. Nach einer Reihe von Tests und weniger als zehn Tagen hatte ich zu Hause eine medikamentöse Abtreibung, umgeben von meinem Partner und meinen Mitbewohner*innen. So einfach war das.




***




Diese Abtreibung hat mir gezeigt, dass alles, was ich mir vorgestellt hatte, alles, was ich im Zusammenhang mit einer Schwangerschaft befürchtet hatte, falsch war.




Mein schlimmster Albtraum war buchstäblich (ich hatte tatsächlich davon geträumt, und bis heute ist es einer der realistischsten und erschreckendsten Träume meines Lebens), eine Schwangerschaft zu leugnen. Zu spät zu erkennen, dass ich schwanger war, und keine Abtreibung mehr vornehmen zu können. Ich hatte schreckliche Angst davor, gezwungen zu sein, ein Kind zu bekommen. Und doch hatte ich Angst davor, mich für eine Abtreibung entscheiden zu müssen; Angst davor, dies nicht tun zu können, falls es doch zu einer Schwangerschaft kommen sollte; Angst davor, Schuldgefühle zu haben, zu leiden, etwas zu verlieren. Doch als der Moment tatsächlich kam, zögerte ich keine Sekunde. Keine Sekunde des Zweifels. Selbst meine Abneigung und mein Ekel gegenüber gynäkologischen Untersuchungen traten angesichts dieser neuen Notwendigkeit in den Hintergrund. „Es“ musste einfach geschehen.




Es war diese Diskrepanz zwischen meinen imaginierten Ängsten und meiner tatsächlichen Erfahrung, die sich in meiner Reaktion auf den Test zeigte: Ich versuchte, eine starke Emotion zu empfinden. Ich versuchte zu weinen, weil ich erwartete, dass mir zum Weinen zumute sein würde. Ich versuchte zu lachen, weil ich dachte, ich sei eine starke Reaktion schuldig – eine Emotion, eigentlich irgendeine Emotion, aber eben eine Emotion. In diesem ersten Moment wurde mir bewusst, welche Last gesellschaftliche Vorstellungen und Normen mir seit meiner Geburt auf die Schultern gelegt hatten.




 

 

 

 

 







Childfree – Wähle deinen Charakter aus, und das Spiel beginnt




Ein Feel-Good-Larp, um aus der Rhetorik des Leidens auszubrechen




In dieser Woche begann ich, ein Live-Action-Rollenspiel (LARP) zu schreiben. Es handelte von drei Paaren mit unterschiedlichen Zusammensetzungen, Wünschen und Lebensgeschichten; zunächst im Wartezimmer einer Frauenarztpraxis, dann beim Arzt und schließlich in verschiedenen familiären Interaktionen. Die drei Paare bestanden aus zwei jungen heterosexuellen Menschen ohne Kinder, die sich in einer ungewollten Schwangerschaft befanden, zwei heterosexuellen Menschen in den Vierzigern in einer Patchwork-Familie, die ebenfalls mit einer ungewollten Schwangerschaft konfrontiert waren, sowie einem schwulen, lesbischen und/oder Trans-Paar, das eine medizinische Schwangerschaftsunterbrechung anstrebte (je nach Besetzung variierten die Geschlechter der Figuren ebenso wie die Methoden der Schwangerschaftsunterbrechung – die in der fiktiven Spielwelt legal war). Das Larp sollte, glaube ich, die unterschiedlichen Erfahrungen, die Urteile anderer und der Familie, individuelle Gefühle und die Bedeutung sozialer Beziehungen hervorheben. Jedenfalls war mit dem Ende meiner Abtreibung auch die Zeit zum Schreiben vorbei, und ich legte das Larp-Projekt beiseite (ich habe vor nicht allzu langer Zeit versucht, es wiederzubeleben, aber der Ansatz funktionierte für mich nicht mehr, obwohl er seine Qualitäten hatte).




Fast zwei Jahre später stieß ich jedoch auf zwei LARPs zum Thema Abtreibung, die mich durch das, was sie vermittelten – offensichtlich ohne es selbst zu wissen –, tief beeindruckten. Geschrieben von Menschen, von denen ich keinen Zweifel hatte, dass sie für das Recht auf Abtreibung eintraten, konzentrierten sich beide Spiele bei der Darstellung der Erfahrung – die eines heterosexuellen Paares, das mit einer ungewollten Schwangerschaft konfrontiert ist – auf … „die möglichen Zukunftsszenarien“ des „Kindes“.




Ich kann nicht einmal sagen, dass ich mich darüber aufgeregt habe. Ich war einfach nur sprachlos. Wie können Abtreibungsbefürworter*innen ihren Diskurs auf das Leid ausrichten, das durch die Beendigung eines potenziellen Lebens verursacht wird? Verdammt, da gibt es wirklich etwas Kulturelles, das es an der Wurzel zu bekämpfen gilt.




In einem Facebook-Kommentar unter einem der Beiträge, die mich zu diesen Spielen geführt haben, habe ich geschworen, als Antwort darauf ein „Feel-Good“-LARP zum Thema Abtreibung zu schreiben. Nun ja; „Childfree“ ist streng genommen kein Feel-Good-Spiel – es versucht nicht gezielt, positive Emotionen hervorzurufen. Dennoch ist es ein „Feel-Free“-Spiel: Und das ist wahrscheinlich sogar noch besser, denn was der Schwangerschaftsabbruch für mich war, war in erster Linie die Erfahrung einer Befreiung – einer Emanzipation von den gesellschaftlichen Normen, die bis dahin unbewusst meine Vorstellungen bestimmt hatten.




Es ist diese Befreiung, die „Childfree“ euch erleben lassen möchte.




 

 

 

 

 




Zurück zu den materiellen Lebensbedingungen




Ich kann es mir nicht verkneifen, noch eine gesellschaftliche Anmerkung zu machen. Es liegt auf der Hand: Wenn meine Erfahrung so positiv war, dann deshalb, weil ich auf keinerlei Hindernisse gestoßen bin und von kompetenten und hilfsbereiten Menschen angemessen, effizient und freundlich begleitet wurde, mit denen ich offen sprechen konnte und die mich zu keinem Zeitpunkt verurteilt haben. Dass meine Erfahrung so positiv war, liegt daran, dass ich in einer großen französischen Stadt lebte, nur einen Katzensprung von einer „Planing Familial“-Praxis entfernt, die frei vom Einfluss von Abtreibungsgegnern war. Dass meine Erfahrung so positiv war, liegt daran, dass ich von meinen Freundinnen – und bis zu einem gewissen Grad auch von meiner Familie – begleitet und unterstützt wurde und von einem Umfeld profitierte, in dem es mir materiell möglich war, unter guten Bedingungen eine medikamentöse Abtreibung vornehmen zu lassen. Dass meine Erfahrung so positiv war, liegt daran, dass ich rechtlich volljährig war und selbstständig reisen konnte, und daran, dass ich nicht arbeitete und meine Universität Abwesenheiten nicht genau überprüfte, sodass ich weder eine Beurlaubung beantragen noch mit meinem Arbeitgeber oder meiner Universität sprechen musste. Dass meine Erfahrung so positiv war, liegt daran, dass Frankreich zu dieser Zeit das Land auf der Welt war, in dem der Zugang zu Schwangerschaftsabbrüchen und anderen Verhütungsmitteln am einfachsten war. Es ist wahrscheinlich auch heute noch eines der besten Länder, aber dass dies so bleibt, obwohl es ganze Departements gibt, in denen es keine Ärztinnen gibt, die Schwangerschaftsabbrüche durchführen, sagt viel über den Zustand der Welt und den weltweiten Rückgang der reproduktiven Rechte aus.




Abtreibung als Verhütungsmethode




Es mag Sie überraschen, dass ich Abtreibung als Verhütungsmethode einordne, während sie im Allgemeinen gesondert betrachtet und als fast isolierter Akt dargestellt wird, der mit keinem anderen vergleichbar ist. Abtreibung ist jedoch tatsächlich Teil der Empfängnisverhütung: Sie ist eine Methode, die darauf abzielt, die Entscheidung, Kinder zu bekommen (oder nicht zu bekommen), zu steuern, damit eine fruchtbare Person nicht schwanger wird. Sie ist die letzte verfügbare Verhütungsmethode, die wir so weit wie möglich vermeiden wollen, aber ihre Existenz ist absolut entscheidend und ein integraler Bestandteil des Verhütungsprozesses. Darüber hinaus nutzten mehr als 70 % der Menschen, die auf eine Abtreibung zurückgegriffen haben, physische oder hormonelle Verhütungsmittel: Das bedeutet, dass der Zugang zu Verhütungsmitteln keineswegs eine Ablehnung der Abtreibung rechtfertigt, denn keine Verhütungsmethode ist zu 100 % zuverlässig und wirksam, selbst bei strikter Einhaltung der Anweisungen (was, das sollten wir nicht vergessen, äußerst kompliziert ist und seltsamerweise nur für „Frauen“, die die Pille nehmen, zu einem moralischen und Schuldgefühle auslösenden Argument wird, nicht jedoch für jede Person, die sich einer Behandlung unterzieht). Und diejenigen, die gegen Abtreibung sind, wissen das ganz genau, da sie genau diejenigen sind, die den Zugang zu Verhütungsmitteln einschränken wollen, weil ihnen kulturell akzeptable Argumente fehlen, um diese ganz abzuschaffen…


Die Debatte über Leben und Nicht-Leben beiseite lassen




Um zu verstehen, wie Abtreibung in das Kontinuum der Verhütung passt, kann es zudem hilfreich sein zu wissen, wie wir – und sei es nur gegenüber uns selbst, um unsere eigenen Vorstellungen zu hinterfragen – auf das Argument vom „Leben“ des Embryos oder Fötus reagieren können. Tatsächlich werden die Bedingungen der Debatte – wie so oft – von Konservativen vorgegeben: ob Abtreibung legalisiert werden soll oder nicht, die Festlegung der maximalen Schwangerschaftsdauer, die Kontrolle des Zugangs dazu … all dies dreht sich um die Frage „Wann beginnt das Leben?“, und wir geraten in die Falle, versuchen zu müssen, diese zu beantworten.




Die Antwort auf eine solche Frage kann jedoch nur philosophischer, ja sogar theologischer Natur sein: Keine wissenschaftliche Antwort ist in der Lage, die Debatte zu beenden. Es handelt sich um eine moralische Frage. Das „Violinisten-Argument“ ersetzt diese Frage durch eine andere: nicht mehr „Wann beginnt ein Leben?“, sondern „Kann eine Person gezwungen werden, das Leben einer anderen auf eigene Kosten zu erhalten?“. Das „Violinisten-Argument“ ist ein Gedankenexperiment aus einem Artikel von Judith Jarvis Thomson aus dem Jahr 1971 mit dem Titel „A Defense of Abortion“, in dem sie sich eine Situation vorstellt, in der der weltbeste Geiger, der an schwerem Nierenversagen leidet, neun Monate lang an Sie angeschlossen werden muss, um zu überleben. Würden Sie das akzeptieren? Und würden Sie es auch noch nach neun Jahren akzeptieren? Wo würden Sie die Grenze ziehen? Schließlich steht das Leben des besten Geigers der Welt auf dem Spiel … Dieses Gedankenexperiment lädt uns dazu ein, über die Debatte darüber hinauszugehen, ob der Embryo und später der Fötus lebt oder nicht: Das (potenzielle oder tatsächliche) „Leben“ des Embryos oder Fötus ist für die Abtreibungsdebatte irrelevant. Ob es sich um ein Leben handelt oder nicht, ist irrelevant: Wir müssen uns vielmehr fragen: „Kann eine Person gezwungen werden, ihren Körper zu veräußern und ihre Lebenszeit zum Wohle eines anderen aufzugeben?“ Die Antwort lautet natürlich: Nein. „Niemand ist moralisch verpflichtet, große Opfer zu bringen – in Bezug auf seine Gesundheit, alle anderen Interessen und Anliegen, alle anderen Pflichten und Verpflichtungen – neun Jahre lang oder auch nur neun Monate lang, um eine andere Person am Leben zu erhalten.“

 oder ein großartiges Video von 

PhilosophyTube

, das das Experiment auf die Bühne bringt und es in aktuelle Debatten einordnet – komplett mit Untertiteln in mehreren Sprachen.




Viel Spaß beim Spielen,

title: İstanbul'u sel aldı: 1.277 su baskını, bir ölüm, 15 heyelan, binlerce yardım çağrısı
content:
İstanbul Valiliği, 14 Ekim günü sabah 06:00 ile 20:00 arasında kesintisiz süren olağanüstü yağışların 1.277 su baskınına yol açtığını, kentte 15 heyelan, 47 mahsur kalma, 13 ağaç devrilmesi ve iki çatı uçması kaydedildiğini bildirdi. Ayrıca 808 konut, 280 iş yeri ve 76 araçla ilgili ihbarlar alındı. 




Valilik açıklamasında şu bilgilere yer verdi:







“AFAD, İBB, İlçe Belediyeleri başta olmak üzere tüm kurumlar 8 bin personel, 2 bin araç ve iş makinası ile sahada yağış nedeniyle oluşan olumsuzluklara müdahale etmektedir.”







Kent genelinden alınan 2 bin 518 ihbarın ilgili müdahale ekiplerine yönlendirildiği bildirildi. 




Beykoz'da metrekareye 194 kilogram yağmur




İstanbul'un ilçeleri arasında yağış miktarı farklılık gösterdi.




Valiliğin verilerine göre Beykoz-Ömerli'de metrekareye 193,84 kilogram; Arnavutköy'de 125,9, Sarıyer-İTÜ Maslak istasyonunda 124,72, Çatalca'da 75,2 kilogram yağış kaydedildi.




Buna karşılık Kartal'da 14,3, Bakırköy'de yalnızca 6,8 kilogram yağış ölçüldü.




Yağış özellikle İstanbul'un bazı kuzey ve batı ilçelerinde yoğunlaştı. 




Yollar ve alt geçitler sular altında kaldı




Sağanak, özellikle Esenyurt, Başakşehir, Sultangazi ve Bayrampaşa'da ciddi su baskınlarına yol açtı.




Esenyurt Haramidere Sanayi Bölgesi'nde iş yerlerini su bastı. Başakşehir İkitelli'de araçlar suyla dolan yollarda ve alt geçitlerde mahsur kaldı.




Sultangazi'de yolların göle dönmesi nedeniyle yayalar yürümekte zorlandı. Bayrampaşa'da iş yerlerini korumaya çalışan esnaf, biriken suları kendi imkânlarıyla tahliye etmeye çalıştı.




Alt geçitlere ve bazı metro istasyonlarına su girmesi ulaşımda aksamalara neden oldu. Trafikte kalan araçlar ve toplu taşıma duraklarında biriken yolcular, yağışın günlük yaşam üzerindeki etkisini artırdı. 




Fatih'te 14 yaşındaki çocuk elektrik akımına kapıldı 




Sel felaketinin ilk ölüm haberi akşam saatlerinde geldi. Fatih'in Balat Mahallesi'ndeki Çukurbostan Parkı'nda 14 yaşındaki M.I., bir su birikintisine bastığı sırada elektrik akımına kapıldı. Bilinci kapalı olarak hastaneye kaldırılan çocuk, tüm müdahalelere rağmen kurtarılamadı.




İstanbul Valiliği olayla ilgili soruşturma başlatıldığını açıkladı. 




Sel sularında sürüklenen kadın kurtarıldı




Esenyurt'un Dereyolu Hürriyet Mahallesi'nde suya kapılan bir kadın, metrelerce sürüklendikten sonra çevredekilerin yardımıyla kurtarıldı. 




Sarıyer Ayazağa'da ise saat 19.00 sıralarında bir İETT otobüsü sel sularında sürüklendi. Mahsur kalan yolcular otobüsün tepesine çıkarak yardım bekledi. 




Perşembe günü okullar tatil, motosikletler trafikten men edildi




İstanbul Valiliği, 15 Ekim Perşembe günü kent genelindeki resmi ve özel eğitim kurumlarında yüz yüze eğitime bir gün ara verildiğini duyurdu.




Valilik ayrıca kamu kurumlarında çalışan hamile ve engelli personelin, gazilerin ve belirli koşullarda sekiz yaşından küçük çocuğu bulunan kadın çalışanların idari izinli sayılacağını açıkladı.




Motosiklet ve benzeri iki tekerlekli araçların trafiğe çıkışı da 14 Ekim saat 21.00'den başlayarak ikinci bir talimata kadar yasaklandı.




İstanbul Valiliğinin 19.49'da yayımladığı resmi açıklamada özellikle bodrum katlarında oturan yurttaşların su baskını tehlikesine karşı önlem almalarını ve zorunlu olmadıkça dışarı çıkmamalarını istendi. 




Felaketin boyutları




İstanbul'da birkaç saat içinde felaket boyutlarına bürünen olağanüstü yağışın etkisi, yalnızca su baskınlarıyla sınırlı değildi. Heyelanlar, elektrik çarpması tehlikesi, sürüklenen araçlar ve toplu taşıma sistemindeki aksamalar kent altyapısının farklı kesimlerinde sorunlara yol açtı. 




İstanbul'un sel tarihinde yeni bir felaket




14 Ekim'de Beykoz-Ömerli'de metrekareye düşen 193,84 kilogram yağış, İstanbul'un ekim ayı ortalaması olan 66,3 kilogramın yaklaşık üç katı. Bu miktar, kentin tarihsel yağış rekorlarına yaklaşırken bazı istasyonlarda kaydedilen en yüksek günlük değerleri de aşıyor.




İstanbul daha önce de benzer felaketler yaşadı. Eylül 2009'da Ayamama Deresi ve çevresindeki selde 31 kişi hayatını kaybetti. Temmuz 2017'de Silivri'de 2 saat içinde 118 kilogram yağış ölçüldü. Eylül 2023'te Arnavutköy ve Başakşehir'de 125 kilograma ulaşan sağanakta 2 kişi yaşamını yitirdi. 2026 felaketi, şiddetli yağış açısından istisnai boyutlara ulaşmış olsa da, İstanbul'un sel geçmişinde benzer felaketler yaşanmıştı. 




1.277 su baskını, 15 heyelan ve sel sularında sürüklenen araçlar ve Fatih'te 14 yaşındaki bir çocuğun su birikintisinde elektrik akımına kapılarak ölmesini içeren 14 Ekim bilançosu, İstanbul'un  hala 2009'dakinden daha güvenli bir kentsel yaşam sunmaktan uzak olduğunu gösterdi. 




(AEK)

author: Sophia Cope
title: DHS Inspector General Finds That TSA is Not Properly Safeguarding Passenger Facial Recognition Data
content:
EFF legal intern Gabrielle Ladun was the principal author of this post.

The Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General (DHS OIG) has published a summary of findings from its audit of the Transportation Security Administration’s (TSA) facial recognition technology. While the detailed findings are classified, the summary states that the OIG’s audit uncovered a “significant weakness” in the technology’s ability to protect the privacy of passenger data. This has massive privacy implications for the millions of passengers who travel and don’t opt out of the TSA’s biometric surveillance technology verification process.

TSA uses facial comparison technology for identity verification of airline passengers. A camera takes a photo of passengers to verify that their provided identification matches their live photo. Although TSA states that it is “committed to protecting traveler privacy,” the audit highlights that this has not been the case.

The OIG found that TSA’s Credential Authentication Technology 2’s (CAT-2) vendor “was able to access and extract sensitive passenger information, including driver’s license and passport images, during system troubleshooting and enhancements, without TSA’s knowledge.”

The OIG further admonished the agency:

TSA lacked clear policies, did not track when this data was extracted, could not verify that extracted information was properly deleted, and did not notify passengers when their biometric and biographic information may have been stored. As a result, although passenger information was generally protected during routine operations, weaknesses in vendor oversight created a risk that sensitive personal information could be retained or exposed.

We hope the TSA will fix these issues. The OIG summary states:

We issued one finding and three recommendations to strengthen controls, improve oversight, and ensure transparency and the proper handling of passenger data. TSA concurred with all three recommendations. Two recommendations are open and resolved, and one remains open and unresolved.

EFF has a long history of opposing governmental use of facial recognition technology. As the OIG’s audit underscores, this technology presents privacy risks associated with unsecured data, unauthorized access, and data breaches. The government’s use of this technology also creates a mass surveillance system and facilitates the creation of warrantless biometric records for unconsenting parties.

The biometric data captured by this technology is not without errors. There have been multiple instances of law enforcement agencies using facial recognition technology to misidentify and arrest innocent individuals.

Given that facial recognition technology is prone to mistakes, combined with the OIG’s audit revealing significant privacy weaknesses, it is imperative that travelers remember that opting out is possible. TSA’s own website emphasizes that travelers who wish to decline to have their photo taken for facial comparison can do so without any delay, disruption, or recourse.

Considering the data protection weaknesses exposed by the OIG’s audit, EFF will continue to oppose this governmental system of mass surveillance and spread awareness to ensure that no one is forced to relinquish their biometric data without consent.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Most Americans Say Trump’s Presidential Profits Are Illegal or Unethical
content:
Meanwhile, Trump reportedly ousted Guilfoyle because he was upset that she was making money off his presidency.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

A strong majority of Americans believe that President Donald Trump is profiting illegally or unethically from his presidency, polling finds.

AP-NORC poll results released Tuesday find that 41 percent of U.S. adults say that Trump has acted illegally in personally profiting from his position, while another 18 percent say that those actions are unethical, for a total of 59 percent. In contrast, only 18 percent of people say that he has done nothing wrong.

Even a sizable proportion of Republicans, at 32 percent, believe that Trump has acted illegally or unethically in seeking private gain, the poll found.

Meanwhile, an even larger proportion believe that Trump is prioritizing his personal profits while acting as president. Fifty-six percent said he is prioritizing his profits “a lot,” while 19 percent said “some.” This stands in stark contrast to only 23 percent of people saying that he is prioritizing the country “a lot” and only 11 percent saying he’s focusing on “people like me.”

Corruption allegations have become rather common during Trump’s second term.

Trump has disclosed making $2.2 billion in income in 2025. Much of those profits came from the president’s crypto schemes and his meme coin that he launched three days before his second inauguration. His promotions of these schemes have often been openly corrupt; at least twice, for instance, Trump has encouraged buyers to become the biggest holders of the coin in order to gain access to an exclusive dinner with him.

Trump and his team hardly try to hide his many other avenues of income that are boosted by his presidency. His financial team trades prolifically, often in relation to his decisions. His practice of hosting foreign leaders and power brokers at his resorts has multiplied during this term. Earlier this year, Truth Social unrolled a program to allow traders and banks to buy access to Trump’s Truth Social posts — which often move markets — at the “fastest” speed, allowing them to access information quicker than others could react.

Trump has openly bragged about the power of wielding the Oval Office; earlier this year, he said that his children have “inside information” whenever they make any sort of investment or purchase. He has also defended his profits, claiming that he doesn’t “get involved” with his personal finances and that “we have funds that run my money.”

But Trump is still aware of the public perception of corruption surrounding his administration. This week, he ordered the ouster of U.S. ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports found that she had asked a Trump donor to pay off a $100,000 credit card bill in exchange for access to the administration.

According to the Wall Street Journal, Trump grew incensed at Guilfoyle because he was upset that she was profiting off of his presidency. His aides, meanwhile, were concerned about more headlines describing the Trump administration’s self-dealing ahead of the midterm elections.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. title: Registro de la Marcha por la Resistencia, 12 de octubre en Temuco
content:
Convocada por familiares de los Presos Políticos Mapuche y pu lof en resistencia, se realizó en temuco este 12 de octubre la Marcha por la Resistencia, la cual comenzó a eso de las 11 de la mañana y cruzó las principales calles de la ciudad. Los más de mil participantes hicieron ayekan en las afueras de la cárcel de temuco, en apoyo a los presos políticos mapuche del módulo comuneros.




Dejamos a continuación las palabras de autoridades y vocerías que se dieron durante la jornada.










Lonko Arturo Catalan Trangol
















Lonko Ignacio Ñancuvilu, Kiñel Mapu Makewe,



















Machi Fidel Tranamil Nahuel













Kvyen Candia Rain, lof Metrenco, Kiñel mapu Makewe. Familiar del preso político mapuche Luis Tranamil Nahuel, quien fue trasladado durante el mes de agosto hasta el CCP Biobío permaneciendo alejado de sus familiares hasta hoy.



















Familiares de los 19 PPM del Caso Grollmus realizan lectura de carta enviada por los comuneros recluidos en el CCP Biobío.













Palabras de la Voceria y Familiares de los 19 Presos políticos mapuche de la Franja lavkenche recientemente condenados en el Caso Grollmus, destacan las más altas condenas en la historia judicial reciente contra el pueblo mapuche.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Advocate says chiefs, grassroots working to get 145,000 registered First Nations to vote in Alberta referendum
content:
An Indigenous political activist and advocate says chiefs in Alberta, along with grassroots organizers says they’re doing everything they can to get First Nations people out to vote in the Oct. 19 referendum which could open a path for Alberta to pursue a formal separation process.

With the vote less than a week away, a key strategist says mobilization has been underway since Premier Danielle Smith introduced legislation making it easier for separatists to mount a successful petition to force a referendum.

“It really started in May 2025 when the chiefs called an emergency meeting, and the response back then was to her first legislative piece, Bill 54. The chiefs came in very firm 100 per cent opposed to separation prepared to fight. They ordered her by letter, and they all signed off on the letter to cease and desist on her separation intention,” Cara Currie Hall told APTN News in an interview.

Bill 54 was an omnibus bill that received Royal Assent in May, 2025. It included a number of changes related to the electoral process in Alberta including lifting the ban on corporate and union political donations for provincial elections and direct democracy processes like referendums and introduced a $5,000 annual contribution limit and a $5 million general election spending limit for political parties.

The separation question is number 10 on the ballot. It reads: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”

Voters are then given two options to choose from: Option 1: Alberta should remain a province of Canada or Option 2: The Government of Alberta should commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.

Currie Hall was a key figure in the Rock the Indigenous Vote movement in Canada in 2015 and helped organize Indigenous voters in the United States to back Barack Obama in his presidential run. She’s lending her considerable political savvy to the chiefs in Alberta and contends it was easy to see what Smith’s intentions were in making legislative changes.

“Because by then, [Smith] already lowered the threshold of signatures required to advance a referendum, and she lowered it from 60 per cent required signatures… to only 10 per cent, which is how she got away with only needing a hundred and seventy seven thousand signatures to push forward for a referendum. So, she accommodated that right from the get go.”

Currie Hall has been working alongside chiefs and grassroots people at her home First Nation of Maskwacis, 96 km south of Edmonton, to inform members of the importance of this vote. That work follows legal challenges mounted by several First Nations against Alberta over the constitutionality of the referendum.

Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation and the Blackfoot Confederacy (including Siksika Nation, Piikani Nation, and Blood Tribe with a total of at least five to six distinct First Nations/groups) brought successful judicial reviews and legal challenges that led the Court of King’s Bench to quash the separation petition and rule that the province breached its constitutional duty to consult.

Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation is suing the Alberta government, the chief electoral officer, and the federal attorney general in a separate lawsuit over Bill 14 and the separation petition process. Sturgeon Lake Cree said the referendum breached the treaties which pre-dated the province of Alberta.

APTN requested an interview with the chief but were advised he is not giving interviews at this time. Instead, in an emailed statement Sunshine said they’ve been informing and educating members “ever since Danielle Smith announced there would be an unconstitutional, expensive, and divisive referendum…”

“We hope that when all votes are counted Albertans will have repudiated this farcical anti -Treaty, anti-immigrant, and anti-democratic process,” Sunshine said.

Onion Lake Cree Nation which straddles the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary also revived a separate lawsuit against Alberta’s broader Sovereignty Within a United Canada Act over related constitutional and treaty concerns. It claimed the provincial legislation infringes on constitutionally protected treaty rights.

The Alberta Court of Appeal ruled that the province failed its duty to consult Treaty First Nations regarding a separatist referendum question and petition drive. The court affirmed that pre-existing treaty agreements supersede provincial political efforts.

Currie Hall said the chiefs have stood firm united against the referendum since the former chief of Mikisew Cree Nation, Billy-Joe Tuccaro threw a copy of Bill 54 in the air at a news conference.

“And he said, ‘this is what we think of your bill. It’s garbage. You’re on treaty land.’ So, the chiefs are very steady and very firm in the pushback and the rejection of any efforts for referendum. And, so the chiefs united…they did the cease and desist. They went to court. They won in court. And, the courts determined that the referendum was unconstitutional,” Currie Hall said.

Currie Hall likens the chiefs’ fight against separation to what the Crees of Quebec did in turning back that separation initiative during the 1995 Quebec referendum.

“And it was the Crees under the leadership of Matthew Coon Come, who was the grand chief at the time, that defeated Quebec and saved Canada,” Currie Hall said.

Coon Come lent his voice and support to Alberta chiefs at the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) Annual General Assembly on July 16, where chiefs passed a landmark resolution put forward by Confederacy of Treaty No. 6 First Nations Grand Chief Joey Pete, alongside Coon Come who was appearing as a proxy from the Cree Nation of Nemaska, Que.

“No province has the legal authority to alter, diminish, or extinguish Treaty Rights or the constitutional relationship between First Nations and the Crown,” the resolution said.

Grassroots boots on the ground getting the vote out

Meanwhile, Currie Hall has been getting help on the ground in Maskwacis from her sister Shelli Yellowbird.

“In Alberta, we only have 145,000 First Nations that are registered (to vote), that’s small” Yellowbird shared in an interview with APTN.

“On the ground, [there are] a lot of uncertainties and not understanding the real purpose and intention of the October 19 vote, but also to a lot of misconceptions about why should we vote. But a lot of it is actually pretty good. The boots on the ground initiative is working really well in terms of getting to the grassroots people, where everybody’s got an assignment to do. Mine is strictly social media blitz,” she said.

Yellowbird has been creating TikTok videos with some getting shared more than 30,000 times.

“And then it works by going door to door. We are using every means that we have in the community, the radio, social media, and word-of-mouth-signage,” Yellowbird said.

Yellowbird described their efforts as “a four nation initiative” at Makwacis primarily at Sampson Cree the biggest nation in Maskwacis. Ermineskin Cree Nation is also doing its own work alongside Montana First Nation and Louis Bull Tribe, the smaller nations that make up Maskwacis.

Yellowbird is hosting a rally at the nation on Saturday, Oct. 17 which will coincide with rallies and protests by First Nations across Alberta. There will also be a rally at the Alberta legislature on Sunday, a day ahead of the referendum.

Advance polls open through Friday

Advance polls opened Monday with some voting locations having to stay open extended hours on Tuesday, “to reflect late location openings,” according to Elections Alberta. It was to afford voters the fully advertised number of hours to vote.

“Late openings were due to various and separate technology issues that have been resolved,” it said.

Of the 311 total advance voting locations open Tuesday, 17 were affected.

And voters will need some time to ponder all ten questions on the referendum ballot.Aside from the contentious separation question, they’ll also be answering “yes” or “no” to nine additional questions, ranging from immigration to abolishing the Canadian Senate. A video by Indigenous social media creators says “No to the Nine, Option 1 Stay on Question 10,” in an effort to simplify the ballot choices for voters. Questions one through five which voters will vote “Yes” or “No” to deal with immigration and voter eligibility requirements. These questions focus on shifting immigration and social spending controls away from federal models, covering increased provincial control over immigration levels and job priorities, restricting provincially funded services to citizens, permanent residents, and approved statuses, implementing 12-month residency requirements for temporary residents to receive services, introducing newcomer fees for select services, and requiring proof of citizenship for provincial voting. Questions six to nine deal with Constitutional changes which voters will say “Yes” or “No” to. author: Hope Pisoni
title: Meta Has Paid Far Right Accounts for Their Posts Ahead of the Midterms
content:
An invite-only program for content creators has accounts promoting white supremacy, anti-LGBTQ, and neo-Nazi rhetoric.

An invite-only program for content creators has accounts promoting white supremacy, anti-LGBTQ, and neo-Nazi rhetoric.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

On September 14, far-right influencer Chaya Raichik, known online as Libs of Tiktok, attacked a Washington state high school on Facebook for displaying a Pride flag. “Hey Mercer Island High School, why does your profile photo display a mutilation flag??” she wrote, tagging the school’s account in the post and attaching a photo of the entrance.

A few weeks before, on August 27, neo-Nazi webcomic artist StoneToss posted a strip that used Tim Curry’s death to mock transgender suicide rates. And earlier this month, right-wing political commentator Benny Johnson shared claims that Democrats will “transition your kids while you’re at work” and “hand out gas cards to illegal aliens.”

Meta pays these creators for making posts like these. In 2024, the tech giant unveiled a new invite-only program called Facebook Content Monetization, designed to streamline earnings for creators. Many creators celebrated the move, with some reporting a major increase in their earnings through the program.

However, that program has recently come under scrutiny. In August, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported that Meta invited accounts promoting white supremacist and neo-Nazi ideologies. And after reviewing Meta’s monetization data, Uncloseted Media identified 29 accounts with histories of anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric that have been invited to the program. These include the three aforementioned accounts as well as podcaster Candace Owens, who has blamed gay men for child abuse in the Catholic church, and Turning Point USA, which has been connected to an assault on a queer Arizona State University professor. Meta did not respond to Uncloseted Media and The 19th’s requests for an interview or for comment.

With the midterm elections looming, some of the accounts Meta pays through the program have been spreading political misinformation. In the first week of October, for example, Benny Johnson made 14 separate Facebook posts connecting the Democratic Party to election fraud.

Courtney Radsch, director of the Center for Media and Digital Governance at Open Markets Institute, said that promoting hateful rhetoric and misinformation like this is especially dangerous during an election season where the increasingly authoritarian Trump administration, which Meta has courted since its inauguration, has openly discussed attempts to interfere.

“Amplifying and enabling harassment campaigns and centering fringe conspiracy theories through algorithmic curation and monetization opportunities has led to a dissolution of democracy in America,” Radsch told Uncloseted Media and The 19th. “This administration is dismantling democratic oversight and increasing authoritarian control. … You can’t look at your platform policies on monetization without looking at the context in which this is occurring in the U.S. with rising technofascism.”

Meta launched its Facebook Content Monetization program to incentivize more creators to post on Facebook, which has faced an aging user base and competition from newer apps. Those incentives can be substantial — within the program’s first year, content creators who accepted Meta’s invitation to join reported huge increases in their payouts, with some calling it their most lucrative platform. One creator told The Hollywood Reporter that she consistently earned $20,000 to $30,000 per month, while another said his monthly earnings often hit six figures.

While most accounts aren’t big enough to rake in that amount of money, Meta also motivates smaller accounts to join. Starting in 2025, they launched a side program called “breakthrough bonus” that advertises up to $5,000 and an automatic onboarding into Content Monetization for creators from other platforms if they start posting regularly on Facebook.

SK Smigiel, a content creator who posts about LGBTQ+ education and activism under the username justsaysk, joined the program through the breakthrough bonus initiative in April. They say Meta would offer them payouts for completing certain “missions.” For example, Smigiel says they earned $500 a month for posting 10 reels. They say other missions included using trending hashtags and audio or cross-posting to relevant groups. These incentives initially convinced them to post on Facebook due to their poor earnings on Instagram, but they didn’t stick around.

“When I post on Facebook, I don’t even open the post that I’ve made because I already know that … probably 99 percent of the engagement is negative towards me,” Smigiel told Uncloseted Media and The 19th.

Uncloseted Media identified accounts enrolled in the program via data compiled by What To Fix (WTF), a Dutch nonprofit focused on tech accountability. The Meta Monetization Archive is a searchable database of information collected from disclosures released by Meta.

Belén Luna Sanz, policy manager at WTF, said the program represents a broader shift in industry practices. While advertisers once paid content creators directly with companies like Meta taking a cut, platforms now collect all ad revenue and pay creators themselves.

“They’re only paying you royalties depending on how much engagement you are creating on your content,” Sanz told Uncloseted Media and The 19th. Jason Hong, a professor of computer science at Carnegie Mellon University, says that while inflammatory and misleading content may go against Meta’s policies, both the company and the people posting it are financially incentivized to promote it. “We know that things that get people really angry get a lot of engagement, we know that disinformation and misinformation … also gets lots of engagement,” Hong told Uncloseted Media and The 19th. “[Meta is] at a fork in the road, and one path is about the morals and ethics and well-being of society and democracy, and on the other path is a really big pile of money.”

Since Meta launched the program two years ago, WTF has identified over 18 million accounts in the program. But Sanz says the selection process has been opaque and describes the program’s rollout as “reckless.”

“[The program requires] little to no verification of their identity, there are not enough safeguards and their monetization policies are enforced in a very non-transparent way, so it’s hard to tell whether they are enforcing it properly or not,” Sanz said.

Uncloseted Media found numerous posts that seemingly violate Facebook’s content monetization policies, which state that “content may be subject to reduced or disabled monetization if it depicts or discusses [debated social issues] in a polarizing or inflammatory manner.” Those issues include race, religion, sexual orientation, political affiliation and more.

Libs of TikTok, for example, has called the organizers of an LGBTQ+ pride event “sick sick freaks,” accused pro-LGBTQ+ teachers of wanting to “indoctrinate your children” and decried the “lgbtq groomer cult.” Other posts may violate content monetization policies forbidding “derogatory words” and “hateful conduct,” including Raichik using a slur to describe the usage of the term “sex assigned at birth.”

Meta also states that misinformation, which they define as “content that has been rated false by a third-party fact checker,” is “ineligible to monetize,” even though the company ended its third-party fact-checking last year, leaving no clear mechanism to enforce the prohibition. Meta states that “repeated violations of [content monetization policies] could lead to a temporary or permanent ban on your Page or profile’s ability to use our monetization tools.” However, as of the Monetization Archive’s most recent update on September 15, all of the accounts discussed above are actively enrolled in the program. The Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) has designated several individuals in Meta’s program as extremists. These include Tucker Carlson, who has agreed with claims that gender-affirming care allows adults to “basically molest and abuse children”; James Lindsay and Jack Posobiec, who helped popularize “groomer” rhetoric against LGBTQ+ people; and Alex Jones, whose infamous conspiracy show InfoWars received an invitation prior to its acquisition by The Onion. It also includes Libs of TikTok, which is known for stoking anti-LGBTQ+ harassment — 2024 reports by NBC News and The Washington Post cumulatively found over 80 instances of violent threats against institutions like schools and businesses connected to its posts.

“There does need to be discussion and diversity of opinion allowed in the public sphere,” Radsch said. “However, there is a difference between rational debate and harassment.”

Reports from WTF suggest that Meta doesn’t consistently uphold the program’s other rules either. Despite Meta’s policies stating that “political and government entities are ineligible for monetization,” including “current elected and appointed government officials” and “political parties,” WTF found hundreds enrolled. In addition, Uncloseted Media confirmed membership of at least 8 official Republican Party pages, including the Republican Party of Georgia.

In recent years, Meta has courted the Trump administration and its far-right allies, including influencers. Last August, the company hired Robby Starbuck, an anti-DEI campaigner who has promoted conspiracy theories claiming that pesticides turn children gay, as an adviser on preventing “political bias” in its AI systems. And in April, Meta sponsored a party celebrating Isabel Brown, a Daily Wire host who has advocated for people to leave their LGBTQ+ “lifestyles.” Brown and Starbuck are both enrolled in the content monetization program.

Radsch said that being able to control who gets monetized grants Meta significant power over political narratives.

“That can be problematic because it means that they can pick winners and losers, they can pick ideologies, they can discriminate at will, and we have very little way to know whether that’s happening,” Radsch said.

The stakes are high given the upcoming midterms. Misinformation that the 2020 presidential election was rigged inspired the Jan. 6 insurrection. Still, Meta monetizes accounts which spread similar claims. Libs of TikTok has said, “Democrats want to cheat,” and Johnson responded to reports of new plague cases in Russia by implying that Democrats would use them to rig the election.

“There’s a level of commitment with trying to preserve electoral integrity that needs to be present, especially when there are very delicate elections coming up,” Sanz said. “Disinformation should not be rewarded financially — this is something that even they have in their own policies for monetization.”

Sanz has a “wish list” of new accountability policies that could push back against the anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric and political disinformation being disseminated through this program. These include labeling monetized accounts and adding mechanisms for users to report monetization policy violations.

Hong added that platforms should restructure their algorithms and monetization systems to consider factors other than engagement.

“I wish that Facebook would have more kinds of metrics, like societal or individual well-being,” Hong said. “These are kinds of things that would be far better for society, but it is a corporation and this is what they’re trying to do because this is the mandate from the top.”

While Meta is protected from many forms of legal action in the United States, there may be a path to legal accountability in other jurisdictions. In 2022, the European Union passed the Digital Services Act (DSA), which, among other provisions, requires large online platforms like Facebook to mitigate the potential harms of content disseminated on their platforms. WTF filed a complaint against Meta in European courts last month arguing that by monetizing 11 accounts sanctioned by the E.U. for alleged involvement in pro-Russia propaganda campaigns, the company failed to meet the DSA’s risk mitigation obligations.

Perhaps most importantly, Sanz emphasizes that social media monetization needs more public attention.

“Creator monetization is a very ill-explored area,” she said. “Although there is a good amount of legislation here in the E.U. that gives us a playground to try to incorporate much more responsibility when it comes to monetization, I do think that globally this needs to be the case.”

Note: Jones and Raichik did not respond to requests for comment.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

title: As Inflation Goes Up, New Poll Shows 4 in 10 Struggle to Pay Basic Necessities
content:
The latest Consumer Price Index report shows that inflation has gone up 3.7 percent over the past year.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows inflation has increased over the past month (and the year overall), as millions of Americans say they are struggling to make ends meet or pay for basic necessities.

According to the CPI report, which was published on Wednesday, consumer prices shot up by 0.6 percent from August to September. Year-over-year prices have increased by 3.7 percent.

That yearly rate is higher than previous reports in 2026. On average, the annual inflation rate, which is included in each monthly report, has been around 3.3 percent since the start of the year. The latest CPI numbers are also higher than they were immediately before Trump returned to the White House in 2025 — according to the December 2024 CPI, the inflation rate was 2.9 percent.

Costs for staple food items have increased over the past year, with ground beef prices up 5.4 percent, fruits and vegetables up 3.7 percent, bread up 3.3 percent, and fish/seafood up 6.9 percent. Energy costs are also markedly higher than they were last year, increasing by 10.9 percent overall, including a 21.5 percent increase in gas prices compared to September 2025.

Analysts largely attribute higher energy prices to Trump’s war against Iran, which began in late February and resulted in the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil is normally transported. The week before the war began, gas prices across the U.S. averaged around $2.937 per gallon. As of Wednesday, prices are $4.333 per gallon on average, a 47 percent increase over the past seven months.

While prices for gasoline have been higher in the past, those increased costs were temporary. This week, the U.S. broke a record set in 2022 for the most days in a calendar year where average prices for regular gasoline have been above $4 per gallon: 158 days total since the start of 2026.

On gas costs, the Trump administration has promised throughout the war that higher prices would be short-lived.

“Rest assured, to the American people, the recent increase in oil and ​gas prices is temporary, and this operation will result in lower gas prices in the long term,” former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said in March.

Asked by reporters about continuing high costs for fuel, Trump said in April that “gas will go down” and will “drop like a rock” as soon as the war is over. In June, he made a similar statement on Truth Social, writing that “Gas prices will plummet, and Affordability will be far better” than in the Biden years.

Earlier this week, Trump appeared to ignore entirely the fact that most Americans are feeling economic pinches, falsely stating during one of his campaign speeches that “prices are coming down very fast” right now.

The president promised on the 2024 presidential campaign trail to lower prices for groceries and other consumer goods, and to produce $2 per gallon gasoline shortly after entering office.

New polling demonstrates Americans are struggling, despite Trump’s rosy assessments.

According to a recently published Pew Research Center survey, 60 percent of Americans say they don’t have enough income to lead the life they desire. The poll also showed that 53 percent say they don’t have emergency savings that could help pay expenses for three months, and a third of respondents (32 percent) say they worry every day or almost every day about health care and debt costs.

Seventy percent of Americans have had to cut back their spending habits for “extras” — going out to eat or streaming services, for example. And 44 percent say they have had trouble paying for at least one basic necessity over the past year.

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s 

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.




But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?




The history beneath the headline




Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier 

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.




Across the region, 

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers 

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.




These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s 

The Forgotten Queens of Islam

 

challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators 

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 




Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this 

hadith

 against women’s political authority:




«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»




Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a 

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a 

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.




PAM’s promises and its record




Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi 

documents 

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures 

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.




PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008, 

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.




PAM’s 

2026 programme

 promises improved widow pensions, childcare, safe transport, a women’s enterprise fund and labour inspection. The commitments leave inheritance equality, abortion reform and decriminalisation of consensual same sex relations unaddressed. Mansouri called for 

banning child marriage

 without exceptions in 2024, yet PAM’s electoral programme 

omits that commitment

. Employment can support independence, but a wage does not cancel criminalisation or unequal property rights. The programme leaves those constraints intact.




Even PAM’s narrow promise to increase women’s access to paid work confronts a record of failure. The government 

promised to raise women’s economic activity rate above 30 

per cent. Morocco’s statistics agency, HCP, recorded 

20.9 percent in 2021

 and 

19 percent in 2025

. That leaves 81 per cent of women aged 15 and over outside the labour force, compared with 31.5 per cent of men. Women’s unpaid work nevertheless sustains households. As a governing coalition since 2021, PAM shares responsibility for the policies that failed to reverse this decline. Promising 21.2 percent by 2031 requires explaining what will change beyond the deadline.




Women in traditional Moroccan attire exploring a bustling outdoor market in Tiznit. Photo by 

YOUSSEF elbelghiti

 /Pexels 




Mansouri’s housing record reveals the distance between reconstruction and recovery. As Marrakech mayor and national housing minister, her 

portfolio included 

earthquake reconstructio

n

. Yet in June 2026, 

Al Haouz survivors protesting 

in Marrakech reported still living in damaged homes at risk of collapse, nearly three years after the earthquake devastated the High Atlas. For women managing care in unsafe housing, delay narrows possibilities for work or study. An unfinished house can become an unfinished independence.




Moreover, PAM must form a coalition government because it lacks a parliamentary majority. Istiqlal’s 

conditions for joining

 the PAM-led government include defending a socially conservative conception of the family and its values. Such alliances protect established family hierarchies. Protection must include a woman’s ability to leave a marriage, raise children independently or refuse the family’s expectations. Support must not entrench dependence. PAM could also govern with parties from the established left, including the Socialist Union of Popular Forces (USFP) and the Party of Progress and Socialism (PPS). Both have participated in previous governments. Their participation would not itself guarantee a feminist programme: the question is which commitments Mansouri’s government would adopt




Within Morocco’s political landscape, the Alliance de la Gauche offers a substantive point of comparison because of its explicit commitments to legal equality and social justice. The Alliance brings together the Unified Socialist Party (PSU) and the Federation of the Democratic Left. Its programme

 

pledges to abolish child marriage without exceptions, eliminate ta’sib

 (which can assign residual inheritance to male relatives) and comprehensively reform inheritance law. These commitments would challenge legal mechanisms that sustain women’s dependence. Whatever coalition Mansouri forms, advancing equality requires confronting those mechanisms, rather than merely broadening the government’s political composition.




For left parties to make a substantive difference, their commitments must extend to how care is funded and shared. Nancy Fraser’s

 

analysis of capitalism’s care contradiction

 shows how economies depend on care while undermining the resources sustaining it. Cuts and inadequate services transfer obligations into households, often onto women. A feminist left must confront that transfer and defend bodily autonomy, rather than expect class justice automatically to produce it. 




When representation preserves hierarchy




Morocco’s first female prime minister follows earlier examples of women’s leadership in other Muslim-majority countries, including 

Pakistan

, 

Bangladesh

 and 

Tunisia

. Their experience challenges religious arguments against women’s leadership, but also the assumption that representation guarantees emancipation. In 2025, 

women’s labour force 

participation in Pakistan stood at 24 percent and 38.6 percent in Bangladesh, against roughly 80 percent for men. In Tunisia, Najla Bouden’s 2021 appointment accompanied 

an authoritarian concentration of power

. Patriarchy can accommodate a woman at the summit while preserving the laws, economic dependencies and hierarchies that subordinate women below. 




Emancipation requires changing how power is organised, exercised and distributed.




Women’s leadership can also lend credibility to conservative projects. Italy’s Giorgia Meloni government 

allowed anti-abortion

 groups access to counselling centres. This risks exposing women seeking abortions to pressure against their decision. Japan’s Sanae Takaichi 

defends 

compulsory shared marital surnames and male imperial succession. Their ascent to power leaves those constraints on other women intact. 




And the rise of Germany’s Alice Weidel, who raises two sons with a Sri Lankan-born female partner while 

leading the far-right AfD

, which opposes same sex marriage and expanded adoption rights and demands tighter immigration restrictions, is another example. Her presence makes the party appear more open than the freedoms it would extend to others. Rwanda’s former Minister of Family and Women’s Development 

under the interim government in 1994

, Pauline Nyiramasuhuko, 

was convicted of genocidal crimes,

 including responsibility for rape. Together, these cases expose the danger of treating gender as a guarantee of solidarity.




Patriarchy survives through the incentives and penalties that organise social life. 




Feminist sociologist Deniz Kandiyoti’s

 

concept of “patriarchal bargains”

 explains how women seek security within patriarchal systems, sometimes enforcing the restrictions they navigate. A mother may limit her daughter’s choices because she fears the consequences of disobedience. For women in political office, the question is whether they use their authority to dismantle the conditions that make obedience a price of security.




What freedom requires




Which women are recognised as entitled to freedom? Kimberlé Crenshaw’s 

intersectionality

 challenges separating gender from racialisation. Class, disability, sexuality and citizenship shape whether a woman can exercise a right. A professional’s independence may depend on another woman’s underpaid domestic labour. 




Feminism must confront that unequal distribution of freedom.




Poverty makes institutional failure harder to escape. In 2025, nine 

maternal deaths

 at Agadir’s Hassan II Regional Hospital prompted demands for accountability. Women unable to purchase private care depend on public provision. In Morocco, rural Amazigh women 

face barriers 

to services and information in their language; agricultural workers have 

described

 low pay and sexual violence. Celebrating Amazigh queens means little if living Amazigh women cannot reach a hospital or work safely.




Dependence is also enforced through law. Morocco’s article 490 

criminalises sex outside marriage

, exposing sexually active unmarried women, including single mothers, to prosecution. Single and divorced mothers need independent parental rights, 

children born outside marriage

 can be denied paternal maintenance and inheritance. Article 489 

criminalises same sex relations

, threatening lesbian, bisexual and queer women’s intimacy. Transgender women lack

 

legal gender recognition

 and face

 

policing of their gender expression

 under Article 483, whose prohibition of public indecency can be applied even when no nudity is involved.




Safety requires rights that survive disapproval. 




Rights also require that institutions be accessible for women. In its 

2017 review of Morocco

, the UN disability committee identified inaccessible courts and healthcare, and restrictions on legal capacity. Disabled and neurodivergent women need accessible services, bodily autonomy and the means to live independently with dignity.




Migration status creates another fault line in women’s access to protection. Political theorist Françoise Vergès’s

 

A Decolonial Feminism

 insists that feminism must confront racism and capitalism together. This shifts the question from whether women gain power to which women that acquired power protect. A 

2023 study of 151 migrant women

 attending healthcare facilities in Rabat found that 76.2 per cent reported gender based violence during migration, while only 9 per cent of survivors had filed a complaint. Pan-African feminism must make access to protection a measure of political progress. 




Women’s advancement cannot be measured only among those the nation recognises as its own.




I want equality that dismantles the arrangements through which patriarchy makes obedience a condition of survival. A woman needs a home she can keep, an income she controls and laws that recognise her authority over her own body. Inheritance, abortion, housing, the right to love and collective labour rights belong together because freedom requires power over the conditions of one’s life.




For girls, that begins with accessible schools, protection against violence and child marriage, and a future they can choose. A right that poverty renders unusable remains, in practice, a privilege.




PM Mansouri’s appointment enlarges what women can imagine. Its feminist significance depends on whether power becomes less concentrated and freedom more accessible to women still impoverished, marginalised or criminalised. Patriarchy can accommodate exceptional women; emancipation must reach those it keeps expendable. Women’s liberation cannot rest on the hierarchies that decide which women can be sacrificed.




 




Ayah Kareem is a Moroccan feminist researcher, writer and activist whose work connects political analysis with collective organising. She has an academic background in political science and human rights and is a Thomson Reuters Foundation mentee. Drawing on decolonial and intersectional feminism, she examines the patriarchal institutions that make inequality ordinary and the struggles that make it contestable.
