title: Indigenous Just Transition in The Arctic
content:
This is going to be a collaborative event between Ungeirr Umkveraasenaar, or the Icelandic Young Environmentalists, and the Indigenous Environmental Network. Maybe we can go around and you guys can give a little introduction about yourselves. Sure.

Huang’a a’ka, pang’a’anang naka pang’a’u yu, huang’a a’taka, a’anatirma, naka kirstinuga pás, huang’a sivunga rumi. I come from St. Lawrence Island. I’ve been with IEN since 2021, and I work on organizing against climate geoengineering.

Kweyanaipaplusi maunga, huang’a a’akaluk, ungelaksirmiu runga, angayukang maktaklu Charlie. I a’anukwa’apu’a makigaklu anaktiyuk asii, janililu Charlie, chinirmiu, ungelaksirmiu. Thank you everyone for welcoming us here today.

I’m Adrienne A’akaluk Blatchford. I’m from Unalakleet, Alaska, which is up on the Northwest Coast in the passageway to the Arctic. We’re right on the coast of the Bering Sea in the heart of the Norton Sound.

And I work with Indigenous Environmental Network as a geoengineering outreach organizer with a focus on Alaska and the Arctic. Hello, thank you for having us as the host.

My name is Thomas Joseph. I’m a Hoopa Valley tribal member from the Six Rivers National Forest in Northern California. I am also Shoshone Paiute from the Sierra Nevadas. Paiute is what we call it, the land of flowing water.

I’m down there by Yosemite and the Half Dome area. I am here with the Indigenous Environmental Network as their carbon pricing educator. And again, thanks for having us.

Yá’át’ééh. My name is Talia Boyd. Older women from my community who love to have the time of their lives shared with me.

Greetings, everyone. My name is Talia Boyd. I’m the mining organizer for IEN.

I’m based in New Mexico, originally from Arizona, and I hail from the Navajo Nation in the Southwest. And I’m very honored to be here with y’all and share this space and time. Thank you.

Awesome. And a little bit about me for any of you who don’t know me. My name is Isla.

I’m originally from Wales and I’ve been living here in Iceland for over five years and I’m the education representative for the Icelandic Young Environmentalists. So how about we just go straight into things and you guys can give us a little bit of an oral presentation about your work and everything that you do and then we’ll get started with the panel Q&A afterwards. Sounds good.

Thank you. So I want to kind of do a little bit of an introduction on who is the Indigenous Environmental Network. Over 30 years ago the United States, we’re kind of seeing that return back to that, was having a really hard time addressing the mining operations of uranium in the southwest and the Indigenous people came together as they were the ones that were being directly affected by these mining operations that was being used for the production of uranium for the purpose of war.

And so the Indigenous peoples from that region rallied together to try to protect their communities against the high rates of cancers and other issues that was plaguing their communities to no avail. The state governments wouldn’t listen to them. The national governments wouldn’t listen to them and so they seen that it was in their best interest to take this fight to the international space of the United Nations and that’s when the Indigenous Environmental Network was formed with the purpose and intent of taking the struggles of the mining and the struggles of the health impacts of mining to a global positioning.

The Indigenous Environmental Network has been active in the United Nations space since then and in various different causes pertaining to the Paris Climate Agreement, water issues, mining issues, also very active in the Convention on Biological Diversity and we continue to play a role of Indigenous networks across Turtle Island. So we come from impacted communities of Indigenous peoples. Frontline community is another term that’s often used from across Turtle Island of communities that are faced with deforestation, faced with dams, faced with any type of harm that we see against our Mother Earth.

In these past 30 years IEN has now expanded its network to be globally and so we have Indigenous organizations that we work with across the globe and in North America we have a strong positioning on mining operations which is Talia Leeds and geoengineering and carbon pricing which I do but we also do a lot of other work pertaining to just transition and many other things that you can find on our website at IENEarth.org. Thank you. Great. I wanted to share a little bit about the two histories Thomas talked about.

The duality that we have to keep in mind, the recognition that the history of why we are in this work and what our priorities are in terms of the Arctic and climate change and then the history and the purpose behind the Arctic Assembly which is the meetings that we are attending. So I come from St. Lawrence Island and Akula comes from very nearby and their community also experienced a lot of the same things we did. The history that we carry is around colonization and how the purpose behind colonization was always resource extraction, resource extraction happening from Indigenous people’s lands and waters and to the detriment of our health, our welfare, the health of our ecosystems and as a violation of the sacred or the original instructions that we have carried forward through millennia.

And particularly this was done through military tactics and the military has also harmed our communities by creating bases on or near our communities or where we practice subsistence activities and other cultural activities and those bases have contaminated our lands and contaminated our waters and so we suffer the health effects and so we see all of these as connected because the military was used to colonize and the purpose behind colonizing was resource extraction. So we always come back to that and we see those issues like permeating throughout all of the issues that we’ll talk about today including carbon markets, carbon pricing, geoengineering, mining, even in the energy transition. But I was going back as I do whenever I come to the Arctic Assembly and looking at the web archives of when they first formed and some of the stuff on here is interesting.

I just wanted to read some of the wording. The Arctic is the fastest warming place on earth. This is from their website in 2013.

As a result it is moving to the center of the geopolitical stage and is playing an increasingly important role in globalization, economic development, energy exploration, environmental protection, and international security. So it’s just kind of environmental protection is just kind of sprinkled in there a little bit but the priority is clearly economic development. And if you look at the articles like I could go you can go and look at who created it, who was on their first board, who was on their first panel, but some of the articles that they attached.

Could Western Alaska become the new Panama Canal? Energy, indigenous communities, and the Arctic Council. Arctic climate change opens new shipping routes. So these are the articles that they cited as the foundation of the initial meetings that they were having and I wanted to read one excerpt just to kind of give the context of what the purpose was behind this meeting and like holding that reality in the messages that they appear to be spreading versus what is actually being done.

Owing to the vast economic opportunities and environmental, social, and geopolitical challenges it presents, the Arctic is an emerging as an important topic of debate. With an estimated 25 percent of the world’s undiscovered oil and gas reserves, and with climate change making shorter maritime routes through Arctic waters possible, the rewards of successful economic development are plentiful. Like that’s how they started out.

And then this is really interesting. They say, however, the remote pristine frontier is home to some of the world’s harshest conditions making energy development, maritime trade, and tourism increasingly difficult and dangerous. The Arctic is also home to indigenous communities whose livelihoods are likely to be challenged by both the effects of climate change and increasing external human activity in the region.

So those are just, yeah, a couple of things that I wanted you to keep in mind and I wanted to hand it back to Thomas to look at the history of carbon pricing. Thank you, Pananga. I remember my first time here in the Arctic region.

I was invited up here by Pananga Pagawi and other indigenous peoples from Greenland and the Alaska region because they told me, they came the year before, and they told me that there is a lot of talk and dialogue that’s being discussed in this Arctic circle pertaining to carbon markets and the continued commodification of our Mother Earth. And this is something that I have specialized with the Indigenous Environmental Network for quite a few years now. And when we look at the CDMs on where carbon markets came from, which is the Clean Development Mechanism, which was created out of the Kyoto Protocols, which is basically the foundation of the Paris Climate Agreement.

And so when we go that far back, we have to also understand that it was the strong arm of Al Gore at the time, who was the Vice President of the United States, that really forced these governmental nations into accepting a clean development mechanism or a carbon market mechanism, which we see as indigenous peoples is just the continuation of commodifying our Mother Earth for the profitable gain of the elite few. We also see it as a mechanism to continue colonization and white supremacy, as that’s what these northern global nations are pushing and addressing. The world did not want clean development mechanisms.

They didn’t want to put a price tag on carbon because they didn’t think that that was the route to go. But because of the strong arm of the United States, they were able to get clean development mechanisms into the Kyoto Protocols. And so we see a shift now, how the United States is not even a signer of the Paris Climate Agreement, and they have pulled out.

So their influence in that space has dramatically changed, but yet it is the foundation of how the world is addressing climate change. We now see in Article 6 of the Paris Climate Agreement and market mechanisms as a way to, how they see in their eyes, bring carbon out of the air, because we know that greenhouse gases are real. We know that that’s what’s warming our planet, and that is what is causing climate change.

But instead of reducing gases at source, or reducing the burning of fossil fuel, they’re simply offsetting it. So they’re saying that they could do offsets through RED, which is reducing emissions through deforestation and forest degradation, and RED Plus, which even expands that into nature-based solutions and other products. But that’s still just a continuation of commodifying our Mother Earth.

And now if we look at climate change, one of the root causes of climate change is capitalism, is that we continue to see our Mother Earth as something that we can make profit of, that we can continue to separate ourselves from, and think that it is here just for the profitable gain of a select few, and not that we’re in relationship with our Mother Earth, not that that relationship is reciprocal, like Indigenous peoples believe. And so when we look into even biodiversity offsets that are now being pushed, it calls that relationship into question. As humanity, are we going to continue to move forward with the desire of just raping and plaguing our Mother Earth? Are we going to try to find some type of balance and reciprocal relationship with her, so that she can heal, and that we may be able to move forward and not experience this climate chaos that’s coming our way? We see that in Nepal.

We see that with the mega El Nino that’s going on right now in California. So we will continue to experience this. Even the Secretariat has said, we have reached 1.5, we will start experiencing mega catastrophes with climate change.

But yet, what we’re seeing is just us doubling down on mechanisms that has caused climate change. I brought up colonization earlier. When we look at the world’s biodiversity, 80% of the world’s biodiversity is in the tenure of Indigenous peoples.

And so for these global elite countries to be able to maintain their economic growth, to be able to maintain their markets, they need to gain access to these unceded territories of Indigenous peoples. And that’s how they do it, is through carbon markets, through biodiversity offsets, through the 30 by 30 initiative, which is being pushed through the CBD, the Convention on Biological Diversity. And so, you know, this is just continuating the ability to access unceded Indigenous lands and further colonize Indigenous peoples, and move us away from an understanding that what we really need to do is rebuild our relationship with our Mother Earth, not to see her as a commodity just to be used, but understand that our reciprocal relationship with her is vital, and not just the humanity of humans, but in all things living.

And so when I came up here to my first Arctic gathering, I seen what they were telling me about. I seen how these Arctic nations were lifting up examples from all across the world, not even the Arctic, from New Zealand, on mangroves that are being introduced as carbon offsets in the New Zealand area. And we see how Nepal and that region is being considered the third Arctic for the purpose of offset projects on sprinkling, these guys will get more into that, but sprinkling basically fiberglass on top of the ice.

And so it’s just a continuation of us continuing to commodify our Mother Earth and not understand that we really need to address root causes, which is capitalism, which is colonization and patriarchy, and the continuation that we always need to develop new market mechanisms or new systems to gain wealth. So we need to have that system change. But when we keep on focusing on false solutions like direct air capture, which is alive and well here in Iceland, we’re not going to be able to really focus on keeping the fossil fuels in the ground, and making sure that we’re limiting the amount of carbon that’s being burnt and not simply offsetting it.

Thank you. I’m just going to snowball off of what Thomas said, because before I get into what I’m going to talk about with geoengineering, he said something really profound one time that just kind of made carbon markets and these schemes that they are implementing within our governance systems, these colonial governance systems. When you think about the world’s forest and the oceans and the rivers and Mother Earth, and we see these climate disasters, she’s already struggling to breathe, right? We already know that.

We’ve exceeded 1.5. And these carbon market schemes and these false solutions make it sound like they’re putting a new forest, or there’s a new emerging ocean, or there’s these rivers that are already leaching things like mercury, because of the melting permafrost in them, that all of a sudden they’re appearing out of nowhere for these carbon markets, right? And that’s not what’s happening. We’re seeing extractivism continue to grow. We’re seeing this sort of monetary wealth through this extractive industry pile more, right, to do business as usual on top of all of it.

And that’s led us into from fossil fuel dependency into a tech regime that has emerged from false solutions like geoengineering. And when we think about geoengineering, it’s such a far-fetched concept when you’re first learning about it, right? It’s like a sci-fi movie. There’s two different types that are really focused on, especially in the Arctic, with solar radiation management and carbon dioxide removal.

And Thomas had just mentioned, you know, we have the facility right out here, just out of town. And when these false solutions first started popping up here in the Arctic, we seen a lot of the focus on the Arctic is melting, we need to save the Arctic, because we know that the rest of the world depends on this ice cap and this old ice, right? When you think about the Arctic Ocean and where the passageway comes up through and the world perceives it as this frozen place all the time, well, it took a millennia for that ice to form, and it’s taken a hundred years for it to melt because of extractivism, because of colonialism, because of after imaginary wealth, when you think of money and the way that it is focused in our lives. The villagers have been speaking from us.

They feed us all these lies about you need daycare, you need childcare, you need education. We’ve always had those systems within our communities, within our social systems of wherever we come from, right? And so this colonial practice has led us to these false solutions, saying that if we can introduce a way to control the climate, then we can keep the world at a critical level. And so that’s when folks that started doing these carbon capture projects, the marine carbon dioxide removal, the solar radiation management, I’m sorry, is there a T-next in here anywhere? Sorry, guys, I’ve been really sniffly all day.

I went from the latitudes to the seas, and the Arctic has caught me again. But geoengineering has been a huge focus at Arctic Assembly for years. The first year that we had attended, we had gone in and they were talking about a solar aerosol injection project, and they have this huge, beautiful display, and PhD candidates, so much PhD candidates, doctorates, scientists, renowned university folks that had come in, and they’re from Ivy League colleges that are standing there saying, yeah, we’re going to spray sulfur dioxide over the Arctic, and once we deploy, it’s going to have to happen for 100 years, and 5% of the world’s population is going to perish doing it, but it’s going to be a sacrifice to the rest of the world.

And we’re sitting there, and you’re saying, and by the way, the 5% will be Indigenous people, marginalized communities, and the majority of it will be in the Arctic. Not even a blink of an eye. And this is an international platform where there are decision makers from the pan-Arctic coming here to talk about saving the world by spraying toxic chemicals into the atmosphere to literally kill people, animals, ecosystems, so they’re well synthesized.

And then we see projects like the Arctic Ice Project, which was formerly known as Ice 9-11, which is a, the idea was to increase the surface albedo of the ice by sprinkling glass beads, microscopic glass beads, which were formed by scientists at 3M who had previously worked for Chevron, and NHP as an engineer, and she has over 300 patents, came up to the Arctic, and without required consent, without proper processes processes to assess the environment that she was going to be introducing huge amounts of new substances to, had no connection to anybody in the Arctic, just came in and started doing it on their own free will, and hiring local Indigenous students at a college up north. And when we got wind of this project, we immediately saw red flags. We started pushing back, but we found that a lot of these geoengineering projects, these fossil solutions that are rooted in extractivism, are crowd-funded and have huge hedge funds that come in as a guide, as nature, they’re going to conserve nature by introducing these projects in the world to keep being, continue doing business as usual.

And so the science is rooted in all of the things that Thomas has talked about, and the foundation of the Arctic Assembly is been based on the sacrifice zone, creating new sacrifice zones, not only in Arctic Indigenous lands, but lands worldwide, because what happens in the north is going to impact the rest of the world. And so once we started organizing around, pushing back on these projects, Thomas’ family had joined us all the way down in California in Menlo Park, where Leslie Fields, one of the founders of the Arctic Ice Project, had organized a fundraiser and a golf course, a very prestigious golf course in Menlo Park. And so a group of Alaska Native folks had gone down, a delegation that IAN Kavanaugh had put together with IAN and Thomas’ family joined us.

Yeah, yeah, so we bought this, we spent thousands of dollars on purchasing a VIP ticket, and immediately they denied our entrance and said that it was still, that it was already at capacity. So we got some folks that we were working with down there, and they also applied and got in immediately. And so they went in and were able to infiltrate this fundraiser.

But it didn’t last long, and they caught on with the folks that were with us outside when we were picketing and protesting. And they came out and wanted to try to see, so the police showed up and said, sorry, we can’t do anything, this is legal here, and tried to have us removed. So we continued that, but it brought attention, right? That’s where we started, and we continued for five years.

No, 19 to 25, yeah, six years. 24. So yeah, five years, we continued to push back against this project that had moved, started in the Bay Area and then Minnesota on Indigenous lands, on a lake there, and all the way up to a camp which we had deployed, and then we started attacking on Arctic, like Arctic species of fish, and yeah, and birds, and was doing false reporting.

And it comes here to the Arctic Assembly without false reporting. And the guys, of course, that were giving this case to the Arctic, I watched Al Gore’s, her claim was, I watched Al Gore’s documentary, touched my heart, it made me want to save the world. So these projects continue to not only allow them to do business as usual, but create sacrifice zones in other Indigenous communities, not only in the Arctic, but the rest of the world.

And so geoengineering is another dangerous way for the elite to continue doing what they do, by extracting, and stealing, and killing Indigenous people throughout the world. We see that within our communities. And it isn’t only the impacts of the introduction of all of these foreign substances, but it also is our mental health, right? Without our connection to the land, and without our way of being, since we always have our mental health struggles, we have suicide clusters, we have cancer clusters, we have autoimmune diseases that are unexplained.

We have experiences at such a high level that we’re in a constant state of grief as Indigenous people. And so it isn’t only what we’re seeing on the surface, but also the subsurface of who we are. And so this geoengineering, these fossil solutions, these carbon market mechanisms, all of these different ways that they’re claiming a way to advance science, to save the world, is a shield and almost like a blind for them to continue doing what they want to do in our land.

And so we recognize that, and we continue to push for free pirate consent, and meaningful government-to-government consultation. And when we say that, we’re not talking about these colonial governments that we see, but also our traditional government systems, because that’s how we function within our community. So I’m going to leave it there, below air, if she wants to.

Yeah, just add a couple things. So as we feel continued, she left our fifth ice project. I think they figured her out because she had done the experiments outdoors.

And so then they changed their company name and said, we’re not doing outdoor experiments. And they started doing like all those experiments on those species. And then she formed her other, another company, called Wheel.

title: Le hussard noir tombe du toit / une émission de Minuit Décousu
content:
Après notre émission sur le début du mouvement lycéen à Lyon, on continue à suivre la mobilisation en passant cette fois la porte des établissements actuellement vides pour voir ce qu'il reste des fameux hussards noirs de la République et comprendre l'origine du malaise qui a poussé autant de jeunes dans les rues.




Cette semaine, cela fait déjà près d'une vingtaine de jours que le mouvement lycéen et désormais également étudiant s'est emparé des rues lyonnaises quasi quotidiennement. Partout, les lycées ont encore leurs portes solidement fermées voire barricadées de peur de la résurgence des rassemblement lycéens aux portes des établissements, malgré la répression inédite menée conjointement par la préfecture et le rectorat. Depuis notre dernière émission, où l'on écoutait dans des entretiens fleuves des lycéen-nes lyonnais-es nous parler de leurs premiers blocages, de l'organisation et des perspectives du mouvement, la répression a tenté de dégager la mobilisation des abords des établissements pour lui faire gagner la respectabilité des mobilisation sociales traditionnelles. Pourtant, la jeunesse continue de prouver jour après jour sa détermination à poursuivre le mouvement, selon son propre agenda.




Pour cette émission, on voulait aller voir ce qu'il se passait en interne dans les établissements scolaires pour comprendre l'origine du malaise qui a poussé autant de jeunes dans la rue. On est donc allés tourner dans la manifestation du 13 octobre à Lyon, où l'on écoute à nouveau des lycéen-nes, mais aussi des étudiant-es nous parler de l'avancée de leur mobilisation et la manière dont les établissements du second degré et du supérieur tentent coûte que coûte de mater la révolte en interne en gardant leurs portes fermées. Dans cette même manif', on s'est entretenu avec des profs de lycées de quartiers populaires ayant connu de nombreux blocages qui nous expliquent concrètement ce qu'il se passe dans les établissements fantômatiques depuis ces 20 derniers jours. . On écoute aussi une camarade prof de lettre en réseau d'éducation prioritaire renforcé (REP+) de banlieue lyonnaise, qui revient à notre micro sur les évolutions de l'éducation ces 10 dernières années, sur l'absence complète de démocratie dans les bahuts et sur le fossé grandissant entre l'ordre et la morale pronés par les adultes et les désirs de révolution des jeunes. Pour saupoudrer le tout d'un peu d'histoire, on est allés repiquer les archives du mouvement lycéen de 1971 à Villeurbanne dans le 2ème numéro des 

Informations Rassemblées à Lyon

 (IRL).




L'émission s'écoute sur notre 

audioblog

, ici, et un peu partout en podcast. Bonne écoute !




 

 

 

 

 

 










Minuit Décousu, c'est un fanzine radiophonique nocturne sur 

Radio Canut

 (Lyon et alentours), 

Radio Vassivière

 (Limousin) et 

Cause Commune

 (Paris/IDF). Semaine après semaine pendant une heure, on en découd avec la nuit et on tire les fils de sons, de textes, d'archives et de voix qui s'entremêlent.

title: Universities fire dozens amid pressure from Zionist billionaires (Electronic Intifada)
content:
Ali Abunimah Rights and Accountability 14 October 2026

Universities in the United States and Canada have fired, suspended and harassed employees for speaking out against Israel’s genocide in Gaza, often using ostensibly neutral disciplinary procedures to conceal politically motivated retaliation.

That is the finding of a new report from the Academic Freedom Initiative, a project of the Middle East Studies Association (MESA).

“Lessons in Repression: Silencing Campus Workers on Palestine Since October 7, 2023” is the first systematic study of retaliation against university employees for their Palestine-related speech and activism in the two countries.

The report draws on a database of 196 incidents recorded through 20 August 2026 and in-depth interviews with 31 targeted employees.

Of those incidents, 76 – nearly 40 percent – resulted in termination, while 59 involved suspension or campus bans.

Both tenured professors and precariously employed instructors and staff have been targeted. Of 134 cases in which racial or ethnic identity was known, nearly two-thirds involved people of color. Some 16.5 percent of those targeted identified as Jewish.

Most retaliation had nothing to do with classroom teaching. More than half the incidents stemmed from other on-campus activities, including protests, while only 11 percent concerned alleged classroom interactions.

Another 16 percent of cases arose from off-campus speech and 12 percent from social media posts, “suggesting that teaching is a relatively less common context provoking punishment.”

Major drivers of the repression include pressure from wealthy pro-Israel donors, government interference and the political loyalties of university administrators and trustees, the report says.

Growing financial dependence of universities on wealthy benefactors, alongside austerity and the widespread use of precariously employed workers, also makes institutions more vulnerable to political pressure.

At the University of Pennsylvania, for example, trustee Cheryl Peisach is married to the treasurer of a family foundation that donated $100,000 to Canary Mission in 2023.

The notorious pro-Israel blacklisting website publishes dossiers attacking students and academics who support Palestinian rights.

US immigration authorities have admitted to using its dossiers to target Palestine activists.

In another case at Penn, a tenured professor faced a vicious online harassment campaign over her support for Palestine, including hundreds of messages containing rape and death threats.

The donor funding her endowed chair withdrew support. According to the professor, a dean told her that donor pressure had led the university to encourage her retirement. She retired in June 2026.

Billionaire Bill Ackman demanded a blacklist of Harvard students who disagreed with his views, while billionaire Leon Cooperman threatened to stop donating to Columbia University following a Palestine solidarity walkout.

Pressure from the Trump administration has reinforced the crackdown.

During the last two months of 2023, the US government opened more federal “anti-Semitism” investigations against universities than in all previous years combined.

Dozens of institutions agreed to government monitoring, including sharing the names of students and employees accused of anti-Semitism, to close investigations.

Harvard provided a notable example of such cowardice. Even as it fought a Trump administration lawsuit falsely portraying Gaza solidarity protests as anti-Jewish terror, the university boasted of its own crackdown on alleged anti-Semitism rather than defend its students’ right to protest Israel’s genocide.

A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit in August, finding that the government had failed to plausibly allege any ongoing violation of civil rights law.

Six congressional hearings between December 2023 and July 2025 subjected university leaders to McCarthyite interrogations over alleged failures to combat anti-Semitism.

In Illinois, Northwestern University journalism professor Steven Thrasher was suspended shortly after being singled out during one of these hearings and was later denied tenure and terminated. He is currently suing the university for discrimination and violations of his First Amendment rights.

The repression has also affected Canada, where provincial ministers have publicly accused academic staff and students of anti-Semitism, attacked discussions of Palestine and genocide, and demanded the removal of pro-Palestinian statements from university websites.

The crackdown has often been brutally overt.

More than 3,000 anti-genocide protesters, mostly students, were arrested or detained on US campuses by July 2024. Faculty and staff were affected by police violence.

At Indiana University, seven faculty members were arrested while trying to protect protesting students from government forces.

One professor recalled stepping between students and state troopers armed with assault rifles.

“I was arrested trying to preserve the safety of those students,” he said. He was banned from campus for a year and has received death threats.

The university itself pushed for criminal charges against the arrested faculty, but, according to the report, the county prosecutor “refused to press any charges, believing the constitutionality of the arrests was dubious at best.”

In January 2026, a federal court ruled that Indiana University had violated the First Amendment rights of Palestine solidarity protesters it banned from campus in 2024, including students and faculty.

The court also found the university’s ban on overnight expressive activity unconstitutional and ordered related disciplinary reprimands expunged from their records.

But MESA finds that much of the repression has taken less visible forms.

University administrators have relied on lengthy investigations, vague allegations, fabricated policy violations, non-renewal of contracts and non-disclosure agreements to punish employees while concealing their political motivations.

In many cases, the investigation itself is a form of repression.

“The complaints themselves have been the punishment, have been the intimidation and were designed to be,” Judith Norman, a professor at Trinity University in Texas, said of the repeated, baseless anti-Semitism accusations she faced.

Some allegations were astoundingly petty.

One professor was summoned to an anti-discrimination office after two students complained that the professor’s use of the term “state of Israel,” rather than simply “Israel,” supposedly made them feel alienated from the learning process.

In another case, a professor had to attend a meeting to face questions about a class he had taught two years earlier. The “accusations” included his use of the term “Jewish settlers” to refer to Israeli settlers, who, as the report notes, “due to Israel’s discriminatory laws, are by definition nearly always Jews.”

Investigations frequently drag on for months or years, with employees denied basic information about the accusations against them or meaningful opportunities to defend themselves.

Some investigators displayed open hostility or political bias, conflating criticism of Israel with hatred of Jews, or themselves expressing pro-Israel, anti-Arab, anti-Muslim views.

Universities have also increasingly subjected teaching materials to political surveillance.

By August 2026, seven US states had mandated public access to course syllabi, exposing instructors to scrutiny and complaints from political activists with no connection to their classrooms.

Another prominent tactic is what the report calls “networked harassment.”

Pro-Israel social media accounts and activists generate outrage against academics, sometimes unleashing torrents of racist abuse, doxxing and violent threats.

In one striking case at the University of Pennsylvania, a tenured professor faced a vicious campaign of online harassment after declining to participate in a documentary produced by a Zionist student activist.

Targeted over her personal social media posts about Palestine, she received hundreds of hate emails, most demanding that she be raped, along with death threats and other abuse.

“Because if somebody says, ‘you should be raped’ enough, you do watch your back a little bit,” she told MESA.

The harassment was followed by demands from donors, university trustees, alumni and outside groups that she be fired.

Rather than defend their employees, university administrators often capitulate to the harassers’ demands, even amplifying the attacks themselves.

None of MESA’s interviewees reported that their universities took action to protect them from online incitement.

The personal consequences have been devastating.

Nearly half of the documented incidents involved financial harm. Employees lost jobs, health insurance, housing and career prospects, while accusations of anti-Semitism inflicted lasting damage on reputations.

Amid intensified kidnappings and deportations by ICE, the US immigration agency, the risks for international scholars are even greater.

A tenure-track professor facing retaliation feared that losing her job would also mean losing her immigration status.

“Without my work visa, then I don’t have a status in the country. I have two kids here and a [non-citizen] husband,” she explained.

A professor who had been arrested and suspended described the continuing fear he experienced simply going to work.

“Every morning I come to my office, and I put my key in the door. I wonder if it’s going to work. Did they change the lock? Did they fire me and not tell me?”

“I don’t feel safe at this university,” he said, opining that if the institution’s president decided he had to go, “I don’t feel that there is even one level or layer that would try to stop them from firing me.”

The damage extended far beyond those directly punished.

The report documents pervasive self-censorship, with academics increasingly reluctant to discuss Palestine or criticize Israel – effectively fulfilling a key goal of the repression campaign.

Targeted employees also described profound disappointment with colleagues who refused to defend them.

Some condemned the “abject cowardice” of tenured professors who were the least likely to speak out, or provide moral and material support.

Interviewees also criticized faculty and administrators who privately expressed sympathy but remained publicly silent.

“Notably, pre-tenure faculty and students were more likely to provide support, despite being in a more precarious position than their tenured colleagues,” the report states.

Yet the report also offers lessons for resisting repression.

MESA urges workers to document everything, understand their rights, build alliances and join unions and professional associations. It calls on university administrators to defend academic freedom rather than merely proclaim their commitment to it.

It also recommends that institutions reject the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s so-called definition of anti-Semitism, which conflates criticism of Israel and its Zionist state ideology with anti-Jewish bigotry.

Far from impartial, the IHRA is a self-selected group of countries including Israel, the United States and other Western states that are Israel’s principal allies and arms suppliers.

Israel’s lobby has aggressively pushed for widespread adoption of the IHRA definition as a way to muzzle and smear supporters of Palestinian rights.

One significant victory came at the City University of New York, where a coordinated campaign involving unions and Palestine solidarity activists secured the rehiring of three of four contingent instructors dismissed after participating in a pro-Palestine demonstration.

The experience highlighted the importance of openly confronting the pro-Israel motivations behind the repression rather than treating it solely as a matter of employment rights.

As one professor involved in the organizing explained, “the more direct the political message about Palestine was, the more powerful the movement became.”

author: Ju-Hyun Park
title: Progressives Shouldn’t Call on Trump to Restore Military Exercises in Korea
content:
More than 20 Democrats signed a letter calling on Trump to maintain escalatory policies against North Korea.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The Korean Peninsula was thrust back into the spotlight this August following a surprise announcement from U.S. President Donald Trump that the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield joint U.S.-South Korea military exercises would be partially cancelled. In his typical meandering style, Trump simultaneously claimed the decision stemmed from his “very good relationship” with Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) President Kim Jong Un, and his growing frustration with the Republic of Korea (ROK), which he said had rebuffed his calls to join the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. While politicians and the media clamored over whether the decision was justified, few questioned the basic assumption that the U.S. military protects the Korean people or regional stability.

Trump’s up-and-down engagement with the DPRK has been a recurring story throughout his political career. It is one of the most ridiculed aspects of his presidency, and also one of the most misunderstood. At the root of this is a persistent ignorance concerning the true nature of Washington’s history and interests in Korea.

Democrats soon moved to convey their disapproval. DropSite News leaked a letter signed by 22 Democratic members of Congress expressing “alarm” at Trump’s decision, essentially urging the president to maintain a commitment to a cycle of military escalation and brinksmanship in Korea. “This decision has strained a 73-year alliance and risks undermining readiness, security, and deterrence on the Korean Peninsula,” the signatories warned. The letter was quietly published by House Democrats after the leak.

To be sure, there is much to criticize about the manner and purpose for why the Trump government made this choice to scale back these war drills in August. But it is important to recognize that Trump’s decision had little effect on the military situation. Ulchi Freedom Shield is a significant series of war drills, but it is far from the only one. In 2025, U.S. Forces Korea conducted 274 days of similar war exercises. Cancelling just a few is a drop in the bucket, and did nothing to meet his stated goal of advancing dialogue with the DPRK — which would have required stepping back from the prevailing framework of denuclearization.

So what was Trump’s purpose? In the weeks since, it has become apparent that Trump’s decision was a maneuver to pressure Seoul to concede on other matters: deliveries on the ROK’s promised $350 billion in tariff-related investments to the U.S., and joining the war on Iran. Today, South Korea is seeing a growing protest movement to prevent Seoul from capitulating to this pressure. The real issue is not Trump’s reduction of military drills; it is the U.S. war machine in Korea, and Democrats are part of this problem.

Calls for elected Democrats to drop their hawkish rhetoric on North Korea have gone unheeded. At a time when Washington is engaged in numerous destructive wars around the world, many of them escalated under Trump 2.0, the old guard of the Democratic Party is stubbornly clinging to a Cold War vision of the Korean Peninsula that can only lead to further escalation and instability.

The U.S. military has occupied Korea since 1945, when Washington made the decision to divide the peninsula into separate occupation zones, rather than permit the Korean people to organize an independent government. The U.S. military occupation in the south waged a brutal counterinsurgency war to crush a series of popular rebellions, and established the Republic of Korea (ROK) under the lead of Syngman Rhee, a staunchly pro-U.S. and anti-communist political figure. Even before the official start of the Korean War in 1950, the U.S. and ROK killed over 100,000 Koreans in the south alone.

Opposing war drills in Korea is fundamentally about opposing the violence of military occupation and Washington’s role in prolonging the Korean War.

The war itself brought only further destruction. In the south, the U.S. designated civilian refugees as enemy combatants, leading to atrocities like No Gun Ri, in which U.S. soldiers massacred hundreds of Korean refugees after evacuating them from their homes south of the 38th parallel. The U.S. backed the ROK state in its extermination campaign of political enemies, known as the Bodo League Massacre. In the north, the U.S. Air Force pursued a relentless bombing campaign that expunged the landscape of virtually all civilian structures. By the signing of the armistice in 1953, the U.S. had dropped 635,000 tons of explosives and over 37,000 tons of napalm in Korea — more than was used in the entire Pacific Theater of WWII.

A peace agreement has never formally concluded the Korean War. This makes the Korean War the longest-running overseas conflict in U.S. history. The war has left deep scars on the Korean people, but also upon U.S. politics. It was an undeclared war — a “police action” undertaken solely by executive fiat, a reverberating backdrop to all U.S. politics since 1945. Korea became the lab from which the U.S. could test its ideologies, technologies, and geopolitical maneuvers, executing heinous atrocities and setting the stage for countless Cold War interventions to come. To fight the Korean War, the U.S. quadrupled its military spending, directing much of it toward the restoration of military industry and the construction of overseas bases.

From the Cold War to the “war on terror,” the U.S. has continued to structure its economy and politics through permanent war on the Global South. If U.S. progressives today wish to dismantle the machine of endless war that dominates Washington, the legacy and present reality of Korea today must be confronted honestly.

U.S. intervention and occupation are far from being guarantors of democracy in Korea. This was made evident on the night of December 3, 2024, when then-President Yoon Suk Yeol declared martial law, to the complete surprise of the South Korean public. Yoon’s failed self-coup revived the traumatic memory of Chun Doo Hwan’s 1980s martial law regime which, under the aegis of the ongoing U.S. war against North Korea, used martial law to enforce anticommunism in South Korea through the policing and repression of everyday life, including the massacre of civilians. (Independent journalist Tim Shorrock has exposed the U.S. role in the most infamous atrocity of the 1980s, the Gwangju Massacre, in which ROK paratroopers deployed from the DMZ massacred up to 2,000 people.) Yoon and his co-conspirators planned similar atrocities against the people of South Korea, and have even been accused of attempts to restart the Korean War through a series of drone incursions into the DPRK’s airspace in late 2024. While Washington claimed it had no prior knowledge of his plans, it is unlikely that Yoon would have acted if he felt it threatened U.S. patronage.

Elected officials of any party will not change their tune without pressure. That pressure must begin from the grassroots.

In Korea, the U.S. military presence is woven into the fabric of everyday life. Communities living near the 80 different U.S. military bases and facilities in Korea contend with the daily realities of environmental pollution, military accidents, and violence against civilians. For more than 80 years, the U.S. military has exploited access to Korean land, oceans, women, markets, and technology. The occupation manifests as oil leaks, noise pollution, stray bullets, and drunk drivers. At times, more severe incidents also occur. In 2025, the ROK Air Force accidentally bombed the city of Pocheon during a U.S.-led war drill. Pocheon sits in the vicinity of multiple U.S. firing ranges, and this was the 30th major military accident in the city since 2000.

The U.S. military occupation does not protect the Korean people, and U.S. military activity there is not undertaken as a favor to an ally of equal standing. The U.S. holds operational wartime control of the ROK Armed Forces, and dangles the possibility of eventually returning military sovereignty as an incentive to keep Seoul engaged in war drills. Both governments claim the drills are strictly for defensive purposes. Yet in reality they rehearse Washington’s aggressive military doctrine for Korea, which includes the deployment of nuclear weapons against the Korean people and plans for regime change in the DPRK.

These are the realities behind the bipartisan rhetoric surrounding the U.S.-ROK relationship. Opposing war drills in Korea is fundamentally about opposing the violence of military occupation and Washington’s role in prolonging the Korean War to justify its permanent, destructive, and wasteful military occupation of the peninsula and the Western Pacific.

Elected officials of any party will not change their tune without pressure. That pressure must begin from the grassroots. In 2024, Nodutdol, a grassroots anti-imperialist diaspora organization, launched the US Out of Korea campaign for precisely that purpose. We have since mobilized and educated thousands of people, and garnered the support of hundreds of organizations.

An international progressive movement for Korea is already rising, driven by the long struggle of the Korean people themselves. The question U.S. progressives face is whether to embrace this cause as their own.

This summer, Nodutdol took an international delegation of 26 progressive activists from six countries and territories to bear witness to the U.S. occupation firsthand. We visited communities struggling to preserve the local environment and their homes from U.S. base expansion. We spoke to activists fighting to preserve the historical memory of U.S. military sexual violence and femicide. We marched alongside nearly 10,000 protesters in Seoul on the anniversary of Korea’s liberation from Japan under the banner of a familiar slogan: U.S. out of Korea.

An international progressive movement for Korea is already rising, driven by the long struggle of the Korean people themselves. The question U.S. progressives face is whether to embrace this cause as their own.

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump’s New Press Sec Faces Scrutiny Over Lawyer Claims, Anti-Abortion Views
content:
Zacharia’s claims of being a lawyer and her spreading of anti-abortion disinformation have received renewed examination.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Following White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia’s first appearance before the media on Tuesday, numerous aspects of her background have come to light — including her staunch anti-abortion views and that she may have lied about her résumé.

Zacharia has claimed she is a lawyer, noting that she graduated from law school at Pepperdine University. However, no record of her passing a bar exam in any state exists, which is generally a requirement before a person can practice law. In states without that requirement, would-be lawyers usually have to submit an application to the state’s bar association, but there is no record of her applying in those jurisdictions either.

Asked by reporters this week where she passed the bar exam, Zacharia responded, “When I moved to China.” But critics have pointed out that a person cannot take a state bar exam while outside of the U.S.

White House press secretaries are not required to have an educational degree, let alone be a lawyer. However, the fact that Zacharia has possibly misled others about her personal history raises the question of whether she can be forthright or honest in her new role.

Perhaps more concerning are Zacharia’s views on reproductive rights. From November 2023 to February 2026, she served on the board of advisors for an organization called “White Rose Resistance,” an anti-abortion group that stole its name from a Nazi Germany-era resistance group that had nothing to do with the issue.

The contemporary White Rose Resistance has pushed for charging people with murder if they receive an abortion or help to facilitate one. On the organization’s FAQ page, the group downplays the possibility of a death penalty sentence for those found “guilty” of having an abortion while also not outright denying that it could happen.

After leaving the organization, Zacharia has pushed an anti-abortion agenda through the use of disinformation. In an interview from October 2026, she pointedly stated that “the abortion pill has the same chemicals that they used…in camps in Nazi Germany” — a verifiably false claim.

The decision to hire Zacharia as the Trump administration’s new press secretary could indicate that the White House may focus on abortion following the upcoming midterm elections. Indeed, according to a report from The Washington Sun, the Department of Justice (DOJ) has been instructed to move more slowly on abortion-related cases until after November, picking up attacks on abortion rights and access once the elections are over.

Abortion rights proponents have decried the appointment of Zacharia.

“Donald Trump is handing the anti-abortion disinformation movement one of the biggest megaphones in government,” Reproductive Freedom for All President and CEO Mini Timmaraju said in a statement. “Katie Zacharia is the latest anti-abortion extremist Trump has installed in his administration. We must put a check on their fringe agenda this November and block their plan to ban abortion after the midterms.”

On Tuesday, Zacharia stumbled at many moments during her first appearance as press secretary, and only took three questions from reporters (from Trump-friendly news outlets) after giving her initial remarks. Sources close to the White House said it was a rough start for her.

“You either got it or don’t. And she don’t got it,” one source connected to the administration told Politico.

“She needs to get much better, fast. Otherwise, she’ll break Scaramucci’s record,” a White House official said to MS NOW, referring to former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci, who only served for 11 days in Trump’s first term.

author: Andrea DiP
title: Em Israel, conferência da extrema direita exalta Flávio Bolsonaro
content:
Nos dias 06, 07 e 08 de outubro, a cidade de Jerusalém sediou a “National Conservatism Conference”, ou “NatCon” (algo como Conferência sobre Conservadorismo Nacional), evento que reúne algumas vezes ao ano políticos conservadores nacionalistas de extrema direita da Europa, Estados Unidos, Israel, Reino Unido e, algumas vezes, da América Latina.




Mas digamos que nossa região não é tão importante para eles, a não ser quando se fala contra a imigração de “países pobres” – nestes casos, os discursos nos colocam como quintal dos Estados Unidos, ou interessam a alianças que podem servir às suas causas. Sei disso porque já participei de outra NatCon em Bruxelas em 2024 e tenho me infiltrado nesses eventos transnacionais da extrema direita europeia desde 2022.




A NatCon é financiada pela Fundação estadunidense Edmund Burke, que tem entre seus principais doadores a Heritage Foundation. A Heritage Foundation, por sua vez, é uma das principais geradoras de diretrizes políticas para a atual administração Trump. Seu presidente, Kevin Roberts, descreve explicitamente a missão moderna da Heritage Foundation como a de “institucionalizar o Trumpismo” em uma 

entrevista

 para o New York Times. Roberts foi um dos palestrantes da conferência em Jerusalém. E a Heritage está de olho no Brasil: em março deste ano, Paulo Figueiredo e Alexandre Ramagem 

participaram

 de um evento da fundação em Miami, como revelou a 

Pública

.




Eu estava lá nesta edição da NatCon, que reuniu políticos israelenses de extrema-direita, figuras europeias que enfrentaram medidas disciplinares por suposto antissemitismo e figuras nacionalistas cristãs e de extrema-direita dos Estados Unidos, como bem definiu o jornal britânico 

The Guardian

. 




O foco principal estava no apoio às políticas e medidas de Benjamin Netanyahu contra os palestinos, a defesa do Estado de Israel, da conquista de territórios na Cisjordânia e na celebração e endosso de ações dos colonos israelenses que agem como uma milícia na região, cometendo todo tipo de barbaridades, como contei um pouco 

na minha última coluna

. Também foram defendidas ações “anti-terrorismo” e anti-imigração na Europa e Estados Unidos e o combate ao que foi chamado de “red green alliance” (aliança verde e vermelha), que é como a extrema direita tem se referido à parte da esquerda progressista que protesta contra o genocídio do povo palestino. Uma das principais referências dessa aliança seria, na visão destes radicais, o prefeito de Nova York, Zohran Mamdani. Alguns palestrantes também atacaram ferrenhamente a comunidade LGBTQIA+, sobretudo as pessoas trans, e falaram da importância de criar grandes famílias, ter muitos filhos, mas sem se misturar com pessoas de diferentes culturas.




Um dos discursos mais violentos veio de Sebastian Gorka, subchefe de gabinete do presidente e diretor sênior de contraterrorismo no Conselho de Segurança Nacional dos Estados Unidos, que participou ao vivo e online da Casa Branca. Gorka é um dos aliados de Eduardo Bolsonaro nos EUA, a quem 

foi apresentado

 por Steve Bannon.




Ele defendeu que existe hoje uma nova religião: “a religião da esquerda”.




“Seja ela preenchida por ambientalistas adoradores de Gaia como Greta Thunberg, seja pelo altar do DEI (Diversidade, Equidade e Inclusão, em inglês)”, disse. Seu discurso misturou a Irmandade Muçulmana com marxismo, se estendeu para ligações entre o Hamas, e a “mã do Irã”. “A Aliança Vermelho-Verde é real. Os islamistas trabalhando com os marxistas é real”. E finalizou parafraseando Trump: “Se você planeja machucar americanos ou matar inocentes, nós vamos encontrar você e nós vamos matar você”.




Foi neste clima de Conferência que o nome de Flávio Bolsonaro foi citado e aplaudido pelos presentes – cerca de 300 pessoas.




O europarlamentar Harald Vilimsky, que lidera a delegação do Partido da Liberdade da Áustria (FPÖ) no Parlamento Europeu e atua como vice-presidente do grupo “Patriotas pela Europa”, foi quem levantou a bola:







“Quero que a Europa fique ombro a ombro com Israel, com aqueles que, em termos de fé, são nossos irmãos mais velhos. Quero a parte conservadora dos Estados Unidos em nosso campo, não os Republicanos apenas no nome, mas os verdadeiros conservadores. Isso é algo que realmente poderia ser um divisor de águas no desenvolvimento internacional. Quero a Argentina com o presidente Javier Milei em nossas fileiras. Quero o Chile com o Presidente José Antonio Kast ao nosso lado. Quero Flávio Bolsonaro no Brasil.”







Foi quando a plateia explodiu em aplausos. Ele completou: “Brasil, Japão e tantos outros países apenas para se juntar a uma ideia, algo como ‘patriotas globais’. Um grupo forte, uma rede poderosa, uma força enorme pelo conservadorismo”.




O evento foi tratado como estratégico pelo governo de Netanyahu. Bezalel Smotrich, ministro das Finanças, autoproclamado “fascista homofóbico” e extremista sancionado internacionalmente, esteve presente.




Também marcou presença o rabino Shmuel Eliyahu, que em 2023 pediu o lançamento de uma bomba atômica sobre Gaza e que já havia sido intimado a responder a um processo disciplinar por incitação racista contra os palestinos. Da Europa, estiveram presentes o ex-chefe da agência de inteligência interna da Alemanha Hans-Georg Maaßen, para quem Angela Merkel “abrir as portas” do país para imigração em massa e Balázs Orbán, deputado do Parlamento húngaro e ex-diretor político do primeiro-ministro Viktor Orbán.




Essa foi uma das conferências mais violentas que já cobri. Os afetos movimentados nesses três dias foram o ódio, o ressentimento, o nacionalismo extremo, a xenofobia, o orgulho da crueldade. E são essas pessoas, que movem esses afetos, que querem estar “ombro a ombro”, “nas mesmas fileiras” com Flávio Bolsonaro. E você? De que lado quer o presidente do Brasil?

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Ehsan Salah
title: Sudan, Egypt to pursue joint border security, as public tensions flare after deadly mine bombing
content:
In the aftermath of the bombing of a mine in the 

Halayeb Triangle

 that left scores of Sudanese miners dead, Egypt and Sudan are discussing a new security framework along the countries’ shared eastern border.

 




That framework would provide for joint coordination to pursue what both sides regard as security risks arising from organized crime, Sudanese and Egyptian officials 

told

 Mada Masr.




The push toward closer coordination comes amid public outcry in Sudan and diplomatic concern in international quarters over the killing of scores of artisanal miners in the disputed 

Halayeb Triangle

 on Saturday.

 




That public outcry was accentuated on Monday when a gunman killed two Egyptians in a main market in southern Khartoum in what Sudanese security officials involved in the investigations told Mada Masr was a retaliatory attack.




The shooting took place at around 2 pm near the 

Export Development Bank in the Local Market

, a security source in 

Khartoum State police

 told Mada Masr.

 Three Egyptians were targeted in the market’s commercial area. 

Two died at the scene, while the third was taken to the 

Omdurman Medical Corps Hospital 

for treatment.




Ali al-Laouta, a vegetable seller at the market, witnessed Monday’s shooting. 

He told Mada Masr that he noticed a man wearing a 

military uniform bearing the badge of the joint force of military-allied armed movements buying some items in the market.

 




He then suddenly pointed his weapon at the three Egyptians shopping nearby, opened fire and fled the scene, Laouta adds.




Police patrols and security units responded to the scene and tracked down the suspect, a source in the Khartoum police’s criminal investigations department told Mada Masr. The suspect initially resisted arrest, opening fire on security forces, but officers eventually subdued him, seized the weapon used in the attack and took him into custody, the source said.




One member of the arrest unit was shot in the leg during the exchange of fire, a security officer involved in the operation said. The injured officer was hospitalized and is in stable condition, he added.




The suspect is a member of the “support forces” — a wide range of armed formations that fight alongside the Sudanese military in the current war — a source informed of the preliminary investigation told Mada Masr.




Sudan’s military-led government adopted a wartime policy that put the joint force, its main battlefield ally, in charge of protecting state institutions and supporting security operations in cities under military control. That has left the alliance with a heavy presence in urban areas. 

But a 

string

 of violent incidents involving joint force members in recent months has stoked public concerns and prompted authorities to review the policy and seek to curb the allied group’s urban presence.




The source informed of the preliminary investigation told Mada Masr that the suspect was subjected to intensive questioning about his military affiliation and how he had obtained the weapon used in the attack.




The interrogating officer told Mada Masr that, in his initial statement, the suspect said he had shot the Egyptian men in retaliation for his brother’s death in Saturday’s strikes.




The shooting comes amid a wave of polarization in Sudanese public opinion following the deadly airstrike near the Sudanese-Egyptian border that killed scores of Sudanese people.




The shooting adds more complexity to an already charged public sphere.




Sudanese lawyer Oweis Salah Eddin al-Iraqi urged authorities to disclose the facts related to the miners’ deaths directly to the public, saying the case had become a matter of public concern and that any mishandling could provoke backlash.




Many in the public and political arena are viewing the shooting in the context of wider accountability for the miners’ deaths.




Viewing the market shooting in isolation from the attack on the miners would offer an incomplete assessment of the situation, said Adel Ibrahim Hamad, the head of 

Sudan’s Ashigga Party.

 

The party was re-established by former members of the Democratic Unionist Party, drawing inspiration from an earlier party of the same name that called for union with Egypt.

 The revived party focuses on national issues, paying particular attention to Sudanese-Egyptian relations.




Discussion of Monday’s shooting, Hamad argued, must begin with the original incident, saying Egypt’s response was disproportionate to the violation, “if any.”




“Approaching the discussion from any other angle, such as platitudes about the strategic relationship [between the two countries] and the need to prevent an isolated incident from affecting it, would distract from a recurring Egyptian failing in handling Sudanese issues,” he said. 




For journalist Majed Mohamed Ali, Sudanese authorities have seriously underestimated the political and security consequences, at an especially complex and sensitive geopolitical moment, in their handling of the miners’ deaths. 




While he insisted that Monday’s shootings came down to the actions of an individual, Ali warned Khartoum and Cairo against allowing their opponents further opportunities to exploit the miners’ deaths. “The matter should be closed by clarifying the facts, identifying who is responsible and holding them accountable,” he said. “The Sudanese government must also take responsibility for securing the borders and regulating miners’ activity in accordance with the law.”




Two days after the strike, the Transitional Sovereignty Council issued its first comment on the incident, announcing the formation of a fact-finding committee to investigate the deaths of the Sudanese miners. 




While the statement said Egyptian and Sudanese leaders had remained in contact since the attack to establish the facts, Egypt’s military announced later that evening that it had launched the third phase of its campaign against illegal gold mining in the Eastern Desert, citing the protection of national resources and the imposition of Egypt’s “full sovereignty” over its territories, without acknowledgement of the incident. 




According to a senior Sudanese diplomat, TSC Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan is paying close attention to the matter amid mounting public pressure to uncover the circumstances surrounding the attack and identify those responsible. That level of attention reflects heightened public concern in Sudan and the need to manage the strikes’ repercussions through state institutions and official channels, while safeguarding Sudanese citizens’ rights and ensuring the incident is treated seriously, the source said.




The diplomatic steps are intended to convey Khartoum’s position to Cairo clearly and facilitate cooperation between the relevant authorities to complete the investigation and address questions raised by the incident, the diplomat added.




Sudan has put forward a proposal for a joint security matrix to govern how incidents and activities in border areas are handled, define the responsibilities of relevant agencies and establish coordination mechanisms, according to the diplomat. The proposal also calls for the activation of surveillance and field monitoring procedures in areas prone to such incidents, he added.




The matrix could include direct communication channels between relevant agencies in both countries, clear procedures for reporting and verifying incidents and mechanisms for sharing information on movements and activities requiring security intervention. It could also prompt a review of how authorities respond when incidents affect citizens or people working in border areas, the diplomat said.




The proposal’s significance lies in the shift from responding to each incident separately toward an institutional mechanism for managing border risks and preventing the recurrence of similar incidents, the source added.




Activating surveillance mechanisms would require practical coordination between the relevant Sudanese and Egyptian agencies, potentially through a new joint committee 

similar

 to the long established bodies overseeing other aspects of Sudanese-Egyptian affairs.

 

This would necessitates clearly defined 

administrative and security responsibilities

 and a mechanism for exchanging information and verifying reports, the source said.

 All adopted measures would need to respect the sovereignty of both countries and the rules governing activities in border areas, the source added. 




An Egyptian official briefed on Egyptian-Sudanese relations confirmed that Cairo is considering establishing a joint security presence on the border alongside the Sudanese military to ensure border security. 




Egypt has pointed to the plan in discussions with African Union officials, during which Saturday’s strikes were criticized. 




An informed diplomat said Egypt had informed AU officials of its ongoing coordination with Sudan on measures and criteria for joint border management.

The post 

Sudan, Egypt to pursue joint border security, as public tensions flare after deadly mine bombing

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.
