title: Sağlık Bakanlığı: Eşitsizlikleri devam ettirmekte kararlıyız!
content:
Sağlık Bakanlığı İstatistik Yıllığı (SBİY) 2025 Haber Bülteni, 30 Eylül 2025, çarşamba günü, saat 17:00’de 

(!)

 yayımlandı. İlki 12 yıl önce, 2014 yılında yine eylül ayının son günü SBİY 2013 Haber Bülteni olarak yayımlanmıştı. Bülten, istatistik yıllığından yaklaşık üç, dört ay önce daha az sayıdaki veri grubunu kapsayacak şekilde yayımlanıyor. Bununla birlikte, ölümlülük, aşılama ve hizmet kullanımıyla ilgili bir önceki yılın verilerine 9-10 ay sonra da olsa ulaşabilmiş oluyoruz. Ve Türkiye’nin dokuz ilinin bulunduğu coğrafyada yaşayanların, AKP’li yılların bundan önceki 16 yılında olduğu gibi, 17nci yılında da değişmeyen bir biçimde sağlık ve sosyoekonomik eşitsizlere mahkûm edilmiş olduğunu görüyoruz. Bu haftaki yazıda söz konusu durumu ve AKP’li Sağlık Bakanlığı’nın verileri kendine saklamak gibi bir özelliğini kendilerinin sunduğu kaynaklar üzerinden ele alacağım.



















ERİŞ BİLALOĞLU YAZDI




Yeni Bir Sıfırlama Çabası mı: Türkiye’de Bebek Ölüm Hızı




29 Ocak 2015










AKP’li bakanlık verileri kendine saklıyor




AKP tarafından 2002 yılında kurulan 58. Hükümet’e kadar sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleriyle ilgili veriler yıllardır istatistik yıllıklarıyla düzenli olarak kamuoyuyla paylaşılıyordu. Ancak 

58. Hükümet ve o kabinenin Sağlık Bakanı Recep Akdağ ile birlikte, sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleriyle ilgili veriler kamuoyundan 2011 yılına kadar saklandı, 

paylaşılmadı. Dünya Sağlık Örgütü başta olmak üzere, Türkiye’nin üyesi olduğu uluslararası kuruluşların talebi üzerine, bir AKP Hükümeti ve Sağlık Bakanı olarak ilk defa 2011 yılında, 2008 yılına ait veriler “Sağlık Bakanlığı Sağlık İstatistikleri Yıllığı 2008” başlığında Bakan Akdağ’ın önsözüyle yayımlandı. O nedenle Türkiye’nin 2003-2007 yıllarına ait sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleriyle ilgili verileri diğer yıllar gibi düzenli bir biçimde bugüne kadar paylaşılmadı.




Sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleriyle ilgili istatistikler, 2011 yılından sonra, Sağlık Bakanlığı ve Türkiye İstatistik Kurumu (TÜİK) tarafından düzenli olarak yayımlanıyor. TÜİK, özelikle doğurganlık ve ölümlülükle ilgili verileri Merkezi Nüfus İdaresi Sistemi (MERNİS) üzerinden iller düzeyinde, sağlık harcamalarıyla ilgili verileri Hazine ve Maliye Bakanlığı ile Sosyal Güvenlik Kurumu (SGK) ve yerel yönetimlerden ve “Hanehalkı Bütçe Anketi” çalışması üzerinden, hastalıklarla ilgili verileri de “Türkiye Sağlık Araştırması” üzerinden sağlıyor. Sağlık Bakanlığı da bu verileri kullanıp yaptığı hesaplamaları ve sağlık kurumları, sağlık emekçileri, ilaç, sağlık hizmetleri kullanımı vb. verileri Türkiye’nin makro düzeyde ekonomik ve sosyo-ekonomik yapıya göre gruplandığı 12 bölge, İstatistiki Bölge Bilgileri Sınıflaması-1 (İBBS-1), üzerinden paylaşıyor. Bununla birlikte, 

Sağlık Bakanlığı kaynakları üzerinden 81 ilden herhangi birinin sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleri verilerini, durumunu öğrenebilmek mümkün olamıyor. 

Çünkü Sağlık Bakanlığı illerin verilerini yayımlamayı uzun zamandır tercih etmiyor.










Tabip Odası Bebek Ölümlerine Önlem Paketini Açıkladı




25 Eylül 2008










Bebek ölüm hızı önemli bir toplumsal sağlık düzeyi göstergesidir




Toplumların sağlık düzeyinin değerlendirilmesi ve izlenebilmesi amacıyla “bebek ölüm hızı”, “beş yaş altı ölüm hızı” ve “doğumda beklenen yaşam süresi” uluslararası alanda sıklıkla kullanılan, kabul görmüş üç değişkendir. Bunlar aynı zamanda, ülkelerin gelişmişlik düzeyi göstergeleri arasında da yer almaktadır. Çünkü, bu üç gösterge bir ülkede, bölgede, ilde vb. öncelikle beslenme, barınma, alt yapı ve eğitim başta olmak üzere, sosyoekonomik koşulların durumu ve sağlık hizmetlerinin ulaşılabilir olup olmamasıyla sağlık hizmetlerinin niteliğinden doğrudan etkilenmektedir.




Gebeliğin herhangi bir döneminde, canlı doğan bebeğin, birinci doğum gününü göremeden ölmesi, nüfus bilim (demografi) ve tıp alanında bebek ölümü olarak kabul edilmekte, tanımlanmaktadır. Bir ilde, bölgede ve/veya ülkede yıl içinde canlı doğan her bin bebekten kaçının birinci doğum gününü göremeden öldüğü de bebek ölüm hızı olarak tanımlanmaktadır. Bebek ölümlerinden doğumdan sonraki 

ilk ay içinde gerçekleşen

ler neonatal ölüm, birinci aydan sonra gerçekleşenler de postneonatal ölüm olarak adlandırılmaktadır. Neonatal 

ölümler genellikle anne adayının sağlık, beslenme ve eğitim durumuyla doğum öncesi izlemlerin yapılıp yapılmaması ve doğum koşullarıyla ilişkilidir.

 

Postneonatal ölümler

in de 

bebeğin aşılama başta olmak üzere, sağlık hizmetlerine ulaşıp ulaşamaması vb. ile beslenme, barınma vb. ailesinin sosyoekonomik düzeyi, yaşam koşullarıyla doğrudan ilişkili

 olduğu bilimsel araştırmalarla gösterilmiştir.




Türkiye’de ve OECD ülkelerinde bebek ölüm hızları




SBİY 2025 Haber Bülteni’ndeki verilere göre, Türkiye’de 2025 yılında gerçekleşen bin canlı doğumdan 5,0’i doğumdan sonraki birinci ay içinde, 2,7’si de birinci ay ile 12. ay arasında yaşamını kaybetmiştir. Toplamda da bin canlı doğumdan 7,7’si birinci doğum gününü göremeden ölmüştür. Başka bir ifadeyle, Sağlık Bakanlığı tarafından Türkiye geneli için 2025 yılı bebek ölüm hızı binde 7,7; neonatal ölüm hızı binde 5,0 ve postneonatal ölüm hızı da binde 2,7 olarak bildirilmiştir.




Türkiye, yayımlanmış son verilere göre, üyesi olduğu Ekonomik Kalkınma ve İşbirliği Örgütü’ne (OECD) üye 38 ülke arasında, 2024 yılında BÖH en yüksek Meksika (binde 12,5) ve Kosta Rika’nın (binde 10,2) ardından binde 8,9 ile üçüncü sırada yer alıyor. Türkiye, benzer gelir, “kalkınmışlık” düzeyindeki ülkeler arasında toplumsal sağlık düzeyi en kötü olanlar arasında yer almakta ve bu durum yıllardır değişmemektedir.




AKP Hükümeti iddialı: Türkiye’de eşitsizliklerin en derin yaşandığı coğrafya yine değişmedi




TÜİK ve Sağlık Bakanlığı başta olmak üzere, İBBS-1’i kullanan kurumların gruplamasına göre, 

Adıyaman, Batman, Diyarbakır, Gaziantep, Kilis, Mardin, Siirt, Şanlıurfa ve Şırnak

 olmak üzere 

dokuz il

in bulunduğu coğrafya 

Güneydoğu Anadolu 

bölgesi olarak tanımlanıyor. Türkiye’de 

anadili Kürtçe ve Arapça

 

olan yurttaşların en yoğun olarak yaşadığı iller

den oluşan Güneydoğu Anadolu, AKP’nin düzenli olarak verileri yayımlamakta olduğu ve iktidarının son 17 yılı boyunca her yıl bebek ölüm hızının en yüksek olduğu coğrafya olma özelliği taşıyor.




İBBS-1’de yer alan bölgeleri, bebek ölüm hızının en düşük (en iyi) olduğu bölgeden en yüksek (en kötü) olduğu bölgeye doğru sıralandığında, ilk sırada en iyi durumda olan Batı Marmara’da 5,6; ikinci sıradaki İstanbul’da 5,7; Batı Anadolu’da 6,0; Doğu Marmara’da 6,1; beşinci sırada yer alan Doğu Karadeniz’de 6,2; Batı Karadeniz’de 6,4; Ege’de 6,9; sekizinci sıradaki Orta Anadolu’da 7,5; Kuzeydoğu Anadolu’da 7,8; onuncu sıradaki Akdeniz’de 8,2; Ortadoğu Anadolu’da 9,6 ve son sırada yer alan Güneydoğu Anadolu’da 11,5’dir.




Sayılarla eşitsizlikler




2025 yılında canlı doğan bin bebekten Batı Marmara’da 5,6’sı, Güneydoğu Anadolu’da ise 11,5’i birinci doğum gününü göremeden hayatını kaybetmiştir. Aralarındaki fark iki katından daha fazladır (

Hız oranı

=2,04). Bu durum, 2025 yılında bebek ölüm hızının en iyi/düşük olduğu Batı Marmara’da ölen her bir bebeğe karşılık, bebek ölüm hızının en kötü/yüksek olduğu Güneydoğu Anadolu’da iki bebeğin birinci doğum gününü göremeden öldüğünü göstermektedir.




Güneydoğu Anadolu, 2025 yılında Türkiye’de binde 11,5 ile bebek ölüm hızının yanı sıra, binde 7,2 ile neonatal ve binde 4,3 ile de postneonatal ölüm hızlarının en yüksek olduğu bölge konumundadır. Hız oranı 

neonatal ölüm hızı için 2,0

; 

postneonatal ölüm hızı için

 de 

2,4 

olarak hesaplanmıştır. Sağlık Bakanlığı’nın verileriyle yapılan hesaplamalara göre, her üç toplumsal sağlık düzeyi göstergesi açısından Türkiye’nin en kötü durumda olan bölgesi; İBBS-1 sınıflamasında Güneydoğu Anadolu olarak adlandırılan ve esas olarak anadili Kürtçe ve Arapça olan yurttaşların en yoğun olarak yaşadığı illerin bir araya getirilmesiyle tanımlanmış olan coğrafyadır.




Başka bir ifadeyle, bu coğrafya diğer bölgelere göre bebek ölüm hızının en yüksek olmasına neden olduğu bilinen beslenme, barınma, alt yapı ve eğitim başta olmak üzere, sosyoekonomik koşulların durumu ve sağlık hizmetlerinin ulaşılabilirliğiyle sağlık hizmetlerinin niteliği alanlarında da diğer bölgelere göre en kötü, eşitsizliklerin en fazla olduğu bölge durumundadır.




Sağlık eşitsizlikleri önlenemez değil




Türkiye’de sağlıktaki eşitsizlikler de gelir dağılımında, işsizlikte, eğitimde olduğu gibi uçuruma dönüştü. AKP iktidarının yarattığı sağlık alanındaki bu utanç tablosunun ancak toplumsal eşitsizlikler ortadan kaldırılarak yok edilebileceği biliniyor. Bunun için de 

sınıfsal dayanışma ve mücadele gerekiyor

. “Barış ve Demokratik Toplum” süreci tamamlanıp, silahlı çatışmaların sonlanması kalıcılaşıp, 

normalleşme aşaması başladığında

 ittifakların, ortak mücadelelerin ve dayanışmanın önü daha da açılacak. Umudumuz, toplumsal muhalefetin amasız, fakatsız açık desteğiyle bu aşamanın bir an önce başlayabilmesi ve 

eşitlikçi, barış içinde bir toplumsal yaşantı için “gerekenlerin” hep birlikte hayata geçirilebilmesi

.







Kaynakça




Kunt A E, Mackenbach J P., Measuring Socioeconomic Inequalities in Health, EUR/ICP/RPD 416, WHO, Copenhagen-28, (1994).

author: Chris Walker
title: Report: Trump Is Having Second Thoughts About Livestreaming Military Execution
content:
Trump isn’t “particularly enthusiastic” about Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream a military execution in December.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump is reportedly asking advisors if he should go through with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream a military execution later this year.

Trump has publicly indicated that he’ll make a final decision on the matter soon.

“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it,” Trump said. “Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did.”

“I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I’ll make a decision,” Trump added.

But according to reporting from Axios, Trump is questioning whether the execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan should be televised, asking his advisers for their views on the matter.

Hasan was convicted of killing 13 soldiers at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009. He was shot during the rampage, and is now a paraplegic, paralyzed from the waist down. Hasan is set to be executed by a firing squad in December.

The president “didn’t sound particularly enthusiastic” about a live, national showing of the execution, a source close to Trump said to the publication, adding that “he’s calling around, doing the Trump thing, asking people what they think.”

The livestream event “might not happen,” another source confirmed.

Trump’s public statements about the death penalty reveal that he has errant views about capital punishment. Multiple studies have shown that there is no evidence supporting the idea that the death penalty can act as a deterrent, or that the threat of capital punishment somehow lessens violent crime. Indeed, several years of data demonstrate that the homicide rates in states with capital punishment are higher than in states without the death penalty.

Trump is also wrong about what “the military would like to do.” While there isn’t widespread data to demonstrate most servicemembers’ views one way or another, some officers have spoken out against the planned livestreaming of Hasan’s execution.

“It takes away everything America stands for when we do public executions,” one Army officer said in an anonymous comment to CNN. “The generational harm caused by allowing troops in uniform to stand in front of a man in a wheelchair and watch him get shot to death is irreparable.”

Several religious leaders, including Pope Leo, and a bipartisan cadre of lawmakers, have also spoken out against livestreaming the execution.

Despite Trump’s reticence about this specific event, he has been an outspoken proponent of expanding the death penalty, including for non-lethal crimes such as drug dealing. In his first week in office, he signed an executive order peddling the the false claim that the death penalty is “an essential tool for deterring” crimes, calling for the attorney general to seek the death penalty for crimes involving the killing of law enforcement officers, or when the defendant being charged is an undocumented immigrant.

In an op-ed published last week, Truthout’s board of directors president Maya Schenwar decried the death penalty in all of its forms, describing the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee as an act of torture and Hegseth’s decision to livestream Hasan’s execution as part of a larger “pro-death penalty fervor.”

“The brutality is the point. The torture is the point. The murder, not only state-sanctioned but state-celebrated, is the very point,” Schenwar wrote.

A cohesive life-affirming agenda rejects not only executions, but also the inherent violence of incarceration, policing, deportation, imperial wars, and military aid to genocidal forces. It makes no excuses — let alone expansions — that prop up or prolong the existence of these institutions in ‘kinder, gentler’ forms.

“Let’s not allow ourselves to give in to the inertia of our brutal present, in which death by hanging is a mercy. Let’s envision the cohesive, life-affirming agenda that embraces a future for all of us, a world in which the torture of Christa Pike — or anyone — is unthinkable,” Schenwar concluded.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Nairobi, Kenya, October 13, 2026: For 42 years, Kenya has committed to ensuring women’s equality in marriage and family life. In 1984, the country ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), and Article 2(6) of the Constitution makes the treaty part of Kenyan law. Yet in reality, this promise remains unrealised. Women in Kenya can still lose their homes when their husbands die, struggle to claim property they helped build, and face barriers to leaving marriages marked by violence. Kenya’s record on women’s rights is currently under scrutiny as the CEDAW Committee reviews the country’s implementation of the Convention during the Committee’s 93rd session at the United Nations in Geneva. The Global Campaign for Equality in Family Law, Equality Now and Kenyan partners, including Come Together Widows and Orphans Organization (CTWOO), have submitted a shadow report providing a civil society account of what happens on the ground in Kenya in relation to Article 16 of the CEDAW Convention. What CEDAW Article 16 means for women in Kenya Article 16 of CEDAW protects equality inside the family. This includes equal rights when spouses marry, during marriage and when it ends, with equal say over parenting, property and decisions about children. It protects the right to belong in a family, to be safe in it and to prosper in it, from marriage through widowhood. The Committee’s guidance on violence against women extends that protection to safety at home. That commitment is tested at every stage of family life. When a couple registers a marriage, when unpaid care counts towards family wealth, when a woman seeks a divorce, when a widow tries to keep her home and when a woman needs protection from violence. These are not separate failures but different ways in which equality can exist on paper and be denied in practice. Kenya has made real progress. Article 27 of the Constitution guarantees equality, and Article 45(3) applies that guarantee to spouses at every stage of marriage. The Marriage Act of 2014 brought many marriage laws into one statute, and the Matrimonial Property Act of 2013 recognised non-financial contribution to family wealth, reforms that the Federation of Women Lawyers in Kenya and other women’s organisations helped advance through strategic litigation, legislative proposals and community education. Marriage registration and women’s property rights in Kenya Equality in family life starts with being able to prove a marriage exists. The Marriage Act requires registration, yet it costs Kenya shillings 3,900, and both spouses must appear before the registrar. Only 19.3 per cent of married women aged 15 to 49 had registered their marriage in the 2022 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey, while the shadow report finds no fee waiver for poor households and no county registration drives to help make it easier for couples to register their marriages locally. For a family living on the World Bank’s international poverty line of US$3 a day, the fee equals ten days of income. Many families pass land down the husband’s line, so a wife who cannot prove her marriage can struggle to claim the family home and land after a divorce or a death, and courts have been inconsistent about the consequences of non-registration. Free registration for poor households and mobile registration teams in every county would remove the barrier. Kenya recognises unpaid contribution in property division, but no formula says how to value it, and in 2023 the Supreme Court held that Article 45(3) does not give spouses an automatic half share. Women must still establish their contribution to matrimonial property over the years, including non-monetary contributions such as childcare and housework. A presumption of equal sharing, supported by judicial guidelines on valuing unpaid work, would help turn the constitutional promise of equal rights into equal outcomes. Divorce, access to justice and women’s safety The question is not only whether Kenya has laws protecting women’s rights, but whether women can use them. Fees, distance from courts and lengthy proceedings stand between many women and justice, and Kenya’s divorce law is largely fault-based, so a petitioner must prove a ground such as adultery, cruelty or desertion. In 2022, the Court of Appeal ruled that the three-year wait to seek a divorce in a civil marriage is unconstitutional when a divorce is justified sooner, yet Parliament has not amended the Marriage Act. Chiefs, elders and clergy can also pressure women to reconcile, even where violence is present, but mediation cannot replace a court for a woman who fears for her safety. Widows’ rights in Kenya: more than a succession issue Kenyan law treats widowhood mainly as a succession issue, yet being widowed also determines who keeps property, dignity and safety. CTWOO’s August 2025 widowhood survey found that approximately one third of respondents faced eviction from their home or land after a spouse died and around a third were excluded from inheritance decisions. CTWOO recorded 139 cases involving widows in May 2026 alone. The Law of Succession Act ends a widow’s life interest in her husband’s estate if she remarries, a rule that does not apply to widowers. The High Court declared it unconstitutional in the Ripples International case in September 2022, but the provision remains in the text of the statute. The Widowed Persons Protection Bill, 2026, tabled in Parliament in May and drafted with input from CTWOO and Equality Now, would bring protections now scattered across succession, family and criminal law into one framework. Muslim women and equal protection under Kenya’s Constitution Here, the Constitution’s guarantee of equality meets a constitutional limitation. Article 24(4) allows that guarantee to be qualified “to the extent strictly necessary” for Muslim law in the Kadhis’ courts, covering marriage, divorce and inheritance, and the Law of Succession Act does not apply to the estates of deceased Muslims. In practice, Muslim daughters can receive half their brothers’ inheritance share, while Muslim wives have fewer routes to divorce than their husbands. Kenya’s Supreme Court has found that any departure from equality under Article 24(4) must be strictly necessary and proportionate. Equality Now and its partners therefore call for Article 24(4) to be repealed so that the constitutional equality guarantee applies equally to all women. Gender-based violence, reproductive rights and the risk of rollback The Africa Data Hub has documented the killings of at least 1,069 women in Kenya between 2016 and 2025. Section 43(5) of the Sexual Offences Act excludes lawfully married people from the section that defines unlawful sexual acts, creating a marital rape exemption. Usikimye’s accountability audit also notes that Kenyan law does not define femicide. Harmful practices persist, including child marriage, where data remain scarce, and female genital mutilation (FGM). A review of 68 prosecutions under the Prohibition of Female Genital Mutilation Act by the American Bar Association Center for Human Rights found that 76 of the 137 identifiable accused people were survivors themselves, including 11 girls under 18, and only eight were cutters. The Act also has a gap. In 2021, the High Court found in Kamau v Attorney General, a case in which Equality Now was an interested party, that the Act leaves out Type IV practices such as pricking and piercing, and directed the Attorney General to propose amendments. Article 16 also covers decisions about the number and spacing of children. Article 26(4) of the Constitution allows abortion in defined circumstances, yet the Penal Code criminalises it. In April 2026, the Court of Appeal held that abortion is not a fundamental right and acknowledged the absence of a clear regulatory framework. Kenya’s reservation to the abortion provision of the Maputo Protocol, Africa’s treaty on women’s rights, also contradicts the Constitution. The shadow report finds that, since the Committee’s last review in 2017, most of CEDAW’s recommendations remain unimplemented, while the Linda Jamii constitutional amendment proposal and the National Policy on Family Promotion and Protection have raised concerns about rolling back protections for women, as Equality Now has documented. The pushback has also included the Family Protection Bill of 2023, which seeks to criminalise same-sex conduct, and calls for Kenya to adopt the regressive Draft African Charter on Family, Sovereignty and Values. Yet Article 45 recognises the family as the natural and fundamental unit of society while giving spouses equal rights. Protecting the family and protecting the equality of each member are therefore part of the same constitutional duty. Commitments Kenya should make after the CEDAW review Align the law. Kenya should amend provisions that conflict with the Constitution, CEDAW and the Maputo Protocol. The Widowed Persons Protection Bill 2026 should be enacted, and a stand-alone law on femicide introduced. The Protection Against Domestic Violence Act needs to be fully operationalised, and the Sexual Offences Act must be amended to remove the exemption for marital rape. Article 24(4) in Kenya’s Constitution that exempts Muslim women from constitutional protection also needs to be reformed. The government should also lift reservations on Article 14(2)(c) of the Maputo Protocol, which protects women’s access to medical abortion in specified circumstances, and align the country’s laws and policies with the Constitution’s protections for women’s reproductive health and rights. Implement existing decisions. Court rulings on widows’ inheritance, divorce and FGM, and the recommendations of the government’s Technical Working Group on gender-based violence should change the statute book and practice, so that women are not forced to litigate the same rights repeatedly. Make rights accessible and protect the gains. Fee waivers, marriage registration drives, legal aid and community education would lower the financial, geographic and procedural barriers, because discrimination rooted in culture and religion outlasts a new law. Kenya should also keep its constitutional and treaty guarantees intact against rollback. Equality in marriage and family life benefits every family in Kenya Equality in marriage is not only a women’s issue; sons, fathers, grandparents and children all bear the cost when a family loses its home, its land or its safety. Kenya has the Constitution, the court rulings and a Bill before Parliament to build on. Today’s review offers a chance to turn 42 years of legal promises into equality that families can feel at home. title: Trump Admin Is Reportedly Offering Children as Young as 5 $3,000 to Self-Deport
content:
The offers are meant to “coerce” the children into giving up on their immigration cases, an immigrant advocate said.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

ICE is offering children as young as 5 years old $3,000 “incentives” to voluntarily depart the country, legal advocates have reported, as the Trump administration works to separate immigrant families under the hammer of their mass deportation machine.

Bloomberg Law first reported on the offers, citing attorneys and immigrant advocacy groups who say that the offers are sometimes given to children who lack legal representation. The offers, they say, are a method of forcing children to take a deal so that they drop their legal challenges before they have gone through their time in the court system.

Shaina Aber, executive director for the Acacia Center for Justice, told Bloomberg Law that the tactic is “part of a larger pattern of really trying to coerce children, bully children, intensify pressure on children so that they abandon their cases.”

“It’s part of this deport-at-all-costs policy that seems to be in particular targeting children,” Aber went on.

The offer is being made by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) attorneys as well as immigration judges. In some cases, judges are telling children that it is a one-time offer and giving them no time to consider it, forcing them to make a decision “on the spot” even though “they might not understand what the longer term consequences are down the line,” Aber said.

Another group, the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, said that it and similar groups have received the emails from ICE’s Office of the Principal Legal Advisor offering a “$3,000 incentive” for children. Michael Lukens, head of Amica, told Bloomberg Law that the latest offer came to his office this week for an 11-year-old.

The reporting shows that the Trump administration’s policies toward child deportations are even more extreme than previously thought. Last year, NBC reported that the Trump administration was offering children aged 14 and older $2,500 to self-deport or voluntarily leave the country, according to a Department of Health and Human Services memo.

Indeed, reports have since found that the Trump administration is carrying out this policy even in cases where the children were living with their families, in cases likened to President Donald Trump’s family separation policies from his first term.

The Department of Homeland Security didn’t confirm or deny the payments, saying that the administration is supposedly working to reunite children who come to the U.S. unaccompanied with their families.

According to a tracker maintained by the Marshall Project, as of August, the federal government has deported over 22,500 children since January 1, 2025. ICE arrests of children have only continued to escalate throughout Trump’s second term, with over 8,500 children having been arrested thus far — including 562 children and babies under 4.

author: Stephen Prager
title: Air Force Major Who Called for Trump’s Impeachment Held in Solitary Confinement
content:
Some legal experts say Jason Watson’s confinement for 24 hours a day could amount to illegal pretrial punishment.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Air Force Maj. Jason Watson was arrested July 1 on the steps of the US Capitol after calling for the impeachment of President Donald Trump. According to his lawyer, he’s now being held in solitary confinement 24 hours a day in what some legal experts say could amount to illegal pretrial punishment.

The Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ) contains provisions barring officers from engaging in public political activities that are typically protected for civilians, including criticizing the president and other elected officials.

Prosecutors have charged Watson with violating them when he participated in a news conference calling for Trump to be removed from office over his launching of military actions against Iran, Cuba, and Venezuela without congressional authorization.

After the speech, Watson stood on the Capitol steps holding a sign that read “Impeach, Convict, Remove” and was arrested after he refused to move.

Before he was charged, Watson gave a CNN interview on August 17 in which he continued to criticize Trump, accusing him of “flagrantly violating the Constitution” and “breaking the law.”

He acknowledged that he could face severe consequences as a result of his speech: “We just have to be willing to accept that we can change what is happening in our country if we are just willing to pay a price for it,” he said.

One day later, he was arrested while on duty and taken into pretrial confinement. He now faces a general court-martial, the military’s most severe trial, which is capable of imposing lengthy prison sentences.

“Cruel and unusual form of punishment.” U.S. Air Force Maj. Jason Watson is headed to the most severe form of military trial — a general court-martial — after calling for President Trump’s impeachment while in uniform at the U.S. Capitol. His attorney reveals that Maj. Watson… pic.twitter.com/7izEA47Gh2

On Friday, Watson’s lawyer, Christopher Mutimer, told CNN that after nearly two months, Watson is “still in solitary confinement 24 hours a day,” which he said amounted to “cruel and unusual” punishment.

“Even if he gets an hour to eat or to exercise, he is alone,” Mutimer said. “He is literally by himself, with his thoughts, in a room where the light never turns off all day.”

In an essay published Sunday by writer Monte Mader, Watson himself acknowledged spending his days in isolation, revealing that his Bible had only recently been returned to him and that he had little access to news.

Watson described the conditions of his confinement as the reality one must accept when choosing to engage in nonviolent resistance.

“Walking this path,” he said, “means exposing oneself to violence while refusing to retaliate against it.”

Major Jason Watson is NOT a Democrat. His protest was NOT about party politics. It was about what he believes his oath requires of him—and the price he’s willing to pay for speaking out. Everyone has seen the arrest. Now hear the courageous powerful speech that came first: pic.twitter.com/MMRoiYPV7K

After his July 1 protest, Watson had been restricted to Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling in Washington. Though the base reportedly has a confinement facility, following his detention, he was instead moved to a county jail in Maryland.

During Watson’s September 18 preliminary hearing, Maj. Joshua Wendell, the hearing officer, said Watson could not be confined with civilians and was therefore kept in solitary confinement.

“He was placed in confinement because of the law, which puts him in solitary confinement,” Wendell said, according to Stars and Stripes.

Article 13 of the UCMJ “forbids punishing a service member before trial and forbids pretrial restraint more rigorous than the circumstances require.”

Mutimer has pointed out that solitary confinement is “usually reserved for individuals who are disobeying or are violent, and injuring other people,” and usually only for “a day or two, or a week.” Watson, he said, has “been in there for months now.”

Rachel VanLandingham, a former Air Force judge advocate and professor of law at Southwestern Law School, told Common Dreams that this “seems to be a blatant case of illegal pretrial punishment given that the nature of his pretrial restraint does not seem necessary to either ensure his presence at trial or to prevent foreseeable serious criminal misconduct.”

“Solitary confinement is rare, and must be justified,” she said. “What, is the administration so afraid of this major’s words that he cannot talk to anyone?”

Military defense attorney Cody Harnish, who attended Watson’s preliminary hearing, has raised concerns that his detention could be unlawful and that his especially harsh treatment was political in nature.

“I represent people at court-martial in the military, who are accused of doing some very bad things,” he said during an interview this weekend with Meidas Defense. “They are not in pretrial confinement.”

Harnish noted other abnormal aspects of Watson’s preliminary hearing: He was denied the ability to wear his uniform and instead arrived handcuffed, unshaven, and wearing an undershirt, which pointed to the possibility that he was facing degrading treatment.

He also pointed out that Watson had submitted a request to resign his commission in exchange for avoiding a court-martial, but that the request was denied in 24 hours.

“Nothing gets processed in the military that fast,” he said, suggesting that this could indicate influence from senior Pentagon officials.

During his second term, Trump has used members of the military for political purposes in ways that have challenged longstanding norms of political neutrality. This has included hosting overtly political rallies before uniformed troops, screening them for ideology, and purging senior military officers deemed disloyal.

Harnish suggested that the Trump administration was seeking to make an example out of Watson for speaking out against the president.

“When someone speaks out against this administration in the military,” he said, “they’re going to crush him to silence anyone else in the ranks from ever thinking about it.”

content:
Στη «Μικρή Σκηνή», στις εγκαταστάσεις του πάλαι ποτέ στούντιο «Αγροτικόν» στην Κάτω Τούμπα, την Τετάρτη 14 Οκτωβρίου 2026, στις 21:30, θα παρουσιαστεί στους δημοσιογράφους, σε φίλους/ες ο διπλός δίσκος του Νίκου Παπάζογλου «Επιτόπια ηχογράφηση, Θέατρο Δάσους, 18 Αυγούστου 1986».




Πρόκειται για το ηχητικό ντοκουμέντο της συναυλίας που έδωσε ο Νίκος Παπάζογλου πριν 40 χρόνια, μπροστά σε περισσότερα από 4.000 άτομα εντός του χώρου του Θεάτρου Δάσους, και με άλλα τόσα τριγύρω στον δασικό «εξώστη». Ο Νίκος Παπάζογλου ερμήνευσε εκείνο το βράδυ τραγούδια της «Εκδίκησης της Γυφτιάς» (1978) και των «Δήθεν» (1979) με διαφορετικές ενορχηστρώσεις, τραγούδια από το πρώτο προσωπικό του «Χαράτσι» (1984), και παρουσίασε για πρώτη φορά κομμάτια από τον επερχόμενο δίσκο του «Μέσω νεφών» (1986), που ηχογραφούνταν την ίδια περίοδο, στο νέο «Αγροτικόν», στην 

Επταλόφου 14

, στην Κάτω Τούμπα.




Για την ενέργεια και την ιστορία πίσω από τον δίσκο, που κυκλοφορεί 15 χρόνια μετά τον θάνατο του Νίκου, σε παραγωγή «στρόγγυλοι δίσκοι», καθώς και για το μοναδικό και αυθεντικό αποτύπωμα του καλλιτέχνη στην εθνική και παγκόσμια μουσική σκηνή θα μιλήσουν:




Απόστολος Λυκεσάς, Δημοσιογράφος, Συγγραφέας


Γιάννης Θ. Πετρίδης, Δημοσιογράφος


Θεόδωρος Προύσαλης, Συγγραφέας, Μουσικός


Αναστασία Γρηγοριάδου, Δημοσιογράφος, Ραδιοφωνικός Παραγωγός


Χρήστος Μέγας, SoundEngineer, Μουσικός Παραγωγός


Θάνος Καζαντζής, Percussionist, Sound Engineer


Διανομή https://www.b-otherside.gr/

author: Kourosh Ziabari
title: Trump’s Genocidal Rhetoric on Iran Deserves Legal Consequences, Scholars Say
content:
As Trump repeats annihilation threats against Iran, legal scholars implore other countries to step in.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

US President Donald Trump’s threats to destroy Iran have become so frequent that they often don’t make headlines. One recent exception, though, was during his 38-minute speech at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly on September 22, in which Trump mentioned Iran 17 times.

“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before? Maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East, or even the world,” he blustered. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”

Using a mix of warnings and expletives to address Iranians, Trump falsely claimed that Tehran had refused to negotiate an agreement over its nuclear program. On both occasions when Iran was militarily attacked, in June 2025 and February 2026, it was in the middle of diplomatic talks with Trump’s envoys.

“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he added during his speech at the international organization founded in 1945 to preserve global peace and security.

The U.S. military operations in Iran, an extension of the U.S.-Israeli aggression launched in February, have largely been on hold for the past few weeks as American voters gear up for the midterm elections in less than a month — with the unpopular war remaining a hot-button issue. But White House officials have sought to preserve momentum for the conflict through continued combative rhetoric, and Trump has led the charge with occasional social media outbursts and inflammatory monologues.

The UN address is far from the only time that Trump had resorted to annihilatory language to describe his intentions with Iran. “I have a big decision coming up,” Trump told Axios earlier in September. “Do I want to go in and annihilate them, or do I not?”

“My question is, if and when I want to destroy the entire country, when do I do it?” he told Fox News days after his speech at the UN. In October, TIME published an interview in which the publication asked him to clarify his annihilation comments. “Yeah, I would do that. It’s possible.… Because by annihilating Iran, we’ve created peace in the world. With Iran, I don’t think you could ever have peace.”

Most notably, in a widely criticized Truth Social post on April 7, he wrote, “a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again,” prompting calls from several members of the Congress for his impeachment under the 25th Amendment to the Constitution, including Rep. Steve Cohen (D-Tennessee), Rep. John Garamendi (D-California), and Rep. Jan Schakowsky (D-Illinois).

Different sections of the amendment have been invoked in the past when the sitting presidents were incapable of discharging their duties. For example, on November 19, 2021, former President Joe Biden invoked Section 3 of the 25th Amendment to undergo a medical surgery and his vice president Kamala Harris took charge as acting president for 85 minutes. Still, the fourth section of the amendment laying out the authority of the vice president and cabinet members to remove the president has never been invoked.

On April 30, a group of 30 psychiatrists and psychologists published a statement declaring that Trump was contending with a serious mental health impairment. The statement, which was entered into the Congressional Record by Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Jack Reed of Rhode Island, argued that if the signatories were called to adjudicate the president’s fitness to fulfill the obligations of his office, they would confirm that “he lacks the capacity to do so.” Still, that option has not been raised by Vice President JD Vance or members of Trump’s cabinet.

“Trump’s statement was certainly genocidal in character, in the sense that it appears to demonstrate the intent to destroy the Iranian people as a protected national group, in whole or in part,” said Heidi Matthews, an assistant professor of law at York University in Toronto, referencing the U.S. president’s chilling Truth Social post.

“Direct and public incitement to genocide is considered an ‘other genocidal act,’ in that it is a crime independent of whether or not genocide is actually carried out,” she told Truthout.

Matthews, who is also the co-director of York University’s International and Transnational Law Intensive Program, believes the legal framework to interpret these remarks has already been established: “It is certainly reasonable to consider this statement both in terms of the crime of incitement to genocide, and also as constituting an unlawful breach of Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state.”

Meanwhile, some Iranians listening to Trump’s remarks while grappling with the consequences of his aggression are concerned that the most powerful leader in the world may follow through on his rhetoric and take actions with irreversible consequences. The United States possesses nearly 5,000 nuclear warheads, and the decision to use them rests with the president.

Yalda Hasheminezhad, a 42-year-old cartoonist from Ardabil in northwestern Iran, said her reaction to Trump’s threats was a mixture of “sorrow and disbelief.”

“As a human being and as an artist, I cannot tolerate this much injustice, oppression, and violence,” Hasheminezhad told Truthout. “Behind each killing, there’s a human being, there’s a life, there’s a family, and it’s impossible to be indifferent to it.”

“I hope that one day, instead of making decisions on how to annihilate each other, people decide to live and try to make each other’s lives more peaceful. Yet, I feel that Trump isn’t a stable person and acts like a child who easily forgets what he said a few minutes ago,” she added.

In addition to his graphic comments, in recent months Trump has consistently expressed contempt for Iranians and used his Truth Social platform to publish AI-generated visuals depicting violence across Iran, including the critical Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf, which he has vowed on multiple occasions to destroy.

In one Truth Social post on September 6, he portrayed himself wielding a sledgehammer, shattering a sandstone-like map of Iran. Trump has also regularly threatened to attack civilian infrastructure; civilian sites were openly targeted during the height of U.S.-Israeli attacks.

Still, Trump’s public gestures toward Iran have been mercurial. After the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding was signed by Tehran and Washington on June 17, Trump temporarily shifted his rhetoric and praised the Iranian leadership as “very rational people” who were “nice to deal with.” At a White House dinner on June 25, he promised American farmers that they’d be able to sell their products to “the lovely country of Iran.” Once the ceasefire agreement collapsed, he went back to his more violent language.

Many international leaders have shrugged off Trump’s rhetoric. In September, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney downplayed Trump’s threat to “annihilate” Iran as speaking the “language of war.” But legal scholars specializing in the study of mass atrocities disagree, arguing that incitement to violence, even if not carried out, has been deemed criminal under international law.

“I do not think that dismissing these remarks as simply the language of war is either accurate or helpful,” said Craig Martin, co-director of the International and Comparative Law Center at Washburn University School of Law.

“These statements were clearly threats designed to coerce Iran into conceding, and they threatened actions that would have been unlawful under international law … the threats themselves may have been unlawful and even risen to the level of constituting a war crime,” he told Truthout.

Since the beginning of the war, Trump has made four international trips and met several foreign dignitaries, including at the 36th NATO Summit in Ankara in July. Throughout this time, his counterparts have rarely criticized his frightening statements. Scholars of international law believe world leaders should call out the harm of Trump’s rhetoric and align their foreign policy with their international legal obligations.

“Third states are legally obligated to ensure respect for the rules of international humanitarian law and to prevent genocide, making it imperative that leaders recognize Trump’s threats for what they are: unlawful and potentially criminal,” York University’s Matthews said, pointing to discursive double standards in safeguarding international law, which are making illegal wars more frequent.

Since September, when a United Nations fact-finding mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States has committed war crimes in Iran by targeting civilian sites, specifically an elementary school in Minab killing more than 120 children and a sports hall in Lamerd, the question of accountability has been debated more widely.

This comes at a time when the U.S. State Department has sanctioned the International Criminal Court and clarified its determination to “dismantle” the UN-affiliated judicial system in a bid to avert future legal proceedings implicating members of the current administration and Israeli officials.

“Neither the U.S. nor Iran have ratified the Rome Statute for the International Criminal Court, but Trump could theoretically be prosecuted by another state under the well-established doctrine of universal jurisdiction,” said Marjorie Cohn, professor emerita at Thomas Jefferson School of Law and former president of the National Lawyers Guild.

“Another state could also file a case with the International Court of Justice, asking for an advisory opinion about Trump’s war crimes and genocidal threats against Iran,” she told Truthout.

But the structures of international law continue to determine the context of relations between countries, even if they have been increasingly weakened. The United Nations General Assembly remains the largest global forum for consensus-building on key issues, the Security Council makes decisions directly affecting global peace and security, and the UN’s humanitarian agencies are facilitating critical aid to war- and poverty-stricken regions.

Gabor Rona, a professor of practice at the Cardozo Law School in New York, says the bodies of international law known as jus ad bellum and jus in bello, which dictate why and how wars should be fought, are being overlooked. Still, these laws have been enshrined in the UN Charter and remain binding.

“It is forbidden to target civilians, civilian infrastructure, cultural property, hospitals, and to cause long-term and widespread environmental damage,” Rona told Truthout. “Trump’s threats violate jus ad bellum and constitute a threat to violate jus in bello. These are the types of international crimes for which Nazi leaders were prosecuted at Nuremberg.”

“Despite ongoing serious problems and conflicts, the past 80 years have seen unprecedented advances in peace, diplomacy, human development, health, welfare, education, life expectancy, etc. These advances are in no small part a product of the post-World War II international order that is now at grave risk,” he added.

Trump has suggested that he will likely resume his bombing operations in Iran after the midterms. He also rejected a new diplomatic proposal by the Iranian delegation visiting New York for the UN General Assembly and doesn’t appear to have a clear vision of why he is continuing the war. Many Iranians are adjusting to the new reality of uncertainty and violence, and some of them are ignoring his bombast.

“When I first heard him [Trump] saying a few months ago that he would do something annihilatory, I was truly scared, because we were in the middle of the war, and I was seeing he was striking different places and people were rushing to the north,” said Shabnam Assad, a 40-year-old civil engineer in Rasht.

“But over time, I saw that he’s a capricious person and changes his mind a lot, and generally, both I and many people I know have really stopped following the news. We don’t believe in anything anymore, and are simply coping with the economy,” she told Truthout. “I have concluded that I should not waste my life and time on things like this.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Elon Musk Becomes the Largest Known Donor to This Year’s Midterms
content:
Alex Gibney, director of the new documentary Musk, discusses the rise of the world’s first trillionaire.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

We speak with the Academy Award-winning director Alex Gibney about his new documentary Musk, an expansive, nearly four-hour examination of the world’s first trillionaire and how he has amassed unprecedented power in business, technology and politics. The film traces Elon Musk’s early ventures and the rise of SpaceX and Tesla, examining the role of government support in their growth. It also explores his acquisition of Twitter, now X; his alliance with President Donald Trump and the MAGA movement; and his role in the Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, whose cuts devastated federal programs, including USAID.

Gibney says Musk has carefully crafted an image of a “polymath” who can solve the world’s most pressing problems, but that he is really “kind of a ruthless businessman” willing to do whatever it takes to succeed, including “a series of elaborate cons” to win government support for his companies.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

The world’s richest man is pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into the November midterm elections in an effort to help Republicans hold on to their Senate majority. Elon Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, has reportedly funneled more than $366 million into Republican groups and his own super PAC, according to The New York Times. That makes him by far the largest known donor to this year’s midterms. Musk and President Trump have appeared together at three events over the past two weeks, praising one another, after a very public falling-out last year. And Musk is doing all this while overseeing a sprawling business empire that’s benefited enormously from federal contracts.

We spend the rest of the hour on a new documentary about Musk and the unprecedented power he’s amassed in business, technology, politics and beyond. The epic, nearly four-hour-long film by Academy Award-winning director Alex Gibney is called simply Musk. Gibney says he set out to answer two fundamental questions: How could Musk amass so much power, and why had we given it to him? This is the film’s trailer.

ELON MUSK: What are the odds that we are in base reality? Like, we are in a simulation.

ANNOUNCER: Give it up for the greatest capitalist in history!

ALEX GIBNEY: Elon Musk is one of the most controversial figures in the world, so I decided to make him the subject of my next film. But it soon became clear Elon would not participate.

UNIDENTIFIED: Between what SpaceX has accomplished and what Elon has been saying they will be doing, there is a big leap.

ELON MUSK: Gonna build a city on Mars.

ADAM BECKER: When Musk says that the future of humanity is to colonize Mars, he is selling us dreams. That’s not happening.

MARTIN EBERHARD: When we started Tesla, he agreed to be the lead investor. What I learned in that process is there’s no legal definition of “founder.” You could call yourself a founder.

AWARD PRESENTER: The CEO Performance Award to our founder, Elon Musk.

CORY DOCTOROW: This is a car that lies to you about what it’s doing.

UNIDENTIFIED: As a result, a young woman lost her life, and a young man was forever injured.

UNIDENTIFIED: Twitter is the place where Elon can tell his side of history.

JUSTINE MUSK: Somebody on Elon’s side referred to us as “the breeders.”

UNIDENTIFIED: There’s 14 that are publicly known, but people around Elon believe that there’s many more.

AIDE: This is an order creating a department known as DOGE.

KATIE DRUMMOND: The conflicts of interest are shocking.

KARA SWISHER: The SEC, USAID, the FAA, a lot of these agencies are the ones looking at him.

ASHLEY ST. CLAIR: He had told me, “I can’t be president, but I can help Trump beat Biden.” I say, “I think we’re going to win.” And he said, “I have 10,000 lasers in space. I knew that hours ago.” What are his actual motivations? Do we even know this man at all?

UNIDENTIFIED: We have one person who’s this chaotic and has this much power. It’s completely insane.

AMY GOODMAN: The documentary traces Musk’s early business ventures, the rise of SpaceX and Tesla, the role of government support for his businesses. It also examines Musk’s acquisition of Twitter, which he renamed X; his political alliance with Trump; and his role in the Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, which eviscerated lifesaving federal government programs like USAID. Gibney also examines Musk’s ambitions in artificial intelligence, including his company xAI and the reported integration of its Grok chatbot and other AI models into U.S. military networks.

For more, we’re joined by Alex Gibney, Academy Award-winning director, his new documentary called simply Musk. Alex’s previous films include Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room, Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief and the Oscar-winning Taxi to the Dark Side.

Alex Gibney, welcome back to Democracy Now! Thank you for joining us from Maine. Why don’t we start off by talking about the resistance to even getting this film out, as it’s being released in theaters around the country this week? The Musk empire threatened to sue you. You had platforms saying they wouldn’t run the ads. Explain what is at stake right now.

ALEX GIBNEY: Well, even before the movie was premiered at the Venice Film Festival, Elon Musk’s lawyer, Alex Spiro, threatened to sue us over something that they claimed was in the documentary, but it wasn’t.

In terms of the ads, it was really interesting. We produced the trailer, the trailer you just showed, and then we wanted to run ads for that trailer on YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and X — of course, X. All of those platforms denied our ads. We appealed. They denied again. We appealed again. They denied again. They said that they were political advertisements, and on that basis, we were refused the ability to place them there. Then, there was an article was written exposing this, and mysteriously, YouTube and Meta said, “Oh gosh, sorry, just a mistake.” TikTok still won’t run the ads, and X claims they are, but so far as I know, they’re not. What it does testify to is this enormous sort of shrinking of political discourse because these massive platforms, which are controlled by tech oligarchs, are limiting speech.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Alex, what is it that got you to decide to do a film on Musk in the first place?

ALEX GIBNEY: It’s a good question. Some people came to me and asked me to do it. This goes back to 2022, long before he had hitched his wagon to Trump. And I wasn’t sure I wanted to do it initially, but I was convinced by a friend that it was about 21st-century power. And so it was. I just didn’t realize how much his economic power was going to fuse with political power at the time I started.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: What I found especially fascinating in the film is I, like most Americans, assumed that what most people know — knew originally about Musk was of Tesla, and you tell a different founding story about Tesla than most people are commonly aware of. Could you talk about that and his battle with — was it Martin Eberhard?

ALEX GIBNEY: Sure. I mean, it’s interesting. Most people think that Elon Musk is the founder of Tesla and also the prime inventor of the technology at Tesla, and that just isn’t true. He was an investor, not an inventor. The real inventor was a man named Martin Eberhard. He and his partner Marc Tarpenning founded Tesla. They were the ones who came up with the original technology of the lithium-ion battery pack, which is the thing that gives Tesla so much torque. And they also had the original business plan of starting at the high end of the market and, as people began to adopt the car, driving costs down.

Musk came in, invested in the company, and after a while, they had a falling-out. And Musk engineered Martin Eberhard’s departure. Eberhard sued for money he thought he was owed, and Musk would only agree to settle the lawsuit if Eberhard agreed to say that Musk was what he wasn’t, which was the founder of Tesla —

AMY GOODMAN: I mean, this is unbelievable.

ALEX GIBNEY: — which I find very interesting. I mean, to go to that —

AMY GOODMAN: I wanted to interrupt for one second, because I wanted to go to a clip from your documentary that goes to this, the documentary Musk describing the origins of Tesla.

ALEX GIBNEY: When Musk fired Eberhard, Musk refused to pay him what he claimed he was owed. A lawsuit followed, and it was settled only when Musk was able to claim that he was what he wasn’t: a founder of Tesla.

MARTIN EBERHARD: What I learned in that process is there’s no legal definition of “founder.” You could call yourself a founder. There’s nothing illegal about that.

MARTIN EBERHARD: Sure. Why not? You should be. You’d be a good founder. I have with me the incorporation papers for Tesla Motors, and you’ll see his name is nowhere on them.

AMY GOODMAN: So, Alex Gibney, take it from there. It’s really astounding.

ALEX GIBNEY: It is astounding. And what’s astounding is that Musk would go to such lengths to sort of embrace this lie. And I think there are a number of reasons for that. One is he wants people to know — or, he really feels it’s important for people to think that he’s this polymath, this sort of Leonardo da Vinci-like figure, when, in fact, what he is is a kind of a ruthless businessman — with some talents, we should all admit, but not an inventor.

And the other thing that’s interesting, too, is that when it comes to Silicon Valley, being a founder is what entitles you to all sorts of money, and the ability downstream, even when your company’s economic fundamentals don’t justify a big valuation, to pitch people on the idea that, “Don’t worry, we may not be making money now, but in the future, you’re investing in this man, Elon Musk, who’s a genius. He’s an inventor. He’s all these things” — which of course, he isn’t.

AMY GOODMAN: I wanted to go to the amount of government money — that’s taxpayer money — that has gone into all of these businesses, ultimately, all of these companies, recognizing that they get involved with the military — he’s running, what, the future of war for Hegseth at the Pentagon now — that that’s where the biggest bucks are. But go back to the beginning, to how he positioned Tesla, and then going into SpaceX, and recognizing what would get him the money and what wouldn’t.

ALEX GIBNEY: Well, it’s interesting, because, particularly with SpaceX, I mean, Musk has always positioned himself as this kind of free-wheeling entrepreneur who did what he did just by the dint of hard work and independence. But, I mean, SpaceX, for almost all of its existence, has been more or less a socialist enterprise. It had one customer, and that’s the government of the United States. Tesla benefited early on, particularly under the Obama administration, from a number of loans and subsidies for EVs, and also the state of California helped to subsidize Tesla early on. So, Tesla itself as a company would be unimaginable without those subsidies and never would have made it.

The other thing that he’s done, particularly at Tesla, is when he ran out of government subsidies and his ability to get money from venture capitalists, there was only one place left to go, and that was the stock market. So he started making increasingly bold, outlandish and, really, fictional claims about his company in order to get a high valuation, which is what allowed Tesla to, you know, prosper.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And could you talk, as well — in the film, you go into the various situations where Musk really almost — practically pulled a scam on government. The rechargeable — the swapping of batteries in Tesla that enabled him to be able to get a hold of all of these EV credits from California, could you talk about that, as well?

ALEX GIBNEY: Sure. I mean, you know, very early on, in order to get this money from the government, he had to engage in a series of elaborate cons. And maybe the first one is the most outlandish and the most interesting. He had this big demonstration where he claimed to solve the essential problem of the EV. And what is that essential problem? It’s range. Everybody worries about range, you know, because unlike a gas car, you can’t pull into a gas station and juice up your battery. Well, Musk held this big demonstration where he said, “Oh yes, you can. We have a thing called a battery swap.” And he holds this big demonstration where something strange underneath the the chassis of the car happens, and he claims to be swapping out a battery, and that for that, because he did it once, he was able to get an extraordinary subsidy from the government of California.

But the thing is, you know, he claimed that he was going to try to do that on a grand scale so that people really could do this. He had one battery swap station. There was a journalist there who observed that it never happened. Nobody ever went in. Well, people tried to go in, but there were no battery swaps because, you have to understand, the battery in a Tesla is a thousand pounds. OK? And it’s usually covered with sealant and stuff like that. But Musk, you know, sort of gulled the government of California into thinking it could be swapped out like double-A batteries. So, it was really an outrageous con.

AMY GOODMAN: What about the self-driving cars, what you describe here in this documentary, the information that Tesla would not reveal the number of people who died? Explain what took place in the settling of these lawsuits so that information would not come out.

ALEX GIBNEY: I think the thing that we have to understand about Tesla’s attempt to, you know, develop self-driving cars was that it was always a stock market play, because, otherwise, you were just an ordinary car company. But for years, he was touting his technology. And his technology was basically a camera technology. The cameras in the cars, you know, take stock of what’s going on around them. It feeds data to the system. AI then, you know, teaches the car how to drive on roads. That’s the theory of it. OK? But he also never put in the redundant systems that Waymo has — radar and lidar, and so forth and so on. So, the problem came between the distance of Musk’s hype and pitch and what the cars could actually do.

There’s a famous ad that they ran in 2016 called the “Paint It Black” ad, from the Rolling Stones song that, you know, accompanies it, where you see a car driving itself and says — and it’s touted as a technology that in fact exists, but, really, at the time, that technology couldn’t tell the difference between a red light and a green light, which is a pretty fundamental issue that you need to sort out for safety in a car.

And as a result, as you say, over 60 people lost their lives as a result of Autopilot failures. And in the case of many lawsuits, they were able to be settled so that the information about all of this wouldn’t come out. There was one very powerful lawsuit brought by a woman who died, who was a pedestrian, who was literally killed by a runaway Autopilot Tesla, and one of the things that was discovered was that Tesla was effectively hiding evidence from them, which they were able to obtain with the help of a Russian hacker, which showed that Tesla knew very well how and why the car malfunctioned, but they weren’t sharing it with the investigators. As a result, there was a rather large judgment against Tesla, the first one.

And I think, you know, going back to the campaign contributions, if I may, I think that this issue of fraud at — or, alleged fraud at Tesla is one of the investigations that he was facing when he hitched his wagon to Trump, and I strongly believe that one of the reasons he’s flooding the political campaigns with so much money now is he wants to avoid investigations in the future.

AMY GOODMAN: This is a critical point. But I want to go back to your documentary, Musk, featuring rare interviews with people previously in Musk’s inner circle, including Ashley St. Clair, the former conservative influencer, mother of one of Musk’s kids. She says she was offered a nondisclosure agreement in exchange for financial support, but she chose not to sign it, saying she felt a moral obligation to speak publicly about her experience. Musk has disputed her account of a $40 million offer with $100,000 a month. This is a clip from Musk featuring Ashley St. Clair.

ASHLEY ST. CLAIR: If you were to ask someone on the right what they think of Elon, he’s a free speech god; and someone on the left, he’s just someone who sends hateful tweets, and he’s lost his mind. Both are very comforting, but both are completely insufficient to the immense amount of power and influence he has.

AMY GOODMAN: And this is Ashley Sinclair from the trailer for Musk.

ASHLEY ST. CLAIR: He had told me, “I can’t be president, but I can help Trump beat Biden.” I say, “I think we’re going to win.” And he said, “I have 10,000 lasers in space. I knew that hours ago.” What are his actual motivations? Do we even know this man at all?

AMY GOODMAN: So, let’s go to who spoke to you, Alex, and who wouldn’t speak to you — I mean, Ashley St. Clair would not sign a nondisclosure agreement — and the fear of retribution that others had, and then go to your point that you’re making about — I mean, it goes to DOGE, as well, taking out the very agencies and inspectors that would be investigating him if Democrats win.

ALEX GIBNEY: That’s right. So, I think that — I mean, look, I talked to hundreds of people, or myself and my team talked to hundreds of people, many people off the record, some on background. But it was tremendously hard to get people to come on camera to speak. Over time, we were able to get some key people — Reid Hoffman, you know, who was part of the PayPal Mafia, knew Musk early on; Justine Musk, his first wife; Ashley St. Clair, you showed; as well as a number of people involved in the origin of his companies. So, you know, it took some doing, but I think there was a tremendous amount of fear that Musk would either sue them out of existence or would launch sort of vitriolic attacks on them on X, which has a kind of ramification, because once you start the rage loop on something like X, all sorts of crazy people come out of the woodwork, and the next thing you know, you’re being doxxed or you’re being chased. It can be a very scary thing. But some very courageous people were — you know, did come forward, and it was tremendously helpful in order to give dimension to this character.

But I do want to — you know, a lot of people have gone to sort of the ideological underpinnings of Musk, and I think, to some extent, those are overdone. I think he’s always behaved in a very pragmatic way. I mean, when he needed money from Barack Obama, he was, you know, liberal. But then, when he — you know, in 2024, when he suddenly hitched his wagon to Trump, it seemed like, “This is the guy I believe in. It’s his ideas that are so important.” Well, he was also facing a tremendous number of civil investigations into his companies for abrogating workers’ rights, for pollution, for all sorts of other things, and a criminal investigation into possible fraud at Tesla.

Now, once Trump is elected, Musk is put in charge of the Department of Government Efficiency, which really had nothing to do with waste, fraud and abuse. Its two goals, as far as I’m concerned, were, one, to destroy the regulatory state — and he starts first with the agencies that are regulating him — and then, the next thing, I think, that, you know, was a kind of key goal for DOGE, for Musk, was the access of federal data, not only classified information, but also access on all of us, from our Social Security data, our Medicare data, so forth and so on.

You know, the DOGE boys, which we all — whom we all remember as these callow kids from some of Musk’s companies going into federal agencies and literally knowing nothing about them and cutting jobs here, cutting jobs there, a little bit like, you know, firing the pilot while he’s flying the plane, without any regard to how damaging or dangerous that might be. So, you could say that they were reckless and “What were they doing?” and it was crazy, but, actually, there was an ulterior motive here. All these kids were very savvy about how to access IT and data at these federal agencies. They had what’s called super admin status, which meant that they could see data across the silos that are normally put in place either to protect our privacy or to protect classified information. And I’m told by heads of IT at those agencies that moving that data to SpaceX, for example, would have been as easy as a drag and drop — you know, taking a computer file and putting it into a folder. So, that’s a really terrifying idea. Now, we don’t — I can’t prove that that’s what he did, but I strongly suspect it is.

AMY GOODMAN: Alex Gibney, we want to congratulate you on your film, Academy Award-winning director. His new documentary is Musk. We hope to do Part 2 and post it online.

Happy birthday to Miguel Nogueira! And an early happy birthday to Juan González!

By the way, Steal This Story, Please!, the documentary about Democracy Now!, will be viewable online for the first time in an exclusive special event starting tonight at 8 p.m. Eastern. If you live in the U.S. and Canada, you can watch the film in your own home and be part of the post-screening question-and-answer with me and the filmmakers Tia Lessin and Carl Deal, moderated by the Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Maria Hinojosa. Find out more at StealThisStory.org. Join us and help support the impact of this film that celebrates the importance of independent media. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González, for Democracy Now!

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

title: “Καμία δίωξη στον κόσμο του αγώνα” – συγκέντρωση την Τετάρτη 14/10, 09.00, στα δικαστήρια Χανίων
content:
Από την Ανοιχτή συνέλευση για την κρατική δολοφονία του Κώστα Μανιουδάκη:




Καμία δίωξη στον κόσμο του αγώνα




Τετάρτη 14 Οκτωβρίου & Τετάρτη 21 Οκτωβρίου | 09:00 | Δικαστήρια Χανίων







Από το καλοκαίρι του 2024, οι 4 μπάτσοι δολοφόνοι του Κώστα Μανιουδάκη έχουν κατηγορηθεί για ανθρωποκτονία με ενδεχόμενο δόλο σε ήρεμη ψυχική κατάσταση από κοινού. Μόλις τους τελευταίους 10 μήνες, η υπόθεση ξυλοδαρμού μέχρι θανάτου του Κωστή προχώρησε στην κύρια ανάκριση και ολοκληρώθηκε, επιβάλλοντας στους δολοφόνους απαγόρευση εξόδου από τη χώρα και εγγυήσεις 20.000€ για τους 2 μπάτσους και 5.000€ για τους άλλους 2. Οι μπάτσοι δολοφόνοι παραμένουν στις θέσεις τους, ένοπλοι, ενεργώντας μέχρι και σήμερα «τυχαίους» ελέγχους.




Η ανοχή και η επιβράβευση του κράτους στα δολοφονικά εγκλήματα των ένστολων φονιάδων του, έρχεται (και) μέσω του δικαστικού συστήματος: μέχρι και σήμερα, τους έχει δώσει το ελεύθερο να μηνύουν με κάθε τρόπο τον κόσμο που αγωνίζεται, από τους συγγενείς του Κωστή μέχρι τα μέλη της ανοιχτής συνέλευσης. Αντί, λοιπόν, να προχωράει ο προγραμματισμός της δίκης για ανθρωποκτονία από πρόθεση, προχωράνε οι μηνύσεις που κάνουν οι ίδιοι οι δολοφόνοι. Περιττό να πούμε πως στην περίπτωση που στη θέση των μπάτσων, κατηγορούνταν κάποιος «φτωχοδιάβολος», οι διαδικασίες θα κινούνταν με γρήγορους ρυθμούς.




Καλούμε σε συγκεντρώσεις αλληλεγγύης στα δικαστήρια: στις 14/10 για τον αδερφό του Κωστή, τον οποίο μήνυσε η Κ. Μόσχου επειδή «την προσέβαλε στο διαδίκτυο», και στις 21/10, για τα 4 μέλη της ανοιχτής συνέλευσης που μήνυσε ο Μ. Γεωργιάδης το 2024, επειδή όταν τον είδαν να σκίζει τις αφίσες μας και, χωρίς να γνωρίζουν ποιος είναι, τις υπερασπίστηκαν. Για την τελευταία μάλιστα μήνυση, έχουν οριστεί τους προηγούμενους μήνες 3 δικάσιμοι στις οποίες ο Γεωργιάδης δεν εμφανίστηκε.




Να τεθούν άμεσα σε διαθεσιμότητα οι τέσσερις μπάτσοι δολοφόνοι




Στέλιος Λιανιδάκης, Μανώλης Γεωργιάδης, Κωνσταντίνα Μόσχου και Σήφης Τσιχλάκης




Να ξεκινήσει άμεσα η δίκη των τεσσάρων μπάτσων δολοφόνων
