author: Daron Letts
title: RCMP charge Chesterfield Inlet youth withfirst-degree murder
content:
Police have charged a Chesterfield Inlet youth with first-degree murder following the death of a man in the hamlet early Friday morning.




Nunavut RCMP issued a news release about the incident Tuesday.




Officers arrived on scene at 1 a.m. following a report of gunfire and located a man “with injuries consistent with a gunshot wound,” the release said.




The victim was transported to the local health centre, where he was pronounced dead.




Police arrested a youth and the Nunavut RCMP Major Crime Unit laid charges that same day.




The youth, whose identity is protected by law, is in custody and scheduled to appear in court in Iqaluit on Nov. 16.




It’s unclear what, if any, relation there is between the accused and victim.
















RCMP are not providing any further details, the release said.

author: Dion Nissenbaum
title: Meet the Right-Wing Activists Urging Trump to Take Extreme Action in Elections
content:
“The president needs to completely declare a national emergency,” said longtime Trump ally Mike Lindell.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Since being released early from prison in June, former Colorado election clerk Tina Peters has been granted extraordinary access to the halls of power in Washington.

Peters said she has traveled to Washington seven times, visited the White House at least twice, and met with senior officials at the Justice and Commerce departments — remarkable access for someone on parole after a 2024 felony conviction for tampering with voting machines in an attempt to show that the 2020 election was rigged against President Donald Trump.

She’s a high-profile example of a group of Trump supporters and conservative activists trying to lay out a roadmap for the president to follow. They are urging him to take more extreme steps to try and influence the outcome of an election that many polls suggest could end Republican control of Congress. But as the election closes in, the activists are now voicing increasing concerns that the president and his administration aren’t going to act on their ideas.

Peters isn’t shy about what she wants. The 71-year-old activist is pushing the Trump administration to use emergency powers before the November election to scrutinize voting machines across America, though that’s something most experts and lawyers say it can’t legally do.

“A lot of people would say that we just need to go rogue and declare this radical emergency and we need to shut everything down,” Peters said last week on an election activist livestream on Rumble. “The encouraging part is that there are already orders and laws in place that allow them to do what they need to do.”

Other conservative activists pushing for changes to election administration include:

Cleta Mitchell, head of the Election Integrity Network and a Trump ally, who is pushing for the Commerce Department to examine foreign-made parts in voting systems as potential national security risks that should be addressed before November.

Mike Lindell, a longtime Trump ally who has spent years promoting claims that voting machines were used to manipulate U.S. elections, who wants Trump to declare a national emergency and prevent the use of electronic voting machines in November.

Peter Ticktin, a Florida attorney representing Peters and longtime Trump friend, who said Trump might have to declare martial law if the election results are in question.

Steve Bannon, a longtime Trump ally and former White House chief strategist who hosts the influential right-wing podcast War Room, who has repeatedly urged Trump to use emergency powers to require voter identification at the polls and send ICE agents to polling places.

James Mills, head of the Georgia State Election Board, who sent a letter last week urging the Trump administration to compel his state to make election software updates before the November election.

A wide array of lawyers, voting rights groups, civil rights leaders, and Democrats have denounced the ideas as an unconstitutional attack on the nation’s electoral process. But such criticisms haven’t deterred Trump from trying to advance a variety of proposals to impose more federal control over elections.

Federal courts have blocked Trump from advancing key pillars of two executive orders that would have transformed the U.S. Postal Service into a ballot regulation agency, eliminated grace periods for ballots arriving after Election Day, and required all people to provide documented proof of citizenship to register to vote.

With most of his efforts at election oversight blocked, Trump has left open the possibility he might heed the calls of supporters urging him to take drastic action before November.

“Let me just say that stranger things have happened, OK?” Trump said in an August interview with Wayne Allyn Root on Real America’s Voice, responding to a question about declaring a national security emergency as a way to assert more authority over elections. “I’ll leave it at that.”

The Trump administration has laid out an Election Day plan that includes dispatching 1,000 election monitors to look for any problems in key states, establishing FBI command posts across the nation, and military monitoring of potential cyber attacks from hostile nations. Pentagon officials have said they have no plans to send armed forces to polling places on Election Day. But the Trump administration has stopped short of foreclosing the possibility that ICE or armed federal agents could operate near or in polling places, a move that could cross legal lines.

Sean Morales-Doyle, senior director of the Brennan Center’s Voting Rights and Elections Program, said federal laws and precedent make it extremely unlikely that Trump would be able to take any meaningful steps to seize voting machines before the election. And that may not be the ultimate goal, he said.

“The point of this concerted campaign to undermine our elections from this administration is really not about changing the rules, because even they know the president lacks the authority,” said Morales-Doyle. “It is about sowing confusion, chaos and distrust and undermining public trust in our elections.”

Peters appears to be the person who has had the greatest access to Trump administration officials in recent months. Trump had lunch at the White House with Peters and Ticktin in late June, just four weeks after Peters was released from state prison. Peters returned for a second visit last week, Ticktin told Votebeat.

Mitchell and Peters have focused their efforts on persuading the Trump administration to use existing authority to compel the Commerce Department to examine voting machines to determine if they pose a national security risk because they contain parts from other nations, including China.

Mitchell argues that a national emergency declaration that Trump declared in 2019 gives him the power to compel action by the Commerce Department. Earlier this year, Justice Department official Keith Olsen reportedly tried to get the Commerce Department to classify voting machine components as national security threats, which could lead to them being banned from use in the U.S. But investigators found no evidence to support the claims, Reuters reported, and the idea was scrapped.

Mitchell, in an interview with Votebeat, expressed frustration that the Trump administration has not placed enough importance on the concerns and blamed people working for the president for not doing enough to address election issues.

“I can call the president anytime I want to — and I have,” said Mitchell, who declined to say when she last spoke to Trump. “I told the president this: I wish that the people in your administration knew or cared as much about election integrity as you do.”

Neither the Commerce Department nor the White House responded to requests for comment.

Mitchell said she signs every message to administration officials with the same sign-off: Tick-tock.

That’s the same message Ticktin said he has been trying to convey.

“We are running out of time,” said Ticktin, who characterized the threat from Chinese-made parts in voting machines as akin to an act of war.

“This is getting serious enough and critical enough that it might even require, at some point, martial law,” said Ticktin. “People say: ‘Ticktin’s crazy.’ If I’m not crazy and what I am saying is true that China is attacking us in some way, well then we’re really in a state of belligerence with China and, sooner or later, it’s going to be too late to change things in a peaceful way.”

Ticktin suggested that federal forces could help seize voting machines in places where the count is in question, and potentially hand-count ballots.

Ticktin’s call represents the most extreme — and most unlikely — idea being pushed by election skeptics.

Mitchell, Peters, and others have been urging the administration to take more strategic steps to address their concerns.

A focal point for the group is Georgia, where Mills surprised members of the state elections board by sending off a letter urging the Trump administration to order major changes to the state’s voting equipment before the November election.

The letter asked the Justice Department to force state and county officials to install software updates before the November election. It also asked the Justice Department to prevent QR-code-based tabulation in Georgia and require Georgia to end its use of the codes in six months. But installing new software would require time, money and resources — all of which are in short supply for Georgia in the weeks leading up to the election.

Trump has long focused his ire on Georgia, where he lost the 2020 presidential election by fewer than 12,000 votes — less than 1% of the ballots cast. Mitchell joined Trump on a call to Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger after the election where they pressed him to change the results before the results were certified. Earlier this year, the FBI searched Fulton County’s election hub and seized more than 650 boxes, including ballots, from the 2020 election. The results in Georgia this fall will be pivotal to partisan control of the U.S. Senate.

Beyond Georgia, others like Bannon and Lindell keep pressing the president to issue a new national security declaration to prevent the use of electronic voting machines to tally votes at all.

“The president needs to completely declare a national emergency,” Lindell said. “The president can just make a national argument and say, ‘Hey, we’re going to go paper ballots, hand counting.’”

But making such a declaration wouldn’t allow Trump to ban voting machines or require states to count all ballots by hand. The Constitution grants the president limited control over elections, which are usually handled by state and local officials with direction from Congress.

At the end of the day, said Morales-Doyle, the most important thing voters can do is make plans to cast their ballots in ways they feel safe and secure.

“At this moment, when democracy has come under such unprecedented and pointed attacks, it is more important than ever that people invest in democracy and that do so in defiance of all this,” he said.

Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization covering local election integrity and voting access. Sign up for their newsletters here.

author: Daniel Hunter
title: Why we need to think outside the box this election
content:
This article 

Why we need to think outside the box this election

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







This election is not like any other. You’ve heard that before, and so have I. But after decades of “this presidential election is the most important election in your lifetime,” I have finally conceded that this 

midterm

 election may be the most important election in my lifetime — because it will be the ultimate test of whether Trump and MAGA have succeeded in their authoritarian consolidation of power. 




And so it’s appropriate that many groups are trying new things ahead of this election — because the old playbook alone won’t get us there.




No Kings.

 On Oct. 17, No Kings is going to try something it hasn’t tried before. Instead of another mass march, the coalition is holding 

No Kings: Vote Early

, a 

nonpartisan day of action

 in which communities will host block parties, BBQs and local protests to make a voting plan together and vote early where local rules allow. Organizers say it’s 

“not purely a protest

,” but rather a nonpartisan action to encourage voter participation. The idea is to treat voting not as something we do alone, but as something we do together. I’m not old enough to remember it, but people used to go to the polls with their neighbors and make an event of it. This is bringing back that collective spirit.




(It’s easy to host. Go 

here

 for all the info you need by Thursday Oct. 15.)




Election Holiday.

 Another experiment is popping up for the Nov. 3 election — 

Election Day: Our Civic Holiday

. This group (which I’m a part of) rests on a simple idea: treating Election Day as a day for showing love for democracy by doing our civic duty. Vote, help someone else vote, become a poll worker or observer, or find another way to participate in civic life. The idea is to translate that into a cultural vibe, like Valentine’s Day, but for a different form of love — love for democracy and our neighbors.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










These are two experiments among many in how we protect elections in new ways under new circumstances. (I’ll be writing more about possible post-election actions later.) Neither solves the problem on its own, but both actions build on the understanding that stealing an election gets much harder when there’s a large blowout. Hungary is the reminder. As I 

wrote in April

, Orbán’s defeat was so decisive that he conceded before all the votes were counted, with turnout 

near 80 percent

, the highest since their transition to democracy. As Micah Sifry put it, it was “

too big to rig

.”




New tactics aren’t easy — and it’s worth reminding ourselves of that.




The trap of the winning tactic




Until now, No Kings has been known for one thing: enormous marches, each bigger than the last. Organizers 

put the first at five million, the second at seven million, and the third, in March, at more than eight million

. When a tactic works like that, the pressure to keep repeating it is immense.




I’ve seen this up close. After Greta Thunberg began her Friday walkouts, Fridays for Future grew and grew. I was working with 350.org — a global environmental organization — at the time and we provided a lot of the backend technical support to help it grow. That growth created tremendous pressure and helped drive movement at the United Nations and in many countries. (You can certainly argue it contributed to the Inflation Reduction Act, which — despite significant cuts — has some parts that are still 

very active

.)




But every tactic eventually peaks. As Saul Alinsky put it, “A tactic that drags on too long becomes a drag.” Suddenly an organization named for leaving school on Fridays needs to improvise — and that’s hard.




Student protesters asked me to write the 

Climate Resistance Handbook

 to try to assist Fridays for Future (and others) to break out of their tactical doldrums.




Occupy Wall Street

 hit the same wall. In Philadelphia, where we had an encampment outside of City Hall, my ears still ring with painful, shouted debates over whether we could do anything other than occupy. The argument largely won out that occupying is the thing that held us together — and like most occupations around the country (but not all!), we never tactically transitioned.




That’s the pull: The familiar tactic feels like the glue. The drive to stay the course is strong. And it takes a strong decision-making process to break out.




Many of us know this tactical challenge: endless weekly vigils and letter-writing with no changes. Worried about this dynamic in my anti-casino organizing group, I once made us promise we would only use the same tactic 

once

 — resulting in new tactics like 

citizen’s search warrants, Philly’s Ballot Box or the public filibuster

. 




So No Kings deserves congratulations for breaking the mold. Yes, many would love to see something more escalated that increases the level of risk-taking — but it’s worth just underlining how difficult it is to change course at all. So greeting this pivot with encouragement makes all pivots more possible.




The strategic logic




Why put so much energy into the election? 




I’ve regularly argued there is 

so much more than elections

. And Trump’s attempt at consolidation is happening in places where elections alone won’t save us. Take the military, where Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plans to purge 

20 percent of the military’s top leaders

. He’s already blocked and purged many women and Black leaders. Many view his attempts as a long-term purge to keep control of the military. (The military is hardly defensive and has its own ways of pushing back — including the extensive leaking about the 

eight sailors in the USS Abraham Lincoln strike group who attempted suicide.)




But the elections remain critical both as a narrative (exposing Trump’s unpopularity!) and also because Congress (for all its faults) remains a key pillar in allowing the theft of congressional money, putting in radical judges, co-signing his corruption and so much more.




Previous Coverage

 

What D.C.’s election defense under occupation can teach us




Trump knows this, which is why it is such important contested territory for him. In September, Trump led the crowd at the Republican National Convention in a pledge to 

“cheat like hell”

 (

Newsweek

 

claimed he was joking

 — but I’d say the intent is hard to dismiss). The 

Callais

 decision echoes widely as the single largest loss of Black political power in recent memory. 




Trump hopes terror can keep us from voting. In March he signed an 

executive order restricting mail-in voting

, and while courts have 

kept the restrictions from taking effect this year

, the fear it stoked is already having an impact. Trump is adding more fuel by making up stories of noncitizen voting. Why? So he can actually steal the election. I lay out 18 ways the regime might take our votes away in 

this scenario guide

.




If nothing else, remember that a 2028 election becomes far easier to steal with a willing Congress. You don’t need a strong imagination to picture a Trump-led Jan. 6 insurrection under current Republican leadership ending in a fully effective coup backed by Congress and the Supreme Court. That becomes much harder with a hostile Congress.




All of this brings us back to why the midterms matter and the context of why collectively voting early and supporting each other on Election Day matters.




Why turnout is protection




Mass participation can overwhelm a system and make the likely accomplices of would-be election thieves less willing to go along. Trump can try to control the narrative, but the mechanics of theft require a chain of accomplices: election deniers in the certification process, state actors, and behind them businesses and supporters who quietly approve. That’s why folks at May Day Strong launched the 

Business for Democracy Pledge

. By signing on, businesses commit to oppose obstacles to voting and, if results aren’t honored, to close ranks in defense of the election. It pulls potential accomplices back before they cross the line.
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













Then there are the efforts to recruit more voters, like the Oct. 17 Vote Early Day coming up soon — a chance to mix large-scale decentralized actions for an electoral good. Or the 

Election Day: Our Civic Holiday

 effort where we’re not asking for a federal policy change. We’re asking people to treat the day differently. Vote if you haven’t. Help someone else vote. Make it visible.




We’re trying to feed into the energy by reminding everyone to stay active on Election Day, Nov. 3, by:







making sure you’ve voted, and that the people around you have too




becoming a poll worker or 

nonpartisan observer




joining Singing Resistance, Souls to the Polls, or Joy to the Polls, and meeting any interference with positivity




connecting with rapid-deployment teams or people already at polling sites, not to confront ICE, but to redirect and escort voters so everyone eligible gets to vote.







You can 

share the word at election.holiday

. Businesses can support the campaign by pledging to give their employees time off to do their civic duty through 

Time to Vote

, the coalition founded by Patagonia. And if you’re still looking for roles to support the election, find them at 

We are Ground Control

.




All of this is part of the pre-election plan: Get large numbers of people voting against an awful regime. There’s an abundant range of opportunities to help protect our election. I hope you find your role.




This article 

Why we need to think outside the box this election

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.

Health officials in Pennsylvania have announced another death related to measles, the sixth overall in the state and the U.S. since the beginning of this year.

author: Mada Masr
title: State security prosecution renews detention of 6 Matsda2sh journalists for 15 days
content:
The detention of six journalists from fact-checking platform Matsda2sh was renewed for 15 days on Tuesday evening, pending further investigations, according to their lawyers. The renewal was ordered by the Supreme State Security Prosecution during today’s hearing in Case 8083/2026.




The journalists Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emaira, Abdallah Kadry, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Adel, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal are being investigated in the case, registered with the Supreme State Security Prosecution, and were questioned again by prosecutors in sessions on Tuesday.




The journalists’ lawyers told Mada Masr that questioning began around 1 pm and continued into the evening at the prosecution’s headquarters in the Fifth Settlement. The sessions revisited previous lines of questioning, including questioning about wages, the managerial structure of the platform and the way work was organized, with no new evidence presented to the journalists.




All six journalists have been held at Badr 1 Prison since they were brought before the prosecution early last week. Their lawyers said they are due to receive their first family visits starting Thursday, as well as to be granted dedicated time for exercise.




Security forces arrested the six Matsda2sh journalists in the span of24 hours 

during a campaign 

launched on September 28 which targeted the fact-checking platform’s team across several governorates. 




Their whereabouts remained unknown for five days, during which they were denied access to their lawyers and prevented from contacting their families, in 

violation

 of the counterterrorism law under which they were detained, according to 

EIPR

. They appeared before the Supreme State Security Prosecution on October 4 when investigations began.




The prosecution is investigating the six journalists for several offenses, including joining a terrorist group, spreading false news, misusing social media and receiving foreign funding.




Several journalists told prosecutors during their interrogations that they had been subjected to torture and forced to record video footage in custody of themselves reading fabricated confessions, according to the 

Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights,

 whose legal team is leading their defense. The Journalists 

Syndicate

 subsequently filed a complaint with the prosecutor general, calling for an investigation into allegations that the journalists were tortured at National Security Agency facilities before being brought before the prosecution. The 

Interior Ministry

 denied the allegations two hours after the syndicate issued its statement.




Three of the detained journalists were referred to the Forensic Medicine Authority on October 6. The 

prosecution

 said the following day that forensic reports found no injuries on their bodies or signs of violence having been used against them. 




EIPR 

responded

 to the prosecutor’s statement by noting that prosecutors had refused to hear the journalists’ testimony as victims in the torture complaints they filed against the officers responsible for their detention at National Security Agency facilities. EIPR also said the prosecution had not summoned or heard testimony from the officers named in the complaints or witnesses to the incidents. It also noted that the journalists had not claimed to have visible injuries but had reported being subjected to torture, ill-treatment, threats and physical and psychological coercion.

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Tablets Make Communication Easier Behind Bars – But Deaf People Are Left Behind
content:
This story was co-published with

 

Truthout

.




Tablet computers have revolutionized communication inside prisons for hearing prisoners. Prison systems from across the country — including in 

New York

, 

California

, and 

Illinois

 — have 

distributed tens of thousands

 of tablets to incarcerated people, which they can use to call home, watch movies, message loved ones, or attend virtual classes (although they are often 

charged predatory fees

 for accessing these benefits). As of 2022, 

25 state prison systems

 had tablet distribution programs, according to the Electronic Privacy Information Center. 




But as the rollout of such tablets continues, many deaf incarcerated people have been left behind. 




Disability justice organization HEARD points out that 

it’s 

unknown

 how many deaf people are incarcerated in U.S. prisons, but a 

2015 report

 by the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated that 6.2 percent of incarcerated people in 

state

 and 

federal

 prisons have a hearing disability, which would equal about 71,000 people.




Daniel Valenzuela, who is deaf, is incarcerated at Danville Correctional Center in Illinois. Last year, the Illinois Department of Corrections (IDOC) 

distributed tablets

 to all incarcerated people. But IDOC blocks videophone capabilities, preventing Valenzuela from communicating in his primary language, American Sign Language (ASL).  




In September, Valenzuela sued the IDOC director for violating the Americans with Disabilities Act.




“I have six kids, four grandkids, and one of my sons is in the military. I cherish and love my family so much,” said Valenzuela in a 

press release

 announcing the lawsuit. “I just want to tell them happy birthday and I am so grieved when I can’t call because I don’t want them to think I forgot.”




There are at least three other deaf individuals at Danville who primarily use ASL to communicate, according to the 

complaint

 filed by Disability Rights Advocates, Equip for Equality, and the law firm Much Shelist. 




“Across the Illinois Department of Corrections, people can use tablets to communicate with their loved ones, which has been a game changer in removing restrictions on communication,” Valenzuela’s attorney, Rachel Weisberg, the directing attorney at Disability Rights Advocates, told 

Truthout

. “But for Mr. Valenzuela and other deaf people who use American Sign Language, that same access simply isn’t available.” 




IDOC did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.




Last year, in addition to distributing tablets to incarcerated people, IDOC 

announced

 it would provide every incarcerated person with 775 free domestic phone call minutes per month. In a press release, 

IDOC said

 that these initiatives, working in tandem, “enhance family connections and increase access to technology that supports rehabilitation.” 




But deaf prisoners are excluded from accessing these critical programs. 




Unlike hearing prisoners who can use their tablets to make calls from their cells, Valenzuela must get a guard’s permission to walk to another building to use the one videophone that’s available to him. In at least one instance, Valenzuela had to go out in the pouring rain to use the videophone, according to the complaint. 




“When prison officials don’t communicate with deaf/disabled people in ways they can understand, they may be written up for being ‘non-compliant.'”




The videophone is often unavailable because the unit itself breaks down, the prison is on lockdown, or a guard denies his request, according to the complaint. Last year, Valenzuela was unable to speak with his family during the holidays because the phone was not working for 54 straight days, from November 2025 to January 2026. However, if the tablets malfunction, there are several backup phones that incarcerated hearing people can use, the complaint says.




“We’re asking for equal access, as that’s what the law requires,” said Weisberg. “Equal access is not static — it must reflect the benefits currently offered to others and account for the needs of people with disabilities as technology and communication systems evolve.”




These issues are not limited to Illinois. Advocates say incarcerated deaf people have to contend with discriminatory communication practices in prisons throughout the country.




“In prisons where we’ve seen scores of deaf/disabled people, there may only be 2 videophones,” Kah Mendoza, the communications coordinator for 

HEARD

, told 

Truthout

 in an email. “We’ve seen deaf/disabled incarcerated people on lockdowns for weeks with no way to call home.”




HEARD is a deaf-led prison abolitionist organization that advocates for the rights of and provides support to deaf/disabled incarcerated people. Mendoza says the organization uses deaf/disabled to describe people who are deaf or hard-of-hearing and/or experience any form of disability.




In 2022, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) 

published a rule

 mandating that correctional facilities with more than 50 incarcerated people provide access to video calls for people who communicate in ASL. However, correctional agencies have ignored or attempted to sidestep the FCC mandate, said Mendoza. 




Within prisons, deaf people are often isolated and excluded from programs and religious services, and unable to participate in counseling sessions or communicate with medical staff. They’re also at risk of being disciplined for their disability, said Mendoza. When prison officials don’t communicate with deaf/disabled people in ways they can understand, they may be written up for being “non-compliant,” he said. 




In an 

essay published

 in 

The Marshall Project

, Jeremy Woody wrote that when he was taken to a disciplinary hearing while incarcerated in Georgia, his hands were cuffed behind his back. A guard wrote, “guilty or not guilty?”, but with his hands restrained, he was unable to write his answer or communicate in ASL.




“The responsibility should be on prisons and jails to provide reliable access, not on incarcerated people to overcome barriers that the system itself created.”




“They said, ‘OK, you have nothing to say? Guilty,’” he wrote. “That infuriated me. I started to scream. That was really all that I could do. They sent me to the hole, and I cried endlessly. It’s hard to describe the fury and anger.”




Last year, Disability Rights Advocates 

settled a lawsuit

 with the Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC) filed on behalf of deaf incarcerated individuals who alleged that they were unable to participate in programming and services because TDOC denied them ASL interpreters, videophones, and captioning.




The settlement requires TDOC to provide sign language interpreters for intake and orientation, medical and mental health appointments, educational and vocational programming, religious services, and discipline and parole-related proceedings. The agency must also provide videophones at every facility housing a deaf person.




Mendoza says by denying access to communication, “deaf/disabled incarcerated people can be effectively cut off from other human beings in ways hearing people do not experience.”




“Access to communication is not a luxury,” he said. “Deaf/disabled people should not have to fight repeatedly for basic access to information and communication while they are incarcerated. The responsibility should be on prisons and jails to provide reliable access, not on incarcerated people to overcome barriers that the system itself created.”

Tablets Make Communication Easier Behind Bars – But Deaf People Are Left Behind

The Appeal

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Emergency Care for Christa Pike Was Delayed After Prison Botched 911 Call
content:
Emergency dispatchers were left scrambling after prison officials were unable to verify that the call was legitimate.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Newly released 911 calls show that prison officials neglected to provide basic details when calling for emergency care for Christa Pike after Tennessee officials botched her execution last week.

Emergency dispatchers were left scrambling after the prison official who made the first 911 call, roughly an hour after the lethal injection process began, was unable to provide the code for the prison facility, despite it being needed for confirmation by dispatchers.

This caused emergency care for Pike to be delayed by roughly half an hour as the chemicals wreaked havoc on her body. Her lawyer, at one point, made a call saying that she needed “immediate life-saving care” from first responders.

The revelations raise further questions about Tennessee prison officials’ protocol for executions. Witnesses present for the execution attempt on September 30 said that it was apparent during the procedure that officials were not prepared for the injections to fail, despite the high rate of failure for lethal injections.

The calls were released by Nashville’s Department of Emergency Communications (DEC) after information requests by news outlets, and posted online by the Nashville Banner. A transcript of the first call shows the caller, whose identity is redacted, being repeatedly asked for the verification code for the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, which is needed for emergency dispatch to the prison. The prison official said they don’t know the code.

“I don’t have a code,” the caller said. When the dispatcher asked for a callback number, they gave the number for a cell phone, the transcript shows. The caller also seemed unsure about Pike’s age when asked, saying, “I believe 50.”

After that call, DEC placed a call to the Metro Fire Dispatch, where both the emergency dispatcher and the metro fire employee shared disbelief that the prison official didn’t know the procedure.

“How do they not have a code?” the fire dispatcher asked. “There’s nobody there that knows the process?”

“I guess since this is a special case, they may not know. But I don’t know why they don’t have the code…. [Riverbend] is the one place where you definitely need a code,” the emergency dispatcher said.

The lack of a code led officials to be unclear about whether or not the call was legitimate. The call also did not originate from Central Control for the state’s Department of Correction, as it would normally, leading to further confusion. As a result, dispatchers began reaching out to other prison officials in attempts to verify the call, while also trying to triangulate first responders.

Central Control was initially not even aware that that first call had happened. An employee told dispatchers not to send an emergency response because they “didn’t call anybody” and “would have been the one to call you guys.”

In another call, the DEC dispatcher expressed that they were “trying to find out if this is an actual thing that is happening … or if this is someone that is just basically prank calling or like swatting us.”

After the flurry of phone calls, and as a first responder was waiting at the gate of the prison to enter the facility, a Central Control employee was eventually able to confirm the legitimacy of the request — roughly half an hour after the initial 911 call. Medics later made sure to confirm that the prison officials knew where they were transporting Pike in the ambulance.

Pike was discharged from the hospital back to prison last week. She was initially unconscious and in critical condition after the execution, as the physician administering the procedure was seemingly unable to find a vein after going through at least seven needles. Ultimately, her lawyers said, they probably injected the drug into the tissue rather than into her bloodstream, causing her to be the first known person to survive a lethal injection attempt after the drugs had already been put into her body.

Pike has since regained consciousness, regained movement in her arms, and has been able to walk with some assistance. The horrific ordeal has sparked renewed calls for the abolition of the death penalty.

Despite this, state officials have left the possibility of attempting to execute Pike for a second time open, her lawyers said.

και ο διασώστης και ακτιβιστής 

Ιάσονας Αποστολόπουλος

 συζητούν με θέμα “

Όταν τα κράτη δολοφονούν τους μετανάστες. Μια εισαγωγή στην θανατοπολιτική της Ελλάδας και της Ευρωπαϊκής Ένωσης σε βάρος των μεταναστών”.

Μετά από 3 σεζόν παραστάσεων, διθυραμβικές κριτικές και 2 διακρίσεις -τη βράβευση του Θανάση Τριαρίδη με το βραβείο «Κάρολος Κουν» για το έργο, και την υποψηφιότητα του Νίκου Στεργιώτη στο βραβείο «Δημήτρης Χορν

 για την ερμηνεία του- η παράσταση-φαινόμενο συνεχίζει την πορεία του.

author: Alex Brown
title: At Least 39 Data Center Measures Will Be on the Ballot This Year in 8 States
content:
A recent poll finds 65 percent of respondents oppose the construction of AI data centers in their local community.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

In the course of a single election cycle, the backlash against data centers has grown from an issue at local planning commission and city council meetings to become a flashpoint in state and federal races across the country.

Candidates who once touted data centers as an economic boon have backtracked, and voters in at least three dozen cities, counties and townships will consider ballot measures in November that could ban data centers in their communities. Analysts say the opposition to data centers has come from Republican and Democratic voters alike.

“The people are speaking, and they’re speaking in one voice in opposition to this infrastructure,” said Tatishe Nteta, provost professor of political science at UMass Amherst. “It is not something that people desire in any shape, form or fashion. This potentially could be the issue that gives you the status of a former member of a city council or a former member of Congress.”

Last month, UMass Amherst published a poll, directed by Nteta, showing that only 11% of Americans would support the construction of an artificial intelligence data center in their local community. The poll found that 65% of respondents oppose the construction of such facilities.

Local and national activists have a long list of grievances against data centers, which tech companies are aggressively building to provide the computing power for artificial intelligence platforms. The rapid buildout of data centers is expected to strain the electrical grid and drive up energy costs, some forecasts show.

Opponents are also concerned about the facilities’ pollution, water use, noise and conversion of farmland and other open spaces. Many developers are also building private, “behind-the-meter” natural gas plants to power their data centers, increasing concerns about emissions and public health.

Some activists also object to the artificial intelligence technologies the sites will power, which threaten to disrupt the economy, replace workers, erode critical thinking skills and mental health and even — according to some tech executives — potentially kill all humans.

“For so many years, Ohio rolled out the red carpet to become a tech hub,” said Nick Owens, an attorney with Conserve Ohio, a campaign seeking to block data center development. “Unfortunately, what we’ve become is a tech dump.”

Activists across the country have lashed out at elected officials from both parties who have offered state and local tax breaks in order to entice data center developers. They’ve also called out local officials for negotiating deals behind closed doors and signing non-disclosure agreements with large tech companies.

“The politicians are chasing the grassroots, they aren’t leading on the issue,” said Anthony Elmo, public education defender with Good Jobs First, a policy group that tracks government subsidies related to economic development. “(Politicians) who were very pro-data center a year ago are now coming out against them due to political factors.”

Tech companies have launched their own political efforts to respond to the backlash. Industry leaders argue that artificial intelligence is key to the nation’s economic competitiveness. They note that the data center boom has created many construction jobs and increased property tax revenue in communities desperate for more money.

Leading the Future, a tech-backed Super PAC, has invested in federal and state campaigns in support of both Republican and Democratic candidates who support artificial intelligence. Josh Vlasto, the group’s co-leader, argued that the narrative around data centers has conflated the industry at large with its worst offenders — speculative projects that disregarded local opposition and failed to meet environmental standards.

“(Voters) want the jobs in their communities, they want the revenue, but they want the risks and downsides mitigated and addressed,” he said. “There is backlash in communities that don’t want them, but if you look to the states that are building and doing it right, these data centers are being welcomed and generating a massive amount of revenue. If this is done correctly, I could see this issue turning drastically in a different direction.”

An investigation earlier this year linked Leading the Future with a news website that used AI bots posing as journalists to solicit quotes for stories that promoted industry talking points. Another investigation found that a dark-money group tied to Leading the Future paid lifestyle influencers to promote artificial intelligence by highlighting the threat of competition from Chinese AI.

The Data Center Coalition, a membership association for tech companies, did not respond to a Stateline interview request. Amazon, Google and OpenAI — industry leaders that have pushed for data center construction — did not respond to Stateline inquiries. Think Big, an associated PAC of Leading the Future that supports Democratic candidates, did not respond to an interview request.

Across the United States, data centers currently use about 49 gigawatts of electricity, according to the website US Data Center Map. New projects planned or under construction total nearly 350 gigawatts — roughly a quarter of the country’s current electrical generation capacity.

While data centers have long powered our online infrastructure, many of the “hyperscale” facilities being built to support artificial intelligence are much larger and use vastly more power.

Ohio has become the political epicenter of the data center backlash. Like many states, Ohio agreed to sales tax exemptions for data centers in the 2010s in order to secure investment from tech companies. In recent years, the state has seen a boom in construction, with 154 operational facilities and 84 more data centers in the works — more than all but three other states.

“Our attraction in Ohio was a very minimal regulatory framework, plentiful farmland and plentiful water,” said Nick Owens, the Conserve Ohio attorney.

Owens, like many data center activists, became engaged on the issue when he learned that a large project was planned in his rural community in Brown County. Owens is a lifelong Republican and was a 2024 delegate for President Donald Trump, who has called data center opponents “backwards and poor.” He said politicians from city councils to the White House have failed to hear residents’ concerns.

“The dysfunction and unresponsiveness of government at all levels is truly sickening and frightening,” he said. “Conversely, it’s one of the most beautiful things I’ve ever seen, people coming together across communities, putting partisan differences aside and uniting (to oppose data centers).”

Conserve Ohio has worked with community activists across the state to draft ballot initiatives to ban data centers, change zoning regulations or require voter approval for large facilities. In total, Ohio municipalities will vote on 21 ballot measures related to data centers. Nationwide, 39 measures in eight states will be on the ballot this year, according to Ballotpedia.

In elections earlier this year, four local ballot measures across the country were decided with overwhelming opposition to data centers.

Jen Belt is the leader of Protect Grove City, an Ohio nonprofit backing a ballot measure to block development in that community.

“This is the first issue that I’ve seen Grove City united in such a way,” she said. “It is red, it is blue, it is every age, it is every socioeconomic status. It kind of gives you hope.”

Three communities in Kansas will vote on data center bans in November, including Ottawa, a city in the eastern portion of the state where residents have fought back against a proposed data center. Michael Lewis, with the nonprofit group Ottawa United, which has led the campaign, said locals were outraged when city commissioners announced the planned development.

“Everything was negotiated without public input, it was all done behind closed doors until they brought it out and approved it,” he said.

Lewis serves as vice chair of the Franklin County Democratic Party and is running for state representative. But the data center backlash has been so strong that his allies on the issue include the secretary of the Franklin County Republican Party and GOP state Rep. Rebecca Schmoe, his opponent in the general election.

The issue has been a focal point of statewide races as well. U.S. Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio, a Republican, has come under attack for championing tax breaks for data centers during his time as lieutenant governor. His Democratic opponent, former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown, has run ads calling him “the face of data centers.”

Last month, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a memo that data centers are “the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” The Washington Post reported. Husted has drafted a bill that would require state utility regulators to consider making data centers pay to cover the costs of their own electrical infrastructure needs. Senate Democrats blocked the bill last month, calling it “toothless” political messaging.

In Pennsylvania, both gubernatorial candidates have distanced themselves from their previous support for data centers. Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, until recently a staunch data center advocate, issued a moratorium on new data center permits last month, amid attacks from his Democratic opponent.

“Republican candidates know this is a losing issue and one that can do damage to their already questionable electoral positions,” said Nteta, the political science professor. “It’s a unique issue that brings together Americans in ways we don’t usually see.”

Vlasto, with the pro-data center Super PAC, said candidates calling for statewide bans on data centers are overcorrecting.

“Each community is going to make their choice,” he said. “Some communities are just not going to welcome data centers. From a political position, it doesn’t seem like preventing communities that want to build data centers is a palatable position either.”

Elmo, with Good Jobs First, said even longtime data center opponents are surprised at how quickly they have become a top political issue. He said tech companies and politicians who once promoted data centers have now joined calls for “responsible” development.

“This issue puts (politicians) between a rock and a hard place between the grassroots and their wealthy tech donors,” he said. “If the industry you’re trying to regulate immediately agrees with everything you’re suggesting to regulate them, I’d suggest that those regulations are not extremely effective.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Andrew Crocker
title: As Federal Court Rules ALPRs are Mass Surveillance, EFF Gets Disappointing Ruling
content:
In an extremely disappointing 

ruling

, a California trial court dismissed 

SIREN v. San Jose

, our case challenging the city of San Jose’s warrantless searches of its vast stores of automated license plate reader (ALPR) data. EFF and the ACLU of Northern California represent SIREN and CAIR California, two non-profits that serve San Jose residents, in this case.




Make no mistake: We believe this ruling is wrong on the law, and we will appeal. The ruling ignores the importance of landmark rulings from the U.S. Supreme Court regarding the invasiveness of aggregating collected data on an individual over time, including 

one issued just months ago

. It also severely underestimates the harm that ALPRs cause, in San Jose and around the country. 




San Jose’s ALPR surveillance system is inescapable. It blankets the city’s streets in nearly five hundred cameras that continuously photograph every car that passes by and retains the collected data for a month or longer. In our briefs, we argued that law enforcement officers who warrantlessly search the resulting ALPR database are violating the California Constitution’s ban on unreasonable searches and its guarantee of privacy. The court disagreed, explaining that based on one California appeals court case involving individual streetlight cameras, people do not have a reasonable expectation of privacy when driving on a public road. This is wrong. Networked ALPRs are not individual streetlight cameras. Their net effect of tracking and mapping cars as they travel reveals patterns of life, intimate relationships, and much more.




Fortunately, there are signs that the tide is turning against ALPRs in the courts. Just a day before the ruling in our case, a federal district court in Oklahoma called ALPRs “a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance” 

and decided

 that a law enforcement officer’s warrantless search of ALPR data violated the Fourth Amendment. The officer was observing traffic on an Oklahoma highway when he saw a woman driving a car with California plates. According to the court order, the officer began following the woman “for no apparent reason” other than her out of state plates. While following her, the officer decided to run the woman’s license plate number through 

Flock’s ALPR system

 – again, with no apparent reason other than her California plates. The Flock search returned at least 30 days of data, allowing the officer to track the car across at least three states, over the span of a month, from a single search.




The facts of this case demonstrate how ALPRs allow law enforcement to grab a breathtakingly vast sweep of information about a car (and the driver within) with no more effort than a Google search. It’s true that when a person drives on public roads, they can be observed, including by police. But as the Supreme Court 

has

 

explained

, we don’t expect law enforcement to be able to secretly track and store 

every

 movement our cars while we’re driving. The federal court in the Oklahoma case aptly illustrated this difference in societal expectations:




We might reasonably expect our friends and family to tell us something like: “Hey, I saw you out driving by the store last week.” But we do not expect people we know—let alone strangers, and especially not law enforcement—to randomly approach us to say: “Hey, I have been following your car for the last 30 days, and here is a detailed log of every place your vehicle has been with supporting photographic evidence. I am also going to share this information with law enforcement throughout the country so they know your whereabouts, too.







This decision is the first of its kind, and EFF will continue working to ensure that it is the first of many. Outside the courts, we’ve seen people across the country step up to reject ALPRs at the 

state

 and 

local

 level. EFF will continue challenging this technology 

on every front

 as well.




Related Cases: 

SIREN and CAIR-CA v. San Jose

author: Joe Sandler Clarke
title: Scottish Government’s Deal With IDF-Linked Firm ‘Breaks Boycott Pledge’
content:
The Scottish government has been 

accused of failing to live up to its Israeli boycott policy

, by agreeing to a multimillion-pound deal with a company linked to the country’s military.




GE Aerospace said on Monday it was 

spending £30m

 to modernise Glasgow’s Prestwich Airport, as part of a partnership with Ayrshire Growth Deal, the National reported. The project is led by the Scottish and UK governments, as well as three local councils. 




The US firm’s jet engines are used by Israeli military planes in Gaza, 

Campaign Against Arms Trade

 and other advocacy groups have said. In September, GE Aerospace 

shareholders raised concerns

 that the 

company had exported parts for military aircraft

 engines to countries accused of human rights abuses, including Israel. 




Scottish first minister John Swinney has said Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, and last year announced his government 

would not give public money

 to companies supplying arms to the country.




“We will pause new awards of public money to arms companies whose products or services are provided to countries where there is plausible evidence of genocide being committed by that country,” he said at the time, “that will include Israel.”




The Scottish Green party have accused Swinney’s Scottish National Party (SNP) of failing to live up to this commitment with the airport renovation deal. Green MSP Laura Moodie told 

the National

: “How can this possibly be reconciled with a policy of boycotting, divesting from and sanctioning companies that arm and support Israeli forces?”




The news of the GE Aerospace deal came just a few days after the Scottish government  partnered with Barclays on an 

upcoming bond issue

. The bank has 

come under pressure

 for its ties to firms doing business with the Israel Defense Forces (IDF). The Bureau of Investigative Journalism recently reported the bank had agreed to work with a firm that makes 

parts for IDF drones

.




A Scottish government spokesperson defended the agreement with GE Aerospace.




“The primary market of GE Aerospace’s Scottish company is not defence,” they said. “Where this is the case, the Scottish company must complete a self-declaration confirming that it does not supply military equipment, technologies, or services to Israel or Myanmar.”

author: James Green
title: Trumponaro: como um governo de Flávio pode imitar a presidência de Trump no Brasil?
content:
Enquanto apoiadores do presidente Lula se 

mobilizam

 para reverter os resultados do primeiro turno da disputa presidencial e garantir um quarto mandato liderado pelo Partido dos Trabalhadores, acho importante considerar que tipo de presidência o Brasil teria caso Flávio Bolsonaro fosse eleito em 25 de outubro.




Obviamente, todo cenário político nacional é único. Um eventual futuro governo Bolsonaro poderia ser bem diferente da forma como Donald Trump tem governado desde que retornou à presidência em 2025. 

No entanto, dada a afinidade declarada da família Bolsonaro com o clã Trump — bem como com suas políticas e práticas —, vale a pena considerar em que medida um novo presidente, governando com uma forte base de extrema-direita no Congresso, poderia adotar elementos da cartilha política de Trump, caso suba a rampa em 1º de janeiro de 2027.




Observadores políticos vêm notando uma defasagem de dois anos entre os eventos políticos recentes nos Estados Unidos e no Brasil. Trump assumiu o poder em 2016; Jair foi eleito dois anos depois. Biden derrotou Trump em 2020; Lula venceu as eleições de 2022. Apoiadores de Trump invadiram o Capitólio em 2021; o exército de defensores de Bolsonaro invadiu Brasília dois anos depois, em 2023. Trump retornou ao poder em 2025; o Brasil poderá enfrentar uma nova presidência de Bolsonaro em 2027. Embora processos históricos distintos raramente apresentem uma relação de causa e efeito tão nítida, parece que os dois campos de extrema-direita mantêm um diálogo constante sobre a melhor forma de conquistar e consolidar o poder.




Trump rapidamente celebrou a vitória de Bolsonaro por uma margem de 1,9% em 4 de outubro, embora, 

na mensagem publicada nas redes sociais

, tenha confundido o Brasil com a Índia: “125 milhões de pessoas votaram hoje no primeiro turno da eleição presidencial da Índia. Os resultados saíram logo após o encerramento da votação, no MESMO DIA!” Ele também aproveitou a ocasião para fazer comentários bombásticos sobre uma de suas principais obsessões: “Em Detroit, Filadélfia, Califórnia e em inúmeras outras cidades e estados dos EUA, os resultados — com números muito menores — frequentemente levam semanas para serem fraudados… digo, calculados. A votação na América é CORRUPTA!!!”




Enquanto Jair Bolsonaro baseou parte de sua campanha eleitoral de 2022 em críticas à confiabilidade do sistema brasileiro de votação eletrônica, o campo da direita manteve-se em silêncio sobre o processo de votação desta vez. Parece haver fraude eleitoral quando se perde, mas não quando se ganha. Ironicamente, Trump elogiou as eleições brasileiras por utilizarem procedimentos de votação que o próprio presidente dos EUA classificou como fraudulentos em seu próprio país.




Se os apoiadores de Lula reverterem o resultado do primeiro turno e vencerem por uma margem estreita no segundo turno, tanto Bolsonaro quanto Trump contestarão o resultado.

 A Casa Branca poderia insistir que o segundo turno das eleições brasileiras foi fraudulento e que Bolsonaro foi legitimamente eleito presidente, o que provocaria uma crise nacional e internacional sobre a legitimidade do novo governo de Lula.




Já se Flávio Bolsonaro derrotar o presidente Lula, provavelmente seguirá o exemplo de Trump, revertendo quase todas as políticas e programas do governo atual.

 A exemplo da ordem executiva de Trump emitida em 20 de janeiro de 2025 — seu primeiro dia no cargo —, concedendo perdão aos apoiadores que invadiram o Capitólio dos EUA na tentativa de anular os resultados da eleição presidencial americana de 2022, Flávio prometeu um perdão presidencial para seu pai (condenado por organizar uma insurreição contra o novo governo Lula) e para aqueles que invadiram a Praça dos Três Poderes em apoio ao plano de Bolsonaro.




Embora um perdão presidencial possa extinguir a pena de prisão restante de Jair Bolsonaro, ele não anularia a condenação do Supremo Tribunal Federal nem restauraria seus direitos políticos. Portanto, os aliados políticos de Bolsonaro poderiam buscar uma anistia legislativa que restaure plenamente a elegibilidade de Jair Bolsonaro.




Flávio pode governar pela vingança, assim como Trump 




Logo no primeiro dia de sua presidência, Trump anunciou uma campanha de vingança contra seus oponentes políticos, por meio de ações judiciais retaliatórias e de outras medidas administrativas. Flávio pode repetir essa estratégia.




Alvo 1: Moraes




No Brasil, sem dúvida, o primeiro alvo seria Alexandre de Moraes, que conduziu o julgamento e condenação de Jair Bolsonaro. Como o ministro — juntamente com outros membros do Supremo, incluindo dois indicados pelo pai de Flávio — está envolvido no escândalo do Banco Master, Flávio pode utilizar esse cenário para pressionar um movimento de impeachment contra Moraes. 




O ministro já é um alvo declarado da família. O irmão de Flávio Bolsonaro, Eduardo — atualmente foragido da Justiça brasileira e vivendo nos Estados Unidos —, juntamente com Paulo Figueiredo, pressionou com sucesso a Casa Branca de Trump para que impusesse tarifas de 50% ao Brasil, condicionadas à retirada das acusações contra Jair Bolsonaro. Eles também convenceram o governo dos EUA a aplicar a Lei Magnitsky ao ministro da Suprema Corte, impondo-lhe sanções financeiras severas por supostas violações de direitos humanos, embora 

Jim McGovern

 — o congressista americano autor da legislação — tenha declarado nas redes sociais que a lei não se aplica a este caso.




Alvo 2: movimentos sociais




Outro alvo da ofensiva direta de Trump tem sido as organizações da sociedade civil que criticam as políticas do presidente. Flávio pode repetir esse ataque aqui no Brasil.




Durante o mandato de Jair Bolsonaro, o presidente já atacou movimentos sociais ambientalistas, que chamou de organizações terroristas. Devemos esperar que essa investida se intensifique significativamente caso Flávio chegue ao poder.




Alvo 3: Constituição




Desde o seu retorno à Casa Branca, a estratégia política de Trump tem sido adotar medidas que parecem violar flagrantemente a Constituição dos EUA: tentativas de negar a cidadania a pessoas nascidas nos Estados Unidos, a imposição de tarifas de 50% em 2025 sem aprovação do Congresso e o congelamento de verbas autorizadas pelo Legislativo, entre outras medidas.




Flávio Bolsonaro declarou que pretende alterar a Constituição e mencionou algumas possíveis medidas legislativas, embora mantenha seus planos gerais em termos vagos.

 Diante da tentativa de insurreição de 2023, que violou os princípios fundamentais da Constituição de 1988, resta saber se ele respeitará o Estado de Direito, especialmente tendo um grande bloco de apoio de extrema-direita no Congresso. 




Alvo 4: Imprensa




A liberdade de imprensa também pode sofrer ataques, visto que Trump baniu veículos de comunicação cuja cobertura de seu governo lhe desagradava.

 Até o momento, a grande mídia brasileira não parece muito preocupada com essa ameaça à liberdade de expressão e à liberdade de imprensa, e vários grandes conglomerados de mídia demonstraram preferir Flávio a Lula.




Mas se o primeiro for eleito e decidir perseguir quem faz reportagens desfavoráveis, quem o impedirá? Com a maioria no Congresso e uma Suprema Corte em desordem, não há mecanismos de controle do sistema capazes de impedir que o possível futuro presidente desfira um ataque frontal à liberdade de imprensa ou aos críticos mais contundentes da extrema-direita no país. 




Alvo 5: Programas sociais




Quando Trump retornou ao poder nos Estados Unidos, trouxe consigo um plano detalhado, o Projeto 2025, concebido para reduzir o tamanho do governo federal e eliminar programas que os conservadores consideravam incompatíveis com sua agenda. Trump convocou Elon Musk para realizar o “trabalho sujo”, e o trilionário obteve grande êxito ao cortar drasticamente programas governamentais e os empregos das pessoas que garantiam o sucesso dessas iniciativas. O grupo político de Bolsonaro anunciou a intenção de cortar gastos públicos, mas apresentou poucos detalhes sobre seus planos. No entanto, dada a postura ideológica de que “menos Estado é melhor”, pode-se esperar cortes severos semelhantes no Brasil. 




Sem dúvida, um dos primeiros alvos serão as universidades públicas brasileiras. 

Os ataques de Trump a Columbia, Harvard e outras universidades de renome mundial — sob a alegação de que os administradores haviam falhado em conter o antissemitismo nos campi — serviram de pretexto para forçar essas instituições a eliminar todos os programas de diversidade, equidade e inclusão.

 Tais programas eram mecanismos importantes para garantir que o ensino superior de qualidade fosse verdadeiramente acessível a todos os segmentos sociais, e não apenas aos brancos de classe média.




Não há absolutamente nenhuma garantia de que um novo governo de extrema-direita em Brasília manteria os atuais programas de ação afirmativa, sob o argumento de que são discriminatórios, racistas e parte de uma conspiração de esquerda para controlar as mentes dos estudantes universitários. Nenhum programa estará imune a tentativas de desmantelamento. 




Alvo 6: Soberania




A soberania brasileira também estará em jogo. Em todo o mundo, observadores que acompanham os Estados Unidos consideram muitas das declarações de Trump meras fantasias delirantes de uma pessoa instável. Propor a anexação do Canadá e da Groenlândia, ou mudar o nome do Golfo do México para Golfo da América e do Lago Ontário para Lago América, parecem iniciativas nacionalistas absurdas para agradar à sua base.




No entanto, a ideia de Trump de invadir a Venezuela e a declaração de que organizações criminosas brasileiras são grupos terroristas — que o governo dos EUA teria o direito divino de destruir — refletem, na verdade, o desejo de consolidar a América Latina e o Caribe como um quintal neocolonial dos Estados Unidos. 

Um acordo sobre terras raras favorável aos EUA, mas com poucos benefícios para o Brasil, é claramente uma das primeiras prioridades na agenda de um presidente brasileiro que se considera 100% alinhado ao atual governo norte-americano. 




Mais alvos: Itamaraty, direitos LGBTQIAPN+ e meio ambiente




A lista é interminável: expurgos no Itamaraty, processos administrativos contra funcionários públicos, ataques aos direitos LGBT+, a continuidade das privatizações de empresas estatais, o desmantelamento da proteção às terras indígenas e o fim da preservação ambiental. Com uma vitória eleitoral — por menor que seja —, Bolsonaro, assim como Trump, declarará ter recebido um mandato popular para implementar seu programa, ignorando a vontade da outra metade do país que não apoia seus planos para o futuro do Brasil. 




As 

pesquisas mais recentes

 nos Estados Unidos indicam que os Democratas conquistarão o controle da Câmara dos Representantes e, possivelmente, até do Senado, formando uma frente para conter as piores intenções de Trump nos próximos dois anos. Enquanto o Congresso dos EUA se inclina à esquerda em repúdio às políticas do atual presidente, o Brasil pode enfrentar quatro anos piores que a gestão de Jair Bolsonaro. Embora uma rejeição generalizada a um possível novo governo Bolsonaro possa surgir após cerca de um ano de mandato, não há cenário plausível que preveja um freio semelhante ao que a extrema-direita pretende impor nos próximos quatro anos, caso os apoiadores de Lula não consigam reverter o resultado das urnas. 




O destino do país pode depender de algumas centenas de milhares de votos.
